headline: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights
trail_text: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost
body_text: It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes. The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs. This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children. But now, starting from the upcoming spending review, which kicks off next year, projects that can be shown to bring down costs in the future will be protected via a new piece of jargon – a preventative departmental expenditure limit, or PDEL. “It could end up being quite a major change in how the government runs spending reviews, and the entire spending framework,” said Stuart Hoddinott, at the Institute for Government thinktank, which had called for such a system to be implemented. Officials in the Treasury agree, with one calling it an “important reform”. That is, however, about as straightforward as it gets. The budget document uses Andy Burnham’s new spending to prevent rough sleeping as an example of the sort of thing that would qualify. A few other areas would seem likely: for example, public health programmes to prevent future illness, and Sure Start-type early years schemes. But beyond that, no one really knows what might or might not qualify for PDEL status. Departments say they are waiting for Treasury guidance, which has not yet been drawn up. “A lot depends on the definition,” Hoddinott said. “While it sounds simple, it becomes quite difficult when you think about how it will work in practice, as you could make any argument that almost all types of spending are preventative.” Government officials agree, with one making the point that, in theory, the Ministry of Defence could argue all its spending is preventive, given the very obvious costs to the country of fighting a war, let alone losing one. There is therefore the potential for a new variant of the endless spending-review tussles between departments and the Treasury, as ministers try to protect their pet projects from future plunder. But what is perhaps just as important is the symbolism. Some other governments around the world protect specific preventative budgets – public health, for example – but this is believed to be the first time one has introduced this as a blanket policy. Government officials are billing the decision as part of a wider focus under Burnham to try to deal with knotty and neglected issues that have longer-term costs and repercussions, including rough sleeping and adult social care. One said: “Too often government departments have ended up raiding these types of budgets to fund short-term measures. This is an attempt to combat that as part of a wider push to transform the way the state operates.” Those whose work revolves around trying to generate long-term benefits to the public are cautiously delighted. “This does feel like a really good thing,” said Greg Fell, Sheffield city council’s director of public health and the president of the Association of Directors of Public Health. “There are a lot of questions about how it will work. Is it about preventing future acute demand, or creating the conditions for communities to thrive? Those are different things and they require a different mindset and way of operating. And with some spending, it might take decades to realise the benefits. “But as a country we have never been very good at this sort of thing, so it’s up to all of us to make sure it works.”

headline: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes
trail_text: Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
body_text: The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10. The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already. “A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events. “First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.” Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”. He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”. Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit. “I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before. “That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.” His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU. Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility. Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence. “Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine. “Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

headline: Streeting says he began stockpiling food weeks ago amid rising threat to UK
trail_text: Defence secretary says value for money and modernisation key for spending to ‘fight the wars ahead’
body_text: The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, says he started stockpiling food and water weeks ago in case of a national emergency, as he talked up the threats to the UK and said his department had already begun ramping up its spending in response. Streeting spoke after the chancellor, John Healey, said he wanted defence spending to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 and 3.5% by 2035; having already asked Whitehall departments to find 1% cuts in their budgets for long-term investment to fund defence spending. “I’m glad the message is getting through because my mum got in touch and said ‘payday is coming up, how much do you think I need to buy because I’m just budgeting to the end of the month?’ I’m glad that people are beginning to think about their own household resilience, making sure we’ve got sufficient supplies of bottled water, canned goods, battery-powered torches. These are all just commonsense things for the everyday challenges,” Streeting told the Times. The defence secretary says he has bottled water, a first aid kit and a battery-powered torch on standby. He added that he was stockpiling baked beans, sweetcorn, red kidney beans, tuna, protein bars and nuts. Streeting, who recently urged all Britons to follow suit, said he had started setting aside the supplies because he wanted to “lead by example”. He told the Times he was determined the UK should be able to deter its adversaries and “should deterrence fail, to be ready to defeat them”. Streeting said: “That is the core job. We should never lose sight of that,” adding that any additional spending must be done carefully. “Spending more money badly is not virtuous,” he said. He also told the newspaper that value for money and modernisation needed to be balanced in order to ready the UK to “fight the wars ahead”. In June, Healey’s resignation as defence secretary was one of the final nails in the coffin of Keir Starmer’s premiership. The man who now serves as chancellor in Andy Burnham’s government accused Burnham’s predecessor, as well as the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk with inadequate funding for the defence investment plan (Dip). “You have been unable and the Treasury has been unwilling to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats. I would not be able to accept a Dip settlement that does not give our forces the resources they need. I am now left with no other option than to submit my resignation as your defence secretary,” he wrote. Announcing his first budget on Wednesday, Healey said he was now fully funding the defence investment plan. He reiterated the target of defence spending reaching 3% of GDP; prompting the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, to say the UK was on “a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato allies in The Hague”. But Healey was criticised for leaving details of his plan to reach that target until next year’s spending review. Besides spending, Streeting also discussed oversight of service personnel, telling the Times the courts were in the middle of an “active campaign” to “smear the reputation and integrity of our special forces”. He also left the door open to scrutiny of special forces and the UK’s nuclear weapons by MPs and peers on the intelligence and security committee, saying they could be trusted.

headline: Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham
trail_text: John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth say devolving power further is up to Holyrood and Senedd – not Westminster
byline: Peter Walker, Bethan McKernan and Andrew Sparrow
body_text: Scotland and Wales’s first ministers have told Andy Burnham that decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK. After Burnham held discussions in Glasgow with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth about localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive. However, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, caused friction before the summit by criticising Swinney’s government for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further. Streeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is: ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government across Scotland?’” Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the talks, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there. The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues. “There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” Burnham said. “I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.” Ap Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government. He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.” Swinney’s comments after the summit took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”. Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which the Welsh government said amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”. Plaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland. The SNP-led government is frequently irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”. Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the elections in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming prime minister, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”. He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas. “Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends. “Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”

headline: Pedestrianisation won’t save Oxford Street
trail_text: Letters: Oliver Schick writes that there is a limit to how much footfall is beneficial. Plus letters from Iain Nelson and Tom Hardy
body_text: The real causes of the problems seen in Oxford Street (The long read, 22 October) are high rents, the chaotic system of business rates and the replacement of many smaller footprints with larger ones; these are the main factors that have made the street less viable. The large flagship shops depend on being surrounded by good-quality small businesses to attract customers. Much of what the mayor of London is doing here is a de facto part-privatisation – stopping up a very important public highway for a large number of users of “unwelcome” modes of transport, to benefit private landowners. Rather than buses being a main culprit here, it is much more likely that the gradual downgrading of bus services along Oxford Street has contributed significantly to its decline. The strategic mistake of routing Crossrail along Oxford Street – long after this plan lost its part-justification (dating from when it was conceived decades ago) of stimulating the West End – has caused the dangerously high footfall levels that have become a main motivation for pedestrianisation. The Crossrail route should have been changed to connect Heathrow and Stratford through centres in south London, but we have to live with it now. There is a natural limit to how much footfall is beneficial for urban centres, and disadvantaging everyone who doesn’t want to get there by underground railway isn’t going to change this. The factors at play that have weakened Oxford Street are not unique to it, and none of them will be affected by these actions from the mayor of London, who is largely powerless to address them without central government taking corrective action. Oliver Schick London • I like to see Sadiq Khan contributing to the Guardian, but on this occasion I have to quibble with his description of Oxford Street as “our nation’s high street” (We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too, 26 October). I live on the border of Wales, and whether a street in London is pedestrianised or not is entirely irrelevant to me. It’s not my high street and never will be. Iain Nelson Selattyn, Shropshire • Credit where credit is due. Contrary to accusations at the time that businesses had suffered, footfall on Oxford Street actually increased by 13.5% as visitors were drawn to the utopia that was Extinction Rebellion’s blockade in April 2019 – a harbinger, in microcosm, of what a greener, less polluted world might look like. Tom Hardy London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Public sector an ‘afterthought’ to North Sea oil jobs, says Unison leader
trail_text: Andrea Egan calls for same political focus on teachers, care sector and NHS and says Jackdaw decision ‘a serious misstep’
body_text: The leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas. Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, said too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea. “There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.” North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave the go ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield following huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad. The decision caused anger among climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will further escalate the crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on the more controversial Rosebank oilfield is expected before the end of the year. After Wednesday’s budget, which factored in the project’s approval in its forecast, the Guardian revealed some Labour MPs were lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decided to block Rosebank. Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. She said ministers should instead focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of employees in the public sector, which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years. “It’s time for the government to get its priorities straight: invest in clean energy, invest in the public services that communities rely on – to the benefit of us all.” There is a split among the UK’s main trade unions on allowing fossil fuel companies to drill in the North Sea. Unite and GMB, which represent many oil and gas workers, back more licences, while Unison and the National Education Union oppose more drilling as part of a wider drive to create long term sustainable jobs and tackle the climate crisis. One concern among unions is that jobs in the rapidly growing renewables sector are often not unionised and therefore not as secure or well paid as in those in the oil and gas sector. However, last week Unison announced a new recognition deal with the UK’s largest energy company, Octopus Energy, known as a progressive organisation with a focus on renewable energy. The GMB union had been attempting to gain recognition at Octopus but the company said Unison “stood out for its commitment to the energy transition”. Egan said it was an important step to securing good, secure jobs in the renewable sector. “Unison is proud to be leading the way as the clean energy union. We urgently need more well-paid, unionised jobs and to transition away from fossil fuels at pace. This agreement is a step in the right direction on both counts.”

headline: UK side-hustle tax-free allowance to rise to £3,000 next year
trail_text: Up to 1.4 million people could benefit from change to trading allowance announced in budget, with some saving hundreds in tax
body_text: The amount Britons can earn from a side hustle without paying tax will rise to £3,000 next year in a fillip for those who make extra cash from hobbies or reselling. Up to 1.4 million people could benefit from the change announced in the budget, with the chancellor confirming the tax-free “trading” allowance will increase from £1,000 to £3,000 in April 2027. The number of Britons with a side hustle has exploded in recent years, with reselling clothes, tutoring and dog-walking among the popular avenues to create extra income at a time when household finances are under pressure. Last year, 2.6 million people made money selling goods through platforms including eBay, Vinted and Etsy, according to data provided by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) to accountancy firm Lubbock Fine. In 2024 the number was just 450,000. Currently, people can earn up to £1,000 a year from a side hustle without paying tax but above this you may owe tax if your total income, including your main job, is above the £12,570 personal allowance. Out of the 1.4 million people, an estimated 400,000 will see their tax bill go down, with an average saving of £380. Meanwhile, about 100,000 people will no longer have to report their trading income to HMRC. Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said that for people with a small side hustle, the more generous allowance “doesn’t just save tax, it also takes the hassle of admin off their plate”. As a result, she added: “You can spend more time working for yourself and less doing paperwork for HMRC. It means you can make £3,000 before you have to think about doing a self-assessment tax return.” Coles said people who were making more than £3,000 would have the choice to use the allowance or subtract business expenses and capital costs when calculating their profits for tax purposes. Jane Hawkes, a consumer champion and the founder of the Lady Janey blog, said side hustles were a great way to turn hobbies, skills and spare-time activities into extra cash and “increasing the allowance should make this easier without wholly unnecessary red tape”. But, she added: “It’s important that people understand their tax obligations, particularly the distinction between selling unwanted personal belongings and trading for profit, so they don’t inadvertently fall foul of HMRC rules.” Selling your own clothes or other items is not taxable if you’re selling them for less than you originally paid as you are not making a profit. Rules came into force last year requiring platforms to inform HMRC about their sellers and how much money they made. HMRC now receives data about every seller who made 30 sales or €2,000 (about £1,700) on any platform in the past year.

headline: TUC leader expects wave of union recognition in private sector over coming year
trail_text: Paul Nowak says ‘hundreds, if not thousands’ of employers could sign access agreements as ‘transformative’ rules come into force
body_text: The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, is predicting a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces come into force. From Friday, as part of Labour’s Employment Rights Act, unions will have the right to enter workplaces or communicate with staff electronically. From January, employers will be obliged to inform workers of their right to join a union. “I think it potentially could be transformative,” Nowak said. “This could open up large parts of … the private sector, where unions have been trying to get a foothold but have been hampered partly because of the legal framework. It gives us a real opportunity.” He added: “My prediction would be that by this time next year, we’ll have signed hundreds, if not thousands of new recognition agreements with employers, taking that union voice into the private sector in particular.” Polling carried out for the TUC by YouGov suggests 62% of workers would support a trade union negotiating on their behalf on pay and conditions, but 36% of those who are not members of a union say they would not know how to join one. Nowak pointed to a flurry of recent deals, citing agreements between John Lewis and Usdaw and between the GMB and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as evidence that some employers are responding even before the rules have come into force. “What we’re seeing is a whole range of employers, who have recognised that the legislation is changing, that the political climate is changed and are now reaching voluntary agreements with unions,” he said. Just over a fifth of the UK’s workforce are trade union members, down from more than half in 1979, before Margaret Thatcher came to power. Under the new rules, there will be a formal process to request access to a workplace if a union cannot agree with the employer, which will be overseen by the regulator, the Central Arbitration Committee. Previously, unions trying to win the right to represent a workforce have sometimes had to do so from outside the building – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to win recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago. Nowak said Labour’s new approach “changes the mood, and I think it brings us much more into the European mainstream, which is that unions are part and parcel of the workplace”. The access rights are the latest element of the government’s upgrade to workers’ rights to be implemented. Rights to sick pay have already been extended and further changes, including restrictions on zero hours contracts, are yet to come into force. Some employers have complained about the potential costs of the new regime, but Nowak insisted good bosses need not worry. “Genuinely, employers have got nothing to fear from this. They shouldn’t see their staff wanting an independent voice as somehow a negative verdict on them. You can work for a good, successful organisation and still want a strong, independent union voice.”

headline: Security guard who protected Nigel Farage on campaign trail was facing rape charge
trail_text: Ryan Dinnage – who accompanied Reform UK leader on walkabouts before local elections – was later jailed, raising questions about vetting failure
body_text: One of Nigel Farage’s security team who accompanied him on the local election campaign trail this year was facing a rape charge and was later jailed for eight years, raising questions about a failure of vetting. Ryan Dinnage spent time protecting Farage in April and May, but in June was convicted of having raped a woman while she slept in a caravan at the Royal Windsor horse show. Dinnage was seen beside Farage on walkabouts on at least four occasions on Reform’s local election campaign trail this spring: in Llandudno, Conwy County; Waterlooville, Hampshire, Worthing, West Sussex, and Downham Market, Norfolk. He had been charged in 2025, three years after the crime took place at the equestrian event in 2022. Reform UK acknowledged Farage was provided with protection by Dinnage, and said his services had been supplied by a third-party contractor who had assured them he had been vetted. A spokesperson for the party said: “As soon as we found out, we were shocked and disgusted and he ceased to be used by Reform.” However, the episode raises questions about how a security operative facing a charge of serious sexual violence could have been put in a position of responsibility near a senior politician and members of the public. Reform UK did not answer further questions about whether the party was continuing its relationship with the third-party contractor, and whether any action was taken against them. A Labour spokesperson said: “Nigel Farage must urgently explain at what point Reform UK became aware that they allowed a man charged with rape to directly interact with the public on their behalf. They must also urgently make clear what action they have taken to prevent such a situation happening again. “Farage and his party are lurching from scandal to scandal and the public are rapidly seeing who they really are. In recent weeks Farage has shrugged off vile misogyny and Reform has an appalling track record when it comes to standing up for women. It’s time Farage showed some leadership for once, got his house in order, and realised the buck stops with him.” Farage is generally accompanied by a large security team, and has spoken of threats being made against him. The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism, including against Farage. Over the summer, counter-terror police reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London. The Reform UK leader has repeatedly said he accepted a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne in order to pay for his security for the rest of his life. He has previously turned down taxpayer-funded security from the government, which included a bodyguard, a car, and a trained driver, deeming it to be inadequate. Dinnage, then 32, of Croydon, was sentenced to eight and half years in prison in July. According to Thames Valley police, his offence took place in the early hours of 16 May 2022, when Dinnage entered the caravan where the victim was sleeping and raped her. He was reported to police later that day and arrested the next day. Reform is not the only party in the spotlight for a vetting failure in recent weeks. The Conservatives were criticised, by Reform UK, for having employed a former election candidate, Jack Ross, who was filmed by an undercover reporter appearing to discuss the cost of hiring contract killers. Ross had worked as a consultant in Kemi Badenoch’s office. Ross is facing an investigation by the Tories after he was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter: “What do you want done?” and apparently offering to “broker” the services of an alleged far-right paramilitary group. Police in Scotland have said they will be reviewing an Al Jazeera documentary in which Ross was filmed seemingly making a range of comments about what a contract killer could be employed to do, and talked about using far-right groups to create disruption on the streets. • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

headline: British Council’s £197m debt should mostly be written off, MPs say
trail_text: Commons report calls on Foreign Office to bail out soft-power flagship reeling from job cuts and asset sales
body_text: Ministers should explore writing off a crippling £197m loan to the British Council by converting as much of it as possible into “a grant or similar”, MPs have said. The Commons public accounts committee said the government lacked a “positive vision” for the council, whose soft power value to the UK is put at £1bn a year. The MPs called on the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to set out what more it could do to support the council and its work. Despite slashing a third of its headcount and selling off historical assets, the council’s future remains precarious because a £60m Covid-era FCDO loan on commercial terms has grown to £197m. The loan was agreed by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government when the pandemic shuttered the council’s English teaching and exams business overseas. The loan was due to have been repaid this year but was restructured to be cleared over the next 15 years. Even with a turnaround plan to reduce staffing by a further 25% as well as dispose of more assets and close operations in nine countries, the council forecasts it will not generate an operating surplus until 2029–30, according to the committee. The report said: “The FCDO should write to us on what steps could be taken to offset the loan against the soft power value provided by the British Council and convert as much of the loan as possible into a grant or similar.” British Council staff across Europe have staged widespread strikes and protests against the cuts. The planned further job losses will mean numbers will have almost halved since 2020, with more than 2,000 full-time equivalent posts lost since 2021. The report called on the FCDO and the council “to work together to set out a positive vision for the future of the British Council that will build on its soft power value to the UK”. “It seems to the public accounts committee that the future of the British Council is still precarious and both it and the FCDO need to carefully monitor the situation as partners so that the British Council can confidently demonstrate to the world that the UK values its work in providing soft power,” it said. The committee said it recognised the council’s “inestimable value” and called for a “more collaborative tone” in relations between the FCDO and council, where there has been “a lack of trust”. Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the committee, said: “With the council seeking a leaner operation at a time of continuing precarity and obvious vulnerability for its finances, it needs the government’s help to continue its vital work, not to be simply pursued as a debtor. The FCDO says the British Council must adapt to survive. That may be true – but it will fail to do so without the government’s full-throated support.” The council is an arm’s-length body of the FCDO as well as an established charity and a commercial organisation. It operates in just under 100 countries and claims a reach of more than 700 million people a year. The majority of its income is from its teaching and exams business, while grant-in-aid from the FCDO accounts for about 15% of its annual revenue. The funding is used to support the council’s three charitable objectives: cultural relationships, the English language and education.

headline: Save Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of cars
trail_text: Letters: Readers respond to Simon Jenkins’s article on the west London crossing
body_text: Simon Jenkins is a great defender of our national heritage, having produced many books on the subject and frequently written in the Guardian against aggressive modern architectural horrors. How shocking, then, to find him arguing for the replacement of Hammersmith Bridge simply to provide for yet more cars on the roads (Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October). He claims that the principal cause of congestion is “London’s epidemic of roadworks”, when actually it’s the fact that there are just too many cars trying to use a road network that isn’t designed for them. Furthermore, he says that, in its present state, the bridge “merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross it” – and yet between 12,000 and 15,000 people use it every day. Reopening it to motor traffic (and increasingly heavy cars have massively contributed to the current state of degradation of the bridge) would bring little benefit. Well over half the households in Hammersmith and Fulham don’t have access to a car, and there are very good public transport links in the area; there is even a well-thought-out plan put forward by the Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group to run driverless electric “pod” vehicles to provide for those who are unable to walk across Hammersmith Bridge. And quite apart from the huge difficulty involved in enabling the tearing down of a Grade II* listed structure (where’s our doughty defender of national heritage now?), there is no effective business case for replacing it at enormous cost to provide for yet more cars, when for both environmental and health reasons (particularly because of the pollution they cause), the whole emphasis should be on reducing our reliance on cars. If only someone in authority would summon up the courage to tackle the motoring lobby. Dr Richard Carter Putney, London • Simon Jenkins is right to castigate the different London authorities that have failed to replace Hammersmith Bridge over a period of seven years. No other capital city in Europe would allow such a prolonged truncation of a major transport artery, preventing vehicles from crossing the river. London is not a unitary authority and its mayor does not have the powers of his peers in other capitals to raise the finance to pay for the cost of a new bridge. The lack of joined-up thinking appears to be baked in to the planning processes of the different relevant authorities. This sorry state of affairs in south-west London has led to permanent traffic chaos along the Upper Richmond Road and the hell that is Putney High Street during rush hour. Were it not for the British obsession for so-called “heritage” projects, we could have had a temporary bridge capable of carrying traffic years ago. Instead citizens are obliged to walk or pedal their way across a wonky bridge in order to get to the other side for the sake of a misplaced nostalgia for Victorian engineering feats. Julian Heddy East Sheen, London • The outdated photograph published with Simon Jenkins’s off-beam article on Hammersmith Bridge suggests decrepitude, when the reality is quite different. Thanks to £55m of investment by Hammersmith and Fulham council, this iconic, Grade II* listed bridge has found a successful new purpose as an active travel crossing, with 15,000 people a day walking and wheeling across its reopened main carriageway. I know of no “growing body of opinion” calling for its replacement. On the contrary, the settled local preference has moved to build on this success with a proposal to introduce a fleet of lightweight, autonomous electric shuttles to fill the public transport gap to ensure all residents can cross comfortably and safely. Community-led Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit is working with Ohmio UK and partners to deliver this vision. Traffic on neighbouring bridges and the wider road network is down compared with before the bridge closed to motor vehicles, while Barnes’s local economy is booming, aided by the ebike revolution. There is no credible business case for spending hundreds of millions bringing back polluting, dangerous and exclusionary through traffic. With the mayor targeting a 27% reduction in car traffic by 2030, the priority must be to build on this success, not undo it. Charles Campion Chair, Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit • Simon Jenkins is a respected commentator on London’s heritage and built environment, with a deep understanding of the costs of maintaining historic infrastructure. We share his commitment to London’s bridges, but not his views on how the City Bridge Foundation’s charitable funds should be used. We maintain five Thames bridges: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium and Blackfriars, spanning centuries of engineering history. Their upkeep requires sustained investment and commitment, demonstrated by our current £15m Blackfriars Bridge refurbishment, repairing more than 2,000 cast-iron balusters and repainting the entire structure. Our endowment exists to meet these responsibilities in perpetuity. It is not a general fund for London’s infrastructure, nor is its value a measure of money freely available to spend. Alongside maintaining and supporting our bridges, where there are funds available, we make grants to charities tackling inequality and disadvantage across London. These funds are made for charitable purposes and governed by the legal and regulatory arrangements that apply to our work. They cannot simply be redirected to pay for the restoration or replacement of a bridge outside our remit. We recognise the importance of London’s bridges to the people who rely on them every day, but other Thames crossings are the responsibility of other organisations. We share knowledge and experience with those responsible through industry groups. For nearly 900 years, the legacy of Bridge House Estates has helped keep London’s bridges standing while supporting charitable work across the city. We are proud of this legacy and the charity partners working alongside us to build a fairer London. Paul Martinelli Chairman, City Bridge Foundation

headline: Female Lib Dem MP accuses Nigel Farage of shoving her in parliament
trail_text: Caroline Voaden says Reform UK leader grabbed her by the arm and tried to push past her in incident in May
body_text: A female Liberal Democrat MP has accused Nigel Farage of shoving her aside at the state opening of parliament after which one of her male colleagues intervened. Caroline Voaden gave her account of the incident in May this year after Farage revealed on Wednesday that there had been a “physical altercation” in parliament which meant he had decided to avoid the budget. Voaden told the Guardian: “He was trying to get out of the chamber and instead of just asking if he could go past, he said: ‘Let me past’. I turned round and said: ‘No, you can wait your turn like everyone else’. He grabbed me by the arm or the shoulder, pushed me to one side and tried to push past me. One of my colleagues tried to stop him because he thought I was going to fall down the stairs. And then we all shuffled down. “Quite deliberately, he grabbed me by the arm from behind and pushed me to one side so that I fell into a colleague or the wall on the other side. I was really taken aback and really angry because I think you just don’t behave like that in any workplace, let alone the chamber of the House of Commons. It was rude. It was nasty.” Voaden said she had complained to the serjeant at arms who she believed had written to Farage asking him to apologise. She also raised it with the speaker. “Nothing ever came of it,” she said. A Reform UK source said it was “not true at all, it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel. This is typical Lib Dem dishonesty in an attempt to stay relevant.” The male Lib Dem MP who intervened is understood to be Max Wilkinson, with sources saying he put a hand on Farage’s shoulder, “fairly gently” grabbed him and said he could not do that to another MP. Reform sources also suggested a video from the Commons showed her account was wrong, but the Lib Dems said the incident took place before the footage started. The row erupted after the Reform leader said he had skipped John Healey’s budget speech in the Commons on Wednesday because his seat reservation had been moved and he decided to give it a “wide berth” in order to “avoid conflict” in the chamber. He claimed he had been involved in a “physical altercation” with another MP on the day of the state opening of parliament in May. It later emerged his reservation had been removed by Commons staff as it did not have the proper date stamp. Daisy Cooper, the Lib Dem deputy leader, told Sky News on Thursday morning that her party’s MPs were involved in the May incident mentioned by Farage. She said: “My understanding – I didn’t see it, I wasn’t there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that. “I didn’t see it, I didn’t witness what happened, but that was several months ago. “And let’s be really clear: it’s Reform UK that had a problem at their conference with bundling female journalists and members out of their hall. So, we’ll take no lessons from them on this.” Afterwards, Voaden posted on social media in response to Farage’s claim that he was at risk of “another physical altercation”: “We both know that’s not true Nigel don’t we? “I’m still waiting for the apology you were required to write to me … Though I won’t hold my breath.” When asked for a response to the accusations, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s shadow chancellor, said: “You know what? I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates. “The thing about Reform politicians is, yeah, we love parliament, the institution of parliament. I go there every day. I speak in parliament. I represent my constituents. “But I’m much more interested about, actually, the issues, trying to change this country, getting out and about outside of the bubble. And I’m not interested in even responding, dignifying the nonsense that Daisy Cooper is talking about there.”

headline: The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is
trail_text: John Healey aced the morning-after media round because his Martin Lewis measures left nothing to challenge him on
body_text: Maybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments. But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when you don’t make any massive tax or spending commitments, there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call it the Martin Lewis budget. In fact, Healey and Lewis now seem unable to get through the day without spending some time with each other. They certainly can’t stop talking about one another. It’s becoming unhealthily co-dependent. The gods of small things. It had been billed as the “breathing space” budget. A budget to help get everyone through the coming year more or less alive. No hiding under tables or breaking open the emergency supplies of baked beans. Apocalypse averted. But the breathing space might just as well have been for the government. Difficult decisions delayed. Hope that we all wake up in 52 weeks’ time and the world looks like a less frightening place. And even if it doesn’t, it will always have had a year’s grace. A chance for the Tories and Reform to implode. You can always hope. Come the traditional morning-after interview with the chancellor on the Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson seemed uncharacteristically subdued. Normally he’s a terrier on occasions like these. There’s never been a budget that Nick wouldn’t have been able to do far better himself. But this one? This one was something you might find on the consumer affairs programme, You and Yours. And the BBC was in the process of axing that. So the 20 minutes passed with little fuss. More a softball back and forth. Healey started with his usual infectious brand of pessimism. He was born to be the bearer of bad news. The poster boy for assisted dying. Everything was absolutely terrible. He wasn’t quite sure why anyone was still bothering with anything. If it had been up to him he would have ended the interview before it had started. There was nothing to say. Other than that, given the chance, he wouldn’t have started from here. Brexit, the pandemic, Ukraine, Iran, energy prices. The world was screwed. Britain was screwed. Lie back and prepare for the worst 10 years of your already miserable life. Nick tried to find a reason to believe. Couldn’t the chancellor have made just a little more effort? Having a plan to have a plan wasn’t the usual budget fare. Healey, AKA Dr Death, shrugged. It was one up on having a plan to not have a plan. By now Robbo was audibly struggling. How could he put it politely? In the third year of a government with a 160-seat majority, surely Healey could have been a little more ambitious. This wasn’t exactly the big transformation that had been promised. Could he even say if he would bring down the benefits bill? Apparently he could. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Dr Death. Cue panic stations in the Treasury. Within seconds of Healey opening his mouth, dozens of government spinners were on the phones to every journalist to tell them they hadn’t heard what they had just heard. There had been collective false consciousness. When Healey had said that he would be bringing down a benefits bill that everyone agreed was too high and that the country could not afford, what he had really meant to say was that he would not be bringing down the benefits bill that he had no idea how to pay for. Fag packets gratefully received. That was about as close to news as we got. Maybe it was just that while Healey was having one of his better days, Robinson was having one of his worse ones. Because he had also sounded uninterested in his interview with Andrew Griffith an hour earlier. An exercise in box-ticking rather than revelation because the shadow chancellor never has anything useful to add on the day after. Sure enough, Griffith insisted that he would have done everything differently while never going into the details of how. At which point, Robbo opened half an eye and observed that if it was really that easy, how come the Tories hadn’t fixed it when in office? Indeed, Nick continued, it could be argued that Labour had been left to clear up the mess the Tories created. “I’ve never shied away from saying that the Tories have a chequered record,” Griffith said defensively. Er, I’m not sure that’s entirely true, Andrew. Your usual line is that history started in 2024 and that everything is the Labour government’s fault. That just left time for Robinson to remind the shadow chancellor that he had been part of the Treasury team that had defended the Liz Truss mini-budget even as it was being shredded. “I will never publish plans without saying where the money is coming from,” said Griffith, before announcing £30bn of planned tax cuts without specifying which benefits he would cut to pay for them. Fair to say, he’s not a man who seems to learn from experience. Once in the Truss image, always in the Truss image. The final piece of the Thursday jigsaw was the verdict from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. In the past this has been enough to completely destroy the reputation of some chancellors. I could never look at George Osborne in quite the same way after the IFS had rubbished one of his budgets. It’s one thing to be thought of as an economic quarter-wit. What’s really devastating is to have it proved. Helen Miller, the IFS director, looked a bit knackered. She and her team had been up most of the night, going through both the budget and the OBR figures line by line, searching for the fatal flaw. And she was gutted to announce that there actually wasn’t one. There was as little in the budget as had first appeared. She announced that she was grumpy about some measures. Disappointed in others. Another was cack-handed. The tax system had been made more complicated, not less. Yet, all in all, these were minor gripes. “This chancellor is hoping that things get better without actually needing to do anything,” Miller said in conclusion. I don’t think that’s right. Healey never travels in hope. Like the rest of us, he’s pretty confident everything is going to be worse in a year’s time. But he had got himself some breathing space. headline: Reform UK launches its own ‘newspaper’ with Farage on front page
trail_text: Party aims to build a ‘significant national publishing operation’ as first edition of the Reformer is distributed
body_text: Reform UK has launched what it is calling a newspaper, featuring large pictures of Nigel Farage, which the party hopes will replace mainstream media for its supporters. Though the party is hiring qualified journalists to write its newspapers, the only “reporter” credited with writing articles is Farage, the party leader. Political parties often put out pamphlets made to look like newspapers in local areas during elections, but it is unusual for a party to put out a paper nationally, year-round. The party has said it wishes to build a “significant national publishing operation” as well as its TV channel hosted on YouTube. In his first column for the publication, Farage writes: “We have had enough of what we say and do being distorted by the media. So instead, we want to talk to you directly, and make sure that you get our message straight from the Reformer.” Its front-page story features a photograph of Farage smiling and posing with a labrador, with the headline “Nigel Farage: we will fix broken Britain”. Other stories include “Clacton result: Farage 22,239, Establishment 0.” This refers to the byelection called by Farage after he resigned his Essex seat following revelations about an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The gift was revealed by the Guardian earlier this summer. The other main parties declined to stand in the ensuing byelection, with the result that Farage’s main opponent was Count Binface. One piece advertises Reform’s plan to use the Royal Navy to send back migrants who travel across the Channel in small boats. It says: “A Reform UK government will launch Operation Fortress. Prime Minister Nigel Farage will order the Royal Navy to stop the boats and return the illegal immigrants to France. Not one will make it to Britain.” Military experts have criticised this plan, saying the navy should not be used as a ferry service. Other articles include a short tribute to Ann Widdecombe, the Reform politician who was killed in her home in July, featuring a quote from Farage, and another piece by Farage in which he vows to declare a national emergency should he become prime minister. Other features include updates on local Reform politicians’ progress on filling in potholes and picking up litter. Reform insiders said the first edition was “rushed” and to expect more news and features in subsequent editions, coming monthly. Roles at the publication are still open, with 12 journalist jobs including executive editor, website editor and multimedia reporters/producers advertised online. Reform sources said they thought the newspapers, being delivered to homes across Britain and available in the lobby of the party’s Westminster office, would drive up membership rates. Those who join the party using the cut-out form included in the newspaper are offered a free mug and badge. Rather than being kept on the news stands in the lobby of Millbank Tower, where Reform has its headquarters, the Reformer is kept behind the desk at reception and available on request. The party says the paper has been sent to 15 million people across the country. Readers of the publication are also urged to sign up as Reform candidates in the May 2027 local elections. A report by Printweek revealed that the paper has been printed by Walstead Group, which has contracts with several of the UK’s leading newspapers including the Sunday Times and Sun on Sunday. The paper is reportedly being led by Mick Hume, the founder and former editor of the online libertarian-right politics magazine Spiked, and is part of Reform’s drive to build a “national publishing operation” with a digital newsroom and expanded video content. Though the first edition of the free paper does not appear to contain any exclusive news stories, budding reporters hoping to join the Reformer need to be able to produce scoops. A job advert states: “Reform UK is building a seven-day digital newsroom at its Westminster headquarters and is looking for hard-working, NCTJ-qualified multimedia reporter/producers who can report, write and publish high-quality content at speed. The role sits at the heart of the party’s ambition to build the Reform UK website into a significant national publishing operation.” It adds that applicants need to come up with original stories “rather than relying solely on rewriting or republishing material already available elsewhere”.

headline: He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harm
trail_text: Armed with 98 measures, a rictus grin and a decidedly comedy-free speech, the chancellor at least offered us – and Labour – some breathing space
body_text: It was as if John Healey was taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can all think of plenty of chancellors who have done untold damage. Take a bow George Osborne. It might just have been better if the doctor that Healey had chosen to impersonate was not Dr Death. John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed. Not everyone can have a naturally sunny disposition. His face seems to be carved out of despair. But it would be a big help if, when called upon to make his most important speech of the year, he didn’t reinforce the impression when he opened his mouth. A one-way journey to the slough of despond. “I’m very sorry to let you know, Mr Crace,” he would say with Voldemort delight. “But your cancer is now terminal. You have months to live.” And just when you are trying to process what he’s said and are preparing to say your goodbyes, he would let you know he had made a mistake. You only had weeks to live after all. He would then smile wanly, pat you on the shoulder before moving on to kill off his next patient. You wouldn’t be seeing him again. Healey began with a few cheery words. Cheery by his standards, that is. This was a budget for working people. People often talked about global headwinds. John was here to let us know that these headwinds were more like a storm. Make that a hurricane. One we’d all be lucky to come out of alive. The wars in Iran and Ukraine, the rising cost of energy. The whole world was basically screwed. He knew the government had suggested we all stockpile food and water ahead of the apocalypse, but frankly we might as well not bother. Why prolong the agony? “Fresh hope for Britain’s future,” he said. The word hope died on his lips. Only Healey can send you into a vortex of existential futility with an attempt at optimism. Even the normally upbeat Andy Burnham who was sitting next to him looked lost in his own sense of pointlessness. Not even a glimmer of a smile. The main reason he had appointed Healey was because he could be relied on to do his bidding. To deliver the kind of budget Andy had in mind. Ed Miliband was far too much his own man. But Burnham hadn’t factored in the aura of gloom. The one consolation was that even John couldn’t be as depressing as Rachel Reeves. But Healey was working on it. Give him time. Most budget statements try to tell a story. To create a coherent narrative of the state of the economy, the government’s plans to stimulate growth and fix the problems they inherited. Even when the problems the chancellor is inheriting are the ones they created. But Healey was going to try a different approach. Just a series of unstructured, random spending announcements. Dr Death’s Seven Last Words on the Cross. Most budget speeches also contain the odd joke. Or what passes for a gag in the minds of MPs. None of them are going to get gigs at the Edinburgh fringe. But on the few occasions that the mirror cracked and Healey’s mouth tried to form a rictus grin, his words fell flat. Turns out that not everyone finds telling people they have nothing to live for quite as funny as John. Worse still, he is a man with no sense of timing. He makes Ed Balls sound like a comedy giant. There was the obligatory reference to Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and the hand that the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, played in it. That should have been fertile comic ground as it has the benefit of being true. Four years on, we are all still suffering PTSD. Everyone apart from the Trusster, who believes the real problem was that she was forced to reverse £70bn of unfunded tax cuts. But Healey couldn’t land the punchline. Labour backbenchers were willing him to succeed, but they still couldn’t bring themselves to laugh. The only really funny moment was completely unintentional, when Healey said that the energy secretary had opposed Jackdaw. That was supposed to be kept an open secret, not broadcast to the world. The Tory benches couldn’t contain themselves with forced laughter. The chancellor tried to redeem the situation by ad-libbing that at least the opposition was still awake. Which was more than could be said for many Labour backbenchers. Fresh hope and breathing space, Healey said again. It had become his only leitmotif. And, yet again, it felt like another nail in the coffin. The world was in turmoil, the country bouncing from crisis to crisis and the chancellor was doing not very much. Or rather he was doing a lot – he announced 98 different measures – but none of them amounted to a lot. Not that anyone was going to complain about getting £100 off their council tax or not having to queue up at the post office for your Amazon returns. These things do make a difference. It was just that we were waiting for the big reveal. The major surprise. But time passed. And passed. And none came. There was a promise to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but no details of how. It was the miserabilist’s dream. Growth baked in at less than 2%, living standards predicted to fall. A sense of drift. But maybe it was all deliberate. A country put on palliative care because it wouldn’t survive extreme surgery. Healey had said he had called an early budget because it was time to inject some urgency into the public finances. But many of the really big decisions had been kicked into the long grass. He had said the budget was to give the country some breathing space. It felt as if the government were the ones who needed the breathing space. Kemi Badenoch’s response was similarly underwhelming. Then she had rather shot herself in the foot by admitting that the country had been paralysed and miserable under the Tories. She even found herself agreeing with some of Healey’s measures but her overall assessment – Was that it? – was echoed by many Labour MPs. Not that Kemi had any answers herself. None to be taken seriously, at least. At his own press conference, a disinhibited Nigel Farage had just sounded mad. There is no appetite for the Tories or Reform. So a breathing space it is. headline: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham
trail_text: Prime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of options
body_text: Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum. In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this. Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote. A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards. “The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.” The letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options. “It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.” It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnham has talked up as a possibility. The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month. Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail. “I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum. “We hope the summit will lead to some important, concrete steps. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit. “Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.” Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.” Challenged by Badenoch at PMQs about his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum. In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”

headline: Volunteer, 78, says Reform official likened her to Nazi collaborator for teaching asylum seekers English
trail_text: Mair Godley claims Essex councillor Carl Johnson told her she was ‘facilitating the invasion’ by giving language lessons
body_text: A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English. Mair Godley and her husband, Nick, 77, a former chair of Wethersfield parish council, live near the former Wethersfield military base in Essex, where the Home Office accommodates hundreds of asylum seekers. The couple said the accusations were made against Mair Godley at a parish council meeting on 14 October. Reform took over control of Essex county council after the elections in May 2026, ending 25 years of Conservative control. The Reform councillor, Carl Johnson, attended the meeting to update members of the parish council about local issues for which it has responsibility, including repairing potholes and “Operation Vanguard”, which involves private security guards patrolling Essex town centres. Wethersfield is the larger of two former military sites the Home Office uses to provide mass accommodation for asylum seekers. The other is at Crowborough in Sussex. Nick Godley challenged Johnson at the meeting about the potholes and whether Operation Vanguard was needed to protect local people against asylum seekers. He said crime and antisocial behaviour incidents in nearby Braintree, where asylum seekers sometimes go to, were low. In response, Johnson asked if anyone in the room had been helping the migrants at Wethersfield and “facilitating the invasion”. Mair Godley said she had previously volunteered to help teach English to the asylum seekers at the facility. Johnson then reportedly said that by doing so she might as well have been helping Germany during second world war. He said he didn’t want to bring his daughter up to be raped and murdered by asylum seekers. In a Facebook post the week before the parish council meeting, Johnson had written that people who enter the country “illegally” received things including clothing and accommodation for free while “the rest of us” had to pay for items. “I have never known a country to actively facilitate its own invasion and population replacement,” he wrote. “This is treason.” According to the draft minutes of the parish council meeting seen by the Guardian the discussion became heated and Johnson was asked to leave the meeting to “restore order”. Mair Godley said: “I’m nearly 79 years old. I felt violated by his comments. How dare he say that to me? I certainly told him at the meeting, ‘you are not wanted here’. He has left a really bad taste.” Nick Godley said he had had a “fairly challenging” discussion with Johnson about Operation Vanguard. It was after he had raised concerns that it had been introduced without consultation that Johnson accused Mair Godley of being akin to a Nazi collaborator by helping asylum seekers to learn English. “It was a member of the public who attended the meeting who suggested forcibly that he should leave. Cllr Johnson’s behaviour was shocking,” said Nick Godley. He has lodged a formal complaint about Johnson’s comments at the meeting with Essex county council. A spokesperson for the council said: “We comment on complaints made at a point where they have been investigated and a finding of a breach has been made, but not before that point.” Reform UK and Johnson have not responded to repeated requests for comment.

headline: Schrödinger’s racism, Nige’s latest wheeze to try to dodge his associates’ bigotry
trail_text: We are apparently to believe Raheem Kassam calling Kemi a ‘Nigerian scammer’ was racist and not racist at the same time
body_text: Back to the future. Some of us can remember the days when the key to surviving a nuclear war was to kneel down under the kitchen table and keep your eyes closed till you were incinerated or died of radiation poisoning. Now the government wants you to hoard some baked beans and a few litres of water in the hope of getting through the next three days. But when the apocalypse does come, you can bank on there being one survivor. The politician with seemingly limitless powers of regeneration. As one party of his dies, so another rises from the ashes. Fuelled not by water and tinned food, but by alcohol and grievance. Somehow, Nigel Farage is always the victim in his own story. The man who is forever misunderstood. Nige must be the unluckiest politician alive. The man who has only ever wanted the best for everybody – deporting immigrants is clearly in their own best interests, even if it involves death or torture – keeps getting mired in scandal. There’s the money. Of course there is. Plenty of it from – how shall we put this? – unorthodox sources. But there’s also the racism. Why is it that so many who are close to Farage and his organisation turn out to be bigots? How can his message of love and peace to all men be so tainted? It’s happened so often now that you could forgive Nige for being a little grumpy. Last week one of his closest friends was at it again. Raheem Kassam, touted as Reform’s next chief of staff, called Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”. You and I know exactly what he meant. The leader of the opposition was like a West African phonejacker who rang you up and tried to scam your bank accounts. It was a fairly obvious racist slur. One designed to denigrate. Only it wasn’t quite so obviously racist to Reform MPs themselves. Robert Jenrick called it a bit of forensic journalism. At least that’s what he implied by describing Kassam as a journalist. Danny Kruger was even more confused. There again, he often is. He’s meant to be the intellectual and moral compass of Reform, but just appears dim-witted and spinning helplessly in space. He thought “Nigerian scammer” couldn’t be racist because he couldn’t conceive of any of Nigel’s friends being racist. Try a little harder, Danny. It was third time unlucky – that word again – as Nige took on his first proper morning media round in months. It didn’t end well for him. Car-crash TV. On BBC Breakfast, the presenter Sally Nugent quickly cut to the chase and it soon became clear that Nige doesn’t take it well when an intelligent woman asks him tricky questions. He likes to think of himself very much as a man’s man. Somehow being interviewed by a woman is a sign of disrespect. Or maybe he’s still tetchy about having given a press conference to a near-empty hall the day before. First Nige tried to claim Kassam had not been a former chief of staff – he had in one of Farage’s previous lives – and was on the point of saying he wasn’t even a friend. But then he had a brainwave. “He’s Indian,” he said. “He’s of Indian heritage.” As if that somehow precluded all Indians – all black and brown people, for that matter – from being racist. A suggestion, dare one say it, that is racist in itself. Nige clearly believes in a hierarchy of racism. If he believes in racism at all. Maybe we’re just all stuck in a doom loop of cultural relativism. We just need to chill out a bit. Next Farage tried to play the word dissociation game. Just because Kassam had used the words “Nigerian scammer” in conjunction with one another, it didn’t necessarily mean the words were in any way connected to form a single image. All he had done was to state two truths. Kemi was of Nigerian descent, though for the purposes of this conversation he was prepared to concede that she might also be part British. And she was a scammer, because she had said things that were demonstrably untrue. Much the same could be said of Nige, mind. Maybe in his own mind he also longs to be outed as a scammer. Back in the BBC studio, Nugent wasn’t having any of this and kept at him. Did he think it was racist? “No, I don’t,” said Nige. Perhaps a bit over the top, but definitely not intentionally racist. Farage had spoken, Schrödinger’s racism. Something could be racist and not racist at the same time. In any case, he couldn’t be held responsible for any of the social media posts his friends and supporters made. It was his curse that so many in Reform expressed themselves in racist language. He had no idea why he had become the last refuge for so many bigots. Things took on a more surreal turn later that morning when Kassam contacted a Guardian journalist to give an update on the situation. He said that Nige had given him a ticking off for a tweet that was neither “clever nor funny”. Just a shame Farage couldn’t have used his position as the leader of Reform to make that same point on the BBC hours earlier. Kassam went on to say that, in hindsight, his tweet could have been better phrased and timed. He also claimed Kemi was a con artist for turning the Tories into a version of the Lib Dems. That will come as news to both the Tories and the Lib Dems. The Tories have been shadowing Reform to the right for the last two years. The real sorry-not-sorry moment came when Kassam suggested he had spent too much time in the US recently. Over there, out-and-out racism was an acceptable rite of political discourse. People could say what they want. The trouble is that we Brits had lost our sense of humour. It was now a thought crime even to make a racist joke. Time we all lightened up. What was needed was more politicians who called Kemi a “Nigerian scammer” not fewer. This isn’t quite the end of it. Because Kassam’s new found contrition may not be all it seems. While his pinned “Nigerian scammer” tweet has been deleted, on Tuesday morning he was again posting about “Kemi Scammenoch” on X. If this is remorse, it’s still in its early days. Maybe one should treat Kassam and Farage as one and the same. When they show you what they are, believe them. • On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. Book tickets here or at theguardian.live • This article was amended on 28 October 2026. An earlier version said a tweet by Raheem Kassam referring to “Kemi Scammenoch” had been deleted. In fact, the tweet remains.

headline: Shabana Mahmood urged to grant visa to former Weather Underground activist
trail_text: Home Office refused entry to Judith Clark, 77, invited by RSC to speak about restorative justice after her time in prison
byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
body_text: Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour.
