Judith Clark, 77, was the inspiration for Walter’s portrayal of prisoners in the Donmar Warehouse all-female Shakespeare trilogy, including Brutus in Julius Caesar and Prospero in The Tempest. Clark had been invited to speak about rehabilitation and restorative justice at a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Julius Caesar in Stratford-upon-Avon next month, but her application to visit Britain was refused last week. She had also hoped to attend the UK launch of her daughter Harriet Clark’s first novel, The Hill, on 5 November. Kennedy said that while the Home Office had rules governing visas for people with serious criminal convictions, there was also ministerial discretion, which should be exercised in Clark’s case. “This is a woman in her 70s who served a long sentence for political activism, which involved no violence on her part, and whose clear remorse and exceptional works within the prison system led to her early release,” she said. “She was deemed to pose no threat to US society and in my view she poses no threat whatsoever to the UK’s national security.” Walter said immigration rules designed to protect the public should allow flexibility in exceptional cases such as Clark’s. “There is no other purpose behind the short visit she wants to make other than to reward us with her presence as a speaker in our post-show conversation and to celebrate her daughter’s first book launch,” she said. Lloyd said Clark had become a touchstone for the creative team’s understanding of repentance, redemption and rehabilitation during the making of the Donmar trilogy. “To say she did her time and turned her life around is an understatement,” she said. “To have her speak in the UK would be an inspiration in the realm of restorative justice.” Clark joined the student movement against the Vietnam war in the late 1960s and became involved in the Weather Underground, a radical organisation that emerged from the American anti-war movement. She was later involved in the May 19th Communist Organization, which pursued armed revolutionary activity. In 1983, she was convicted for her role as a getaway driver in an attempted robbery of a Brinks armoured truck in New York in 1981, during which a security guard and two police officers were killed. She was sentenced to three consecutive terms of 25 years to life. In 2017, the then-New York governor Andrew Cuomo commuted her sentence, allowing her to seek parole. She was released in 2019, after serving 37 years. During her incarceration at Bedford Hills correctional facility in New York, Clark helped establish an Aids education and support group, developed programmes to help mothers maintain relationships with their children, raised service dogs for veterans and first responders and helped build a college education programme. She has since worked in criminal justice reform and support for formerly incarcerated women. In 2025, she became director of the Survivors Justice Project, which works to secure legal relief for survivors of domestic violence facing prison sentences. Walter and Lloyd met Clark while researching their Shakespeare trilogy, which reimagined the plays as productions staged by women in prison. Walter said Clark had helped her understand Brutus, the politically conflicted character in Julius Caesar, who struggles with the moral consequences of his actions. Her story also informed Walter’s portrayal of Prospero in The Tempest. “By the time I met Judy she had developed into one of the most exemplary and evolved human beings I have ever met or am likely to meet,” Walter said. The RSC has invited Clark to take part in a post-show discussion entitled Can Art Save Lives? It would also include a company member introduced to theatre after prison through the charity Clean Break. Kennedy first met Clark more than 30 years ago at Bedford Hills while making a television documentary about women in prison. “Her remorse for her participation in criminal conduct was very evident to all who were involved with her,” she said. In her own letter supporting her visa application, Clark said she had publicly disavowed her actions and apologised for the harm she had contributed to a decade into her sentence. She spent the remainder of her imprisonment trying to turn her remorse into work benefiting the prison community, families and those harmed by crime. Clark hoped to visit Britain from 4 to 15 November with her wife, Cheryl Moch. Her daughter has said that The Hill draws on her own experience of visiting her mother throughout her imprisonment. Despite their separation, she wrote, Clark had found ways to mother her. A Home Office spokesperson said: “It’s our longstanding policy not to comment on individual cases. “All applications for entry clearance in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the Immigration Rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

headline: How has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power?
trail_text: From ‘everyday fixes’, party management and communications to long-term plans for care and pensions, the PM’s six key acts so far
body_text: Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street promising to transform the way Britain works, restore hope and bring an end to years of political division. One hundred days later, the prime minister has announced a series of measures aimed at making everyday life easier, he’s reopened the debate over Britain’s relationship with the EU and set out plans to overhaul public services. He has also managed to maintain an unusually visible public profile, appearing regularly on social media and even taking part in a charity edition of Channel 4’s Gogglebox. Burnham has said he’s been surprised by the public’s appetite for change, insisting his first budget on Wednesday would offer some breathing space for households and businesses. But the early weeks of his premiership have also exposed tensions between immediate political wins and the structural changes he has promised. Here is how his first 100 days have unfolded in six key ways. Quick policy wins Burnham made a series of what Downing Street calls “everyday fixes” central to his premiership, targeting everything from electricity bills and bus fares to misleading discounts, subscription traps and antisocial behaviour on public transport. One of his first announcements, the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills across Britain, took effect on 1 October. The government estimates an annualised saving of £45 for a typical household, although the temporary measure is funded only until March. Other announcements have yet to take effect. A £2 cap on participating bus services in England outside London and new rules making subscriptions easier to cancel are due to start in January. The bus measure also involves trade-offs. It is partly funded by switching international climate finance from grants to loans, a decision criticised by development charities. The strategy is intended to demonstrate that the government understands ordinary frustrations and can respond quickly. Yet questions remain about whether a collection of relatively modest interventions can significantly improve living standards. The VAT cut on electricity bills is not likely to help struggling households, who are more likely to be reliant on gas than electricity. Rough sleeping and social care Ending rough sleeping was among Burnham’s earliest commitments, drawing on his experience as the mayor of Greater Manchester. The government initially allocated £442m to tackle the problem, and announced a further £432m on Sunday, bringing its commitment to £874m over different funding periods. Burnham wants everyone sleeping rough in England to be offered a route off the streets or appropriate support before Christmas. But the success of the initiative will depend on whether people can access suitable accommodation and the services needed to help them remain housed. And it remains unclear how exactly the prime minister hopes to keep people from going back on to the streets and not staying permanently in temporary accommodation. A big proposal is Burnham’s plan for a national care service in England, which he intends to help finance by reforming the state pension triple lock from 2030. The government plans to legislate during this parliament, while maintaining the existing guarantee until then. But the savings from changing pension uprating are uncertain and depend heavily on future economic conditions. Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, welcomed Burnham’s proposed changes of the triple lock but said “it will not be the answer to funding universal social care”. Party management Burnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. His appointments have included members of the Socialist Campaign Group, bringing MPs from Labour’s left into government roles. But he has disappointed a lot of soft-left MPs who campaigned for him after the Labour conference in 2025, when he made a number of media appearances attempting to prove he could replace Keir Starmer. His failure to include many of those from Mainstream, Open Labour and larger soft-left factions has been noted from MPs in the new intake, and those who have been in the parliamentary Labour party for a long time. Disagreements have emerged, particularly over immigration. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, faces opposition from Labour MPs and some cabinet colleagues over proposals that could require some migrant workers to wait 15 years before securing permanent residence. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, declined to endorse the specific proposal before being forced to clarify her support for the government’s broader approach. Burnham backed the principle of earned settlement but stopped short of committing to every detail of Mahmood’s proposals. A government source believes Burnham has avoided public rows so far because he is “taking his time to get policy right”, but they added, “isn’t it strange that a sitting cabinet minister had to apologise for making a joke … clearly we’re not one big happy family”. Difficult decisions Beyond the everyday fixes, Burnham has begun confronting choices that divide opinion within his own party. He has reopened discussion of Britain’s relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit has damaged economic growth and weakened immigration control. On Monday, he revealed his personal desire to see Britain rejoin the EU during his lifetime, while ruling out abandoning Labour’s manifesto red lines during this parliament. Energy policy has presented another dilemma. Last week, the government approved the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield, arguing that domestic production would support energy security and employment. The development is expected to create only 27 new direct jobs and safeguard 273 existing positions. Environmental groups argue that further fossil fuel production undermines Britain’s climate commitments, while domestic gas does not automatically reduce household bills. Communication Burnham has drastically changed the way Downing Street presents itself. The prime minister’s social media updates, which are pretty much daily, his collaborations with public figures including Mo Farah and online creators, and his appearance alongside Steve Rotheram on Gogglebox have taken his message beyond the traditional Westminster audience or those who avidly follow politics. His approach has attracted substantial online attention and made short, accessible explanations of government announcements a recognisable feature of his premiership. Andrew Chadwick, professor of political communication at Loughborough University, has described Burnham’s collaborations with influencers as generating a “constructed sense of authenticity”. But there is a big difference between attracting audiences, of all ages and backgrounds, and explaining policy and persuading voters that measures will actually help them. What do the public think? Labour has recovered ground in the polls, although the measures of how satisfied the public are seem slightly more complicated. As soon as Burnham entered No 10, the party’s ratings rose to 23% then reached 26%, overtaking Reform UK on 24%. After the Labour conference, an Ipsos survey conducted between 15 and 22 October put the party on 32%, eight points ahead of the Conservatives, with Reform UK on 20%. But 66% of those surveyed expressed dissatisfaction with the government’s performance, against 23% who were satisfied. Meanwhile, YouGov polling conducted earlier this month revealed 46% viewed Burnham favourably and 42% unfavourably. His net favourability rating had fallen from 13 points in August to four points. Despite this, Opinium pollsters declared: “Burnham remains the only party leader with a positive net approval rating and holds a commanding lead over both Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage on who would make the better prime minister.”

headline: UK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summit
trail_text: Business secretary says focus for November summit will be trade and youth mobility, but talks will also include ‘future options for relationship’
body_text: British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept. Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc. “They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible. “We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.” Reynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.” He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said. A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU. The Labour MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.” The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago, Andy Burnham says to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said. “What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.” Burnham made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU. Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll. The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now]. “Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

headline: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims
trail_text: Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group
body_text: AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research. Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG). It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool. Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry. The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric. It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed. The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states. Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications. It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools. Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.” Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers. “Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”

headline: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement
trail_text: Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend
body_text: Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue. Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels. Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue. It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option. “He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship with Europe is best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said. “He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.” She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU. Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with the European Union looks like.” In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU. On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in the Labour manifesto.” Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum. When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.” Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing. “The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit.” Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU. Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.

headline: Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak
trail_text: Move comes after claims that killer had history of using threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons
body_text: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak. It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons. Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse. In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.” Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes. Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak. The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident. Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months. “Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said. “It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene. “It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been. “Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.” Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct. The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid. Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice. “Since Henry was murdered, we’ve fought tirelessly for answers to questions no family should ever have to ask. The emotional toll of that fight, on top of the unimaginable grief of losing Henry, has been immense,” the family said. “We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for. “Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have.” Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. He has been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the court of appeal on 5 November. Kiran Kaur, Digwa’s mother, was also jailed for three years for assisting an offender after she removed the knife used by her son. The knife was found by police at their family home along with more than 20 other weapons.

headline: Brexit deal is not good enough for British public, says Andy Burnham
trail_text: EU exit has damaged economy and failed to bring promised benefits, says PM, but he rules out big pre-election changes
body_text: Brexit has not “played out” like it was promised to the public, has weakened the economy and the current deal is not good enough, Andy Burnham has said, while ruling out any major changes in the current parliament. The prime minister said Britain had ended up with a “harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign” and it had not helped to control the small boats crisis. Backing the home secretary’s tougher immigration rules, he said Brexit had weakened the UK’s ability to control its borders as it could no longer send people back to Europe. When asked directly on Monday whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, Burnham told Good Morning Britain: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.” Explaining why he even brought up the possibility of “going all the way” in terms of closer relations with the EU, Burnham said: “Looking back at Brexit … I don’t think it has played out as people said it would at the time. We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign. “It’s weakened our economy. It’s also weakened our control of immigration, and that might surprise people because that was the big issue, but the small boats crisis has risen since and we have a different form of immigration now.” He added: “I am not going to say at the moment that the deal we’ve got is good enough for Britain. I don’t think it is good enough.” Burnham said he would not “move away from the red lines in Labour’s manifesto”, adding: “I’m not proposing rejoining [the EU] in this parliament. We’re way, way away from that at this particular point in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better.” There are concerns among Labour MPs who represent leave-voting constituencies in the north of the England and the Midlands that reopening the Brexit debate could create opportunities for Reform UK. Asked about the fact that 65% of his constituents in Makerfield voted to leave the EU, the prime minister said: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing. The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit … What I can do though is make practical steps to make the arrangements work better.” Emphasising the negative impact Brexit had had on Britain’s control of immigration, the Labour leader said: “I think we’ve got weaker control now. The reason the small boats crisis has arisen is because we can’t return people, and people know we can’t do that in the same way that we used to be able to.” Burnham said he hoped the UK-EU summit on 20 November could yield a deal “which would be good for British food manufacturers, because they’ve been hit hard by Brexit”. He said he backed “the principle” of the home secretary’s controversial plan to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency. Burnham said Shabana Mahmood was right to pursue the plans based on the principle that “settlement is a right to be earned not just something that is granted automatically”. He also ruled out calling an early general election, despite polling suggesting Labour was still enjoying a “Burnham bounce”. “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” On Wednesday’s budget, Burnham said it would offer people and businesses “breathing space”, claiming it would give Britain “a little bit of light at the end of the tunnel”.

headline: UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income
trail_text: Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated
body_text: The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year. Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027. The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income. However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates. Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”. Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said. The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget. The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target. The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence. Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget. She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set. “Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut. “The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.” Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries. The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m. The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m. The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support. The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank. An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review. “Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

headline: Cabinet ministers back Burnham’s call for debate on return to free movement with EU
trail_text: PM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concern
body_text: Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers but risked a rift with “red wall” Labour MPs, who say it could jeopardise Brexit-voting seats. The prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU. Burnham also revealed his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in their manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll. The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now]. “Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.” His remarks were supported by Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, as well as Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe. However, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those Labour MPs who have previously been more cautious about closer ties with Europe, while a number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU. Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she would “like to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be, and then put that to the people at a general election”, and Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means”. A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion include Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. At a New Statesman event during the Labour party conference in September, however, Mahmood said rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”. One senior minister under Keir Starmer said the reopening of the debate on free movement was “brave” given how divisive it had been in the Brexit years. “It’s a question of timing. Public opinion is of a place where you can start to have this debate,” he said. “Theresa May, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer: what they were all trying to do was get as close as possible without freedom of movement. There is now the a possibility of being brave and making the case on single market and free movement without going for rejoin.” Labour MPs with pro-Brexit seats have expressed scepticism about rejoining the bloc, including Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement. One red wall MP said they thought debating free movement was the right thing to do but many colleagues in the north-east, especially in coastal areas, had begun to raise serious concerns. “These MPs are definitely raising the alarm,” they said. “Andy may have to work out if he can win without them, which is brutal but true.” Another Labour MP from a Brexit-voting area said it would “undoubtedly put seats at risk to Reform” but that Burnham was making an argument from a position of strength, having taken the party to higher poll ratings in recent weeks. Worries were brought up publicly on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “1 million young people that are out of work”. In his party conference speech last month, Burnham fired the starting gun on the argument about rejoining the EU as one potential route, but his latest comments suggest he appears to be favouring the option that would avoid a referendum. Although Labour’s manifesto pledges no return to free movement and the single market, Burnham signalled it could still be up for discussion at next month’s EU summit. Burnham’s comments at the weekend drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”. “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added. Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move more freely for jobs within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services. Luke Tryl, a polling and focus groups expert at the More in Common thinktank, said on Sunday that people tended to be less concerned about free movement given years of high non-EU migration but would be more exercised about EU budget contributions or joining the euro. During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote. Burnham’s decision to open the debate on free movement was welcomed by some businesses, which have grown frustrated at the lack of progress on the issue, and on reducing the extra paperwork required to do business with EU customers since Brexit – both seen as obstacles to faster economic growth. The British Chambers of Commerce lobby group called for the Treasury to analyse the various economic options for different forms of EU-UK relationships. Most economic studies have concluded that a closer EU relationship would benefit the UK economy. William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said the common understanding strategy agreed by Keir Starmer in May 2025 was “approaching the ceiling of what can be achieved”. This week’s budget is expected to underscore the damage to the economy from Brexit, including from a drop in net migration. The Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said that if migration falls by 300,000 over the next five years it would translate to a hit to government tax revenues of £4.7bn in 2029-30, reducing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre. The Institute for Fiscal Studies, another thinktank, estimated that lower net migration estimates would reduce the chancellor’s “headroom” by between £1bn and £5bn by 2031-32, depending on how the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) chooses to model the expected reductions in population. The OBR has previously estimated that Brexit barriers to trade and free movement have caused a long-term hit of about 4% of UK output.

headline: Former Tory candidate suspended over contract killer claims was adviser in Kemi Badenoch’s office
trail_text: Sources close to Tory leader say Jack Ross, who faces party investigation after undercover report, worked as social media consultant
body_text: A former Conservative election candidate who was suspended after he was filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers worked as a consultant in Kemi Badenoch’s office as recently as last year. Jack Ross is facing an investigation by the Tories after he was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter: “What do you want done?” and apparently offering to “broker” the services of an alleged far-right paramilitary group. Police in Scotland say they will be reviewing an Al Jazeera documentary in which Ross was filmed making a range comments about what a contract killer could be employed to do, and talked about using far-right groups to create disruption on the streets. It has now emerged that he was working in 2025 in the leader of the opposition’s office, which can draw on taxpayer funds to pay staff. By that point, Ross was CEO of Turning Point UK, which was already involving itself in anti-migrant street protests, and listed its chief operating officer as Nick Tenconi, the leader of Ukip. Sources close to Badenoch said Ross was contracted as a junior social media external consultant in her office. However, a Tory staffer familiar with the role of Ross at that time said: “Jack would come and go in the office and a few people raised their eyebrows, but it was brushed under the carpet because he got the party clicks on socials. “He would have been in the same room as Kemi and she would have been aware of him. Some MPs were uncomfortable about it, but senior figures were clear that social media clicks were more important.” Ross was reported by Al Jazeera to have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offered to have people killed for money. Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened. Ross replied to this saying: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.” On another occasion, Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought. Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.” Ross, who stood unsuccessfully as a Conservative local election candidate, became CEO of Turning Point UK (TPUK) in 2021, the British offshoot of the US campaign group established by the late rightwing American activist Charlie Kirk. Ross became a fixture of the British rightwing scene, appearing regularly on GB News and joining the conservative thinktank the Bow Group. TPUK was intended to be a campus-based offshoot of the US group and initially endorsed by leading Tory figures such as Priti Patel and Jacob Rees-Mogg. Early members included younger rightwingers such as Tom Harwood, who went on to become a GB News anchor. However, it began reinventing itself as a street-protest group after the addition of Tenconi, who has worked closely with Ross, as its COO. Tenconi, as leader of Ukip, has been at the forefont of leading immigration protests in recent years, blending anti-migrant rhetoric with Christian nationalism. Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Badenoch after Kirk’s death TPUK has not responded to the allegations but Tenconi staged a stunt outside King’s College London on Thursday in an imitation of the campus-based events held by Kirk. A gazebo with TPUK branding was surrounded by students and protesters chanting in opposition. Al Jazeera filmed Tenconi in the company of Ross in 2022 as they discussed the formation of a “new right” which would include the engagement of far-right activists who could cause disruption on the streets, as well as what Tenconi described as the “winning over” of sympathetic MPs. A Tory spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.” Ross and Tenconi have been approached for comment.

headline: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
trail_text: Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November
body_text: Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc. The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU. Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU. In an interview with the Sunday Times, he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.” Burnham has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union. It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029. Burnham acknowledged freedom of movement had “very significant challenges associated with it”, but he suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade. “It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times. “Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.” Burnham will meet EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. He argued there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe. Migration was one of the dominant topics of debate during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign. In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics. Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however. Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic. It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016. Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc. He said he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro. Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency. The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.” Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe. The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

headline: Andy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bullet
trail_text: PM and the Liverpool mayor prove to be naturals at watching TV, with a genuine connection and sense of fun
body_text: On nights like this a man can feel like he’s slipped through the looking-glass. I’m sitting on the sofa watching the TV, poised to make some gags about the prime minister and the mayor of Liverpool, who are themselves sitting on a sofa at No 10, poised to make some gags about what they are watching on TV. Life doesn’t get more meta. The saving grace is that this episode of Gogglebox is a charity special for Stand Up to Cancer. Andy Burnham has requested that any journalist writing about the programme makes a donation to SU2C. I’m happy to oblige. Cancer is costing me a great deal more than money. Meet Andy Bloke and his best mate, Steve Bloke. Two career politicians who still manage to look and sound vaguely normal. Not totally normal, mind. In real life, Steve Bloke would have said to Andy Bloke: “This is a total shithole you’re living in.” And Andy Bloke would have replied: “I know. It’s been a complete tip since Boris was here. You can’t get rid of the stains.” You can’t deny that Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke are naturals at this. Not so bland that you want to turn off, a genuine connection with one another and a sense of fun that can’t be faked. Kemi Badenoch is reportedly annoyed she wasn’t invited on the programme. The reality is that she’s dodged a bullet. Kemi just doesn’t have the woman of the people shtick. It’s something you’ve either got or you haven’t and she really doesn’t. If you let her on Gogglebox the only laugh you would get from her would be if she was livestreaming an execution from the US. Mind you, it’s a slow burn. At first Andy and Steve look like they are feeling their way into the programme. But then so do the other celebs, Joe Lycett and his aunties, Stanley Tucci and his wife, Felicity, and Paul Whitehouse and Lenny Rush. The bantz feels a bit contrived and Andy Bloke – a Cambridge English grad – fails to recognise a photo of Margaret Atwood. If Steve Bloke had been more on the ball, he’d have taken the piss mercilessly. But Andy and Steve are nothing if not a team. They’ve got each other’s backs and bond over filling in the blanks on members of the royal household in Only Connect. “The king will be pleased with me at our next weekly meeting,” says Andy Bloke. He probably will be. I suspect Camilla will have made Charles watch this. The Man of the People meets the King of the People. Halfway through, we get a reminder that this isn’t all about the laughs. There is the story of Callum who died at the age of 16 from brain cancer. Then the story of a woman whose mother died of pancreatic cancer when she was 11, was diagnosed with cervical cancer shortly after her child was born and whose husband died of bowel cancer a week after diagnosis. Sometimes shit really does happen to good people. All the celebs were fighting back tears. Andy was no exception. “I’d like to see Match of the Day,” says Paul Whitehouse. “Why? To hear how crap Spurs are?” Lenny joked. Careful, Lenny, careful. We might be past the watershed but it’s still way too early for gags about Spurs. But some football would have been nice. Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke would have been in their element. You could have made an entire programme of the pair of them pissing themselves laughing as Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League. It might even have earned a Bafta nomination. For some reason, Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke were excluded from watching an X-rated natural history about some young birds that haven’t yet learned to fly and are so dim that they literally just stand there as tortoises eat them alive. Well, not all. One bird managed to hop on top of a tortoise shell. Though not before the tortoise had taken a chunk out of a wing. A happy ending of sorts. The celebs couldn’t quite believe they were being forced to watch such ultra-violence. Normal service was resumed with a mercifully brief excerpt from Strictly Come Dancing. Brief because none of the real celebs had any idea who the celebrity contestants were. Andy Bloke admitted he still had PTSD from watching Ed Balls crashing around the dancefloor. Steve Bloke wisely helped himself to another beer. Maybe this was the way they used to do business when Andy Bloke was also a mayor. We ended on an upbeat note. The Celebrity Traitors. Steve Bloke had no idea what was going on so Andy Bloke tried to fill him in as they cracked up over some crisps, pork scratchings and Skips. Me neither. I guess that was one were you had to be in the room. “You should be quite good at this,” Andy Bloke said, encouragingly. “You can generally spot the wrong ’un in the room.” I guess that depends on how often you’ve been in the same room as Michael Gove. Claudia Winkleman was announcing that the murder would be done in plain sight by boring a Faithful to death. Steve Bloke had the solution. Just make them watch the proceedings in the House of Commons. Boom boom. Neither Steve nor Andy Bloke had much to say about Ross Kemp’s worrying levels of paranoia or Jerry Hall’s complete charisma bypass. How do you bore someone who is already boring? That could have been a question for Only Connect. Maybe we had come full circle. Or perhaps their gags about Rupert Murdoch got cut in the editing suite.

headline: Reform UK braces for Farage standards verdict over undeclared £5m gift
trail_text: Party insiders say they expect initial verdict to be against leader and are preparing to appeal against adverse findings
body_text: Nigel Farage’s Reform is braced for a negative report from the standards commissioner over his failure to declare a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and plans to appeal against any adverse findings. The party is on tenterhooks over the report, with multiple Reform insiders saying they are readying for a fightback through the appeals process and fully expect the initial verdict to find against their leader. Any attempt by Farage to oppose a negative verdict could mean the process drags on for months, as an MP under investigation has the right to present further evidence to the standards committee as well as to appeal through the independent expert panel. After any appeals process, and if parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, Farage could end up facing a second byelection in his Clacton constituency. This would require a recall petition, triggered by signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over six weeks. Farage was interviewed by the standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, last month and the party expects to be notified of the verdict at any time. While it awaits the findings, Reform has been overhauling its HQ operations, having been destabilised by undercover investigations by Channel 4 and ITV in recent weeks and fallen in the polls. The Channel 4 reporting with the investigative group Verbatim has led to a police inquiry into alleged attempts to orchestrate illegal overseas donations, as well as the suspension of James Orr as head of policy and Dan Jukes as Farage’s communications chief. They deny wrongdoing and an internal party report has cleared them, but the matter remains under police investigation. The ITV reporting uncovered racist councillors and election candidates for the party caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. One Reform insider said the ITV documentary in particular was extremely bad and showed the party’s vetting had not been up to scratch, despite its claims to have professionalised. But they said the party was well on its way to bringing in changes in its organisation. Harvey Griffiths, Reform’s new treasurer, has been taking a central role in handling day-to-day party business, while Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary, has taken on the role of getting to grips with vetting. There have also been departures. Aaron Lobo, its former head of operations, has moved to a new role running a Reform-focused TV channel, which is hiring dozens of “journalists” to increase communications directly to voters. Amar Johal, a former government lawyer who had been working for the party as head of policy, has taken on the role of acting head of people operations and is said to be a rising force within the party. Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s polling guru and former campaign lead, has been asked to return to play a role as an informal sounding board on strategy for the party. Raheem Kassam, a former communications chief for Farage now based in the US, has been playing an unofficial role as an attack dog mostly aimed at the Tories, including calling Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”, which has been condemned by the Conservative chair, Kevin Hollinrake. While Jukes, who was a longtime aide to Farage, was considered a loss, the party’s communications are now being handled by Ed Sumner, its communications director, and Miles Goslett, a former journalist. The mood at Reform is said to be down but less bad than expected given its polling slide, partly because of the £72m gift from two donors, Harborne and Ben Delo. The Guardian reported undercover footage from Verbatim this week in which Orr suggested Harborne could be caught by the forthcoming overseas donor cap, given he has only been a registered domestic voter in the UK since June. However, Reform has insisted the money will not have to be handed back. The party has begun a hiring spree since the windfall and is planning to take on 400 campaign managers in target seats. It has also sent a mailshot directly to voters – a move that may be repeated in the coming weeks. Farage has been under investigation over the £5m gift from Harborne just before the last election in 2024 since shortly after the Guardian revealed it in May. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not a political one, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

headline: Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets
trail_text: PM’s revelation follows launch of advice for households to have enough water and food to get by in civil emergency
body_text: Andy Burnham has said he has stockpiles of beans, soup and Twiglets in case of a civil emergency, as he said a new government campaign was not a reason for panic buying. The prime minister was questioned on his domestic supply situation after the Be Ready campaign advised households to have enough bottled water and long-life food to keep going in case of an emergency, such as one caused by a weather event or a cyber-attack. Asked on BBC Radio 5 Live whether, like Angela Rayner, he would make sure his emergency supplies included a bottle of sauvignon blanc, Burnham said: “I’m not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you’re in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you’ve done the hard work. “I’ll stick to the basics, I think. I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by for too long without those.” The campaign says people should ensure they have at least three days of supplies, including water, in case of an emergency, which is similar to advice given to citizens in some other European countries. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the nation also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure. The advice was general and longer-term, Burnham told 5 Live, rather than urgent. “It’s not about panicking, is it? It’s just about being prepared and having a sensible amount of supplies in the home … These events, sadly, in the world that we’re in are becoming more likely, and therefore it’s just sensible to be prepared.” Asked about a message from a listener who was worried about supplies running low as people tried to stock up, Burnham said: “It’s not about panic buying. I understand what your listener is saying there, but it’s about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation.” Speaking earlier to the BBC, the Treasury minister James Murray admitted to being less prepared. He said: “I’ve got quite a lot of coffee in my house … it’s for individual people to take choices. I’m not going to say: ‘Here’s a government shopping list.’” He added: “I’m not going to pretend I’ve followed all that advice myself yet.” He said the advice was in part a matter of bringing the UK into line with other countries. He told BBC Breakfast: “If you look at, say, Ireland or other countries in Europe like France and Netherlands, they’ve had this system for quite a long time, the idea of having a bit of stuff at home to protect yourselves in case something goes wrong. “So it’s quite normal in other countries. I think it’s a bit more interesting here because we haven’t really talked about it as a country in recent years.”

headline: Potholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed?
trail_text: New PM has prioritised small fixes to show voters Labour can make a real difference, and government insiders are delighted at the public’s reaction
body_text: In the first episode of Armando Iannucci’s political satire The Thick of It, the hapless minister Hugh Abbot is in the back of a taxi, frantically brainstorming for an on-the-hoof policy he can announce to the assembled national press. “So you want something sexy and eye-catching, and that is free and universally popular and instantly applicable. No one can possibly object to it,” says the addled junior adviser Ollie Reeder. “Well, really, you should have said something before then, because I’ve got a file about that fucking thick of that back in the office.” After a three-month micro-policy blitz from Downing Street, the question now being asked is: did Reeder pass said file on to the government’s battalion of special advisers? In the past week Andy Burnham has vowed to clamp down on social pariahs blaring out TikTok videos on public transport, outlaw “rip-off” private car park fines and – on Thursday – fill in potholes in 7,000 miles of England’s roads. Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan to remove VAT from electricity bills, a £2 cap on single bus fares across England and take action on “auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas. The idea is simple, says one policy adviser. “People expect the government to be able to do something about things which are unfair – big or small,” they said. “It sends a message that the government is on people’s side, its ready to act, and it can genuinely make a difference.” Government insiders say the policies are not the product of standing around in a circle, throwing a stress ball and shouting out ideas. “There isn’t someone with a whiteboard brainstorming new bicycles for special constables,” says one, furthering the Thick of It comparison. Instead, the everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office. “We did this sort of thing under Keir too,” said another source. “But under Andy it’s a whole different thing; he’s put rocket boosters under it.” In the first days of his premiership, Burnham gave his close ally Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, the job of establishing taskforces for three core areas – cost of living, public control and regeneration. One government source said: “There is a very intentional drumbeat of those because they do make a difference, but also it’s constantly showing people that we understand where those frustrations and low-level pressures are.” Ideas are “kicked around” between the cost of living taskforce in the Cabinet Office and the policy unit in No 10, with all departments encouraged to feed in. “There’s a sort of filtering up process,” the source said. “It’s quite a sprawling sort of cross-government approach.” Another said that while some departments were better placed to find “not hugely spendy” fixes, every minister was encouraged to contribute. “I think a lot of people had sort of resigned any hope that the government can actually get things done – and this is showing them that, yes, actually, we can,” another source said. The small policy announcements have been, one delighted adviser said, a roaring success. Another source said: “Some people are very snotty about it, but in a world where it’s really hard for a government to cut through, this is working. You put some ideas through the grid and you often don’t know if they’re going to fly. But when you see one go gangbusters, it’s kind of like Christmas morning.” One single fact policy idea dominated the news cycle for an entire day. Another generated tens of thousands of posts on X. Burnham’s faintly hokey video on antisocial phone use garnered 2m views. “It helps that he’s just really good at it,” the source said. The small-fix policies have not been appreciated by everyone. Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said the UK was “going down the pan and our prime minister is faffing around tweaking parking tickets” – despite trying to implement the policy himself when he was a Conservative minister. The former Olympian Sharron Davies said: “As Paris burns our prime minister has stopped people playing loud music on buses & trains,” leading some to question whether she expected Burnham to invade the French capital. Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, has been dismissive, saying in a speech this week that cracking down on loud music on public transport was a “job for ticket inspectors, not the prime minister”. Reprising the theme at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the leader of the opposition implicitly accused Burnham of fiddling while Rome burns. “We are spending more on interest payments than we do on schools, the army and the police combined,” she said. “Meanwhile, the prime minister is worrying about loud music on trains. This is not serious.” Across the dispatch box, Burnham hid his delight at her response behind a disappointed look. “I’m not going to apologise for doing the small things that help people have better lives,” he said sombrely, while his advisers likely high-fived in private. Regardless of the reaction of Burnham’s opponents, the focus on minor grievances is a canny strategy that appears to be working, said the pollster Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. In recent polling, when people were asked whether Burnham understood the pressure of high energy bills on ordinary people, 45% said he did. When the same question was asked about Starmer, that figure was 23%. “I think the Tories and Reform have got it dead wrong on this,” Tryl said. “People bring this sort of stuff up in focus groups all the time. It cuts across left- and rightwing voters. People care about immigration, about the NHS – but they also care about everyday frictions.” But behind the scenes there is an acknowledgment that a focus on ticking off small things from the PM’s to-do list will be significantly more challenging in moments of crisis. There has to be a “twin-track” approach, said one insider. “It’s combining a big picture, long term, dismantling 40 years of neoliberalism and addressing questions about ownership and control, but at the same time tackling more immediate daily bugbears,” they said. “What you’ve seen so far is these smaller level interventions, but the bigger structural, longer term piece will be in the 10-year plan.” While the everyday fixes may be popular, the sugar-high they produce could be short-lived, said Ed Shackle, the head of qualitative research at the policy consultants Public First Global. “The government should be under no illusion that as soon as any real substantive event rears its head, any small popularity boost will be instantly blown away,” he said. “Quick fixes are popular, but they are a poor substitute for fixing the big issues the public care about.”

headline: Briton facing forced separation from baby son after Sweden orders his deportation
trail_text: Exclusive: Photographer Simon Montgomery told ‘state’s interest in regulated immigration’ outweighs his family concerns
body_text: A British photographer is facing deportation from Sweden and forced separation from his 16-month-old son after authorities ruled in favour of the country’s immigration interests. Simon Montgomery’s application to remain after the birth of his son last year was rejected on several grounds by Sweden’s migration agency, a decision that was then upheld by the migration court. He is appealing to the higher migration court, arguing that he has EU freedom of movement rights as his son is a German citizen through his mother. “I am not here because I want to be in Sweden, I am only in Sweden to be with my son,” he said. The couple separated shortly after the child was born but Montgomery, who grew up without his father in his life, said he was determined to stick around and be there for his newborn. The pair have legally recognised joint custody, with a parenting agreement that meant his time with his son increased as he got older and no longer needed night-time breastfeeding. He said he saw his son three days a week and took an active part in his care and daily routine with a “stable parenting plan” agreed via discussions with the municipal family law service. He moved to Sweden after Brexit so was not entitled to any withdrawal agreement residency rights, but applied to stay on the basis he was the father of an EU citizen. Montgomery said it was shocking that Sweden was prepared to separate a son from his father, even though the child had rights under EU law as well as international conventions. “Everything in Sweden is about the children’s right to both parents,” Montgomery said. “But this seems to be ignoring all of that, when it comes around to immigration. Sometimes I feel like people don’t know what happens here. That’s why it’s so important to have these stories told. “Everyone’s so friendly here; society works and things are nice. And when you tell them what’s happened, they just look shocked. They think you must have done something wrong, and when I explain I have done nothing wrong they just don’t understand.” Montgomery said he was unable to leave Sweden to see elderly relatives in the UK for fear he would be blocked from returning to be with his son. “It’s almost like torture in some ways, like having to make these decisions between staying to fulfil your parenting roles and not being able to visit my 98-year-old grandmother back in the UK and say my goodbyes,” he said. His residency application, made when his son was six months old, was rejected last December by the migration agency on the grounds there was no evidence he had “actual care” for the child, who at that point still stayed overnight with his mother. It also said he was free to maintain a relationship with his son from afar as he could enter the country visa-free and “still have the opportunity to visit the child in Sweden”. He appealed against the decision but the court this month sided with the authorities, which assessed, according to the ruling, that the “state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs your interest in the protection of your private and family life in a proportionality assessment”. Montgomery said he was taken aback by the court’s suggestion he did not need to be in Sweden full-time because he could visit his son by entering the country as a visitor. “Because I can come here visa-free, [they say] it shouldn’t interrupt my parenting ability. That’s crazy because I look after my son three days a week now … and overnights are about to start very soon.” According to court papers, the decision to reject an application for residency and a simultaneous decision that he should be deported was made “primarily on the grounds that he had not demonstrated that he met the conditions for the right of residence as a family member of an EEA citizen”. His lawyer argued that if he were “forced to leave Sweden, this would undermine the process and create instability for his son”. They added: “His son is an infant and is in a critical attachment phase where it is in his best interest to have both parents physically present and actively involved.” They argued that the boy’s father’s presence was “particularly important” because his former German partner did not have a family network to rely on if she was sick or at appointments. “Deportation would constitute a disproportionate interference in their family life,” they said, arguing that the lower migration court had interpreted “actual care” – evidence of a child’s relationship with a parent – “too narrowly on the grounds that the son primarily lives with his mother”. They alleged forcibly separating a son from his father would violate article 8 of the European convention of human rights. Montgomery is appealing against the case to the higher court but said he wanted to share the story so people understood how immigration law was being implemented. Sweden’s migration agency has been approached for comment. The German government said it could not comment on the case.

headline: Reform snowflake Zia Yusuf demands safe space from ITV’s racism hunters
trail_text: How can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?
body_text: The world has gone mad. What has happened to the country when you can’t even have a bit of racist and sexist banter with your mates at work? Time was when up to 20 million viewers would settle down to watch Till Death Us Do Part, for 30 minutes of laughter with Alf Garnett moaning about black people while calling his wife “a silly old moo”. That was a Britain that was worth living in. These days the thought police are everywhere. The wokerati from London, Oxford and Cambridge who are out to ruin everyone’s lives. What’s wrong with letting sleeping racists lie? Well, Zia Yusuf has had enough and he’s not going to take it any more. After the ITV exposé which revealed racist remarks by members of the party, he has posted a six-and-a-half-minute video on social media promising extreme retribution against the undercover journalists who posed as Reform-friendly. You have to love the irony. Because for the past six months, Zia has been posing as something he isn’t: the shadow home secretary.
