Now he may be equally as half-witted as Chris Philp, but the last time I checked, they weren’t the same person. Maybe Zia has a crush on the Philpster. Longs for the gym bod and absence of brain. Zia isn’t even an MP. When the Gorton and Denton Reform association prefer the dislikable Matt Goodwin, you know how loathed you are. Hoping to add some gravitas by sitting in front of a union jack in a wood-panelled room, Zia prepares to address the nation. And it turns out that he’s not the slightest bit bothered that some Reform members are racists and misogynists – it was probably as much of a surprise to him as it was to the rest of us. What really seems to bother him is that ITV didn’t ask permission to film colleagues being racist. Which is a bit like being annoyed that Pete Hegseth wanted to broadcast a live execution because it wasn’t being streamed on pay per view. Zia has clearly never heard of undercover public interest journalism. And he’s crushingly disappointed by the deception. He had imagined that ITV would have taken the trouble to personally write to him, asking permission to film people being racist. And he would have happily let them do so. Because then everyone would have known exactly what was going on. I mean, think of the possible consequences of not doing it this way. It might turn out that there were dozens of other undercover journalists in Reform. All just hoping to catch each other out. No one at Reform HQ might be who they say they are. There was no knowing where any of this could end. It was quite possible even that Robert Jenrick was a plant. That his defection from the Tory party had been a plot dreamed up by Kemi Badenoch. A long game to place one of the least trusted and least talented Conservative politicians at the heart of Reform. And it had worked brilliantly. Nigel Farage had taken the bait and had appointed Honest Bob as his so-called “shadow chancellor”, making Reform look more and more like a care home for unsuccessful Tories. Job done with Nige tanking in the polls. Some day in the future, Kemi would reward Jenrick with a peerage. The Conservative establishment looking after one another as usual. How things ought to be. First, though, Zia was promising retribution. He wasn’t just alleging that crimes had been committed by ITV. He was stating it as a fact. Which might get a little awkward for him. The most detailed crime was that ITV had directly affected the outcome of a council election in which Reform had lost one ward by 24 votes. The facts were this, apparently. ITV had paid their journalists to put a curse on the 200 leaflets they had been asked to distribute by Reform so that the people reading them voted for Labour and the Conservatives. Sometimes you wonder if a man can actually be this dim. At which point you have to consider if the whole video is a double bluff and that Zia is also a Tory stooge who has managed to embed himself at the heart of Reform. That his desire to deport women and children is just a front. Because first, the journalists weren’t being paid by ITV to canvass for Reform. They were being paid to be undercover journalists. And second, the idea that 200 leaflets could swing 24 voters is clearly absurd. Of the 200 leaflets it is likely that all 200 of them would have been put straight in the recycling. A leaflet changes the mind of about one person in 10,000. Leafleting is something parties do for their own benefit. To make them feel like they are doing something useful. Having got all this off his chest, Zia wanted to express his hurt. His disappointment. The psychological damage that had been done to Reform activists and workers in HQ. Men and women who had been entitled to believe they had been in a safe space, where racist outbursts would be well received and applauded. Only now they had been forced to consider the possibility that some people might find them offensive. How could that possibly be right? The violation had been so severe that Zia had been forced to issue a Reform Victim Support card for those most badly affected by the ITV investigation. Much like the yellow card that people with cancer get given. Find yourself on a crowded train full of foreigners and you just brandish the card and all black and brown people are obliged to leave the carriage and give you a seat. And if the police come across a dishevelled-looking man wearing a teal tie and babbling about how foreigners have ruined the country, they can call the hotline number on the back of the card and a Reform outreach worker will come and pick them up and take them to a refuge. Who would have guessed that the snowflake slayer in chief would turn out to be the biggest snowflake of all? Hiding in plain sight. “We will never give up,” Zia concluded. On day one of a Reform government, perhaps Nige would create safe spaces where people could be as abusive to foreigners and women as they liked. This was a Britain of which we could all be proud.

headline: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
trail_text: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage
body_text: Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic. Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum. He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party. The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America. Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016. It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year. Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner. The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015. The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad. AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law. The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi. The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”. Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project. Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.” He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership. The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region. Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico. Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead. The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran. According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point. Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US. In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence. Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists. Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016. Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel. In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated. It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now. In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”. At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.

headline: Burnham to become first PM to appear on Gogglebox in episode filmed at No 10
trail_text: The PM is heard having a long discussion about crisps in the trailer to the show, which is in aid of Stand Up To Cancer
body_text: From ranking his favourite crisps in the pub to complaining about people watching TikToks out loud on the train, Andy Burnham has made efforts to show he has the common touch. Now he will become the first prime minister to appear on the TV show Gogglebox, in a special charity episode on Friday. He will review the television shows of the week alongside the mayor of Liverpool city region, Steve Rotheram – a close friend. Others featured in the episode will include the pop band Sugababes and the comedian Joe Lycett. The show was filmed inside No 10. In the trailer, viewers are introduced to “good friends Andy and Steve” and Burnham can be heard saying: “Might have some crisps out here, do you want any?” They then have a long discussion about crisps. Rotheram responds that he has brought Quavers with him. Burnham offers his friend Skips, pork scratchings, Twiglets or bacon fries to go with a beer. He is heard throwing the packet to Rotheram and it appears to drop on the floor, after which both laugh uproariously. Channel 4 said: “Nothing is off limits as Gogglebox continues to celebrate the simple joy of watching television together. They’ll be sharing hilarious, honest and often unexpected reactions to the week’s biggest television moments as well as poignant stories, all in aid of Stand Up To Cancer.” A source close to Burnham told the Guardian he liked Gogglebox and had enjoyed watching the show. No 10 said he had a longstanding commitment to supporting charities, building on his work as the mayor of Greater Manchester and continuing in office as prime minister. In 2017, Jeremy Corbyn, then the Labour leader, appeared on the show. During his episode he shared his recipe for coddled eggs while watching a Nigella Lawson cookery programme. Stand Up To Cancer is a joint national fundraising campaign from Cancer Research UK and Channel 4 that brings Britain together to speed up progress in cancer research. More than £127m has been raised to date, funding 73 clinical trials and research projects involving more than 13,000 cancer patients. More celebrity TV critics are to be announced. The show airs this Friday on Channel 4 at 9.05pm.

headline: Wanted: new No 10 adviser to help citizens deal with rise of AI
trail_text: Andy Burnham advertises for policy experts in technology, economic growth and cost-of-living challenges
body_text: Andy Burnham is to recruit a number of advisers to plug gaps in No 10, including an expert on how AI will affect society. The roles advertised by Downing Street give a glimpse into the biggest challenges facing the prime minister – and what he has decided to prioritise. The new hires will flesh out the threadbare No 10 policy unit – where many of the roles are still vacant after Keir Starmer’s departure. Senior sources have said the prime minister wanted to take time to recruit advisers. The adviser on AI, who will be expected to have “deep expertise” in the sector, will be expected to lead preparations for the impact of the AI boom on the workforce, amid significant concerns for lower-level professional services jobs, in particular for new graduates. They will also be expected to be the main adviser to Burnham on frontier AI, the effects and benefits of AI in public service transformation and other major societal impacts. Several cabinet ministers have openly expressed concerns about the UK’s readiness for the impact of AI on the workforce and economy, as well as the dangers of unregulated systems. In his Labour conference speech on 28 September, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said there were “daunting” dangers of AI, saying they could not allow technological advances “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”. Burnham will also hire an adviser to develop policy on greater public control over everyday essentials – with a roving brief across transport, energy, housing, water and the environment. The adviser will be asked to focus on the cost of living. The job advert specifically demands an individual who can “bring challenge and external perspectives into policy development”. Burnham is known to be frustrated with the cautious and limited options presented to him by Whitehall on areas where he is seeking greater public control. The Guardian reported on Tuesday that Burnham had told officials to rip up their plans on how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical choices for what to do with the stricken company, including options that could cost more taxpayer money or carry higher legal risk. Burnham will also recruit an economic adviser to replace Starmer’s aide, Minouche Shafik. The job, which will examine growth and macroeconomic policy, requires “a strong understanding of the economic, fiscal and political context shaping government decision-making”. Before he became prime minister, Burnham took advice from Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, as well as from Richard Hughes, a former chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Jim O’Neill, a cross-bench peer and former Treasury minister. However, none have agreed to take roles in No 10. Haldane and O’Neill have been critical of Burnham’s economic approach since he entered government, particularly on increased public spending and a lack of growth-oriented policies. Other roles will include a new adviser on Scotland, an adviser on work and welfare who will report to the new growth director, as well as another post working across immigration, security and justice, looking at cross-border crime, exploitation and illegal migration.

headline: Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives
trail_text: Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
body_text: Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public. Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to the National Archives show. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS. At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general of MI5 approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him. However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved. “In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.” Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.” MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.” He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”. Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party. In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928. Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney. The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died. Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937. While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public. One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.” Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files. MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war. The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained. A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”. However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.

headline: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn
trail_text: Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
body_text: Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said. The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat. “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.” The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating. The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters in November and January last year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them. Russia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months. The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on the Ministry of Defence to draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030. The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked. “There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy. It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy. The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added. None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress. However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer. Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact. In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.

headline: Former Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claims
trail_text: Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
body_text: A former Conservative election candidate has been suspended from the party after he was seemingly filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to “broker” the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links. Jack Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought. Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.” Police in Scotland say they will be reviewing and assessing the Al Jazeera documentary – Contract Killers and the Far Right – for any criminality. Ross is the chief executive of Turning Point UK, a spin-off from the campaign group founded by the murdered US Republican commentator Charlie Kirk. Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, after Kirk’s death. A profile page for Ross on the website of the Bow Group, a Conservative thinktank that lists him as a research fellow, states he has advised MPs and candidates on political and digital strategy. He has been pictured alongside Boris Johnson and other high-profile figures including James Cleverly, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Liam Fox. Ross was reported by Al Jazeera to have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offers to have people killed for money. Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened. Ross replied to this: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.” The Scottish paramilitary contact was then filmed at a London hotel offering to arrange different types of killings, ranging from a hit-and-run that could be made to look like drink-driving to a stabbing. The meeting took place after Ross, apparently acting on behalf of the Zimbabwean government, had reportedly paid thousands of pounds to the Glasgow activist to organise a fake political rally in support of lifting UK sanctions imposed on the African country. Ross said: “I have had a few things and some of the Zims [Zimbabweans] have said to me they want stuff done. They wanted a fucking shooter.” He said he had asked them to talk to the paramilitary, adding: “I said I was not putting fucking prints on anything.” While TPUK was launched as a student movement, it has become increasingly involved in anti-migrant street protests. Its chief operating officer is Nick Tenconi, the leader of the far-right UK Independence party, who visited the Conservative conference in 2022 with Ross. Ross was filmed in 2022 telling an undercover reporter they should chat to him about what they wanted, adding “keep it simple” and then listing the various violent options that could be bought for cash, including murder. A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.” At another point, Ross expressed concerns that journalists could be recording the sort of things he was saying and could pass them to police. “The journalist will put it out there and then the police will pick it up and fuck you,” he said. “You’ve got to think that what we were talking about and had someone film it we’d be fucking done for conspiracy.” Tenconi was filmed alongside Ross as they outlined a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble. Tenconi said: “So let Labour get in. So we build the new right and we have these armies … so, three-pronged. We keep winning MPs over. Then we build the second prong, we build an army, and that’s street demos, protest, just fuck things up, basically.” A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the documentary. It will be reviewed and assessed for any criminality.” Al Jazeera reported that Ross had “completely” denied its investigation’s findings, claiming that everything he said to the undercover reporter was not meant seriously. Ross, who was a local elections candidate for the Conservatives, was approached by the Guardian for comment through TPUK. Tenconi was also approached for comment via his party.

headline: Gas go-ahead ignites oily response from Trump, while speaker seems ready to blow
trail_text: The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sad
body_text: When is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too. There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin. Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current one. Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint. Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash. The speaker was less than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day. For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week. PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality. Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster. By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water. For the rest of PMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget. It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which? That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad. As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour. How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.

headline: Reform UK fined for failing to declare it was publisher of campaigns material
trail_text: Party given additional penalty by Electoral Commission for not paying original fine on time
body_text: Reform UK has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time. Nigel Farage’s party was sanctioned by the Electoral Commission after four items of election material were missing an “imprint” – a declaration of the publisher so voters know who has paid for the promotional message. It was due to pay £1,750 on 23 September, but the fine was increased by a quarter to £2,187 because Reform missed the payment deadline. The penalty was eventually paid on Tuesday. Jackie Killeen, the commission’s director of electoral administration and regulation, said: “The UK’s political finance and imprints laws are there to ensure transparency in both the finances of political parties and the materials produced to influence voters. “As a regulator, we take proportionate action based on the facts and circumstances of each case, as set out in our enforcement policy. We seek to support compliance and deliver transparency, and we will take enforcement action where necessary.” The fine related to three social media accounts run by Reform, on X, Instagram and LinkedIn, that did not have digital imprints between at least November 2025 and January 2026. The party also published an advertisement in the Telegraph in February 2026 without an imprint, promoting its shadow chancellor, Robert Jenrick. The watchdog’s investigation found that the purpose of the advertisement was to promote Reform and its electoral success in the May 2026 elections, so the ad required an imprint. There has also been a separate complaint about the Reform candidate’s election material in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February this year. On that occasion, the party sent out a letter designed to look as if it had been handwritten by the local resident Patricia Clegg, who said she no longer wanted to vote Labour, but who was in fact working for Reform – without including an imprint. The party said it was caused by a printing error, and that the company had accidentally left the imprint off the material. Reform’s censure from the Electoral Commission came as the party said it had reported ITV to the police after the broadcaster’s exposé which revealed racist remarks by members of the party. Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, announced it would also launch a legal challenge against the ITV journalists involved and the broadcaster’s board of directors. The channel’s undercover investigation included footage of Reform councillors and candidates using racist language. In one excerpt, black children were referred to as animals, while in another a Reform member said his area had become infested with Asian families. In a social media video, Yusuf said: “We have reported multiple ITV journalists and their board of directors to the police, and will be taking legal action against all of them. Journalists are supposed to report the news. These ones set out to create it.” He claimed that the undercover ITV reporter who became employed as a Reform press officer had “doctored” her passport to gain the job. He also said two undercover reporters who joined Reform members campaigning in Portsmouth had been reported to the police, as it is illegal to pay someone to canvass for a candidate. An ITV spokesperson said: “ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom broadcasting code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. “All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch, we would fully cooperate.”

headline: Why is Liz Truss trying to be Danny Dyer with her new book?
trail_text: Bank Job, the former prime minister’s forthcoming publication, is about a shady cabal that brought down the bond market. Seemingly she has forgotten that this was her doing
body_text: Name: Liz Truss’s Bank Job. Age: Forthcoming. Appearance: Etiquette dictates that you should never judge a book by its cover. Yes, but do it anyway. It looks like a poster for one of those bad gangster films Danny Dyer used to make, featuring a shadowy set of tough guys – except, instead of Dyer front and centre, there’s Liz Truss. So you’re saying this is a book – by Truss? Yes. The former prime minister’s new book is out next week. Its subtitle is A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government. I have so many questions. Who wouldn’t? The response to her first book, Ten Years to Save the West, didn’t seem to guarantee that she’d get to publish a second. OK, first: how short is short? Amazon states that the book comes in at just 99 pages. For reference, that’s about 13 times shorter than War and Peace, or three times shorter than the 2012 memoir by Tulisa from N-Dubz. Next: who on earth is publishing this? That would be Free Speech Press, which says it is “dedicated to publishing books that challenge conventional thinking”. Its authors include Jennifer Arcuri, who you might remember as that woman who claimed she had an affair with Boris Johnson, and the guy who went viral for saying you can grow concrete. Mike Graham? That’s him. Actually, this is an interesting link: Graham also owns UKLive, the YouTube channel that now hosts Truss’s show. Is that still going? Sadly yes. And by the look of recent videos – which include “Why Britain’s political system is completely broken”, “Britain is becoming a LOW-TRUST society” and “Defund the BBC” – she’s still scratching around the US right’s favourite talking points in the hopes that someone will love her again. What has been the response to the announcement? Are people excited? Well, when Truss announced Bank Job on X, just six days before its publication date, replies variously retitled it as “Bankrupt” and – inevitably – “Lettuce Job”. I suppose we should ask what the book is actually about. It’s the same drum that Truss has been banging since her embarrassment as PM: the country is secretly run by the Bank of England, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility, with this unelected cartel ensuring that Britain will never change. Still, at least it’s nice and short. Exactly – it’s a toilet book, in the sense that it will probably do in a pinch if you run out of Andrex. One last question. Go ahead. The book is about breaking the bond market, and bringing down the government, but … But wasn’t it Truss who did that? Yes, it was her. Do say: “Liz Truss knows who broke the bond market.” Don’t say: “Presumably because Liz Truss owns a mirror.”

headline: Bereaved civil service families could face ‘unjust’ tax bills due to pension scheme delays
trail_text: MPs say ‘chaos’ at Capita-run scheme could mean some claims miss tax-free time limit on lump sum payments
body_text: Bereaved families could face “unconscionable” tax bills because of “chaos” in the civil service pension scheme, the government has been warned. Some lump sum pension payments to families are only tax-free if made within two years of a scheme being told of the member’s death. MPs are now voicing fears that severe delays in the administration of the civil service pension scheme, which is run by the outsourcing company Capita, could push some families over that threshold. They would then be hit with a tax bill calculated at the recipient’s personal rate. The families of more than 1,600 deceased civil servants have been waiting for more than 100 days for their “death in benefit” claim to be processed, according to the latest figures. Some of those have reported struggling to pay bills because of the delay. The Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Commons public accounts committee (PAC), said: “The chaos currently engulfing the civil service pensions scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim.” He added: “It is unconscionable that the families of loyal and dedicated civil servants, who are continuing to suffer through this serious government failing, could potentially face such an unjust financial penalty.” The Cabinet Office, which is responsible for the pension scheme, said it was unable to prevent HM Revenue and Customs from taxing delayed claims, and that affected members would have to claw back the money by taking their case to the Pensions Ombudsman. The ombudsman estimates an 18-month wait to resolve cases because of the volume of complaints from those affected. The PAC has called for a change in legislation to prevent relatives paying the price for administrative delays. The government has already been accused of letting down civil servants and their families by repeatedly outsourcing the 1.7-million-member pension scheme to private companies that failed to deliver. The PAC last year urged ministers to take the scheme in-house after a previous contractor, MyCSP, was blamed for plummeting service levels. However, the £239m contract passed to Capita last December, despite concerns voiced by some that the company was inadequately prepared. The Cabinet Office said it was confident that Capita would offer an improved service. It has since acknowledged that service levels were “unacceptable”. MyCSP and Capita were contacted for a comment. In February, a dedicated email address was set up for unions to escalate cases of severe hardship caused by the delays. The cases referred included claimants at risk of suicide or of losing their homes. Clare Norris has been waiting 11 months for the death benefit and pension payments she is due after her husband died last November. “I was petrified – I am 52 and early death was not part of our financial plan,” she said. “Losing your partner is one of the most difficult experiences anyone can go through. The lack of clarity, communication and basic administrative handling from Civil Service Pensions has made it considerably worse.” Capita said her case would be progressed under a new process. “It remains a high priority and the member can expect to hear on next steps as soon as possible.” Under HMRC rules, in cases in which someone dies under the age of 75, tax-free lump sum payments must be made within two years, otherwise they will be taxed at the recipient’s marginal rate of tax. The Cabinet Office said it was committed to ensuring scheme members were not left out of pocket. “We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure individuals do not experience delays,” said a spokesperson. “If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses.”

headline: Streeting delays defence jobs plan for young people after union pushback
trail_text: UK defence secretary had been due to unveil proposals on Thursday until concerns were raised at 11th hour
body_text: Wes Streeting has been forced to delay the publication of a plan to get more young people into defence industry jobs after pushback from trade unions, the Guardian understands. The defence secretary had been due to announce the proposals on Thursday, but some unions in the sector are understood to have reacted angrily to the plans, accusing the government of bypassing their members and minimising their roles in job creation. The delay risks derailing a planned series of government announcements to tackle the youth jobs crisis, with ministers stating on Monday that jobs plans in business services, construction, technology and defence would be published this week. Streeting is expected to visit Telford on Thursday to unveil a major new gun production facility run by German defence giant Rheinmetall, after promising that the defence jobs plan would “help deliver thousands of opportunities for young people, including an increase in the number of people supported through apprenticeship programmes in the defence sector to at least 14,000 annually by 2035”. But the Guardian understands that unions representing workers in the sector were shown the plan just before publication, and told ministers that they would not support it, forcing the 11th-hour delay. Sources at the Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed the delay, but played down the role of unions in the hold-up, stating there were issues that still had to be worked through, but that it would be published “in due course”. Union leaders are understood to have told ministers that the plan was weak and did not acknowledge the role of unions in promoting “build British” defence policies and the creation of jobs for young people, especially apprentices. Further meetings between the ministers and union representatives are “imminent”, said one source. “Wes Streeting has to recognise that unions have a vital role to play in developing good jobs in the defence industry, but this plan lacked a union voice and the voice of workers who are meant to be at the heart of it,” said a union source. “Any union representing people in this industry can see that this plan doesn’t do the job, and they will have to go back to the drawing board.” A MoD source said that the department had a positive relationship with the affected unions, and downplayed reports of a rift. “This department is looking to create thousands of jobs in defence and a comprehensive plan will be published in due course.” A spokesperson for the MoD said: “The defence jobs plan continues to be developed and will be published when ready. We work closely with trade unions and are committed to our mission to create thousands of well-paid, unionised defence jobs in every part of the country.” The delay will come as a blow for Streeting, who last month said he was overseeing a “ministry for growth”, adding that he was determined the defence industry should play its part in tackling what he called the “moral emergency” of almost 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet). Labour, which is coming under increasing pressure to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, has been keen to demonstrate that the rapid increase in spending will result in jobs in the UK. Last month defence contractors promised to create 40,000 apprenticeships, work experience placements and jobs for young people each year. “I think we have a responsibility, as we’re investing more in the defence of the realm, to do so in a way that boosts British jobs, British industry, and helps to deal with this moral emergency,” said Streeting at the time. “I want the Ministry of Defence to be a ministry of growth and a ministry of opportunity, and that’s how we’re going to direct our defence spending.” The defence jobs plan was due to be published before the publication of former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn’s final report on Neets, which is now expected next month after a delay. Reacting to the pledge made by defence industry players last month, Milburn said the industry had shown “what is possible when employers step up,” adding: “Defence is one of our great industries – it has both the scale and the opportunity to give young people the experience, skills and confidence they need to build a career.”

headline: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations
trail_text: Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m
body_text: A senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backers Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo would be legal under the proposed new foreign donors cap three months before they gave £72m to the party. James Orr, who was then Reform UK’s head of policy and a Cambridge professor, discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim. A reporter was posing as a potential donor when Orr talked to him about “filling the war chest in anticipation” of tougher donations rules, describing it as the establishment trying to “kneecap” the party. Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after Channel 4 broadcast some of Verbatim’s undercover filming in which he appeared to discuss ways to get around funding laws to allow donations from a US-based donor. The matter is under police investigation and he remains suspended, although Reform has released its own report clearing Orr and another official of wrongdoing. The new footage has been shared with the Guardian after a public debate about whether the two £36m donations from Harborne and Delo to Reform UK will be allowed under the cap. The party maintains the donations are legal, pointing out that the retrospective overseas donor cap has not yet been passed into law. In the footage, recorded in July this year, Orr expressed doubt about whether Delo and Harborne would still be able to donate given that, when it does become law, the £100,000 overseas donor cap is to cover party donations dating back to March this year. Orr believed Delo would probably meet the residency test as long as he was not required to have been a tax resident, in which case he would be “stuffed”. He said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge” in terms of avoiding the overseas cap and he “can’t do anything for 12 months” after moving back. Harborne had been living in Thailand until he registered to vote in Hampshire this summer, and Delo has long been resident in Hong Kong, though he has been on the UK domestic register for some years. The new law will limit overseas donors to giving £100,000 a year to a political party. It will apply to donations made after March 2026, and will require any domestic donor who wants to give more than £100,000 to have been resident in the UK for at least a year. In the discussion, Orr was recorded as saying the party was too reliant on Harborne and Delo as “two big whales”. He said the new law was “a retrospective law, which is unheard of. So, we’re going to challenge it in the courts.” Orr added: “We’ll push it through judicial review. And then … so, we’ll have a big fight. But, yeah, the last few days we’ve been working hard on just filling the war chest as best we can, in anticipation of something quite brutal.” On whether the two men would be caught by the overseas cap, he said: “I mean, there’s going to be a huge fight over that. But Ben, I think it’s probably OK, because I think he is … it depends on how they legislate it, they might just say, you must have been tax domiciled here for X period of time, in which case Ben is stuffed.” Orr went on to say: “It depends what … test for moving back you apply. So, under the common law, there’s a two-limb test, which is actually quite a – not a stringent one. It’s a factual thing, a factual matrix test. “How much time you spend in England, do you have a house here, can you vote, do you have any bills that you pay, you know, it’s quite kind of, it’s not tax … So, on that test, Ben meets it, I think. And then the second then is intention. Do you intend to stay, so, evidence that you intend to stay …” Having debated whether Delo would meet the test, Orr said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge”. The Reform official said he would move back to the UK. “But, if he does move back, there’s 12 – he can’t pay – he can’t do anything for 12 months. And, it looks as if they will bring that in.” In his chat with the undercover reporter, Orr also referred to the “complicated backstory” of Delo, a British-born billionaire who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business. He was later pardoned by Donald Trump. Orr also spoke about having spent time on a boat with Ben Delo in the Peloponnese this summer, talking of mixing work and a holiday in Greece, saying: “We went from Athens down to Ben’s boat in Porto Cheli.” Lawyers for Delo said he did not own a yacht. A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back.” Orr did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to electoral laws on overseas funding and dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”. Lawyers for Harborne described Orr’s comments as private speculation that would not be appropriate to comment on and did not represent established facts. Delo’s lawyers did not respond substantively, saying he would not be drawn into speculation about a conversation he was not party to, or the legal effect of a law yet to be passed. They later added that he had taken extensive legal advice on his donations and had previously set out his rationale for making them. Reform has previously said it intends to take legal action against Verbatim and its directors over the undercover filming.

headline: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
trail_text: RAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for Riyadh
byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
body_text: RAF Typhoon fighters are to be used in efforts to protect Saudi Arabia from attack by Yemen’s Houthis, flying protective missions over the country’s cities and critical infrastructure as western allies increase their intervention in the escalating conflict. The operation – the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister – will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, which attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities. The Ministry of Defence emphasised that the role of the fighters – whose number was not stated – would be limited. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis,” it said. An offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen that began in September has gradually escalated into a deadly regional conflict. This month the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia, the backer of Yemen’s officially recognised government. Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, the deadliest incident since September in a war that has claimed 19 lives in Saudi Arabia so far. Dozens more have been killed in Yemen by the surge in fighting. The death toll from Monday’s Houthi missile strike on a Yemeni government training camp has risen to 73, a brutal demonstration of the rebel group’s military effectiveness. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said in a TV interview the UK had agreed to help Saudi Arabia to counter the “outrageous Houthi escalation that we’ve seen in recent weeks” and said the UK was “responding to protect civilians” from attack. HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, speculated that the UK could get drawn further into the conflict in the future, asking: “What does defensive mean?” He asked what the RAF would do if a Houthi attack happened on a Saudi ship in the Red Sea and the British were in a position to stop it. “The UK might say it was defensive but the Houthis would see it as offensive,” he said. Streeting, however, said that the fighter jets’ remit was narrow. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles,” he said. Military advisers said the UK would also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft capable of transporting heavy equipment, in addition to an existing commitment to supply air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets with an RAF Voyager. The refuelling mission has been extended by 90 days. The UK has long been a military ally of Saudi Arabia: BAE Systems has supplied it with 72 Typhoons in a deal originally worth £4.4bn. Riyadh has been considering buying another 48 in a negotiation that has dragged on for years. Though the UK only had a limited involvement in the US-Israel war against Iran, Typhoons from the RAF airbase in Akrotiri, Cyprus, and in Qatar, flew defensive missions in the spring and summer to shoot down missiles and drones launched by Iran and other proxies against Gulf states. Britain’s announcement came a few days after Streeting visited his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where they discussed how to respond to the Houthi escalation amongst other issues. The US has so far stepped up its intelligence support and sent more than 100 military advisers to help the Saudis with targeting, but it has been cautious about providing more direct military support. Donald Trump urged Riyadh on Friday to accept help from Israel, though it was unclear what was on offer. The White House has been trying to de-escalate against Iran and in the Middle Eastbefore US midterm elections in November and with the oil price over $100 a barrel. The US envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, told a conference in Qatar that sending in ground troops against the Houthis “seems fruitless”. The Saudi strategy for dealing with the Houthis, who have been gaining territory along the Red Sea coast, remains unclear. “Allies would be happy to help the Saudis, but they have not been very good at explaining what they want,” said Hellyer. He suggested UK military support could help free up the Saudi military to step up direct attacks on the Houthis, though in the past the Saudi air force has been accused of using UK- and US-made weapons in indiscriminate bombing. Amid some concern that the UK risks being seen as closely aligned to the unpopular US war on Iran, the military intervention was partly justified because instability in the Middle East was driving up energy prices and affecting the cost of living.

headline: Nige seems tired and bored of himself as Kemi conjures a telepathic budget
trail_text: The Tory leader has glimpsed the future and it involves Labour putting every last UK citizen on benefits
body_text: If you’re worried about next week’s budget, then now is your time to chill out. Because Kemi Badenoch has all the answers. The chancellor, John Healey, has been living rent free in the leader of the opposition’s head for the past few weeks. Lucky man. More than that, she has been perched on his shoulder while he sits at his desk in the Treasury and tries to make the sums add up. And – SPOILER ALERT – Kemi has now read the whole speech that hasn’t yet been written and is in a position to give her budget reply more than a week ahead of time. Opposition by telepathy. Or wish fulfilment. If things don’t work out for her in her current job she could apply to be the next Mystic Meg. In a plush room in Westminster on a wet Tuesday morning, Kemi was giving her verdict in front of an adoring crowd of invited Tory members. They cheered every word. Which was kind. Because she won’t be getting that kind of reception next week. Nobody could be worse than Rachel Reeves, she began. Rachel had been the She-Devil who had implemented £70bn of tax rises. But wait. There was someone worse than Reeves. And that was Healey. Logic is not Kemi’s strongest point. No matter. Healey would be worse because he would do less. Fiscal dialecticism. Yup, the chancellor was going to stand up for an hour and say absolutely nothing. Make no changes to anything. This didn’t seem very likely, but we had to take it on trust. Kemi was John Healey’s brain. And Healey doing nothing was worse than Rachel doing something. It sounded as if Kemi rather missed the tax rises after all. But she had a further warning. The Marxist International Monetary Fund were completely wrong to praise the government for its efforts to reduce the deficit. At best, they had been duped by Healey, at worst they were trying to bankrupt the country. Here’s what was going to happen. Labour were going to introduce some fictional cuts to benefits that would never be implemented. Because deep down what Labour MPs really wanted was for everyone to live in a country where they could pick up £80,000 a year in benefits. The sign of a functioning nirvana was a world where everyone could be paid not to work. It didn’t seem to have occurred to Kemi that the reason the benefits bill was so high was primarily because the Conservative government in which she had served had increased them substantially during her time in office. And also because many benefits, such as pensions, she was unwilling to cut herself. Labour was doing the wrong things for the wrong reasons, she said. This opened up several philosophical lines of inquiry. Ontologically speaking, was it better to do the wrong things for the right reasons, even if the results were the same? Or what happened if you did the right things for the wrong reasons? Would you then have to negate everything regardless of the outcomes? It turned out that I wasn’t the only one struggling with Kemi’s reasoning. When it came to the questions from the media, several reporters wondered why, if the welfare cuts that she was proposing were so easy to make, previous Tory governments hadn’t got round to making them earlier. And was it just our imagination, or were the same cuts being used to pay for several different items on the country’s balance sheet? Kemi didn’t miss a beat. The cuts she was proposing were the ones Rishi Sunak would have made if he hadn’t been interrupted by the general election that he himself called. It was all very unfortunate. The Tories had been on the brink of success and if only they had had another couple of weeks, everything would have been hunky dory. Tax breaks for the wealthy and benefits cuts for those that need them, that was the Tory way. Then the reverse ferret. Although she had been in previous Conservative governments, she had never inhaled. She had kept her fingers crossed and her mouth shut. Previous prime ministers had taken wrong steps. But sometimes the bravest thing a cabinet minister can do is to do and say nothing. And no one had been braver than Kemi. “In case you hadn’t noticed,” she said patronisingly to one journalist, “we are under new management.” Only it feels very much like the old management. Kemi was still saying nothing her predecessors wouldn’t have said. It was just one of life’s sadnesses that the scales had only fallen from her eyes when the Tories had been booted out of office. Down in Plymouth, Reform was regrouping after yet another weekend of bad headlines. And the party members who had assembled for the rally didn’t look entirely enthused when the first person sent on stage to act as cheerleader was the charisma-free Danny Kruger. The man who is meant to act as the brains of the party, despite appearing spectacularly dim. “I don’t want to whine,” he said, before going on to do just that. The ITV exposé was just a bit unfortunate, he went on, because he was sure most Reform supporters weren’t racist. “There is no room for that kind of behaviour in the party.” Some of the audience looked a bit disappointed by that. They thought they had been guaranteed a welcome. After a brief and entirely forgettable number from Honest Bob Jenrick – even Reform members think he seems a wrong ’un – out came Nigel Farage. He seemed like a man with the cares of the world on his shoulders. A man who could sense the tide was going out. There was no energy about him as he rolled through a collection of his greatest hits. Forgetting where he was, he even called Plymouth, Portsmouth. That drew a few boos. People like to think they matter a little bit. Nige was just tired and bored of himself. Disappointed with a world that had promised him so much and was now crumbling before him. Hell, why hadn’t the riots even spread to this country? Then he could blame lefties and foreigners. He tried to pass off the stories of racism and financial unorthodoxy as just one offs. Every self-respecting party has a few racists. He didn’t sound as if he believed a word of it. And ITV had exposed a 70% hit rate of undesirables. Those aren’t outliers. Come the end, Nige couldn’t wait to see the back of Portsmouth. Or wherever he was. And it felt as though for much of the audience the feeling was entirely mutual. • On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s year in review event.
