headline: Ex-Greens co-leader urges council groups to reject Zionism policy
trail_text: Exclusive: Adrian Ramsay calls conference motion a distraction and says councillors should maintain coalitions where possible
body_text: Adrian Ramsay, the former co-leader of the Greens, has urged his party’s councillors to reject the newly adopted “Zionism is racism” motion if it will help them stay in power in local government, in a fresh sign of internal dissent over the policy. Ramsay, one of the Greens’ five MPs, said he was pleased that a number of Green council groups had already condemned the policy, which was adopted at the party’s conference and also calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel. Last week, Labour ordered its local parties who share power on councils with Greens to terminate the deals if the local Greens did not disown the policy motion. In a statement to the Guardian, Ramsay, who co-led the Greens in England and Wales for four years until Zack Polanski took over last year, said that while he understood why Green groups might not want to be “bullied” into action by Labour, it was important for them to be clear about the motion and to maintain coalitions where possible. Ramsay expressed his opposition to the motion before the vote at the party conference earlier this month but had subsequently not commented. Such a public call to Green councillors places him at odds with Polanski, who has said he will not seek to overturn the motion, and with the official party line, which stated that the Greens will “not take lectures” from a Labour government that supplies arms to Israel. A series of Green council groups or councillors within them who share power with Labour have already rejected the motion, including Lewes, Warwick, and Rother. Among other groups to have disowned the policy are the Greens in Southwark, who did so to maintain a coalition with the Liberal Democrats. Ramsay said such groups “have been brave in speaking out about such a contentious motion”. He said: “They have supported the Green party’s strong position of calling out the ethnic cleansing and war crimes in Gaza and how this must be combined with upholding the right of both Palestinians and Israelis to statehood and self-determination. Calling out a genocide is more important than debating definitions of Zionism.” Ramsay said his advice to other groups still deciding was to make their opposition to the motion clear if that was what they believed, saying it would “reassure a lot of people in your communities, and it will enable you to continue making a real difference for your residents”. He said Labour’s ultimatum about the policy was “entirely predictable” and it was understandable that Green councillors “don’t want to be bullied into making a statement by a diktat from the national Labour party which has been served on local Labour groups”. It would, however, “be incredibly sad to see joint council administrations fold because of this – especially as the alternative will often be a rightwing coalition that could see services put at risk”, he argued. Green-run or jointly run councils were making a real difference, Ramsay said. “We can’t let this be undermined by a party conference motion which is a distraction from this work, and which I am confident is not supported by most party members.” Speaking to the BBC on Sunday, Polanski defended the motion and said the policy would stand for at least two years, given party rules, but he wanted to amend it to remove the call for a single Palestinian state. He said: “I’m not going to try and overturn it. At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it.”

headline: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water
trail_text: Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control
byline: Kiran Stacey, Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot
body_text: Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility. One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run. Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both. Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court. One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes. “There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said. Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer. Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control. Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies and could rewrite how the bankruptcy regime works for the industry. Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future. But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems. When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR. Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary, made clear her opposition to such a plan before Burnham became prime minister. Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running. Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash. While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright. The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors. Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.” The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company. Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors. Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for Thames Water before it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas. “An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.” Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone. “While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”

headline: ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples
trail_text: While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it
body_text: It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic. Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear. The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags. Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires. The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet. Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants. It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim. Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed. Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war. All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war. Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her? • On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s year in review event. headline: Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’
trail_text: In now-removed post, Miatta Fahnbulleh criticised home secretary’s proposal to extend qualifying period for settlement in UK
body_text: The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration. Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views. In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents. The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers. The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes. Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”. Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”. “I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added. With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions. “I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said. “I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.” In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.” She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion. “We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”

headline: We need to stop disinformation in UK political adverts. Here’s a chance to do so
trail_text: Letters: Alex Tait on a proposed amendment to the representation of the people bill, and Dr Joseph Mullen on Russian interference in the Brexit referendum
body_text: Andy Burnham’s comments about Russian interference in Brexit (Report, 11 October) and the warning by the MI5 chief, Ken McCallum, against exaggerating its impact (Report, 13 October) risk overlooking another serious threat to electoral integrity: disinformation from our own political parties and campaigners. Foreign interference deserves scrutiny, but misleading factual claims in electoral advertising are unregulated, unlike in commercial advertising. We have four sets of rules to ensure an advert for a packet of sausages is accurate, but none for the most important advertising of all – ads that influence how we vote. With our fragmented five-party politics producing increasingly close elections, misleading advertising can be decisive. Brexit was decided by a 51.9%-48.1% vote split. Our research into May’s local elections found that 41.4% of wards in England were won by margins of less than 5%, with nine decided by a single vote. We also identified misleading electoral advertising in some of the closest contests. Regulating factual claims in electoral advertising was a key recommendation of the House of Lords select committee on democracy and digital technologies in 2020. The representation of the people bill, currently going through parliament, offers an opportunity to act. An amendment covering the same scope attracted 37 MPs as sponsors in the Commons, and we are working with peers in the Lords to take it forward. Burnham signed up to our voluntary code for honest electoral advertising in 2024, which forms part of the proposed amendments. We should tackle foreign interference, but we can’t continue to ignore the disinformation put out by our own political parties. Alex Tait Reform Political Advertising • The head of MI5 confirming that Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum is highly significant to the result. The vote share achieved by the leave campaign was 51.9%, as against 48.1% for the remainers. This was a majority of just 3.8%. If Russian interference swayed just 2% of voting intentions, this would erode the much-vaunted majority of the leave group, and remainers would emerge as victors. MI5 should carry out an impact assessment of Russian interference using the most up-to-date AI, and attempt to quantify shifts in voting patterns. This would go a long way towards introducing a new referendum. Dr Joseph Mullen Former senior lecturer, University of Manchester • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
trail_text: Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security
body_text: Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides. The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics. The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes. The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules. Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.” Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter. “That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident. The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead. After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.” The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.” “I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit. “That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.” The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”. Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.” If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax. Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade. An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing. Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”. The timeline for the gift is disputed. Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024. According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP. The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election. Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted. A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit. Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.” They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.

headline: Hywel Lloyd obituary
trail_text: Other lives: Public policy consultant on sustainability who led Labour’s campaign to get elected in rural and coastal areas
body_text: My friend and colleague Hywel Lloyd, who has died aged 61 of a cardiac arrest, was a public policy consultant and Labour party activist with a strong conviction that radical environmentalism should be at the heart of a progressive agenda. Unconventional, energetic and extraordinarily well connected, he brought together people across Westminster, local government and the green movement around a common campaign. He started work in disability employment and public services, before becoming a senior fellow in 2001 at the management consultancy Office for Public Management. Between 2007 and 2010, he was a specialist policy adviser to cabinet ministers – first to Hazel Blears, at the Department for Communities and Local Government, and then from 2009 to Hilary Benn at Defra – overseeing policy on energy, planning, the low carbon built environment, land use, waste and resources. He then returned to OPM for a period, and later worked at the Institute for Public Policy Research, as well as establishing in 2012 his own consultancy, Facilitating the Future, where he continued his work on energy and sustainability. Hywel was always brimming with ideas – some brilliant, some decidedly wacky. To highlight the importance of nature, he offered apples to ministers to persuade them to make Apple Day in October a bank holiday, and organised for Ed Miliband, when Labour party leader, to send a sapling to the Prince and Princess of Wales on the birth of their son George. His biggest mission was to make Labour a party for the whole country. After the election defeat in 2010, Hywel, Jim Knight and others established Labour Coast & Country, determined that Labour did not retreat into an urban comfort zone. For more than a decade, he built the organisation into a formidable campaigning force for rural and coastal communities, and the 2024 landslide victory vindicated this relentless work, with record numbers of coastal and rural seats backing Labour, including the Kent constituency of East Thanet, where I was elected MP. Hywel was born in Southampton to Marlene (nee Lydford), a short-hand typist and homemaker, and Gareth Lloyd, an electronics engineer. He went to King Edward VI school in the city before going on to study chemistry at the University of Bath, where he also became president of Bath Students’ Union in 1987. His first job was working for the RNID, the national hearing loss charity. While he was skilled cross-party coalition builder, he was also a committed campaigner, knocking on doors and organising events. He stood as Labour’s parliamentary candidate for Westminster in 2005, having previously sought selection in Tooting (losing out to Sadiq Khan) and in Torfaen, south Wales. Hywel spent weekends chopping and planting in friends’ woodlands, building enormous bonfires, and hiking across Wales and Scotland. For him, Britain’s landscapes were treasures to be cared for. He gave colleagues saplings as gifts, sometimes lugging them hundreds of miles on public transport. He loved rugby and was very proud of his Welsh roots, following Wales and the British & Irish Lions with great fervour. For many years his partner was Janey, and they remained good friends. He is survived by his brother, Stuart, and his nephews, Ben and Harry.

headline: Andy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport
trail_text: Passengers urged to ‘share the carriage, not the noise’ as guidance sets out £100 penalties for nuisance behaviour
body_text: Andy Burnham has announced a crackdown on “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on public transport, as he extends his promise to give voters “breathing space” in the confines of a train carriage. The prime minister will unveil a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport on Monday, alongside guidance allowing local transport authorities to levy fines of up to £100 for non-compliance. The move makes him the latest senior politician to promise action against people who play videos or music out loud in public spaces, something that about 60% of voters back. Burnham said in a statement: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey. “So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses. “It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.” Under the plan, ministers will issue guidance to local transport authorities in England advising them on how they should use new powers granted under the Bus Services Act, which allows them to set and enforce their own rules on board. The guidance will say authorities should issue fines of up to £100 if bus passengers refuse to comply with a request to stop certain nuisance behaviour. Officials said drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules. That job would be left to transport safety officers or police officers. Train operating companies already have the power to issue fines of up to £1,000 for similar behaviour. Alongside the new powers, the government is launching a poster campaign to discourage people from playing videos or music on their phones out loud on public transport. Under the slogan “share the carriage, not the noise”, passengers will be encouraged to use headphones, avoid making calls on speakerphone and watch videos quietly. The campaign makes Burnham the latest in a series of politicians to promise to tackle headphone dodgers. The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, unveiled a campaign in the summer urging passengers to “travel kind”, including by wearing headphones. The Liberal Democrats have called for bus travellers to face £1,000 fines as well as those on trains. The scramble for politicians to react comes as polls show noise on public transport is a major annoyance for British people. A recent poll by YouGov found voters would back £1,000 fines for people playing music out loud on buses and trains. A separate survey by the same company found that voters listed people talking on speakerphones as one of their top three irritants. Unions, however, said the new enforcement regime would do little to protect transport workers. The general secretary of Unite, Sharon Graham, said: “The government’s proposals are well-meaning but wholly inadequate to tackle the challenges and violence bus workers are facing on a daily basis. The proposed penalties are not going to deal with the issues facing workers.” • This article was amended on 19 October 2026 to add text clarifying that the Bus Services Act applies in England only.

headline: Zack Polanski says application of Zionism is racist and no state has right to exist
trail_text: Green leader in England and Wales calls ‘debates about words’ unhelpful and denies recent motion was controversial
body_text: Zack Polanski has said Zionism in its current form is racist, that no country has a right to exist, and that the Green party motion on the issue was not controversial. The leader of the Green party in England and Wales gave an unapologetic interview to the BBC on Sunday two weeks after his party approved a motion equating Zionism with racism. Polanski did not attend the vote, prompting accusations of a lack of leadership, but he made clear he agreed with the broad thrust of it even if he felt it was unhelpful to have what he called a “debate about semantics”. Asked by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg whether he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said: “I don’t think this is actually controversial. “What’s controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years, including more child amputees than ever in modern history. So when you take that to account, the fact that they’re being murdered because they’re Palestinian – that’s very obviously a racist ideology.” He added: “I think Zionism is racism in the practical application of it. Now the conference had a debate about the motion, about the word. I said I think debates about words are unhelpful, and I still think that.” Asked whether he believed Israel had a right to exist, Polanski, who is Jewish, said: “I don’t think any state has a right to exist under international law,” adding that the idea of a two-state solution was “for the birds” given Israel’s opposition to it. He also insisted he had no regrets about the way he had handled the recent controversy, despite criticism from some prominent Jewish Green members, including Vivien Lichtenstein, the chair of the Jewish Greens. Polanski said: “I’m not sorry at all. Vivien is someone I’ve had respect for and do have respect for, and partly co-founded the Jewish Greens together … Actually, when the Jewish Greens were surveyed about this motion, a majority supported it.” In response, Lichtenstein later said: “Zack should have joined conference online, listened to the speeches for and against and, crucially, spoken for those amendments he supported, then voted. “None of that took an inordinate amount of time. There was no excuse for his not participating.” She also said polling of Jewish greens on the Zionism motion showed they were evenly split, contrary to Polanski’s claims. Polanski’s defiant interview comes after the most difficult two weeks of his leadership of the party since he took over last September, during which he has endured the fallout from the conference vote and lost the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. His strategy of shifting his party to the left, focusing on economically populist ideas and leaning into debates on Palestine and Gaza initially paid dividends, with the party jumping from about 10% in the polls to 18% earlier this year. In recent months, however, the party has tumbled, beset by questions over his tax affairs, a public spat with the police after the Golders Green attack and the recent row over Zionism. He said on Sunday that he was confident voters would return to his party once they had seen more of Andy Burnham’s leadership of the country. “People more and more will see from Andy Burnham a change in rhetoric, but not a change in action, and know the Green party have been right all along,” he said.

headline: Police investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himself
trail_text: Female colleague says she was forced out shortly after incident with Luke Campbell, Hull and East Yorkshire mayor
byline: Josh Halliday North of England editor
body_text: A Reform UK mayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff. Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion and the mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police earlier this month. In an incident first reported by the Observer on Sunday, Campbell allegedly showed a senior female colleague four fully naked and sexualised images of himself in May. The woman said she had felt “shocked, embarrassed and humiliated” and claimed she had been forced out of her job soon after, according to documents submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure at Hull and East Yorkshire combined authority (Heyca). Campbell, who was elected last May, has not responded to requests to comment. It is understood that he has not been arrested in relation to the allegations, which Reform UK has said he “firmly denies”. A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Luke firmly denies the allegations. They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute.” The allegations against Campbell came to light after a year-long ITV investigation uncovered racist comments from a number of Reform UK councillors and a prospective MP. An aspiring Reform UK MP was suspended after telling an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers crossing the English channel should be put in “concentration camps”, in footage due to be broadcast on Sunday night. Nigel Farage’s party said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding that there was “no room for racism” in the party. Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative minister and now a Reform UK member, came to Campbell’s defence on Sunday by claiming that the “sexualised” image was in fact a 2013 magazine cover showing the former boxer posing naked from the waist up after he won gold at the 2012 London Olympics. However, that appears to be at odds with witness testimony submitted as part of an internal grievance procedure at Heyca, where Campbell is mayor. In one document, corroborated by the Guardian, a senior female colleague said Campbell had called her over to a computer screen, where she was shown “several naked and sexualised images” of the mayor. A separate witness said they saw a naked man with a tattoo in one of the images, whereas no tattoo is visible on the magazine front cover. The main complainant said in a witness statement: “I was deliberately exposed to naked and sexualised images involving the mayor in the workplace, without my consent, and was laughed at when I was visibly embarrassed. “In my view, this was unwanted conduct of a sexual nature which violated my dignity and created a humiliating, degrading and offensive working environment.” About three weeks after the alleged incident, the female officer, who was working as a contractor but had accepted the offer of a permanent role, was allegedly told on a Teams call that the offer had been withdrawn. In a separate document, a second colleague said they had felt “uneasy” after allegedly seeing Campbell and two male colleagues ushering over a female officer to look at his laptop, which showed an image of a naked man with a tattoo. The Guardian understands that this second employee recalled comments then being made about Campbell’s tattoo and that they saw the mayor lift his shirt to show the tattoo. A spokesperson for Heyca confirmed to the Observer that a police investigation was under way. He said: “As with all public authorities, the combined authority has a standards process that can be engaged to deal with complaints about members and a complaints procedure that can be used to deal with complaints about officers. “The standards process and the complaints procedure must be carried out in a fair and independent manner.” Humberside police has been contacted for comment.

headline: ‘Damp squib’: Ed Davey can breathe easy as Lib Dem leadership challenge fails to materialise
trail_text: Lengthy meeting heard grumbles about ‘blue wall’ policies and ‘Ming vase’ tactics but no real rancour
body_text: As political showdowns go, this week’s gathering of Liberal Democrat MPs, billed by some as a crunch moment for Ed Davey, was a touch underwhelming. “I had expected a damp squib,” one attender put it. “It was damper than I thought.” Far from generating a mass of opposition to Davey’s leadership, let alone a formal challenge to his position, the lengthy gathering in a Commons committee room on Tuesday evening brought a few minor grumbles, but little else. “My main feeling was a sort of irritation that we were forced to sit through this very long meeting, one where in the main we all aggressively agreed with each other,” another MP put it. This is not, however, the entire story. There is disquiet with Davey’s patient and sometimes cautious leadership style, as shown most dramatically by the sudden resignation a week ago of Charlie Maynard, the number two in the party’s Treasury team, over concerns the Lib Dems were failing to cut through with voters. If Maynard hoped to spark a wider revolt, it did not happen. “It felt like he was trying to light the touchpaper, but it fizzled out instead of exploding,” one MP said. Another was more blunt: “Charlie really has fucked it up. He has zero political nous.” The situation nonetheless remains tricky. Davey led the Lib Dems to a century-best performance in the 2024 election, winning 72 MPs, and is safe for the foreseeable future. That said, frustrations that were already bubbling up before September’s party conference have arguably become more acute since. This is largely the result of the two policy decisions set out by Davey at the conference: a promise of £17bn in income tax cuts if the party is elected, and support for the pensions triple lock, just as Andy Burnham pledged to change it. Both chimed explicitly with Lib Dem efforts to build momentum in the so-called blue wall of affluent home counties constituencies where the party made big gains from the Conservatives in 2024. While just about every Lib Dem MP agrees that protecting these seats and potentially winning more is vital, some worry that Davey is being so careful to not alienate former Tory voters that any distinctively liberal message has been lost. “Making us the party of tax cuts just jarred with activists,” one MP said. “It’s not that we don’t want taxes cut, it’s just that the overt positioning felt incredibly blue wall-y. It’s like we are aping the Conservatives, while they are aping Reform.” They added: “There are levels of nuance here. Ed will be given time to make changes. But there are a lot of unhappy people in the party at the moment, and not just MPs. “Charlie Maynard didn’t help. Now we have to rally around the leader, do all the Operation Big Dog stuff, and we haven’t addressed the issues about who we actually are.” Supporters of Davey argue that he is listening, but also point to the lessons of the 2019 election, when the party had a very clear national message – stop Brexit – but won just 12 seats, with a vote total higher than 2024’s but spread too thinly. “Ed was very clear in the meeting that he understands people’s frustrations,” an MP said. “There are some legitimate grievances. But he has enormous credit built up, and people are prepared to give him the time he needs to make the changes he needs to make.” Thus far, public opposition has come from only a handful of people, also including another MP, Tom Gordon, who called Davey’s argument that the triple lock needed to be saved to protect the pensions of people currently in their 40s “downright insulting”. Some MPs are privately unimpressed by what they view as performative complaints from, as one put it, a “small minority who feel the world fails to recognise their staggering genius”. Another said: “The plea, particularly among colleagues with small majorities, is: please think when you do these things, as it undermines us.” Another factor protecting Davey is the absence of a plan for what would come next. There are ambitious and capable MPs in the 2024 intake, but they lack experience. If Davey was ousted, a leading contender would be Daisy Cooper, his deputy and Treasury spokesperson – who some Lib Dems feel shares the same cautious approach. One MP said: “A lot of people are terrified of a Daisy leadership – it’s the main reason why Ed is still in place. It is politely phrased as a ‘lack of a viable alternative’.” For now, it seems, the party will maintain its own version of Labour’s “Ming vase” tactic – trying to remain sufficiently benign and unobjectionable to hoover up enough tactical votes to gain more MPs, and then perhaps support a Labour government on the condition it introduces the Lib Dem holy grail of a proportional election system. “That’s the big plan: win the seats to deliver PR and then we can be liberals,” one MP said. “But that relies on a lot of things going right.” There is worry, and some disagreement. But as yet, no real rancour. “Some of this is just the usual mid-parliament blues, which the 2024 intake have never experienced,” one senior party figure said. “We are still small enough that we can have individual conversations to sort things out. And we don’t do drama. So there will be no implosion. Just some soul searching.”

headline: Aspiring Reform MP who said ‘you cannot be Muslim and British’ suspended
trail_text: Jason Powell also backed concentration camps as Reform councillors talk of executing grooming gang members
body_text: An aspiring Reform UK MP who advocated the use of concentration camps and said “you cannot be Muslim and British” has been suspended from the party. The activist is one of a number featured in an ITV documentary, which will be broadcast in full on Sunday night and has already resulted in fresh questions about Reform’s vetting process. The year-long investigation included undercover filming at an event referred to as Farage Fest, which was thrown by the party to thank volunteers who helped Nigel Farage get re-elected as the MP for Clacton during the recent byelection. Those attending included Jason Powell, who said he had passed vetting checks to become a Reform parliamentary candidate, and who was recorded as saying: “Anyone who comes across on a boat, as an example, in the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there. “And that’s the first, the very first day … They just need to be rounded up, every single last one of them, and sent to those concentration camps, and then be given an ultimatum. Where are you from? Because you’re going back there. If you don’t tell us, you’re staying here for the rest of your life.” Powell was also recorded as saying that he was “pretty hardline about Islam as well”, adding: “I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, Zia Yusuf [Reform’s home affairs spokesperson] is a Muslim. To me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.” However, Reform has said that two other party figures who were elected as councillors in London and were recorded advocating the mass shooting of grooming gang members were not under investigation. Adam Parkins was recorded as saying that if he was prime minister he “would quite happily do Sunday morning rose garden executions”. David Kerr, a colleague of Parkins on Hounslow council in west London, said: “When it comes to like, yeah, grooming gang perpetrators, like, yeah dude, we just fucking line them up on the wall … line up a few thousand grooming gang perpetrators and machine gun them down.” Kerr and Parkins have been approached for comment. Powell later told ITV that his views were those of British people in general and are not extremist. The Muslim Council of Britain, the UK’s largest Muslim umbrella group, said the suspension of Reform members meant very little given that other cases suggested people were sometimes quietly let back in again weeks later. “The leadership of Reform UK must take full responsibility for the culture of hatred that they have allowed to fester and mainstream within their organisation,” said a spokesperson for the group. Pressure meanwhile is also growing for the resignation of a councillor in London who was elected for Reform and who was recorded by the same ITV investigation, made with Hardcash Productions, allegedly calling for King Charles to be beheaded because he believed the king was secretly a Muslim. Conservative, Labour and Liberal Democrat councillors in the south London borough of Bromley called on Dean Miller, who now sits as an independent, to stand down. Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting, “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”. In a statement released to the media this week, the party said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting. “This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment.” • Undercover: A Year in Reform airs on 18 October at 10.20pm on ITV1, ITVX, STV and STV Player

headline: No action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action post
trail_text: Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’
body_text: No further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, after she was accused of supporting the banned protest group Palestine Action. Helm, a journalist and author who is married to Jonathan Powell, posted on X on Thursday: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.” The Metropolitan police said on Friday the post was “in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”. In an update on Saturday, a force spokesperson said: “On Thursday 15 October, we were made aware of a post on X relating to Palestine Action. “The post was assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold. No further police action will be taken.” Helm was responding on X to a discussion about the Irish author Sally Rooney, who has said she can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action. It is understood there was insufficient evidence that the post was capable of encouraging support for a proscribed organisation. The ban, which began in July 2025, made membership or support of the direct action group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Downing Street has distanced itself from Helm’s remarks. The Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) had called on the police to investigate. The group acknowledged that “spouses are entitled to independent views”, but said Helm’s post “raises extremely serious questions for Jonathan Powell and the government. “Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.” Earlier, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

headline: Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’
trail_text: Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British
body_text: A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”. The comments were recorded as part of the undercover investigation by ITV that has already seen Reform accused of “appalling behaviour” and “extreme racism”. Reform has said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding there was “no room for racism” in the party. In footage due to be broadcast on Sunday, a Reform activist and aspiring MP, who has yet to be publicly identified, described himself as “pretty hardline about Islam”. He said: “If a Muslim’s prepared to de-convert, I’m happy. “But if they want to remain faithful to Islam, then this would be, I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, [Reform home affairs spokesperson] Zia Yusuf is a Muslim … to me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.” Discussing people crossing the Channel in small boats, the same activist said: “In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there.” Excerpts from the investigation released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates within Reform using racist language. In one excerpt, black children were referred to as “animals”, while in another a Reform member said his area had become “infested” with Asian families. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said Nigel Farage’s response to the revelations showed he was “completely unfit to lead”. She said: “Bad apples don’t fall far from the tree. The sleaze, scandals and appalling revelations of racism and rank misogyny piling up by the day go right to the top of Reform UK. “Nigel Farage is incapable of taking responsibility and getting his house in order because he himself shares culpability.” Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting, “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”. In a statement to ITV, the party said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting. “This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment. “There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.” On Friday, Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments he had made were uncovered in the investigation. ITV revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign. In a subsequent Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.” He added: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.”

headline: SNP says campaign for next referendum on independence ‘has already begun’
trail_text: John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK
body_text: John Swinney has said that the second referendum campaign for Scottish independence “has already begun”, revealing a nationwide effort to renew the argument for leaving the UK in his keynote address to the SNP party conference. On Saturday, the Scottish first minister said the SNP would launch its “most sophisticated campaign in history” to convince Scottish voters of the benefits of independence, backed by “a six-figure war chest”. Called Choose Scotland, the campaign will aim to build the consensus for leaving the union. Swinney told the SNP party conference in Aberdeen that the “stars were aligning” for the pro-independence cause, arguing that nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland had panicked pro-union parties. “For centuries, people in the Celtic nations have been told that we are not good enough. Our languages were derided, our cultures suppressed, our histories rewritten,” he said. “When I stood on a stage recently with pro-independence leaders from Wales and Ireland, it certainly upset some of our opponents. “From their point of view, they are right to be worried. Watching us pledge to work together and seeing the love and respect we feel for each other’s nations. Never again can they portray us as separatists.” At the conference, leading SNP figures said a hung Westminster parliament is the most realistic path to securing a second independence referendum in Scotland as the nationalists would probably “hold the balance of power” in forming a future progressive government. The party has just eight MPs in parliament, but recent polling indicates that if a vote was held today, that number would surge at the Labour party’s expense in Scotland, although there is uncertainty surrounding how many seats it would gain. Deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth said her party would welcome an early general election to reenergise the push for independence. “The polling, of course, suggests the SNP would hold the balance of power in a hung parliament and really strong support for the SNP across the country allowing us to regain a number of seats,” she said. The sentiment was echoed by Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, who told a podcast by the pro-independence newspaper the National that they could negotiate another poll if the overall results were tight. “We have a really great opportunity at the next general election to be in a position where that negotiation can seriously start with the next iteration of the Westminster government, whether we have a hung parliament, which is looking very likely, or different coalitions,” she said. “Perhaps now we are talking about a Lib Dem-Labour coalition. The SNP are polled at getting somewhere between 40 and 50 MPs at the general election. That’s huge. “Let’s put it to Westminster and put the onus on them to meet us at the table and set that plan out for us.” The latest MRP polling by Electoral Calculus this week predicted a narrow Labour victory, with the SNP winning 28 seats, although previous polls have indicated they could win even more. In a visit to Lanarkshire on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the Scottish government needed to “move beyond” the question of independence while offering to work more closely on devolving power from Holyrood with Swinney’s administration. The Westminster government would have to grant a second vote on Scottish independence. “I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions. In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people. Right now, too much time is wasted on those dramas. It consumes too much energy,” he said, when asked about the issue. Although it is not in Swinney’s power to call a second independence referendum, he told the conference that another vote could happen sooner than expected. “Our independence is very close,” he said. “Our nearest neighbours will always be our closest friends and our strongest allies. I will always want the very best for the people living in England, Wales and across Ireland. “But friends, in the long arc of history, nothing is static. And those that try to hold on to the past fail to grasp the opportunities of the future. “In this period of history, the nations of the United Kingdom are evolving into a new relationship. That is something to welcome.”

headline: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
trail_text: As Andy Burnham talks up closer alignment with the EU and a poll suggests half in UK would rejoin, the B-word is back on the agenda
body_text: In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.” Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe. This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU. There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing. But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it? Polling evidence may suggest so. A “megapoll” of more than 11,000 people published this month found that half of Britons now support rejoining the EU, with only 28% opposed, and the remainder undecided. Almost 60% think it was wrong to leave. Sliced some ways, the numbers are even more striking: a More in Common survey in June to mark a decade since the vote found that if another referendum was held today across Britain’s 632 constituencies, just 11 would vote to leave (even in Clacton, Nigel Farage’s constituency, 52% supported rejoining). What changed? To the polling expert Rob Ford, a professor of political science at the University of Manchester, there are several key reasons, from demographic change to buyers’ remorse. Brexiters are fewer in number – “a lot of leave voters have died, bluntly” – and both young people entering the electorate and those who did not vote in 2016 skew heavily in favour of Europe. And with the project widely considered a disappointment at best, a proportion of those who opted to leave have switched positions. “Although each is a relatively slow moving and relatively small incremental force, add them together over a decade and it adds up to quite a lot of change,” said Ford. Given the divisiveness and turbulence of the past decade – and the fact many Labour MPs represent constituencies that voted to leave – it is little wonder that some senior Labour figures have expressed nervousness about reopening the debate. “[Burnham] definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division,” one cabinet minister told the Guardian. But the view from formerly Brexit-supporting areas is not necessarily what it was. “Hull East voted 74% leave in the referendum, however I believe the mood has changed,” said Karl Turner, the Labour MP for the constituency since 2010 (he now sits as an independent after having the whip withdrawn). “Constituents tell me they expected Brexit to improve their lives; instead many face higher costs and fewer opportunities.” As a result, he said, they were “increasingly ready to consider the practical benefits of rejoining the EU”. Ford added: “Andy Burnham looks at the data and says, well, I’ve got an electoral coalition that’s 80% remain and becoming more so. The parties to my left that I need to squeeze have a [position] that is even more remain than that. “And the overall balance of opinion in the country is now nudging up towards 60% in favour of remain, sometimes even higher in terms of how many think Brexit is a mistake. Why wouldn’t I move in a pro-remain direction? It’s the direction of travel of the country. The art of leadership is getting out ahead of the trends that are happening and using them to your advantage.” Sara Hobolt, a professor in the department of government at London School of Economics, agrees that the polling data today suggests Brexit could be an effective general election rallying cry for Labour. “This is an issue that a lot of people were quite upset with Keir Starmer and his government for not talking about it. It is something that definitely mobilises the base.” While Labour supporters and those the party wants to win back from other progressive parties overwhelmingly support remain, she points out, the Conservative party is now much more divided on the issue, having lost many of its hardline Brexiters to Reform. “That means that [by putting Brexit back on the agenda] you can potentially do more damage to the right than the left. “But I think probably the main thing for Andy Burnham is that this has been seen in his electoral base as something [that has been overlooked]. ‘You talk about growth? Why are you not talking about Brexit?’ Because overwhelmingly remainers think that a lot of the economic problems we’ve faced over the last decade are due to Brexit.” But if uniting the left before a Westminster election is one thing, winning a future Brexit referendum is a whole other challenge, as the experience of 2016 showed. “There clearly is support for rejoining the EU,” says the More in Commondirector, Luke Tryl, “the question is, how resilient would that be in the face of a referendum campaign?” One factor is, inevitably, Brexit weariness, he says. “The British public are tired. They’ve lurched from crisis to crisis, from row to row, and I think, for some, just the idea of reopening the wounds [is unwelcome]. I think in a campaign rejoin, if it got to that, would start ahead, but I don’t think the headline polling we are seeing now would remain where it is once it was subject to a full back and forth.” Ford agrees – noting that the EU will be resistant to serious discussions so long as there is the prospect of a wholesale reversal under a future Reform government. The risk of bringing up Brexit is not just because the subject is neuralgic to many, he says. “One of the problems during the Brexit years was it was just simply impossible to get a conversation going about all the other pressing issues that mattered. “There is a risk for Burnham, if this thing starts to take life of its own yet again, that the big difficult conversations he wants to have about some of the longstanding structural problems in British society will be harder to have because for a lot of people in the political conversation, Brexit is like catnip – they’ll run straight to it. And then you’re not able to get them to pay attention to the issues you want them to pay attention to.”

headline: Home Office denies British baby living in Thailand chance to meet great-grandfather in UK
trail_text: British father would like to take his family to Lancashire to see ill relative but officials refused visa for his partner, a refugee from Myanmar
body_text: The Home Office has denied a great-grandfather from Lancashire the chance of meeting his five-month-old British great-grandson, who lives abroad. William Cross was born in Thailand on 30 April to parents Matthew Cross, 31, who is from Burnley in Lancashire, and Khin Thant Zin, known as Jue Jue, also 31, a refugee who fled persecution in Myanmar to Thailand. The family live on the island of Koh Tao, famous for its diving schools and a centre for turtle conservation. It is a popular tourism spot and Cross, a mechanical engineer, opened a steakhouse restaurant there 15 months ago. He met Zin on the island and the couple are now engaged. She works in the restaurant managing social media and human resources. Cross’s parents have visited the family in Thailand and have met their grandson. But William’s great-grandfather George Kerr, 74, who lives in Clayton-le-Moors in Lancashire, has multiple health problems and so is unable to fly out to Thailand to meet the baby. Instead, a large family gathering was planned in Burnley for Christmas. Cross said: “My grandfather suffers from ill health and sadly he is unable to travel. He and I have been extremely close all my life and I’m desperate for him to meet his [great] grandchild.” The family have just signed a lease on a new home and have bought some land on the island for later development. They assumed that organising a short trip to the UK for a family Christmas would be straightforward. But the Home Office refused Zin’s visitor visa application, which means the family will be unable to travel. Officials said they were not satisfied she was a “genuine visitor”, and that there was no evidence Zin would return to Thailand because she had not shown evidence of significant family ties there, and she was unable to show sufficient evidence of her income. “Jue Jue has never had a bank account,” Cross said. “Her brother and sister both live on Koh Tao and her mum is planning to move here when her younger sister has finished school in Myanmar.” The visitor visa application process is expensive and cumbersome. “They required documentation from my family to be financial guarantors while we’re in the UK. Passport photos of my grandfather, my mum and dad and me, a typed letter from each of us confirming our commitment to sponsorship, a formal letter of invitation from my parents saying they would be comfortable with my partner being in my home,” Cross said. “We had to travel to Phuket, a journey of two nights and three days from Koh Tao on a ferry and buses, which cost us £400, to complete biometric screening required for the visitor visa application.” There is no right of appeal against this visa refusal so the couple are preparing a new application, although the Home Office refusal letter warns that future applications are likely to be refused “unless the circumstances of your application change”. They also need to buy and provide evidence of return flight tickets even though they don’t know whether the new visa application will be granted. They have to make the long journey from the island on ferry and buses a second time to repeat the biometrics. “By the time we send our next application, the whole thing will have cost us £3,000 with no guarantee of it being accepted,” Cross said. The family are still hoping that baby William will be able to meet his great-grandfather at Christmas. Temperatures on the island rarely fall below 25C, so back in Burnley his relatives have bought warm baby clothes in the hope he will get a chance to wear them. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All visa applications are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

headline: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
trail_text: Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments
body_text: Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash over racist comments that were captured in an undercover investigation. In a Facebook post on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.” Earlier this week, an ITV investigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign. Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post. “The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.” Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham city council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series on Reform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning. In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.” Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation. Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.” Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.

headline: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
trail_text: Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
byline: Rowena Mason, Lisa O’Carroll and Jasper Jolly
body_text: No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”. Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme. The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme. The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures. The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”. This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy. However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU. Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”. They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.” Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share. EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027. But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants. Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc. According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway. This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”. Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China. Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
