A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation. China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars. While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry. Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU. At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”. Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy. “Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

headline: Six-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vetting
trail_text: Former head of Foreign Office Olly Robbins applied for judicial review after Keir Starmer dismissed him in April
body_text: Olly Robbins, the former head of the Foreign Office sacked by Keir Starmer over his role in vetting Peter Mandelson, has received a six-figure payout from the government over his dismissal. Robbins had applied to the high court for a judicial review of the prime minister’s decision to remove him as the top civil servant at the Foreign Office after he was dismissed in April. He was removed from his post by Starmer after the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation from UK Security Vetting (UKSV) to deny clearance for Mandelson. In a statement on Friday, Robbins said he was “grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time”. He added: “I want to thank the FDA [union] for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life.” Dave Penman, general secretary of the FDA, which represents senior civil servants, said: “This settlement may bring an end to the judicial review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government. “The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgment of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations – which is quite the feat. “We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process.” The government will ultimately have to publish how much it has given Robbins in a settlement, which is believed to be six figures but not as much as the record £860,000 given to former cabinet secretary Chris Wormald after he was forced out by Starmer after just a year in post. At the time of his dismissal, Downing Street said Robbins had lost the confidence of Starmer and Yvette Cooper, then foreign secretary, due to his handling of the vetting of Mandelson, who was sacked over the extent of his links to the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Guardian later revealed that Mandelson’s associations with senior figures in China, Russia and Israel had been among the concerns raised by UKSV when it concluded he should be denied clearance. His relationship with Epstein was not among the reasons. Robbins’ legal submission had made the case that Starmer had no statutory authority to dismiss him as the head of the diplomatic service, and that there had been “no fair procedure” and “no process at all” in the dismissal. It also said Robbins had been given “irrational” reasons for being fired. There had been strong support for Robbins within Whitehall, with senior civil servants said to believe he had in effect been sacked for doing what No 10 wanted by swiftly passing Mandelson through vetting, and that the focus should instead have been on the prime minister’s initial decision. The Commons foreign affairs select committee has previously said that Robbins believed he was “delivering the outcome that was wanted” and concluded that his dismissal “seems to have been taken without full due process and the establishment of the facts”. Questions remain about the defence Robbins mounted, both of his own actions and the system through which the national security establishment vets people, and the lack of mitigation put in place to get around the security concerns. The Foreign Office refused to hand over a summary of Mandelson’s security vetting to the official tasked with compiling documents detailing his appointment as ambassador to the US, in response to a Commons motion forcing the release of documents linked to the process.

headline: Jenrick claims Farage has done more to stand against racism than ‘almost anybody’
trail_text: Reform MP defends leader after ITV footage shows official warning Farage he is ‘protecting’ candidate over racist David Lammy comments
body_text: Robert Jenrick has sought to defend Reform UK against fresh allegations that it hosts extremists by claiming that Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism and the far right”. The remarks came after Farage was berated by a Reform official for “protecting” a mayoral candidate who was accused of making racist remarks about the former Labour deputy prime minister David Lammy. The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views. In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy. Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “[Farage] is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime. “And this documentary failed to besmirch his character, which presumably was the ultimate objective.” Farage has made repeated promises over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Further footage released on Thursday shows Farage discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party. The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds did not have a primary loyalty to the UK. Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, but clips from the ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier discussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”. In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate. “He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.” To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.” Jenrick defended Reform’s vetting policy. “In my experience, all political parties have bad apples. I mean, you can see that’s plain to see from the conduct of other political parties. In fact, Councillor Feeney, the one that you presented before I came online, was for a short time a Reform councillor, but for a much greater time a Conservative councillor.” He added: “We actually have very strong vetting, and we invest a huge amount in it, and it’s improving all the time. I don’t know what the vetting is like in every other political party. I can say in the Conservative party, because it was my former party, there is absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors.”

headline: UK could quickly re-enter EU with ‘Switzerland plus’ deal, senior MEP says
trail_text: Bernd Lange, who was involved in Brexit talks, says deal could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties
body_text: The UK could re-enter the EU in a “Switzerland plus” package that could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties with the bloc, the head of a European parliament committee has said. Bernd Lange, who was heavily involved in Brexit negotiations, said: “I would love to see the UK back.” He said the EU missed the UK in decision-making because of its strong history of promoting open markets and democracy. A Swiss style arrangement is often considered a halfway house to full membership of the bloc but involves free movement and regulatory alignment. Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market across more than 100 agreements with a new framework deal. This gives it access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. In exchange, Switzerland agreed to the free movement of people and to pay €375m (£326m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds. Lange, a German MEP who has an important role in the European legislative process as chair of the European parliament’s trade committee, said the Switzerland framework could be a model for the UK, but it was a “passive” agreement that would not involve the country in EU decision-making. “As a step by step [process], of course, there are a lot of possibilities, but I would love to have the UK come back also in the political decision-making process and politically be engaged. So we have the model of Switzerland … Switzerland plus, I would say, as that has some kinds of engagement but not the full membership.” He said the decision about what relationship the UK wanted with the EU was entirely “in the hands of the UK”, but if it opted for something like Switzerland plus, an agreement could be achieved quickly, notwithstanding political hiccups. He was speaking in London, where his schedule includes a meeting with the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, who is part of a team working on the UK’s new position on EU relations. Lange also threw his weight behind Andy Burnham’s call for the EU not to lock the UK out of Made in Europe legislation that would restrict UK suppliers from inclusion in public procurement tenders as well as some corporate contracts such as car fleets. French and German leaders were reportedly close on Thursday to agreeing a proposal that the UK could be included, provided it aligned with the EU’s 2024 tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles. This week the boss of Mercedes said the EU would be making a “deliberate choice” to harm the EU car industry if it did not allow the UK into the Made in Europe package. Burnham has backing from the Netherlands, Germany and Italy. France, which came up with the legislative proposals, was opposed, saying it needed to get the legislation on the books urgently to guard against cheap competition from China, and that allowing the UK and other allied countries in could hold up the lawmaking. Lange said the UK should “of course” be included because it was already aligned with the EU on environmental standards and employment laws. He said France’s position was “not rational” and “also so emotional” but could be born from the desire to be seen as putting France first before next April’s presidential elections, in which Marine Le Pen, who is opposed to globalism, could take power. Locking the UK out of Made in Europe could also cause a legal dispute over the trade and cooperation agreement that allows UK goods to be sold in the single market without barriers as long as they the meet the bloc’s standards. The Made in Europe package, or the Industrial Accelerator Act, is expected to get political approval by the end of the year or early 2027, meaning Burnham does not have much time to get clauses inserted designating the UK as European for the purposes of the legislation. But Lange said there could be time after that, given the processes of the European parliament, where three committees have scrutinising powers. “There are 5,100 amendments,” he said, referring to the protracted process ahead, including one on UK inclusion.

headline: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row
trail_text: UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ by counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions
byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
body_text: Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort. The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity. Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military. He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.” The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries. Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East. Speaking to the BBC after the meeting, Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.” The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis. But it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military. Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy. The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine. Developing the theme, Streeting made a direct appeal to the US audience, saying: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together. “The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”. Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK. “Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said. The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable. It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities. Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.

headline: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy
trail_text: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
body_text: Nigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed. The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Other footage shows Farage himself discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party. The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK. However, while Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”. “He needs to go, I’m getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December. However, Parry was still the candidate three weeks later, while Farage told a press conference that the candidate could stay if he apologised. In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate. “He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.” To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.” Parry was suspended on 26 March after the Guardian reported that he had described members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as “cosplayers” and likened them to “Islamists on horseback”. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said these “latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform”, adding: “Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.” The revelations are the latest in a number of recent controversies for Reform. The full ITV documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on Sunday. A number of councillors have already stood down after segments from the investigation aired on Wednesday showed them making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. The undercover reporter for ITV also met Pochin, Reform’s MP for Runcorn and Helsby, at a time when she was the party’s only female member of parliament. When Pochin was told that a new female press officer was starting work, she was recorded as saying: “Oh thank fuck for that. God! We so need women press officers … They are so fucking chauvinistic. “I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it’s lovely, oh they’re all so welcoming.’ Shit … they just exclude you if you’re a woman. It’s really tough being a girl with all of this alpha male shit going on.” Pochin did not provide a statement when approached by ITV. Reform UK used a statement issued on Thursday to accuse ITV and the company behind the documentary, Hardcash Productions, of using “extreme methods of deception”. It said: “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees. “That same journalist did not limit themselves to recording candid conversations in the workplace. That journalist also sought to find out sensitive security information, travel arrangements, and financial information outside of the scope of this investigation.” Reform went on to claim that ITV had failed to address this in correspondence, despite this conduct being drawn to its attention. “This is at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation,” it added. “There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.” When approached for comment, Parry referred the Guardian to a statement given to ITV. In it he said: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”

headline: Top health official urged to recuse herself from private ADHD crackdown over ties to industry
trail_text: Exclusive: Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessments
body_text: A senior civil servant should play no part in ministers’ crackdown on private attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism clinics because of her recent ties to the industry, MPs have said. Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs are demanding that Samantha Jones, the permanent secretary at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), steps away from any role in plans to toughen regulation of the booming market in private neurodiversity assessments. They say Jones should not be involved because of her links to a company that is one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded neurodiversity assessments, which earned it £26m from the health service in England over the past six years. Ministers are drawing up plans for how to better regulate the “wild west” of private clinics offering assessment, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD and autism that has grown rapidly in recent years as people have struggled to access care via the NHS. The push comes after the government last week accepted the findings of a review by Prof Peter Fonagy, which raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of assessments by private providers of neurodiversity services that had inbuilt “financial incentives” to diagnose and treat people. Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy. She would therefore be expected to advise ministers on how best to strengthen the regulation of private providers of ADHD and autism services. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has vowed to introduce a much tougher regime. Four MPs have called for Jones to recuse herself from any role in those decisions because of her previous ties to ADHD360, a provider of neurodiversity services. Her links to the private ADHD sector represent a serious conflict of interest, they claim. Jones was appointed as the permanent secretary on 22 April 2025. A month later, she was still the chair of and a director of and shareholder in the private care provider Keys Group when, on 16 May, it bought ADHD360, a clinic that has increased its NHS income considerably in recent years. At the time of the £22.5m purchase, Jones was also an operating partner in G Square Capital, the private equity company that owns Keys Group. She sold her shares in Keys Group and resigned her roles there and at G Square Capital before she started at the DHSC on 16 June. Jones has already recused herself from involvement in the department’s decision over whether to extend Palantir’s £330m, seven-year contract with the NHS because of her past work for the lobbyists Carnall Farrar, which advised Palantir regarding the contract. MPs believe her tenure at Keys Group could represent a conflict of interest. Ben Coleman, a Labour MP on the health and social care committee, said: “People will want to feel reassured that future regulation of private ADHD and autism assessments is beyond reproach. Given her recent close involvement with ADHD360, I would encourage Ms Jones to recuse herself from that work, as she has done over Palantir, to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest.” In June, Jones apologised after she was reprimanded by the Civil Service Commission for breaching lobbying rules by failing to ask the (now defunct) Advisory Committee on Business Appointments for prior approval before undertaking work for four healthcare companies. Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “Given Sam Jones oversaw the multimillion-pound acquisition of ADHD360 just weeks before entering the Department of Health, ministers must ensure she recuses herself immediately, just as she has over Palantir.” Jones, 55, was widely admired in the NHS when she ran West Hertfordshire NHS trust in 2013-15. After a role with NHS England, she began working in private healthcare. Boris Johnson as prime minister handed her a key role in Downing Street in 2021. She returned to private health in 2023 and by 2023-24 had paid roles or shareholdings in 13 health or consultancy organisations. Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said Jones’s deep involvement in private healthcare meant she should not have been made DHSC permanent secretary in the first place, saying: “It just defies logic that anyone thought it was a good idea. Surely this must have come up during her recruitment process?” Jones did not answer questions put by the Guardian. The NHS has paid ADHD360 just over £26m for its services since 2020, according to figures supplied by the Tussell public expenditure database. “When it comes to the government’s response to the [Fonagy] review, there should be no suggestion that the top NHS official is being influenced by any past or current links to a major private provider of NHS ADHD services,” said Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. “This issue is too sensitive and complex to permit any conflicts of interest. As a result the permanent secretary should recuse herself from this area of policy.” David Rowland, the director of the Centre for Health and the Public Interest thinktank, said: “The permanent secretary at the department which has responsibility for regulating private ADHD providers appears to have a conflict of interest in this area and so may struggle to remain impartial when it comes to implementing the recommendations made by Prof Fonagy.” A DHSC spokesperson said: “There is no conflict of interest. The permanent secretary has appropriately declared all interests, in this post and when she was a non-executive director [of the DHSC]. She resigned from all her private sector posts before taking on the permanent secretary role at the department.”

headline: Just as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITV
trail_text: How dare the channel reveal more racism and bigotry within Reform just as he was planning a press conference?
body_text: Sometimes the world can be very unfair. As though life is just one cruel joke. How else to make sense of everything? For when the history books come to be written, Nigel Farage will go down as one of the century’s unluckiest politicians. Poor Nige. All he has ever wanted is a better Britain. A country united in a shared vision where everyone gets along with one another. Where people of all faiths and none look out for each other. Where men and women of all colours are treated as equals. Where Nige can teach the world to sing in perfect harmony. So why do so many bad things keep happening to such a good person? Where’s the justice in that? How come Nige has been given a lead role in the rewrite of Little Britain’s Book of Job. Nige as a latter day Old Testament prophet put on Earth to show us all the value of eternal suffering. Because Nige is a decent man. The very best of us. And yet time and again he is made to feel pain. No more so than in the last few months. First there was the money. Few would have batted an eyelid if he had been given £5m by the RNLI. For all he has done to support the work that unpaid volunteers do in rescuing all people in trouble on the sea. Let’s face it, a modern day ministry doesn’t pay for itself and no demigod-like politician can expect to get by on less than £1m a year. Those houses and bottles of champagne aren’t going to pay for themselves. Yet because the £5m came from a Thai crypto-billionaire, suddenly everyone was asking difficult questions. Anyone would think Reform might have crypto-friendly policies. Then there was the Channel 4 sting. And yet again our Messiah was the innocent victim of an establishment plot. Compared to Nige, Jesus had it easy in Holy Week. How could he be expected to realise that two associates whom he had barely known for years might allegedly be trying to secure an illegal donation from overseas? And what were the chances that Nige might be caught on camera giving considered responses as part of a conversation he hadn’t even been listening to? Some days you just can’t buy a break. On Thursday morning, Farage had been scheduled to host a press conference near Southend where we were promised he would spread goodwill to all men with yet another major policy announcement. Only for the event to be cancelled late on Wednesday evening. The official reason given was that Reform didn’t want to clash with the fifth anniversary of the murder of the former Southend MP David Amess. Yet more bad luck for Nige. Imagine only being given five years’ notice to plan your schedule. Or perhaps there was another reason for the cancellation. One related to another sting, this time by ITV, that had sent undercover journalists into the Reform operations room and uncovered the only bad apples in the entire organisation. Again, what were the chances of finding racists and misogynists attracted to a party that loved women and people of all colours? How could this ever have happened? The chances were slimmer than winning the EuroMillions lottery. And surely had nothing to do with Nige’s would-be chancellor, Honest Bob Jenrick, saying he would consider allowing soldiers to be able to blow up migrants in small boats in the Channel. What’s wrong with killing a few thousand people for the sake of a greater good? The country is just too woke for its own good sometimes. Then there’s the wannabe home secretary Zia Yusuf, who is on a one-man mission to round up all immigrants – even women and children – and send them back to countries where they may be killed. So again we are left with the question. Why are so many racists attracted to Reform? Let’s take Dean Miller. A vetted Reform councillor from Bromley who was filmed campaigning during the Makerfield byelection. Quite how extensive the vetting process was is anyone’s guess. “Tell us, Dean. Are you in any way prejudiced against people of colour?”. “Absolutely not. I just don’t want them anywhere near me.” “That’s great. Thanks Dean. Welcome to Reform.” Anyway, Dean was caught on camera saying that it was kill or be killed with illegal immigrants. “They’re all fucking black and they’re like animals,” he said. “I’m not a racist, but you know what I mean.” Yes, Dean. We know exactly what you mean. And he couldn’t have been clearer about his intentions towards the king. Charles was a Muslim and deserved to be beheaded. It’s a view. When Miller was asked for a comment before the film is aired this weekend, his defence was that he had been on heavy medication at the time. And suddenly that all made sense. Because I too am on regular medication both for my psyche and for my heart. So I chose to reread the common known side effects of one of my drugs. And there among the small print about causing faster breathing, fever, muscle stiffness and drowsiness, one thing stood out. “Never take in the presence of a black person or royalty. Can make you prone to racist outbursts and in extreme cases can provoke urges to kill the monarch.” I guess I must just have been extremely lucky so far. Miller was not the only one to have been caught out this way. Others – also apparently vetted – declared that all foreigners were parasites, that the UK should have a 1% limit on all immigrants and made disgusting comments about a female Reform councillor. Raymond Dunning said he was so far-far right it was unbelievable. Then there were those who thought it best to try to sound moderate until after they had been elected. Then the gloves would come off and they could give foreigners hell. And in the middle of all this we have the saintly Nige. Scratching his head and wondering why all this was happening to him again. He hadn’t come in to politics to stir grievance and division. He was the god of love, the man of peace. Others among the Reform elite knew exactly where the blame lay. And it wasn’t with the innocent men who had been caught saying the only racist and sexist words they had ever said. Dicky Tice and the former Tory MP Ben Bradley were pointing the finger at ITV for daring to do its job properly. It was outrageous they had recorded Reform councillors going about their everyday jobs. Every man and woman was entitled to be as racist as they like in the comfort of their workplace. For now, Nige was determined to rise above it. He would survive. He was doing God’s work. Just a shame that God didn’t seem to like him much.

headline: Labour councils told to end agreements with Greens who do not condemn ‘Zionism is racism’ policy
trail_text: Party chair calls on Labour groups to end local deals if Green councillors do not reject motion attacked as ‘antisemitic’
body_text: Labour councils who share power with the Greens have been told to terminate agreements if their Green partners do not condemn the party’s new “Zionism is racism” policy. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said groups working with Green party politicians must review their agreements and end them unless they reject the controversial motion, which Andy Burnham has called “antisemitic”. The policy, which was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton at the start of the month, equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. It also rejects a two-state solution and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said on Thursday it had written to the Green party of England and Wales to seek more information about the motion “and assess its practical implications and potential impact”. Several individuals and groups had said they planned to contact the watchdog to argue that the new policy risked breaching equality laws. On Wednesday, Burnham ruled out Labour having a partnership with the Greens. Asked about the motion during prime minister’s questions, Burnham said: “It is wrong. It is antisemitic, and this side of the house will have nothing to do with it.” Burnham went on to state that Labour would not “support a partnership with a party that holds [the] position that has recently been adopted”. Giving further details of Labour’s response to the motion, Phillipson said Greens who were working with Labour in local government would be asked “to make clear that they reject this position and to call on their national leadership to reconsider” the policy. She added: “We have asked local Green groups to respond as a matter of urgency. Where they are unable to provide that assurance, Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end. This isn’t an issue of party politics, it’s about doing what is right and upholding the values anyone holding public office should share. “The Labour party fought hard to address antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics. We have a responsibility to uphold those same standards in our relationships with other parties.” Responding to the announcement, a Green party spokesperson said: “For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong. Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic. “Whilst Labour continue to try to meddle in our internal democracy, arm a genocide and lock up protesting pensioners, we will not take lectures from them.” The Guardian understands that local Green party councillors are unlikely to face disciplinary measures if they do condemn the motion, as the party has a highly decentralised structure and no whipping system. Several MPs and the former leader Caroline Lucas have already stated their opposition, and dissent about policy is tolerated. Southwark Greens have already disowned the policy to maintain a coalition with the Liberal Democrats. The binding anti-Zionism policy motion was passed on 4 October by 1,022 votes to 813. The 1,022 votes represented 0.4% of the Green party membership. Four of the Greens’ five MPs opposed the policy, while the group representing European Green parties expressed dismay at the move, which runs counter to their support for a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, abstained from the vote to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which he lost. In a statement on Thursday, the EHRC said it had received complaints about the policy breaching the Equality Act, “including concerns that Jewish people could face discrimination because of their beliefs following the adoption of the motion”. It added: “We recognise that many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable following the party’s motion. Political parties, like all duty-bearers, must comply with the Equality Act and take steps to avoid discrimination including on the grounds of race, religion or belief.” Affected councils Derbyshire Dales Lib Dem-led coalition Broadland Lib Dem-led coalition West Suffolk Labour-led coalition Arun Lib Dem-led coalition Havant Labour-led coalition Lewes Green-led coalition Rother Coalition led by local independent group Runnymede Coalition with Lib Dems, Greens and local independent group Wealden Green-led coalition West Oxfordshire Lib Dem-led coalition West Sussex Lib Dem-led coalition North Somerset Lib Dem-led coalition West Devon Independent-led coalition Monmouthshire Labour minority-led coalition Coventry Labour-led confidence and supply agreement with the Greens Stafford Labour-led coalition Warwick Green-led coalition Sheffield Labour-led coalition

headline: John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget
trail_text: Speaking at IMF meeting, chancellor says he will stick to fiscal rules while recognising business and living costs
body_text: John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules. Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs. “I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space – but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future,” he said. The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills, but Healey is expected to announce a further package of energy support at his 28 October tax and spending statement, before what is expected to be a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January. He said: “The prime minister’s talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living.” Healey also reiterated his insistence that he would be sticking to the spending plans set out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves at last year’s spending review – and that cabinet colleagues would have to find any additional resources within their existing budgets. “When the second half of a spending review is in place, there are pressures on departments, and colleagues are doing a good job of managing with what they’ve got,” he said, adding: “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things.” The UK has been praised by the IMF this week for setting out a plan to tackle its deficit, with the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urging the government to “stay the course”. Healey stressed he would stick to the rules set out by Reeves. “We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF’s backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn’t just a forecast for the future, but there’s some evidence of performance already.” He declined to say whether he would increase taxes on banks, or raise capital gains tax, to offset the expected pressure on his budget from higher energy prices and government borrowing costs. “If you think back to the run-up to previous budgets, the speculation about what was set to be in those budgets was actually deeply damaging,” he said. “It led to people cashing in their pensions early when they didn’t need to. It led to people holding back or not investing in their businesses when they didn’t need to. So I’m just not going to get drawn into any speculation.” Healey, a former defence secretary, also hinted he was working on an additional package of support for Ukraine, to be announced at the budget. He said: “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine: military, diplomatic and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with [Vladimir] Putin targeting these energy systems with thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching. “The step back from this is that the future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.” Healey and the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, chaired a meeting of G20 policymakers on Thursday morning, in the absence of the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent. The chancellor will fly back to London on Thursday evening to put the finishing touches to the budget.

headline: Burnham v Swinney: will the UK PM overshadow the SNP’s conference?
trail_text: Prime minister presents new kind of challenge for SNP, and his Scottish visit will loom large over its big event
body_text: This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party conference. But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup. Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister. The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died. “I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.” Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil. Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence. Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront. Even among SNP voters, he is popular. Polling by PF Global found that 46% of Scots have a favourable view of Burnham, far higher than the Labour party itself, and double Keir Starmer’s when he left power. Only Swinney is more popular than the prime minister among SNP voters who supported yes in 2014, reaching a level not seen for a Labour leader since Jeremy Corbyn. Despite this, SNP figures have sought to capitalise on Burnham’s stance on the EU in their quest for a second independence vote. “We are in a situation where Andy Burnham is actively and unilaterally opening up the conversation about whether we are able to go back to results of referendums and relitigate those decisions while saying that that same democratic principle does not apply to the people of Scotland,” said Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry. “The idea that the union can continue to exist in its current form is absolutely farcical.” In Aberdeen, the SNP is hoping to draw a line under a bruising few years after Nicola Sturgeon’s resignation and the subsequent fraud conviction of her estranged husband and former SNP chief executive Peter Murrell, who is serving a five-year prison sentence for embezzling £400,000 from the party. A proceeds of crime case against Murrell is scheduled for early December. In May, the SNP won a fifth successive election, but only enough to form a minority government in Holyrood. Despite the victory, Sturgeon criticised a “lack of vision or big picture thinking” in the campaign in the opening to her memoir. Swinney has said they were still good friends. Some SNP figures wonder how much they owe to the unpopularity of Starmer. The party also faces challenges on multiple fronts: Reform has as many MSPs as Labour in Holyrood with 17, while the Scottish Greens won a record 15 seats. The Tories have showed that they can still win seats, defeating the SNP in Aberdeen South in June. Despite the potential for a standoff between Swinney and Burnham, there is growing appetite in Scotland for collaboration between Westminster and Holyrood. Since the May elections, there has been a sharp rise in Scots who support a closer working relationship between the UK and Scottish governments. Polling by Ipsos has found that 42% of Scots would feel happy about the SNP-led Scottish government working with London, up 12 points since Starmer was in charge in May. Just over half of Scots believe that the country is going in the wrong direction, up six points in the same time period. This conference, the SNP has invited speakers from other separatist and pro-independence parties. Sioned Williams, deputy first minister of Wales, will give a fraternal address on Friday. Gillian Mackay, a Scottish Green party MSP, will speak at a panel about the right pathway to independence on Saturday. “We understand, and members of the SNP know, that this is bigger than the SNP. Obviously, I fundamentally believe that the SNP will be the party who secures independence for Scotland. But that runs so much deeper throughout the Scottish population than just those who vote for the SNP. I do think that it is important at this moment to harness and to build on that support as broadly as we can,” said Bird. • This article was amended on 16 October 2026. Peter Murrell was the chief executive of the SNP, not the chair as an earlier version said.

headline: Parents of Chloe Moffat want Treasury staff held to account over her death
trail_text: Exclusive: David and Anne Moffat to meet permanent secretary after coroner found Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to employee taking her own life
body_text: The parents of a woman who killed herself after facing disciplinary proceedings at the Treasury will call for anyone found to have contributed to their daughter’s death to be held to account. A coroner found in August that the Treasury had “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death after the 26-year-old personal assistant was called into a surprise disciplinary meeting about anonymous complaints alleging she had disclosed sensitive information at work, which she denied. The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report, seen by the Guardian, acknowledges the department’s role in her death and commits to safeguards so this does not happen again. A review of the civil service by the Cabinet Office found that the conditions Moffat was subjected to had been replicated in other disciplinary meetings. “We have some tough questions to ask,” David Moffat, Chloe’s father, told the Guardian before a meeting with the Treasury’s permanent secretary, James Bowler. “We do want to know that staff have been held to account. The coroner didn’t ask for that, but obviously that is very important. Chloe was held to account; we need to know that the managers and HR staff are being held to account.” Moffat’s managers declined to allow her to bring a colleague to the meeting, did not give her any advance notice of it, and refused to tell her whether she was likely to lose her job. They also removed access to her director’s email and changed her work responsibilities. This was despite the meeting being described as “informal”. Moffat left the meeting “devastated” and convinced she would lose her job, the coroner found, and the next morning she took her own life. She had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years, “loved her job” and had an “exemplary employment record”, the coroner heard. During the inquest, Moffat’s line manager was asked if she would have done anything differently and told the court: “No, I think we did all we could at the time with the information and advice we were given.” Moffat’s parents have spent the year since she died fighting to get answers from the Treasury, which initially did not take any responsibility. “It has taken us a long time to get to this point, and they have not helped us in any form,” said Anne Moffat, Chloe’s mother. “Now we are also trying to think how we want lessons to be learned so no other young person suffers in the same way as Chloe suffered. So we are looking at Chloe’s legacy, to ensure that there is learning across all organisations in HR departments.” They say they have not had the chance to grieve properly yet and are thinking about holding a second celebration of life for Chloe. David said: “The funeral was in some ways uplifting as so many people chose to join us, but we didn’t really know what we knew now. We want to revisit it and have a more joyful time and celebrate Chloe as the person she was.” The prevention of future deaths report issued by the coroner found there was still a risk at the civil service due to its disciplinary procedures. The civil service has put in place multiple safeguards to address these issues. Documents seen by the Guardian read: “HM Treasury has accepted the findings in the report in full. In direct response to the inquest findings, HM Treasury immediately stopped using informal fact-finding meetings for allegations of potential serious or gross misconduct, introduced strengthened procedural and wellbeing safeguards, and issued urgent interim guidance.” This guidance includes allowing staff to have a supporter in disciplinary meetings, giving proper notice of any such meeting, and informing staff if a dismissal is not likely. The Treasury is also hiring an on-site occupational therapist to support staff wellbeing. Of this, David Moffat said: “We feel a lot better than we did about it going through the inquest. This is a step forward, but we still have some difficult questions to ask the permanent secretary.” The coroner heard that during the disciplinary meeting, Moffat repeatedly asked for her best friend at work to be allowed to come in for support. This was not felt by her managers to be “appropriate”, the court heard, despite the obvious distress the young woman was in. The department has now changed its policy. An email sent to staff at the Treasury last week, seen by the Guardian, reads: “Where concerns may amount to minor misconduct, these will continue to be handled informally. You will be able to ask to bring a colleague with you for personal support if you would like.” Anne Moffat hopes other young people will not be put in the same position as Chloe. “It is so avoidable what happened, and such a waste. I wish we had known the risks. As parents we are still taking a bit responsibility that we could have done things differently. And if we had, the result wouldn’t have been so catastrophic.” Chloe’s friends have been keeping her memory alive by running marathons for Shooting Stars Children’s Hospice, a charity for which her mother used to work, and volunteering for Samaritans. Her parents hope their experience can stop other families from going through the same tragic event. “We are hoping when we see the Treasury they will give us more reassurance and work with us on how Chloe is remembered,” Anne said. “We so miss having Chloe now. Our lives will never be the same again as we have lost her through something that was so preventable.” A HM Treasury spokesperson said: “The Treasury’s deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague. Our response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report sets out the action we have taken following this tragic case. An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

headline: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and misogynist comments
trail_text: Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views
body_text: Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday. Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters. Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, making Islamophobic remarks, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”. Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues. Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”. Chris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post. Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel. Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs. The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”. “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said. The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”. “They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added. Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.” The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party. The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.” • Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on 18 October at 10.20pm on ITV1, ITVX, STV & STV Player • This article was amended on 20 October 2026 to add detail that some comments were anti-Muslim.

headline: ‘We’re doomed anyway’: young people disheartened about the future are splashing out on the present
trail_text: Spending $8 on a matcha every day seems worth it when the alternatives – like saving for a house – feel virtually unattainable
body_text: An Tran treats herself to experiences like concerts and movie tickets. The 21-year-old Sydney law student, who is working towards paying her tuition fees, says many of her friends spend their spare money on matcha, Labubu toys and trending makeup items. Tran, who moved from Vietnam two years ago, says she appreciates what she has in Australia but can understand why young people like her are concerned about the future. “We feel like we’re doomed anyway so why should we save?” she says. Young people feeling disheartened about the economy are choosing to spend their money in the present – regularly buying “little treats” such as takeaway coffees or even “doomspending” if it feels like there’s no point saving for the future. “If we believe in the future, we are much more likely to be able to defer gratification in the pursuit of it,” says brand strategist Eugene Healey. Healey says “little treat” culture – a pattern of consumer behaviour where people, especially younger people, buy “affordable, everyday luxuries” like matcha or lunch – has come about because traditional milestones feel out of reach. The rationale works like this: buying an $8 matcha five days a week for 48 weeks works out to $1,920 a year. Even if you saved that money, the median house price in Australia’s capital cities combined is now $1.1m and the median unit price $738,778, according to Cotality research published this month. Saving $40 a week and not getting to have a matcha during the work day may not seem worth it if even a 10% deposit feels out of reach and future job security is uncertain – especially amid the disruption to white collar industries caused by AI. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads Housing affordability has reached its worst on record, according to the Housing Industry Association, as rising borrowing costs have eclipsed the recent retreat in prices. The average homebuyer nationally needs to save more than eight years for a deposit, and more than nine years in Sydney. A recent report from realestate.com.au found that a typical household earning $125,000 a year could only afford 12% of the homes for sale across the country – also a historical low with the previous low watermark being 14% in 2008. Australians on lower incomes are virtually shut out of the market. The analysis showed that a household earning $76,000 could afford just 2% of homes on the market. Meanwhile, workers’ wages have barely kept up with inflation since cost of living exploded from 2022, making it harder to save. Healey says the social contract, where working hard and saving for the future ensured you would get ahead, has broken down. “Not only are you paying into the system with superannuation, but there is no guarantee now that if you do well in school, get a relatively good job [and] accrue university debt, that you’re going to be able to enjoy … even a fraction of the prosperity that previous generations took for granted,” he says. Healey says doomspending is “perhaps a more advanced version or symptom of the same underlying feeling”. Cambridge dictionary, which began tracking the word last year, defines doomspending as spending money that you cannot afford in order to make yourself feel better, which people sometimes engage in when they feel anxious and uncertain about the future. “It’s not merely just, ‘Oh, things are a little expensive here and there [and] the major things are expensive, I deserve a little treat,’” Healey says. “It’s a quite significant paradigm shift [to]: ‘I don’t believe in what the future is going to look like any more … It’s much more rational for me to spend that money in the present and to enjoy what I have in front of me.’” Terry Rawnsley, a senior economist at KPMG, says it is a “perfectly rational decision” to spend money on things that make you happy now, when the alternative – buying a home in the future – is unattainable. Rawnsely says this phenomenon isn’t just evident among people in their early 20s, but also for some millennials in their 30s who have found that “things haven’t worked out for them as it has for previous generations, and so they are having a different mix of priorities in their lives”. “This is where superannuation has probably given people a financial safety net when they retire, as it was designed to do so,” he says. Kayshini Logeswaran, 28, a business analyst in Sydney, says she has a “good, stable job” but saving up for big things like overseas holidays still feels out of reach. Logeswaran says companies’ shifting of roles to AI and general cost-of-living pressures are making her more fearful of the future. She considers indulging in some little treats worth it if they make her feel good in the moment. “Whenever I go out or go for a walk I always make sure I get my favourite coffee: it’s something that keeps me happy and sane,” she says.

headline: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape
trail_text: We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply
body_text: John Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget. The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say. Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so. Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now. Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out. More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property. It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing allowed a property Ponzi scheme to develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity. Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels that deny younger generations the chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security. UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitating leasehold/freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?). The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities. Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers. And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse. The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”. In an academic article published in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.” The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market. Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start. It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy. There was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000. Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500. The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term. Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell. There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”. However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discredited help-to-buy scheme for new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness. Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth. However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.

headline: Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption
trail_text: London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open
body_text: Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works. Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period. Passengers travelling between London, north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period. Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works. Engineers hope to use the quieter festive days to carry out about £152m of works to improve reliability and capacity. The biggest engineering work is expected on the lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough. Most Great Western services to Wales and the west of England will start and finish at Reading, with some services diverting around Oxford to London Euston, from 27 December until 4 January. The work also means Elizabeth line services west of Paddington and Heathrow Express services will not resume after Christmas until 31 December. Birmingham’s main station, New Street, will be closed from the start of Christmas Eve until 29 December to replace overhead power supplies. No trains will stop or pass through, with rail replacement buses serving the city centre. Passengers using east coast mainline services run by LNER and other operators may wish to avoid travel on Christmas Eve. Work at Doncaster means trains between London, north-east England and Scotland will be partly replaced by rail replacement buses from Newark to York, adding two hours to journeys. The Great Eastern mainline out of London Liverpool Street will be closed for 10 days from Christmas Day for track replacement in east London, meaning no Greater Anglia or Elizabeth line rains will run through the area, with no direct trains from Norwich to London. TransPennine services between Leeds and Manchester will be slowed for six weeks from Christmas Day with the closure of Huddersfield station. Network Rail’s group director, system operator, Anit Chandarana, said: “Christmas is a time when many people want to be with family and friends, and most of the railway will be open to help them get there. We have worked with train operators to keep services running wherever we can on the busiest travel days and to provide alternative journey options where work affects the usual route. “We are sorry that some passengers will face disruption. The days between Christmas and new year are by far the quietest of the year and give us the best opportunity to complete major projects such as the power supply upgrades at Birmingham and Paddington. Our teams will do everything they can to keep people moving, and we urge passengers to check their journeys before setting off.” • This article was amended on 2 November 2026. An earlier version said that Elizabeth line services west of Paddington and Heathrow Express services would not resume after Christmas until 31 January; that should have said 31 December.

headline: Avanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summer
trail_text: Intercity train operator’s compensation bill likely to top £70m this financial year amid rise in claims across network
body_text: Avanti West Coast paid out more than £20m to passengers in just three months this summer in refunds for disrupted journeys on Britain’s main intercity rail network. The intercity operator paid out almost as much in a four-week period to 25 July – £9.3m – as its annual profits for each of the past two years. It repaid a further £12.2m in the subsequent eight weeks. The “delay repay” compensation bill for slow-running or cancelled services has been spiralling upwards across the railway network in recent years, according to official figures, with Avanti the biggest payer – although never before at this scale. Most train operators are yet to publish this year’s payouts. According to the most recent published financial figures from the Department for Transport (DfT), covering all operators, the total passenger compensation for delays rose to £150m across the railway in 2024-25, up 8% compared with the previous year, of which about 27% was Avanti’s payouts (£40.5m). Fare inflation and efforts to make passengers aware of their rights have contributed to the industry’s soaring bill, as well as the delays themselves. Compensation has become increasingly automated and some operators now proactively repay passengers who have been delayed. Under the contracts that replaced the franchising system since the pandemic, train operators’ income comes from fees paid by the DfT instead of depending on fare revenue, with the taxpayer instead taking any profit or loss from ticketing income or refunds. Avanti, which is due to be taken into public ownership next year as part of Great British Railways, paid out more than £50m in 2025-26, and is expected to pay out more than £70m this financial year. As heatwaves hit the railway, fewer than half of Avanti trains ran on time in July with passengers delayed by an average 19 minutes, according to figures from the Office of Rail and Road. Its peak payout period also covered the incursion of a large herd of cows on the tracks for several hours one Tuesday. Long-distance operators typically pay out the largest sums, with customers more likely to claim owing to the expense and the chance of delays reaching the 60-minute threshold where fares are refunded in full. Avanti and GWR are unusually generous among long-distance operators in paying compensation for delays after 15 minutes, when passengers are eligible for refunds of 25% of the fare paid. GWR, which runs trains from Wales and the south-west to London, and LNER, which runs London-Scotland trains on the east coast mainline, were the next highest refunders in 2025, paying back £29.7m and £28m respectively.
