The number of compensation claims filed by passengers across Great Britain’s railway reached 9.1m in 2026, up almost 10% year on year, with 80% of the claims approved, according to data from the Office of Rail and Road. An Avanti West Coast spokesperson said: “We apologise to customers affected by train delays. A range of factors can impact service performance, and we are working closely with our industry partners to improve punctuality and reliability across the network. “To make it as easy as possible for customers to claim compensation when things don’t go to plan, we are committed to ensuring that customers are able to promptly receive any compensation for delays and offer automatic delay repay for journeys delayed by 15 minutes or more.” According to Avanti, between May to August this year it was directly responsible for only 23% of those delays, with Network Rail or other operators responsible for the majority, as well as external factors such as trespassers on the line. GWR said the increase in its delay repay payments this year was “driven largely by repeated heatwaves, with prolonged periods of unprecedented temperatures affecting both trains and railway infrastructure”, including track defects, points failures, speed restrictions and train cooling issues. The operator said the payments recognised “the impact of disruption and helping maintain confidence in rail travel”, adding: “We’ve recently made efforts to increase publicity of the scheme, with clearer, more frequent announcements onboard delayed trains and on social media disruption updates.” LNER, which compensates customers only after 30-minute delays, did not provide updated financial data. According to DfT research, about half of disrupted passengers claim compensation, but an increasing number are satisfied with the process and results. Most train operators now resolve more than 99% of claims within 20 days, according to data from the rail regulator. A DfT spokesperson said it was “acting to tackle the root causes of disruption” and making it easier for passengers to get refunds, adding: “Under Great British Railways, we will make it quicker and easier to claim compensation through an easy-to-use service, which will also be available wherever passengers purchase their tickets.”

headline: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports
trail_text: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough
body_text: A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars on Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less. More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq ⁠100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough. The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. ⁠The index has fallen ⁠more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure. Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported stronger profits for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profits in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations. Amazon fell 1.8% after reporting weaker profits for the summer than analysts expected. The company also disclosed that it had spent more this year than anticipated. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12%, wiping $500bn from its market capitalization, to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make AI investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI datacenters have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build-out of datacenters. A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward. Such losses overshadowed an otherwise mixed day for the rest of Wall Street, with the S&P 500 roughly evenly split between gainers and losers. Expectations are high broadly for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month. The Associated Press contributed reporting

headline: BP profits hit ‘obscene’ 18-year high as Iran war drives up oil refining margins
trail_text: Oil giant comes under fire from climate campaigners, as its earnings reach $8.46bn while ‘innocent civilians suffer’
byline: Jillian Ambrose, Damien Gayle and Lauren Almeida
body_text: BP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an 18-year high of $8.46bn (£6.3bn), as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices. The energy company hailed a “banner quarter” on Friday, with its underlying replacement ⁠cost profit – a key measure of its income – almost quadrupling in the three months to the end of September, from $2.2bn in the same period a year ago. The jump meant BP’s quarterly profits hit their highest level since the $8.9bn recorded in 2008. BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told Bloomberg TV: “It really was a banner quarter for the refining business. We had very strong margins from the BP-operated refineries, we also had very strong underlying performance. We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market.” However, climate crisis campaigners said it was outrageous that BP was profiting so handsomely on commodities causing serious damage to the environment. It is just over a week until diplomats will meet in Antalya, Turkey, for the Cop31 UN climate summit. Recent climate-linked disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal will be at the forefront of many delegates’ minds. There are likely to be tensions with fossil fuel producing countries, which have sought to stymie calls for a transition to clean energy. BP’s strong results also come as motorists in the UK face high fuel prices, with diesel now at 198.79p a litre, according to estimates from the RAC. The cost of petrol has also risen, with an average price of 172.92p a litre, compared with 132.83p in late February, before the latest conflict in the Middle East began. Jonathan Noronha-Gant, of the campaign group Global Witness, said it was “obscene that polluters are continuing to cash in on the fallout of the war in Iran, making more bumper profits from spiralling oil prices while innocent civilians suffer. “These massive profits come as ordinary people across Europe are struggling with the rising cost of living, with many struggling to afford to heat their homes as winter arrives,” he said. Danny Gross, of Friends of the Earth, said: “As millions of households brace themselves for a cold winter, huddling under blankets and clutching hot-water bottles as they struggle to pay their bills, BP is raking in huge profits while doubling down on gas and oil production and slashing investment in renewables.” Although the link between fossil fuels and climate breakdown has been known for decades, scientists directly linked carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel companies to dozens of deadly heatwaves for the first time a year ago. Yet more heatwaves swept across Europe this summer, with separate research suggesting they led to a record 50,000 excess deaths. As people in cities sweltered, infernos tore through forests and brush in parched rural areas. France experienced its largest area burned on record and fires blazed in usually cooler regions, such as the Cairngorms in Scotland. In the Pacific, a supercharged El Niño is brewing, with water temperatures reaching more than 3C higher than usual. The weather phenomenon is likely to be the most extreme of its kind in at least 1,000 years, dumping vast amounts of extra heat into an atmosphere already warmed by climate breakdown. “The climate crisis is not an abstract future threat,” said Clémence Dubois, head of global campaigns at 350.org. “People are facing deadly heat, destroyed livelihoods and growing insecurity now. Governments are being forced to find money to protect their populations, while fossil fuel companies are forecast to make extraordinary profits.” Record oil company profits come as the UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the North Sea’s Rosebank oilfield, after approving a licence for the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield earlier in October. BP’s quarterly earnings were bolstered by higher profits from the oil refining business as the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined fuels such as diesel and gasoline soared, earning almost $47 for each barrel produced. Although global oil prices have remained below the peaks recorded during the 2022 energy crisis, the pump prices for fuels, including diesel, have risen to all-time highs across the UK, Europe and the US in recent months because of severe disruptions to refineries in the Gulf region and across Russia. BP’s earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergies reported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel. headline: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’
trail_text: Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses
body_text: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit. Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets. Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars. Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic. Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist. TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis. An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report. Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets. The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025. The company said: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.” Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks. Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”. In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.” Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. “It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic. Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, including the FBI and the US Secret Service. Tether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m. The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to hackers. Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system. Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system. A spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.” The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment. Coinbase, another major cryptocurrency exchange, said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation. In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

headline: Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed
trail_text: With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct
body_text: ‘It was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one former Poundland boss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain. Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains. Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats. Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted to offer support to the high street. Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade. The chain’s potential demise comes after Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring specialist which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner in June last year, rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the whole chain by Martin Property Group. While the Northern Irish firm is still in talks about taking on Poundland, it is understood its offer amounts to about £15m. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood. This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News. One source who knows Poundland well said that Gordon Brothers had already taken about £10m in fees and interest out of the chain in the last year and that wanting another £30m was “egregious”. Gordon Brothers did not respond to a request for comment and has not confirmed this figure. Gordon Brothers said earlier this week that options for the whole and parts of the business “are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders”. Sources close to the process said Gordon Brothers was unwilling to accept the Martin deal as the latest offer includes only about £7.5m up front and the rest over the next two years, leaving uncertainty for creditors, staff and suppliers. One source said Gordon Brothers had sought bidders for the whole of Poundland but “the market had spoken” and only one little-known financial bidder with no history of running a large retail chain in the UK had come forward who might only go on to break up Poundland itself. Instead, the restructuring specialist is understood to believe that suppliers and staff would be safer with the “trusted established retail operators” who have already put forward firm offers for parcels of outlets that amount to about half of Poundland’s stores, which could be converted to their formats. A deal may yet be agreed with Martin over the next 10 days, especially with political pressure from Andy Burnham. On Friday, he told the Telegraph: “We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.” For now, Gordon Brothers appears more keen on a break-up after losing faith in the likelihood of Poundland finding a route to long-term profitability amid tough times on the high street and heavy competition. Rapid inflation on the cost of goods and labour, energy and business rates in recent years has forced Poundland to take a hit on profits and sell products for more than £1, including items for £5 or more. In the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited. High inflation – triggered first by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and then the Middle East conflict – has exposed a business model which always appeared to have a shelf life. In most supermarkets a two-litre bottle of milk costs over £2, a pack of KitKats is at least £1.50 and a tin of Heinz baked beans is about £1.40, according to the price comparison site Trolley. Cutting the size of Poundland has, meanwhile, reduced its scale, making it harder to get good deals from suppliers to protect margins. Poundland has also admitted that it made mistakes in recent years, including putting its Pepco clothing ranges into stores, which proved unpopular with UK shoppers. The expansion of cut-price chains such as Savers, The Range, B&M, The Works and Home Bargains alongside budget online rivals such as Temu, Shein and Amazon means the cheaper end of the UK retail market is now very crowded. Meanwhile, the low-wage shoppers that make up the core of Poundland’s clientele have little spare cash for non-essentials amid rising household bills. Those with more to spare have more options in their supermarket shop, where they are increasingly locked in by loyalty-card-linked discounts. Poundland’s pre-tax losses widened to £85.3m in the year to September 2025, from a loss of £45.4m in 2024, as sales at its outlets in the UK, Republic of Ireland and Isle of Man slid almost 12% to £1.55bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House. In September Poundland said its revenues had returned to growth, up 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period, but sources said the business was not generating enough cash to pay off its loans. US-headquartered Gordon Brothers has a long history of involvement in selling off the assets of UK high street businesses, including offloading the stock and and fittings of failed retailers such as Toys R Us. It previously owned the British fashion brands Laura Ashley and Ben Sherman, where it oversaw the closure of their stores, and it recently bought LK Bennett, which has also closed its stores this year. One advisory expert said Poundland’s owners had intended the buyout to be a rescue operation rather than a break-up but ultimately: “Gordon Brothers has ended up doing what Gordon Brothers do. Leopards do not change their spots.” He said Gordon Brothers was likely to “come out looking like the worst version” of a restructuring firm. The number of stores likely not to find an immediate buyer “might not be as catastrophic as half” but it was unlikely buyers would be found for all, he added. Poundland’s possible demise is part of a wave of consolidation of similar outlets over the past decade. Poundworld closed its 350 stores in 2018, and Poundland bought its rival 99p Stores in 2015. Poundland then closed about 200 of its then 800 UK stores in a restructuring last year. Poundstretcher was bought by Majestic Wine’s owner, Fortress, in 2024. Poundland itself has a rocky history during which it has passed in and out of the hands of investment firms. Founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, the company was listed on the London Stock Exchange in 2014 at a value of about £750m by its then owner, the buyout firm Warburg Pincus. Just two years later, Poundland agreed to a £597m takeover by Steinhoff, the South African retail conglomerate, after the British chain struggled to digest the takeover of 99p stores. By 2018, Poundland had to seek new investment after an accounting scandal at Steinhoff and was hived off into Pepco, a company formed from Steinhoff’s European retail business. Poundland was then preparing to rejoin the London stock market when the Covid pandemic hit in 2020, scotching those plans as high streets across the UK closed down for months. Last year, with costs rising, Pepco was looking to sell. Gordon Brothers stepped in, snapping up the struggling chain with its £1 deal. It remains unclear whether someone new will flip another coin to bet on turning Poundland around.

headline: How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?
trail_text: The incident at Binance could be the biggest theft of any kind in history. We answer some key questions
body_text: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a $6.3bn heist that, according to experts, is likely to be the work of North Korea. This is not the first time a crypto market has been targeted by hackers, and the rogue state has a track record of this type of theft. Here we answer some key questions about what’s happened: Just how big a deal is this? It could be the biggest heist of any kind in history, according to Elliptic, a consultancy specialising in crypto-related crime. The incident, which took place late on Thursday, is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto hack, the $1.5bn one targeting the Bybit exchange last year. Elliptic says there does not appear to be anything comparable in the pre-crypto era. “This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” says Tom Robinson, the consultancy’s chief scientist. “Before Bybit, that record was held by Saddam Hussein, who took $1bn from the central bank of Iraq in Baghdad on the eve of the 2003 Iraq war. The Binance theft is more than six times larger.” So what exactly is cryptocurrency? This digital asset operates online, outside the traditional financial system. There is no physical version of the most popular form of crypto – bitcoin – or its peers, such as Ethereum, Ripple and Dogecoin. A cryptocurrency such as bitcoin runs on a combination of encryption, which is the sort of technology that keeps your WhatsApp messages safe, and peer-to-peer networks that allow computers to connect without a central server (think of the music-sharing sites like Napster at the turn of the century). In short, the owner of a bitcoin (or part of a bitcoin; you can buy them in fractions) has access to a private key – like a long password – which is needed to access the funds. These transactions are all stored and displayed on a publicly available ledger, like a school register, known as a blockchain. You typically store your private keys in a “crypto wallet”. There are varying estimates for how many cryptocurrencies there are but Coingecko, which monitors the market, claims there are more than 22,000 coins. The entire market is worth about $2.7tn, so it is not a surprise that hackers and rogue states looking for funds are interested in a corner of the global finance industry that has so much money, is largely unregulated and is vulnerable to digital thieves. And what is a cryptoexchange? A cryptoexchange is where you buy, sell and trade digital assets such as bitcoin. They host your crypto wallets, which are typically “cold”, meaning they are not connected online and can be kept safer from hackers. A smaller amount sits in “hot” wallets which are linked to the internet so they can be used for quick withdrawals, making them of greater interest to hackers. Binance is the world’s largest of these exchanges in terms of the number of trades it carries out every day – at a value of about $95bn daily. How was Binance hacked? It does not appear that private keys were hacked. Instead, a Binance engineer’s laptop was infiltrated, which in turn allowed the attackers to drain “hot” wallets. Binance later added that there were “additional points of breach” in its systems as well as the laptop. “Hackers rarely crack the cryptographic keys themselves,” says Robinson. “They instead target people with access to those wallets. Binance says the attack involved a compromised engineer’s laptop, along with other points of breach. This gave the attacker a way into Binance’s internal systems. From there, they made Binance’s own systems sign transactions that sent the funds to the attacker.” More than $2.5bn of the $6.3bn was taken in one transaction alone. “Crypto exchanges are safer than they used to be, but not immune to attacks such as this,” says Robinson. “This hack shows that even the biggest exchange can be breached through one employee’s laptop. What matters most for customers is whether the exchange can cover the loss. Binance says it will repay everyone from its own funds.” How do the hackers get hold of their haul? They will have to “cash out” the crypto and turn it into legitimate money, known as fiat currency. Chainalysis, a crypto research firm, has said the attackers used “never seen before” laundering patterns to exfiltrate the affected assets. Phil Larratt, a senior director at the consultancy, says the thieves will now try to convert the crypto into fiat money in a process that “takes weeks and months, if not years”. “The process is patient and sophisticated,” he says. Laundering methods used by crypto hackers include visiting less scrupulous exchanges, using swapping services that exchange one type of crypto asset for another, and accessing brokers who will convert crypto to cash in exchange for a cut of the proceeds. Do we know who did it? This attack has been attributed to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, a name assigned to it by the US government. The communist state, short of cash and hamstrung by sanctions, has a strong track record of crypto hacking. TraderTraitor emerged from Lazarus, a group working from North Korea’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, a military intelligence agency. Last year TraderTraitor was blamed for the $1.5bn theft from the Dubai-based Bybit. Elliptic and two other crypto analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea. Elliptic said some of the funds taken from Binance have already been traced to wallet addresses used in a cryptoexchange hack last month that is also thought to have been carried out by operatives from the rogue state. Rafe Pilling, the senior director of threat intelligence at the cybersecurity firm Sophos, says North Korea had previously hacked conventional financial targets such as the Bangladesh Central Bank and even cash machines. But crypto delivers bigger potential rewards, he says. “Crypto is less well regulated, easier to move, easier to launder and that makes it a more enticing target for North Korea. And as a result you have groups like TraderTraitor that are specialising in attacking crypto firms and getting away with huge payments.” Are my crypto investments safe? Any guarantees will be coming from Binance itself, rather than any regulatory or government-backed safety nets. The exchange said in a post on X that it would “cover all losses” and “user funds are safe”. It also said it had frozen about half the funds targeted in the hack, stopping the thieves from making off with that tranche of cryptocurrency. In Australia, you can claim a capital loss on your tax return if you can offer proof that a crypto asset was lost or stolen. However, most customers won’t have any legal protections. Crypto users are not covered by formal deposit protections in countries such as the US, UK or Australia if things go wrong, including if an exchange is hacked or ever goes bankrupt. Customers of regulated banks are guaranteed capped refunds – up to £120,000 per customer per bank in the UK, and $250,000 in the US – but only if the lender goes out of business. It will not pay out claims if there is a hack but the bank keeps operating.

headline: ExxonMobil and Chevron top estimates for Q3 as Americans feel gas price pain
trail_text: Business is booming for two biggest US oil companies, with both benefiting from higher prices and record production
body_text: ExxonMobil and Chevron reported better than expected quarterly results on Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production. The boon for oil companies has simultaneously been a major pain point for consumers, who say the higher cost of living, especially gas prices, will affect how they vote in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Gas prices for consumers are an average $4.20 a gallon, according to AAA, nearly $1.20 a gallon higher than a year ago. In a recent Harris poll for the Guardian, 36% of voters said the rising cost of living is the single most important issue this election. Besides the disruption caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine that have driven up the cost of fuel, Exxon is also seeing strong production in its fields in Guyana and the Permian Basin in the south-west. Chevron said its results include one month of production in Venezuela where it is making a big investment. Utilization at Exxon’s US Gulf coast refineries was at 100%, and Gulf coast diesel production was at the second-highest on record. The price of diesel, currently about $6.32 per gallon, is up 71% since last year, according to AAA. Regular gasoline is up about 38% in the past year as well. Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chair and CEO, said investments such as the expansion of its Beaumont refinery in Texas have contributed to an increase in its distillate production by approximately 40% since 2019. For the third quarter, net income more than doubled to $3.72 per share. On an adjusted basis, profit totaled $4.23 per share, easily topping the average analyst estimate of $4.12 per share. Revenue during the three months ended in September rose 33% to $113.16bn, also beating estimates. The company, based in Spring, Texas, also raised its quarterly dividend to $1.07 and set a $20bn stock buyback plan. Houston-based Chevron said on Friday it earned $9.9bn, or $5.06 per share, during the third quarter, as revenue surged 36% to $67.8bn. Its results handily topped estimates. Chevron, the second-largest US oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. Last month it announced it will invest $7bn over the next five years in Venezuela. It said on Friday that following an accounting-related change during the quarter, it was now including those results. In pre-market trading, Exxon shares rose 1.9%. The stock is up 64% in the past 12 months. Chevron shares rose 1.1%. At a recent rally in Georgia on 24 October, Donald Trump told the crowd – despite, he noted, warnings from his advisers not to – that higher gas prices had ultimately been a blessing for all Americans. “Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas and they’re coming to Oklahoma and they’re coming to Louisiana and they’re taking that oil,” Trump said. Trump said that “fake headlines” would claim that he “is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump”. “But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m gonna say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune,’” he said. The Associated Press contributed to this report

headline: UK house prices grow at slowest pace in two years as mortgage rates rise
trail_text: Average price for property stands at £273,566 in October, flat on previous month, says Nationwide
body_text: UK house prices grew by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years, as higher mortgage rates put off potential buyers. The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566 in October, flat on the previous month and down from 0.8% in the year to September, according to the lender Nationwide. The slowdown in the market comes as buyers face higher borrowing costs. This month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years. The average stood at 5.99% on Thursday, according to the financial information provider Moneyfacts, while the average two-year rate was not far behind at 5.97%. There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages. While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week the monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%. Robert Gardner, the chief economist at Nationwide, said the Middle East conflict had fed concerns around inflation, driving up expectations of higher interest rates. Property prices are likely to fall further, he said. “Surveyors report that new buyer inquiries remain weak. “Consumer sentiment dipped noticeably in October, with households becoming less confident about the outlook for the general economy as well as their own financial situation in the year ahead.” Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, added that the impact of rising mortgage costs “eclipses any support measure announced in this week’s budget”. This week the chancellor, John Healey, confirmed the government’s new £4.7bn Your First Home scheme, which is designed to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”. Bill added: “The absence of major shocks from the chancellor may produce a modest relief bounce in coming months. However, asking prices will need to reflect the much tougher financial landscape that buyers face.” Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said the government’s new scheme could provide a “modest boost” to the market but that prices were likely to remain subdued next year.

headline: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
trail_text: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective
body_text: Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October. Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking. South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week. However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally. Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground. Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating. South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007. In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song. The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen. Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question. Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open. For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed. The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging. However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated. Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed. “The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said. “There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.” Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts. “The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.” In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said. While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

headline: Hold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happen
trail_text: The chancellor’s budget giveaway is, unfortunately, a reflection of how life works in the global aerospace business
body_text: It wasn’t a “nothing” budget for engine-maker Rolls-Royce. The company was handed £1.25bn from public coffers to part-fund the development of a next-generation engine for single-aisle commercial planes. The chancellor buried this giveaway in two short sentences in the stodgy middle of his speech, presumably because it would look too much like a case of corporate welfare just after he had grumbled about the £14bn extra we’ll be paying in debt interest this year. And it’s not as if Rolls is on its uppers. The pride of Derby is the UK’s most radically improved major company of the past few years. It sits in fifth spot in the FTSE 100 index, sporting a market value of £105bn, and has enough spare cash to spend up to £9bn on share buy-backs this year. But there had been an air of inevitability about this subsidy ever since the company’s chief executive, Tufan Erginbilgiç, talked earlier this year about how he would “appreciate” financial support from the government in developing the UltraFan engine. Appreciate? What he meant is that other governments would cough up if the UK didn’t. That, unfortunately, is how life works in the global aerospace business. Subsidies are a down payment on the jobs and factories that can follow. Germany, reeling from the woes of its carmakers, would love to have a bigger slice of the hi-tech UltraFan action (and has a role in the gearboxes anyway). The US aerospace industry is a study in how generous defence contracts subsidise civil operations. Healey couldn’t ignore those facts of aerospace life. What’s more, one can see how the possible long-term return on the £1.25bn could turn out very well. “The single biggest opportunity in aerospace over the next 50 years is to secure a UK engine position on next generation narrow body programmes,” said the government’s strategy document for advanced manufacturing. Aircraft engines are high-value products. About 80% would be exported, doing wonders for the national balance of payments. Projections of “tens of thousands of highly skilled jobs” eventually are credible. The big “if” is that Rolls hasn’t yet got a slot on a narrow-body programme. The company exited that market a couple of decades ago; its civil aircraft side currently only supplies engines to the smaller wide-body long-haul market. Rolls needs to get on to either the Airbus or Boeing narrow-body programmes, and success or failure won’t be known until some time around 2030. Thus the government is only contributing to a joint 10-year £2.5bn research and development programme, including a “demonstrator” engine to show off the gas turbine tech. There will be spillover benefits for defence capability but, ultimately, UltraFan needs to be on a civil project. It is a big bet – and Rolls, even if it wins, will need a corporate partner at a later stage. The point, though, is that the UK government had to get behind the UK runner in this race. One trusts the guarantees on UK jobs and investment, beyond the 3,300 roles supported initially, will be written in triplicate in the final agreement. That must be a fundamental condition of support on this scale. But this is an occasion to hold your nose. Rolls is plainly not a corporate pauper but, yes, it is justifiable to shove £1.25bn its way. Andy Burnham’s “reindustrialisation” talk would otherwise ring very hollow.

headline: Eight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report finds
trail_text: Angela Eagle tells industry ‘people are sick of excuses’ as pollution levels remain high despite billions in investment
body_text: Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after the environment watchdog said their companies continue to pump effluent into Britain’s waterways at “unacceptable” rates. “People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”. There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, in 2025, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry. The watchdog’s environmental performance assessment ratings of water companies added up to 16 “stars” out of a possible 36, a fall from 19 the previous year, and the lowest score since the process began. Changes could be imposed on the industry, Eagle warned: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and-branch reform cannot wait.” The UK is one of only two countries in the world where the provision of water is fully privatised. The other is Chile, where water privatisation was imposed in the 1980s by a military dictatorship. Overall, there were 2,666 pollution incidents in England in 2025 – a 40% increase on 2016, the EA said. Thames Water had the most, followed by Anglian Water, United Utilities, Yorkshire Water and Southern Water. The Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Eagle was preparing to take “further action”, with “tougher consequences” for executives at failing companies. Defra said it would “set out a clear set of improvement actions”, such as “tackling leakage”, “reductions in pollution incidents” and “improving customer satisfaction”. Rules that took effect last year would block bonuses for executives at companies receiving a one-star rating. Environmental campaigners called for stronger action. “This is a system that rewards shareholders and creditors while our rivers, wildlife and bill payers lose out,” said James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action. Thames Water, the worst offender, ought to go into special administration immediately, he said. “Ministers must end the failed privatisation experiment, review alternative models including public ownership, and give regulators the power to make polluters pay not the public.” The pollution figures came as the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat pooled their data in a joint report for the first time – a step towards combining currently fragmented regulatory responsibilities under a single watchdog. But Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said a new regulator “must be more than a merger of existing institutions”. “It needs a clear legal duty to restore nature, strong environmental targets and the powers and resources to enforce the law across the water industry, industrial agriculture, and chemical companies,” he said. Water UK, the industry trade body, said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough. “While more than half of all pollution incidents last year were caused by blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies, there is clearly more work to do. “It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth and end sewage entering rivers and seas.” • This article was amended on 30 October 2026 to more accurately reflect the findings of the Environment Agency’s report that, owing to changes made during the editing process, had not been clearly set out.

headline: Union in plea to save Poundland from administration, with 12,000 jobs at risk
trail_text: Gordon Brothers files notice of intent to begin process after rejecting management-backed rescue bid
body_text: The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland. It bought the struggling chain for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025. Only one bidder, Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, was interested in buying the entire chain and working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, the chief executive. Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer, which was worth less than the £30m in debts that Gordon Brothers took on when it bought the chain. The threat of administration leaves thousands of shop workers facing uncertainty in the run-up to Christmas. Rival cut-price retailers, including Poundstretcher, The Range and B&M, have reportedly expressed an interest in taking on some Poundland stores. Bally Auluk, national officer of the Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers, said: “It has been an incredibly distressing week for Poundland staff who have had to watch from the sidelines as a multibillion-pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1. “We are urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider and to prioritise a unified buyer who will protect the livelihoods of [more than] 11,000 people.” Williams wrote to workers this week saying the rejection of the bid from Martin Property Group was “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”. The board of Poundland said on Thursday: “We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment.” The board said the notice of the intention to appoint administrators had been filed “in order to bring stability” as “despite enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole”. Poundland would be “working closely with our advisors to identify and deliver the best possible outcome”. Gordon Brothers hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal in August to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m, fuelling fears of a breakup, despite improved trading. Poundland, founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, was the first UK-wide chain based on a single price. However, it now offers a broader range of price points and goods in a similar way to its rival Poundstretcher, which was founded in 1981. Rising costs and heavy competition from chains such as Savers, Home Bargains and B&M, as well as from the major supermarkets, have meant pound shop chains have been gradually disappearing. Poundworld closed its 350 stores in 2018, and Poundland bought its rival 99p Stores in 2015. Poundland then closed about 200 of its then 800 UK stores in a restructuring last year. In 2020, Poundstretcher was due to close about half its then 270 stores in a rescue restructure but it now has more than 300 outlets after being bought by Majestic Wine’s owner, Fortress, in 2024. The board of Poundland said the latest sale process for Poundland had attracted offers from several established retailers “which collectively cover a significant part of the business” and that “offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs”. Five initially interested parties include the US company Fortress, which is thought to want to take fewer than half of Poundland’s stores to add to its existing chain. CDS, owner of The Range, and B&M are understood to be considering a bid for at least some stores.

headline: US economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7%
trail_text: Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom
body_text: The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace. Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace. The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven ⁠business investment has more than ⁠offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East. The change is in stark contrast to households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%. The consumer price index, a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September. Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”. Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely. Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation. But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending. Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment, measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.

headline: Lloyds executive criticises Healey for linking bank tax rises to energy bill support
trail_text: Chief financial officer says he hopes budget measure is temporary as sector provides loans that fuel growth
body_text: A senior Lloyds Banking Group executive has criticised the chancellor for linking bank tax increases to energy bill support for UK households, as he warned the government against extending the higher levy beyond March 2028. Lloyds’s chief financial officer, William Chalmers, acknowledged that the economic environment was “challenging” but said the government should not seek to ease pressure on households at the expense of the banking sector as it provides loans that could fuel UK growth. “Ultimately, it is important that the UK banking sector is able to deliver banking services to businesses and households and communities in a cost-effective way, in order to promote UK growth,” he said, adding that it was also important that the sector stayed internationally competitive. “We therefore very much hope that yesterday’s tax increase is indeed a temporary measure, to help ensure the business environment remains consistent with supporting long-term investment,” Chalmers told journalists during an earnings call on Thursday morning. The comments came less than 24 hours after the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans to double the bank surcharge, which is levied on top of corporation tax, to 6% from January. He said the increase would be “time-limited”, lasting 15 months, in order “to pay for immediate support on energy bills”. However, Chalmers questioned the government’s decision to tie bank taxes to rising energy costs, amid concerns that doing so could open the door to an extension, or a further rise in the levy, after the 15 months expire. “We hope this tax rate is limited,” he said. “When we look forward, what impact, if any, will energy prices have on that? Well, I don’t see an obvious linkage between energy prices and bank taxes. “In fact, if anything, it makes it even more important that we’re able to lend into the real economy and secure growth, which is the best defence against energy price impacts that might otherwise be there on the UK economy.” While the Treasury has promised to legislate for the 15-month tax-rise limit in the financial bill, senior bankers and industry lobbyists have privately questioned whether a further energy crisis could throw that limit out the window. Some pointed to Spain, where a two-year windfall tax on banks, meant to alleviate cost of living pressures in 2022, was ultimately extended a further three years, and increased from 4.8% to 7% for the country’s largest banks. “We are a major taxpayer,” Chalmers said: “We paid around £1.8bn of corporate taxes year to date, and it is important to us that we have a stable and a predictable tax regime.” Lloyds revealed on Thursday that its third-quarter pre-tax profits almost doubled from a year earlier, from £1.2bn to £2.3bn. However, that increase largely reflected the £800m hit it took last year after setting aside another £800m for compensation relating to the motor finance scandal. The bank’s results were also supported by a 10% rise in net interest income, which measures the difference between what it charges borrowers and what it pays to savers, showing the bank continued to benefit from higher interest rates. Net interest income has risen across the banking industry, as inflation expectations – driven by higher fuel prices triggered by the war in the Middle East – pushed up interest rates.

headline: Shell profits double to $10.8bn as Iran war pushes up margin on oil
trail_text: Energy firm to return $5bn to shareholders as climate campaigners criticise high profits
body_text: Shell has doubled its profits in the last quarter after the Middle East conflict drove up the price of oil and gas and created shortages in the global market. Shell reported on Thursday morning that it made an adjusted profit of $10.8bn (£8.1bn) in the July-September quarter, up from $5.432bn in the third quarter of 2025. The results beat analyst expectations for a rise to $10.33bn. The company also raised its share buyback programme – it plans to return $5bn to investors for the next three months, up from $3bn in the last quarter. “Shell’s relentless focus on operational performance enabled very strong results in a quarter with continued severe disruption to the global energy system,” the Shell chief executive, Wael Sawan, said. Climate campaigners criticised the jump in profits, which pushed Shell’s shares up by 3% in early trading on Thursday morning. “As fossil-fuelled storms, floods, and soaring costs wreck communities, oil executives like Shell’s Wael Sawan are popping champagne on the deck of a sinking planet. We are paying with our lives and pay-cheques while they cash in on our misery,” said Philip Evans, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace. Shell’s profits were also higher than in the second quarter of this year, when it made $9.836bn. Shell told investors earlier this month that it expected the profit margins at its refineries to climb to $42 for each barrel of fuel produced in the July to September period, far above the margins of $24 a barrel in the second quarter of this year. These margins are also significantly higher than the previous record for petroleum products of about $28 a barrel, set in the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war, due to shortages in the global market caused by severe damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia. Shell’s gas production has been hard hit by the Middle East crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf. The company’s prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels ⁠of oil equivalent ‌per day fell by a third as the Middle East war unfolded. Europe’s benchmark gas price index reached an average of almost €64 per megawatt-hour in the third quarter, up from more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the global oil price benchmark averaged $94.90 a barrel, up from $69.10 a barrel in the same quarter last year. The steadily rising commodity prices helped lift the market value of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company, now the largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index. Shell’s share price rose to a record high of more than £40 a share earlier this month as the global oil price climbed towards $117 a barrel, the highest price in six months.

headline: Toblerone owner sues British vegan chocolate brand over chunky shape
trail_text: Catherine’s Originals denies Mondelēz claims in London high court of ‘passing off’ and trademark infringement
body_text: The owner of Toblerone is taking legal action against a tiny British vegan chocolate brand that it claims has been copying the Swiss chocolate bar’s famous chunky shape. Mondelēz has filed papers at the high court in London accusing Catherine’s Originals of “passing off” and trademark infringement with its O’bar – a length of chocolate divided into segments each with a rounded semi-oval hump. The 200g bars cost £9.20 for a milk or plain variety, and as much as £10.55 for more exotic flavours such as pumpkin spice or cinnamon swirl. A standard milk chocolate Toblerone can be bought for £2.50. Catherine’s Originals, founded by the then teenager Catherine Dodd in 2021, makes its chocolate in Walberton in Sussex, England, and sells them via markets, online or by subscription. Dodd said the shape of her bars reflected an O for Originals. “We stand firmly behind the product and identity we’ve created,” she said. “We strongly disagree with the claim concerning O’bar and are working with our legal team to defend our position. Honestly, it’s fairly frightening for a small business we’ve put so much care and hard work into building. But being a smaller business does not mean being afraid to stand up for what we’ve created.” The brand’s legal adviser, Stephen Lowry of Brandsmiths, added: “Our client disagrees with the claim and considers O’bar to have its own distinctive design and identity. We look forward to addressing the matter through the appropriate legal process.” Mondelēz International, which also owns Britain’s Cadbury and Belgium’s Côte d’Or chocolate brands, said: “The iconic Toblerone shape is one of the most recognised and distinctive product designs in the UK and across the world, and has been a hallmark of the brand since 1929. “We have a responsibility to protect our trademarks and intellectual property, which we take seriously. We have attempted to resolve this matter constructively and directly with Catherine’s Originals over several months but unfortunately have been unable to reach an agreement. We cannot comment further on ongoing legal matters.” The budget chain Poundland was forced to delay the launch of its Twin Peaks bar in 2017, which had two humps rather than the single peaks of Toblerone, after a legal warning from Mondelēz. The bar eventually relaunched, after Poundland modified the colour of the packaging and the shape of the bar, and is still on sale today. Toblerone itself was forced to change its packaging in 2023 to remove the image of the Matterhorn mountain peak. That came after some of the chocolate bar’s production was moved outside Switzerland, falling foul of marketing restrictions relating to the use of Swiss iconography. • This article was amended on 29 October 2026. An earlier version said Belgium’s Côte d’Or was a coffee brand. It is in fact a chocolate brand.

headline: Thames Water creditors to vote on emergency £2.4bn loan as cash runs low
trail_text: Campaigners say costly new funds will lead to higher bills, which company denies
body_text: A group of creditors to troubled Thames Water are poised to vote on whether to grant an emergency £2.4bn loan to keep the company afloat, as campaigners raise concerns it could add £40 to each household’s bills in interest alone. A consortium of creditors, called London & Valley Water, will vote on Thursday on whether to increase a funding facility for the debt-laden utility company to £5.4bn to keep it operating to autumn 2027. The company’s class A creditors, which include BlackRock, Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, last year granted it a £3bn loan at a 9.75% interest rate. This month, Thames Water said it needed a further £2.4bn cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its extensive debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”. Thames Water has previously said that customers will not be on the hook for the interest on the £3bn loan, but it has almost run out of money and not paid down the debt. Analysis by the campaign group We Own It showed that the £2.4bn loan, if it is granted on the same terms and added to bills, would cost £40 per household in interest alone, and £454 per household if the entire loan amount was included. London & Valley Water insisted it would not be added to bills. Andy Burnham is now deciding whether to allow a takeover deal by the water company’s creditors, which would entail writing off fines and reducing environmental commitments. He is also mulling whether to nationalise the company or take another form of state control. Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners have said Burnham should instead put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “Since privatisation, £11.9bn has been extracted from Thames Water. They have already had more than enough of our money. If they cannot survive without yet another excruciatingly expensive bailout, this government must let them go bust and bring them into special administration, followed by permanent public ownership.” The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames Valley. It has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away in 2024, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy. In 2025, Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat MP for Witney, along with campaigners and junior creditors, unsuccessfully took the water company to court over the £3bn loan. On the proposed £2.4bn loan, he said: “The creditors will likely hand Thames Water yet another massively overpriced rescue loan, which customers will end up having to pay for. “This is just another short-term fix, paid for by customers and taxpayers. The government has had more than two years to make up its mind. It’s time it did so. Put Thames Water into special administration now.” The creditors have approved 15 previous consent requests from Thames Water. The company said this month it had so far drawn £2.65bn of the £3bn available under the “super senior” facility. Prof Dieter Helm, an economist at the University of Oxford, doubted that a turnaround of Thames Water could be “properly funded” and said further loans were merely postponing an “inevitable” special administration. He said: “The future investment programme for the turnaround will not be properly funded. Thames – and indeed much of the rest of the industry – is caught between a political rock and a political hard place.” Conquest added: “During a cost of living crisis, this government cannot continue to reward Thames Water’s failures at our expense.” Burnham has been looking at ways to take control of Thames Water in an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control. He has urged his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a list of policies for the utility company. One option under consideration is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run. A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Additional liquidity from creditors will enable the investment to continue uninterrupted while the business seeks a recapitalisation. Customer bills are set by Ofwat, and this funding does not add any costs for households.” A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “No customer bills will be used to pay for the costs of Thames Water’s rescue financing. These costs are borne entirely by the class A creditors. “Creditors have stepped in to provide the billions of pounds of private capital needed to ensure Thames Water’s record infrastructure investment programme can continue, avoiding the need for any government financial support or taxpayer funding.”

headline: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
trail_text: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
body_text: The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years. Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement. Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%. Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week. During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations. “Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.” The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”. “The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said. September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”. Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”. “I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said. Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases. Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year. “The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month. The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School. “Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said. Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months. The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters. By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise. “If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
