On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

headline: Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world
trail_text: The chancellor is right to focus on pure affordability, but £100 handouts and delayed decisions won’t shield consumers from the next wave of price hikes
body_text: Amid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher energy prices that have resulted from the Iran war have pushed up inflation, are eating into households’ incomes, are a drag on businesses – and are the main reason why the forecast for GDP growth next year was cut from 1.6% to just 1%. And energy was the focus of Healey’s sole surprise in his consumer-facing policies – the £100 payment to 20m households in A-D council tax bands to help with fuel bills this winter. It will be funded, in effect, by tapping the banks for a few quid for 15 months via the bank surcharge. But the chancellor will know that £100 won’t look generous when the bills land. Gas prices are still rising, and leading supplier EDF’s latest prediction is that the regulator’s price cap will be hiked by £466 in January, pushing the annual rate for an average household to £2,189. When Labour took office in July 2024, talking naively about taking £300 off bills over the life of the parliament, the cap was £1,568. No surprise, then, that the messaging on energy is shifting. Here is the passage in Healey’s speech that hinted at big changes ahead: “Today I’m setting a new course on energy: to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe. From this point, our Labour government’s priority is first and foremost cheaper energy, with clean power key to achieving this.” Thank goodness for the reset towards affordability. It is long overdue. The biggest impediment to economic growth, including the prime minister’s longed-for “reindustrialisation”, is the cost of energy in the UK. There is little Healey can do about international gas prices, but he can do “deep reform of our energy system”, as he put it. So what’s the plan? That, unfortunately, is where the “new course” turned blurry. Take the promise to introduce “a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills”. The ambition is laudable, because energy bills have become littered with levies and charges – everything from socialising unpaid consumer energy debt to funding Sizewell C – that should more naturally be funded from general taxation. It’s about time the Treasury took an interest in such hidden taxes. But the costs don’t disappear just because they are placed within a new framework. The tough question is how much a chancellor is willing to fund from Treasury coffers in the interest of lower upfront bills for consumers and business. It is not a small question, because wide-ranging definitions of levies can produce figures as high as £15bn. It’s good that Healey is demanding no new levies (unless they bring down bills), but that’s not the same as hacking into the existing thicket. Funding for green hydrogen projects is being taken on by the Treasury, which is a start. But come back in next year’s spending review, it seems, to discover the size of Healey’s scythe. More urgency is needed. There was a bit more clarity on the electricity generation side. “This government will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid,” said Healey. That reads as a strong hint that offshore wind commissions will be slowed until prices fall (which probably requires a fall in borrowing costs for developers) and the upgrade of the grid is more advanced. Very sensible: sequencing matters, as the alarming costs of “wasted wind” demonstrate regularly. But Healey’s ambition to “break the grip of international gas prices” by switching older renewables projects on to lower fixed-price contracts is not new. Ed Miliband, when energy secretary, said the same. The test is how hard ministers are willing to twist the arms of renewables owners, who are very attached to arrangements that give them jackpot revenues when gas prices are high. The basic tension remains: for consumers to win, somebody has to be paid less than they were expecting. So, yes, one can applaud the change of tone and direction. A reset in energy policy to prioritise affordability was bound to arrive eventually. The drive to clean power also had to be a drive to cheap power. But one cannot yet say the new approach is joined-up. Policies to drive the electrification of homes and transport were not turbo-charged, which they need to be to reduce long-term dependency on gas and oil. And “deep reforms” to the electricity market are, to put it gently, a work in progress. More urgency needed.

headline: Business secretary writes to Poundland owner as administration fears build
trail_text: Jonathan Reynolds’ team has written to Gordon Brothers, which bought retailer for £1 last summer, to ‘establish the facts’
body_text: The business secretary’s team has written to the owner of Poundland amid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening to overshadow John Healey’s budget. Sources said that Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm that bought the 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, looks set to appoint administrators to the struggling retailer. Jonathan Reynolds has written to Gordon Brothers to establish the latest situation at the company, which employs 12,000 staff. The company rejected the only bid to take on the group – which includes the 50-store Dealz chain in Ireland – as a solvent company in its entirety, from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, earlier this week. It is understood Gordon Brothers is poised to file a notice of intention to appoint the advisory firm AlixPartners as administrator, potentially as early as Wednesday. This legal measure would protect Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. Three independent directors appointed to help oversee a sale have quit amid disquiet over the move towards insolvency. The timing of the move threatened to overshadow Healey’s first budget as chancellor, amid longstanding complaints from companies over costs imposed by the government on businesses. Barry Williams, the boss of Poundland, wrote to workers saying the rejection of the bid from Martin Property Group was “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”. An improved bid from the Northern Irish firm has not been ruled out. However, sources said that Martin’s bid fell well short of Gordon Brothers’ hopes to recoup the £30m in debts it took on with Poundland. The bid is understood to be worth more than £15m, with only a portion upfront. One industry source said that suppliers to Poundland were already beginning to hold back on deliveries, making it tougher for the group to secure a rescue bid. Industry insiders said Gordon Brothers wanted to move quickly as Poundland was flush with stock ahead of the busy Christmas period. A quick break-up of the chain, with parcels of stores and stock sold off, would lead to a maximum return for the restructuring specialist, sources said. “Gordon Brothers has a simple choice. It can accept an offer from Martin Group, worth at least half of the £30m which it secured for £1, or get significantly more than that by busting the business,” a source said. “The only thing that can change this is if they feel the moral or public relations duty.” Reynolds has instructed his chief strategic business adviser, David Bickerton, to “establish the facts” regarding Poundland’s potential collapse, as first reported by the Financial Times. He is understood to have contacted Gordon Brothers but not Poundland’s management team, which had backed the Martin Property Group bid. A business department spokesperson said: “We know this will be a concerning time for Poundland employees, their families and communities across the UK. “This is a commercial process and ultimately a decision for Poundland’s owners, so it would not be appropriate for the government to comment further.” Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more cash – up to £30m – and keep more jobs in place long-term by breaking up Poundland and selling off the stock and stores to a variety of retailers. There could be as many as eight interested parties, including the US investment firm Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and the owner of The Range. B&M is thought to be interested in taking on at least some outlets. However, one industry insider said: “Who is going to take on 600 high street stores?” He predicted that up to 500 could be left without a buyer in the event of a break-up, leading to significant job losses. The general secretary of the Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers, Joanne Thomas, said: “I am calling on the government to do everything it can to save 11,000 jobs, which are mainly done by women and part-time workers. “Over the past five years, around 250,000 jobs have been lost in the retail sector. Job security is a key priority for a successful economy; therefore, I urge the government to grant the retail sector the same priority and strategic support it provides to other vital industries.” Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.

headline: ‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget
trail_text: OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis
body_text: British households face a “grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said. As John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued its report showing a sharp downgrade for growth in 2027, household disposable incomes and the public finances, despite the measures taken by the chancellor. Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help with soaring energy costs, the watchdog said household disposable incomes after taking account of inflation would fall by 0.6% next year. The downgrade - compared with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes that the OBR was forecasting in March – was driven mainly by higher energy costs. While forecasting a modest recovery from next year, the OBR warned that families were facing among the weakest decades for growth in real household disposable income on records dating back to the 1960s. Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said disposable incomes in 2029, after taking account of inflation, were on track to be only 1% higher than in 2019 – before the onset of the Covid pandemic. “It’s a pretty grim picture”, David Miles of the OBR said. “If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are right now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income,” he said. “That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.” As the impact from Donald Trump’s war hits British households, businesses and the government finances, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for countries worldwide. Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support. He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule, which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring. As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans. As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March. Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills. However, with the fallout from the war steadily mounting, the OBR warned that Britain’s resilience to the conflict that had been recorded so far this year would begin to fizzle out. While it upgrades its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, it slashed its estimate for next year from 1.5% to 1%. Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise. Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund had issued growth upgrades for the UK within recent months. “There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said. However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled. With a tentative pause in the fighting while Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain. Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

headline: GSK shares dive as weaker vaccine sales unnerve investors
trail_text: British pharma company one of biggest fallers on FTSE 100 despite better than expected financial results
body_text: Shares in GSK slid on Wednesday despite the UK drugmaker reporting better than expected financial results, as investors were unnerved by weaker sales of its respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and shingles vaccines and recently launched medications. Britain’s second-biggest pharmaceutical company reported a 19% decline in pre-tax profit to £1.9bn in the July to September quarter and £318m of restructuring charges, with more to come. Core operating profit and core earnings per share rose 5% and 1% respectively, however, beating analysts’ expectations. Shares dived as much as 7% at one point on Wednesday, and despite later paring back such losses to a 3.8% drop, it was the second-biggest faller on the FTSE 100 index of blue-chip businesses. Luke Miels, who took over from Emma Walmsley as GSK’s chief executive in January, has announced a number of acquisitions, including a £7.9bn US cancer specialist and a major cost-saving programme in July to speed up drug development. GSK said turnover in the third quarter was £8.9bn, a 5% rise compared with the same period last year thanks to strong sales of its HIV, cancer and lupus medications. Vaccine sales, however, dipped 2% to £2.6bn, with sharp declines for the shingles shot Shingrix, down 5%, and the RSV vaccine Arexvy, down 24%, partly the result of tough year-on-year comparisons, while sales of meningitis vaccines rose 12%. Sales of the recently launched asthma drug Exdensur also disappointed analysts. Referring to Arexvy, Miels said: “When we look at our market share versus Pfizer, we still have leadership there. We are getting good orders outside of the US, so I think we need to just see what happens over the next couple of months to have the full picture.” Investors are also worried about the loss of patent protection for GSK’s blockbuster HIV drug dolutegravir towards the end of the decade, which means other drugmakers can make cheaper, generic versions. GSK has set a goal of generating more than £40bn in total annual revenue by 2031 as it rebuilds its cancer business. Miels said the company was slightly ahead on its three-year cost reduction plan to save £1.9bn a year, which involves simplifying operations to invest more in research and development (R&D). The restructuring will cost the company £2.4bn, and most of these charges will come this year and next. The impact on the UK was relatively limited, Miels said, with some cuts to support jobs such as in human resources and procurement at its headquarters in central London and in hubs in Poland and India. “You never want headquarters to be too big; I want people on the bench in the lab,” he said. GSK is also reorganising its vaccine business in Belgium, with increased use of digital tools and automation expected to lead to about 1,200 job losses, but the country will continue to produce the bulk of its vaccines. GSK had nearly 67,000 employees globally at the end of last year, its annual report showed. GSK stuck to its annual forecasts, with R&D spending set to grow faster than sales. It expects to begin 22 late-stage studies of new medications by the end of the year. Miels said Shingrix had the “potential to grow next year”, describing it as “a remarkable product”. He pointed to two large studies of the vaccine to assess the reduction of dementia risk, as well as its effects on major adverse cardiovascular events such as heart attacks and strokes, with the first data available in 2029 and 2027 respectively. Both studies could be “transformative” for the shingles vaccine, he added. Britain’s high street chemists have reported a rise in demand for the shingles vaccine after studies showed a correlation with a reduced risk of dementia. “We’ve got a lot of studies that show a correlation. We’re trying to demonstrate causation,” Miels said.

headline: The RBA has primed the market for an interest rate rise. But what will it mean for unemployment?
trail_text: Central bank forecast that unemployment might have to move even higher makes it clear how much more the RBA cares about inflation than full employment
body_text: Back in July, the June inflation figures killed off chances of a rate rise; yesterday, however, the September inflation figures all but guarantee a rate rise next week. The September figures are a bit quirky because the Bureau of Statistics published both the monthly and old quarterly ones. The monthly measure had annual inflation jumping up from 4.0% to 4.3%; while the quarterly measure – which the RBA has in the past said was more important – remained steady at 3.9% (and if anything fell very slightly): Click here if this graph does not display But that did not matter: all focus was on the 4.3% number, even though monthly figures are much more erratic and subject to jumps and falls in certain prices. In September, as was the case in July and August, petrol prices were the big driver. Automotive fuel rose 9.4% in the month. They also look set to rise another 7% when the October figures come out next month: Click here if this graph does not display It means that around half of the increase in inflation in September came from fuel prices. This was followed by holiday costs, which always go up at the start of spring: Click here if this graph does not display The impact of petrol prices over the past three months is, of course, all driven by oil prices oddly refusing to react to either the RBA raising rates or Donald Trump declaring mission accomplished in Iran: Click here if this graph does not display The impact of petrol prices since June on overall inflation is obvious when you look at inflation with and without those prices. Without petrol prices, inflation would be at 3.6% – well below the 4.3% official rate: Click here if this graph does not display And yes, 3.6% is higher than the Reserve Bank would like, but it does perhaps give an indicator of what we are dealing with here. Inflation isn’t galloping ahead due to domestic pressures; rather, it is remaining higher than the RBA’s target due to the flow through of oil prices into costs (including holidays) and directly in fuel prices. We are also seeing the impact of AI datacentres on inflation. As with last month, once again the price of games increased. That’s because we are not talking about board games, but those which require computer chips – the same type that are in such high demand for datacentres. The ABS noted that the 15.5% price rise for games, toys and hobbies in the past year was “driven by price increases in memory and storage components being passed on to consumers”. So that’s nice: enjoy paying more for Grand Theft Auto VI. But look, anything I tell you here isn’t going to make a lick of difference. The RBA is going to raise rates next week. Before the CPI release, the odds were about 61%. Afterwards they rose to 87% and a rise to 4.85% is fully priced in to happen in December: Click here if this graph does not display What is interesting, though, is it makes it clear just how much more the RBA cares about inflation than its other mandate of full employment. When the September unemployment figures of 4.7% were released, the market quite rightly dropped the likelihood of a rate rise to a less than one in five chance. But the RBA was clearly not happy with that. Last week, the deputy governor of the RBA, Andrew Hauser, participated in a fireside chat to Citigroup investors. He made it clear the RBA was not happy with things, saying “the inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in the August report”. He further said that there is “an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3% to 3.5% is the new normal … that is the central banker’s nightmare”. And boom, the odds of a rate rise increased from 22% to 51%, and they kept going up. Click here if this graph does not display That means the RBA can now easily justify raising the rate next week – after all, they primed the market to do so. Hauser yesterday walked back his comments somewhat when the RBA appeared before the Senate estimates committee. He said that it was surprising “how well anchored inflation expectations remain”. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here And as for the increases in unemployment? That is rather less of a concern for the RBA. Greens senator Nick McKim asked Michele Bullock whether she was “worried … about the pace of the increase in unemployment, specifically what rise in unemployment would give the RBA cause for a reasonable concern that we would head into recession?”. He asked this due to unemployment rising from 4.1% in January to 4.7% in September. Claudia Sahm, a US economist, argues a 0.5% rise in the three-month average of unemployment over a year is the point at which an economy enters recession conditions. Right now, Australia’s three-month average unemployment rate has risen 0.45% in the past year, and if the October rate remains at 4.7%, it will break through the 0.5% mark: Click here if this graph does not display Bullock replied: “We’re not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate at this stage. We do forecast that it has to gradually move up … I can’t be specific about what that number is. What I can say is we think that it’s probably above where the unemployment rate is at the moment.” So that’s nice. Sleep well knowing that Australia’s unemployment rate is rising but the central bank will increase rates again, knowing it might send it up even higher. Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

headline: Australia’s inflation rate rises to 4.3%, fuelling fears of fifth interest rate hike this year
trail_text: CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis
body_text: Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with a key gauge that strips out volatile prices also elevated, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week. The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred measure of consumer prices, called underlying inflation, came in at an annual 3.6% to September. RBA officials have strongly indicated the board may need to lift borrowing costs further to drag price growth back toward its 2.5% target, citing concerns of a “materially worse” inflation outlook. The CPI release comes shortly ahead of the central bank’s next monetary policy decision on 3 November, when most economists are tipping another cash rate increase. The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, described the inflation numbers as “too high” at Senate estimates on Wednesday, shortly after the data was released. He said there was a “nightmare” risk that longer-term inflation expectations would pick up, making it harder to get inflation out of the system. “We don’t think it is necessarily crystallising yet, but it is a particular risk,” Hauser said. The cash rate, which informs lending rates including mortgages, already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years, after four rate hikes in 2026. A fierce political debate has erupted in Australia over what is driving the cost-of-living squeeze, with critics pointing to a mix of high fuel prices caused by the Iran conflict, government spending and poor productivity. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said on Wednesday that while “we accept our part in the fight against inflation”, high oil prices and a recovering private sector were the main causes of the rise. “The most important thing that can happen for Australians under pressure is to see an end to this war in the Middle East,” Chalmers said. “This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living and for inflation, right around the world.” Growing unease CPI figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday show that costs for everyday goods and services are rising at the same time as unemployment lifts, making life uncomfortable for households. Transport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran. While higher fuel prices are trickling through the economy, there are price pressures everywhere. Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs were up 5.2%. Stephen Smith, partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the RBA had “little appetite to allow inflation expectations to drift higher after such a prolonged period above target”. “The difficulty is that the economy is already slowing. Household spending is subdued, the labour market has softened and the housing market has weakened,” Smith, who is expecting a rate rise next week, said. The escalating expenses have fed into the growing political unease in Australia and elsewhere, as voters express their discontent with cost-of-living pressures. Housing, which is the single biggest category in the CPI, was the largest contributor to annual inflation, according to the ABS, followed by transport costs. Builders have been passing on higher costs for materials and labour for new dwellings, while electricity prices are also elevated. Josh Gilbert, market analyst at eToro, said inflation was turning into a “higher-for-longer” story in Australia. “Anyone holding out for rate relief may need to pack plenty of patience, because another hike looks imminent after today,” Gilbert said.

headline: Plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs say
trail_text: The public accounts committee has said the risk to billpayers is ‘extraordinary’
body_text: The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog. MPs on the public accounts committee (PAC) have warned the government that the cost of the Sizewell C nuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48bn, leaving bill payers on the hook to provide an extra £9.8bn to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12bn over its 60-year operating life. Taxpayers and consumers face a “high level of risk”, according to PAC, after the government agreed to take a near-45% stake in the nuclear plant, which is considered a successor project to the heavily delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear plant in Somerset. Under the terms of the multibillion-pound deal, which will be paid for through taxes and energy bills, the UK government holds a 44.9% stake while French state nuclear developer EDF has a 12.5% stake. The rest of the funding has come from private investors including the British Gas owner Centrica, which holds a 15% share, alongside the Canadian investment group La Caisse, which holds 20%, and the investment manager Amber Infrastructure, which has a 7.6% stake. The UK government was forced to take a larger than expected share of the project after buying out Chinese state nuclear developer CGN, which had been allowed to hold a 20% stake in Sizewell C before national security concerns emerged. The watchdog warned that while the British public could be called on to shoulder multibillion-pound cost overruns, the nuclear project’s private investors would only need to put in an extra £30m. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the PAC chair, said: “The high level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers for the construction of Sizewell C is extraordinary. Private investors look set for significant returns on their investments, while customers are likely to be saddled with higher energy bills.” He urged the government to “focus on the successful delivery of this project”, and in building confidence in the UK’s nuclear industry more broadly, so that taxpayers will “never be put in this position again”. A government spokesperson said the report “completely ignores that investors are incentivised to complete construction as cheaply and quickly as possible” through the terms of the deal. “Once operational, Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system, cutting costs for families up and down the country, and the project is already making good progress with over 2,000 workers on site,” the spokesperson added. Sizewell C is projected to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn, with construction completing between 2039 and 2043. The committee has called on the government to provide the scenario analysis it used to underpin its cost estimates for the project within the next three months. It also asked ministers to provide an update on the project’s development every six months to keep track of its progress. Critics of the project, including Alison Downes of the Stop Sizewell C campaign group and Prof Steve Thomas of Greenwich Business School, who provided joint evidence to the committee, have suggested that the cost of abandoning the project today would be lower than the cost of paying inflated energy bills over 60 years “multiple times over”. They called on the government to rule out using this funding model for future nuclear projects. “All it offers is a free ride for investors and financial pain for households,” they said in a joint statement. Tom Greatrex, the chief executive of the Nuclear Industry Association, said Sizewell C would provide “clean, reliable and constantly available power” that could save households billions from paying the cost of balancing the grid or building extra network connections. “Currently, the consumer is footing a bill of £2.8bn so far this year to manage a dysfunctional grid, paying both for wind to stop generating at some times, and for gas-powered backup at others,” he said. • This article was amended on 28 October 2026. Costs for Sizewell C are regulatory threshold projections, not a government estimate as an earlier version said.

headline: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny
trail_text: A regulator to keep the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank on mission is starting to look essential
body_text: Two winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and now John Healey is going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn. Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing. Cue, also, another round of debate about whether Healey is engaged in fancy financial footwork to get around the constraints of his fiscal rules. Reeves rewrote those rules in her first budget in 2024 to allow the value of financial assets – such the NWF and BBB’s loans and stakes in companies – to be netted off against the public debt. To fans, the principle makes sense. As long as the PuFins’ assets maintain their value and cover the interest on the government’s extra borrowing (a critical condition), it’s a way to boost investment. More critical projects can be built sooner, and possibly more cheaply; more companies may prosper to the eventual benefit of the public purse. Critics, such as the right-leaning Centre for Policy Studies in a report last week, see a “financial wheeze” that disguises the true level of government borrowing and stores up trouble, as the Blair-era private finance initiative did. The thinktank called for the wings of the PuFins to be clipped. Healey, it is safe to assume, will ignore that advice. The PuFins fall squarely within his theory for growth – the idea of “crowding in” private investment and spreading money around the regions. In Healey’s support, one can say state-backed co-investment vehicles are not new. Governments of all hues have used them. George Osborne even launched a Green Investment Bank. And the NWF, despite its misleading name (it’s not a Norway-style wealth fund), to some degree merely replaces infrastructure lending that might have been done by the European Investment Bank in pre-Brexit days. As for the BBB, its focus on “scale-up” capital for young, fast-growing companies is designed to address a gap that has been a source of grumbles for decades. Both institutions are useful. There are questions, however, about potential overuse. Are the NWF and BBB sticking in all cases to their core role of “additionality”, the idea that PuFins should bring something extra to the party? They are not meant to be substitutes for private capital. They must crowd in rather than crowd out. The line can appear blurry at times. This column has questioned the £25m that BBB invested in Kraken Technologies, the software firm being spun out of Octopus Energy. How was that a case of “helping smaller businesses get the finance they need”? Kraken was valued at a thumping £6.45bn, so wasn’t a small firm; and £25m was a rounding error within a wider $1bn fundraising. Similarly, the Centre for Policy Studies surely has a point when it wonders why the NWF lent to Scottish Power, “an investment-grade company with an investment-grade Spanish parent” on projects to upgrade to the electricity grid. The NWF’s ability to make long-dated loans probably helped the financing, but regulated utilities are supposed to be big enough to stand on their own feet. Weren’t there better targets for the NWF’s loans? To be fair, the websites of both the NWF and BBB are stuffed with case studies that fit the government’s priorities uncontroversially. For example, the latter’s follow-on £100m investment in Oxford Quantum Circuits, a quantum computing firm, was big and on-message. And, so far at least, the promise of gilt-like returns is intact, or not disproved. The BBB cites a “3.9% five-year adjusted return” but says the number would be higher if one was counting only its commercial activities. In the case of NWF, it’s too soon to tell: last year’s return on equity was -2.6% but a gilt-like number was only ever promised in 2030-31. The requirement to co-invest with hard-nosed private investors is probably helpful. But there’s still the issue of being additional. “Assessing additionality is not a precise science, but rather an exercise in judgment,” concedes the NWF in its impact framework. An Office for Budget Responsibility-style body to scrutinise those judgments is starting to look essential. As the allocations from the Treasury increase, there is a risk that the definition of “additional” gets stretched. At the moment, the PuFins are only ultimately answerable to their sole shareholders, the Treasury (NWF) and the business secretary (BBB). The Institute for Fiscal Studies, in its pre-budget assessment, said: “If the government follows the spirit of the guidelines, and aims to construct a portfolio of investments that align with government priorities and generate a profit, the cases where investment can occur through PuFins may turn out to be relatively limited.” That sounds like good advice. For the time being, there’s a fair argument there is room for more. The Resolution Foundation argues that, notwithstanding the extra £5.8bn from Reeves, the NWF’s capacity has “barely kept pace with inflation”. But policing the PuFins, and ensuring they stick to their “additionality” brief, is surely equally important. There will be problems if they behave like gannets. • This article was amended on 28 October 2026. The sole shareholder of the British Business Bank is the business secretary, not the Treasury as an earlier version said.

headline: HSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxes
trail_text: As John Healey’s budget decision looms, lender reports 32% rise in profits
body_text: A top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK over tax increases expected to be announced in Wednesday’s budget. HSBC’s chief financial officer, Pam Kaur, said there was “no pressure”, particularly from shareholders in its cornerstone Hong Kong market, to shift out of London despite lobbyists warning higher tax bills could drive big banks’ business abroad. HSBC on Tuesday revealed a 32% rise in third-quarter profits to $9.6bn (£7.2bn), alongside plans to give $2.7bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Lobby groups have for months warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills, with the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, saying he could even scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if Britain became “hostile” to banks. A handful of wealthy businesspeople have already said they are leaving the UK, with some criticising Labour’s tax policies. The Guardian revealed earlier this month that the chancellor, John Healey, was planning to tax Britain’s banks in Wednesday’s budget. He is likely to reverse the previous Conservative government’s cuts to the bank surcharge. “Irrespective of what happens on taxes, we are there to support our customers, and that is what we will do,” she told journalists during a media call on Tuesday. “We are very comfortable, we are domiciled in the UK and we remain in the UK. So that question is just not on the table,” Kaur said. HSBC has a strong shareholder base in east Asia, where it makes the bulk of its profits, and has twice been pushed to shift or split its operations in reaction to UK policies. That includes in 2015, when growing regulatory burdens and a new bank levy led HSBC to consider shifting its headquarters out of London to Hong Kong. The Conservative government later scaled back the levy to cover only UK-based assets, in a boon to HSBC. HSBC later faced pressure to separate the bank’s profitable Asian business from the rest of its operations in 2022, amid anger that the UK had forced the bank to cancel its dividend during the first Covid lockdown. Kaur gave broad backing to Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, saying the bank was “very encouraged by the government’s growth agenda”, adding that the bank would “just have to see how businesses and customers react”. The lender’s profit in the July to September quarter was boosted by higher interest rates, lower loan losses and smaller legal provisions compared with last year. However, its UK-listed shares fell 5.4% on Tuesday, causing it to lose its status as the biggest company on the FTSE 100. Kaur speculated that investors may have expected stronger forecasts for net interest income – which is the difference between what banks charge for loans versus what they pay out in deposits. HSBC’s net interest income rose to $9.3bn in the third quarter, up from $8.8bn a year earlier. That metric has been a flashpoint for groups campaigning for a UK bank tax, including the Trades Union Congress, which said bank profits have been driven by higher interest rates rather than their own improving performance. However, HSBC said its net interest income grew in the third quarter as a result of hedging strategies and a growth in deposits in Hong Kong, while UK deposits stayed flat. The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said HSBC’s results still showed banks could comfortably shoulder higher taxes. “Some in the finance lobby have tried every which way to stop tax rises in the budget. But these results make it blatantly obvious banks can afford to contribute more.” Abhijay Sood, an economist at the New Economics Foundation thinktank, said HSBC’s strong profits would be “difficult news to swallow for households struggling with rising mortgage costs”. He added: “Like other big banks, its profitability has depended on keeping interest rates on savings accounts low, and a stealth subsidy from taxpayers via the Bank of England due to quantitative easing. “While the rumours of a bank tax change in the budget are welcome, it is unlikely to go far enough … “The chancellor should go further by clawing back the stealth subsidy, and use this to fund inflation-busting investment and keep the essentials of life affordable for ordinary people.”

headline: Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’
trail_text: Administrator BTG says 738,144 firms struggling as calls grow for more support for private sector in budget
body_text: The number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to provide more support to the private sector in Wednesday’s budget. There were 738,144 businesses in “significant” financial distress in the third quarter of this year, up 1.6% compared with the same period last year, according to BTG. That is the highest level since the administrator’s closely watched “red flag” report began in 2004. The UK’s support services, construction and real estate sectors were among the most vulnerable, with the highest numbers of businesses in significant distress – at 118,695, 108,340 and 99,908 respectively. The hospitality industry was hardest hit this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866. Struggling food and drug retailers rose by more than 7% to 19,269, according to BTG, which is one of the UK’s biggest insolvency practitioners and changed its name from Begbies Traynor in February. The growing strain on UK companies comes as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to give his first budget on Wednesday, against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East disrupts the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis. The chancellor has vowed to use the budget to provide households and businesses with more “breathing space”. Mark Fry, the chief executive of BTG, said British businesses were “battling a combination of rising employment costs, inflationary pressures, higher energy prices and elevated borrowing costs. “Crucially, these pressures are not only affecting small businesses’ ability to operate, but also larger businesses’ ability to compete on a global stage,” he said. A freedom of information request by BTG also found that British businesses still owed £27.3bn in arrears to HMRC in VAT, corporation tax and PAYE at the end of August. About £24bn has been recovered since arrears reached a peak of £51.3bn during the Covid pandemic, compared with a pre-pandemic total of £11.4bn. “With £27.3bn owed to HMRC, high levels of recovery activity and record financial distress across the economy, many companies are approaching this budget from a position of financial weakness rather than strength,” Fry said. “We hear from businesses that structural hurdles, weight of red tape, employment legislation and the tax burden alongside high interest and energy costs will need to be tackled if this is to be a budget for business.” Last week the prime minister, Andy Burnham, promised that his government would “slash red tape” for businesses, with plans to make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses.

headline: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises
trail_text: British Retail Consortium says ‘dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs’ being kept from consumers
body_text: Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers. The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out. It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday. Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year. The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month. Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly. Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year. Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.” She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up. The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents. The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow. Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs. Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project working in partnership with over 200 hundred families. She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants surveyed for the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold. One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.” The report involves responses from 76 participants, of which 73 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month. Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued. “Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

headline: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs
trail_text: Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes
body_text: The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say. Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest against school underfunding, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures. Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis as households grapple with high and rising prices. The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude but the grievances are common. Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France but soaring energy costs were having a major impact. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter. More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state. France’s high public debt, stagnant economy and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position. France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund. Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%. Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity. “If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said. “It’s a warning signal.” Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver. “One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said. The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows. In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom. “All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, adding France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”. “The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.” President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending. “There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said. The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory. France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position. That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011. Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long. “We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.” While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes. “At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.” • Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

headline: The regime change we need for Thames Water
trail_text: Letters: Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton
body_text: Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question. Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed. Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name. The Cunliffe review’s single water regulator closes one gap. It leaves the larger one: water is still regulated apart from the air, land and soil it moves through, though sewage in a river is a land, soil and water problem at once. The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator, with a duty of candour, for air, water, land and soil, with three plain service duties: the service is delivered to standard, the money raised is spent on the service, and the charge is fair to the household that pays it. That, not ownership alone, is what a well-regulated industry looks like. Terry Barker Honorary professor of environmental sciences, University of East Anglia • Your report that Andy Burnham has instructed his team to explore radical solutions to the Thames Water crisis is welcome. But one solution already exists: the special administration regime (SAR), which could bring the company under temporary public control to stabilise and restructure it in the public interest. The forthcoming clean water bill may revisit legislation enabling greater public ownership, but reform must not delay action under existing powers. The Water Industry Act 1991 provides for special administration where statutory conditions are met. Thames Water’s financial instability, service failures and environmental record provide compelling grounds. We at River Action urge the government and Ofwat to petition the high court to place Thames Water into an SAR. A creditor deal will not address the causes of its decline. An SAR offers restructuring that prioritises customers, communities and the environment over creditors. The government should also commission an independent feasibility study of alternative ownership, governance and financing models, including public, mutual and not-for-profit options. No new legislation is needed: the powers and grounds to intervene in Thames Water already exist. Water is an essential public service. Its future must be secured in the public interest. James Wallace CEO, River Action • If Thames Water is effectively bankrupt, I can’t see why shareholders should get compensation. Broke is broke. Rather than old-style nationalisation, I would turn it into a social enterprise and put it under the control of its engineers. There would be no shares, no dividends, and all profits would be reinvested in infrastructure, such as pipes and new reservoirs. Philip Clayton London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees
trail_text: Application made for group claim seeking compensation for companies for alleged overcharging on customer card payments
body_text: Visa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees. The law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have lodged an application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal in hopes of pursuing a group claim that would compensate companies who, they claim, have been overcharged on customer card payments since October 2020. The claim will centre on multilateral interchange fees, which are set by Visa and Mastercard and then paid by businesses through their banks every time a customer pays by card. The argument is that the lack of competition has left businesses at their mercy – and paying higher fees on debit, credit and prepaid cards – as a result. The case will hope to claw back fees charged over the past six years, as well as interest on those losses. Sources close to the claim estimate that it could be worth about £5bn, based on the number of businesses allegedly overcharged between 2020 and 2026. A spokesperson for Mastercard defended the interchange fees, saying the potential group claim was “speculative” and part of a “growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation”. The case is being funded by Bench Walk Advisors, a London-headquartered firm that launched in 2017 and makes money from backing lawsuits. It is being led by Stephen Allen, a British businessman and former travel sector executive who has been pursuing Visa and Mastercard through a number of group legal actions since 2021. If the application is successful, an estimated 1m UK-based businesses, organisations and charities with less than £100m in revenues will be automatically included for compensation, unless they opt out. Their claims could be worth several thousands of pounds each. Larger businesses would have to actively opt in to be included in the claim, and could be due tens of millions over the claim period. However, it could take years for the case to reach a conclusion. Visa and Mastercard last year agreed to pay a combined $167.5m to settle a class action lawsuit in the US which accused the two companies of conspiring to keep ATM access fees artificially high. That lawsuit was originally filed in 2011. Commenting on the latest group claim application, a Mastercard spokesperson said: “We strongly disagree with the basis of this claim. Interchange plays a vital role in supporting the UK payments ecosystem, and ensures people and businesses can pay and get paid quickly and securely. “This speculative claim does nothing to support UK businesses or consumers and instead reflects the growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation. It is exactly the type of claim the UK government’s recently announced proposed opt-out class action reforms [put out for consultation this summer] are directed at preventing.” A Visa spokesperson said: “Visa continues to believe that interchange is a critical component to maintaining a secure digital payments ecosystem that benefits all parties, including consumers, merchants and banks.”

headline: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears
trail_text: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran
body_text: European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East. Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating. The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections. Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel. Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%. Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid. Meanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill. European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.

headline: Drive reindustrialisation from No 10 North or risk failure, MPs tell Burnham
trail_text: Ninety-plus Labour MPs warn civil service lacks skills to drive growth where it is needed and plan should be steered by Louise Haigh from Manchester
body_text: Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said. The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode”. John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”. However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work. “The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says. The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues. The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy. And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry. Andy MacNae, the MP for Rossendale and Darwen, who chairs the group, said: “I’ve got absolutely no doubt about Andy or John’s commitment to this, but there is a kind of inertia in government, within the civil service, within economic orthodoxy, that still says that growth policy is about cities – it’s about the places that are already doing well.” Instead, he said, reindustrialisation must be about “delivering jobs to the places that need them most.” He added: “It’s about making things again, and it’s about making the things that give us national resilience in a turbulent world.” He cited the government’s recent decision to nationalise British Steel, adding that reindustrialisation involved policies across government, from procurement to education. Steve Yemm, the MP for the former mining constituency of Mansfield, said: “Countries around the world are reindustrialising, yet too many in Whitehall still treat industrial policy as dangerous nostalgia. We need the prime minister’s full backing to challenge those outdated assumptions.” A third member of the group, Lorraine Beavers, the MP for Blackpool North and Fleetwood, said she was enthusiastic about the promise of reindustrialisation for constituencies like hers, but said: “If I have learned anything since becoming an MP two years ago, it’s that Whitehall doesn’t fix a problem unless it is told to.” In its industrial strategy, published while Keir Starmer was prime minister, Labour identified eight sectors ripe for growth, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and defence. In his conference speech, to which Healey had invited a young apprentice who had worked on building a new Mersey ferry, the chancellor said Labour would “get Britain growing. With hope for our young people. With good work, good jobs and a new age of industrialisation.”

headline: Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work
trail_text: Pilots report pressure to extend working hours and fears of penalties for declaring themselves unfit to fly
byline: Carmen Aguilar García and Sarah Marsh
body_text: Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report. The findings, based on a survey of almost 7,200 captains and first officers by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), include pilots reporting insufficient rest, pressure to extend working hours and fears of being penalised for declaring themselves unfit to fly. Almost a quarter (24%) of pilots admitted they usually continue flying rather than report themselves unfit due to fatigue, while another 16.8% said they call in sick instead. In aviation, fatigue can result from long duty hours, insufficient rest, irregular schedules and flying across time zones, which disrupt the body’s natural sleep cycle. It is a significant safety concern because it can impair pilots’ judgment, slow their reactions, reduce alertness and impair responses to unexpected situations. Under European aviation safety regulations, airlines are required to have systems in place to identify, monitor and manage crew fatigue. The survey, conducted in August, found that three-quarters of respondents had experienced at least one microsleep – a brief, involuntary episode of sleep – while operating an aircraft in the previous four weeks. Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta reported the highest levels of microsleeps. More than a third said they were not getting enough rest to prevent fatigue from building up over time. Despite the prevalence of exhaustion, only one in three pilots said they usually reported themselves unfit for duty when fatigued. Half admitted they had operated a flight in the three months before the survey when they should have declared themselves too fatigued to fly. Almost half of the respondents said they feared negative consequences from management if they reported themselves unfit because of fatigue, while just 11.9% trusted their airline’s fatigue reporting system. Ian Holder, the managing director of the aviation safety consultancy Baines Simmons, said the results showed persistent differences in how airlines and national authorities manage fatigue. “This survey captures how European pilots experience fatigue risk management in practice,” he said. He stressed that the findings represented pilots’ first-hand experiences rather than a direct measurement of aviation safety outcomes, but said the consistency of the results over three years highlighted areas requiring attention. Holder pointed to Finland and the Netherlands as evidence that stronger fatigue reporting cultures were achievable. Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta were among the most likely to fear management reprisals and the least likely to trust the reporting systems. The proportion of pilots who said they would fly when fatigued was higher in Spain, Ireland and France. Two in five of the pilots working for airlines based in Spain and a third of those working for Ireland- and France-based airlines said they usually fly when fatigued. That compares with only one in 10 of the pilots flying for an airline based in the UK. Only 15.6% of pilots at low-cost carriers believed their airline managed fatigue risks well, compared with 18.6% at ACMI or wet-lease operators – companies that supply aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance to other airlines. Almost two in five pilots said they had used commander’s discretion – allowing captains to extend crew working hours or reduce rest periods in exceptional circumstances – at least once in the month before the survey. But nearly 70% expressed concern about refusing to extend their duty, suggesting that a measure intended for exceptional situations may be accompanied by significant pressure on flight crews. Pilots at low-cost and wet-lease operators, as well as those working for airlines registered in Ireland and Malta, reported the greatest concerns. Capt Tanja Harter, the president of the ECA, said airlines and regulators should take responsibility rather than leaving pilots to manage the risks themselves. “This cannot be simply left to us – the pilots – to manage, while we are on the flight deck and expected to bring our passengers safely to their destination,” she said. She urged the European Union Aviation Safety Agency to strengthen fatigue management rules and ensure airlines comply with requirements for non-punitive reporting and the proper use of commander’s discretion. “Waiting for another three years to discover that nothing has changed is simply not an option,” Harter said. “The problems are identified, solutions are there, and we as the European pilot community are ready to contribute. What is needed now is the political will to act.”

headline: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
trail_text: VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs
body_text: Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump. The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections. The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners. Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year. Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars. It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia. Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US. The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US. Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US. “We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.” Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”. However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

headline: Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive
trail_text: Blaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulation
body_text: Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape. In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”. Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness. Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since. Thatcher unleashed the City with her “big bang” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”. It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”. With Labour back in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis. Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before. Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a “boot on the neck” of British business. There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons. First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example. When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. Its Employment Rights Act is the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow.
