It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year. The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expected increase in bank taxes in the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes. When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said Barclays would be able to absorb them. “I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to prompt growth. “This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signalling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.” Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax. It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations. The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills. The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.” Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”. He told the Times: “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”

headline: Economy set to worsen, with higher unemployment and weaker growth on the way, Jim Chalmers reveals
trail_text: Treasury is revising all the numbers for the midyear budget update as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead
body_text: Jim Chalmers has revealed December’s midyear budget update will project weaker growth and higher unemployment, as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead for the Australian economy. Two days after a senior Reserve Bank official foreshadowed the potential for another interest rate rise in under two weeks’ time, the treasurer in a speech on Friday morning will say “higher inflation is putting people under pressure, tighter monetary policy is weighing on domestic activity, and we can see that in the softening of the labour market”. “Treasury is in the process of revising all the numbers for the midyear update,” Chalmers will say, according to speech extracts seen by Guardian Australia. “Higher interest rates and higher inflation are likely to mean softer growth and slightly higher unemployment.” With the Albanese government already suffering the fallout from its ambitious tax reforms, the deteriorating economic situation will be a further blow to Labor and Chalmers’s popularity into the new year. Australian households are deeply pessimistic about the outlook and Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “things have to get worse before they get better”. • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Jobs data last week showed unemployment reached 4.7% in September, the highest in nearly five years. Despite this, financial markets on Thursday lifted the probability of a Melbourne Cup day rate hike to nearly 60%, according to ANZ. Kearns said the full impact of this year’s four interest rate hikes were yet to fully flow through to the economy – and that was before the prospect of a fifth. “The unemployment rate will increase further from here and we are yet to see the full decline in housing prices, so they are two pretty high-profile things that will impact how people feel about the economy,” he said. “We could be seeing unemployment at 5% and that will be a difficult threshold for the government.” ANZ economists on Thursday said they now expected capital city home prices to eventually fall by 13.5% – a record peak-to-trough fall – before regaining some ground in 2028. With little end in sight for the Middle East conflict, high fuel costs could also be a pain for motorists through the festive season and summer holidays. Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, agreed that “the next six to nine months will be pretty challenging”. “Growth needs to slow. The RBA is facing an inflation challenge that’s worse than they thought it would be as recently as August,” Auld said. By this time next year, however, the economy should be sailing in smoother waters. “Hopefully by that point we should have lower inflation than we have today,” Auld said. “That would be a step in the right direction.” The government will hope for an economic tailwind before the next federal election in 2028. But Kearns said Chalmers’ policy options were limited for now, as any additional cost-of-living relief threatened to exacerbate the inflation challenge. “The challenge is that the government has been criticised, and probably fairly, for contributing to inflation through high government spending. “But if they pull back on government spending to reduce inflation, they will be gonged for contributing to the rise in unemployment.”

headline: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
trail_text: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz
body_text: Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May. Yemeni Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield. Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday. It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely. Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt. Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf. However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman. Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%. Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year. American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”.

headline: Sainsbury’s expects challenging run-up to Christmas as households feel squeeze
trail_text: Supermarket urges government not to ‘further aggravate’ pressure on costs for businesses in next week’s budget
body_text: Sainsbury’s has warned of a “pretty challenging” market in the run-up to Christmas as households are “finding it tough” and food producers face rising costs. Simon Roberts, the chief executive of the UK’s second biggest supermarket, called on the government not to “further aggravate” pressure on costs for business in this month’s budget. He said it was “important this government does not repeat what we have seen in previous budgets” in raising business rates and employers’ national insurance contributions. “That’s been really hard,” he said. After Sainsbury’s and other industry leaders met government ministers last week, Roberts said he believed “this government is really listening to business” especially on helping to create more jobs for young people. Roberts added that food inflation was not “anything like” some of the high levels forecast earlier in the year but suggested high energy and fertiliser costs could push up food prices next year. Roberts said that in a more unsettled global environment the UK needed to “improve food resilience and grow and produce more at home”. He called on the government to increase tax breaks that support investment in technology – including irrigation and reservoirs – on farms, as the climate crisis is expected to lead to more hotter, drier summers such as this year’s. Shares in Sainsbury’s fell by about 3% on Thursday as the retailer revealed slower than expected sales growth of 2.6% in the six months to 12 September, with growth almost halving to 1.9% in the second quarter from 3% in the first. Strong online grocery sales – up 9% – and a 6% rise in sales of the retailer’s premium own-label Taste the Difference range helped with growth. Roberts said sales had slowed as shoppers had kept a tight rein on the number of items they bought because of a “focus on the cost of living” and had reduced spending on clothing and “big-ticket” items, such as furniture, at Argos. Sales at the catalogue shop were down 1.8% and Sainsbury’s general merchandise and clothing sales were down 3.4% in the half. The growth figures for grocery and clothing were also dented by comparison with last summer, when Sainsbury’s and other retailers experienced a boost to trade after Marks & Spencer and the Co-op were affected by cyber-attacks. Pre-tax losses for the half year widened to £63m from £14m a year before. However, the company reported a 5.2% rise in underlying profit to £366m, excluding the Argos catalogue shop, which is in the process of being sold off. The deal is expected to complete in February and the businesses to be totally separated by 2029. Sainsbury’s said it now expects an annual underlying profit of at least £1.02bn, slightly more than the £975m previously outlined. Charles Allen, a senior retail analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said the figures suggested Sainsbury’s was not expecting to increase profits in the second half of the year against a “tougher competitive backdrop as inflation returns and rivals prioritise sales growth”. Roberts refused to comment on speculation that Sainsbury’s was set to buy one of its rivals – amid reports that it had entered, and ended, talks to buy Morrisons earlier this year. However, the group said it planned to open 10 supermarkets and 25 convenience stores by March, which some analysts said reduced the need to seek a merger with a rival.

headline: Waitrose opens first new supermarket in eight years in north London
trail_text: Grocer launches Cricklewood store as part of £1bn investment plan, with Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, to follow next month
body_text: As part of a £1bn investment plan, Waitrose has chosen Cricklewood in north London as the location for its first supermarket in eight years. The upmarket grocer will open the store on Thursday and another supermarket in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, next month. It also plans four smaller stores next year, including a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge). In 2024, Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, said it planned to open up to four large supermarkets and 100 convenience stores over five years and would also refurbish a number of outlets introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections. The company has since ditched these specific targets and said it wants to focus on finding the right locations for new outlets. Tina Mitchell, the retail director at Waitrose, said: “Our supermarkets provide the ultimate showcase for everything that sets Waitrose apart – from our unmatched quality and industry-leading welfare standards to the expert service of our partners.” This year the company – led since January by the former Tesco executive Tom Denyard - also plans to refurbish 29 stores. After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems which led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. However, the chain is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, which now has a higher share of the grocery market, under some measures, after opening a number of new food-led outlets. Sales at Waitrose rose 4% in the six months to 1 August. However, its underlying operating profit slid by £7m to £103m as it invested in keeping prices down and improving its loyalty scheme. It was also hit by higher energy costs during the summer heat wave. Waitrose’s parent company, the John Lewis Partnership – which is owned by its staff – reported a £98m pre-tax loss in the half-year to 1 August, as sales fell at the department stores despite heavy investment in updating the outlets. The company has been reducing the number of staff it employs directly as it tries to trim costs. On Wednesday, the partnership announced it had signed its first company-wide union recognition deal. The collective agreement with Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, comes ahead of new rights of union access in workplaces that come into force at the end of this month. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said: “Usdaw already has members working within the business and this agreement will strengthen that presence and help us in supporting and representing members across the partnership. We now look forward to growing our membership and influence within the partnership and to working with the partnership’s management on finalising the details of how the agreement will work in practice.”

headline: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
trail_text: Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zero
body_text: Andy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?” It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year. Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain. While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel. Meanwhile, hydrogen and biomethane have barely taken off as alternatives to gas for those industrial processes that require higher temperatures than electricity can achieve – tricky for a government pursuing “reindustrialisation”. Fourth – and this one must alarm Downing Street – the global energy market has simply become less reliable. The strait of Hormuz can close overnight. The US president can threaten to ban diesel exports. Russian ships prowl the North Sea. Even the nice Norwegians, with an eye on their own energy consumers, scrapped a planned electricity cable to Scotland in 2023. It is no longer a world of always-available “just in time” supply. Thinking has shifted to “just in case” scenario-planning. And a truly scary scenario would be disruption to the 725-mile Langeled pipeline that is the primary route for gas supplies from Norway, 40% of the UK’s consumption last year. The pipeline is a security vulnerability if ever there was one (if you doubt it, watch Sky News’ recent report). Now we have the start of an answer to Burnham’s “where should it come from?” question. The Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, has finally been approved to produce in time for winter. About time, too. All the arguments from pragmatism were in the field’s favour. As this column has said in the past, less North Sea gas would inevitably mean more imported liquefied natural gas, with the extra carbon emissions created by chilling the fuel to -160C for shipment and then “regasifying” it at the other end. Such cargos were 20% of UK gas imports last year, mostly from the US. It already feels absurd that the 24m UK households with a gas boiler burn any gas at all from the shale fields of Texas and Pennsylvania. Why increase the exposure if lower-polluting supplies are available off Aberdeen? More UK North Sea gas production won’t lower the price for consumers much, if at all. But that was never the argument. It was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security that comes with having domestic volumes piped straight into the national gas network. Jackdaw is not a gamechanger – it will be 6% of UK North Sea gas production at peak – but it’s definitely worth having while the UK is still using gas, which will be at least as long as the field’s 11-year life. The next question is whether other “tie-back” gasfields in already-explored areas, such as Tornado, west of Shetland, will follow. The line in the government’s announcement about “asking the regulator to consider urgent cases that could benefit from similar measures now” suggests so. Rosebank, also near Shetland, is a trickier political proposition because it’s mostly oil, which is more polluting, and will be producing for longer. But the arguments aren’t wholly different. The common elements are still jobs, investment, taxes and the government’s ability to impose higher environmental standards during the production stage. Meanwhile, the “it’s all exported” objection to Rosebank misses the fact that the UK oil industry operates within a European network. If the UK had more than four refineries (compared with nine at the turn of the century), a chunk of Rosebank’s output might be processed at home. As it is, some – perhaps the majority – will come back to the UK as petrol, diesel and jet fuel once it’s been refined in Rotterdam or elsewhere in north-west Europe. Take a step back and the North Sea debate is really about how much oil and gas it is sensible for the UK to produce itself on the way to net zero. On the current trajectory, only about a third of consumption will come from domestic sources on a net basis. Even offshore lobbyists reckon a boost to North Sea production would only get the ratio up to about a half, albeit the figure would obviously increase if consumption of fossil fuels can be made to fall faster. Nobody is talking about the UK becoming a net exporter again. Commitment to net zero by 2050 was intact, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted. We wait to see what the new “energy wealth fund”, which will reinvest oil and gas revenues into renewable and low-carbon projects, means in practice. But the financial logic is sound: recycle the receipts from the old system to quicken the transition. Electrification, enabling consumers to make use of lower-carbon energy, is still the main story. The bizarreness in the government’s previous approach was that, even as it proclaimed the virtues of “clean homegrown energy” such as wind, solar and nuclear, it pursued an approach that maximised imports when it came to oil and gas. Many, including the general secretary of the GMB union, Gary Smith, pointed out the flaw: it was hard for the UK to claim real climate leadership if it was simply off-shoring emissions. In a small way, Jackdaw addresses the UK’s extreme reliance on imports. It is a step towards a joined-up commonsense approach to energy security. The real transition test remains the pace at which the UK stops using fossil fuels.

headline: Cost-of-living crisis? You wouldn’t know it by looking at these companies’ profits
trail_text: We are so locked into believing the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should
body_text: It is always quite striking just how greatly the overseers of the economy defend the status quo in order to ensure company profits keep rising. Right now, Australians are suffering from a cost-of-living crisis. It’s pretty obvious why this is happening. Exhibit 1: Click here if this graph does not display And exhibit 2: Click here if this graph does not display But we too often default to the view that oil prices are rising, so petrol prices must also rise and nothing can be done about it. We are so locked into believing that the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should. Well this week Ampol released its third-quarter report to the ASX. It noted that the growth in its operating profits “reflects the strength of the integrated supply chain to capture the benefits from prevailing market conditions”. Yep, the “benefits”. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here It also reported that the “escalation of geopolitical tensions in the Middle East in recent weeks and ongoing constraints in supply of fuel products … continue to be net favourable for Ampol’s integrated supply chain”. Yep, “net favourable”. This isn’t about them selling more fuel. It’s about them increasing margins at Ampol’s Lytton refinery. Ampol noted that the margin in the third quarter of US$23.92 was more than double what it was a year earlier (US$10.62). This accords with earlier reports from Ampol showing just how good the US and Israel war on Iran has been for them: Click here if this graph does not display It’s why Ampol’s net profit in the first half of this year was up a rather stunning 376% from $180.2m to $857.2m. Then there is Viva Energy, which owns the Geelong oil refinery and supplies, among others, Shell-branded fuel. It has announced “strong first half earnings”, with its operating profit up 154% from $304.9m to $774.4m. Again, this did not come from more sales – the volume of fuel it sold only rose 1.3%. It’s pretty astonishing when you are outperforming even the gas companies: Click here if this graph does not display So yes, oil prices are going up, but let’s not pretend the companies that are importing the oil are struggling. No, they are passing on the costs and then some, as we can tell from the increase in the prices charged by the petroleum and coal product manufacturing companies compared with the cost of their inputs: Click here if this graph does not display This is important because on Wednesday at his fireside chat the deputy governor of the Reserve Bank, Andrew Hauser, was asked about strong “corporate profitability” and whether companies needed to adjust “to a lower level of profitability over time in order to get the balance right … in order to have the social licence to operate”. It was a good question, and in reply Hauser suggested “companies are extremely conscious … about what is called in the trade their social licence” before talking about small business and then future problems with AI companies. But we don’t need to ponder what will happen in the future, because the problem of excessive profits leading to hardship for workers is happening right now and the RBA is saying nothing. And as for caring about their social licence, companies care about ensuring their marketing budgets are spent making them look like good corporate citizens rather than actually being so. They also spend an inordinate amount lobbying governments to ensure any concerns about social licence are overlooked. Consider that Japanese gas companies, including Inpex, are currently complaining loudly about the proposed gas reservation policy and agitated against a 25% tax on gas exports because (as it wrote in a Senate committee submission) “Inpex’s contribution to Australia extends beyond taxation”. In August Inpex reported that the times were very good, despite its Abu Dhabi operations being disrupted. It noted that “despite continued uncertainty surrounding the Middle East situation, full-year profit is expected to be a record high ¥510.0 billion, supported mainly by higher sales prices and stable operations at Ichthys LNG”. That Ichthys LNG operation is rather beloved by our current minister for resources, Madeleine King. Back in 2018, when she was the shadow minister, she attended the celebration of its first LNG shipment and said “it plays a vital role in the economy of Northern Australia and will continue to contribute to the Australian economy for decades to come”. More recently she crowed about how “this project provides resilience and security for Japan”. That’s nice. Especially given so much LNG is exported to Japan that it sells more of that gas to other countries than is used each year in all of eastern Australia. And it sure is good to know that Inpex’s profits are going to reach a record high due to the Ichthys LNG project, given how much it pays in tax and royalties that helps Australians: Click here if this chart does not display Gotta love that social licence. But don’t worry, I’m sure when AI firms make massive profits that increase inflation and pay little tax our governments and central banks will speak up and households won’t again be hit with higher interest rates or cuts to services. Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

headline: Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn
trail_text: Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September
body_text: Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget. The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August, overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, throttling the flow of fuel through the strait of Hormuz. Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March. Official figures showed the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest last month: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn. Payments on some government bonds rise in line with inflation. The ONS said higher inflation had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone. Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year, but still £6bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had expected. The twin pieces of bad news underline the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure. The ONS said a rise in the cost of motor fuels was the single largest factor pushing up inflation in September. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p a litre from August compared with a fall of 0.2p in the same period last year. Diesel, which is often refined in the Middle East, rose by 10.7p a litre last month compared with a fall of 0.4p a litre in September 2025. Air fares, which are heavily affected by the price of fuel, dropped in September by much less than usual after the traditional summer peak. In better news for the chancellor, the cost of clothing fell slightly and food prices growth remained steady at 1.3% as competition among supermarkets offset increases in transport costs. Rising prices make it even more likely that the Bank of England will raise interest rates from their current 3.7% level when its monetary policy committee (MPC) meets next month. Rate setters are concerned that inflation will jump above 4% next year as the price of a wider range of goods increases in response to higher oil and gas prices. September’s reading commits the chancellor to raising most working-age welfare benefit payments from next April by more than expected. For instance, the 3.5% rise will uprate weekly child benefit by 95p, to £28 for the first child. It also means a bigger than forecast inflation-linked rise in business rates in England. The tax firm Ryan said this could raise more than £1bn in extra receipts for the Treasury and would be paid mostly by organisations in the hospitality, leisure, education, health, transport and utility sectors. September’s CPI reading came in lower than the 3.9% wage growth figure for the three months to July, meaning that the state pension will almost certainly rise by the latter figure under the formula that dictates the triple lock. Healey blamed the inflation rise on the war in the Gulf. “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide,” he said, adding that his budget would “drive for growth in every postcode” to improve living standards. Charlotte O’Leary, an economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said the run of three months of rising annual inflation was likely to continue through the winter, even if there was some resolution to the conflict in the Middle East. “Higher fuel and transport costs will likely push up food prices, and January’s large price cap increase will land as household energy demand peaks. Given this, inflation could reach 4%, double the Bank of England’s target, by early 2027,” she said. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI, said the higher than expected inflation rate meant it was almost inevitable that the MPC would raise interest rates when it met on 5 November, but he cautioned against persistent rises in the cost of borrowing. “Raising interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and further tightening risks weakening an already fragile economy,” he said.

headline: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
trail_text: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
body_text: France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets. With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%. The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks. Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living. Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges. No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending. France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action. International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans. Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies. “The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

headline: UK government borrowing rises to £24.5bn as John Healey prepares for budget
trail_text: Government paid £10.9bn in debt interest, the highest September figure since records began
body_text: The Treasury ran a higher than expected budget deficit of £24.5bn last month as rising inflation pushed up the interest paid on government debt, increasing pressure on John Healey before his budget next week. Official figures show the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn. Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs. The Office for National Statistics said this had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone. Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago. The £24.5bn monthly deficit on the public finances was up from £17bn in August, and £1.9bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had forecast. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing is £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year but still £6bn higher than the OBR expected. The data underlines the impact of the Iran war on the public finances, before the budget next Wednesday. Healey has been keen to stress his determination to stay within the fiscal rules set out by his predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves. However, he is widely expected to accept a slimmer financial buffer, or “headroom”, against those rules than the £24bn Reeves had built up at the time of her spring forecast. Higher inflation tends to be good for tax revenues but it also squeezes how much government departments can achieve within fixed budgets. Receipts from income-related taxes were up more than 7% on the same month last year in September, and corporation tax by 9%, aided by stronger than expected economic growth – but these higher receipts failed to offset the rising debt interest bill. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI Strategy, said the latest data was “an unwelcome reminder of the pressures facing the chancellor ahead of next week’s budget”. Healey is under pressure to provide relief from rapidly rising energy costs. Greg Thwaites, the interim chief economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the public finances figures suggested he would have to take a cautious approach. “The support must be temporary and targeted given the state of the public finances. Borrowing is already off track this year, debt has hit £3tn, and markets are closely scrutinising the government’s ability to keep on top of the public finances,” he said. The Conservative shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said the figures showed Labour should do more to tackle the deficit. “Government borrowing of more than £3tn – the highest in history – and rising inflation show Labour has lost control of the economy,” he said.

headline: How might Andy Burnham tackle Thames Water debacle?
trail_text: A look at some of the options after PM is urged to consider radical alternatives to deal with stricken company
body_text: Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. Here are some ideas the prime minister is being urged to consider. Emergency legislation Burnham must introduce emergency legislation immediately to protect the supply of water for the public, said Richard Murphy, tax accountant and the brains behind Corbynomics. A new state-owned company, with a management team in waiting and all the necessary steps ready to take over the existing company’s systems, has to be put in place now. “A prime minister who cannot deliver water to maybe a quarter of the UK’s population would not be someone to be trusted with anything else. Andy Burnham has no choice but to address this matter, now,” said Murphy. The 1971 nationalisation of the Rolls-Royce aeronautical engineering company, to protect the national interest after it collapsed into receivership, could be used as a blue print. A similar national emergency exists now to protect the supply of water, Murphy said. Murphy said that, in essence, Thames Water was financially insolvent, with real doubt about whether it could survive into 2027. It was failing in its regulatory obligations, including to maintain clean water supplies and keep rivers and beaches clean. Use Emergency legislation should ensure that the nationalisation is of the assets and undertakings of Thames Water, and not of the company itself. All financial liabilities of Thames Water would be left for the old company to settle. The government should not acquire them. The new company needed to be structured within days, said Murphy. “There is no time to wait.” Public control – probably via the courts Burnham must be prepared to go to court to take Thames Water back into public control, said Ewan McGaughey, professor of law at King’s College London. Moody’s has estimated a one-off cost of £14.5bn in 2019 to bring water into public ownership. But privatisation, said McGaughey, would cost up to £22bn extra for bill payers from 2025 to 2030, or £176 a household a year, in returns on capital to shareholders and banks, as set by Ofwat’s price review. McGaughey believes that this year public ownership of failed water companies will cost closer to £0, using the special administration procedure within the 1991 Water Industry Act. The higher the repair bills, the less that creditors or shareholders deserve under UK law, international law and our investment treaties, he said. He advises Burnham to prepare to go to court – creditors will probably sue – but they have no reasonable prospect of success. McGaughey says privatised water and the regulators have failed so badly that England pays among the highest bills in Europe, while nearly every river is illegally polluted, taps run dry and a trillion litres of water is leaked each year. Shareholders have taken over £85.2bn in dividends, and creditors more in interest, since privatisation in 1989, evaporating UK investment, shipping capital overseas and leaving billions of pounds in sewage treatment and pipe repair costs. These polluters should not be paid a penny more to run our water, McGaughey said. The government should bring our accounting practice up to international and European standards, by separating public corporation borrowing from the national debt, so that the borrowing of a publicly owned company does not contribute to national debt. Strip Thames of its licence Continuing the theme of using the special administrative powers of the 1991 legislation, Cat Hobbs of We Own It wants Thames Water’s licence taken away immediately. Hobbs has written to the government and water regulator, Ofwat, calling for bill rises to be blocked and for Thames Water to be brought into public hands. “It is absurd that Thames Water is now asking its creditors for a further £2.4bn to stay afloat – this saga has dragged out since July 2024 when the company was first in breach of its licence conditions,” said Hobbs. Under the 1991 act, companies can have their licences removed if they are insolvent or if they fail to fulfil their statutory duties to provide water, protect the environment and properly manage wastewater. Hobbs told Burnham his government should be using this power and facing down threats from the water industry and the prospect of a legal challenge from special administration under the 1991 act. Public ownership of water would deliver savings of £3bn to £5bn a year over time from cheaper financing costs – no shareholder dividends, less expensive debt. Taking water into public ownership would reduce the cost of living burden as well as freeing up money for infrastructure. The government should make it possible for new publicly owned water companies to borrow to invest on their own account – rather than adding to the national debt – as is standard practice elsewhere in Europe. Hobbs pointed out that when Network Rail’s debt of £31bn was transferred to the public sector, bond yields fell from 3% a year to 2.2% a year.

headline: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax
trail_text: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interview
body_text: Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview. Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust. “We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.” In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”. “How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” he wrote on X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!” “Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added. The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have been spending millions fighting against. Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year were being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry. “We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said. When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.” Kirby also maintained that fares were still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.

headline: What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?
trail_text: Decision has implications for household energy bills, the UK economy and the climate crisis
body_text: About four years and six energy secretaries after it was given the green light, the Jackdaw gasfield has been given consent to begin production 150 miles east of Aberdeen. So what does this long-awaited decision mean for the Labour party, household bills, the economy and the climate crisis? Does this break a Labour manifesto promise? No, because although the party vowed to “not issue new licences to explore new fields” in the hydrocarbon-rich basin, it made clear it would honour licences granted before it came to power. These fields include Jackdaw, which was granted a licence in 2022, and the larger Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, which was approved the following year. Oil and gas licences give broad permission to explore an area for fossil fuels but consent is still needed to extract them. Although Jackdaw and Rosebank had both, they were blocked from starting production after a legal challenge by campaigners at Greenpeace and Uplift early last year. That ruling compelled the companies behind the project to resubmit their applications with extra information on the climate impact of the fuels produced. Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norway’s state oil company, Equinor. Adura also hopes to develop Rosebank in conjunction with Ithaca Energy. A decision on Rosebank’s new application for consent is expected later this year. Will the Jackdaw decision lower energy bills? Probably not. Household bills are based on the price of gas in the UK wholesale market, which is determined by international prices that have soared amid disruptions to global supplies. These have included the loss of Russian flows to Europe and disruption to Gulf exports to buyers around the world – shocks far too big for the relatively small output from Jackdaw to outweigh. The Tories have claimed drilling could still help to lower bills under their plans to use tax revenues to cut VAT on gas and electricity bills for three years. However, this does not mean energy costs are fundamentally lower – or sustainable. Meanwhile, Labour has cut VAT from electricity bills from this month until next March and ministers are understood to be planning to offer billions in energy bill support for low-income households at next week’s budget. What about the UK’s carbon emissions? Gas from Jackdaw could release between 23.6m and 35.8m tonnes of CO2 equivalent over its 11-year operational lifespan, but the carbon impact of new North Sea fields is “not clear cut”. That’s the view of the Committee on Climate Change (CCC), which advises the government on meeting its legally binding climate targets. There are two sorts of emission to consider: first, the “scope 1 and 2” kind, created from getting fossil fuels out of the ground and transporting them to users. These are relatively low in the British North Sea and make up about 3% of the UK’s total. In fact, the CCC has said there might be “emissions advantages” to the switch because scope 1 and 2 emissions from UK gas are by some estimates four times lower than from US and Gulf fossil gas imports. The second, far bigger impact is from the “scope 3” emissions created from burning the fossil fuel. Although Jackdaw’s gas would release CO2 when used in homes, businesses, factories and power plants, there is no evidence it would lead to higher overall gas consumption. As Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in July: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from?” A better way to reduce UK emissions would be to replace gas boilers and fossil fuel vehicles with electric alternatives powered by low-carbon sources. What about the impact on global emissions? Here, too, the answer is unclear. Some academics have suggested that more UK oil and gas would push up fossil fuel production globally unless output fell elsewhere. In 2024, the CCC said new fossil fuel developments would have a “minimal impact on UK carbon budgets” but if others followed the UK’s lead in increasing production, the cumulative impact could lead to “an oversupply that would pose a risk” to international targets. It urged the UK government to “reassess whether further exploration for new sources of fossil fuels” was aligned with its global climate obligations. This supports the government’s ban on new licences but would not rule out Jackdaw – which is not a new source. Moreover, a global oversupply of fossil fuels does not necessarily lead to greater emissions. In 2025, China’s crude oil imports hit a record 11m barrels a day but its emissions continued to fall because it was building its crude stocks to a record high of 1.4bn barrels. In short, emissions are largely due to energy consumption, not energy production. So if consumption continues to decline, emissions will fall regardless of the amount of fossil fuels made available in the global market. Where does this leave the UK’s climate agenda? Green groups have argued that allowing North Sea developments to move ahead would undermine the UK’s role as a climate leader and weaken its ability to use climate diplomacy to encourage other nations to adopt green energy policies. However, their opposition has been focused less on Jackdaw and more on the impact of the larger Rosebank scheme, which Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary turned foreign secretary, described as “climate vandalism” while he was in opposition. If the government goes on to also give consent for this project it could fuel accusations of climate hypocrisy at the top of the cabinet, undermining the UK’s ambition to be a global climate leader. John Gummer argued as the CCC chair in 2022 that an end to UK exploration “would send a clear signal to investors and consumers” and “help the UK in its diplomatic efforts to strengthen climate ambition internationally”. So what might the economic benefits be? The North Sea is an ageing hydrocarbon basin in terminal decline but supporting new projects still offers economic benefits, including higher tax revenues from oil and gas companies, income tax from well-paid workers and job creation within the industry and its supply chain. Offshore Energies UK, an industry body, has promised the government that approving Jackdaw and Rosebank could provide £1.4bn in tax revenues by 2029, rising to £3.8bn by 2034. It has also claimed the fields could support a peak of more than 3,500 jobs during the construction phase and 880 jobs with an average salary of £85,850 over the lifetime of the fields. Green groups reject these figures, arguing they overstate the economic benefits. Regardless, they are still relatively modest in the context of the broader economy. What about the new energy wealth fund? Alongside the government’s decision to back the Jackdaw project, it set out plans to set up an energy wealth fund, which will use tax revenues from North Sea fossil fuel profits to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects. The government will set up the fund with £2bn, and it will grow as oil and gasfield tax revenues flow into it over time. This should help to support the UK’s green industries and even “help reduce energy bills over the long term”, according to Burnham. The idea echoes the approach of Norway, which has channelled its own North Sea revenues into a sovereign wealth fund for more than 30 years. Today that $2.3tn fund is the largest of its kind. The UK may wish that it had done something similar in the early 1990s when tax revenues were higher – but the fund could still offer a top-up to schemes to help reduce the country’s long-term reliance on fossil fuels. Given the disputed impact, why is the debate so febrile? The North Sea has become a totemic issue. For some, the basin is steeped in nostalgia for a long-gone period of British economic success and innovation, while for others it is a reminder of the UK’s longstanding contribution to the climate crisis and its responsibility to take action. “It has sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change,” the CCC’s former chief executive Chris Stark told the New Statesman in 2024. “It means we haven’t got the political capital to deploy on the heat pump story, or the electric vehicle story. That’s where the action needs to be.”

headline: NatWest cracks down on 13,000 staff attending office two days a month
trail_text: Union furious as bank scraps remote-first policy from February 2027, forcing all UK employees to come in at least twice a week
body_text: NatWest has ordered 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days from two days a month to two days a week, angering its staff union. The banking group, which serves customers under the Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands, will require all of its nearly 40,000 UK staff to follow a strict two days a week office schedule from February 2027, abolishing a remote-first policy for thousands of employees. Unite said it was a “kick in the teeth” for the 13,000 employees who attend the office only two days a month, and accounted for some of NatWest’s lowest-paid workers, including staff involved in technology, security, data analytics and human resources. The union said the change would pile additional financial pressure on staff already struggling with rising living costs, while undermining flexible arrangements for those with caring responsibilities or disabilities. Many had also structured their lives around flexible working agreements that were expanded during the Covid pandemic, it said. “This is yet another kick in the teeth for workers who have suffered years of real-terms pay cuts and who are struggling to make ends meet,” said the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham. “NatWest’s decision is completely out of touch with the realities facing its workforce,” she added, noting that thousands of staff would face higher travel and childcare costs as a result. “For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce. NatWest must ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers.” The bank said its policy was meant to “help teams collaborate,” echoing arguments made by other banks ranging from JP Morgan to Revolut, which clamped down on remote working, saying it harms the training of younger staff. Last month Barclays was forced to push back its return-to-office plans after a staff backlash, backed by Unite. It had ordered staff to come in at least three days a week from early October, up from two days a week. The bank eventually softened its stance and allowed some staff to delay the requirement until next year. Some staff at NatWest – including traders, branch workers and relationship managers – are already required to be in the office four days a week. Others, including its communications, administrative and analytics staff, work a hybrid schedule where they are in six times a month. A NatWest spokesperson said: “Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we’ve also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers – helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another.” The bank added: “We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we’re giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition.”

headline: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts
trail_text: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says
body_text: Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict. Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%. “You’re going to see air fares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see ⁠the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months,” O’Leary told a news conference ‌in Brussels. Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be 70% higher across 2026 – estimated to average $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits. Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February. However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high. “We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” O’Leary said. Ryanair’s hedging contract for 2027 covered 15% of its fuel costs at $85 a barrel, he added, whereas spot rates are currently hovering at about double that level. EasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July, adding it had hedged 62% of its fuel requirements for the first half of 2027 and 37% for the second half of the year. The airline announced in October it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule in an attempt to save fuel. During his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule, after the federal government’s decision to increase its aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January. O’Leary is the latest executive to warn of the downbeat outlook for aviation. Industry leaders have said some carriers will struggle to survive the fuel price shock. Passenger surveys have shown travellers are braced for higher fares and are prepared to spend more, but airlines do not know how long consumers will be able to afford pricier tickets.

headline: Thames Water creditors secure former Labour minister to drive rescue deal
trail_text: Stricken UK water supplier lines up John Hutton as independent chair designate if takeover goes ahead
body_text: The group of Thames Water creditors pursuing a £10bn rescue deal for Britain’s largest water supplier has lined up a former senior Labour minister to chair the company, as it tries to win over the government. The creditor consortium, called London & Valley Water, said on Tuesday that Lord John Hutton had been selected as independent chair designate of the Thames Water board, if the consortium’s deal is approved. Creditors have been locked in talks with ministers and regulators for months over the future ownership of the debt-laden water company, which has 16 million customers in the south of England. Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames and present him with more radical options for the stricken company, the Guardian reported this week. Before he became prime minister, he said he would nationalise Thames. The company has been battling to stave off bankruptcy for years and is running out of cash. It recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn. The creditor group said Hutton would be supported by Mike McTighe, a telecoms and turnaround specialist, who is leading Thames’s overhaul. McTighe had been lined up as the new chair in August to replace the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if the creditors’ takeover is approved by the government. McTighe has now been appointed vice-chair designate and is expected to work closely with the management team. Hutton served in Tony Blair’s and Gordon Brown’s governments as work and pensions secretary, business secretary and defence secretary and has experience ‌across public policy, energy and infrastructure. He has chaired the Nuclear Industry Association, Energy UK, and manufacturing association Make UK. Other roles include chairing the Association of Infrastructure Investors and London Luton Airport, and serving as non-executive director of Scottish Power Energy Networks. Hutton said: “I am looking forward to being part of the new leadership at Thames Water and helping get this hugely important business into a better place. “People living in London and the Thames Valley have the right to expect the highest possible standards of customer service and proper environmental stewardship from their water company, and that will be our focus as we look to the future.”

headline: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
trail_text: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday
body_text: India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn. Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday. Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians. Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential. On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday. Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares. The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share. At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company. However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer. It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year. Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure. Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working. “What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

headline: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline
trail_text: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money
body_text: An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut. Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”. The US tech company said services were starting to come back online as of 1pm London time, and were back online for most customers by 3pm, but not before critical financial transactions and legal proceedings were disrupted. That included the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales, which failed to work throughout the morning. The issue was believed to have delayed several hearings, as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody but need to attend court. Meanwhile, bank customers at high street lenders and leading digital bank Revolut were left in limbo as services including card payments, cash withdrawals and transfers were disrupted. By 5pm most Revolut services were still marked on its website as having problems, with only six out of 27 services listed, including support chat and internal transfers, said to be working. The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage. The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority is also understood to be speaking with the tech firm. Halifax, owned by Lloyds Bank, said on X that some of its customers had been unable to log in via the app and online. Revolut said its app was down because of a “service disruption” affecting several services, but insisted that customers’ funds and data were safe. The outage was affecting new and current customers, hitting its sign-up, sign-in, card payment, transfer, ATM withdrawal and cryptocurrency services. In a statement, Revolut said: “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.” A spokesperson for Lloyds originally said that customers were having issues with “certain online services” on Tuesday morning but that they were aware of “similar issues affecting other organisations”. By the afternoon, the banking group issued an update saying: “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to [have] all our services back to normal soon.” HSBC customers had also been complaining online that they were struggling to access their accounts. A spokesperson for the bank said: “Our services have returned to normal following earlier access issues. We continue to monitor the situation closely and thank customers for their patience.” This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and the Bank of England since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer. Their response is already facing scrutiny by the influential Treasury committee of MPs, whose chair Meg Hillier wrote to the regulators asking for details about how they reacted and a sense of the total impact on the UK financial system. Hillier has asked for an initial response by 4 November. The property portal Rightmove was also reportedly affected by the Google cloud outage, and NewsThump, the satire and spoof news website, was struggling to load. Reports suggested Royal Mail and DPD had also suffered disruption. Google said: “We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.” An FCA spokesperson said: “We are aware of the incident affecting services provided by Google and are engaging with them and affected firms to understand the impact. “People need to be able to access their money and make payments, so we expect firms to fix issues quickly, keep their customers informed and ensure no one is left out of pocket.”

headline: Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7% as John Healey’s first budget looms
trail_text: Latest ONS data presents mixed picture ahead of budget amid slump in job vacancies and analysts warning labour market is ‘running on idle’
byline: Phillip Inman Senior economics writer and Graeme Wearden
body_text: Unemployment in the UK has fallen unexpectedly in the final snapshot of the jobs market before John Healey’s first budget next week. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, from 4.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had forecast a rise to 5%. In a further boost to the chancellor, the figures also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3 million. However, a slump in the number of job vacancies illustrated what some economists said was an economy moving sideways. After hitting a peak of 1.3m in the period after the pandemic, vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic. Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation thinktank at Lancaster University, said the fall in unemployment “should not make the government complacent ahead of next week’s budget”. He said: “The UK is still amid a jobs drought with vacancies at their lowest for over 12 years outside of the pandemic.” Vacancies fell particularly sharply across the construction sector, suggesting Britain’s builders cut back on hiring last summer. Data on wage growth was mixed. Stripping out bonuses, average pay growth rose to 3.7% from 3.6%. However, when bonuses are included the rate fell to 3.7% from 3.9%, indicating that only a few workers received bonuses. Wage growth in the UK remains above inflation, which was 3.1% in August and is expected to rise to 3.4% when figures for September are published on Wednesday. The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates in response to higher prices at next month’s meeting of the monetary policy committee (MPC). The pound rose against the dollar after the labour market figures were released, by about half a cent to $1.3352, as investors bet on the increased likelihood of a rate rise from 3.75% as early as next month. Members of the MPC are split on the need for further increases in the cost of borrowing with some, including the Columbia University professor Alan Taylor, arguing that the committee needs to wait several months to see whether costs and wages continue to rise. Financial markets expect interest rates to rise to between 4.75% and 5% by the middle of next year, although the consultancy Capital Economics said recent improvements in the labour market were modest and the central bank would probably cap interest rates at 4.25%. Ellie Henderson, an economist at Investec, said lower unemployment and higher wages would make a majority of the MPC nervous about leaving interest rates on hold. “The MPC will collectively decide to increase the Bank rate by 0.25 percentage points at the next meeting in November, framing it as a ‘risk management’ move, in case the data were to turn or energy prices move even higher,” she said. “Sterling markets seem to agree, with the pound strengthening on the numbers, gaining modestly against both the US dollar and the euro.” Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, described the labour market as “running on idle” with employers limiting recruitment and pay awards “in response to surging cost pressures and pre-budget policy uncertainty”. He said: “The continued fall in vacancies is a flashing red warning light for the labour market, suggesting that a damaging side-effect of this year’s AI-fuelled economic growth has been weaker hiring demand, compounded by elevated employment costs.” The ONS estimated there were 715,000 unemployed young people aged 16 to 24, down by 28,000 on the quarter. Harrison of the Work Foundation welcomed the drop, but said ministers should be more focused on the number of jobless young people remaining at 54,000 higher than 12 months ago. The secretary of state for work and pensions, Pat McFadden, said: “Today’s figures show the resilience of our labour market with unemployment falling and the UK’s employment rate now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty.” But he conceded that many young people needed support to enter the labour market. “That’s why we are working with industry, to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system.”

headline: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders
trail_text: As long as Healey doesn’t go overboard, a small turn on surcharge dial will not seriously undermine flow of capital
body_text: Everyone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less interest will be paid on deposits and loans will cost slightly more, meaning we’ll all be worse off eventually. In terms of economic theory, it’s coherent, it should be said: in an ideal world, a chancellor would strive to lower costs of capital at every opportunity. In the real world, however, John Healey faces multiple competing demands, even from within a business lobby that extends well beyond the banks. As this newspaper revealed last week, the chancellor is likely to increase bank taxes in his budget next week. In the current climate of trying to “stay the course” on the fiscal rules by finding some money from somewhere, tapping the banks is a reasonable policy. Or, at least, better than most alternatives. First, today’s conditions for banks are plainly gentle: defaults are historically low and interest rates are high. Banks’ returns on tangible equity – a better guide to how they are doing than pure profitability – are heading towards 20%. Most non-financial firms would love such a number. Provided Healey doesn’t go overboard, the flow of capital is not going to be seriously undermined when the starting point for banks’ returns is so good. Second, all the indications suggest Healey will indeed opt only for tweaks. If the mechanism is the surcharge that banks pay on top of corporation tax at 25%, then an increase to 8%, from 3%, would amount to £2bn-ish extra from across the sector. He may not even go that far. Analysts at UBS calculate that a doubling of the surcharge to 6% would reduce UK banks’ profits only by about 2% on average, with a roughly 3%-4% impact for the domestic-focused banks, meaning NatWest and Lloyds. That cannot be called a violent change in the operating climate, or a devastating blow for the shareholders or the equity-incentivised executives. Dividends or share buybacks may be trimmed a bit, but the share prices for both banks are up by a fifth in the past year. Third, we’ll have to wait to see whether any move by Healey is part of a wider financial services package that could include bank-pleasing elements. There’s always scope for another hack at the thicket of regulations, for instance. Or help on capital buffers. And, if Healey is really as pro-growth as he claims, he’d consider this column’s perennial pre-budget suggestion to scrap or cut stamp duty on shares – a move that would seriously improve UK companies’ cost of capital (see Tax Policy Associates’ paper) and do wonders for banks’ wealth-management divisions. The point is that a small turn on the surcharge dial is better than other ways of extracting the odd billion or two for the banks. A windfall tax would be too arbitrary. Changing the way banks’ deposits are remunerated at the Bank of England would look like interference in the central bank’s independence. The surcharge is a well-understood mechanism. None of which, one suspects, will stop the howls of complaints from banks, or halt the grumbles about the loss of competitiveness versus other financial centres. But an extra £2bn, or less, from the financial services sector simply doesn’t sound like a gamechanger if Healey acts as expected. Even JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, who likes to play politics at budget-time with his proposed new London headquarters, might reflect that some other European capitals – Paris, say – don’t look like a bed of roses.

headline: New Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’
trail_text: Transport hub will offer through trains between Leeds and Manchester with ‘turn-up-and-go’ service
body_text: A new railway station will be built in Bradford to “transform how people travel across the north”, the government has announced. The station will be at the heart of the Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) scheme, built on the current Bradford Interchange site but allowing through trains between Leeds and Manchester. With the promise of more frequent and faster services, it is expected to support new homes and jobs for the West Yorkshire city, located alongside its Southern Gateway regeneration project and connecting to the proposed tram to Leeds. Approval of the station, which is expected to be built by the mid-2030s, has been regarded by northern leaders as a critical sign of political commitment to improving rail links across the north, after long delays in delivering pledged upgrades. The Department for Transport said that NPR would allow a “turn-up-and-go railway” for passengers from Bradford, with sufficiently frequent trains running across the north for people not to need to check timetables.
