But technology isn’t waiting for regulation to catch up and Fisk says his synthetic twin clients are blurring the lines between real and fake. “It’s becoming almost impossible to detect, that look and feel, the difference, particularly when you see it on a mobile device,” he says. ‘We’re watching a race’ William Saunders leads a small Sydney based start-up, Hyperknown, that’s trying to cut similar deals. He says athletes are beginning to realise that if they don’t monetise their AI image, others will. Earlier this month, the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without their consent. This was prompted by a complaint from the players’ union, which is considering whether stricter rules should be negotiated. “Sportsbet shows us what happens when companies and technology get ahead of consent,” Saunders says. “Volpato represents the counter-move: people establishing their rights before others start making decisions about their identities. “We’re watching a race between what technology can do and what people have actually authorised.” Many in the Australian sports industry, including content creators, bookmakers, broadcasters and athletes themselves, have started embracing the technology. Earlier this month, Australian cricketer Travis Head personally appeared in an ad for the broadcaster Kayo. He joked that his AI clone had already finished filming the ad, before throwing to vision of him riding a flying kookaburra. Brand deals and endorsements have become major money makers for athletes, with some securing multimillion dollar contracts. It remains unclear whether brands will be willing to pay as much for an AI clone, as opposed to the real deal. But Saunders, whose company has only just launched, says the opportunities are enormous. He talks of AI clones selling products in foreign languages in nations athletes have never visited. “The next trust signal won’t just say ‘made with AI’,” he says, referencing a tag often used by social media companies. “It will say ‘made with this person’s permission’. “AI can make content abundant. It can’t manufacture someone’s permission. That’s becoming a new commercial requirement.” ‘A tangle of different interests’ Jonathan Harlen, an expert in intellectual property law at Southern Cross University, says the rise of AI brokers is “the obvious next step” in a “supercharged global market”. From a legal perspective, he says this new industry presents “a tangle of different interests and rights” that need to be carefully negotiated. “While copyright already subsists in voice recordings, artistic works and cinematographic images, it is only recognised where there has been human authorship, as well as a degree of independent or creative human effort involved in the making of the work,” Harlen says. “It doesn’t apply to AI reproductions.” Celebrities and athletes do have some protection against AI-generated content using their image and voice without consent. But these “passing off” laws only apply when public figures can prove they have suffered an economic loss. This has not slowed an explosion of deepfakes generated by increasingly sophisticated off-the-shelf software. In the UK last month, a campaign was launched by some the world’s top footballers, including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, which highlighted their concerns about deepfakes and the inability for regulation to slow their explosion. This campaign was backed by the global player union, Fifpro. One offshore casino used a deepfake video of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year. Not all unauthorised deepfakes will be unwanted, however. Fisk says a heavy-handed crackdown on “fan art” using AI tools might be counterproductive. “You don’t want fans to use your image and put you in [content] using brands that you don’t use, or saying something that you would never say,” he says. “Obviously, anything with religion and drugs, or whatever it might be, you have to be very, very careful. So it does complicate things a bit, but the opportunities are phenomenal.” But in this emerging realm, the consequences may be hard to predict.

headline: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle
trail_text: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back
body_text: Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels. The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”. Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.” Johnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”. * * * This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are 315 hyperscale datacentres waiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day. Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as an inevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It established five AI growth zones to push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change, turning down calls for a moratorium and insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole. * * * Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it is estimated spending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 – more than double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation. The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughly half of the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing a furious backlash, with three-quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it for increasing energy bills, threatening water supplies in drought-hit areas and spewing out toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporary datacentre bans. Loudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it is home to more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.” The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.” The UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, who overturned a council decision blocking the scheme. Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.” Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.” In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as the heart disease and dementia research powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AI facility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.” * * * On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales. Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 1,314,000 megawatt hours (MWh) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff. The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands. Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says. Elias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus. She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part in protests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.” It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.” Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homes built under the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.” Like many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.” Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.” Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements. There are more than 100 other planned UK datacentres aiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.” * * * A stone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff. “Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.” Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.” Many of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner. The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says. Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.” Although the datacentre will employ only up to 125 people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.” Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.” Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents. * * * The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administration welcomed the building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales. In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is a Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says. Carter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years. Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing a moratorium on new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.” However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power. * * * A soft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage. Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut. Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”. The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens. Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.” Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.” • This article was amended on 26 October 2026. An earlier version said the datacentre would use 150 megawatts of electricity a year; this should have been measured in megawatt hours (MWh), and would be 1,314,000 MWh.

headline: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
trail_text: After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’
body_text: Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace. The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”. AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do. “The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X. While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October. Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking. However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace. Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun. After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said. “Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read. In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced. “That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote. In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

headline: We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram
trail_text: Letters: Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms
body_text: I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara (The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October). Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience. This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 book Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now. Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy. His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever. By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being. In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them. Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen. A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind. Guy Edmondson Hipperholme, West Yorkshire • Georgina McNamara’s article really resonated with me. I haven’t deleted Instagram, but I check it very infrequently now. While I didn’t post all that often, the compulsion to document experiences and turn moments into posts or stories, rather than being in the moment, was always there – and with it, the eventual anxiety about whether anyone had liked what I had posted. I also realised that comparing my day-to-day life with others’ carefully curated highlights was making me unhappy: an endless stream of holiday photos made me keenly aware of how long it would be until I would next have a break, while other fitness instructors posting photos taken from strategic angles made me worry that I wasn’t as flexible as them in comparison, or that my technique was poor. After reading some books and articles on cutting back on smartphone use, I took a number of steps to reduce my phone use, and used the One Sec app to trigger a breathing exercise whenever I opened Instagram. It made me realise how often I checked Instagram as a reflex, and that I could be devoting this time to other activities that I found more fulfilling. The few occasions that I do check it these days, I find it a bit overwhelming. I find that my mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me, appreciating what I see as a moment that doesn’t have to become a post or a story. And if I take a photograph of something, it’s because I like it, not because I’m concerned about whether someone else will. Laura Dobie Glasgow • I deleted my Instagram account after getting pregnant with my second child. At first, I muted it; when I returned, the algorithm had decided that, with all the information it had gathered on me, I must have taken a break due to baby loss. It bombarded me with images and messages about baby loss, until it realised this wasn’t the reason and started to fill my algorithm with “two under two” narratives. The juxtaposition was stark and insensitive. It felt awful. I realised I didn’t want this platform having information about not just me but my family as well, and I hated that by feeding into it (with likes on obsessed-over images and funny captions), I was allowing it to dictate some of my parenting decisions through algorithms and advertised content. Since leaving it, my motherhood journey has been much happier, simpler and in my control. I completely agree that it’s the change that works! Stefanie Withey-Jones London • I enjoyed Georgina McNamara’s account of leaving Instagram, particularly her observations about the time spent checking reactions and seeking validation. However, there is an important distinction to be made between sharing our lives and seeking approval for them. I use social media to share photographs with friends and family because I enjoy letting people I know see what I have been doing. For me, that is about connection, not validation. There is another pleasure too that is rarely mentioned: unexpected reminders of photographs posted one, five or even 10 years ago. A holiday, a familiar face or an ordinary moment that I had forgotten suddenly reappears, bringing back the feelings associated with it. It’s not just the memories themselves I treasure, but the unexpected joy of being reminded of them, often when they’re furthest from my mind. The problem, perhaps, is not posting our lives online, but allowing other people’s reactions to determine how much we value those experiences. Nicky Atkinson Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex • I lasted only six weeks on Instagram. Unlike Georgina McNamara, I came to the party late, in my 60s. Almost immediately, I resented the way that posts were pushed into my feed. In no time at all I was spending hours watching posts of horse sanctuaries in the US and feeling depressed and resentful at whole sections of society. So I deleted my account – no small feat in itself, as the process is determined to keep you there. Afterwards, I felt relief at getting back hours of my own brain time, but for months, I would think: “I could just pop on and look at x, y, z.” I’m glad that I’m off, and scared at how quickly I became addicted. Now when I look around I see that I am the only person on the bus or train who is not looking at a screen but at the outside world, and thinking for myself. Dr Hilary Redden Aberdeen • The one change that worked? I deleted all social media from my phone and instead installed the Guardian app with a subscription to news and well-curated content. No more time-wasting, bottomless doomscrolling for me. Do it, kids! Cecilia Scott Woking, Surrey • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company
trail_text: Anthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the vision
body_text: Last year, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, warned that artificial intelligence could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs and that in six months it would be writing 90% of code. Neither of those predictions came to pass. Now, in a report Anthropic published on Thursday, the company said it was hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as it increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents. Anthropic says AI has changed the way work gets done, and as a result, restructured employment at the company. The report suggests its changes foreshadow the future of work more broadly: as more companies adopt AI agents, software engineers could face a tougher job market while entry-level tech workers struggle to build necessary skills and experience. “As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift,” Anthropic’s report reads before offering a potential future. “One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue.” In its report, Anthropic touts its “deep adoption of AI”, which it claims resulted in “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts”. By outsourcing some coding and sales-related tasks to AI agents, Anthropic said it raised productivity within a few months. From May 2026 onwards, AI agents logged more work hours than human employees, the report said. Employees now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents, more than double the amount a year ago, based on Anthropic’s analysis of their chat summaries. It also says since March 2025 – soon after the release of its agentic AI coding tool Claude Code – entry-level technical hires dropped from nearly 30% to 9%, and headcount dropped from about 21% to 14%. It attributes the shifts to AI usage, and described its workers as merely “a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents”. While the report provides a small glimpse of the inner workings of the AI heavyweight, some AI researchers are skeptical that it will herald big changes across companies or industries. Instead, they say the findings are probably Anthropic’s attempt to drive its valuation ahead of its initial public offering – similar to how SpaceX boasted about proposed space datacenters to boost its market debut in June. Anthropic’s claims seem to back some tech executives’ view that AI is behind recent waves of corporate layoffs, but research complicates that. Morgan Frank, a Case Western Reserve University researcher on how AI and technological changes affect workers, recently posted a paper that’s in peer review showing that AI-exposed job markets deteriorated well before the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Claude a few months later. State unemployment claims reveal that job markets tanked starting at the beginning of 2022, months before ChatGPT’s release, according to the paper. “It doesn’t appear that the launch of ChatGPT corresponds to any major increase in loss or worsening outcomes,” he said. Frank said several factors could explain recent job losses, including cutting pandemic-era hires and “AI-washing”, where some bosses credit AI for layoffs they might have made anyway. Julián Posada, a Yale social scientist, also questions Anthropic’s motives for publishing its report. “It is written from the perspective of a company that wants to sell shares, a company that really wants people to invest in it,” said Posada, author of the book Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence. Unlike an economics study, the report lacked an independent assessment by outside auditors, Posada said. Its figures and graphs only tell part of the story, without revealing how Anthropic’s workers feel about their work or how they are actually engaging with the models, he said. Dylan Baker, lead research engineer at the non-profit Distributed AI Research Institute, was also curious about how Anthropic’s developers feel about the changes. Shifting some software development to AI, while hiring few entry-level workers and having the remaining engineers wrangle AI agents seems “shortsighted”, they said. Baker is also surprised by Anthropic’s human “bottleneck” characterization. “That’s such a strange way to put it,” they said. “It fundamentally misunderstands how software is written, architected and designed. It’s such a social, interpersonal and human process.” Anthropic’s report quotes an unnamed engineer, who described facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention”. That doesn’t sound like a fruitful work environment, Baker said. “I wouldn’t think really thoughtful, well-designed products are coming out of that team.” As generative AI products proliferate, a majority of Americans are wary of AI, with particular concerns about AI-related job losses, according to Pew Research Center. In its report, Anthropic suggests that tech employers should offer their workers stock ownership, posing this as a potential solution to rising concerns. “It is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout,” it said. Anthropic did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. Anthropic, which could debut on the stock market as soon as November, released its employment report one day after pledging to commit 5% of its shares to the “public good”, though it did not provide details. Critics noted that philanthropy has long doubled as a reputation builder used by tech titans like Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg. But Anthropic, and its claims that it is improving how work gets done could face tougher scrutiny as it nears its IPO. A draft of the company’s S-1 filing revealed that Anthropic had an $80bn net loss over the first half of this year, and that it received a junk credit rating in June. Considering Anthropic’s slowing revenue growth, investors now project a valuation of $1.5tn, down from earlier estimates of $2tn or more. At the same time, Anthropic’s cloud computing partner, CoreWeave, has become swamped in AI debt and its stock is plummeting, fueling concerns that the AI bubble may begin to deflate. Regardless of when or whether the bubble pops, software engineers and other tech workers will surely be affected, Baker said. The question is how that will play out. “My hope is that there is a reckoning, a reassessment or re-evaluation of how much this has always been about human work,” they said.

headline: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
trail_text: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude
body_text: In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss. Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee. In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare. The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France, India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee. Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern, with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.” Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.” Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied: “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?” Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways. “The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said. Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits. While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College. “Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.” In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project. Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products. If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement. In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE. Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise. The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods. Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

headline: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features
trail_text: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI
body_text: As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative. That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model. The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to the previous versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside. Upgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics. The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina of top adventure watch rivals. The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes. Specifications Case size: 49 x 44mm Case thickness: 12mm Weight: 63g Processor: S11 Storage: 64GB Operating system: watchOS 27 Water resistance: 100 metres (10ATM) Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWB Sensors: HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeter Vitals and readiness The Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way. The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal. watchOS 27 and AI The Ultra 4 runs watchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to the Series 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year. The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on a modern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications. Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while the sound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful. But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”. Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed. Sustainability Apple says the battery should last more than 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £95. Damage repairs cost £539. The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in its environmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices. Price The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349). For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from £369, the Watch SE 3 costs £219 and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from £860. Verdict The Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone. The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others. Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet. That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before. Pros: great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support. Cons: no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.

headline: Elon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s Skydance
trail_text: Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery
body_text: Elon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison. The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news. The investment follows Paramount’s recent $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery, a huge acquisition that brought the media companies together under the Skydance name. At the head of the new media empire is David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison. The Guardian has contacted Musk and Skydance for comment. The cash infusion solidifies an alliance between two of Trump’s richest monetary backers. In September, Semafor reported that Paramount executives had considered Musk as an equity investor, citing his close ties to Larry Ellison, who invested $1bn in Musk’s acquisition of X in 2022 and also $45m in support of Trump’s re-election bid in 2024. Musk spent more than $290m on Trump’s re-election bid and has spent more than $350m backing Republicans in the current US midterm elections. After the merger, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, who previously led Mattel, informed employees that the integration would involve layoffs, stating: “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce.” The company’s leadership – which now oversees Paramount and Warner Bros’s movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN – has set a target of more than $6bn in cost savings over the next three years, a goal that Los Angeles county officials estimate could lead to the loss of 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles alone. Prior to the merger, a coalition of 12 states, including California and New York, sued Paramount, arguing that the deal would “extinguish” competition and result in “higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television”. In September, a settlement agreement required Skydance to release at least 30 films and more than 180 television shows annually, while ensuring that CBS and CNN maintain editorial independence.

headline: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
trail_text: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault
body_text: Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services. The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault. In the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked. The website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included the Internet Archive, Wikipedia and 4Chan. The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties. Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug. However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.” The flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards. In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”. Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday. CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”. The PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP. Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free. It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it. Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” it said in a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.” “Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” the NSA said. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.” The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem. China’s industry ministry urged organisations to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP, and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys. The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.

headline: What is PHP and how serious is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns?
trail_text: An estimated 70% of websites use the open-source language. What is the identified vulnerability in it?
body_text: Website owners faced millions of attempts to exploit a serious security vulnerability in their programming language, it has emerged, triggering a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem. The newly discovered vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that underpins most websites, allows hackers to carry out cyber-attacks and steal data if not fixed. What were the vulnerabilities and why did they affect so many sites? What is PHP? PHP is an open-source scripting language that is more than 30 years old and used across much of the internet. Content management systems and publishing template systems such as Wordpress are built on PHP. An estimated 70% of websites use PHP, with millions of sites affected by the vulnerabilities. Wikipedia and Facebook are among those. In the UK alone, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to organisations with affected systems, while government websites in France, the Netherlands, Canada, Japan and Germany were taken down temporarily as a precaution while a fix was added. What is the vulnerability? According to the PHP Foundation, the not-for-profit that maintains PHP code, the issues “sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling”. The two vulnerabilities were labelled by the security vendor Hadrian as a “PHP2Shell exploitation”. The vulnerabilities work by corrupting the memory in a website through a request that can then be used to launch an attack and could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”, according to the US National Security Agency. How was it discovered? Historically, researchers and cybersecurity experts would test systems for vulnerabilities and patch the issues when they were discovered – or patch when one system was attacked and a vulnerability was identified. Artificial intelligence has now sped up this process as AI can be thrown at systems to identify potential issues that might not have been spotted by a human, and can do so in a much shorter time frame. The PHP Foundation said it had worked with Anthropic’s frontier model to scan its code, and had PHP put into OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, which discovered the issue at the same time as a researcher, Ryan A, in mid-August. The disclosure of the vulnerabilities had been embargoed until 22 October, to give websites time to fix it. But according to the PHP Foundation, it discovered the two vulnerabilities had begun circulating on forums and social media on Tuesday and so brought forward the disclosure. The UK’s NCSC said this had created a 12- to 14-hour window for people to look for the vulnerability in websites before they could be patched. How bad is it? The breadth of the vulnerability appears to be unprecedented. As the PHP Foundation has said, the issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: “Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions.” Coupled with the sheer number of sites that rely on PHP, that makes it a massive problem that should be fixed as soon as possible. Now the flaw is out in the wild, Hadrian said it was seeing “exploitation happening at scale”. However, so far no major hacks appear to have occurred. In the 24 hours since the vulnerability was announced, the NCSC said it had not seen any successful hacks. How long will it take to fix? Patches are already available, and the reason a number of websites went down in the past few days was that people were working to patch their systems immediately. A number of the websites returned quickly. Security companies have recommended patching straight away, and where it cannot be done immediately, systems should be taken offline. “Shutting down a service for a few hours costs far less than a compromised server,” Hadrian said. However, it will depend on businesses and governments being aware they need to patch, and doing so quickly. “The immediate challenge is not simply installing a patch, but finding and managing every instance where PHP is running,” said Don Smith, the vice-president of threat intelligence at the cybersecurity firm Sophos Counter Threat Unit. Sigi Goode, a professor of information systems at the Australian National University, said the sites that went down while a fix was carried out were not the problem. “The bigger concern is the websites that are not down today. Users should be wary of these, as they are clear targets.” Did someone leak the vulnerability and break the embargo? A number of security companies did break the embargo after the leak, according to the PHP Foundation, but Amazon Threat Intelligence said in a blogpost that it had identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to four days before the public disclosure. “While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” it said. On the day the embargo was due to lift, but before it had lifted, Amazon also identified “multiple proof-of-concept exploits for the vulnerability”. These are non-harmful demonstrations that a vulnerability exists, without actually using that vulnerability to launch an attack – akin to testing a door to see if it has a faulty lock. Is AI making the internet more vulnerable to these sorts of issues? With AI, it is much easier to find vulnerabilities. AI agents can now identify issues that would have taken humans months or years to find, and they are also finding ones people were not aware of. It is why more updates have been issued lately for software on phones or computers and this is predicted to continue as AI exposes more software glitches. In an age of software dependency, that is likely to mean more money being spent on cybersecurity at all levels of the economy, from small to large businesses. Part of the problem is that – with the exception of the most frontline models – AI is very easy for everyone to use. It leads to something of a race between people trying to protect their systems, and hackers looking to take advantage of AI-discovered vulnerabilities. “Threat actors move fast, especially with the help of AI, and this will likely be a priority target for them over the coming hours and days, so it is crucial organisations monitor PHP and web-server processes for unusual processes, command execution or other signs that an attacker may already have gained a foothold,” Smith said. Some on social media have also pointed to a prescient cartoon by Randall Munroe, who is behind the web comic XKCD, about the reliance of modern infrastructure on projects maintained by small groups or one person. The PHP Foundation operates on financial contributions and maintains the language with only 13 full-time and part-time engineers, compared to the billions invested into developing AI.

headline: Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill
trail_text: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth tax
body_text: Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires. The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where Meta’s headquarters are located. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years. Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of these new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company. Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel and the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has described Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs. “Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week. “In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.” Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings. The company’s shares slid by more than 6% when trading opened on Wall Street on Thursday, helping to drag the tech-focused Nasdaq index down 2.5% amid a wider selloff of AI-linked stocks. In a separate case, on Wednesday a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn following a trial that found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data. Meta also revealed that it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago. Reuters contributed to this report.

headline: Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world
trail_text: Precautionary takedowns come as experts say vulnerability in PHP, which is used by 70% of sites, could be exploited
body_text: Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites. The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks. WordPress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday as a precautionary measure until they could be patched. The organisation behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”. Because a fix is now public and AI tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers ⁠jumped to get ahead of the updates. AI was powering a “race to exploit”, said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet”. Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at Surrey University, said: “It was very surprising and troubling because of the extent to which PHP was used around the world. PHP issued a patch very quickly. The big thing is for everyone using it to get that in to make sure their systems are safe. “The troubling part is there is going to be a long tail of websites who may not be maintained as well and they are going to remain vulnerable, which means we may see weeks and months of ongoing attacks. For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly.” Woodward said there was a window of opportunity for bad actors. “There is this race and some people unfortunately don’t even know they are in the race.” OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they used models available to the public. Cybersecurity company Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on 1 August and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The vulnerabilities remained hidden ‌in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said. In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said its security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy “honeypot” systems on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding that it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo. In a statement, the White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday. In the UK, websites belonging to Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford councils were taken offline. In France, local government websites including that of the Paris police prefecture went offline on Wednesday, as did in the Netherlands the national digital identity service, the website of the house of representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre. The Australian Signals Directorate was temporarily affected by the outage overnight local time, with the national cyber defence agency noting other government websites may have been similarly affected.
