Moye said after the verdict, the jury “expressed a profound disbelief” that the company would hire an expert who would make claims “without any foundation”. “[3M] were trying to reset the narrative,” Moye said. “And they hired an expert who’d never touched the machine.” A 3M spokesperson said that “after independently reviewing the facts and reaching his own conclusions”, Autenrieth “used AI as a tool in preparing his report”. Autenrieth’s legal counsel Janina Wojtkowski said ChatGPT didn’t produce his opinions or replace his “professional judgment” but assisted in formatting, structuring and drafting amid “severe deadline constraints”. Performance boost? Not so much As companies and workers muddle through the unknowns of early AI adoption, costs are still coming into focus, while broad productivity gains remain elusive. In a study published in May, University of Pittsburgh researchers concluded that productivity didn’t rise after companies invested in AI and cut staff. Although executives have been overwhelmingly optimistic about AI’s potential impacts for years, “management optimism does not effectively translate into … better performance,” the paper states. More than 112,000 job cut announcements in the US so far in 2026 have mentioned AI, making it a top reason for layoffs, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Earlier this year, Meta paused its practice of tracking employees’ computer activity to train its AI, according to Reuters. Meta also recently told employees that their adoption and usage of AI tools would no longer be part of performance reviews, the Information reported. Meta did not respond to a request for comment. Mark Ma, University of Pittsburgh professor and researcher on the AI layoff study, said leaders are focused on short-term performance, “which is why they tried to rush ahead by investing in AI and laying off workers”. But companies’ share prices tend to dip after they announce AI-related layoffs, he noted, suggesting that “the stock market also does not think these will work out.” “A lot of these mistakes could have been avoided,” Ma said. “Now I feel some managers have learned their lesson.”

headline: Employees all over the world find themselves monitored by AI at work
trail_text: The latest example of workers under surveillance comes from Co-op, a British consumer cooperative that runs thousands of businesses
body_text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while moving laundry from the washer to the dryer, wishing a robot could do the task for me. Today in tech, we’re talking about workers and AI. Workers under surveillance Employees across the globe are increasingly finding themselves minutely monitored in their workplaces, with tiny changes in their behaviors resulting in negative performance evaluations. The latest example of workers under surveillance and bristling at it comes from Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies in the UK. The company implemented an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers. In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyze and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates. “You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity. Read more: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance The Co-op said it did not recognize the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged. Resentment of workers’ treatment is already translating into policy, a break from the sluggishness of most technology regulations. Across the Atlantic and the continental United States, Governor Gavin Newsom of California signed laws into effect last week that prohibit certain types of workplace surveillance. California’s laws aim to target workplace surveillance measures like heat maps that track employees’ movements, including how long they spend in the bathroom, or having their emotional states monitored. Amazon warehouse workers have previously complained about being timed on their bathroom breaks, for example. And at Kaiser Permanente, a California hospital chain, nurses have said automated systems rated their tone of voice in patient interactions. Read more: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs *** Tell us: Are you being watched at work? Tell us: have you been monitored or assessed by AI at work? Silicon Valley on screen Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg Whom does AI benefit? Two stories recently published in the Guardian’s Reworked series pose the question: who is AI enriching? The first story details how the AI boom is leaving women out of the single largest engine of growth in the US economy. One visible example: Donald Trump’s all-male summit of AI leaders last week: not a single woman in sight as the president preached the power of “superintelligence”. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.” Read more: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind Across AI-related occupations, the median pay of men is $45,000 higher than that of women, partly due to the types of jobs men and women are more likely to have, according to research by LinkedIn: men are still typically hired for higher-paying roles in the AI industry. When pitching investors, one female co-founder of an AI startup said she had found through trial and error that she and her male co-founder are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching. Another story in the series examines how dire working conditions can become under the pressures of AI and automation. Refugees in Kenya are completing tasks for foreign technology companies under bizarre and opaque conditions. The stories of desperate remote data workers used to highlight the low pay and horrid content they were exposed to. Today, workers who spoke to the Guardian say they aren’t even sure they will be paid, as their compensation is tied to a so-called “reward” system that decides whether they receive payment based on the quality of their work. Many of the workers called the system unfair but also said with dismay that they had few, if any, other options. Read more: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay The workers in Kenya also expressed a desperation to earn any money at these jobs before AI could carry out the rote tasks they were assigned. Contrast these stories of unequal benefit with Sam Altman’s recent remarks on a podcast: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” Altman was referring to the consequences of AI like the hack of Hugging Face or the attempted creation of bioweapons by would-be terrorists. Bad, to be sure, but lacking the moral outrage of human consequences. The wider TechScape Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says OpenAI’s release of mathematical findings draws concerns from experts Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies aged 90

headline: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet
trail_text: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
body_text: Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price. The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors. The earbuds and case are almost indistinguishable from the AirPods 4, which makes the case very small and easy to pocket, fitting in the watch pocket of a pair of jeans. The buds are some of the most comfortable open-fit designs available and stayed put when commuting, running for the train and generally going about the day. But for those that didn’t get on with the previous design of the AirPods, these are unlikely to change that, and they have no stability wings or similar to keep them in place for vigorous exercise. The stalk has a pressure-sensitive panel you squeeze once, twice or thrice for playback controls. A squeeze and hold changes the noise cancelling mode or activates Siri. On the more expensive versions with a wireless charging case, the panel is also touch-sensitive for swipe volume controls – the same system used in the AirPods Pro to great effect. Specifications Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case) Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes) Earbud dimensions: 30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mm Earbud weight: 4.3g each Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm Charging case weight: 32.3g/34.7g Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch) Up to five hours of battery life The cheapest AirPods 5 have up to four hours playback with noise cancelling and a case that can charge them four times for a total of 20 hours playback. The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case have longer battery life lasting slightly more than five hours of playback with noise cancelling with a total of 22 hours playback using charges in the case. That’s long enough for a week of commuting, but far behind the best in the business. A compromise for the design and super-compact case. Upgraded sound and noise cancelling The new AirPods have noticeably improved noise cancelling and sound. They produce fairly detailed sound with good separation of tones and can handle complex and overlapping tracks very well. But it is the additional bass that helps them produce a fuller, more rounded sound that wipes the floor with most other open-fit rivals and compares well to many decent earbuds with silicone tips. They may not satisfy audiophiles but they are a great listen. The noise cancelling is equally effective, managing to quiet busy roads, the drone of engines or fans, and dampen background chatter. It struggles with higher tones, such as loud keyboard clicks or the screeches from train wheels, but does as good a job as many similarly-priced noise cancelling earbuds with silicone tips and is miles ahead of the open-fit competition. They suffer a little from wind noise and can’t rival the sound dampening of the best earbuds with tips from Sony, Bose or the AirPods Pro 3, but still do a solid job. The transparency mode is first class, sounding almost exactly like not wearing them at all, which is great for awareness on the street. Call quality is equally good coming through loud and clear with only a hint of sudden background noise when passing something particularly loud. The AirPods 5 support Apple’s various smart features with an iPhone, such as direct access to the new Siri, live translation, automatic volume adjustment, spatial audio, audio sharing, the ability to pause music when falling asleep and optimised battery charging to increase its longevity. Sustainability Batteries in earbuds typically maintain at least 80% of their original capacity for 500 charge cycles. Apple offers a battery service for £49 per earbud or case and replacements cost from £69. The specialists iFixit awarded the earbuds two out of 10 for repairability. The AirPods 5 are made with 40% recycled material, which the company breaks down in its environmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products. Price The AirPods 5 cost £119 (€149/$129/A$219) or £139 (€169/$149/A$249) with a wireless charging case and touch controls. For comparison, the AirPods Pro 3 cost £219, the AirPods Max 2 cost £499, the Google Pixel Buds 2a cost £129 and the Shokz OpenFit Air 2 cost £129. Verdict The AirPods 5 take the comfortable open-fit design of their predecessors and upgrade the sound and noise cancelling to rival many plugged-in earbuds with silicone tips, which is quite a feat. They provide a good amount of bass for a full, detailed sound that’s a great general listen and a step above most open-fit rivals. The noise cancelling is capable of dampening unwanted sound to tolerable levels, comparing well with better than average silicone-equipped earbuds. It can’t match the best plugged-in earbuds, but it is certainly good enough. Apple’s transparency mode and call quality are top-notch, and it’s hard to fault the earbuds for daily use with a compact design that’s easy to pocket. The battery life is a little short, and while they work with any Bluetooth device, I wouldn’t recommend them to people who don’t have at least one iPhone, iPad or Mac. There are few great open-fit earbuds, but if you didn’t get on with other AirPods, these won’t tip the balance. The extra money for swipe volume controls and longer battery life is worth it, if you’re considering them. The fifth-generation earbuds are marginally more repairable than their predecessors, which opens up the possibility of replacing the batteries down the line, but otherwise they are just as disposable as most other earbuds. Pros: comfortable open fit, good sound and noise cancelling, great case, great playback and volume controls, great connectivity, special features with Apple devices including spatial audio, great call quality. Cons: battery life could be better, little passive noise isolation, lack of features when connected to non-Apple devices, no Bluetooth multipoint or higher quality audio format support, difficult to repair.

headline: David Pocock concerned senior Albanese adviser ‘vetted’ bipartisan AI letter that was sent to PM
trail_text: Committee chair rejects criticism that letter was ‘pre-determined’ by the government
body_text: Anthony Albanese’s office signed off on language in a bipartisan letter from a parliamentary committee considering AI policy before it was sent to the prime minister, a move which committee member David Pocock said was concerning. Notes on the letter to Albanese, seen by Guardian Australia, show a senior adviser made multiple edits and wrote “fine” on some content, appearing to approve lines in the letter before the committee wrote to the prime minister on Monday night. Some edits were made as late as 8:55pm, 35 minutes before the Labor MP and inquiry chair, Jo Briskey, and Liberal senator and deputy chair, Jonno Duniam, sent the letter to Albanese, on behalf of Labor, Coalition and crossbench MPs. Pocock, an independent senator on the committee, was asked to provide edits to the letter. He provided that feedback at 9:55pm, not knowing the letter had already been sent. The letter raises concerns about copyright, AI safeguards, sovereign capability and AI literacy. Pocock said he was concerned at the intervention of Albanese’s team. “I respect the committee process and the need to work in a multipartisan way across the parliament,” he said. “I’m concerned that markups on the documents show the recommendations were pre-vetted by an adviser in the prime minister’s office and there was no time for changes to be considered by the chair. “While the letter is broad in nature, after reviewing it in more detail it doesn’t capture the breadth of evidence presented to the committee to date.” Briskey rejected criticism that the committee’s work was “pre-determined” by the government, and confirmed the committee had consulted both Albanese and the opposition leader’s office prior to sending the letter. “It’s been a process by which we’re seeking advice and making sure that this is working across the board … There was engagement right across the panel. Senator Duniam also worked with his side, the opposition,” she said. Briskey said the letter was to show the direction of the committee ahead of handing down its report due 30 November. Duniam said there was “no guidance, no interference” with the committee’s work. “I[’ll] tell you who would be the first person out of the blocks to criticise the government if the prime minister wasn’t showing interest in the committee’s work: it would be me,” Duniam said. “This is an example of the parliament working well. There’s been no guidance, no interference. There has been a lot of discussion, a lot of consultation.” He said others who wanted to sit on the sidelines and “find points of difference” could do so. Pocock said the letter overlooks key concerns articulated by creatives about the global dangers from any changes to our copyright protections in Australia, the need to consider a datacentre levy to capture long term benefit and the need to invest in retraining and upskilling workers whose jobs are displaced by AI. “It also fails to address the urgent need to immediately commence mandatory screening of genetic synthesis imports at all Australian borders,” he said. “After this, I am increasingly concerned that the work of this committee is being used to serve a political purpose rather than provide genuine parliamentary scrutiny and policy input. “We’ve seen enough major party stitch-ups. Regaining the community’s trust, especially on the issue of AI requires robust debate and committee work.” Guardian Australia has chosen not to name the advisers in Albanese’s office. The prime minister’s office declined to comment.

headline: Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival
trail_text: Just 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?
body_text: Name: Wikipedia. Age: 25. Appearance: Patronising and deeply biased. Is this because you haven’t got your own page? Well, yes. But these aren’t my words. They’re the words of Sandi Toksvig. But it has 65m articles across more than 300 languages! It’s the largest knowledge resource ever assembled! That may be, but it isn’t very good at women. According to Toksvig? Yes – and she’s very serious about it. As we speak, she is travelling the world trying to raise money to build something better. She is? Yes. Along with the University of Cambridge, she hopes that her Mappa Mundi project will be an “interactive digital atlas where we can find a home for the vast amount of knowledge that is currently sidelined or deleted”. And a lot of the sidelined or deleted knowledge is about women? It is. She cites the case of Donna Strickland, a Canadian physicist who repeatedly had her draft biographies rejected by Wikipedia, until she won a Nobel prize for her work. Awkward. But it goes broader. By the Wikimedia Foundation’s own estimate, only 19% of Wikipedia biographies concern women. Toksvig puts this down to the site being edited by “mostly white, middle-aged, European men who have both the time and the technology”, she told Cheltenham literature festival this weekend. I didn’t know that. Its content is weighted heavily towards wealthy countries. In 2013, for instance, the Oxford Internet Institute discovered that Wikipedia contained more coverage of Germany than of Africa and South America combined. Isn’t Wikipedia too leftwing anyway? Oh God, are you Elon Musk? This is a claim he has repeated for the last couple of years, to the extent of calling it “Wokepedia”. And what did he do about it? He started his own version – an AI-powered alternative called Grokipedia. And is it better? A paper published in November 2025 discovered that Grokipedia articles are 13 times more likely to contain a source blacklisted by the English Wikipedia community. What’s a blacklisted source? The paper pointed out that, at the time of its publication, Grokipedia included 42 citations for the banned neo-Nazi website Stormfront. Yeesh. Bring on Mappa Mundi! Indeed, Toksvig’s version has better intentions. If nothing else, hopefully it will update Wikipedia’s list of people who died on the toilet to include more women. Do say: “Wikipedia is systemically biased.” Don’t say: “At last, something Elon Musk and Sandi Toksvig can agree on.” • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? headline: Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister
trail_text: Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agent
body_text: An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister. Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity. In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK. “It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.” Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have. “The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said. Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents. Narayan spoke before a parliamentary hearing on AI safety on Tuesday into the issue. Senior figures from OpenAI and Anthropic will be among those giving evidence to MPs on the business, innovation, science and trade committee. They will also be joined by the head of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Henry de Zoete. Narayan confirmed that the institute would gain access to advanced AI models before they were released, after the White House had reportedly placed restrictions on their availability. “I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generations of models, including [Google’s] Gemini … to identify risks early to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe,” he said. The minister added that leading AI companies must “listen” to warnings of safety risks posed by their technology – and not release models if they carried a serious threat. “And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers; investigate unexpected behaviours; and if you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” he said. “I want the labs to be honest.” Narayan said the UK would “play its part” in coordinating an international response to AI safety by making the technology a “central focus” of Britain’s G20 presidency next year. “We know that these challenges cannot be addressed by a single country alone, but by virtue of our capability, by virtue of the foundations of our trust, Britain will play its part,” he said.

headline: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
trail_text: Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents
body_text: Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC. Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”. He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. In a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports. Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”. Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder.

headline: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone
trail_text: A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match
body_text: Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299). The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of its Pro Max predecessors: take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support. But it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than its nearest rival, 38g more than its smaller sibling and heavier still than folding phones. It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap. The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro. Specifications Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi) Processor: Apple A20 Pro RAM: 12GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: iOS 27 Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins) Dimensions: 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm Weight: 249g Battery life for days The 18 Pro Max has the same new A20 Pro chip as the 18 Pro, which is one of the fastest chips you can get in a phone, plus a resigned cooling system that helps maintain peak performance during long gaming sessions. It has the longest battery of any iPhone, lasting almost three days of light usage between charges, actively using the screen for seven hours for apps, browsing, messaging and photos. That is about four hours longer than its predecessor and almost a day longer than the 18 Pro. Even with heavy use, the 18 Pro Max still managed to end the day with about 50% left in the tank, meaning most people will have to charge it only every second or third day. iOS 27 The 18 Pro Max runs the same iOS 27 as smartphones from the iPhone 11 onwards. The new software speeds up app launches and other parts of the system, refines the Liquid Glass redesign from last year and revamps Apple’s AI tools. The new Siri AI chatbot is a significant step in the right direction, able to better understand you and perform tasks. It has its own app to review previous conversations and can see what is on your screen or through the camera. It can also suggest data from your various Apple apps, similar to Google’s proactive tools on the Pixels. But it relies on you using messages and mail, rather than third-party apps such as the WhatsApp or Gmail apps. Sustainability The battery will last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity, and it can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £389. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone seven out of 10 for repairability. It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products. Camera The 18 Pro Max has the same camera system as its smaller sibling, which includes an 18 megapixel centre stage selfie camera in the screen and three 48MP cameras on the back. The three rear cameras are some of the best on a phone, including a 4x/8x optical zoom and 0.5x ultra wide. The big addition for the 18 Pro Max is a variable aperture on the main camera, allowing it to open wider than other iPhones for better low light performance or to narrow to preserve depth of field. But it also allows additional creative photography possibilities, including shooting starbursts. The 18 Pro Max also has new AI-powered focus tracking, improved Photographic Styles for greater customisation, Apple’s new digital negative feature and automatic cinematic mode for video. Price The iPhone 18 Pro Max costs from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299). For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air £1,099 and the iPhone 18 Pro £1,199; the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,279 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra £1,359. Verdict The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s biggest, longest-lasting and most expensive slab phone for 2026. It takes what is great about the regular 18 Pro and supersizes the screen and battery, giving it a run time of up to three days, which is a good half day more than its smaller sibling. That places it shoulder to shoulder with some of the longest-lasting phones available on any platform. But similar to superphones from Google and Samsung, the 18 Pro Max is too big to use one-handed and tricky to pocket. It is also too heavy and made my hand hurt without using a Popsocket or a similar handle attached to it. Otherwise, it is a fairly iterative upgrade on the 17 Pro Max, with the same design and feel. The screen is still one of the very best on a phone, and the improved dynamic island is a useful upgrade. The A20 Pro chip is seriously quick, the cameras are some of the best you can get on a phone and the variable aperture on the main camera opens up some new creative opportunities, even if its impact on image quality is fairly minor. Pros: fabulous 6.9in screen, better dynamic island, very long battery life, great cameras with variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI. Cons: very expensive, very heavy, hard to use one-handed, small upgrade on last year, AI tools still lag top competitors.

headline: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts
trail_text: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
body_text: Companies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences. Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure. Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.” He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring. Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body, has warned there is a “50% chance” of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans. “It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said. Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has been signed by leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems. In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions. Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly. The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons. Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk. “We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

headline: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
trail_text: George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
body_text: The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute. The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson. The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift. “As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson. In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart. “We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said. Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.” He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030. “It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said. “We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.” Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.” Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff. Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said. In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology. Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.” “This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups. “We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said. Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.” He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.” Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards. “For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

headline: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
trail_text: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before
body_text: OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI. The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September. However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported. Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment. OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn. News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July. Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not. Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI. Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race. Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month. OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn. Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn. On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI. SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported. Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.

headline: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts
trail_text: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
body_text: Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts. Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer. Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has provided AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS. The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m. Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices? Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one.” He added: “I think we are very targeted by the people that are targeting Israeli companies. We’re not an Israeli company, but because of our work in Israel we found ourselves in the middle of the row of the Gaza protests.” Watson told the podcast he would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns if the situation arose, saying: “We don’t actually work in that sector, but yes, of course we would.” He called Palantir “the most interesting company on the planet” as he announced his new role last month. The company said his job would be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”. Watson was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, he has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir. Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while he worked for the company in London. The Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the science, innovation and technology committee, which has raised concerns about Palantir, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “Tom is not the first politician to be blinded by tech hype. The key issue is we can’t be so dependent on one company. It’s a US company, subject to US legislation regarding access to our data.”

headline: Anthropic bans users from ‘needless abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude
trail_text: A spokesperson for the tech company did not specify what kind of behavior would be considered abusive
body_text: Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness. The Verge first reported the change in policy. A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is behind the AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”. In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”. Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct. The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare. “We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website. The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has said he cannot rule out the possibility. Meanwhile, Sam Altman, CEO of rival OpenAI, has appeared averse to the idea. “I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue,” he wrote in an X post, days after the New York Times reported on Anthropic leaders’ extensive conversations with religious scholars.

headline: Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says
trail_text: Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency
body_text: Microsoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed through a US visa program for high-skilled workers, JD Vance announced on Thursday. The US vice-president accused the tech company of abusing the H-1B system, which allows those on the visa to work while they apply for and are in the process of obtaining a green card. “Our message to Microsoft is, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a press conference announcing the suspension. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.” Microsoft said the vast majority of its workers were American and 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last year were for extensions or status changes for people who already worked for the company. “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote in a statement. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” The US labor department also said Adobe had been similarly suspended. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” said Keith Sonderling, the US labor secretary, in a statement. Microsoft applied for H-1B visas for nearly 3,700 workers in 2026, making it the fifth largest employer of workers on the visa. Tech companies are the biggest employers of H-1B workers across the industry. Amazon topped the list with more than 9,300 petitions this year. Sonderling said since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe had received about 230,000 approvals for H-1B visas and 100,000 “permanent labor certifications”, a step towards an employment-based green card. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. The Trump administration has set its sights on the H-1B program for some time, arguing that it is rife with abuse. Vance said that, on average, workers hired through the H-1B program were making $20,000 less than US workers in the same position. “So I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played,” Vance said. “You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with.” Immigration advocacy groups have long called for reforms for the H-1B program, though for different reasons. Those in the program are often beholden to their employer because their visas are tied to the company that applied for them, making it difficult to switch jobs if things aren’t going well or if they want to find a job with a higher salary. These groups, like the National Immigration Forum, largely disagree with Vance. They argue that competing for specialized talent from around the world benefits the US economy. “The United States has long benefited from its ability to attract talent from around the world, particularly in STEM, higher education, research, and innovation,” the National Immigration Forum wrote in a September 2026 blogpost discussing proposed changes to the H-1B program. “As countries increasingly compete for highly skilled workers, policies that make the United States less attractive could strengthen global competitors.”

headline: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance
trail_text: Whistleblower says recording and analysis of all probate calls in Co-op Legal Services is oppressive
body_text: The Co-op has become the latest employer to place workers under AI surveillance with an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers. In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyse and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates. A model from OpenAI has been trained to assess more than 50 discrete aspects of each phone call and provide pass and fail scores to managers who use the data to analyse employee performance. One worker said the system can mean their work is monitored by AI for several hours a day as they handle inquiries often from recently bereaved customers. It comes after the Guardian last week revealed Euan Blair’s AI training company, Multiverse, has started using an AI for blanket monitoring of online classroom sessions, which teachers called “remorseless” and “unnerving”, while Multiverse said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”. Experts have voiced fears that increasing AI monitoring of workers risks increasing stress. “You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity and said the AI created a sense of distrust. “It’s different from occasionally being listened to for compliance purposes. [You are] being monitored absolutely every word that you say and every time that you utter something … It just feels really dystopian. It’s the thin end of the wedge.” The Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies, said it did not recognise the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged. It said it supported colleagues with AI, which is a “key aspect of our quality assurance processes” and helps ensure “our clients consistently receive empathetic expert guidance”. The AI monitoring is understood to have been introduced in the last couple of months into the work of dozens of legal services staff. It is used in part to identify ways they can boost their sales performance. The Co-op said the AI is used solely as a support tool, is not a decision-maker, and helps leaders “support colleagues and continuously improve the experience we provide to clients”. Trade unions have begun pushing back against the spread of AI monitoring. In February Burger King in the US announced it would be using the technology to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions, and this summer, Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash. “AI is sold as the solution to every problem, but examples like this make it clear that it can diminish sensible workplace practices and intensify working lives for no reason,” said John Chadfield, the national officer of the Communication Workers Union. “Unaccountable computer systems should not be people’s managers, and these hard-working employees demand far more respect.” “The office is becoming more like a factory now our performance feedback can be given in a more structured way,” said Hayfa Mohdzaini, a senior policy and practice adviser at the Chartered Institute of Professional Development. “Clearly some people have a problem with it. It will be interesting to see how it develops and how much managers need to adjust their approach.” This year, the International Labour Organization warned about the “psychosocial” risks of AI monitoring, including increasing work-related stress. “AI systems are being deployed in workplaces in the absence of a comprehensive regulatory framework,” it said. “Preventing the risk of harm by AI use and operation in this context may not be straightforward.” Caoilionn Hurley, the managing director of Co-op Life Services, which includes legal services, said: “The efficiency of AI over traditional methods allows us to review all customer conversations to ensure we consistently deliver high standards of service, while enabling more informed support, coaching and development for colleagues … Put simply, our goal is to provide expert support combined with empathy and understanding for every client at what can be a difficult time. AI helps us deliver that more consistently, while human judgment, accountability, care and kindness remain at the heart of every client relationship.”

headline: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind
trail_text: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
body_text: There’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI. The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present. “A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.” Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching. Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared with 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI. AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have. “AI is creating some of the fastest-growing, highest-paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.” The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said. “What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs. Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement. ‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’ Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at the investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.” Putatunda said it was not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up. “If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.” Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare. “That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.” The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI. “Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.” When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women. The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a former technology product executive with two decades of industry experience, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies such as Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement. “It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.” Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”

headline: OpenAI’s release of mathematical findings draws concerns from experts
trail_text: Leaders worry OpenAI is not doing due diligence to vet results and that AI models aren’t accessible to broader field of mathematicians
body_text: OpenAI has astounded mathematicians after releasing hundreds of new mathematical findings on Tuesday. The company published over 370 mathematical results across a variety of topics such as algebra, theoretical computer science and mathematical logic, showcasing what some of its most advanced artificial intelligence models are capable of. Last month, the company solved the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the world’s toughest mathematical problems with a $1m reward for anyone who cracked it. The achievement prompted concerns from leaders in the field who say that frontier labs should not be testing the most advanced mathematical problems on proprietary AI models that are not accessible to the broader field of mathematicians. The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, an independent group of mathematical experts, said that it does not endorse the practice. “It is now the case that AI can output mathematical arguments in situations without the human who prompted it being able to understand the arguments, verify them, or take responsibility for them,” a statement from the organization read. “We believe that human understanding of mathematics remains of paramount importance. How, in this new era, can we work towards a new paradigm that includes human understanding of mathematics as part of responsible scholarly output?” To address concerns from the mathematics community, OpenAI announced it would work with the Institute for Advanced Study in order to give “mathematicians a voice in how we move forward”. The company did not indicate, however, that it would stop testing its AI models with these advanced problems. Experts in the field say they worry OpenAI is not doing the due diligence required to vet these results. In an interview with the New York Times, Tristan Buckmaster, a New York University mathematician who was working on the Navier-Strokes problem, said mathematicians who were prompting AI models to solve equations could be providing information that helped the model get to the result. “There’s likely to be a bunch of results where they take someone’s work and then take it to completion,” Buckmaster said. The advisory board has also asked that AI labs grant “equitable access” to their AI models to the global mathematics community. “The use of proprietary internal models by AI labs to do mathematical research risks creating a two-tier system where labs outrun the rest of the field, effectively alienating the mathematical community from its own discipline,” the group wrote.

headline: Privacy watchdog launches investigation into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
trail_text: Commissioner says Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries
body_text: The Australian privacy regulator has opened an investigation into the China-based software company behind the HeyCyan app in Kmart’s $89 smartglasses, following public outrage over the covert use of the devices. In August, Guardian Australia reported Kmart had sold out of the Anko-branded discount version of Meta’s smartglasses that can capture images and record high-definition video, which led to widespread concern and calls to ban or restrict their use. The glasses were removed from Kmart’s website as of Wednesday. The retailer has been approached for comment. A GetUp petition has had more than 55,000 signatures calling to restrict the use of what has been labelled as “pervert glasses”, and councils around the country have looked to ban the glasses in public spaces such as swimming pools. The federal government is also considering a restriction on use in government workplaces. The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses at the time. Kind wrote to Kmart and BDI Technology, retailers for the glasses, as well as Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the glasses. She also wrote to Meta – for its Ray-Bans glasses – and Google which is planning its own smartglasses. In a blog post on Wednesday, Kind announced an investigation has been opened into Shenzhen Qingcheng after it failed to respond to inquiries, “as well as concerns arising from third party analysis of the technology itself as well as the entity’s privacy policy” None of the other companies will be investigated as part of this process, Kind said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The privacy commissioner also highlighted the difficulty in applying privacy law to individuals who may use the devices given the privacy act only applies to companies and Commonwealth agencies – not individuals. “Retailers that sell smart glasses – for example on an e-commerce website – or companies that manufacture them, may not have any Privacy Act obligations if they do not collect any personal information with respect to those devices,” Kind said. “Instead, the entity providing the software at use in the device is likely to be the entity that collects and holds the information for the purpose of privacy law.” Kind said that potential changes to the privacy act proposed by the government would strengthen how privacy law would apply to surveillance wearables such as smartglasses. “The most substantial change will be the replacement of the ‘reasonably necessary for an entity’s functions and activities’ test with a ‘fair and reasonable’ test,” she said. “The new test will require an entity to look at a range of factors, including the extent to which an individual had genuine choice in the collection of their personal information, as well as the best interests of the child where children are involved.” Kind said she hoped the community would “find comfort” in the proposed reforms as it would raise the bar over what personal information smartglasses can collect. “These reforms are likely to become increasingly necessary as we face subsequent generations of surveillance wearables and connected devices, from personal assistant gadgets to ambient recording badges.” Researchers at the University of Sydney in August analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”. In a subset of these videos, about 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage. Canterbury-Bankstown and Sydney City are among the councils in Sydney to have banned the glasses from some venues, as well as Brisbane in Queensland, and Yarra city council in Melbourne. Shenzhen Qingcheng was approached for comment.

headline: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns
trail_text: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments
body_text: Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to carry out the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites. The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajaani are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure. It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google, had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA). In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres. On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation. The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said. Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.” If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine. In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”. The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.” Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.” One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities. “The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.” • This article was amended on 16 October 2026 to correct a misspelling of the town of Kajaani.

headline: Is regulation enough to stop AI systems killing us all?
trail_text: Letter: Martyn Thomas wonders how any rational person can argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient
body_text: Once again a frontier AI model has been withdrawn because it fails safety tests (OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing, 28 September). There is the usual call for “independent oversight and regulation”, though never any explanation of how this would work or, most importantly, what evidence should persuade a regulator that an AI system is adequately safe. There is a long engineering tradition of regulating safety-critical software systems, such as those controlling aircraft or nuclear power stations; international standards require “safety cases” – rigorous analyses that show that the possible hazards have been identified and controlled and that the probability of an accident is extremely low. Typically, the safety case should show, with a probability of at least 99%, that an accident that could cause multiple fatalities will not occur more often than once in 1,000 years. It is extremely hard to provide evidence for such low probabilities, even for aircraft that at worst might kill 1,000 people in a single accident. The developers of frontier AI systems tell us that their systems might kill the whole of humanity, yet they have provided no detailed risk analyses, no safety cases that could be independently assessed, and no evidence that such safety cases could ever be produced for frontier AI systems. How, then, can any rational person argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient? Policy must be based on rigorous analysis of the facts, not on fantasy. Martyn Thomas Fellow and emeritus professor of IT, Gresham College • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe
trail_text: A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence
body_text: For more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe. Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground. Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.
