Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all. “It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.” Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators. Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.” Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon. The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter. “We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.” Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year. “This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois. Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles. One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos. Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes. Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”

headline: Elfi Evans obituary
trail_text: Other lives: Carmarthenshire vet who treated animals from cats to elephants
body_text: My father, Elfi Evans, who has died aged 90, was one of a rare breed of truly omnicompetent practising veterinary surgeons, as at ease treating cats and dogs as he was carrying out caesarean sections on horses and cattle, in his native Carmarthenshire. Ever industrious, Elfi also ran a smallholding at the family home, where he reared sheep, grew vegetables and developed a number of environmental projects with the help of the Welsh government’s Tir Gofal (Care of the Land) scheme to support the natural biodiversity of the region. The third of five sons, Elfi was born in Bancycapel, Carmarthenshire, to Margaret (nee Williams) and William Evans, and grew up on the family farm there, becoming used to hard work from a very early age. Speaking exclusively Welsh at home, his first experience of English came about during the second world war, from the exchanges he and his brothers had with the Italian and German prisoners of war working on the farm, and American soldiers stationed nearby. At the age of 15, against his father’s wishes, Elfi stayed on at Queen Elizabeth grammar school in Carmarthen. He had ambitions to study engineering but, persuaded by his father that a veterinary degree was the better option, he started a BVSc at Liverpool University, travelling the eight-hour journey between his home and Liverpool on his Lambretta scooter at the start and end of each term. After graduating in 1960 and working for a period as a vet in Chwilog, north Wales, he returned to Carmarthen to set up his own practice, The Ark, assisted by his wife, Ann (nee Cadwaladr), whom he had met at Liverpool at combined medic and vet physiology lectures and married in 1962. By the 70s Elfi’s veterinary practice had developed into a three-partner operation, responding to increasing demands from the farming community across Carmarthenshire – as well as the rise in ownership of cats, dogs and more exotic animals, including an elephant, Valli, kept by the Skanda Vale religious community. In the early 80s he moved the practice to larger premises and started to specialise in diseases of sheep. Elfi retired from the practice in January 2001, but it was short-lived as his knowledge and skills were urgently required throughout that year with the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth crisis across the UK. He and Ann had taken on and transformed the run-down smallholding near the village of Nantycaws in the late 80s. There, Elfi created ponds to attract and support wildlife and planted native species of trees within traditional orchard environments. The non-native fir trees, which he planted to provide shelter for the young saplings, were harvested over many years and given away as Christmas trees in return for donations, raising tens of thousands of pounds for the oncology department at Carmarthen hospital, where Elfi had been successfully treated for cancer in the early 90s. Elfi is survived by Ann, his three sons, Winston, Gavin and me, and eight grandchildren.

headline: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe
trail_text: Archaeologists uncover jewellery, cosmetics and coins in cabinet sealed since eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79
body_text: Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii. The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii. The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern. But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury. The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified. “A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park. “It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.” The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson. The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said. Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home. The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project. There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century. “It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters. “So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.” Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city. A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

headline: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag
trail_text: Oxford study shows Manx shearwaters lose direction when their body clocks get out of sync
body_text: Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation. The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey. But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles. Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues. Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said. Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time. Writing in Science, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction. “For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.” Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.” Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows. “It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said. “Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”

headline: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?
trail_text: Experts say symptoms such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss can be a warning sign – but there are other factors too
body_text: TikTok is rife with influencers warning of “ferritin face”, a term they use to describe the pallor, dark circles, dry skin, and hair loss claimed to indicate low iron stores. But is this based on fact or fiction, and when is it time to head to the GP? What is ferritin? Iron is not made in the body, so typically we consume it in our diet. Ferritin is the protein responsible for storing iron in the body, particularly in the liver, and releasing it in a controlled manner. By measuring ferritin levels, which can be checked via blood tests, it is possible to get an snapshot of the body’s iron reserves, although experts warn such levels are not always a reliable guide. Blood ferritin levels of less than 30 micrograms/L indicate an iron deficiency, according to guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. However “a level below 50 might be a pointer of iron deficiency,” said Sue Pavord, professor of practice in medical haematology at Oxford University hospitals. Can low ferritin change a person’s appearance? The symptoms influencers describe, such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss, can be caused by a variety of factors, including genetics, stress and dehydration. But experts say low iron stores can have an effect. “Iron is needed for every single cell of the body. So if you are iron deficient, you will be very fatigued, have brain fog, your skin will look dull and saggy, you’ll look pale and tired,” said Pavord. “While we can’t diagnose iron deficiency from the face, it might be a suggestion that there is iron deficiency.” Prof Toby Richards of the University of East London and the Iron Clinic added such changes were particularly pronounced in people with very low iron stores. “They tend to be the really sick patients,” he said. Why might people have low ferritin? “Periods and pregnancies are the most common [causes],” said Pavord, but others include not getting enough iron – either from dietary choices or because of poor absorption, as can occur with coeliac disease. Low ferritin levels can also arise as a result of blood loss linked to gastrointestinal problems, such as gastritis or polyps. “We also sometimes see it in athletes because of the high demand for iron on their bodies,” she added. What should people who are worried they might have low ferritin do ? Richards said those who are at high risk of low ferritin – such as people who have heavy periods, are pregnant or have had children, or are vegetarian or vegan – should ask for a blood test, adding that should include a full blood count, ferritin level check, and test for levels of B12 and folate. “This is a proper disease, and to put it into perspective, it’s the leading cause of disability in women of reproductive ability,” he said. Pavord also said those who are concerned about their ferritin levels should ask for a blood test, adding it was important to understand the cause of iron deficiency. “Older people suspecting iron deficiency would need a proper clinical assessment and investigations to look for a source of bleeding from the bowel,” she said. Pavord said it is possible to buy iron tablets over the counter at a pharmacy. “Taking iron tablets without confirming iron deficiency is not really going to do you any harm, particularly if you’re a young woman, because you’re losing a lot of iron with periods,” she said. But Richards noted many products do not necessarily contain the appropriate dose. “If you are iron deficient, you need to be on a full treatment dose … and then repeat your blood results in three months’ time,” he said. “What’s marketed is normally the lower dose supplements Is the social media focus helpful, or problematic? Pavord was positive about the increase in awareness. “We need to stop normalising iron deficiency,” she said. “Many women are just exhausted trying to cope with their periods, cope with their pregnancies, cope with their young children and their busy jobs, and we need to stop normalising fatigue.” Richards agreed. “ Anything that raises the plight of women in this area is a good thing,” he said. However Dr Asiya Maula, a GP from the private firm The Health Suite, was cautious. “The risk with social media trends is that people may see themselves in a list of symptoms and assume they have a deficiency without checking whether that is actually the cause,” she said.

headline: Jean Phillips-Martinsson obituary
trail_text: Founder of an international organisation to encourage research into the rare genetic disorder Prader-Willi syndrome
body_text: In 1984 Jean Phillips-Martinsson, a British woman living in Sweden, came across an article in the Lancet. It was about Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS), a rare genetic condition named after Andrea Prader and Heinrich Willi, two of the three Swiss paediatricians who discovered it in 1956. It was a lightbulb moment for Phillips-Martinsson, who had been in limbo for 14 years, wanting to know why her son, Anders, born in 1970, was floppy and unable to suck as a baby, and later had behavioural problems and was constantly hungry (hyperphagia). It turned out these are all key signs of PWS. Phillips-Martinsson contacted the article’s author, who was able to diagnose Anders. She said her first thought was, “Are we alone in Sweden?”, and through the endocrinologist Martin Ritzén she was put in touch with four other families with a PWS child. They had all felt similarly isolated, and when they met for coffee on in April 1986 at Phillips-Martinsson’s house in Stockholm she said: “It was an extremely emotional situation for us all.” She and the other parents wanted advice on PWS, which causes behavioural and mental health issues as well as constant hunger and weight gain. So that year she set up a Prader-Willi Syndrome Association in Sweden. But she knew it was too small to be effective: the condition is so rare (estimated to affect between one in 15,000 and in one in 25,000 people) that a global charity with a wider reach was essential. It helped that she had networking and research skills, and could speak several languages. With a background in PR and translating, over the next few years she poured her energies into researching PWS. She discovered fledgling PWS charities in other countries, including the Netherlands, the US and the UK, and in November 1986 attended the PWS-UK’s conference in Bristol. In 1988 she was excited to hear from the American geneticist Dr Suzanne Cassidy. Thanks to a new technique called high-resolution analysis, geneticists knew that PWS resulted from an anomaly on chromosome 15. Research was taking place across the world, but it was not coordinated, and Cassidy wanted to bring researchers and doctors together in an international conference. Phillips-Martinsson and Cassidy met in 1989, forming an organising committee for a conference to be held in the Netherlands in 1991. During the next couple of years, a time she described as “being drowned in correspondence”, Phillips-Martinsson drummed up support from researchers, doctors and parents around the world, and secured sponsorship from the Swedish company Kabi Pharmacia, the World Health Organization and Nato. While much of the conference was devoted to scientific developments, Phillips-Martinsson championed the families, making sure one day of the conference focused on the concerns of parents and caregivers. The conference opened in May 1991 in the Netherlands, with 200 delegates from 22 countries. They voted to form the International Prader-Willi Syndrome Organisation (IPWSO) with Phillips-Martinsson as its president. She served in this capacity until 1998 and remained its guiding force and honorary president to the end of her life. As president, Phillips-Martinsson networked extensively to bring more countries into the IPSWO fold, and supported the setup of national organisations in many countries in Europe and beyond. She travelled widely, speaking at PWS conferences in Europe, the US, Australia and New Zealand. On her watch, IPWSO began its programme of international conferences every three years. They put out regular newsletters, a vital mouthpiece for their community, and disseminated information about developments, such as clinical trials into growth hormones (now a standard treatment). To reduce global inequality, IPWSO lobbied for genetic testing, working to provide free diagnostic testing for people in underserved countries. IPWSO also created information resources on subjects such as diet, behaviour and education, and in 1992 established the first residential care facility for adults with PWS. It was in Sweden and Phillips-Martinsson’s son Anders became one of its first residents. Born in London, Jean had an elder sister, Diana. Her father Emmanuel’s original surname was Isaacs but he took his fiancee’s surname (Phillips) when he married. He ran a furrier business, and died when Jean was four. His wife, Iris, served in the Women’s Royal Voluntary Service during the second world war. Jean attended Claremont school in Esher, Surrey, and, aged 16, spent a year at La Chatelaine finishing school in Switzerland, where she learned French. She also learned skills such as which petit fours to serve and how to treat servants, on the assumption she was going to marry well, but this was not her goal. Instead, in 1957 she went to Neuchâtel University to study French and then trained as a secretary in London. A passionate European, in 1952 she got a job in Paris with the Organisation for European Economic Development, first as a secretary and then as an interpreter, slipping out in the evenings to hear singers such as Edith Piaf and Yves Montand in the Montmartre nightclubs. In 1958 she returned to London, managing to freelance as a PR consultant and a foreign correspondent for several newspapers including the Manchester Guardian. Four years later the Guardian sent her to cover the British Trade Fair in Gothenburg, Sweden, where she stayed on, finding PR work with advertising agencies. On a skiing trip in Romania with Swedish friends she met Sven Martinsson, a teacher of children with special needs, and they married in 1966. They lived in Gothenburg, where Phillips-Martinsson gave seminars and workshops on cross-cultural relations, and she wrote a book, Swedes As Others See Them, which was published in 1979. After several miscarriages, in 1970, aged 40, Phillips-Martinsson became pregnant with Anders. When he was born it was clear something was wrong, but no one knew what the problem was until she came across the Lancet article about PWS in 1984 and her life took a new direction. In 1994, Phillips-Martinsson moved to Tunbridge Wells, in Kent, with Sven, who died in 2008. There she enjoyed singing in local choirs and playing tennis. In 2019, Anders also died, aged 49, and she established the Jean Phillips-Martinsson Fund in 2020 at IPWSO to continue to finance its work. In her 90s she was still heavily involved with the organisation, joining online meetings during Covid and giving a presentation at the 11th IPWSO conference in Limerick, Ireland, in 2022. Diana died in 2021. Phillips-Martinsson is survived by her stepchildren, Arne and Karin, from Sven’s previous marriage, two nieces and a nephew. • Jean Phillips-Martinsson, medical campaigner, born 11 April 1930; died 28 September 2026

headline: Did you solve it? A magical melody from the Mozart of math
trail_text: The solution to today’s puzzles
body_text: Earlier today, I set a puzzle by UCLA professor Terry Tao, who is widely regarded as one of the world’s top mathematicians. Here it is again with solutions. The magic money plant In an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant: a regular plant produces a single coin per day a mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.) At the start of the game, a player has a certain number of mother plants, regular plants and coins, but not more than nine of each. Suppose that I begin on Day 1 with a mother plants, b regular plants and c coins. 1. How many coins do I have in total at the end of days 2 and 3? 2. Find an expression for how many coins I have at the end of Day X. 3. At the end of Day 10 I have 427 coins. What are a, b and c? Solution 1. Day 2: 4a + 2b + c. Day 3: 9a + 3b + c Workings: At the end of day 1 the number of coins is is a + b + c. Each mother plant has also produced 2 seeds, but these have not yet grown into regular plants. On day 2, these plants produce a coin each, so there are 2a of these, added to another a from the mother plant and the a from day 1, makng 4a. The regular plants produce another coin each, making b in total to add to the b from day 1. This gets us 4a + 2b + c for day 2, and the same reasoning gets us the above expression for day 3. 2. aX2 + bX + c We calculated for X = 1, 2 and 3. You hopefully saw the pattern emerge. The number of coins produced by the mother plant and her descendants is the square of the day. 3. a = 4, b = 2, c= 7. When X = 10, there are 427 coins. Thus 100a + 10b + c = 427. So a, b and c must be 4, 2 and 7. The answer was in the question! Tao said he suggested this puzzle because he likes the way it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve a problem. “It turns out that the number of coins at day X is given by a polynomial, aX2 + bX + c. In modern algebra, we have realized that polynomials are very similar to numbers in many ways: for instance, one can add and multiply two polynomials together much as one can add and multiply numbers. For this problem, it is more than an analogy: on day 10 (X=10), the value of the polynomial aX2 + bX + c is just the three-digit number abc (assuming that a,b, and c are at most nine). So one can now read off the desired unknowns a, b, c just by inspecting the digits 4, 2, and 7 of the given coin value 427.” The idea that polynomials behave like numbers is one of the themes of Tao’s first book for a general audience, Six Maths Essentials. I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks. Six Maths Essentials by Terence Tao is out tomorrow. You can buy it at the Guardian Bookshop. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

headline: ‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’
trail_text: As all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable - and experts predict it’s around to stay
body_text: Maxxing is not a new concept. Dungeons and Dragons players have been “min-maxing” character stats for years; Will Smith was maxin’ and relaxin’ in the 90s; as far back as the 40s, the term was used in game theory. But in the past few years, as all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable. We’re personalitymaxxing to charm our peers and sleepmaxxing to get the best possible rest; the Pentagon brags about “lethalitymaxxing”. The explosion in the word’s use has made it Dictionary.com’s word of the year for 2026. To choose each year’s word, Dictionary.com staffers investigate search trends, social media and the news, “and then we ask ourselves what’s telling the most compelling story of the year”, says Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. “This year, maxxing stood out because it really connects to so many different parts of life. People are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI during the workday, cozymaxxing on a Friday night.” While “maxxing” has been around in various forms for decades, it’s the phenomenon of “looksmaxxing” – putting your physical appearance above all other concerns, and going to extreme lengths to improve it – that has fueled the recent rise in the word’s use. The message board 4chan is responsible for a vast amount of current slang, according to the linguist Adam Aleksic, and looksmaxxing has roots in online “incel” communities that use it. But the suffix has emerged from the shadow of 4chan. As associate editor of Among the New Words, which tracks emerging terms in a quarterly journal, the linguist Kelly Wright and her colleagues have documented examples of the term’s use since 1990, when it appeared in a D&D context, through looksmaxxing-related 4chan posts in the 2010s to YouTube discussions of “vibemaxxing” (“adding to my energy”) and Substack posts on “vocabularymaxxing” (“because there are some thoughts you’ll only have if you have the words for them”) in 2025. Wright sees the word as particularly creative – it can “apply to anything”. Dictionary.com data bears this out: by August 2026, it was being used 19 times as often in digital media as its monthly average in 2025. And these days, it says far more about our social media-driven compulsion to optimize than it does about inceldom. “If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed,” writes Jennifer Donnelly, a researcher at RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences, at the Conversation. That comes with risks, she writes, as it suggests there is some kind of endpoint to the improvement process. “But health, wellbeing, social relationships and lifestyle habits aren’t really something we complete,” and maxxing can fuel “constant self-surveillance, self-criticism and the pursuit of an idealised ‘optimal’ self”. In fact, that obsession is emerging on both ends of the words we use: terms recently added to the dictionary include “prefixes that mean ‘much more’ – things like ‘hyper’, things like ‘ultra’, ‘super’”, Johnson says. The suffix benefits from being “infinitely customizable but instantly recognizable”, Daria Bahtina, a continuing lecturer in the UCLA department of linguistics, writes in an email. “You can attach the pattern to practically anything while still sounding like you are participating in a particular linguistic and cultural moment.” Saying you’re “proteinmaxxing” feels much cooler than just saying you’re eating more protein. Its popularity could also be, in part, simply related to its sound. “The sound structure of a word tells us a lot,” Wright says, “and maximalism is trending.” A similar string of sounds – “maxx” – “was maybe a little primed to get picked up”. Bahtina and Johnson agree that it’s unlikely most people using “maxxing” are thinking about any incel connections. Still, Bahtina wonders if its constant usage could help elevate its origins into the mainstream. “Someone encounters pheromone-maxxing or some other allegedly annoying but innocent version,” she writes, “and suddenly there is a linguistic breadcrumb trail into a much broader ideological ecosystem.” So can we expect “maxxing” to stick around as a suffix – will it have the staying power of “-gate”, which has denoted scandal ever since Watergate, or will it go the way of “-licious”, which stretched from Bubblicious bubble gum to Destiny’s Child’s Bootylicious, but, as Johnson notes, has largely disappeared? It’s difficult to predict, the linguists say. Once a slang term gets a mainstream platform, it often loses its cachet. But “I don’t think it’s going to fizzle out,” says Wright. It’s not just young optimizers who’ve embraced it: “Middle-aged people really love this word. Corporate brands love this word. So it’s going to have some staying power.”

headline: Can you solve it? A magical melody from the Mozart of math
trail_text: Terence Tao grows coins
body_text: Today’s puzzle is set by Terence Tao, who may be the world’s most famous mathematician. Tao, aged 51, has been a global phenomenon since the age of ten, when he became the youngest competitor at the International Maths Olympiad, a record he still holds. For the last three decades he has been a professor at UCLA, where he has been garlanded with prizes, and where one of his colleagues famously said: “Terry is like Mozart: mathematics just flows out of him.” Tao is a very visible leader of the field, not only because of his scientific contributions and collaborations, but also because he writes the most widely-read blog in research level maths. When Open AI earlier this month stunned the community with the release of hundreds of proofs of long-standing open questions – the “mathpocalypse” – his blog has become one of the most important forums for the community’s response. This week Tao publishes Six Maths Essentials, his first work aimed at a general audience. The puzzle below reflects ideas in the book. He said: “I like this puzzle in that it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve the problem: working out small examples by hand can give some valuable initial intuition, but it will be algebra that lets you solve the entire problem in a civilized amount of time.” The magic money plant In an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant: a regular plant produces a single coin per day a mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.) headline: Plague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreement
trail_text: Letters: Responding to an editorial on a potential plague outbreak, Dr Darren Mann deplores delays to the agreement, while Kent Buse says Britain could do more
body_text: Your editorial on the silence from Siberia after a worker died at a plague research institute there is right that the lack of information is the real worry (The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information, 18 October). But the deeper failure is not Russian. It is that, six years after Covid, we still have no agreed system for sharing pathogens, or for sharing what is made from them. I spent three decades in Hong Kong, through bird flu, Sars and Covid, working on outbreak surveillance and sample-sharing between Hong Kong and the UK. It is also where this territorial argument began. In June 1894, two bacteriologists arrived to investigate the plague. Kitasato Shibasaburō was given lab space and immediate access to the bodies. Alexandre Yersin was refused access to the dead, and worked from a straw hut, having to appeal to the governor for his share of cadavers. Access to the material was allocated by favour, not by need. The organism carries the name of the man who was shut out: Yersinia pestis. The pathogen access and benefit-sharing annexe to the World Health Organization pandemic agreement is the same argument in modern dress, and it has stalled on the same point. Poorer countries are asked to detect and share dangerous pathogens quickly. In return, they want a binding guarantee of what follows: 20% of real-time production of vaccines and treatments, half donated and half sold at cost. In article 13, the global supply chain and logistics network provides for a more equitable distribution of personal protective equipment. Richer countries prefer all that sharing to stay voluntary. The agreement cannot open for signature until this is settled, and it has now been deferred to 2027. All pandemics start with a rumour. The next pandemic is likely to be something we have never seen before, and whoever first holds the samples will not be us. If we cannot agree what they get in return, we should not be surprised when they are slow to hand them over. Dr Darren Mann Former medical director, Cabinet Office Covid-19 PPE taskforce • Your editorial on plague in Russia is right that the system is fraying, but wrong to treat Moscow’s silence as an aberration. It is the predictable product of rules that member states built without teeth. The International Health Regulations oblige governments to notify the WHO within 24 hours, yet provide no verification, no sanctions and no independent monitoring. States mark their own homework through annual self-assessments. The amendments in force since last September add an implementation committee that is, by design, consultative only. Member states, Britain included, chose this. They then starved the WHO of assessed funding, leaving it dependent on the goodwill of the governments it is meant to hold to account. Britain accepted the amended regulations in July 2025 and, with the United States gone, is among the WHO’s largest government funders. Ministers should raise Russia’s non-reporting formally within the WHO rather than leave Washington to make the only public request. The UK should table proposals for independent verification and a public compliance register when the pandemic agreement’s pathogen-sharing annex returns to the assembly, due by May 2027. And it should volunteer for the WHO’s Universal Health and Preparedness Review, a peer review that only 11 countries have joined and Britain has not. A government cannot demand transparency it declines to practise. The recent UN declaration on pandemics will mean little unless the governments that signed it are held to account. Kent Buse Co-CEO, Global 50/50 • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data
trail_text: This gives the company an advantage in tracking objects in orbit, raising national security concerns and fears of greater control over the space industry
body_text: The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor. The access also raises new national security questions, industry observers say. The move comes after Musk’s Doge in 2025 fired many of the federal government’s nascent space traffic control program’s staff, and the administration has twice attempted to financially gut the department, called the Traffic Coordination System for Space (Traccs). The moves were widely viewed in the industry as an attempt by Musk to privatize space traffic control. The defense department has now granted SpaceX access to its most precise data on potential collisions among satellites and other space objects, which will give Musk’s companies an advantage over competition that offers a similar service. SpaceX and the Space Force signed the new contract. The commercial US space market is expected to grow to a value of nearly $2tn in value over the next decade, and the unprecedented access to military data appears to be another step toward Musk asserting monopoly control over commercial space activity more broadly, said Cole Donovan, a former Traccs employee now with the Stand Up for Science non-profit. “It’s making a company the de facto source for space traffic coordination within the US,” Donovan added. “It’s like giving a trucking company control of all the traffic lights, which they can switch to red whenever it’s their competition’s turn to go.” Traccs manages thousands of satellites, debris and spacecraft, and helps prevent up to 50,000 near-collisions, called conjunctions, daily. SpaceX and Space Force did not respond to requests for comment from the Guardian, but in a statement to Breaking Defense acknowledged the move. “The Space Force is engaging with several companies to exchange commercial data sources for access to sections of the controlled, unclassified information, high accuracy catalogue, where it provides benefit to the US government,” a spokesperson told the outlet. SpaceX has been expanding its power over launch and other space services, while growing closer links with the US government. Multiple industry observers have said since the Trump administration took over that they fear a “vendor lock” scenario in which the government is overly reliant on SpaceX because it has such immense influence and is so technologically advanced. The first Trump administration established Traccs to take over commercial space traffic control from the defense department. But Traccs has never been fully funded or staffed, and has struggled to take root. The latest move by the military comes at a crossroads for Traccs as the administration, Congress, and industry debate what to do next. The administration in fiscal year 2026 tried to largely defund the $65m program during the budgetary process, but Congress re-inserted the funding. The administration has again proposed slashing the budget to nearly zero in fiscal year 2027, but the House again reinserted the funding. Several employees of commercial space companies have told the Guardian since early 2025 that there is wide support in the industry for Traccs because it would level the playing field. But the administration’s apparent move to privatize and consolidate power with a Trump ally is consistent with its broader approach to governance, Donovan said. However, a former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) official who spoke on the condition of anonymity said SpaceX has largely been “remarkably responsive to space safety concerns” and they do not fault Starlink for stepping into a space that the government has failed to adequately address. “My greater disappointment is with the government’s failure to fulfil its responsibility to establish a coherent space governance framework that provides guidance, transparency, and a level playing field for all operators,” the official said. Musk’s growing lower Earth orbit empire includes a massive satellite constellation belonging to Starlink, a broadband internet company that is a subsidiary of SpaceX. It operates about 11,000 satellites in orbit, and could have as many as 20,000 in the coming years. For the first time, the Space Force has given a commercial company “enhanced” access to the US Space Command’s most detailed, secure version of its High Accuracy Catalog (Hac) of on-orbit objects. This includes Vector Covariance Messages (VCMs) made up of tracking data collected from military sensors, telescopes and radars on the ground that track the paths of satellites and other space objects in lower orbit that are down to about 10cm (3.93in) in size. The military largely uses the radars and data for monitoring other countries’ satellite positions, but it is also utilized to track commercial spacecraft and objects to avoid collisions. The latter is part of the responsibility that the military no longer wants, and was supposed to hand off to Traccs, Donovan said. Instead, SpaceX has been given access to the data. The VCM data is valuable to Starlink because the company uses its own “Stargaze” system to track other satellites and space objects. Stargaze is made up of thousands of cameras and radars mounted on Starlink satellites. It can only see objects that are down to about a half meter in size, and is not as accurate as the military’s system. The military “radar data is an extremely valuable tool to supplement Stargaze,” Breaking Defense quoted a SpaceX employee stating during an industry conference. The government is receiving something in return for the data – access to Stargaze cameras and sensors. “The more observations and data that [the military] has, the better,” Donovan said. However, the VCM data is designated as “controlled unclassified information” and has been closely held by the military because it could expose the limits of defense capabilities. The defense department has also wanted to prevent the reverse engineering of satellite sensors it uses to monitor other nations’ defense satellites, observers say. In terms of ethical conflicts, the access is another example of the Trump administration rewarding a donor with business opportunities with the federal government, said Craig Holman, Capitol Hill lobbyist for Public Citizen, a government accountability non-profit. “Elon Musk has bought his way into the favor of President Trump and with it, unlimited riches and lucrative government contracts in the space industry,” Holman added. “[His] political investment is paying off very, very handsomely – as was intended.”

headline: ‘It’s magic’: scientists rediscover how to make ancient Roman colour-changing glass
trail_text: Exclusive: Optical engineering that went into 1,600-year-old Lycurgus Cup has baffled experts for centuries
body_text: The Romans’ proficiency in the art of glass-making has produced some of the wonders of antiquity, but few of their creations better a 1,600-year-old masterpiece which sits in the British Museum. Depending on where a light source is positioned, the Lycurgus Cup changes colour, from jade green under normal lighting to ruby red when lit from behind – an astonishing feat of optical engineering that has confounded historians and glass-makers for centuries. Now scientists from the University of Sheffield have replicated its remarkable optical behaviour, using an ancient recipe derived from a fragment of the Roman “dichroic” (two-coloured) original. Dr Lisa Hollands, a technician at the university’s school of chemical, materials and biological engineering, said that replicating it has been “a labour of love” and “people have tried it before with limited success”. She added: “To me, it’s magic.” The fourth-century original bears a mythological frieze depicting the legend of King Lycurgus from the sixth book of Homer’s Iliad. Carved in deep relief, it shows the triumph of the god of wine, Dionysus, over Lycurgus, who is ensnared by a vine. In 2022, it was recognised as one of the seven glass wonders of the world by an international panel. Hollands worked with Prof Caroline Jackson, a leading Roman glass expert, in conducting the initial research. Then came the challenge of embedding into glass nanoparticles of gold and silver – each a thousand times smaller than a grain of sand. A thick molten glass was created and, as it cooled from well over 1,000C, gold and silver nanocrystals started to grow around particles within it. Hollands said: “White light is made up of many different colours and you see this when there is a rainbow in the sky. Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of light and in certain conditions they block certain colours due to the light affecting the electrons in the atoms. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through. If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green colour we see.” She added: “If the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’” Sheffield commissioned Elliot Walker, a glass artist, to bring the effect to life in a contemporary glass sculpture that pays homage to its “ancient twin” by combining the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture, with the globe replaced by a cup. “For me, it’s a connection with the Roman makers,” he said. It will be unveiled at the Millennium Gallery, as part of the university’s Festival of the Mind from 6-15 November, before a permanent display at the Turner Museum of Glass. Ian Freestone, emeritus professor of archaeological materials at University College London, said that, although a similar-coloured glass was replicated in the 1960s, Sheffield’s project is much closer to the actual green and red shades of the Lycurgus Cup. “This is more ambitious and more precise,” he said. “I was excited because, for the first time, I was getting a feel of just how difficult it was to get these colours. This will help us understand how the Roman craftsmen actually worked.” He added: “The colour was quite dependent on conditions in the furnace. If the glass went in a different position in the furnace, then the colour came out differently … The fact that the colour is so sensitive to the position in the furnace suggests that it would have been very difficult for the Romans to control the colour. It makes me think that, with the Lycurgus glass, they hit the jackpot.” Freestone spoke of the significance of the red-green colours, noting a theory that they symbolised the ripening of the grape: “The depicted scene has grape vines pulling Lycurgus into the underworld. So it could have been used in a drinking ceremony of some sort.” A letter supposedly written by Hadrian to his brother-in-law in Rome reads: “I have sent you parti-coloured cups that change colour, presented to me by the priest of a temple … I would like you to use them at banquets on feast days.” • This article was amended on 26 October 2026. The caption on the video originally said it showed the Lycurgus Cup; in fact, it shows a sculpture made to replicate the colour-change effect.

headline: Australia offers astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg for space mission to International Space Station
trail_text: Australian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 mission
byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science
body_text: The federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to the International Space Station. The mission, slated for 2028, will mark the first time a qualified astronaut has flown to space under the Australian flag. The ESA offer for Bennell-Pegg to join a future ISS mission garnered support from philanthropists and the Australian space industry, but has previously described by the office of the science minister, Tim Ayres, as “a very expensive undertaking” which no government alone could fund. Announcing the decision on Friday, Ayres said:“The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost. “We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6m in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments.” Bennell-Pegg is director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency (ASA) and completed astronaut training with the ESA in 2024. She is not the first Australian astronaut, but she is the first to qualify under the Australian flag. Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power, both Australian-born, went to space as US citizens on Nasa missions. Elaine Hyde, a dual Australian and US citizen, last year took a suborbital flight aboard Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin NS-30. In May, the ASA announced it had entered into “treaty-level discussions” with the ESA, which “would establish a formal framework for enhanced cooperation between Australia and Europe”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In August, Ayres and the assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, wrote to state and territory leaders asking them to “partner” with the federal government to fund the mission. The letter, according to The Australian, described it as a “complete Australian mission that includes locally developed experiments and technology”. South Australia, where the ASA is headquartered, has publicly committed to supporting Bennell-Pegg’s space bid. “South Australia stands ready to partner with the commonwealth in what should be a national endeavour,” the premier, Peter Malinauskus, said. “Katherine Bennell-Pegg has the potential to inspire a new generation to dream big and address the single biggest challenge to our economy which is productivity. “Australia has a massive shortage of young people taking up the fields of science, technology, engineering and maths, and we need more of it if we’re going to grow the nation’s productivity … Nothing would motivate young people more to take up these fields of endeavour than seeing Australia’s first ever flagged astronaut in space.” A campaign to secure Bennell-Pegg’s spaceflight mission was supported by entrepreneurs Dick Smith and Jim Whalley – who had each pledged $1m funding for the mission – and former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who said on social media that the “project makes long-term economic sense for Australia beyond the usual sensibilities of the Treasury bean counters”. Richard de Grijs, a professor of physics and astronomy at Macquarie University, said of Bennell-Pegg: “She is qualified, she has undergone significant training, so she is set to go up if a suitable mission can be found. “The government has actually contributed quite a lot of money to that education already,” he said. The ASA paid $466,000 for Bennell-Pegg to complete her astronaut training at the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany. “There is an inspirational value in sending a citizen from your country to space who is also the Australian of the Year … but the question is, is that worth $100m?” De Grijs said. “It’s a lot of money, but on the other hand, it might actually lead to returns that are way more than the estimated number.” De Grijs pointed out that Australia was also involved in “inspirational spaceflight” by another means: an Australian-built lunar rover, named Roo-ver, will be sent to moon on a Nasa mission in 2030. Darin Lovett, chair of the Space Industry Association of Australia, said the industry had “a strong track record of return on investment”. “For around $100m, less than the price of a single coffee for every Australian adult, this is not a ticket to space. It is a down payment on Australia’s future in one of the defining industries of this century.” In a speech Bennell-Pegg delivered earlier this month, she described space as “a gateway – a lure – into the full breadth of STEM fields. Especially for those that dream of going up there.”

headline: Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests
trail_text: Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning
body_text: Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests. Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly. Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning. “One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.” Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions. The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats. They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat. Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day. On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl. The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference. Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food. Dr Adriano Lameira, a primatologist and evolutionary psychologist at the University of Warwick, who was not involved in the work, described the results as fascinating. “Effectively, hearing others clearly having a good time, orangutans placed their food order: ‘I will have what they are having, please!’” he said. Cartmill added the results suggest it is not only the quantity or frequency of a reward that can be important when learning associations. “What our work is showing is that it’s also about the state of the animal when they are learning that association,” she said. “Who you are in that moment – the context, the emotional states, what you’re feeling, what you’re thinking about – can also influence and can carry over in how you remember these things that you’ve learned.” The findings, she added, could have applications to humans, including in educational environments. “Students might learn at similar rates if they are in a good mood or not, but our research suggests that they would value information more if they learn it when they are in a good mood,” Cartmill said. She added that could be useful in helping to understand why some information is more trusted or why students choose to continue studying certain subjects. “If a student is anxious when they are learning maths for example, it might impact whether they prefer maths versus other subjects when choosing what to pursue in the future,” she said.

headline: Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery
trail_text: Study pitting preschoolers against adults mostly in their 20s finds fear of failure and anxiety hamper the grownups
body_text: Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away. Now researchers say they know why. While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this notion, finding adults outperform preschoolers on creative tasks but generally feel less confident and more anxious doing them. Dr Mathias Benedek, the senior author of the study at the University of Graz in Austria, said: “Children are so intrinsically motivated and absorbed in play that we often mistake their engagement with greater creative ability.” Writing in the journal Plos One, the researchers asked 92 preschool children aged four to seven and 70 adults largely in their 20s to complete three tasks. The first involved coming up with as many creative uses for a tin as possible in three minutes; the second involved drawing anything they liked with no stated time limit; and the third involved drawing an imaginary animal within eight minutes. The results were then rated by judges on originality, usefulness and overall creativity. Participants were also asked to rate how much they enjoyed each task, how motivated and confident they felt, and how anxious they were doing it. The judges deemed the work by adults to be more original, useful and creative than that of children, particularly when clear goals and time limits were set. Conversely, children reported feeling more confident, motivated and less anxious completing tasks. “Adults outperformed children, demonstrating higher creative potential, but they had far less confidence. We need to look at what makes adults so anxious about their original ideas being rejected,” Benedek said. He said children approached tasks with greater intrinsic motivation and enjoyed the process of play, “whereas adults place more focus on the goal or objective”, limiting their enjoyment. As a result, children experimented more freely and treated mistakes as part of the process whereas adults, wary of judgment, often dismissed unusual ideas before trying them. The study, conducted at the University of Graz in Austria in collaboration with UCLouvain in Belgium and Yale University, has limitations. Among them, the research is based on a snapshot comparison of just two age groups, making it hard to draw conclusions about the impact of ageing on creativity. Children are also more likely to pick extreme answers on rating scales and have obvious differences in cognition. Nonetheless, Benedek and his colleagues suggest that the idea of creativity fading as we grow into adulthood is a misconception. “Adults don’t lose their creativity, instead they lose the confidence to use it,” Benedek said.

headline: Tesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backing
trail_text: Billionaire, on SpaceX earnings call, says ‘I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies’
body_text: As SpaceX released its second-ever public earnings report on Tuesday, Elon Musk declared his support for combining the aerospace and AI company with his electric vehicle company, Tesla. He said both companies had created special committees to explore a potential merger, but have not reached any agreement on terms of a transaction. “Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders and these special committees are, uh, consist of independent directors,” Musk said on the call. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees.” Musk also expressed his backing for the move, while cautioning about the hurdles involved achieve it. He stated that it would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said, adding it would require shareholder approvals and special committees at both firms. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.” The company revealed a far better financial quarter than Wall Street projected. SpaceX company, which encompasses rockets, artificial intelligence and satellite communications, reported a 161% growth in revenue year over year, driven by its Starlink and AI segments. The company declared $14.58bn in revenue against analysts’ projected $12.72bn. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents and a net income of $4.4bn. The company’s stock, which started the day down about 8% for the year, shot up 2% in after hours trading immediately after the results. Musk appeared alongside SpaceX’s president, Gwynne Shotwell, and CFO, Bret Johnsen, at his Starlink factory in Texas to deliver the earnings report, touting the company’s growth and plans for future rocket developments. Musk also highlighted its artificial intelligence segment, which the company refers to as Super Intelligence, that drew $7.6bn in revenue and now outperforms its Connectivity business, which provides internet services. Musk’s company once again found itself in the spotlight in recent weeks as investors have speculated about the potential merger with Tesla, the second-most valuable part of the tech mogul’s empire. Musk has also been at the center of geopolitical tensions after Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, last week accused SpaceX of restricting access to its military-grade Starlink internet service. The disruption in service to Starshield allegedly led to several failed Ukrainian combat missions and left the country more vulnerable to Russian drone attacks, as well as highlighted how global internet infrastructure has come to rely on Musk’s products. Musk denied responsibility for the disruption, stating that Starshield was controlled by the US government, not SpaceX. The White House has likewise denied hobbling Starshield. Moments before the SpaceX earnings call on Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the throttling of Starshield, citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter. Musk faced no questions about the reports on the investor Q&A portion of SpaceX’s earnings call. While SpaceX’s role in international affairs faces scrutiny, Musk has taken on a resurgent role in US domestic politics. The world’s richest person has contributed $366m in political spending this election cycle, backing Republican-aligned Super Pacs and pouring money into influencing key midterm races. Musk also agreed earlier this month to co-lead a Pentagon project on the future of warfare, bringing him back into government work after his time as the de facto leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge). Musk recently pledged to give every child in the US one of his SpaceX stocks next year, which Donald Trump stated would be facilitated through the president’s “Trump accounts” initiative that creates savings plans for children. The prospective share giveaway is a rare display of philanthropy from Musk, who has criticized traditional aid organizations and has taken credit for dismantling the world’s largest single provider of humanitarian aid by gutting the government agency USAID. “Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” Musk posted on X, the social media company he owns. Tech leaders such as Musk have faced increasing public pushback over their extraordinary accumulation of wealth and power in the US, while this year AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic both announced big investments to their grant-making and non-profit arms. Musk’s announcement came after Anthropic announced earlier this week that it plans to donate 5% of its shares to a newly created public benefit fund within the company. Tesla will also reveal its latest earnings this week, with Musk set to deliver the quarterly report on Wednesday. The company’s stock received a slight boost this week after it unveiled its new Tesla Roadster 2 electric sports car, which Musk showcased in a dramatic demonstration that included the vehicle using pressurized air tanks to briefly lift off the ground and perform aerial stunts.

headline: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others
trail_text: Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking
body_text: From politicians taking bribes to bullying and harassment in City firms, leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel. Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in others, general compliance can swiftly turn into widespread rule-breaking. Dr Lucas Molleman, from the University of Amsterdam and the first author of the research, said the goal was to explore how individuals make decisions about rule-breaking in a social context. “Many people think of themselves as making sort of autonomous decisions, especially in these individualist cultures that we are from, like Netherlands, the UK,” he said. “But in actual fact, in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.” Writing in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Molleman and colleagues report how they recruited 750 people in the US to take part in an online experiment, with the participants approximately evenly split between Republicans and Democrats. The researchers asked each participant to complete an online task in which they saw an animated “shooting star” moving across a row of 100 squares as its intensity varied. Participants were instructed to pick the square that lit up most intensely to receive a monetary reward. However, participants received greater rewards for selecting squares further to the right of the correct square, and smaller rewards for selecting squares further to the left. Participants were then shown whether another participant had followed the rules or broken them, the extent of any rule-breaking, and their political affiliation, and asked if they wished to update their choice. The process was repeated six times. The results revealed participants showed large degrees of rule-breaking even in their initial choices, with 23% of choices involving squares with the highest reward. However, the choices of others mattered: seeing others following the rules slightly reduced an individual’s rule-breaking, while seeing others making small beneficial violations – choosing a square a third of the way to the right, beyond the correct square – slightly increased rule-breaking. Crucially, seeing others flagrantly flout the rules by selecting a square even further to the right led participants to greatly increase their own level of rule-breaking. In some cases they went beyond the violations they had observed. The team say the findings were stronger when a participant had the same political leanings as others – something Molleman said chimed with other research, suggesting people who are politically aligned are more influenced by each other. The researchers used computer simulations to explore how the behaviour they had observed in the experiments would play out in a large group. The results showed that a situation could quickly get out of hand. “A minority of escalating individuals, exceeding the rule violations they observe, they might cause a whole collective to spin out of control,” Molleman said. However, he noted that about a third of participants consistently followed the rules even though it did not lead to the largest reward. Prof Stephen Reicher, of the University of St Andrews, in Scotland, who was not involved in the work, said the study had limitations, including that the experiment was abstract and there was no penalty for rule-breaking, meaning the relevance of the work to real-world examples remained unproven. Reicher also stressed that the results went against the concept of contagion, instead showing that whether we are influenced by others depends on who those others are. “This is important because it implies that, say, we don’t riot simply because we see others rioting,” he said. “In fact, many people who see rioting respond by helping clear up after riots.”

headline: Mayer Hillman obituary
trail_text: Pioneer of ideas about the climate crisis and road safety, and a champion of walking, cycling and children’s mobility
body_text: In the late 1990s, the social scientist and author Mayer Hillman predicted that, in the future, our children and grandchildren would ask us what we did to prevent global climate catastrophe. Twenty years later Greta Thunberg, addressing the UN, thundered: “You are failing us. But the young people are starting to understand your betrayal. The eyes of all future generations are upon you.” Twenty-five years ago, Hillman also warned that public denial of the climate crisis would only begin to crack when people in the global north were personally affected – by the creation of millions of environmental refugees from uninhabitable parts of the world, for instance, or after their homes had been flooded several times over and they could no longer insure them. Hillman, who has died aged 94, not only anticipated social and environmental problems decades in advance of most other people, he also came up with solutions that seemed outlandish at the time but are now considered unremarkable. In 1984 he proposed energy audits and thermal ratings for buildings; in 2007 EPCs (energy performance certificates) were rolled out across England and Wales. In the early 90s, he suggested that road intersections should be raised to pavement level to give priority to pedestrians, a now commonplace practice. Cycle lanes and 20mph speed limits – Hillman was advocating these more than 40 years ago. Increasingly, his energies were taken up with the climate crisis. His 2004 book, How We Can Save the Planet, described it as “the most serious environmental threat that the world has ever faced”. He dismissed individual gestures as futile, even though he had not flown for decades. In an analogy with the consensus around wartime rationing, he proposed carbon rationing as the only way to prevent serious damage, foreseeing a time when people would pity someone passing in a car – a sign of an emergency requiring them to use up a precious part of their annual carbon quota. Soon, though, he came to believe that it was too late to save the planet, any lame protest about human beings’ need for hope airily brushed aside, as though if Hillman himself could tolerate its absence, so too would most people. Born in West Hampstead, north London, to Scottish Jewish parents, Mayer (known as Mickey by family and many friends), was the youngest of three boys. His father, David, an orthodox Jew who fled the pogroms in Lithuania to settle in Glasgow, was a portrait painter and stained-glass artist; his mother, Annie, a GP. At the outbreak of the second world war, Mickey and his brothers, Ellis and Harold, were evacuated to homes in Rickmansworth, Hertfordshire. His gentile hosts offered him meat and fish, which, coming from a kosher home, he politely declined; Hillman was vegetarian thereafter. All three boys would come home for the Sabbath, leaving school early on Fridays to take the train to Finchley Road station. On Sunday evenings, they returned to Rickmansworth. After two years, their father acceded to their request to come home on condition they stay on at the Rickmansworth school. So, until the end of the war, they did the same journey in reverse, getting up at 6.30am, making their own sandwiches, and walking to the station. The experience proved formative: Hillman would later contrast what he called his “free range” childhood with the “battery” lives experienced by children in the 21st century. At 22, after qualifying from the Bartlett School of Architecture at University College London, he became partner in a newly established north London firm of architects. While there, in 1956, he co-designed for a competition a prototype for the first pedestrian-oriented new town in the UK. Several years later, he decided to switch professions: the catalyst was Colin Buchanan’s influential 1963 report Traffic in Towns, which, while it recognised the potential downsides of rapidly growing car ownership, nevertheless argued for reorganising cities to accommodate it. Hillman disagreed and embarked on a doctorate at Edinburgh University, examining the social and environmental aspects of personal mobility and making the case for reducing the need for motorised transport. By then, in 1964, he had married Heidi Krott, who had come to Britain from Vienna in 1939, aged two, in her refugee mother’s arms. A research post at the thinktank Political and Economic Planning, later the Policy Studies Institute (PSI), where he stayed for the rest of his career, allowed him to develop his most innovative thinking. In a 1979 report, Walking Is Transport, co-written with Anne Whalley, Hillman deplored the omission in national transport data of journeys of less than a mile, most of them walking. Unusually for a male researcher of the time, he recognised that this rendered women’s chief mode of travel invisible (15 years later, walking was added to official research data). From the early 70s, Hillman was also studying children’s independent mobility. His co-authored report One False Move (1990), comparing 1971 survey results with 1990, revealed a dramatic drop in children’s independent travel: where previously 80% of seven- and eight-year-olds had gone to school unaccompanied, 20 years later only 9% were doing so, the rest accompanied on foot or driven there, mostly by their mothers (Hillman alert again to the implications for women, in exhaustion and their ability to work outside the home). The reduction of child deaths over this period did not mean the roads were safer, he maintained. On the contrary, child road deaths were down because the roads had become so dangerous that they had been purged of children by fearful parents, dramatically curtailing children’s freedom. Indeed, “stranger danger” should be redefined, he argued, since far more children were killed by strangers behind the steering wheel of a car or lorry than by any other means. “Danger should be removed from children rather than children from danger,” he concluded. He never actually retired, but his output dropped off after 2018, when the PSI closed. An impassioned advocate of cycling for environmental and health reasons, as well as for the way in which it made the world accessible to children, Hillman rode his bike round London into advanced old age. He was full of contradictions: proud of his Jewish background yet an avowed “militant atheist”, cheerfully apocalyptic, dogged but big-hearted. Heidi died in 2017; Hillman is survived by his sons, Josh and Saul, and three grandchildren, Jasmine, Eva and Rafi. • Mayer Hillman, social scientist, born 30 October 1931; died 25 September 2026

headline: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis
