trail_text: Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows
body_text: Patterns of antibodies in people’s blood could predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) a decade before diagnosis, according to research that raises hopes for catching the condition early. Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main forms of IBD, are typically treated only after symptoms appear, when the gut has already been damaged. But scientists found that the immune system sends warning signals up to a decade before diagnosis, paving the way for potentially earlier detection and even prevention. “For too long we have only been able to treat inflammatory bowel disease once the damage is done, and for many people that is too late,” said Dr Arno Bourgonje at the University Medical Centre Groningen in the Netherlands and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York. “What we have shown is that the disease begins years before symptoms appear, and the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis,” Bourgonje added. “This is not yet a test that can tell someone they will become ill, but it is an important step towards catching the disease earlier and, one day, preventing it.” At least 3.8 million people worldwide live with IBD, an immune condition that drives chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, causing pain, diarrhoea and fatigue. The exact cause is unknown, but a misfiring immune system, genetics and microbes living in the gut can all contribute. Treatment relies on anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing drugs, but many patients do not respond, and a significant number go on to have surgery to remove damaged sections of bowel. Longstanding inflammation also raises the risk of bowel cancer. This has prompted scientists to look for the earlier signs of disease, in the hope of identifying people at risk before damage begins. Bourgonje and colleagues at Mount Sinai and the Medical University of Vienna ran tests on blood samples taken from US military personnel. They examined 2,000 samples from 500 people, 200 of whom later developed Crohn’s disease, and 200 who went on to develop ulcerative colitis. The remaining 100 developed neither condition. The blood samples were screened for antibodies that the immune system might have churned out in response to hundreds of thousands of fragments of proteins from bacteria, viruses, food and even the body’s own tissues. In people who went on to develop Crohn’s disease, antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus, which causes glandular fever, were more common, and the differences were already visible a decade before diagnosis. The signal was strongest in those who later developed more severe, complicated disease, which can narrow the bowel or create abnormal channels. People who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies against one of the body’s own proteins. The findings, published in the journal Gut and presented at the United European Gastroenterology meeting in Barcelona, need to be confirmed in other groups of people, and the results show a link rather than proving the infections cause IBD. But the hope is that IBD could eventually follow the path of type 1 diabetes, where a blood test can identify people whose immune systems have begun attacking the pancreas before any symptoms appear, allowing treatment that delays the onset of disease. James Lindsay, a professor of gastroenterology at Barts Health, who was not involved in the research, said the study provided “important insights into the causes of Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, potentially adding new tools to help identify those at risk of IBD”. But he cautioned that the techniques were “very much a research tool” and not yet ready for the clinic. Marianne Radcliffe, the chief executive of Crohn’s & Colitis UK, a national patient charity, said: “For people affected by Crohn’s and colitis, research like this is an important step forward. Every new insight helps build a clearer understanding of how these conditions develop, including the changes that may occur years before symptoms appear.”

headline: Margaret Hamilton obituary
trail_text: Pioneering software engineer whose work was critical to the Apollo moon landings
body_text: Apollo was a bold, innovative project. It tested the boundaries of technology and human achievement, and took people to the moon. However, one thing it failed to challenge was the prevailing hierarchy. Nearly everyone involved in Nasa’s space programme in the 1960s was male and white. If you weren’t, you needed to be exceptional at what you did. Margaret Hamilton, who has died aged 90, was one of those exceptional people. Without her input, sending spacecraft into lunar orbit, and putting Neil Armstrong and his successors on to the surface of the moon, might have been impossible. Hamilton directed the software engineering division at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Instrumentation Laboratory, which had been charged with developing the computer systems for Apollo. The result of this work was the Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC). This provided the astronauts with a computer-linked keypad, similar in appearance to a calculator and known by the acronym DSKY – short for Display and Keyboard – which they used for navigating and controlling the direction and manoeuvrability of the spacecraft. In the Gemini missions, which preceded Apollo, astronauts used joysticks to control the spacecraft. AGC removed that necessity, leading to a more precise flight path while freeing the crew for other tasks. It was the first computer in the world based on the silicon-integrated circuits that are now mass-produced and found in everyday electronic devices such as smartphones, televisions and laptops. One AGC controlled the command module, which remained in orbit around the moon, while a second controlled the lunar module (LM), which descended to the surface. The astronauts could briefly take manual control as the LM approached the landing site, but otherwise AGC flew the two spacecraft automatically. In July 1969, Apollo 11 became the first mission to put humans on the moon. As its LM, codenamed Eagle, began its descent, alarms went off inside the module. Mission control considered aborting but Hamilton, listening in from MIT, had run the simulations so many times that she realised what had happened: a radar switch had been inadvertently left active. She had seen this during simulations when Armstrong’s companion Buzz Aldrin had made the same error during training, and had previously instructed two of Apollo 11’s mission controllers, Steve Bales and Jack Garman, that unless it happened repeatedly they need not abort. Via the flight controller, Gene Kranz, they reassured Armstrong the alarm could be ignored. Five minutes later Armstrong informed the world: “The Eagle has landed”. Hamilton told the Times in 2019 that the Eagle’s safe landing was “maybe the most exciting moment of my life,” coupled with the realisation of “the things we’d gone through to get there … everything came rushing through my mind”. She was born in Paoli, Indiana, the oldest of four children of Esther (nee Partington) and Kenneth Heafield, both teachers. Early in her life, the family moved to Michigan, where Margaret graduated from Hancock high school in 1954, going on to study mathematics at the University of Michigan and then at Earlham College, in Richmond, Indiana. She gained her BA in 1958, the year she married James Hamilton, a fellow student at Earlham. The following year they moved to Boston, where James was to study law at Harvard and where their daughter, Lauren, was born. Hamilton found work in the meteorology department of MIT, where her first role was developing weather-prediction software, alongside Edward Lorenz, the mathematician and meteorologist and founder of modern chaos theory. Her talent immediately became apparent and she was assigned work on the US air-defence systems before, in 1965, responding to an advert from the Instrumentation Laboratory – also a department of MIT – seeking people to develop software to send humans to the moon. She was successful, becoming the first programmer for Apollo at MIT, and, of more significance, the first woman working on the project. Within three years she was made assistant director, and soon after became director of the team of about 100. Unsurprisingly, she was the target of sexism, some which would have led to disciplinary action today – but rarely from her fellow programmers. She told MIT News in 2009: “Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did … There was no choice but to be pioneers.” As well as her deep knowledge, her insistence on running and rerunning programs searching for glitches was invaluable. One day, Lauren was playing with the command module simulator when she accidentally activated a program called P01 while the simulator was in mid-flight. It crashed the system. Hamilton took note, and when, during the flight of Apollo 8 in 1968, P01 was activated accidentally, her knowledge meant the problem could be fixed mid-mission. Her meticulous approach ensured no software bugs were ever known to have been reported during any crewed Apollo mission. She also earned herself the epithet “the rope mother” because the core memory for Apollo’s onboard computers was woven from strands of copper interlaced through magnets. These had to be meticulously threaded by hand using professional seamstresses. The work was intricate, precise and double-checked by Hamilton at every stage. She even coined the term “software engineering”, to draw a distinction between her work and more theoretical computer science, and to explain to non-specialists what her department’s duties entailed. Once Apollo had been wound down in the early 1970s, Hamilton continued to work at the instrumentation lab. She focused on the Skylab space station and space shuttle programmes, and set up two software companies of her own, Higher Order Software in 1976 and Hamilton Technologies in 1986. Andrew Meade McGee, curator of computing at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC, described her as “a seminal figure in the creation of modern, software-driven computing”. He said: “Her practices, drawn directly from working on the AGC, reshaped the computing industry and software education, and still have influence today. Over the years she has inspired many women into STEM careers. Back then, she was often the only woman in the room during Apollo gatherings of systems analysts, but she proved female engineers could excel when given a foot in the door.” When Hamilton received the presidential medal of freedom from Barack Obama in 2016, he said: “She symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space.” Among many other accolades, she collected the Augusta Ada Lovelace award in 1986 from the Association for Women in Computing, and in 2003 Nasa’s exceptional space act award for scientific and technical contributions. In 2017, a Women of Nasa Lego set was produced, which featured mini figures of Hamilton, the astronauts Sally Ride and Mae Jemison, and the Nasa chief of astronomy Nancy Roman. Last year Hamilton received the Michael Collins trophy from the Air and Space Museum in Washington, which recognises past and present achievements involving the management or execution of a scientific or technological project related to space exploration. It was collected by her daughter, as Hamilton was too frail to travel. Her first marriage ended in divorce in 1967 and two years later she married Dan Lickly, an aeronautical engineer, whom she met at MIT. They were divorced in 1973. Thereafter Hamilton lived with Ron Hackler, a former colleague. He died in 2025. Her daughter survives her. • Margaret Elaine Hamilton, computer scientist, born 17 August 1936; died 30 September 2026

headline: Chris Davies obituary
trail_text: Other lives: Professor of engineering whose work on light metals established him as a leading researcher in the field
body_text: My brother, Chris Davies, who has died aged 61 of cancer, was an academic metallurgist whose research helped to bring about a better understanding of why metals behave the way they do – and therefore how to control their properties during manufacturing. Much of his research took place at Monash University in Australia, where he had moved from the UK in the early 1990s. In particular, his work on the behaviour of light metals and alloys fed into the development of lighter, stronger and more reliable materials used in the making of aircraft, vehicles and medical devices. Chris’s studies also helped to support advances in 3D printing by providing insights into how companies can produce high-performance metal components more efficiently, with less waste and lower energy consumption. Born in Cardiff, Chris was the son of Jack and his wife, Margaret (nee Powell), both teachers of English. He attended Cardiff high school and then gained a degree in engineering at Imperial College London, where he stayed on to do a PhD. In 1992 he moved to Vancouver in Canada to do two years of postdoctoral research at the University of British Columbia, before joining Monash in Melbourne in 1994 and remaining there until his death, initially in a teaching role but thereafter specialising mainly in research. In addition, Chris held a number of leadership roles at Monash over the years, including as associate dean of research, deputy dean of external engagements and deputy dean of operations in the Faculty of Engineering. He was president of the Academic Board from 2016 to 2019, and in 2025 was named to the Monash Honour Roll, a mark of the esteem in which he was held for his integrity, humour and unwavering commitment. Beyond his life in academia Chris loved reading, enjoyed print making, painting and drawing and appreciated music of all genres. He was an avid sports fan, having played club hockey in his younger days, and was a member of the Cardiff Nomads Angling Club. He is survived by his second wife, Sam (nee Lipscombe), whom he married in 2011, a son, Calum, from his first marriage to Louise (nee Hehir), which ended in divorce, and his siblings, Graham and me.

headline: Norman McCubbin obituary
trail_text: Other lives: Particle physicist who worked for many years on projects related to the Large Hadron Collider
body_text: My brother Norman McCubbin, who has died aged 77, was a scientist who worked at the forefront of experimental particle physics. A leading light in experiments that took place on the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s biggest and most powerful particle accelerator at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (Cern) in Switzerland, he spent the last five years of his working life as director of the particle physics department at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) in Oxfordshire, until his retirement in 2012. Afterwards he became a tutor to undergraduates at St Anne’s College, Oxford, and was still in that role at his death. Norman was born in Pinner, Middlesex, the first child of Hugh, an accountant, and his wife, Pat (nee Rosenberg). The family moved to Leicester, where his brothers, Richard and I, were born, and then in 1958 to Kenya for Hugh to take up a post as finance director of the Kenya Farmers’ Association . When Hugh joined the UN’s World Food Programme, the family moved to Lesotho and later, Taiwan, while Norman went to Repton school in Derbyshire as a boarder. After moving on to New College, Oxford, he gained a first-class physics degree and took a PhD. Between 1973 and 1979 he was a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Lancaster and then at RAL, working with the laboratory on the first hadron collider at Cern to study the dynamics of proton-proton collisions. He then worked at Cern as a senior (then principal) scientific officer, where he concentrated on the collisions of heavy ions. From 1990 to 1999 Norman led RAL’s Zeus experiment in Hamburg, studying the structure of the proton, and from 1999 to 2003 he was computing coordinator for the Atlas experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Later he became divisional head of RAL’s particle physics department while continuing with some of his work at Cern until, in 2007, he became the department’s director. In retirement as a stipendiary lecturer in physics at Oxford, he was a popular tutor, relishing the core subjects of thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, relativity and symmetries. More prosaically, he relished answering questions, via video from New Zealand, from his ever-curious seven-year-old great-nephew Hugh, about issues such as gravity, centrifugal force and quantum entanglement. Despite his dedication to his work, family and friendship always came first for Norman. We all basked in his warmth, love, humour and kindness, as well as that illuminating intelligence he wore so lightly. He is survived by me and Richard, two nieces, two nephews, three great-nephews and a great-niece.

headline: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
trail_text: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
body_text: After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour. Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more. The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60. “After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.” The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years. “We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour. The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days. Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom. Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces. Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time. The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward. “Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync. “After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said. Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said. To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote. Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system. The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added. Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

headline: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear
trail_text: Adult excavated in an Iraqi Kurdistan cave died more than 70,000 years ago and bears ‘kill shot’ shoulder wound
body_text: A smooth round hole in the shoulder blade of a Neanderthal who died more than 70,000 years ago may be the oldest evidence so far of a human ancestor being killed by a wooden spear. Archaeologists spotted the distinctive injury after excavating skeletal remains of the adult and other Neanderthals from under nearly 8 metres of rock and sediment in the Shanidar cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. At least five Neanderthals were buried at the same spot over several years, in a depression no larger than a fridge that ran behind a huge boulder near the entrance to the cave. Some of the bodies appear to have been laid on top of others that were still decomposing. “They’re coming back to the same spot to place bodies over a number of years or several decades and that’s really quite unusual in in the Neanderthal archaeological record,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It suggests there’s some kind of meaningful behaviour in depositing the dead there.” Researchers found only partial remains of the injured Neanderthal, an adult aged about 45. The left shoulder blade that bears the wound was found with seven teeth, several ribs and fragments, and a near complete right hand that was leaning against the boulder. Close inspection of the shoulder blade revealed three fractures spreading out from the 1.5cm-wide hole and fragments of bone that filled the wound. The shards were probably punched out of the thin bone when the spear hit, the scientists said. The circular shape of the hole and the pattern of bone damage strongly suggest a wound inflicted by a wooden spear striking the body from the front.But whether it was a hunting accident or an intentional attack – a brutal jab from a foe, perhaps – is impossible to know. Pomeroy said the position of the wound and the force needed to push the spear through the chest, where it would have punctured the lung and probably severed arteries before punching out of the shoulder blade, pointed to a “kill shot” directed at the heart. “I don’t think that’s something you do accidentally,” she said. The spear wound was almost certainly lethal, but the individual was in bad shape before the fatal blow. Examination of the teeth revealed a lower incisor split vertically, leaving only half in place, its neighbours twisted inwards, according to details published in Scientific Reports. “You’d need quite a severe hit in the face to split a tooth like that and to rotate the others,” said Pomeroy. “They might well have needed help because they would have been in terrible pain.” The split tooth was caked in hardened plaque that would have taken at least a year to build up. Chris Hunt, the emeritus professor at Liverpool John Moores University, who co-authored the paper, said Neanderthals at Shanidar were taking ibex as their main prey and could have used wooden spears shaped like modern javelins to kill the animals. Because plant material decomposes so easily, very few wooden objects survive from prehistory, but timber spears from about 200,000 years ago have been discovered in Germany, preserved in waterlogged ground. The pointed end of a rounded wooden spear discovered in Clacton-on-Sea in 1911 is the oldest known at over 400,000 years old. Last week, scientists in Spain described hundreds of wooden imprints and artefacts that show Neanderthals embraced woodwork, making trays, plates, tripods, spears and other items. But proof of fatal skirmishes is harder to find in fossils: we may never know how the wounded Neanderthal at Shanidar died. “Conceivably it was a hunting accident,” Hunt said. “We can’t, however, rule out that purposeful interpersonal violence was involved.”

headline: Cyril Hilsum obituary
trail_text: Government physicist whose radar research paved the way for flat-panel TV and computer screens based on liquid crystals
body_text: Cyril Hilsum’s research into stable liquid crystals and the devices in which they could be used paved the way for the flat-panel television and computer screens that are now ubiquitous in homes, offices and public spaces. Hilsum, who has died aged 101, was leading a Ministry of Defence team at the Royal Radar Establishment (RRE) in Malvern, Worcestershire, in the late 1960s when Harold Wilson’s Labour government, looking to develop a new generation of miniature radar systems, tasked him with creating flat displays to replace the bulky cathode-ray-tube screens used for traditional radar set-ups. Realising the key to flat-screen technology was the emerging science of liquid crystals, Hilsum organised a meeting of liquid crystal researchers – and soon realised there was only one person in the room who really understood anything about them: George Gray, from Hull University. Gray was immediately offered a contract, and began working with Hilsum and Peter Raynes, an optoelectronics expert at the RRE, on fulfilling the government’s brief. By 1972 the three of them had developed a mixture that was suitable for use in screens, made largely of cyanobiphenyls, compounds that remain stable even when heated or exposed to sunlight or ultraviolet light. This gave the resulting screens durability in real-world applications. Although originally designed to support the RRE’s nascent radar technology, the liquid crystal displays (or LCDs) that used the mixture soon found practical uses elsewhere. While the MoD retained the patents, Hilsum persuaded the chemicals company BDH to manufacture and sell the mixtures under licence, eventually netting the government more than £100m in royalties from their use in watches and calculators, and then later in laptops, tablets and phones. Hilsum was born in Stepney, east London, to Benjamin and Ada, who were street traders. A bright boy who had learned to read proficiently by the age of three and spent hours dismantling toys to see how they worked, he went to Raine’s Foundation school in Bethnal Green, after which, during the second world war, he won a scholarship to University College London, which had been evacuated to Bangor in north Wales. He graduated with a degree in physics in 1945 and later a PhD, meeting fellow student Betty Cooper at UCL and marrying her in 1947. He and Betty, who became a teacher, were keen Labour party supporters, and after the war would attend Winston Churchill’s meetings in order to heckle him. After an initial spell working for the MoD in central London immediately after the war, he moved in 1947 to the Admiralty Research Laboratory in Teddington, where he met Alan Turing, who worked at the nearby National Physical Laboratory, and whom he once beat at chess. By 1950, aged 25, he was leading a team studying military uses for infrared light, based at the Services Electronics Research Laboratory in Baldock, Hertfordshire. Hilsum joined the RRE in 1964 to carry out research into gallium arsenide, a semiconductor material that handles high-frequencies, and on the development of radar, transistors and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). In fact his work on semiconductors was as significant as that on LCDs, and included helping to develop infrared lasers that now underpin fibre optic telecommunications. He was also instrumental in developing the Gunn diode, a high-frequency oscillator that generates microwave signals used in motion detectors and proximity sensors, including police radar speed guns – sometimes to his disadvantage, given that he was a fast driver. In tandem, his work on developing miniature radar systems led to Claribel, a device for detecting the trajectory of a bullet, which was used to locate snipers in Northern Ireland during the Troubles. In 1974 Hilsum became the UK’s chief scientific officer, the highest rank for a scientist in the civil service and a position he held until in 1983 he accepted the role of chief scientist, and later research director, at the General Electrical Company’s Hirst Research Centre in Wembley, north-west London. Always a promoter of women in sciences, at GEC he insisted his department hire equal numbers of both sexes. Hilsum served as president of the Institute of Physics from 1988 to 1990, the year that he was appointed CBE. He retired from GEC in 1995. A fellow of the Royal Society, he won the Faraday Medal and in 2007 the Royal Society’s Royal Medal “for his many outstanding contributions and for continuing to use his prodigious talents on behalf of industry, government and academe”. The British Liquid Crystal Society awards the Cyril Hilsum Medal annually for the best contribution to liquid crystal technology. In later years Hilsum built a laboratory in his house in Pinner, Middlesex, where, aged 97, he came up with his final invention – an ink containing sensors to conduct electricity – earning him the last of more than 70 patents. He ascribed his longevity to red wine and chocolate, and was a lifelong reader of the Guardian. Betty died in 1987, and one of their daughters, Karen, also predeceased him, in 1997. Hilsum founded the Karen Burt award at the Women’s Engineering Society. He is survived by their other daughter, Lindsey, international editor for Channel 4 News, and a grandson, Alexander. • Cyril Hilsum, physicist and inventor, born 17 May 1925; died 23 September 2026

headline: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests
trail_text: Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds
body_text: If you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don’t start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar, focus on how they sound instead, research suggests. A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words. Normally, when people learn a language, they try to understand it through the sounds of their native tongue. The more different the foreign language’s sounds and pronunciation are from the native language, the harder the new language will probably be to learn. But the best linguists master even the trickiest pronunciation much more easily. To find out why, researchers at UCL and Tohoku University, Japan, compared the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight changes in pitch, length and tone, in non-speech sounds. Using functional MRI scans, they measured participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between English vowel sounds that do not occur in Japanese. They found that those with higher auditory precision mastered the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners and relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Instead, their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds. With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds. In contrast, those with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native language when processing unfamiliar sounds. The latest findings challenge stereotypes that Britons are less adept at languages. Prof Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, the lead author and professor of second language education at UCL Institute of Education, said: “I do not think British people are biologically bad at languages. The problem is more likely to be that many people receive too little meaningful exposure, combined with teaching methods that do not necessarily train the auditory skills needed to make the most of that limited exposure. “If you only hear and use the language for a small number of hours each week, having a good ear may make a much bigger difference. Learners with high auditory precision can make very effective use of relatively sparse input, whereas others may need much more exposure before unfamiliar sounds begin to become established,” he said. The findings also suggest schools should focus on sounds much more than just grammar and vocabulary when teaching modern languages, he added. “Foreign language education should move beyond an approach based on ‘more practice’ and towards one that develops learners’ ear for language learning in line with their auditory characteristics,” he said. Responding to the findings, Prof Padraic Monaghan, professor of cognition at Lancaster University, said: “Traditional language learning relies on structured practice, but our brains are naturally attuned to acquire languages through exposure. This study confirms how vital listening is to learning, though learners vary in their sound sensitivity at least in the early stages of hearing new language sounds.”

headline: Keith Thompson obituary
trail_text: Other lives: Academic and crop scientist specialising in optimum harvest
body_text: My former husband Keith Thompson, who has died aged 86, was an academic and horticulturalist specialising in the area of optimum harvest, and the packing and storing of fruit and root crops. Working as a crop scientist for the government-run Tropical Products Institute from the 1960s to mid-80s, Keith worked on overseas assignments in many countries including Trinidad, Colombia, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Zambia, Turkey, Thailand and Yemen. He was on a field trip outside Aden in 1986 when the coup happened that sparked the South Yemen conflict. He and his local counterpart trekked to a coastal refinery compound, and Keith and other British nationals were collected by a diverted HMY Britannia, the royal yacht, to land at Djibouti and fly back to the UK. Keith’s souvenir was a Royal Navy sweater to keep him warm. Born in Halifax to Hilda (nee Smith), a mill worker, and Harold Thompson, a lathe-turner at Churchill Redmond metal works, Keith attended Copley junior school. Aged 10 on holiday in Bridlington, his cousin accidentally hit him in the eye with a golf club, and he lost the sight in that eye. Due to missed schooling, Keith failed his 11-plus and at 13 joined Halifax Technical College, leaving at 16 with no qualifications. Horticultural interests led him to enrol as an apprentice gardener for Halifax Public Parks and he gained Royal Horticultural Society qualifications. By 1960 he had added some GCEs and A-level botany and zoology, and gained a place at Wye College, a University of London establishment located in the Kent countryside, to study for a horticulture degree. I met Keith at a graduation party in Canterbury, and we married in 1965. Two years later, Keith gained his PhD from Leeds University, and a daughter, Katie. Recruited by the government’s Overseas Development Administration (ODA), which financed the Tropical Products Institute, Keith and the family set sail to Trinidad, where he lectured in crop science at the University of the West Indies, and our son, Miles, was born. Subsequent teaching and consultancy posts followed, in Jamaica, Khartoum, Seoul and Bogota before returning to the UK and the Tropical Products Institute in 1980, settling in Bromley, Kent, while continuing overseas assignments. In 1987, Keith was appointed professor of crop science at Cranfield University, based at Silsoe campus, Bedfordshire. Many of his PhD and BSc students were from countries where he had worked, and he stayed in that post until retirement in 2000. We divorced in 2004. The same year, Keith settled in Marsden, West Yorkshire, home to the jazz festival that he loved. In 2020, while teaching a course at King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology, Bangkok, he met Pikunthong Nuktamna, a psychology lecturer at Huachiew Chalermprakiet University. They became partners and were engaged. Pikunthong survives him, as do Katie and Miles, nine grandchildren, four great-grandchildren, and his brother, David. • This article was amended on 14 October 2026. Keith Thompson is survived by nine grandchildren, not six as an earlier version said.

headline: Did you solve it? The treacherous puzzle of the round table
trail_text: The solutions to today’s puzzles
body_text: Earlier today I set you these six puzzles. Here they are again with solutions. The round table Three people sit at a round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age. Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left.” 1. What is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth? 2. What is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth? Solution 1. The oldest person must be lying, so the maximum is 2. Here is an example with 2 people telling the truth: 30-40-20 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table) The answer is two. 2. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the minimum is 1. Here is an example with 1 person telling the truth 40-30-20 The answer is one. Seven people sit at a different round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age. Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left, and I am younger than the person two places to my right”. 3. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth? 4. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth? Solution 3. The two oldest people must be lying, so the answer cannot be six or seven. It turns out that the answer cannot be five either. If five were telling the truth, the third oldest would be one of them, and so the three oldest people would have to be arranged in one of the two cases below (suppose the ages are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70). * * * 60 * 50 70 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table) * * * 70 * 50 60 But now there is nowhere for the next oldest (the 40-year-old) to sit and be telling the truth. It is, however, possible for four people to be telling the truth: 10 20 40 70 30 50 60 The answer is four. 4. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the answer cannot be zero. If you order everyone in descending order of ages, no one is telling the truth apart from the youngest: 70 60 50 40 30 20 10 The answer is one. 999 people sit at a third round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age. Each of them says “I am younger than the person three places to my left, and older than the person three places to my right”. 5. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth? 6. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth? Solution 5. We might think about this by colouring the seats gold, silver and bronze in a repeating pattern, like so (in the illustration there are only 21 people, but the idea works for 999 people as well). It can now be seen that each person makes a statement about people sitting on seats with the same colour as them; in particular, the closest people on either side with the same colour seat. Consider those 333 people sitting in gold. The youngest and oldest of these must be lying, so there cannot be 333 or 332 gold truthtellers. But, as the example below helps to illustrate, it is possible for every other gold person to be telling the truth, by seating them with age increasing as we move clockwise around the table. Applying the same reasoning to those seated on silver or bronze, we can have all but six people telling the truth. The same idea with 999 people has 999-6=993 telling the truth. The answer is 993. 6. If the people are sat with age decreasing as we move clockwise around the table, then everybody is lying. The answer is 0. Thanks to Daniel Griller for today’s puzzles. He is the author of the excellent puzzle books Elastic Numbers and A Ring of Cats and Dogs, and Other Curious Puzzles. I’ll be back in two weeks. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

headline: Feelgood factor of human interaction
trail_text: Brief letters: Happy hormones | Fuel costs | Drive-in parking | Guys and girls | Young or old? | Singapore pollution
body_text: Re your report (‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms, 6 October), the US neuroscientist Ben Rein has shown that there is a fundamental difference in our cognitive response according to the type of interaction we have. In-person meetings and conversations show a dramatic increase in serotonin, oxytocin and dopamine – “feelgood” hormones – compared with online interactions. I have been encouraged to speak to people at bus stops. Judith Furner Eastbourne, East Sussex • Re easing winter fuel costs (Report, 6 October), it would benefit everyone if the outrageous daily standing charges were reduced or on a sliding scale based on usage. I can’t be the only person whose standing charges each month are half or more than the energy used. Judith Pearson Sheffield • To your tautology anthology (Letters, 5 October) should be added this sign at a farm shop in the Vale of Evesham: “Large drive-in car park.” Paul Gelling Prenton, Merseyside • Far worse than being called “young lady” (Letters, 7 October) is the ubiquitous use of “guys” in the hospitality industry. Stop it. Megan Parry Wallingford, Oxfordshire • At 91, I object to being addressed as “young man”, remembering that when I was actually a young man I was often called “old man”. Beverley Charles Rowe London • Irony corner: air pollution impairs F1 motor racing in Singapore (Report, 6 October). Martin Datta Lincoln • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights
trail_text: Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
body_text: The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening. Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis. The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday. Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland. The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere. Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said. Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky. According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph. The forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles. “As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.” Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.

headline: Ada Yonath obituary
trail_text: Nobel prizewinning biochemist who succeeded against the odds in mapping the ribosome
body_text: For years, the crystallographer and biochemist Ada Yonath had to contend with the disdain and sometimes derision of many of her contemporaries after she set herself the challenge of mapping the molecular structure of the ribosome. Ribosomes are found in all living cells. Effectively they are tiny factories that synthesise proteins, complex molecules that are vital for building and repairing the tissues and organs of animals and plants. Many scientists believed hers was a fruitless endeavour because ribosomes are so small – sometimes only 20 nanometres in diameter – irregular in shape and lacking internal symmetry. James Watson, one of the Nobel prizewinning discoverers of the double-helix structure of DNA, had tried and failed. But Yonath, who has died aged 87, proved her doubters wrong, and was rewarded with the 2009 Nobel prize in chemistry, only the fourth woman to receive it, which she shared with the biologist Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and biochemist Thomas Steitz. “I was met with disbelief, even ridicule in the international scientific community,” she said later. “I was called a dreamer, a fantasist, even the village idiot. But when I succeeded, it created an overwhelming internal joy and those who once called me crazy or stupid became supporters.” It was in the late 1970s, while being laid up following a bicycle accident, and indulging in some “easier” reading, that Yonath, then a young scientist based at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, chanced upon the article that would lead to her eventual breakthrough. Reading about the biology of polar bears, she learned that the bears pack their ribosomes in an orderly way in their cells prior to hibernating. “These stay intact and functional for months. So, if polar bears knew how to do it, we could too,” she reasoned. Yonath surmised that if she could crystallise ribosomes, she would be able to study their internal structure using X-rays and electron microscopy. However, ribosomes are fragile. Unlike other cell parts, they have no outer protective membrane and are easily damaged. Figuring that ribosomes of organisms that live in harsh conditions were likely to be hardier and more able to survive crystallisation, she attempted to crystallise the thermophile bacteria Geobacillus stearothermophilus, found in austere environments around thermal vents and in desert sands. It took more than 25,000 attempts, but in the mid-80s, Yonath succeeded. She then froze the bacteria at –185°C, to stabilise its internal structure and to protect it from the X-rays, a technique she was an early successful pioneer of, now known as cryo bio-crystallography. Finally, in 2001 and 2002, after almost two decades of research, Yonath’s team succeeded in mapping, in three dimensions, the bacteria’s ribosome. The significance of this discovery extended beyond pure science. Many antibiotics work by binding to sites on a bacterium’s ribosome, stopping it from reproducing. Previously, making antibiotics was a hit-and-miss process because often they would attack human ribosomes as well as those of the bacteria. But, armed with knowledge of the structure of different ribosomes, scientists could now deduce where on a ribosome an antibiotic would bind and so make the necessary structural alterations to the drug. Yonath demonstrated how more than 20 antibiotics function, paving the way for new products, and also studied how antibiotic resistance might be overcome. The Nobel committee specifically noted this work in its citation, highlighting the “fundamental and medically important aspects of ribosome function” leading to “the development of novel antibiotic drugs in the ongoing medical struggle against ever emerging drug resistance among bacterial pathogens”. Born in Jerusalem, into an Orthodox Jewish family, Ada was the elder daughter of parents who had emigrated from Poland to what was then British-mandated Palestine in 1933. Her father, Hillel Lifshitz, a rabbi and grocer, died when she was 11. Her mother, Esther, then moved with her two daughters to Tel Aviv, where she became a clerk. Despite her modest income, she recognised her daughter’s keen intellect and obtained her a place at the fee-paying Tichon Hadash high school, where Ada taught maths lessons in lieu of school fees. In 1959, after two years of mandatory military service, she returned to Jerusalem to take a degree in chemistry at the Hebrew University, graduating in 1962, then a master’s in biochemistry (1964). Four years later she received a PhD from the Weizmann Institute for studies into the structure of collagen using X-ray crystallography. She accepted postdoctoral positions in the US, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Carnegie Mellon University, in Pittsburgh, before returning to the Weizmann Institute, where, in 1970, she began her research into ribosomes and where she remained for the rest of her career. Despite the scepticism of many of her peers, she did receive long-term support and funding from Heinz-Günter Wittman at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in Berlin, frequently travelling to Germany to exchange data and compare notes. In addition to her Nobel prize, Yonath received numerous awards, including the 2007 Wolf prize in chemistry, second only in importance to the Nobel, and was elected as a foreign member of the UK’s Royal Society. Outside her work, Yonath was politically outspoken and critical of the Israeli government. Most recently, she criticised Israeli judicial reforms as a “genuine peril to democracy” and to Israeli scientific enterprise. In 2018, when asked what qualities made a good scientist, she said: “Curiosity, first. Second, curiosity. And third, curiosity. Also, one has to love, and not be afraid of, a challenge.” Her marriage to Moshe Yonath, a schoolteacher, ended in divorce. Her daughter, Hagith, and a granddaughter, Noa, survive her. • Ada Esther Yonath, crystallographer and biochemist, born 22 June 1939; died 31 August 2026 • This article was amended on 14 October 2026. Ada Yonath’s key realisation concerned the crystallisation of ribosomes rather than organisms in order to study their internal structure.

headline: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away
trail_text: Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’
body_text: A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe. Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded. FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does in months or years. These mysterious pulses were first discovered in 2007 and have puzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have an alien origin. In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”. The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record. The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope (JWST). Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”. Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”. There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field. “Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said. More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”. Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen. “[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said. This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe. Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists who first discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”. Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes. Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].” The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.

headline: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies aged 90
trail_text: MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
body_text: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90. In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist. She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity. “I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency. Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended. “It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said. Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. “Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

headline: Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity
trail_text: DNA analysis of oldest living land animal reveal patterns on genes that appear to protect functioning of mitochondria
body_text: The ancient quest to extend human lifespan has received a boost after scientists analysed the genetic code of the world’s oldest living land animal, a giant tortoise called Jonathan. The tortoise, which lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the governor of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, is believed to be 194 years old, making him a contemporary of Queen Victoria and Charles Darwin. Analysis of the animal’s DNA revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing that scientists have discovered. Together, they help organisms to survive by repairing damaged DNA, regulating their metabolism and fending off cancer. But more intriguing to the researchers were chemical patterns on Jonathan’s genes that appear to protect the healthy functioning of his mitochondria, the tiny battery-like structures that power biological cells. Ailing mitochondria have been strongly linked to ageing and age-related diseases. “We’re still trying to work out how ageing occurs and Jonathan gives us a real window on to what happens over a long period of time,” said Stephen Clark, a senior researcher on the project at the non-profit Kallel Foundation. “His mitochondria must be especially stable and that’s an insight into longevity in general. It’s important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.” The insight came when the international team, led by Benjamin Vaisvil, looked at chemical tags that attach to DNA, creating patterns that change over time. The tags, known as methyl groups, typically silence the genes they latch on to. Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how they compared the methylation patterns on Jonathan’s genes with those from other giant tortoises. The patterns on many of his genes were similar to those of other old tortoises, but the patterns on genes linked to mitochondrial function matched those from much younger animals. It is unclear whether, or how much, the chemical patterning contributes to Jonathan’s impressive lifespan. Clark said the team now needed to validate the finding. “How do we test this idea?” he said. “Is there a way that makes the mitochondria young, or can we replace the mitochondria and see if it extends longevity? That’s one of the next steps.” The former senior veterinary officer of Saint Helena, Joe Hollis, took over Jonathan’s care in 2009. He was not faring well at the time. Cataracts had left him blind, he had lost his sense of smell and his beak was soft and crumbly, making it hard to forage. Hollis began hand-feeding him and six months to a year later, the tortoise had regained weight and sported a hard, serrated beak. In April, Jonathan was caught up in a viral crypto death scam when a message from a fake X account posing as Hollis claimed the tortoise had died. The news spread around the world before the Guardian made contact with Nigel Phillips, the governor of Saint Helena, who interrupted his bedtime routine to check on Jonathan. He found him asleep under a tree but “very much alive”. Jonathan certainly appears to be enjoying life. A few months ago, he was found mating with Emma, who shares his paddock. Shortly afterwards, the wife of the governor, who is also called Emma, checked on Jonathan and found him upside down. “Emma [the tortoise] has a very semicircular shell,” said Hollis. “So if you slip sideways fast enough the momentum will flip you right over. It’s phenomenal though. He’s 194. You’re going to have an accident, aren’t you, at 194?”

headline: Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules
trail_text: Henri B Kagan and Kensō Soai awarded prize for discovery that has aided understanding of how medicines work in the body
body_text: The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule. Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality. However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration. How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London. “This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.” The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms. Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution. It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other. Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry. In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time. Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”. Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said. These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai. “It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”

headline: Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?
trail_text: Firms working on reproducing compounds without need for repeated harvesting but conservationists are sceptical
body_text: Many of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When some Aquilaria trees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit. The result has devastated wild Aquilaria populations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree? With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes. Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them. “Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells. Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory. BioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant. The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year. “The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib. “We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.” But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned. “Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline. Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to the Aquilaria tree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant populations,” she said. There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work. Synthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent. “What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said. Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents. Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year. Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows. It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said. “What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”

headline: Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos
trail_text: Belgian physicist praised for work on the IceCube detector that observes the ghost-like particles in Antarctica
body_text: The Nobel prize in physics 2026 has been awarded to a researcher who turned an enormous block of ice at the south pole into a detector for ghostly particles called neutrinos that reach Earth from outer space. Prof Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, led work on the IceCube neutrino observatory, which made the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, soon after it was switched on. To build the observatory, scientists, technicians and engineers embedded thousands of basketball-sized light detectors into a cubic kilometre of ice to detect faint flashes of light that can result when neutrinos from space crash into atomic nuclei. Announcing the prize on Tuesday, the Nobel committee said Halzen won “for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. He receives a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). “It feels strange,” Halzen told a press briefing on winning the prize. “I hope it reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project when no really respectable, conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did.” Neutrinos are mysterious particles that are as elusive as they are ubiquitous. They pass through almost everything they encounter, from people to planets. Every second, billions of neutrinos from the sun pass unnoticed through the body. But every now and then, a neutrino will interact with the nucleus of an atom in a collision that can be picked up by a sensitive detector. Halzen realised that brief flickers of light from neutrino collisions could be detected in clear, glacial ice and in 1988 put forward a plan to convert a chunk of the south pole into a neutrino observatory. The detector uses Earth to shield against the background noise of cosmic rays, and has downwards-facing light sensors to detect neutrinos passing through the planet from the northern hemisphere. Apart from a hostile environment for the team, the site benefited from being far from sources of interference and the risk of vibrations from earthquakes. After the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, scientists working on IceCube identified the first cosmic source of neutrinos 3.7bn light years away. The observatory has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy. Until now, researchers have learned about the cosmos from light, other electromagnetic radiation, and gravitational waves. Neutrinos are considered messengers from the cosmos and provide fresh clues as to how the universe evolved. Halzen, who received the news while travelling in Italy, said he was working on a new proposal and hoped that winning the prize would help in getting it approved. Dr Patrick Dunne at Imperial College London welcomed the prize. “For all of human history the only way we’ve been able to understand things outside our solar system is with light. Detecting neutrinos from astrophysical sources opens up a new lens, so it isn’t overstating things to liken this to when Galileo first pointed a telescope at the stars,” he said. “Neutrinos are the most abundant massive particles and their ability to pass through matter much more easily than light makes them ideal for observing distant phenomena or the inside of extreme phenomena like those seen by IceCube,” he added. Other experiments to understand neutrinos include the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the US and the Hyper-Kamiokande detector in Japan. The observations of cosmic neutrinos have led some scientists to speculate that the ghostly particles could be used by alien civilisations to send messages across the universe. Asked what he made of the idea, Halzen said: “I don’t think I’ll go there. We have enough realistic problems to deal with right now [to] make neutrino astronomy a reality rather than worry about this.” But he added that when astronomers have opened new windows on the universe, they often make unexpected discoveries. “I’m sure this will be true for neutrinos 50 years from now,” he said. On Monday, three scientists won the Nobel prize in medicine for optogenetics, a powerful technique that has allowed researchers to shed unprecedented light on the workings of the brain. The Nobel prize in chemistry is announced on Wednesday.

headline: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain
trail_text: Three scientists to share 12m Swedish kronor prize for their work on ‘light-gated ion channels and optogenetics’
body_text: The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain. Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”. The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists. In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off. Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more. “Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said. The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly. Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse. Further work by the pair revealed that when the genetic instructions for one of the proteins were inserted into human or mouse kidney cells, those cells became light sensitive. Deisseroth took the discovery even further, using rats to demonstrate that by introducing the gene for a channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, it was possible to produce electrical signals in them using light. He and his colleagues later applied the approach to nerve cells in the motor cortex of the brains of mice, allowing them to use light – delivered by tiny optic fibres passed through their skull – to trigger movement in the rodent’s whiskers. Subsequent work in mice showed the approach could also be used to investigate which networks of nerve cells were involved in the formation of particular memories, including fear. While rooted in basic science, the team’s work has already had real-world implications, opening up a field of medicine known as optogenetic therapy. In one trial it was used to partially restore the sight of a man who went blind as a result of retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that results in damage to light-sensitive cells in the retina. In that case, the genetic instructions for making a channelrhodopsin were delivered by means of a harmless virus into retinal ganglion cells in the man’s eyes. He was then kitted out with light-stimulating goggles that captured pictures of the world around him and converted them into single-wavelength images that were projected on to his retina using pulses of light. Prof Botond Roska, the director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel who co-led the study, welcomed the announcement of the Nobel laureates. “This is truly wonderful news. I hope this helps to boost all efforts on optogenetic vision restoration to bring back vision to blind patients,” he said.
