Anna Wedell, a professor at Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology or medicine, said the laureates’ work had provided new possibilities to map which cells were responsible for which functions, and which cells communicated with each other, opening up a new understanding of the function of the brain. “We’ve had anatomical maps and correlations, but now we have a tool that can provide cause-and-effect relationships so we can get a functional map of the brain, exactly pinpoint which cells do what, which cells are responsible for creating behaviours or even emotions and memories in the brain,” she said. Wedell said that by studying animals to understand how a normal, healthy brain worked, it was then possible to explore what happened when thing went wrong – for example in the case of diseases such as dementia, epilepsy and addiction. “By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in the mouse, we can also understand where to look in the human,” she said.

headline: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
trail_text: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory
body_text: Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls. The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC. Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans. Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.” The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with. But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died. Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge. “This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century,” Campbell told the Guardian, but she said this was the first study to look at trauma and cause of death while examining human remains from the tombs. Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye. Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage. The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler. “For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.” Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty. Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”. She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.” Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant. “If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said. • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. An earlier version quoted Rose Campbell as saying this was the first study to examine human remains from the Umm el-Qa’ab tombs; to clarify, this is the first study to do so with the purpose of identifying trauma and cause of death.

headline: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?
trail_text: It’s a powerful analogy that captured the popular imagination, but the biological reality is quite different
body_text: Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles. This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce. A second layer sits wrapped around the first, the so-called mammalian brain. It contains the limbic system, deemed to be the seat of our emotions. It enabled mammals to play, care for and nurse their young and communicate in some crude way. The third and final layer, sheathing all of this and making humans in particular a cut above, is the “neomammalian” brain: the eminently rational cortex. This, it was proposed, provides us with our superior intellect, capacity for language and ability to reason. According to MacLean, it helped to keep in check our primitive, lizard-like impulses and rudimentary emotional reactions. Human behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Frayed tempers, impulsive acts and short termism were signs of the lizard brain winning out. The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check. The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way. MacLean conducted dissections of living creatures to try to prove his theory, but the results, and his interpretations of them, have since been largely discredited. For example, it’s now accepted that many reptiles do actually possess the “mammalian” limbic system, while all mammals exhibit “neomammalian” features previously thought to be unique to “higher” ones like us. Alongside these anatomical observations, there’s the behavioural data too, with many “lower” animals good at problem solving, responding and learning via emotion, and communicating in complex ways. As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. For a start, mammals and reptiles split early in evolutionary terms. Whilst it is true that more primitive functions in our brains evolved earlier in the course of life on Earth, this view of three separate brain systems driving our basic instincts, emotions and logic respectively does not stack up.” Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth. In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements. Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain. So, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of? Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true. • Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author of The 21st Century Brain (Torva). Further reading Seven Deadly Sins by Guy Leschziner (William Collins,£20) How Emotions are Made by Lisa Feldman Barrett (Pan, £12.99) Our Brains, Our Selves by Masud Husain (Canongate, £20)

headline: ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity
trail_text: Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore
body_text: To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral. Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west. In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say. To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said. “The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.” While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.” Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.” While professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.” Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.” The results of the community excavations will be published in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.

headline: All of a flutter: how butterflies avoid being a predator’s lunch
trail_text: Their whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from birds, British study finds
body_text: Naturalists have long wondered how brightly coloured butterflies manage to evade the attention of birds that make a meal of other insects. New research from British ecologists suggests it is not simply a matter of good luck but instead a visual illusion created by their fluttering wings. The study by researchers from the universities of Exeter and Essex concluded that the spots and stripes found on many butterfly wings – combined with their dancing flight – scramble a predator’s sense of the insects’ speed and direction. George Hancock, of the University of Exeter’s Centre for Ecology and Conservation in Cornwall, said very few European butterflies were toxic or unpalatable and they were relatively easy to spot in flight, so they needed something special to stay out of harm’s way. “The illusions interfere with the predator’s most basic visual targeting system and disrupt the final ballistic attack,” Hancock said. “As a result, birds and other predators often miss.” Jolyon Troscianko, also of the University of Exeter, said: “Butterfly wings deform as they fly, clapping together on the upstroke and peeling apart on the downstroke, so their stripes shift angle and point in different directions as they flap. “Combined with their unpredictable flight paths, this patterning creates misleading motion illusions, causing a predator to miss entirely or to strike a less vulnerable part of the wing, such as the hindwing or tail.” The experts compared the mechanism to the “barber pole illusion” – the red and white stripes appear to travel upwards even though the pole is only spinning in place. The breakthrough came when Troscianko put a slow-motion video of a butterfly flying upwards through a “bird-vision” computer model. It seemed to indicate – wrongly – that the butterfly was moving downwards. Troscianko said: “First I checked this wasn’t a coding error, that I’d swapped up and down somehow, but then it dawned on me that this would be a perfect way to confuse attacking predators.” The team looked at hundreds of types of European butterflies and found different patterns created different effects. Swallowtail butterflies were found to be among the best at using motion confusion. Troscianko said: “They are also thought to be closest to the ancestral butterflies, suggesting motion confusion might have been around right at the point when butterflies evolved away from night-flying moths. “Swallowtails have little tails trailing from their hindwings that help increase their levels of motion confusion. They are frequently found with their tails missing and beak-shaped holes cut from their wing edges by failed bird attacks. This fits with our modelling that shows how the wing markings should deflect attacks sideways and behind the butterfly’s vital body and inner wing sections.” The team used a high-speed camera to film butterflies taking off to capture how their patterns behave in flight. To test how patterns might affect attacks, 100 human volunteers acted as “predators”, trying to catch virtual butterflies on a touchscreen. They struggled. The study found that largely white butterflies also managed to dodge predators. The researchers believe that when in flight they appear to move more quickly than they actually do because of the stark contrast they make with their background – which may put out the timing of strikes from predators. Troscianko said the discovery could be used to begin to explain how other animals used motion confusion. “We think it is likely to be far more widespread in nature than previously realised, from the flapping wings of birds to the flicking tails of lizards and fish. It opens up an exciting new research avenue.” The study – Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues – is published in the journal Nature.

headline: Can a mushroom make music? Devon exhibition explores ‘cultural world’ of fungi
trail_text: Exeter museum to host DJ’s ‘collaboration’ with woodland fungi and artist’s map of her own body’s mycobiome
body_text: For one of the installations, a musician spent hours in woodland “collaborating” with fungi to create a soundscape inspired by the electricity they emit. Another is a kinetic sculpture of an extinct fungus that honours Beatrix Potter not for her tales of mischievous rabbits but for her lesser-known skills as a mycologist – a fungi expert. These are just two of the exhibits playing starring roles in a rather extraordinary contemporary art show called Living Labyrinths, at the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery (RAMM) in Exeter, aiming to celebrate the “cultural world” of fungi. Lara Goodband, the contemporary art curator at the RAMM, said it had been five years in the making. She suggested the south-west England was a good place to focus on fungi. “We have great weather for it, warm and damp,” Goodband said. “But also, I think people here have a special affinity for fungi.” She said a wide range of people in the south-west were fungi fans, from the ecologists who study the role they play in soil health to the ravers who enjoy the hallucinogenic properties of some mushrooms and the storytellers who work with the fairytale associations of toadstools. RAMM is also an excellent place for this deep dive because of its Victorian collections of fungi. Specimens of stinkhorn and bird’s nest fungi appear alongside the modern pieces. Goodband said interest in fungi had risen sharply over the past few years, partly after the success of Merlin Sheldrake’s book Entangled Life, which argued fungi provided a key understanding to the planet. “I think we’ve hit a moment,” said Goodband. Among the highlights is a sound installation by the musician, composer and DJ Jason Singh, who spent hours hunkered down in two Devon woods, Fingle and Yarner, for his piece, The Intelligence Below. He said he used biofeedback sensors to measure the electricity coming from mycelium – the rootlike networks of fungi – and translated these into sound. Singh said: “So all the notes that you are hearing are translations of voltage being emitted from the living thing. This is music being generated by the living system of the mushroom. “I’m interested in this idea that all living things generate and vibrate. This is a way for us to try to tune into and connect with other living things.” Singh said he did get some odd looks from passersby when he was out in the woods collaborating with fungi. “But it’s magical being in a space recording mushrooms.” Visitors to the exhibition will also be able to see watercolour studies by Beatrix Potter loaned by the Victoria and Albert Museum. Her work was overlooked in her lifetime but is recognised by modern mycologists. Near them is a recent work called In Balance by the artist Jo Pearl based on a fungus called Potteromyces asteroxylicola, named after Potter in 2023 when it was identified in the collections of the Natural History Museum. Another new piece is by Gemma Anderson-Tempini, who worked with scientists from the University of Exeter’s MRC Centre for Medical Mycology to create a map of her own mycobiome, the fungi dwelling within the human body. Like Singh, Anderson-Tempini ventured out into the Devon landscape to gather material for her piece, Myco-Mother, 2026. She collected pieces of red sandstone from Exmouth and chocolate-brown soil from Killerton, which she ground up to create the watercolours she used. Anderson-Tempini believes her work is a first. “Every one of us is carrying a fungal ecology and until now nobody had drawn it,” she said. “Fungi is fashionable but Sheldrake and the rest stayed outside the body in forests and soil. This work turns it inward.” Living Labyrinths opens on 3 October and runs until 21 February. • This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said that Lara Goodband was head curator at the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery; she is contemporary art curator.

headline: ‘Godzilla’ of weight-loss drugs could provide other important health benefits
trail_text: Though not yet approved by any regulatory agency, Retatrutide could help improve blood sugar levels and reduce inflammation
body_text: The ‘Godzilla’ of weight-loss drugs could help improve blood sugar levels, reduce inflammation and cut a person’s body weight by a quarter, according to the largest study of its kind. Retatrutide mimics three key gut hormones that help control appetite, blood sugar and metabolism: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Unlike other drugs such as Wegovy, which primarily targets the GLP-1 pathway to suppress appetite, or Mounjaro, which contains GLP-1 plus GIP to control blood sugar levels, retatrutide also engages the glucagon receptor, which helps increase energy expenditure. The drug has not yet been approved by any regulatory agency. But the results of the global trial in people living with obesity and type 2 diabetes suggest it could help them shift enormous amounts of excess weight while also providing other important health benefits. “Retatrutide demonstrated substantial reduction in body weight alongside glycaemic control and cardiometabolic risk factors, with a safety profile generally similar to other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonist activity,” the researchers said. The findings from the study, funded by retatrutide maker Eli Lilly, were published in the Lancet medical journal and presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 2,047 adults in eight countries: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, India, Mexico, Romania, Spain and the US. Participants had a body mass index (BMI) of 27 or above and type 2 diabetes. 48% were women and 52% were men. Their average age was 55. In the 80-week phase 3 trial, 1,152 were randomly assigned to receive a weekly injection of placebo (289), or retatrutide 4 mg (292), 9 mg (284) or 12 mg (287), alongside dietary counselling and guidance on physical activity. By the end of the study, those on 4mg of retatrutide lost 11.9% of their body weight on average, increasing to 16.8% with 9mg and 18.8% on 12mg. Those in the placebo group lost 5.1%. Among those on the 12 mg dose, almost half (47%) shed at least 20% of their starting weight and almost a third (31%) lost at least 25%. That compared with 6% and 3%, respectively, with placebo. Additionally, 72% achieved an HbA1c (measuring average blood sugar levels for the last two to three months) of 6.5% or lower, a standard threshold used to diagnose type 2 diabetes, compared with 29% in the placebo group. Retatrutide also significantly improved cardiometabolic risk factors, including blood pressure and lipid profiles, and reduced high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), a marker of inflammation, according to the researchers. The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal. Diarrhoea occurred in 27-34% of participants in the retatrutide groups, compared with 13% in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 14-28% of participants on retatrutide, compared with 8% receiving the placebo. Seven deaths occurred during the trial: two in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group and one in the placebo group, and were deemed unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator. Meanwhile, separate research presented at the conference in Milan and published in the Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women’s Health medical journal showed that in most cases, weight-loss drugs are not associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes in women living with type 2 diabetes. But researchers stressed that more research was urgently needed to address the large evidence gaps and to keep pace with the huge and accelerating rise in women of reproductive age using the drugs.

headline: ‘Starship is in orbit’: cheers go up as huge SpaceX rocket circles Earth for first time
trail_text: Mission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attempt
body_text: SpaceX has sent its enormous Starship rocket into Earth’s orbit for the first time on a milestone flight intended to pave the way for future missions to the moon and Mars. The rocket, the largest and most powerful ever built, blasted off from SpaceX’s Starbase launch facility in Texas at 7.48am local time (1.48pm BST), marking its 14th test flight and first attempt to circle the planet before falling back to Earth. Despite an engine failure on ascent that threatened to prevent Starship from reaching orbit, mission controllers decided it was safe to press ahead with a burn that pushed the ship on to a planned trajectory to take it around the planet. Cheers and applause broke out at SpaceX after initial suggestions that the orbit attempt might be abandoned were quashed and the decision to go ahead was announced. Moments after the orbit burn, Daniel Hewitt, an engineer who was narrating a live stream of the launch, declared: “Starship is in orbit.” Elon Musk’s company has flown Starship in its full form since 2023 but previous test flights have only sought to put the rocket into suborbital trajectories, which are simpler and carry fewer risks for the public. For suborbital flights, the trajectory is such that if the rocket explodes or malfunctions mid-flight, the remnants come down in the Indian Ocean far from populated areas. The risks are harder to control when rockets are on full orbital paths around the planet. Starship soared to an altitude of about 171 miles (275km), with the original aim of completing six loops of Earth in nearly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean somewhere west of Chile. More than an hour into the mission however, SpaceX said Starship would come back early, aiming for a landing about three hours after launch in the north Pacific. Martin Barstow, a professor of astrophysics and space science at the University of Leicester, said: “This is an important milestone for SpaceX, with Starship successfully reaching orbit, and at the first attempt.” The achievement “marks the beginning of the transition from the testing and development phase to becoming a working vehicle able to deliver the large payloads needed to return to the moon,” he added. “Congratulations to the whole SpaceX team. Having this large launch capability will also be transformational for the whole space industry.” On the launchpad, the rocket stands more than 120 metres tall, with the Starship upper stage sitting on the “Super Heavy” booster stage. To remain in orbit, the rocket is required to travel at about 28,000km/h (17,400mph). A successful mission will be a relief for SpaceX and Nasa, who hope to use Starship to carry astronauts to the moon as part of a new era of lunar expeditions. It will also cheer investors after the company’s high-profile launch on the stock market in June. The company’s stock price rose sharply in the initial public offering before falling back. It has since recovered some of those losses. During the mission, SpaceX staff watched the booster launch, ascend and separate from the Starship upper stage, then return to an offshore landing point in the Gulf of Mexico. The company did not intend to catch the booster in giant mechanical arms, as it did after a previous test flight in 2024. Engineers modified the rocket’s hardware and software to overcome glitches that emerged during the last test flight. After stage separation, the booster should flip over and fire its engines to send it back to Earth, but on the last test flight the manoeuvre was ended early because three engines started to clog up with ice. The booster then attempted a landing burn with only eight of 13 planned engines reigniting, leading to a hard landing in the water. On the latest test flight, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites. Three carried cameras to capture images of Starship’s heat shield that will feed into testing for future missions. On coming back to Earth, Starship used its four aerodynamic flaps to control its speed and orientation and bellyflop horizontally towards its designated landing zone in the north Pacific. As it approached the water, the ship righted itself and slowed down before erupting in a ball of flames. Musk has set himself the ambitious target of developing fully reusable rockets to speed up mission turnaround times and reduce the costs of future space travel. But several Starship test flights have ended in failure. In March last year, the rocket exploded soon after launch and scattered debris over the Bahamas. Two months later, Starship span out of control shortly after separating from its booster. A month after that, the rocket exploded during preparations for a test flight.

headline: Gene-edited bananas that don’t go brown could hit UK supermarkets
trail_text: Scientific breakthrough could reduce food waste and make it easier to add the fruit to prepackaged food
body_text: It is the bane of every fruit bowl: sliced banana that turns brown before it has reached the table. But such woes could soon be a thing of the past, with gene-edited bananas that keep their freshly peeled colour now one step closer to reaching British shoppers. According to Tropic, the Norwich-based agricultural-biotechnology company that developed the fruit, the bananas have the same taste and texture but stay “fresh, yellow and appetising long after peeling and slicing”. Gilad Gershon, the chief executive of Tropic, said the flesh of the new banana resisted browning for an extra day or two – and longer if chilled. He added that the innovation could make it easier to add bananas to prepackaged products such as fruit salads and breakfast pots, as well as reducing waste. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) last week approved a marketing notice for the bananas, confirming their precision-bred status – one of two important requirements for them to be placed on the market. According to the Food Standards Agency (FSA), precision-bred status is given only if the genetic changes made could have been achieved through traditional breeding methods. This is different from genetic modification because precision-bred organisms do not contain DNA from unrelated species. Prof Cathie Martin, a project leader at the John Innes Centre in Norwich, who has worked on gene-edited tomatoes, said the next stage for all crops that had received marketing approval – including the new bananas – was a review by the FSA to ensure the safety of the products. “It is not entirely clear how long this will take,” she said. Tropic developed the bananas by using a gene-editing technology called Crispr-Cas9 to alter all three copies of a single gene within the fruit. As a result, they were able to reduce the production of polyphenol oxidase, an enzyme that causes browning. A similar approach has been effective in reducing browning in other produce, including mushrooms. Tropic said the non-browning bananas could reduce food waste and CO2-equivalent emissions along the supply chain by more than 25%. “This could support an annual reduction in CO2 emissions of over 9m tonnes in the banana export market alone,” the company said. A government study found that 1.4m edible bananas were thrown away each day. A third of consumers (30%) said they had discarded a banana owing to a minor bruise or black mark on the skin. Gene editing has been used by researchers to develop sweeter-tasting strawberries, disease-resistant crops and tomatoes that are more compact or high in vitamin D. Regulations for precision-bred plants came into effect in November last year and apply only to England. However, the FSA notes precision-bred foods that are authorised and placed on the market in England can be sold in Wales and Scotland, provided they are not processed further, with similar rules for Northern Ireland. No precision-bred organisms have been granted market authorisation for sale in England. Gershon said Tropic had gained regulatory approval for the non-browning bananas in 10 other countries including Japan, Brazil and the Philippines. The fruit is already being grown in Latin America. A Defra spokesperson said: “Precision breeding offers huge potential to boost food security, cut pesticide use, increase crop yields and enhance disease resistance. “[The non-browning banana] is a great example of how innovation could help to reduce food waste and improve the sustainability of our food system while keeping our world-leading standards in place.”

headline: Did you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
trail_text: The solution to the seventeenth century stumper
body_text: Earlier today I set you a puzzle that Isaac Newton posed in 1679 in a latter to Robert Hooke. I mentioned that the answer is counter-intuitive, and also gave you the hint that it might have something to do with figure skating. Here’s the problem again, with its solution. The tower drop An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land? slightly to the west slightly to the east exactly at the bottom Solution 2. slightly to the east. The Earth rotates from west to east. Our first thought might be that the object falls slightly to the west, on the grounds that as the object is falling the Earth will rotate slightly to the east. But such an argument ignores the fact that the object is originally – like the tower itself – rotating with the Earth. Our second thought might be that it lands exactly at the bottom of the tower. Again wrong! The object lands slightly to the east because as it falls it spins about its axis slightly faster, by essentially the same mechanism that makes a spinning ice-skater spin faster when they pull in their arms. It is in this way, then, that the object lands slightly to the east. The effect is small, but not absurdly so. If the Eiffel tower were on the equator the deflection to the east would be about 11cm. In more technical detail, the result follows from conservation of angular momentum, which is a measure of the momentum of an object rotating about an axis. When an object is falling from a tower, gravity is pushing it towards the centre of mass of the Earth. Yet the object is also spinning in a circle around the centre of the Earth. As the object falls its angular momentum stays the same. Which means that the expression wr2 – where w is the object’s angular velocity and r is its distance to the rotational axis (in this case, the centre of the Earth) – stays the same. Since the value of r decreases during the fall, the value of w must increase, which means that the object spins faster. If it spins faster than the Earth is spinning it will land slightly to the east of the position directly underneath the tower. Thanks to David Acheson for today’s puzzle. He is the author of a new book, Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, which among other things explains the background to Newton’s puzzle in more detail. I hope you had fun. I’ll be back in two weeks. Wonders of Motion by David Acheson is on sale at the Guardian Bookshop. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

headline: Can you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
trail_text: The problem that changed the world
body_text: Today’s puzzle played a pivotal role in the birth of classical physics. The tower drop An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land? slightly to the west slightly to the east exactly at the bottom The answer is counter-intuitive. Or, in the words of Isaac Newton, who posed the problem in a letter he wrote to Robert Hooke in 1679, the answer is “quite contrary to ye opinion of ye vulgar.” Some hints. Think about how the spin of the Earth might affect the downwards trajectory. Also think about what happens when a spinning figure skater pulls in their arms. I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solution. PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Instead discuss your favourite seventeenth century scientists. UPDATE: You can read the solution here. Today’s puzzle was suggested by David Acheson, emeritus professor of maths at Oxford and the author of several excellent popular maths books. His latest is Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, a beautifully accessible introduction to the science of motion. Acheson’s book includes more background about the tower drop puzzle. Hooke’s correspondence with Newton rekindled Newton’s interest in gravity and motion, which ultimately led to his formulation of the mathematical foundations of classical physics in the Principia. Wonders of Motion by David Acheson is on sale at the Guardian Bookshop. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

headline: Earth microbes survive simulated conditions of Saturn moon’s ocean
trail_text: Experiment suggests organisms could live in harsh environment under Enceladus’s icy crust, strengthening possibility moon could support life
body_text: From the moment scientists spotted plumes of water erupting from Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, it became the most tantalising place in the solar system to search for life beyond Earth. Now the case is even more compelling after researchers found that organisms that live in deep-sea waters off Japan can survive the harsh conditions expected in the briny ocean that lurks beneath Enceladus’s icy crust. The microbes, which thrive near hydrothermal vents on the seafloor by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, survived in a brine that mimicked the Saturnian moon’s ocean. The work suggests the distant world may be habitable, if not exactly hospitable, to at least some forms of life. “If we use the cellular definition of life that we understand on Earth today, the experiments tell us that if this organism, or something similar to it, was on Enceladus, there’s a good chance it could survive,” said William Orsi, a professor of geomicrobiology at Ludwig-Maximilian University in Munich. Saturn has more moons than any other planet in the solar system, with nearly 300 known to orbit the gas giant. For more than two centuries, Enceladus, a 300-mile-wide ice ball, did not seem particularly remarkable. But that changed with the arrival of robotic spacecraft. Since the 2000s, observations from Nasa’s Cassini probe and, more recently, the James Webb space telescope have revealed gigantic plumes of water vapour and ice grains spewing from Enceladus and evidence for a huge saltwater ocean under its frozen crust. The seafloor is thought to be dotted with hydrothermal vents that warm the water around them. Last year, scientists found organic substances in samples collected by Cassini as it swooped through one of Enceladus’s spectacular plumes. Orsi and his colleagues wanted to see if they could concoct a miniature version of Enceladus’s ocean to study in the laboratory. By combining water with salts and carbonates and adding powdered rock, they recreated not only the extremely alkaline environment of the ocean but also crucial reactions that take place between the water and the rocky seafloor. The rock-water reactions were active enough to start churning out hydrogen, a process that seems to happen in the ocean on Enceladus. It led the researchers to wonder whether Earthly microbes called methanogens, which survive by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, could survive in the solution. “It was a long shot,” said Orsi. To find out, the scientists turned to microbes originally found near deep-sea hydrothermal vents in the Okinawa trough between Japan and Taiwan. Hydrothermal vents are hot springs on the seafloor that release hot, mineral-rich water. Surprisingly, the microbes grew in the simulated ocean despite its pH reaching 11, which is far more alkaline than the organisms’ known limit. The microbes even adapted their metabolism to cope with low concentrations of carbon dioxide in the water. Details are published in Science Advances. David Rothery, a professor of planetary geosciences at the Open University, said that by showing that methanogenesis – the process that sustains the microbes – was possible in the simulated Enceladus ocean, the work “removes another barrier to the viability of microbial life there”. Orsi stressed that if life ever evolved on Enceladus it could be radically different from that on Earth. Even if similar bugs did somehow arise, it is not clear if methane-making microbes would thrive in the moon’s ocean: his experiments lasted only days. “Could they survive for a year? Could they survive for a million years? We don’t know,” Orsi said. In a second paper in the journal, some of the same researchers describe how ice grains in Enceladus’s plumes freeze and fragment in a way that separates the different constituents of the ocean. If ocean droplets contained bits of alien microbes, these might turn up in a small fraction of ice particles but be highly concentrated within them. That would be “great news” for the search for life, said Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary sciences at the Free University of Berlin, who said it would be relatively easy to identify signs of life with today’s technology. The tantalising science around Enceladus has fuelled interest in a return trip. The European Space Agency’s L4 mission aims to combine a Saturn orbiter with an Enceladus lander that would touch down at the moon’s south pole and hunt for biosignatures in the plumes erupting from its ocean. But scientists face a long wait: with a launch proposed for about 2042, it would not reach Saturn until the 2050s. Dr Rachael Hamp, also at the Open University, who has worked on Enceladus’s plumes, said: “It’s fantastic to see new research pushing our understanding further and providing additional evidence for the potential habitability of this little icy world. I think this makes the European Space Agency’s proposed mission to Enceladus even more exciting.”

headline: Spacecraft returns to Earth after rescue mission for ageing Nasa telescope fails
trail_text: Series of in-flight problems meant Link, a ‘commercial space robot’, could not salvage the Nasa observatory
body_text: A spacecraft that was launched in July on a mission to rescue a decaying Nasa space observatory plunged back to Earth on Friday, concluding a failed mission that will be followed by the telescope’s own demise in several weeks’ time. Link, billed as “America’s first commercial space robot”, lifted off on 3 July from Kwajalein Atoll in the South Pacific islands with the objective of lifting the orbit and prolonging the life of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a satellite that has studied gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events for the last 22 years. It got as close as 7 to 9 miles (12km to 15km) to Swift and was able to take a series of images detailing its condition, but a series of earlier in-flight problems that hampered motion control and communications meant Link was unable to capture the observatory as planned and release it at a higher altitude. Katalyst Space Technologies, the company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, which won a $30m Nasa contract for the salvage mission in September 2024, and put together an ambitious rescue plan inside 22 months, announced in a press release Friday morning that its three-armed spacecraft had re-entered Earth’s atmosphere after 85 days in orbit. Without the altitude lift, Swift, a collaboration between Nasa and Penn State University that was launched in November 2004, will follow its own descent in the coming weeks, and is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in November. “From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of Nasa’s astrophysics division, said in a statement. “While we’ll be sad to see Swift’s mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way – advancing US spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit.” Jared Isaacman, Nasa’s administrator, also praised the mission in a statement. “Nasa should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” he said. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future.” Ironically, Swift’s expected lifespan was shortened by the very intense flare-ups from the sun, which it was sent up to observe. Nasa suspended its observations earlier this year and repositioned Swift to try to minimize the atmosphere’s downward drag while preparing the rescue mission. Electronics issues on board Link after launch rendered inactive two of its three reaction wheels required for maneuvering, and at one point the spacecraft went into a deep spin. Communication and control were restored, but mission managers abandoned the rescue effort last month when it became clear there was insufficient fuel left.

headline: DNA database of UK dogs could help police collar criminals
trail_text: Experts working on database that could identify particular breeds involved in crimes, or rule out canine suspects
body_text: From tracking criminals to sniffing out drugs, dogs have long helped police crack cases. Now experts are hoping a database of canine DNA could offer vital leads. While hair, saliva and other canine material may be found at crime scenes, or on individuals connected to incidents, scientists say they are often not fully investigated. Yet such traces could provide valuable clues, from the identity of a canine perpetrator to evidence a dog’s owner was present at a crime scene. “You might have a human case, kidnapping, for example,” said Prof Denise Syndercombe Court, a forensics expert at King’s College London who is leading the work. “Lots of us have dogs. We live with dogs all the time. And so if you can identify canine material associated with a crime like that, then that can be very powerful in being able to provide intelligence to help solve a human case where there’s no other evidence.” As a result, researchers at King’s College London and the Royal Veterinary College have teamed up to harness the potential of canine DNA. It is not without its challenges. “Forensically, we don’t have loads of DNA,” said Syndercombe Court. “You have a few cells that are left at a crime scene … So you’ve got to make something useful out of that.” One approach is similar to that employed in the forensic analysis of human DNA, which is to focus on very small segments called short tandem repeats (STRs). This technique involves looking at the number of times these small segments are repeated in the DNA, resulting in two numbers for each STR – one inherited from each parent. Syndercombe Court noted the set of numbers provided a virtually unique profile – be it for a human or a dog. What is more, in dogs some sets of numbers are more common in some breeds than others. By focusing on STRs the team has built a database covering 80 different breeds – the first of its kind in the UK. For the 10 most common breeds, including labradors, cocker spaniels and miniature schnauzers, samples were taken from at least 50 dogs of each breed. The upshot is that canine DNA from a crime scene can be analysed and the results either compared with those from a particular dog – allowing that animal to be confirmed or ruled out as being linked to a crime – or screened against the database, potentially allowing experts to identify the breed of dog from which it came. The latter could be particularly useful where the dog thought to be linked to a crime is unknown, or where samples cannot be taken from a canine suspect, or where the sample does not match the DNA of a dog under suspicion. Syndercombe Court said her team now hoped to expand their database to include breeds such as pitbull terriers, American XL bullies and Japanese tosas that are banned in the UK. While the STR analysis focuses on DNA from the nucleus of a cell, the team have also created a database using another approach: sequencing DNA from within mitochondria – the tiny structures that power cells. With many mitochondria per cell, this approach can be useful where there is very little material to work with – although it is more limited as this DNA is only passed from mother to offspring. The focus on doggy DNA has already offered insights for police investigations. In one case, the approach shed light on whether serious injuries sustained by a man were down to another person – as he claimed – or occurred when he tripped over his own dogs as they attacked the accused. Forensic analysis supported the latter. “We looked at the T-shirt [of the accused] and there were holes in the T-shirt,” Syndercombe Court said, adding the team also found DNA from two different dogs on the garment. In another case, the DNA analysis shed light on a sheep attack. “We got some decent DNA from the crime scene, and the police thought it was a particular person’s dogs,” said Syndercombe Court. However the DNA from those dogs did not match the DNA recovered from the crime scene. “So we were not only able to exclude his dogs, which were of a particular breed, but also say the breed of dog that [did] this attack was very likely to be [another breed],” said Syndercombe Court. Dr Nicholas Dawnay, an expert in forensics at Liverpool John Moores University – who was not involved in the work – said research assessing how best to use canine DNA collected from crime scenes was hugely important. “Whether it is a dog attacking a human or livestock or wildlife species, the ability to match the individual dog back to the attack is the primary goal. Obtaining breed information at the early stages of an investigation may help narrow down the pool of possible dogs, which is exciting,” he said. But Dawnay said a big challenge remained regarding the funding of canine forensic casework: “Police budgets are stretched and without effective funding, the benefits of this research may struggle to be realised.”

headline: Glimpses into lives of Roman suburbanites in Bath revealed in rare finds
trail_text: Exclusive: Restoration work at Bath Assembly Rooms unearths Roman ditches containing pottery, coins and fragments of a military helmet
body_text: The restoration of a Georgian building in Bath once frequented by Jane Austen has unexpectedly provided a tantalising glimpse into the life of the city’s Roman suburbanites. A network of Roman ditches containing pottery, coins, glassware and a fragment of a military helmet has been found beneath Bath Assembly Rooms in the north of the city. Experts say the finds expand the known extent of Roman occupation in Bath and suggest further remains are likely to lie under neighbouring Georgian buildings and streets. The Roman baths that give the city its modern name are one of the best-preserved ancient sites in northern Europe, attracting more than 1 million visitors a year. Previous archaeological finds have revealed that in Roman times there were suburbs around the baths complex and, further away, comfortable country villas. But relatively little had been found in an area north of the city, partly because the city’s Georgian buildings and streets are so solid – and well protected by conservation laws – that the sort of construction project that might unearth remains rarely takes place. Marek Lewcun, of Wessex Archaeology, said this made it all the more exciting when Roman artefacts were discovered beneath Bath Assembly Rooms. “There was a gap in our knowledge and this helps fill in a missing link,” he said. Lewcun said the finds suggested the residents of this part of Bath were the sort that might live in the outskirts of a modern city: “So we’re probably looking at the ordinary folk that you might find in a modern suburb today, people who had small shops supplying pottery, bread, things like that. “We are looking at people who had gradually integrated with those who had come from all over the Roman empire. Before they arrived we were living in mud huts, more or less. We’ve gone from that to living in buildings that have got roofs, heating, water.” Lewcun said people with more money or status, such as retired military leaders, were probably living further up the hill in villas. “That may have been the equivalent of retiring to somewhere in the sun today.” The archaeologists found almost 60 fragments of Roman pottery, glass vessels, animal bones, roof tiles, Roman coins and a limestone tessera which may once have formed part of a mosaic floor. Among the most intriguing discoveries was a fragment of a Roman military helmet. This is seen as further evidence that military personnel were involved in the construction of the settlement. A slot for a beam was also found, showing that a Roman building had once stood here. Lewcun and the team were helped by the fact that the builders of Bath Assembly Rooms in the late 18th century did not create deep foundations, knowing the thick clay was strong enough to support the structure. It meant the Roman ditches were left untouched for the 21st-century archaeologists to probe. The bath complex was built by the Romans around mineral-rich hot springs after the defeat of the British queen Boudica in AD60 and 61. Known as Aquae Sulis (the waters of the goddess Sulis), it became a place of pilgrimage for people seeking healing in the apparently curative water. Jane Austen lived in Bath in the early 19th century and visited Bath Assembly Rooms, where dancing, coffee-drinking, billiard-playing and gambling took place. Unsurprisingly, beauty products, wig curlers, wine bottles and tobacco pipes from the rooms’ heyday have been found during the restoration project but the Roman remains are regarded as a joyful bonus. Tatjana LeBoff, the National Trust project curator at Bath Assembly Rooms, described the Roman discoveries as significant. “It’s so wonderful to find Roman remains under our Georgian building,” she said. The £20m restoration project includes refurbishing the upper rooms heavily damaged by bombing in the second world war and conserving 10 original Georgian chandeliers. The building is due to reopen next year with a new Georgian visitor experience and a place for 21st-century assembly.

headline: Baby girls’ greater interest in faces offers clue to nature v nurture debate
trail_text: Study finds overall differences between groups of newborns by sex that are likely to be determined by biology
body_text: The question dates back to the first man and woman: how does the world shape the behaviour of the sexes, and what differences, if any, are present at birth? Untangling the contributions of nature versus nurture has proved challenging for scientists, and controversial at times, but a new study of babies sheds light on at least one aspect of the puzzle. When newborns were played side-by-side videos of a face and a toy, girls spent proportionally more time, on average, watching the face than boys did, suggesting that differences in attention may exist when we are born. Because the babies were only a day or so old it is unlikely the effect was driven by culture or social experience. That leaves biological factors such as genetics and exposure to different levels of testosterone in the womb as the leading suspects. “This is a very active and heated debate in the field of sex differences: what are the causes behind sex differences and how early in life are they present?” said Yumnah Khan, a PhD student at the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge. “What our research shows is that at least some differences are present at a small scale very early on in life.” For the study, babies aged from eight hours to three days old watched a laptop while settled on their parent or carer’s lap. The screen showed side-by-side videos with a young woman’s face on one side and a Newton’s cradle toy on the other. An eye tracker monitored where the babies looked as the video played. Both sexes showed more interest in the video of the woman’s face than the clip of the Newton’s cradle swinging back and forth. But the girls favoured the face over the toy more than the boys did. Details are published in the journal Biology of Sex Differences. The findings, based on tests with 130 babies at the Rosie hospital in Cambridge, reveal average differences between groups of boys and girls; they don’t apply to all girls and all boys. There was still plenty of variation and overlap between each sex, the researchers said. Small differences at birth are unlikely to define how children learn and develop, but they may play a role in some long-observed trends. On average, girls learn to talk earlier than boys, for example, and develop certain social skills at a younger age, too. “If they’re showing heightened social interest from birth onwards, that might facilitate the development of these skills,” said Khan, though this is only a hypothesis. Support for the idea could come from further studies that follow the babies until they are toddlers. Another question the Cambridge team is exploring is whether subtle differences between the sexes at birth have any bearing on people’s vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions. For example, autism and ADHD are more commonly diagnosed in males, while anxiety and depression are more common in females. “That’s the root issue that we’re really trying to understand here when we’re asking are there any differences present in males and females early in life and what causes these differences,” Khan said. Previous work has found similar on-average sex differences in brain structure at birth. These are thought to be driven by hormones in the womb, with male foetuses exposed to more than twice the level of testosterone as females in the first and second trimesters.

headline: Is culture alive?
trail_text: From Mozart to Madonna, dim sum to doughnuts, Shakespeare to Sartre – not all forms of life need DNA
body_text: On Mount Athos, in northern Greece, a monk rises before dawn to sing the same office that has been sung on that mountain for more than 1,000 years. He learned it from older monks who came before him, who learned it in turn in an unbroken chain stretching back to Athanasios the Athonite, in AD963. Over the centuries, individual monks have come and gone, and yet their chants, prayers, oaths, costumes and ceremonies endure. This persistence is remarkable and revealing: cultural traditions endure because they share a fundamental property with biological organisms. They are alive. Not metaphorically, but literally. I believe that human culture isn’t just an accidental add-on to organic life; rather, it’s a separate expression of life in its own right. But first we should define our terms. What is life? There isn’t just one answer; indeed, the lack of a clear definition has become a kind of bad joke among life scientists, who can’t quite agree what it is they actually study. One attribute of life that most biologists would say is critical, however, is the encoding, processing and transmission of information. In organic life, this is the function of genes. Information about how to survive and reproduce is written in DNA, processed by cells and transmitted over generations. Thanks to occasional copying errors and the sifting of natural selection, biological information has evolved to produce the extraordinary diversity of life on Earth today. But millions of years ago, a second kind of self-perpetuating information appeared – one that wasn’t written in DNA or read by cells, but which nonetheless began to replicate and propagate itself through time. And it has evolved and diversified to create the stupefying complexity of the modern world. We call it culture. Cultures consist of knowledge or behaviours transmitted from one individual to another through social learning. We used to believe culture was uniquely human, but animals have cultures, too. Chimpanzees from some parts of west Africa use rocks to crack nuts, for example, but in other parts they don’t, even though the same nuts and rocks are available; in some places they strip sticks of their leaves to fish termites from their nests; and elsewhere they use moss as a sponge from which to drink water. Each population has its own particular way of doing things. Our ancestors were apes who presumably had cultures at least as complex as those of chimpanzees. But then, as the Earth moved in and out of a series of ice ages starting about 2.6m years ago, something extraordinary happened. Culture began to overtake genes as the primary force shaping hominin evolution. We became hunter-gatherers – a lifestyle for which we were ill-equipped genetically, but which nevertheless allowed us to thrive thanks to culture. Cultural innovations accumulated in hunter-gatherer groups – how to knap stone tools, track animals, process a root that would otherwise poison us. Where culture led, genes followed. More sophisticated tools and the control of fire allowed us to prepare and cook food, and consequently our jaws, teeth and guts shrank. At the same time, our brains – organs for acquiring, storing and transmitting cultural information – ballooned. Bigger brains were not simply a consequence of culture – they accelerated it. As brains became better at learning from others, they could acquire and preserve ever greater amounts of cultural knowledge. But the big breakthrough came with language. Language is not only a fundamental part of culture; it’s also our most powerful means of transmitting cultural information. Of course, language couldn’t have emerged fully formed. It must have evolved gradually, from a simple form of communication to a more complex one, akin to the languages we speak today. Once even simple language existed, however, everything changed. Knowledge could be explained. Skills could be taught. Techniques could be learned faster, more accurately and with greater fidelity than mere visual copying could allow. Culture went viral. As brains became better adapted to a world in which some information was available in linguistic form, and able to learn more words and phrases, language itself became gradually more complex, and capable of transmitting more complex cultural information. This positive feedback between language, culture and our neurological hardware turned the human brain into a sophisticated device for the acquisition and production of language. Specific words and phrases weren’t hardwired into our brains, of course, but the ability to learn and use them became hardwired. This capability was entirely new, and constituted a crucial turning point in our cultural evolution, as revolutionary and important as the origin of DNA and the genetic code in biological evolution. Culture and languages diversified wildly as humans spread across the planet, while genetic differences between populations remained minimal. Cultural evolution accelerated away, creating different religions, styles of music, art, farming systems and complex civilisations. It led ultimately to the superabundance of human culture today – from Mozart to Madonna; dim sum to doughnuts; from St Peter’s Basilica to the Taj Mahal; Japanese tea ceremonies to Celebrity Traitors; and from heart transplants to the Hubble space telescope. Life on Earth has evolved in two phases: first, biological, then cultural. But we may now be on the verge of the next critical juncture in the history of life. We’re currently witnessing the emergence of a new kind of information that can perpetuate itself – machines capable of writing their own code. A third form of life and mode of evolution may be beginning, in which case this will be the most extraordinary moment in human history to be alive as an observer. What might this mean for our future? And what can we learn from the past in order to prepare for this new phase of life on Earth? • Jonathan Loh is an honorary fellow in the School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex, and the author of Life Story: From Cells to Civilisations and Beyond (Fern Press). Further reading Becoming Human: A Theory of Ontogeny by Michael Tomasello (Harvard, £20.95) The Social Brain: The Psychology of Successful Groups by Tracey Camilleri, Samantha Rockey and Robin Dunbar (Penguin, £11.99) The Selfish Gene by Richard Dawkins (Oxford, £12.99)

headline: The US air force admitted to deploying weapons in space. Don’t expect the White House to explain why
trail_text: The revelation ‘left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal’
body_text: In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good guys, from Captain Kirk and his crew in Star Trek, to Luke Skywalker’s rebel alliance in Star Wars, battle intergalactic villains with an array of colorful lasers and particle-beam cannons, then the bad guys get dispatched in a spectacular, explosive finale. The messaging coming out of the White House on the subject, by contrast, could not be more vague. This week’s attention-grabbing revelation by air force secretary Troy Meink – that the US has deployed some kind of weapons in space – carried nothing in the way of context or detail, and left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal. And, equally importantly, what he intends to do with it. “You can count the words, and the disclosure, on one hand, so there’s not much there to work with, and we really don’t know what kind of weapons he was talking about,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the aerospace security project and a senior fellow in the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said of Meink’s announcement. “The US is looking for another tool to deter what it sees as concerning Russian and Chinese behaviors in space, so my guess is that revealing it has on-orbit weapons would be your way to do that. “[But] that level of detail needed to make this disclosure effective as a deterrent isn’t there. It could just be a building block, and the US is going to lay out more later with that. To me that would make logical sense, if that was the plan.” What the plan actually is has never been made clear, and Meink, in his announcement, stressed it was unlikely ever to be. “Me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else,” he said. But as Russia and China, both US adversaries, have advanced their own aggressive outer space ambitions and agendas, Trump has responded by placing an ever-increasing focus on militarizing the heavens. During his first term of office, he created Space Force, the first new, separate branch of the US military in more than seven decades. Last month, he signed an executive order designating the first US Space Academy, a proposed joint civilian-military institution modeled on the army and navy training academies at West Point and Annapolis, to be sited at an as-yet unnamed location. This week, Military Times reported plans to recruit and train 10,000 new guardians, as Space Force service members are known, to join uniformed ranks within the next five years. Gen Dan Caine, who as chair of the joint chiefs of staff is the country’s most senior military leader, told the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in Maryland this week, that the armed forces including Space Force must be “prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”. Added to a number of other maneuvers and bold pronouncements Trump has made concerning space in recent weeks and months, it is hard not to see the space weapons reveal by Meink – who holds a civilian position reporting to the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – as a further blending of the traditionally separate military and non-military roles of US space policy. In August, the White House unveiled a national space transportation policy that gives Hegseth, as head of the defense department, new responsibility and authority to determine with the chief of Nasa, Jared Isaacman, who manages all US space launches, and sets an ambitious, expansive federal target of more than 1,000 launch and reentry operations by 2030. The president, meanwhile, has made no secret of his desire for US astronauts to beat China and land on the moon before he leaves office in January 2029; and in March laid out plans, arguably rooted more in optimism than expectation, to invest $20bn (£15bn) on a moonbase to secure for the US the first permanent foothold on the lunar surface. Some analysts see an almost sea change in the way the Trump administration has approached space in pursuit of its geopolitical goals, compared to previous presidents who upheld decades of separation between the government’s civilian and military needs. “The way that the US has structured it since Nasa was established in the late 1950s was we have a civil space organization focused on civil exploration, on science, and then we have the Pentagon,” Swope said. He continued: “There seems to be a tendency to pull them together more than we’ve seen in the past [and] the creation of the Space Academy is just another data point that suggests that at least within the eyes of this administration, the missions are very not just complementary, but very, very similar. “The civilian space agency and Pentagon, [it’s] not just that they complement each other, but that they’re essentially doing the same mission.” Certainly, Trump has become more visible in space circles since inviting Isaacman, at the second time of asking, to lead Nasa. Seen as an ally of Elon Musk, the billionaire SpaceX chief and former political acolyte of the president, Isaacman has proven a staunch Trump loyalist in social media posts and in public appearances. It was the “experience of a lifetime”, Isaacman gushed on X, to accompany Trump on Air Force One to the Johnson Space Center in Houston last month, where the academy announcement was staged before rows of Nasa’s civilian astronaut corps bedecked in their blue flight suits. In a separate, lengthier post, Isaacman defended the need for a space academy with military theming, arguing that US ambitions necessitated “a bright new generation educated and prepared for this environment”. He wrote: “If you understand the increasingly important and contested environment above us, then [the academy] is as timely and necessary today as the Space Force has already proven to be.” The argument that the academy blurs the line between peaceful applications in space and the military, he said, “may be the weakest argument I have seen”, before chronicling a succession of previous Nasa missions and operations that were classified and defense department-based, and noting the agency’s early rockets were modified and evolved from military ballistic missiles. “Nasa’s mission is as peaceful as it is patriotic,” he said. “We explore for the benefit of all humankind, but we go there under our flag. That mission would be impossible without the Guardians standing watch over the domain as we venture outward.” Lori Garver, a former deputy administrator of Nasa during the Biden administration, said that while she saw the academy as potentially helpful to the US space program and its future workforce, she was concerned it conflated the agency’s mission for peaceful, civil space exploration with Space Force’s military goals. “Nasa’s charter and legal foundation calls for a civilian agency separate from the military,” she told the science publication Ars Technica. “Structuring a feeder college along the lines of a military academy strikes me as ill-conceived.” Others say it is difficult, or impossible, for the US to remain committed to the 1967 Outer Space treaty that mandated, among other regulations, that all nations use space for peaceful, non-militarized ends when some countries are blatantly defying it. US intelligence agencies said in 2024 they were monitoring the development of a new Russian space weapon with the capability of shooting down satellites in Earth’s orbit. Lt Gen Gregory Gagnon, head of the Space Force combat forces command, told reporters at the Maryland conference that China was “actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space”, which the country has denied. A Space Force “threat fact sheet” details how Russia and China are both “testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities with the intent to disrupt and degrade US space-enabled capabilities”. So, to Swope, the CSIS analyst who worked for the Central Intelligence Agency’s directorate of science and technology for more than a decade, the US’s declaration that it had deployed space weapons of its own was more significant than the absence of detail. “It’s this idea of space superiority, ‘I want to use space, I don’t want my adversary to’,” he said. “That’s just where we are today. “Is more of that happening in space? I don’t think this announcement is determining that, or even accelerating that. It may be more just a recognition that the US has woken up to it, and we may just not know it because it’s not public.” Another question, he said, is what kind of weapons the US may have. “It has talked previously about systems that operate in the electromagnetic spectrum, for jamming or interference with radio signals, that’s what we know publicly about what is in the US counter-space arsenal,” he said. “War is really bad whether it is confined to Earth or orbit, and maybe we need to have a better thought not just on how we could limit specific types of weapons, but that we want to avoid generally. “You can’t just walk into a quote-unquote space war and expect that not to be ugly.”

headline: Tech billionaires trying to live for ever? That’s a waste of time, says physicist
trail_text: Exclusive: Prof Jim Al-Khalili says he will offer solution to ‘arrow of time’ problem in Royal Institution lectures
body_text: Tech billionaires attempting to live for ever are, quite literally, wasting their time, a leading physicist has said. While some normal people are turning to unregulated peptide injections, cold plunges and supplements in an effort to defy ageing, the ultra-rich are aiming for immortality with even more drastic interventions: the tech chief executive Bryan Johnson has even tried injecting plasma from his 17-year-old son – although he later said he saw no benefit from it. Prof Jim Al-Khalili, who will be giving this year’s Royal Institution Christmas lectures on the topic of time, has said people expending their energy on trying to live for ever may be missing out on the here and now. “We have a finite interval of time in which we exist in the universe.
