A recent study highlighted the potential role of a genetic variant that affects receptors in the brain upon which the drugs work. “People carrying the genetic variant, we found lose about an extra 0.76kg (1.6 lbs) on average, and people who carry two copies of the variant double that,” said Adam Auton, vice-president of human genetics at the 23andMe Research Institute, and the senior author of the study. “For people with two copies, this accounts for about 10% of the weight people might expect to lose on these medications.” Umapathysivam and colleagues have recently published a study into two genetic variants that affect the production of an enzyme, known as PAM, that modifies many hormones including GLP-1. The team found people with such variants appear to show resistance to GLP-1. “GLP-1 resistance simply means a given amount of GLP-1 has less effect on the body,” Umapathysivam said. “The implication for treatment is that a certain dose of GLP-1 in someone with resistance might mean less weight loss, less glucose lowering, less insulin secretion or less slowing to the gastric emptying.” Despite emerging research, it is not yet possible to accurately predict who will respond to weight loss jabs and who won’t. But there are reasons for people like Mercedes to be hopeful. A series of promising new drugs are in development. “Another option is to change patients to a non-GLP-1 based drug called Mysimba [the UK brand name for Contrave]. It works in the same parts of the brain, but just slightly differently and therefore may be worth trying,” said Miras. “It is not available in the NHS, just privately.” For some who struggle to lose weight with GLP-1 medications, weight-loss surgery may be the only option left. And, Miras says, “[A] lack of response to GLP-1 based drugs does not predict lack of response to [bariatric] surgery.” And for those who lose little to no weight on GLP-1 medications, the message is clear. “It’s not your fault and it’s not the drug’s fault either, this is purely luck,” said Miras. “I’ve seen it before, it’s not very common, but it does happen.” Mercedes began GLP-1 medications with huge amounts of hope and expectation. “There was just so much publicity around it. So many people [using the drugs said]: ‘Oh, I forgot to eat lunch,’ that I suppose subconsciously I just sort of ignored the prospect that … the drugs didn’t work,” she said. “I wish I knew if there were other people out there, like me, for whom [GLP-1s] are just not effective at all.” *Some names have been changed

headline: Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers
trail_text: Exhibition opens in former home of William Herschel, who discovered Uranus, and his comet-spotting sibling Caroline
body_text: From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries. A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements. The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment. “It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.” One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785. Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said. “That would have been an unusual thing to talk about back then.” In the basement workshop, where William Herschel built his own telescopes, Weir has installed an LED digital counter that records the distance of Uranus from the Earth as it changes. A key element of the show is to make sure Caroline Herschel gets her share of the credit for the pair’s advances in science. William Herschel was a self-taught amateur astronomer who came to Bath from Germany in 1777. His sister followed, initially as a housekeeper. She quickly became his assistant, recording his findings, helping him with calculations, keeping his telescopes in order but then made discoveries of her own, finding eight comets and becoming the first woman in England to be paid as an astronomer. One of the most striking pieces Weir has created is a tribute to Caroline Herschel’s comet-spotting abilities. Called An Imperfect Account, it features a piece of meteorite and a piece of obsidian in the shape of one of Caroline’s worry beads. Weir said: “William had to persuade her mother to let her come to Bath. He recognised her intelligence and once she got here, they were incredibly collaborative. They drove each other along, they understood each other.” The pieces created by Weir are scattered around the house, meaning the visitor has to look for them. Weir said people were losing the art of observing closely. “The Herschels were masters of long looking, something we are losing by scrolling,” she said. Amy Frost, a senior curator at Bath Preservation Trust, said it was the first time in the museum’s history that contemporary site-specific artworks had been integrated. “It’s really exciting for us – it feels like a thread being created through time,” she said. The exhibition, called The As-Yet Unseen (a quote by William Herschel predicting the discovery of the planet Neptune), runs from 5 September until 3 January 2027. A second exhibition studying the work in photography of William’s son, John Herschel, also runs until January. For full details, see here.

headline: Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months
trail_text: Organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the US
body_text: A genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure alive for a record nine months and successfully acted as a “bridge” to a human transplant in a world first. Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list. Kidney transplantation provides the best survival and quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease, but global demand for human organs far exceeds supply. Surgeons in the US successfully transplanted a kidney from Wilma, a Yucatan miniature pig, into Andrews, after genetically engineering it to be compatible with his immune system. The kidney kept Andrews free of dialysis for a record nine months, the longest period ever recorded, before it began failing and he received one from a dead human donor. It was also the first time a pig’s kidney had been used as a temporary “bridge” to a human transplant. Details of the breakthrough, which offers hope to millions of people whose kidneys have failed, were published in the Lancet medical journal. Andrews, from New Hampshire, described the pig kidney transplant as a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” He was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog, Cupcake, he said. Transplanting genetically engineered pig organs has long been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. But the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days when the patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft survival beyond two months, according to the Lancet. Before the transplant in January 2025, Wilma the pig had received 69 edits to her genome. Some of these were designed to dodge viruses that might pose a risk to humans, while others made the organ more compatible with humans, reducing the odds of immune rejection. The team behind the transplant at Mass General Brigham, a non-profit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, said Andrews successfully lived with the genetically edited kidney for 271 days before receiving a human kidney from a donor. His case represents the longest dialysis-free survival following pig kidney xenotransplantation in a living human, and the world’s first transition to human kidney transplantation, the team said. “The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” said Dr Leonardo Riella, of the Center for Transplantation Sciences and the Division of Nephrology at Mass General Brigham. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner. “Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap – initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right.” After roughly six months, damage developed in the pig kidney’s blood vessels which progressed to organ failure and the kidney was removed nine months after transplantation. After several months back on dialysis, Andrews received a kidney from a dead human donor, which worked well during six months of follow-up, according to the Lancet. There were no new antibodies against human tissue detected, indicating the pig kidney had not made it harder for the human kidney transplant to work successfully. No pig viruses or other pig pathogens were detected at any point. The team cautioned that this was a single patient with no comparison group, and that the outcome reflected careful patient selection and intensive specialist care that may not be available elsewhere. Further clinical trials such as the one Andrews participated in will be needed. But the success opens the door to pig kidney transplants as a bridge for other people facing long waits for a human kidney, they said. “The patients are the true pioneers here,” Riella said. “By stepping forward and being willing to participate in these early stage studies, they are advancing the science. Without their trust and courage, we would not be able to do what we do.”

headline: Rich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning study
trail_text: We round up the winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’
body_text: It’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards. Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”. On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners. Economics: evil rich people Are rich people really worse behaved than the rest of us? Through a series of experiments, psychologists amassed evidence that the upper classes are indeed more prone to behaving badly, from being oblivious to other road users, lying at work and taking treats meant for children. “I’ve followed the Ig Nobels since my early college days. I didn’t think I’d ever win one,” said Dr Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine. Piff and his colleagues found that upper-class drivers were more likely to cut other cars off at junctions and ignore pedestrians at crossings. Wealthier people also appeared more willing to lie at work. In one experiment, volunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children. When the researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled nearly twice as many candies as lower-class people. “The general pattern seems to be that with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships,” Piff said. “Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritise one’s own needs over those of others.” Biomechanics: the definition of kissing Researchers at Oxford University ensured the UK could hold its head high after winning the biomechanics prize. “The whole team is thrilled,” said Dr Matilda Brindle. She and her colleagues investigated the evolution of kissing and needed a scientific definition of the act. They settled on “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, infraspecific oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”. Brindle, who is writing a book on non-reproductive sexual behaviour, has also studied the evolution of masturbation, making her a strong contender to become the Marie Curie of Ig Nobels by winning more than once. “We’re so focused on penises, what they do and why they are important, but all these other sexual behaviours are important,” she said. Physics: The splashless urinal A team of students led by Kavee Thurairajah at the University of Waterloo in Canada worked out that urinal splash is almost entirely eradicated if the stream strikes the urinal at less than 30 degrees. They went on to design a urinal whose shape ensures minimal splash regardless of the user’s aim. “I am very proud,” said Dr Zhao Pan, who runs the lab. Peace: The power of mutual enemies It is natural to want friends that are kind to us, but our friends interact with others in the world in ways that can affect our lives. Dr Jaimie Krems at the University of California, Los Angeles, showed there’s plenty of room for attack dogs in our friendship groups, as long as they target those we dislike. “Sometimes we want our friends to be more vicious and indifferent when they interact with our enemies,” she said. “I’ve felt, in many instances, incredibly loved when people have carried my hate for me and been willing to have my back.” Biology: The science of stepping on snakes Researchers in Brazil donned safety boots to explore what made venomous snakes bite in defence by softly stepping on different parts of their bodies. Pressure on the head triggered most bites, they had found, but the study had been retracted by the Scientific Reports journal as the team did not have ethical approval to step on the creatures. Ig notable mentions The chemistry prize went to an international team that found cockroach milk contains three times as much energy as cows’ milk, while the olfaction prize went to scientists who discovered babies smell wonderful to their parents, but teenagers do not. Other researchers landed prizes for turning mosquito proboscises into 3D printing nozzles, clarifying the aerodynamics of nose blowing, and burying underpants to monitor soil quality.

headline: Abundant common fossils don’t need to be protected
trail_text: Letters: Museums have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, says the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre’s Phil Davidson
body_text: The vast majority of the fossils revealed on this rapidly eroding part of the Jurassic Coast hold very little scientific importance and are not in need of protection or recording (Letters, 28 August). Museums around the world have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, thanks to the efforts of fossil collectors, who since the pioneering palaeontologist Mary Anning (1799–1847) have saved fossils from the same process that reveals them, the action of the sea. The majority of these scientifically important fossils are saved from destruction after the winter storms, not during the peak tourist season in the summer. Allowing tourists to collect and take home their discoveries helps them foster a sense of curiosity and encourages an interest in the natural world, which is especially important for future generations. As in any busy tourist destination, there will always be ill-informed tourists. Some visitors have not worked out which rocks to crack open successfully yet, but the next rough sea or storm will wash new fossils out of the mudslides, and if they are not collected they will be damaged and destroyed by the sea. Here at the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre, our educational charity welcomes in excess of 100,000 visitors a year. It is free for all to enter and learn more about the past, present and future of our amazing coast through our award-winning displays of recent fossil finds. We also maintain the west Dorset and Undercliffs Fossil Recording Schemes and have records of over 600 fossils of scientific importance that have been discovered here, many by members of the public. We work with academics, researchers, landowners and the public to deliver ethical collecting guidelines (fossil codes), which are management tools on this part of the world heritage site. Phil Davidson Palaeontologist, Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivors
trail_text: Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizes
body_text: Memory is an imperfect thing: research shows that recollections of single events – a purse being snatched, say – differ from those about repeated or ongoing events, such as incidents of domestic and family violence. “What our research shows is that compared to a single-event witness, a repeated-event witness tends to report more gist-like details, the overall details of what typically would happen, and the things that remain constant between the episodes,” said Helen Paterson, an associate professor in forensic psychology at the University of Sydney. “Sometimes they confuse one episode with another.” Paterson’s work has important implications for victim-survivors of domestic and family violence and how their testimony is received. “If they’re saying this in trial, it’s defence 101 to say … they’ve made this inconsistency, therefore their whole memory is unreliable,” she said. “But we do know what they do report tends to be highly accurate in that it did happen to them. It’s just they might mix up the episode in which it happened.” Paterson’s work has also found that repeated-event witnesses are perceived to be “less honest, less cognitively competent, and less overall credible than the single-event witnesses – which is pretty concerning that the more repeatedly you are victimised, the less credible you appear to others”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor testimony in such cases, Paterson was awarded a prestigious Eureka prize on Thursday night. Established in 1990, the Australian Museum Eureka prizes recognise the work of Australian scientists and science communicators. Paterson was recognised for excellence in forensic science – one of 19 categories – at an event at Sydney town hall. She hopes the award will help elevate the voices of victim-survivors. “Often we don’t give them the support and encouragement, and we don’t believe them and see them as credible as we should.” Also among the winners was Assoc Prof Jane Tiller of Monash University, recognised for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results. Passed into law in April, the ban will come into effect on 8 October. The legal change will enable scientists to use genomics more effectively to prevent conditions such as cancer and heart disease, Tiller said. “The biggest reason that people don’t want this testing is because of fear of insurance discrimination,” she said. The legal change was a “critical barrier that we needed to remove”. “We want to … start finding young people who we know have very high risks of diseases that we can prevent, and give them the screening, the surveillance, the health tools available to them to prevent or treat those diseases early.” Prof Georgina Long, who alongside the late Prof Richard Scolyer was named Australian of the Year in 2024, won the Eureka prize for scientific research, for her pioneering melanoma work. Four other Australians of the Year have previously received Eureka prizes: Prof Tim Flannery, Prof Ian Frazer, Prof Michelle Simmons, and the late Prof Alan Mackay-Sim. Also among Thursday night’s winners were Australia’s marine heatwaves forecasting tool, developed by the CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology; the Women’s Microbiome Innovation Group, a Melbourne-based research collaboration that discovered that bacterial vaginosis is sexually transmitted between partners; and Prof Yansong Shen of the University of New South Wales, who developed a scalable low-cost process to recover valuable metals and silicon from used solar panels. The Australian Museum director and chief executive, Kim McKay, said: “This year’s winners are tackling some of our greatest challenges: protecting our environment, advancing healthcare, informing public policy and inspiring the next generation of scientists. “World-changing discoveries do not happen overnight. They are built on years of dedication, collaboration and sustained investment.” • In Australia, domestic and family violence counselling is available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

headline: Full-blown adulthood: does it actually start at 50?
trail_text: According to a new survey, that’s the age when people feel most confident and in control of their lives. In other words, they no longer have a chairdrobe ...
body_text: Name: 50 (and thriving). Age: You can work this one out. Appearance: Cool, calm and collected. Also, very tidy. Don’t you mean frazzled? Come on, wouldn’t you say you’re more together now than you were at 20, or even 30? Who says I’m not still in my 20s? Why are we comparing ages anyway? A new survey has found that 50 is the age at which Brits feel “most confident and in control of their lives”. And what source do we have to thank for this? British Gas commissioned the survey of 2,000 British adults. Getting the boiler serviced is one way to feel like a grownup, I suppose. The survey found that recycling, putting clothes away and knowing when bin day is were widely-agreed-upon indicators that someone had “got it together”. What’s wrong with a chairdrobe? It’s a perfectly workable system! It’s a pile of clothes, is what it is. Respondents also said that having a litter-free car, spare batteries to hand and washing up after a dinner party, instead of leaving it till the next day, were signs of adulthood. I knew I was right to buy that bulk pack of triple As. It’s when you’ve got a spare CR2032 battery that you know you’re really nailing it. These do seem somewhat low or arbitrary bars for having your life together. Oh, so you want to hold people to owning a car, or buying a house, or becoming a parent? Not in this economy. True. But surely there are more meaningful markers of maturity than making your bed, or drinking two litres of water a day? As if you do either every day. You’re right, though: the top-rated sign you’ve got your life under control was making regular savings. Surely it’s what’s on the inside that counts for adulthood, not what’s in your bank account. The next top indicators were enjoying your own company, admitting when you’re wrong and saying no to things you don’t want to do. OK, those are way tougher than knowing when bin day is. It does get confusing around the bank holidays … You’re telling me that you have to be 50 to be on top of all this? That’s the average age respondents felt most in control of their lives. But 30% said they felt nowhere near being sorted, while 56% thought no one ever really is. Didn’t we only just discover that the brain doesn’t reach adulthood until age 32, anyway? Yes, that was a Cambridge University finding last year, and probably more credible than this consumer research. So, if you think about it, by 50 you’ve only been a grownup for 18 years. Long enough to know to make your bed. Do say: “Actually, drinking two litres of water a day is excessive for most people.” Don’t say: “Is it bin day?”

headline: Canelo Álvarez wins back world title as Houthi attacks cast shadow over Riyadh
trail_text: Canelo Álvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision win over Christian Mbilli in Riyadh despite regional security concerns
body_text: Mexico’s Saúl “Canelo” Álvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision victory over the previously unbeaten Christian Mbilli in Riyadh on Saturday night. The fight went ahead at Kingdom Arena despite a week of heightened security concerns in the Saudi capital, where the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted missiles and drones launched by Iran-aligned Houthi forces. Several events in the kingdom were cancelled or postponed, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition. Álvarez, 36, fighting for the first time in more than a year, relied on his trademark counter-punching and precise body shots to overcome the aggressive French champion and re-establish himself among boxing’s elite. The judges scored the contest 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in favor of the Mexican. (The Guardian had it 117-110.) “It’s something unbelievable. It feels like my first title. Now, after 21 years as a professional, 16 years ago I won my first title. Now I won that title again. I’m so proud of my team,” ‌Canelo said in English. “I love boxing. That’s why I’m here, because I still love boxing and I enjoy it a lot.” Mbilli, who entered the fight with a record of 29 wins and one draw, sought to unsettle Álvarez with relentless pressure and a higher volume of punches. But the challenger landed the cleaner blows, including a sharp uppercut that staggered Mbilli in the seventh round. The victory marked a significant comeback for Álvarez, who suffered only the third defeat of his professional career when Terence Crawford outpointed him by unanimous decision in September 2025. That loss cost Álvarez his undisputed super-middleweight crown, ending his reign as holder of the division’s four major titles. The contest took place three weeks after a missile strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. A second projectile struck a passenger terminal the following day, according to the Saudi-led military coalition, while several international airlines suspended flights to the kingdom amid the mounting threat to civilian aviation. Turki al-Sheikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority and one of boxing’s most influential power brokers, said earlier this month that Álvarez had personally assured him he would go ahead with the fight regardless of the security situation. “Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh wrote on social media. “He fears nothing.” The escalation threatened Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to establish itself as a global destination for major sporting events. The kingdom has become a dominant force in professional boxing under Al-Sheikh, using its considerable financial resources to attract some of the sport’s biggest names, even as its expanding sporting footprint has drawn scrutiny over its human rights record and accusations of sportswashing. Álvarez made a brief, apparently oblique reference to the circumstances surrounding the fight during his post-fight remarks, thanking family members who were watching from afar rather than ringside. “I also want to thank my family, who are watching me from afar today for the first time,” he said in Spanish. “My siblings, my parents, my daughters, my son, and my wife – who also couldn’t make it due to certain circumstances.” Álvarez did not elaborate on those circumstances or explicitly link their absence to the security situation. Mbilli, 31, had been elevated to full WBC champion following Crawford’s departure from the division, having previously held the interim title. The Cameroon-born boxer fought to a split draw against Lester Martínez on the undercard of the Álvarez-Crawford showdown, ending a run of 29 consecutive professional victories. Saturday’s result improved Álvarez’s record to 64 wins, three defeats and two draws and handed Mbilli the first loss of his professional career.

headline: Lewis Hamilton storms to his first Ferrari pole at F1 Mexican GP with Antonelli fourth
trail_text: Lewis Hamilton took pole position at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, his first for Ferrari, while Kimi Antonelli is well placed as he nears title confirmation
byline: Giles Richards at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez
body_text: Even as Formula One’s young gun Kimi Antonelli remains on course to claim his first world championship on Sunday it was the veteran, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton who gave a salutary reminder that there is very much fight left in the old dog yet as he claimed a spectacular pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix. Hamilton delivered a superb lap for Ferrari to secure his first pole for the team and just beat Mercedes’ George Russell into second. World champion in waiting Antonelli was in fourth place but remains in position to close out the title on Sunday, although Hamilton and Russell, who must win the race to have any hope of keeping the fight alive, have at least locked out the front row. It was clearly a hugely emotional moment for Hamilton at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez to finally nail the top spot for Ferrari in his second season with the team, with the 41-year-old’s 105th pole also his first since 2023. “Thank you so much, that’s been such a long time coming,” he said. “That feels good. I’m lost for words. My first pole with Ferrari. 105 poles, I like that number. “Where there’s a will, there’s a way. It’s all in the mind. For sure, you might feel aches and pains, luckily I don’t, I do all those different things to keep myself young and fit. But I love what I do, and love is not gone.” The title is all but in Antonelli’s hands but the day belonged assuredly to Hamilton who brought the crowd to their feet and earned a rapturous reception with an exemplary lap against very tough competition. His advantage over Russell was ultimately just nine-thousandths of a second. It is an extraordinary feat for Hamilton, coming after his debut win for Ferrari in Barcelona and having endured a very difficult opening season with the team, showing that he has lost none of his edge when he has the right machinery beneath him. His sheer joy in the moment was unsurprising given it had been such a long wait for the British driver. The pole is Hamilton’s first since the Hungarian GP in 2023 and Ferrari’s first since Budapest last year. It is only his second in Mexico, having last taken the top spot a decade ago in 2016. He will, of course, be looking for the win but that alone would not be enough to deny Antonelli the crown. The Italian is 123 points ahead of Russell and 124 in front of Hamilton. If he is 100 ahead after the Mexican GP he will take the title. Russell or Hamilton have to win the race to stay in the fight but even should one of them do so, Antonelli will still be champion if he finishes in ninth place or higher. Anything less than a win for Russell or Hamilton and Antonelli would still be champion even if he failed to finish. Having secured fourth place on the grid, just staying out of trouble would surely be enough for the Italian. If he seals it on Sunday he will become F1’s youngest world champion at just 20 years old and the first Italian to claim the crown since Alberto Ascari in 1953. Charles Leclerc was third for Ferrari and Max Verstappen in fourth on track but has a one-place grid penalty for a clash with Liam Lawson in practice on Friday. The New Zealander who finished in eighth also has a one-place penalty. Lando Norris was in sixth for McLaren. For the opening runs in Q3 it was close at the front of the field with no driver holding a clear advantage. The Ferraris set the pace on the opening salvoes, with Leclerc setting a very strong time of 1min 16.647sec. The two Mercedes could not match him, with Antonelli having to really work the car and managing only seventh on his opening run but Norris came close, one-tenth back. Verstappen, however, was showing great pace and came within four-hundredths of a second of Leclerc. For the final laps Russell found his best form of the weekend to take the top spot only for Hamilton to pip him. Leclerc could not better his teammate, while Antonelli followed them through – he improved but could not match the leaders. Verstappen had a minor lockup in the final sector, costing him his shot and with it the British driver had sealed the place. Oscar Piastri was knocked out unusually early for McLaren. Failing to make it out of Q2, he finished in 13th complaining of a lack of rear grip. Esteban Ocon, meanwhile, has denied reports of a violent altercation with his team after the Frenchman was dropped by Haas from competing in the race weekend. Haas made the shock announcement on Saturday morning that Ocon had been replaced for the rest of the weekend by Ryo Hirakawa, but offered no explanation as to why. The 32-year-old Japanese driver, who has won two World Endurance Championships and the Le Mans 24 Hours, will make his F1 race debut on Sunday. Ocon is set to be replaced next season by the Ferrari junior Rafael Câmara and his sudden removal from competition in Mexico suggests relations between him and the team have broken down. He had an angry exchange with his race engineer Laura Müller during FP2 on Friday, after which he returned to the Haas garage without removing his helmet. Reports followed that a disagreement between Ocon and team staff had surfaced. While Ocon admits the disagreement, he rubbished suggestions that the exchange of views turned physical. “Following the recent decision from Haas F1 Team confirming that I will not be participating in this weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix, I wish to formally address some media reports and speculation surrounding the situation,” a statement from Ocon read. “Last night, a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved. Whilst I acknowledge that this took place, I categorically reject any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature. “I strongly condemn violence in all its forms and firmly believe that disagreements should always be handled with professionalism, respect, and mutual understanding. I kindly ask that speculation be avoided while the matter is being addressed. Further updates will be communicated in due course.”

headline: Mitchell injury blow adds to England’s woes as Northampton sink Gloucester
trail_text: Northampton beat Gloucester 28-14 but Alex Mitchell’s injury makes him a doubt for England’s clash with Australia
byline: Gerard Meagher at DPD Stadium at Franklin's Gardens
body_text: England’s injury headaches are mounting before next Sunday’s autumn opener against Australia with the scrum-half Alex Mitchell a major doubt after limping out of Northampton’s hard-fought victory over Gloucester with another hamstring problem. It is to the credit of Northampton that they weathered that setback, withheld Gloucester’s early onslaught to score 28 unanswered points and see off the early-season pace-setters. Northampton’s last league outing here ended with 119 points scored but this was a victory founded on their defensive resilience with Tom Pearson, back in the England picture this autumn, outstanding throughout. If Pearson’s performance will have pleased Borthwick, Mitchell’s withdrawal will not. He is already sweating on the fitness of the Northampton fly-half Fin Smith, who sat in the stands with an injured calf here, and now has concerns over his half-back partner Mitchell. England begin a crucial autumn series against the Wallabies and Borthwick now has significant concerns in two key positions. Mitchell’s injury is all the more of a worry with Archie McParland, his Northampton team-mate and fellow scrum-half, omitted from the matchday squad against Gloucester due to a calf injury sustained earlier in the week at England’s training camp. It would be rough on Mitchell should he miss out considering it is a fourth hamstring injury of the year and his body language when leaving the field does not bode well. He suffered similar injuries during the Six Nations, at an England camp in May – recovering to take his place in the Northampton squad for the Prem final win over Exeter – and during the summer Test against Fiji. Jack van Poortvliet was England’s starting scrum-half for the summer given Mitchell’s lack of game time but when fit and firing the Northampton Saint is England’s first-choice No 9. “Fin and Archie are both calf, Fin probably not as bad as Archie but it remains to be seen,” said Northampton’s director of rugby, Phil Dowson. “Mitchell has hurt his hamstring but I don’t know how bad. We have to be super careful with Alex and he knows his own body.” This was always likely to be an anxious watch for Borthwick given 10 of the players on show were included in England’s mini-training camp earlier in the week. If he finds himself without both Northampton scrum-halves for the Wallabies Test, Ben Spencer would come into the frame with Harry Randall another option. Borthwick also has problems at hooker with Theo Dan going off early in Saracens’ win over Newcastle amid fitness concerns over Bath youngster Kepu Tuipulotu. Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg have already been ruled out of England’s autumn campaign. Mitchell’s withdrawal here came midway through the first half after he was caught by a Gloucester chaser when covering back to gather a loose ball. Northampton were under the pump by this stage – George Skivington’s side beginning in a manner which befitted their lofty league position. They struck first with a well-worked move after eight minutes. Gloucester’s driving maul has been a lethal weapon this season but while Northampton withstood the drive, they had no answer to the visitors’ quick hands. The captain Seb Atkinson, who this week signed a new contract until 2029, put the excellent George Barton through a gap and he offloaded to Max Llewellyn to score. Will Joseph was next over, showing his acceleration to dash under the posts after a clever pass out the back by Atkinson, who impressed throughout. The form of those two is at least solace for Borthwick, all the more so because Atkinson has just recovered from a knee problem. Northampton had not really got going but managed to find parity at the half-time interval. Both tries came from driving mauls, finished by Pearson and Curtis Langdon. Not exactly the type of scores for which Saints are associated but evidently their canny group of coaches had done their homework. Midway through the second half Northampton turned down a straightforward penalty at goal to kick to the corner. It felt a risk given the scrappy nature of this contest but it ultimately paid off with George Hendy eventually splashing over on the left. With a spring in their step, Saints chalked up the bonus-point score after some nifty footwork from the replacement Rory Hutchinson to move into third in the table, sitting pretty as the league now takes a break until December.

headline: Pakistan win tri-series final as Fakhar Zaman century denies Sri Lanka in thrilling chase
trail_text: Pakistan chased down 326 to beat Sri Lanka in an absorbing tri-series final in Lahore
body_text: This mini-tournament has been a welcome change of pace, carrying more meaning than your bog-standard three-match white-ball slog between two teams. And then there’s the gift of a final. This was a fitting conclusion under the lights in a packed-out Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, settled in the penultimate over as Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by three wickets to win the tri-series. Fakhar Zaman, Pakistan’s hero from the 2017 Champions Trophy final, crashed his way to 127 in a chase of 326. But plenty of work remained after his dismissal, and the new boys needed to stay calm. Arafat Minhas, 21, and Hasan Nawaz, 24, played like old-timers, their partnership of 94 securing the game. Minhas and Faheem Ashraf fell with two runs still required, but Shaheen Afridi finished the evening with a wallop over the ropes. Minhas was particularly brutal, middling four sixes on his way to 61 off 31 balls. Pakistan have got something special brewing, Minhas having decimated England with a six-wicket haul at the start of the tri-series. His left-arm spin was expensive here, but he made up for it. With Sri Lanka setting a target for the first time in the series, Kamindu Mendis was the lead pulveriser in the first half, his 131 ultimately in vain. The left-hander had a Bradmanesque Test average a couple of years ago after hitting five hundreds in his first eight matches, but he’s been waiting for a breakthrough knock in white-ball cricket. Seven years on from his ODI debut, he finally has a hundred, more than doubling his previous career-best. He was helped by in-form colleagues, with Avishka Fernando building an opening stand of 87 and the irrepressible Pavan Rathnayake joining Kamindu for a partnership of 146 inside 20 overs. Rathnayake has had a cracking couple of weeks, and his half-century took him to 427 runs in the tri-series at 106.75, two tons against England to go with a healthy strike rate. His 77 left Pakistan looking lost on another flat one, and they relied on Salman Agha’s part-time off-breaks for their first two wickets. With Rathnayake and Kamindu pushing Sri Lanka to 255 after 41 overs, Dasun Shanaka, unrelenting in his side’s remarkable chase of 430 against England, was waiting for the final bash. Yet Shaheen brought his side back, stopping Sri Lanka from going stratospheric. The left-armer went full to dismiss Kamindu and Shanaka; Haris Rauf went short for his two late wickets as Pakistan took six in the last nine overs. “We had to score another 30 runs,” lamented Sri Lanka’s captain, Kusal Mendis. This was a target well within reach, even for a batting lineup bowled out for 110 by Sri Lanka four days earlier. The chase called for a Babar Azam special at his home ground but Pakistan’s most accomplished batter is struggling for runs, now nine innings without a half-century. There was no unconverted start this time, just a thick edge to a wide slip without a run to his name. Rathnayake juggled before desperately holding on. Maaz Sadaqat had already fallen to Dilshan Madushanka after an errant drive, bringing together Fakhar and Saad Baig on 14 for two. Both are freewheeling left-handers at vastly different junctures, one making his way, the other nearing the end. Both clattered the ball at a similar rate, and Baig, hours before his 20th birthday, advanced to his first international half-century off 52 balls. While Baig perished on 74 with a return catch to Maheesh Theekshana, the Sri Lanka spinner dropped Fakhar on 69 and 106. The left-armers kept Sri Lanka alive. Madushanka’s pace snuck past Fakhar’s swinging bat with 106 still required, and Dunith Wellalage’s spin beat Agha’s sweep. The game was even and boundaries were disappearing for more than 10 overs, the drought only broken when Minhas thumped Shanaka through the covers. With 46 needed from 30 balls, a 15-run over off Shanaka turned the game completely Pakistan’s way, Minhas’ power delighting the stands before Shaheen applied the perfect finish.

headline: Australia collapse on final day as Simon Harmer spins South Africa to series win
trail_text: Australia crumbled on the final day of the third Test against South Africa to lose by 176 runs as the hosts claimed a 2-1 series win at Newlands
body_text: At the start of the fifth day in Cape Town, the contest was set up beautifully: 288 for Australia to chase, a day in which to do it, on a surface that had been sporting but allowed batters to flourish when set. A kettle and a cup of tea later, Australia were ripped open by Kagiso Rabada and gobbled up by Simon Harmer, losing two wickets in the first over, four in the first hour and seven by lunch. Two putrid batting displays back to back, their 99 all out in what should have been an easy draw in Gqeberha, then 111 all out here to lose the match, the series and the world No 1 ranking. During one of Australia’s great former humiliations, the 47 all out on this same ground in 2011, one of the piquant notes was that a young Nathan Lyon top scored from No 11. Fifteen years later, having worked his way up one spot in the batting order, he did so again with 33 not out. That bravery through the second session, taking over from Cameron Green to join captain Pat Cummins, who defended for nearly 30 overs, underlines how dire the rest of the side was. The third-highest score was extras with 16. Some credit goes to the opening bowling menace of Rabada for the way things started, but there was scarcely a wound on the day that was not self-inflicted. Don’t get sucked into the idea that Matt Renshaw was unlucky – a nick past the leg stump is no less an error than a nick outside off, and stepping across to the off side before glancing increases the likelihood that your shot finds the keeper. That was ball three of the innings. Ball six was poor, doomed Marnus Labuschagne, in what must be his last Test innings for at least the foreseeable. Barely a delivery has moved off the seam in this match, but Rabada created one while Labuschagne left a ball that he would once have had the confidence to play. Being hit outside the line didn’t dissuade umpire Richard Kettleborough, in his 100th Test, from unholstering one finger, and one last Labuschagne review for old time’s sake showed a yellow umpire’s call light on the timber. Two in an over might have influenced Travis Head to at least temper a game built on playing Russian roulette with a populated catching cordon, but no. Three overs later, having come close to being caught multiple times, he fulfilled his own prophecy by slicing Rabada to Marco Jansen in the gully. Then came Green’s call for a run, though his defensive prod from Harmer had twirled just a few yards past short leg. Josh Inglis is fast, but Marques Ackerman was right there, getting back and twirling to throw: the first-innings century maker, run out for 4. Welcome to the numerology of Test cricket. In Gqeberha, South Africa were 40 for 4 on the first morning before their captain, Temba Bavuma, turned the game. In Cape Town, South Africa were in effect 40 for 4 in the third innings, from which point Australia’s bowlers coughed up two more centuries. Now, Australia themselves were 40 for 4. But fightbacks were the province of the other team. Alex Carey, with premeditated daftness, hit a reverse sweep off Harmer straight to Jansen behind point for 2. Cooper Connolly, a player in this side without a job to do, thought the best move against an off-spinner ragging it away from the left-hander was a big cover drive second ball. Caught behind. Revise that score to 42 for 6. Mitchell Starc hung in, but was caught at bat pad just before the break, and the match was all but over. A strange sequence followed, with Green soaking up bowling from Rabada, and Cummins from Harmer, turning down singles to retain their configuration. Green had looked so uncomfortable against the spinner that it was not clear who was shielding who. When Bavuma got wise and swung Harmer around to the far end, he got Green first ball, the overthinking batter charging down to defend but totally missing one that ragged back from the footmarks to hit off stump. He lasted 110 balls for 27. Harmer had to toil after that, as Cummins was resolute in facing 90 balls and Lyon enterprising in facing 57, but a move around the wicket trapped Cummins on 11 with a beauty that drifted in to pitch in line and hit the back leg, then Josh Hazlewood was no match for a similar piece of sorcery that bowled the left-hander. A shift of 21.1 overs yielded 6 for 16, highlighting the mystery of why Cummins chose at the toss to give Harmer last use of the pitch, rather than hand that to Lyon, who had been brought into the side, and who got far less reward for his work in the third innings. Meanwhile, 3 for 39 took Rabada to 350 wickets, the fastest by almost a thousand deliveries. His astonishing strike rate of 39.6 balls per wicket is in its own stratosphere: most of the game’s prolific bowlers are in the 50s or 60s. The most wickets at a lower strike rate is 112 from George Lohmann, and that guy debuted in 1886. South Africa are already the reigning world champions, but they’ve spent the last month proving how many champions are in their team.

headline: Fallon Sherrock pulls off shock defeat of world darts No 1 Luke Littler in live TV battle
trail_text: The 15th amateur to challenge Littler in Netflix stream on Friday evening, Sherrock was ‘lost for words’ after winning £501,000 prize
body_text: The name of the programme was Beat Luke Littler and Fallon Sherrock did just that. On one of the biggest nights of the year for British TV and Netflix, there was much at stake: not just £501,000 to any of the 20 amateur challengers who managed to beat Littler in a single leg of darts, but also the jeopardy of whether audiences would choose to watch the streamer’s first UK live entertainment event – or the final of BBC juggernaut The Celebrity Traitors. Netflix also had no idea when or whether the world champion would be beaten at the packed event at Manchester Central arena, hosted by Gary Lineker and Richard Osman, so had put in place contingency plans to have a second place competition should Littler lose within the first few rounds. However, watched by hundreds of his fans, “the Nuke” comfortably beat a range of contestants of differing abilities who had queued up to take part in heats during the summer, including 14-year-olds Mackinley Cooper-Johnson and Jayden Walker. Cheered on by enthusiastic crowds in fancy dress, one contender, the former Irish youth darts player Pearse Mackle, came close to claiming the lucrative prize. But in the end it took about two and a half hours for Littler to lose, to the 15th contender, Sherrock. There was some controversy when it was revealed this month that she was competing: after all, she has an MBE for services to darts, and some people claimed she was not a true amateur, having played at the PDC World Darts Championship and won the inaugural Women’s World Matchplay in 2022. But Netflix classed anyone who has not ever had a PDC tour card as being eligible to take part. “I mean, it’s been tough,” Sherrock said after her victory in Manchester. “Obviously I do see the backlash and I do see all the negative comments. But at the end of the day, I fit the criteria for this. I’ve never had a tour card, and I wouldn’t class myself as a pro really, because all I do is just play darts for the enjoyment of it.” The PDC president, Barry Hearn, who was involved in the audition process, defended the contest. Asked whether Sherrock’s inclusion was unfair, Hearn said: “No, not at all. She’s not a PDC tour card holder. She’s entitled to enter. Why should she be denied?” Despite her experience it was still a shock to the crowd that Sherrock defeated Littler. “I can’t put into words how much this means,” she told Lineker after her win, which was greeted by huge cheers from the delighted audience and a hug from her young son. “I’m really lost for words right now. It was a great moment. Give me an opportunity and I’ll take it every time … I’m really proud of myself.” Littler, a magnanimous loser, said Sherrock had been “world class. I’ve enjoyed every bit of it … everything leading up to this. Maybe, Netflix, we can do it again next year.” Beat Luke Littler was undoubtedly a risk for the streamer but it looks to have paid off as sources said audience numbers stayed steady (they could vote for the order the players appeared in) despite competition from The Celebrity Traitors, and appeared to rise after the end of the BBC show. The show, dreamed up by the Manchester-based production company Workerbee, brings more working-class audiences to the streamer and helps its drive to air more live mainstream events. It echoes similar events in other sports pitting ordinary people against the elite, such as the Million Dollar 1 Point Slam at the Australian Open tennis tournament. Workerbee’s managing director, Michelle Chappell, told the Guardian: “Rick Murray, our CEO, came up with the idea, which was just: ‘Wouldn’t it be amazing if someone could take on Luke Littler.’ It’s a sport event but a big show at the same time and it’s got a sense of humour and real jeopardy.” There was one winner guaranteed, though, in the battle between Beat Luke Littler and The Celebrity Traitors, and that was the global production company Banijay which owns the companies that make the two shows.

headline: Reece Walsh fires clunky Australia to Rugby League World Cup win against Cook Islands
trail_text: The Kangaroos top Pool A with a 66-6 victory in their historic clash in Townsville as Tom Trbojevic scores a second hat-trick in as many games
body_text: Reece Walsh showed if there was anything James Tedesco could do, he can do better with a starring role for the Kangaroos in a partly clunky but otherwise entertaining victory over the Cook Islands in Townsville. Coach Kevin Walters faces a choice between the two brilliant No 1s for the much-anticipated semi-final against either Samoa or Tonga next week, but this only sometimes convincing display showed there is still work to do in camp Kangaroo. It was not quite a horror show on Halloween, given the way Australia improved after the break. But 15 errors will only amplify concerns the Kangaroos – despite their three victories in the tournament and Saturday’s hat-tricks to wingers Tom Trbojevic and Jack Bostock – are still shy of their best. Walsh was the standout with one try, five try assists as well as a hand in another. He shrugged off ankle and shoulder complaints in the second half to spearhead a series of free-flowing attacking forays. The combinations in what appears to be Australia’s first-choice spine of Harry Grant, Tom Dearden, Cam Munster and Grant improved as the match wore on, and were capped off by a late try for Grant off an inside ball from Walsh. A six-try blitz in the first 20 minutes after half-time had earlier ended the contest, though the valiant Cook Islanders were unlucky not to score a second try in the final minutes. Two hours beforehand, the match could hardly have started worse for the underdogs. The Kangaroos’ first kick was fumbled under pressure by winger Cameron Brown, and Australia scored in the ensuing set. It was thanks to an incisive contribution for Walsh, who drew in the right winger Esan Masters then lofted a pass to put Bostock over in the corner untouched. But Australia’s inconsistency has been a feature of this tournament, and it was obvious again after 10 minutes. Grant got caught up with Masters when he was chasing a kick, and the Cook Islands had a set 10m from the Australian line. A dummy from hooker Rua Ngatikaura was enough to fool markers Pat Carrigan and Liam Martin, and a converted try put the Cook Islands ahead. The mistake was compounded when Walsh kicked out on the full from the kick-off, and then Tom Dearden gave up another set with a ruck penalty, but an inexplicable second tackle kick let the hosts off the hook. An error from a wayward Grant pass suddenly brought the Cook Islanders back to the Australian line, but a second poor kicking option let them down. Former Kangaroo Val Holmes was at fullback for the Cook Islands, representing the country of his mother’s birth. Prop Davvy Moale and captain and centre KL Iro were other NRL-calibre players in the side, as well as 20-year-old Warriors’ five-eighth Maui Winitana-Patelesio. The depth was lacking, however, and the side relied on former Eel, 37-year-old Brad Takairangi, at halfback fresh off a season with the Glebe Dirty Reds. To his credit, he looked a player 10 years his junior, with one tackle on Trbojevic flattening the Australian winger. The gulf in class was obvious when the Kangaroos regained the lead with a simple blind side raid down the right, as Trbojevic finished interplay from Grant and Dearden. A Holmes error handed the ball back almost immediately, and the Kangaroos had their third try when Tino Fa’asuamaleaui crashed over. Cam Murray had been named on the bench, but was ill at Friday’s captain run and was replaced by David Fifita. Murray suffered a head knock last week against Fiji, but returned to finish the match and was one of Australia’s better forwards. There had been criticism levelled at the pack over the past two weeks, but Fa’asuamaleaui, Pat Carrigan and lock Isaah Yeo looked predictably comfortable against lesser opposition. Back rower Jacob Preston, whose CV is perhaps the shortest of any among the starters, appeared eager to show Walters that he – rather than Fifita – was worthy of the Kangaroos No 11 jersey with strong running. His first line break led directly to another try, when Dearden found Kotoni Staggs out wide. Preston repeated the feat with seven minutes to go, putting Walsh over this time for Australia’s sixth try. He would get his own midway through the second half. Next week’s semi-final loomed large when Trbojevic and Munster suffered minor ankle injuries, even if both shook them off. But injuries could not be blamed for an ongoing clunkiness in the Kangaroos’ play. The first half ended 28-6, but the Cook Islands almost had a second in a late siege resisted by stout Australian defence. Canberra five-eighth Ethan Strange came on for his first appearance in green and gold in the second half. From his first play the ball Bostock went in for his second try. Again it was Walsh who made the critical contribution, batting the ball on to avoid the jamming defence. For Trbojevic’s second minutes later, it was Walsh once more with the final pass. Those two combined shortly after for Trbojevic’s second hat-trick in two weeks, before Bostock bagged his own triple. But their try-scoring feats will be forgotten when the tournament really begins at Allianz Stadium next Sunday.

headline: He was one of the NFL’s most feared runners. Now Larry Johnson fears what football did to his brain
trail_text: Once among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting toll
body_text: In his heyday, Larry Johnson was the NFL tailback you’d least want to line up against, the steamroller in pads who had defensive players and coaches questioning their life choices on every down. But since Johnson walked away from pro football in 2011, after seven seasons in the league and an All-Pro run with the Kansas City Chiefs, he’s the one doing the soul-searching, grappling with the toll all that gridiron glory has taken on his brain. Johnson, who still cuts a fit and formidable figure at age 46, can scarcely recall his glittering career, much less its highlights. “I go up to maybe 2006, 2007,” he tells me. “Anything before or three years after, I really don’t remember.” When Johnson was thriving as a pro in the mid 2000s, chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, was not yet widely recognized as a risk of playing football. The NFL, however, had evidence that head injuries could cause lasting neurological damage, yet spent much of the decade publicly disputing the link as former players sought disability benefits for neurological problems – and were largely denied. It wasn’t until Will Smith starred in the movie Concussion as Bennett Omalu – the forensic pathologist who sounded the alarm on CTE in American football players after examining the brain of Mike Webster, the Hall of Fame center who died in 2002 after years of cognitive decline and a range of behavioral problems – that Johnson began joining the dots between football and his own personality swings. Johnson has long suspected he suffers from CTE, even though the disease can only be diagnosed after death. A study published on Wednesday of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 found that 74.5% had CTE. Of the nearly 400 players whose brains were donated for postmortem examination, 93.5% showed evidence of the disease. Johnson’s NFL career was defined by physical punishment, and he was a violent runner who welcomed the blows. Ahead of the 2003 draft, Johnson seemed like everything a team could want in a franchise running back. He had size (6ft 1in, 230 lbs) and speed (4.45s 40-yard dash). He capped a four-year career at Penn State by sweeping the Doak Walker Award for the nation’s best running back and the Maxwell and Walter Camp awards for the nation’s best player after rushing for more than 2,000 yards on fewer carries than anyone in history. He had backing from Joe Paterno, when that still meant something, and more hands-on guidance from his father, Larry Johnson Sr – the former Nittany Lions defensive assistant who’s now Ohio State’s associate head coach. But when the Chiefs selected Johnson 27th overall as insurance for franchise running back Priest Holmes, they did so over the objections of head coach Dick Vermeil, who had watched a parade of Penn State runners disappoint in the pros and figured Johnson would be no different. Vermeil singled out Johnson’s preparation habits and maturity, joking that he needed to “take the diapers off”. But Vermeil had to eat his words after Holmes went down with a season-ending neck injury midway through the 2005 season and Johnson stepped in to rack up 1,750 yards and 20 touchdowns in nine weeks. (“Well, he’s a talent,” the coach conceded later.) The following season Vermeil retired and Herm Edwards took over, and the bombastic defensive guru made Johnson the centerpiece of the Chiefs offense. He ran for 1,789 yards on a whopping 416 carries – an NFL record that isn’t likely to be threatened in the current era of pass-happy offense and running by committee. Whenever Johnson publicly shares his CTE fears, fans often find themselves looking back at the season for answers. Was that the beginning? Too many blows? “People forget: I didn’t get hurt during those 416 carries,” he says. “I didn’t really start until 2006. I was in the league for three years – maybe the only first-round pick battling just to dress. If Herm had told me straight up, ‘I’m gonna run you 416 times.’ I would’ve been like, Why can’t we do 500?” Johnson reveled in his star status, famously signing on as an ambassador for Jay-Z’s Roc-A-Fella record label as it was growing into a lifestyle brand. The Chiefs workhorse was frequently spotted partying with LeBron James and other members of Jay-Z’s inner circle at the rapper mogul’s bygone 40/40 Club in New York, helping get Jay-Z in the door with the NFL and paving the way for his later relationship with the league office and commissioner Roger Goodell. Johnson celebrated touchdowns by tenting his hands into a diamond, a gesture popularized by Jay-Z and his associates known as “throwing up the Roc”. But the southern Maryland native never quite cottoned to the scrutiny that came with the spotlight. He was slammed in the press for demanding a trade and threatening to sit out as leverage for a new contract. He clashed with Chiefs coach Todd Haley – questioning his credentials to succeed Edwards – and disparaged fans and media with homophobic slurs, prompting suspensions before he was eventually released by the team. Johnson drew more troubling headlines for his alleged assaults on women: a Kansas City nightclub patron accused him of spitting a drink in her face, and an ex-girlfriend accused him of beating and strangling her at the Bellagio in Las Vegas. Between 2003 and 2012, he was arrested five times in cases involving allegations of violence against women – resulting in convictions for disturbing the peace, domestic battery and assault, with penalties that stopped short of jail time. Johnson shies from blaming football for those incidents, but it’s hard not to wonder what the game left behind in a man so handsomely rewarded for violence – or how much the game messed with his head. Johnson began playing tackle football at age nine, taking helmet-to-helmet hits long before he reached the NFL. Life after football was deeply unsettling for Johnson. “I couldn’t find anything that really will test your manhood and also test your character like football,” he says. “I enjoyed lining up eight in a box and then trying to get five or 10 yards – and then I’m getting 50. As twisted as it may sound, the thing I wanted to do was to die on the football field. I always felt like I had to go to war, like I had to fight even when I don’t have to fight.” He had hoped to transition into nonprofit work, but found the 9-to-5 office environment stifling. A hair-trigger sensitivity to light, noise and group settings made it impossible for him to hold down a job. He fought with the mother of his young daughter, Jaylen, over school pickup schedules; during a two-year court fight, with Johnson’s own mother acting as a go-between, he finally realized he was the one misremembering the times. He enrolled in a master’s program with a cohort of NFL retirees, but says he quit after flipping out on a professor during a group project. All the while, Johnson wrestled with intrusive thoughts and inner voices telling him to harm himself and others. The voices come in waves, he says, “almost like a suggestion. Certain things scare me. I can’t be close to balconies anymore. If I’m walking, I’ll think, What if something falls out of the sky? Just a constant state of paranoia.” To cope, he isolated himself for long stretches and self-medicated with drugs and alcohol – making matters far worse. Johnson’s father had little idea of his son’s quiet suffering until the ex-Chiefs star went public in a 2017 Washington Post profile. Johnson feared that his father might not understand or relate to what he was going through; he went from checking in with his dad for any reason, even if it was just to say he was heading home after a game, to pulling away from his great mentor. The Post article, though, “gave my father new eyes,” Johnson says. “People would tell him, ‘That’s a really good thing your son did.’ I think that made him a little bit more accepting. [Now] we’re back to our relationship – as if I’m still in the house, you know?” Johnson had another major breakthrough around the same time, when the NFL granted him lifetime disability benefits, giving him the financial security to focus on his health without worrying about making ends meet. In a league infamous for publicly denying former players’ claims and using race-norming to limit disability payouts (disputes that were ostensibly addressed in a revised league settlement), that victory shouldn’t be taken lightly. Johnson knows how fortunate he was to last seven years in a league where the average running back’s career is around 2½ years, leaving little time to build a safety net. He believes the modern trend of devaluing running backs only serves a league that’s “trying to lessen payments.” Johnson’s daily life is still punctuated by bouts of confusion. Light and noise still bother him, and he gets irritated anytime he hears himself slurring words or otherwise struggling to put sentences together. But Johnson has better ways of coping. Jaylen is old enough to drive herself – and her dad – around now, sparing him the embarrassment of getting lost on routine trips or confusing the TV remote for a car key fob. Johnson spends a lot of time talking through his feelings with his wife, who knows when to prod and when to leave him be. All of it helps keep the voices at bay, but he still hears them. He likens the intrusive thoughts to a movie. “Yours might last for a scene,” he says. “Mine is like a sequel. Then there’s part three and hidden features. It’s like Marvel at the end of the movie. It engulfs me.” Social media tends to be where Johnson gets in trouble these days, courting controversy with conspiracy theories about Jews, Kobe Bryant’s death and Jay-Z, with whom he has since fallen out. Away from the online fray, though, Johnson keeps a cool head in group chats with former teammates, even as it frustrates him that his peers never want to talk about what they’re really going through. “All they’re talking about is each other’s birthdays and going out and drinking,” he says. “We are in an era where if you admit you were hurt, you’re soft – you know what I mean?” His new dream is to create an app that connects former pros struggling with their mental health with people who understand what they’re going through – former NFL clinicians like Susan Wilson, his team therapist at the Chiefs. “I would love to be able to have a symposium for retired guys,” Johnson says, “so they can hear not only the horror stories, but share their similar histories of how to deal with mental health. It’s been too hush-hush and taboo for such a long time because guys are embarrassed.” CTE researchers are always keen to build relationships with former players, too. Last month, Emory University announced a partnership with the Concussion & CTE Foundation and Boston University on a medical study of former football players experiencing depressive and cognitive symptoms. The study is testing whether an FDA-approved drug that reduces inflammation can also improve those symptoms, recruiting men aged 30–55 in the Atlanta area who have played at least 11 years of tackle football. Whether researchers are any closer to diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients remains an open question. “CTE is both a complex physiological and psychological issue,” says Concussion & CTE Foundation co-founder Chris Nowinski, a longtime advocate. “Learning you have CTE can have a positive mental impact for some, and a negative one for others. That’s why it’s critical to have a multi-pronged approach advancing diagnosis, treatment and mental health support.” Johnson tries not to let his emotions get the better of him when watching football now. He appreciates the safety measures the league has introduced to protect players, but laments what they’ve taken away from the physical brand of football he once defined. It broke the ex-Chief’s heart to see his former AFC rival Chris Johnson opening up about his ALS battle. “To watch these players who could basically run 4.5, 4.4 40s be in wheelchairs, like, that haunts me,” he says. “If this could happen to Chris Johnson or Steve Gleason, it can happen to any of us, right?” In an effort to keep tabs on his own neurological condition, Johnson has taken to posting videos of himself on social media and scrutinizing them for signs of decline – the ultimate mental health self-scout. Early replies describing his delivery as “mean” or “condescending” helped him modulate his behavior and even led to some online friendships. With a firmer handle on his general well-being, Johnson thinks differently about being tested for CTE now, while he’s alive. “When I first said that, it was like, yeah, I would want to know,” he says. “But at the end of the day, I know I would obsess over it. I would be paying attention to every little micro movement and emotion. I would drive myself crazy thinking I don’t have much time, so let me act out. If there was a way we could figure out before then, at least I would know the damage. Whether I know it or whether I can feel it, I know something is there.”

headline: Adil Rashid’s exile cost England but they can right tactical wrongs in Australia
trail_text: The leg-spinner’s absence in the final three games of their tri-series against Pakistan and Sri Lanka was puzzling but there’s no need to panic just yet
body_text: In the end, the beginning was just a little too perfect. When Gus Atkinson struck with the first ball of England’s tour, the rhythm appeared set. They intended to make it four ODI series wins in a row. Sri Lanka had been beaten home and away this year; Pakistan had been embarrassed with the Dukes ball in the summer. Harry Brook’s side were surely heading to the final, right? Alas, he won’t be anywhere near the snappily named KFC Presents Bank Alfalah ODI Tri-Series trophy on Saturday. On two occasions England moved into positions from which games seemed unlosable, yet this thoroughly watchable tri-series refused to turn their way. In making 429 against Sri Lanka, England simply followed their usual formula: thrash their way to a gargantuan total and let scoreboard pressure do the rest. Even as Pavan Rathnayake and Dasun Shanaka swung away, it felt as if England would be fine as long as they produced a three-over period of quiet, forcing the pair to knock it around for ones and twos while the required rate climbed to something ungodly. But it never came as Brook became the first man to finish on the losing side after an ODI double hundred. Three days later Pakistan were 154 for nine chasing 242, with England needing just one small piece of magic. Atkinson thought he had produced it with a yorker that struck Shadab Khan’s pad, with the batter unaware his blade had given the ball a faint tickle on the way. A squiggle on UltraEdge would resurrect the hosts and push the visitors to an ultimately fatal defeat. What jarred, as it did against Sri Lanka, was Adil Rashid’s absence. No one has played more ODIs for England in the last decade than the leg-spinner, who missed the end of the summer with a hand injury. He twirled expensively in the opening game against Pakistan and was subsequently discarded for the next three. Brendon McCullum said that “conditions probably went against” the selection of Rashid, as England favoured the skiddier option of Liam Dawson’s left-arm spin, presumably hoping Dawson would replicate the success of Pakistan’s Arafat Minhas. Yet Rashid’s great value to England since 2015 has been his excellence across continents, conditions be damned. There’s the googly to use if the leg-break isn’t perfect; there are revs through the air if the pitch isn’t helping. While Dawson’s selection did work, with seven wickets at 21.42 and a tight economy rate of five, could he not have played alongside Rashid? The pair have excelled together as the leading wicket-takers in the T20 side over the last 18 months, thriving under Brook’s captaincy, with that group topping the world rankings. It’s surely worth a go next month for three ODIs in Australia, where Rashid has a strong 50-over record and the happy memories of a T20 World Cup win. Sam Curran could also benefit from a trip to Australia, where he was player of the tournament in that World Cup triumph four years ago, taking 13 wickets at 11.38. The left-armer, returning after groin surgery, conceded 103 runs in the historic loss to Sri Lanka, and remains a bit of a mystery eight years after his international debut. Curran started his career as a bowler who could hit the ball sweetly, but he’s been playing in this ODI side as a middle-order batter who doesn’t have to bowl a full allocation, a role Ben Stokes once had. It’s with the bat where he has to really shine. While there were starts in Pakistan, he could do with a statement score, having failed to reach fifty since returning to the 50-over setup a year ago. England shouldn’t get too down about their fortnight in Pakistan. Smashing 400 has become their party trick, the opening partnership has clicked and Brook is mesmerising. Their one chase on this trip crumbled a little too quickly, but the batting looks generally healthy and there is a welcome problem in how to fit Jacob Bethell back into the XI. Tom Banton taking the gloves and Bethell replacing Jordan Cox in the middle order is a potential option. Jofra Archer will return in Australia after a period of rest, his importance growing with each passing game. It would be handy to see him pair up with Josh Tongue, who has had a tough start to his ODI career but still has a spark to him – the ability to open up a game when it seems done. He very nearly brought England back into it when Sri Lanka chased 430, hitting the stumps with back-to-back balls in the final over. England have missed out on a final, which would have been a useful test and an extra game before next year’s World Cup, but upcoming series in Australia and South Africa should help with the homework. There’s no need to panic just yet.

headline: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself puts ‘confronting’ matter behind her to win return race
trail_text: Joanna Wietrzyk claims victory in first event of season in Hamburg after saying in a pre-race social media video that she is ‘truly so sorry’ for events in Beijing
body_text: The Australian athlete who sparked outrage when winning a Hyrox event in Beijing despite soiling herself during the race has returned in style with victory in the first event of the new season in Hamburg. Joanna Wietrzyk won the endurance sports event in China last month but forfeited the points and soon faced a stinging public backlash as footage of her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment with faecal matter running down her legs went viral on social media. The 24-year-old posted a statement on social media with an apology in the aftermath of the incident before stepping away from the public eye. The Melbourne-born athlete returned to speak on a pre-race video this week where she said she was “truly, truly so sorry to everyone that I affected”. Wietrzyk, the world record-holder in the Hyrox women’s solo event, added the attention that had stained her reputation had been “very hard” and “very confronting” to deal with before she put the storm behind her to win the Hyrox event on her comeback to competition on Friday. “I’ve had some time to reflect over the past six to eight weeks of everything that happened in Beijing and firstly I want to say that I’m truly, truly so sorry to everyone that I affected whether they were spectators or participants out on that race floor, for my decision to choose to continue to race,” Wietrzyk said in a post on Instagram. “Having that time to reflect, I’ve really learnt a lot from the situation and I am very, very sorry for it all.” She added: “It has been a very hard situation to navigate for me and very confronting as well, so all the support, whether it was personally or through my team has been honestly so incredible and it goes a far longer way than I can truly express right now. “I’m super excited to go back to doing what I love.” Hyrox is an increasingly popular fitness competition that sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
