The competition launched in Germany in 2017 and is now held in locations across the world with the 2026-27 season to include races in London, Bangkok, Las Vegas and Lyon after the opener in Hamburg. Wietrzyk took an early lead in the Elite 15 competition when winning the fitness event in Hamburg in 56:10.21 ahead of American pair Lauren Weeks (56:24.37) and Vivian Tafuto (57:55.34). Hyrox apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after Wietrzyk was allowed to finish and win the Beijing race in September even as she suffered from a bout of diarrhoea. Co-founder Moritz Fürste said after the event that organisers “made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race”. New rules have since been introduced to give race organisers the power to remove an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers”. Rules were already in place to penalise athletes for minor infractions such as littering on the course, or spitting or clearing their nose on the floor. Wietrzyk was subjected to vitriol when her identity was shared online following the incident in Beijing, prompting Hyrox organisers to warn that anyone sending abuse or threats of violence towards the athlete would be banned from future events.

headline: Red Roses put defeats behind them by crushing USA to extend 35-year streak
trail_text: England bounced back after two defeats against Canada with a comprehensive 55-12 win over USA in their WXV game in New Jersey
body_text: England have seen a lot of records crumble around them in this WXV Global Series but the world champions were not going to let a 35-year winning streak go against the USA. The last time the Eagles claimed a victory over the Red Roses was in the 1991 Rugby World Cup and since then England have won all 22 matches. The Red Roses got back to winning ways and, while their recent losses to Canada displayed the top sides had caught up with the world No 1 team, Friday’s outing against the USA evidenced that outside the top three there is still a gap to be closed. The USA headed into the match at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, New Jersey, in good form with five consecutive wins, including victories over Wales and Ireland, and their No 8 Freda Tafuna has been one of the standouts across all of the teams during the WXV. However, England were able to contain the bright spark and, despite good performances from Alev Kelter and Hope Rogers, the hosts did not have enough firepower. There were two key elements to England’s win: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and a strong second-half performance from the front row. The wing Moloney-MacDonald was dropped from the matchday 23 against Canada last time out but she responded perfectly with four tries. It will be the exact retort John Mitchell would have wanted and the head coach praised the Exeter star afterwards for her consistency. Breaks by players such as Maud Muir gave the visitors the extra few percentages they needed. It was far from a polished performance by England, though. Wasted chances against Canada contributed to both defeats and an error-strewn attack was on display again in the first half on Friday. The Red Roses had some great plays, such as Moloney-MacDonald’s first try, but they could have punished the USA more often had it not been for knock-ons and rogue passes. A disappointing note throughout the match was the empty-looking stands in the 25,000-capacity stadium in New Jersey. The official attendance was not announced but much of the ground had no fans. That was not helped by a 5pm kick-off time but a game of this magnitude deserved a bigger audience than the one that showed up. The last time these two nations met was in the opening game of the World Cup last year. The Red Roses won that 69-7, and once again England got the scoreboard ticking early on. It was less than five minutes before Moloney-MacDonald acrobatically finished, and she added another shortly after. Rogers got a try back and in doing so closed in on the American women’s all-time points record with the score bringing her just four points away. But it was England who held a 17-7 half-time lead after the captain, Meg Jones, scored, then Moloney-MacDonald secured her third and fourth tries early in the second period. Kelter put in a huge hit on Jones and, despite the tackle producing momentum for the world’s sixth-ranked side, it was England who went over through Mia Venner. The Gloucester-Hartpury wing has been impressive in her two starts in this away leg of WXV and she will give Mitchell a selection headache in 2027 if she continues her form. The loss will leave a sour taste for the USA, not just because Bryony Field – England’s replacement hooker – Maddie Feaunati and Sadia Kabeya turned a narrow win into a thumping one, but the hosts’ co-captain Georgie Perris-Redding hobbled off with injury. This game was both teams’ last of the calendar year so the USA will have to wait to bounce back until the 2027 Pacific Four tournament. England will hope they have started a new winning streak to take into the Women’s Six Nations but the important things they will take forward, according to the captain Jones, are the lessons learned from this tour. “We have gained so much feedback from where we want to keep growing and getting better,” she said. “Ultimately teams are getting better, that is the nature of it. It happened in the men’s game, it’s happening in the women’s game and we just have to start being more unpredictable.”

headline: Searle makes difference as Leicester battle to Prem top spot at Bristol
trail_text: Leicester scored four tries at Ashton Gate in a 22-16 win against Bristol that took them to the top of the Prem
body_text: In the end there was a relatively clear winner of this straight shootout for top spot in the Prem. Leicester took the spoils in an error-strewn contest between two sides who began the night in second and third position, scoring four tries to one and being masterfully steered to a bonus point victory by their alert fly-half Billy Searle. Following on from their commanding second-half display in the wet at home to Northampton, the Tigers were far from perfect but had the game’s outstanding player in Searle, whose left boot set up three of his side’s tries in addition to landing two conversions. Bristol, reduced to 13 players in the second quarter by a brace of yellow cards, had their moments but ultimately coughed up possession far too often. The game’s stylistic highlight was a quite brilliant sixth-minute solo try by Louis Rees-Zammit, back to his sharpest on the wing for the Bears, but it takes more than the occasional flash of talent to tame the Tigers. In Adam Radwan they had their own high-speed danger man, with the former Newcastle wing and full-back Freddie Steward both registering first-half tries. Of the England international contingent on view, though, the most eye-catching was Ellis Genge who was a handful in all areas during his 63 minutes, only for the visitors to ruin the prop’s night with a bonus point try from Jamie Blamire within moments of his departure. Modern-day Leicester are not yet an irresistible force but they still have the ability to grind out crucial results. “That was a good gritty win,” stressed Geoff Parling, Leicester’s head coach. “I’m really proud of the team … we’re really pleased with the spot we’re in.” There was something of a throwback feel to the whole evening, with Bristol’s players wearing old-school letters in tribute to the club legends of yesteryear. Leicester were invited to do the same until league officials stepped in and deemed it too confusing. The Tigers’ rugby alphabet used to run the other way, with ABC denoting the front row rather than the outside backs, and asking them to abandon that tradition was borderline heresy. There was a timeless beauty, either way, to Rees-Zammit’s early score. The England tighthead Joe Heyes – entertainingly listed on the teamsheet as ‘Joy Heyes’ – was minding his own business in midfield when the Welsh wing accelerated past him from a standing start before slaloming all the way to the line. Leicester’s response was clinical in a different way, Searle’s cross-kick finding an unmarked Steward who dived over to mark his 100th Prem start in style. The visitors also had a close-range ‘try’ by Chessum scrubbed out for an earlier knock-on but, for a good while, there was little to separate the teams. If Leicester had a slight edge at the scrums the Bears were the more fluent attacking team and Rees-Zammit came close to adding another stunner to his collection,only for his deft chip ahead to elude his grasp. The momentum soon shifted significantly, though, courtesy of two quickfire yellow cards in three minutes for Matías Moroni and Tom Jordan for misjudged tackles. With a two-man advantage Leicester duly went ahead courtesy of another smart kick by Searle, drilled perfectly in behind the cover for the electric Radwan to outpace the cover and slide over. The half-time score of 12-7, even so, still gave the Bears some wriggle room in the closing 40 minutes. The omens did not look great when the Tigers scored again, Searle’s precise boot this time finding Ollie Hassell-Collins in acres of space on the left. But a penalty from Jimmy Williams provided some breathing space and, now restored to 15 players, a massive penalty for the hosts’ scrum altered the mood again. Blamire’s maul score, however, finally settled things, Searle again having an input with a raking kick to the corner. At a time when England’s fly-half pecking order is once again in the spotlight, here was another reminder of his match-winning qualities. On a night full of frustrating moments for both sides, his contribution was even more striking. Bristol huffed and puffed but chances came and went and the steady boot of Williams was ultimately not enough. While Leicester are now top dogs going into the weekend they will need to perform better than this to remain ahead of the chasing pack through the upcoming winter.

headline: Fiesta awaits in Mexico City as Kimi Antonelli speeds towards F1 history
trail_text: Italian 20-year-old is on the verge of becoming the youngest world champion with Mexico City ready for a carnival coronation atmosphere
body_text: An undeniable highlight of this Formula One season, marked by discontent at the new regulations, has been getting swept along by the sheer joy that the world champion-in-waiting, Kimi Antonelli, has displayed on his way to a title he will almost surely secure this weekend at the Mexican Grand Prix. Antonelli was still a teenager for the first half of the year and it seemed fitting to describe him as such. His exuberant embrace of competing for Mercedes at the sharp end of F1 in just his second season was that of any 19-year-old. Like discovering a life-changing new band or how much fun can be had with a cold beer, a wide grin was barely off his face. He is 20 now, still but a stripling and on Sunday at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez if he finishes in ninth place or better he will be F1’s youngest world champion, and the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953. Antonelli has confessed that as a four-year-old he did not recall when Sebastian Vettel became the previous youngest title winner in 2010. “I remember I was playing with Hot Wheels, but I don’t remember him clinching it,” he said. This weekend he will likely embrace an unforgettable moment. Antonelli has shone on track, at home with the complex requirements of the new energy-managed cars, extracting a pace and control such that even his more experienced Mercedes teammate George Russell has been left flailing in his wake. To which traits he has allied a sharp and incisive driving style that has been extraordinary at times and a judgment that has belied his years. That he has done so with such alacrity, especially after a difficult rookie season last year, has surprised many. Not least those team principal Toto Wolff pointedly observed had been questioning whether Antonelli should even be in F1 after his debut season. Doubts now assuredly consigned to the dustbin of history, in the city where Leon Trotsky, who coined the phrase, was killed in 1940. It has been clear how much the Italian loves what he does and how that has informed his performances. At his shoulder through the trials of last season and the triumphs of this, has been Peter Bonnington. Bono, as he is known, was Lewis Hamilton’s engineer across the British driver’s six titles with Mercedes. He and Antonelli have established a close relationship, a friendship, with the Italian taking on board his colleague’s experience and cool head, often referencing him and the importance of their interaction. During Antonelli’s run of five successive victories in the opening period of the season, the last of them was a striking performance in Monaco. Taking an exceptional pole position to deny Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was in fearsome form on the streets of the principality, he then delivered a remarkable race win, including seeing off two restarts. After this, Bono, who often has the avuncular air of an older brother with his young charge, gave an almost disarmingly straightforward explanation of what made his driver so quick. “As soon as he’s happy in the car: happy driver, fast lap time,” he said. The team have adopted an approach to allow Antonelli the opportunity to ensure he could drive in a way that allowed him to truly embrace being himself and in so doing, taking the pressure off. Bonningham described this as “giving him the freedom to do what he enjoys, giving him the freedom to enjoy driving the car, that’s a real big thing and not stressing too much. He’s just a joy to work with.” To trust the youngster’s instincts and talent, when the temptation to micromanage him must have been overwhelming, has worked brilliantly. Even as the opposition caught and at times surpassed Mercedes, Antonelli was able to deliver when a win was not on the table. When it was, as at the last round in Austin, he stepped up to sweep it away with a nonchalance that typified why he is world champion elect. This makes the atmosphere in Mexico City all the more febrile in what is already one of the most vibrant venues on the calendar. Antonelli could barely have chosen a better location to enjoy the celebration of his childhood dream. The fans here embrace F1 with the same passion the Italian has for his trade. With the race coinciding with Mexico’s Day of the Dead, the city and the paddock are adorned with the bright orange Mexican marigolds, the “flor de muerto”. Skulls and skeletons, candles and colour are plentiful to welcome the return of the departed in a joyful, festival lending the weekend an already celebratory air. The F1 faithful are also in good cheer in welcoming home hero Sergio Pérez back to the grid, with Cadillac and his image everywhere in Mexico City. On occasion he appears as a lifesize cardboard cut-out, rather incongruously in a line of fabulously-dressed skeletons. Yet fans will also doubtless revel in having this marvellous venue celebrate F1’s youngest champion in the heady atmosphere of the stadium section of Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. Hamilton has experienced it twice, when he sealed the title here in 2017 and 2018, and the seven-time champion’s assessment of Antonelli’s season was as telling as that of his former race engineer. “You never know how anyone’s going to do under pressure until you see them,” he said. “I could assume that he was going to be fine with the weight you have on you. When you have to do all these appearances and all these things, pulled left, right and centre. But he’s taken it in his stride. He’s a relatively old soul in that young body.” Antonelli was withdrawn from his media duties on Thursday, with Mercedes saying he was unwell and needing to recover properly, but the Italian has stated he would like to finish the job in style and be able to relax for the remaining four races. There is no reason to believe he will suffer from any yips, certainly. He has demonstrated no such weakness thus far, even under the most intense pressure, with team principal Wolff sharing a further insight into why the 20-year-old stands ready to make history. “In Austin, he came to my office sat down on the sofa and said: ‘I’m going to enjoy this one. Isn’t it funny? I’m not thinking at all about the championship,’” Wolff recalled. “I said: ‘Stick to that attitude. You have the best job in the world. Don’t forget that.’ He has the right mindset.” The best job in the world and one he has, admirably, embraced with that irrepressible joy. The right mindset indeed. A deserved champion awaiting his coronation. On this form, not for the last time. In first practice in Mexico City, Ferrari once more opened strongly with Charles Leclerc topping the timesheets, six-tenths up on Antonelli in second, with the Italian apparently fully fit after Thursday’s illness. Many of the teams used the session to allow their rookie drivers to rack up track time with 10 taking part. The Danish driver Fredrik Vesti sat in for Russell and was in third, with Hamilton in fourth. In the afternoon session Hamilton lost vital running time when he retired with a loss of power after 30 minutes. His teammate Leclerc was once more quickest, one-tenth up on Lando Norris’s McLaren. Russell and Antonelli were in third and fourth and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen in fifth, three-tenths back, although the Dutchman was carrying some damage after a clash with Liam Lawson that will be investigated by the stewards.

headline: Australia set 288 to win on final day after South African centurions turn tide
trail_text: Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder hit hundreds for hosts to leave Australia with a last-day chase to win the third Test and the series
body_text: It would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away. Australia’s vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day’s beginning, could only raise that to 1,678 by day’s end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for four in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they were effectively 40 for four in the third innings here, and now have a great chance to do the same. The unlikely basis was Rickelton, a franchise circuiteer who spends most of his year smiting runs or keeping wicket in 20-over blocks. In this series he was monstered in Durban by Josh Hazlewood, out for none and two while pinch-hitting as an opener, then made scant impression down the order with 31 in Gqeberha. He looked like a modern cricketer become anachronism in this ancient form. Yet, while Rickelton strikes at 150 runs per hundred balls across his T20 career, his first-class rate is one third of that speed. There are strings to his bow that are not dyed royal blue by the global Mumbai Indians conglomerate. That was the particular set of skills he employed here, disavowing the lead of his top order the day before in assuming that a placid surface was made for rollicking shots. Instead, he and fellow white-ball dasher Matthew Breetzke absorbed everything that Australia’s freshly rested bowlers could hurl at them. On a pitch without lateral movement, there was still good bounce for the short ball, and increasingly marked turn for Nathan Lyon out of the footmarks. The pair dealt with both, while Rickelton showed a facility to punctuate defence with a single in most overs, keeping the innings at least rolling in first gear. The first session added 62 runs, the lead 102. Still, the lunchtime wicket of Breetzke looked to have turned things Australia’s way, finally impulsive as he pulled to long leg. That ended a streak for Pat Cummins of 372 balls without a wicket, unprecedented in his career, despite some good spells along the way. But Rickelton was now set like cement, and Mulder joined him in that durability, to lunch and beyond. Lyon kept ripping his off-breaks, with an inside edge from Rickelton into Alex Carey’s shin behind the stumps, and umpteen balls that landed safely after deflecting off body or bat, but reward never came. Mulder took the occasional chance attacking spin. Rickelton kept picking off rare bad balls from the quicks, driving down the ground when overpitched, backing himself on the up once the new ball showed no signs of seam. The pair tormented the Australians until well into the final session, Rickelton’s century coming after a slow march through the 90s, the partnership reaching 154 and South Africa’s lead an increasingly daunting 235 on that rapidly wearing pitch, before his departure set off a late burst of activity. Much of it involved the livewire Marnus Labuschagne, out of runs but still a red-cordial kindergarten class in the field, getting vast turn with his leg-breaks as Mulder kept sweeping him outside leg stump, where the only risk was a gloved catch. Yet when Mulder changed tack, repeatedly reverse-sweeping that same line while aiming for the exposed off-side fence, a full toss that would normally disappear over square leg was instead hit to the only fielder in an acre, Inglis at backward point, who spotted Rickelton running and Mulder standing still. Labuschagne at the bowler’s end was quick enough to gather the throw: Rickelton run out for 101. With tired Aussies and 70 minutes to go, things were set up for a Marco Jansen blitz, but he followed the team trend of holing out on the pull, hitting Starc to Lyon for nought. Lyon finally got his first wicket for the day when the opposing off-spinner Simon Harmer shouldered arms on one, big turn doing the trick, then Gerald Coetzee ran himself out for the same score, Labuschagne bobbing up again with a sizzling direct hit from the cordon to the non-striker’s end. Nine down and 251 ahead, South Africa’s lead suddenly looked light. But Mulder fixed that with Kagiso Rabada as support, also taking care of the small personal matter of moving his score from 82 to 115, farming strike for long periods between targeting boundaries. He was finally caught down the ground from a cross-bat shot at Cummins in the last over of the day, trying to hit a fifth six. A neatly apportioned match that already had one full innings occupy the entire first day will now have another full innings occupy the fifth. A target of 288 is perfectly balanced for a match that has been so even. At the last, it must tilt one way or the other, and with it the series.

headline: Bay City Roller can prove top of the pops in fascinating Breeders’ Cup Turf
trail_text: The selection’s excellent second in the Arc de Triomphe is the best form on offer among the European challengers
body_text: The Turf is the highlight of Saturday’s nine-race Breeders’ Cup card for European fans, with 10 of the 14-strong field trained in the UK, Ireland or France, and Bay City Roller (21.36) could be an excellent bet at around 9-1 with British bookmakers to give George Scott a first Breeders’ Cup winner at the second attempt. Stall 13 is not ideal, but there is little obvious pace on his inside and Oisin Murphy managed to get close to the lead from a similar draw in the Arc. A strong second behind Daryz at Longchamp showed that Bay City Roller can act on a sound surface, and he is the top-rated runner in the field on Timeform’s ratings on that form. The short straight, meanwhile, will also play to his strengths if Murphy can get across and sit handy, and then kick coming off the turn. Keeneland 17.10: Ways And Means was nearly six lengths clear in a Grade One last time and should get a better trip from stall two than Explora, her main market rival. Keeneland 17.48: Bacio, the front-running Nunthorpe winner, could face a battle for the lead and Billy Loughnane, on Donnacha O’Brien’s Comanche Brave, will be poised to pounce. Keeneland 18.26: A strong pace should set things up for John Velazquez and Bracket Buster, who ran into traffic problems at Parx last time. Keeneland 19.04: Blue Bolt and Precise are both drawn wide and Mark Casse’s Classic Q, well drawn in three to sit just behind the pace, could be a live each-way alternative at around 16-1. Keeneland 19.42: Englishman and Japanese-trained T O Elvis dominate the betting, but there are negatives for both and the pacy, fast-improving Liam Smith, from three, could well outrun odds of around 25-1. Keeneland 20.20: Charlie Appleby has saddled four winners from five starters in the Mile and Notable Speech, successful at Del Mar 12 months ago, has plenty in hand of the field. Keeneland 20.58: A likely head-to-head between Nitrogen and Fully Subscribed, and Mark Casse’s filly is ideally drawn to attack from the off. Keeneland 22.16: Just seven go to post for the Classic and it promises to set up ideally for Forever Young to become only the second dual winner in its 42-year history. Take Pic to stay in focus after stable switch The classy chaser Pic D’Orhy, already the winner of three Grade Ones and £1m in prize money, was a high-profile stable-switcher from Paul Nicholls to his former assistant, Dan Skelton, over the summer and can make an immediate contribution to the champion trainer’s title defence in the Charlie Hall Chase at Wetherby on Saturday. Pic D’Orhy (2.55) was winless in four starts last season but was just a length-and-a-half away from a fourth Grade One success in the Ascot Chase in February, and also finished a close second on his seasonal debut in Saturday’s race 12 months ago. The 11-year-old remains among the top-rated chasers in training and has often shown his best form when fresh, while good ground is also a positive as Pic D’Orhy tackles three miles for only the third time in his career. Wetherby 1.10 Patrick Neville has his string in exceptional form and Tanking Along could get a soft lead in pursuit of his third win of the campaign. Ascot 1.25 The form of Jet To Vegas’s success at Market Rasen last time was franked when the runner-up won next time up and this should be run to suit. Wetherby 1.45 Dan Skelton is going for a fifth win in six runnings and Kateira, successful 12 months ago, has several pounds in hand of this field. Ascot 2.00 Ben Pauling’s Vanderpoel faded only after jumping the last in the Grand Annual at Cheltenham and could have more to offer this season. Wetherby 2.18 Strong Leader landed this on his seasonal debut 12 months ago and this looks like the ideal day to catch him. Ascot 2.33 The addition of cheekpieces saw an improved performance from Queensbury Boy last time and he remains unexposed at three miles. Down Royal 3.15 Last year’s Ryanair Chase winner, Heart Wood, goes well fresh and could take all the beating in Ireland’s first Grade One chase of the season. Wetherby 3.30 A tactical race in prospect with no obvious pace-setter in the field, and Filibustering could have the finishing speed to take advantage. Ascot 3.43 Messerschmitt is an interesting recruit for Ben Pauling’s stable and still looks on a fair mark on the pick of his Irish form.

headline: Antonelli set for F1 title, Premier League, and NFL action – follow with us
trail_text: Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports
body_text: Saturday 8am (all times GMT) Matchday live Football Join Billy Munday for all the buildup to Saturday’s action in the Premier League and beyond. Breaking news, vibes and reader comments and queries – all are welcome. Contact matchday.live@theguardian.com. 8am Tri-series final: Pakistan v Sri Lanka Cricket With England eliminated, the top two in the tri-series meet in Lahore. Pakistan have won three out of four to get to this stage but that one defeat came when these sides met at the same ground on Tuesday. Sri Lanka eased to an eight-wicket win on that occasion and will fancy their chances of upsetting the hosts again. Tanya Aldred and James Wallace are on over-by-over duty, while Taha Hashim reports. 8.30am Third Test: South Africa v Australia Cricket A thrilling arm-wrestle of a Test match reaches the final day in Cape Town with the series on the line. Geoff Lemon and Daniel Gallan are on the liveblog for what is sure to be a tense conclusion. 12.30pm Chelsea v Manchester United Premier League A rough week for Michael Carrick does not get any easier, with his Manchester United side travelling to Stamford Bridge to face a Chelsea side still smarting from their midweek League Cup defeat on penalties at Anfield. Rob Smyth brings the minute-by-minute action, Jacob Steinberg and Barney Ronay report from Stamford Bridge. 3pm Clockwatch Football There’s a bumper set of 3pm Premier League kick-offs, with Manchester City’s home game against Brighton perhaps the pick of the fixtures. Elsewhere, Leeds visit Bournemouth, Brentford take on Nottingham Forest, Coventry host Sunderland and Ipswich travel to Hull. Tom Bassam brings you all the action from around the grounds in the top flight and beyond. 5.10pm Breeders’ Cup Racing The best Flat horses in the world head to Keeneland in Lexington, Kentucky, for the prestigious Breeders’ Cup meeting. Greg Wood is at the helm for live coverage. 5.30pm Tottenham v Crystal Palace Premier League Two teams who have had slow starts in the Premier League meet in this London derby with the form book suggesting they are heading in different directions. Spurs have won their last two in the league – Palace have suffered back-to-back defeats. Scott Murray delivers the live action and Ed Aarons reports from the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. 9pm Mexican GP qualifying Formula One Kimi Antonelli will surely seal the deal on his first drivers’ championship in Mexico City, where he needs to finish ninth or better to claim the title. Even if he fails, he could still emerge triumphant if neither Lewis Hamilton nor George Russell wins the race. Philip Cornwall brings lap-by-lap coverage of the battle for pole and Giles Richards is at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. Sunday 8am Matchday live Football Rob Smyth has all the buildup to Sunday’s games and the reaction to Saturday’s results. More breaking news, more vibes and more reader comments and queries. Contact matchday.live@theguardian.com. 12 noon Women’s Super League clockwatch Football A big afternoon in the WSL kicks off at midday with third-placed London City Lionesses hosting second-placed Manchester City in a fixture that could say much about whether the London side are genuine title challengers. Chelsea, leading the way on goal difference going into the weekend, travel to Charlton in the 2.30pm kick-off. Luke McLaughlin has the live action across the afternoon while Suzanne Wrack reports from the CopperJax Community Stadium in Bromley. 4.30pm Liverpool v Arsenal Premier League Two giants rumble into the weekend after very different EFL Cup shootouts in midweek. The Gunners were stunned by League Two Fleetwood at Highbury while elsewhere in the north-west, Liverpool edged Chelsea from the spot. Arsenal have not won at Anfield in the league since September 2012. Daniel Harris is on minute-by-minute duty. David Hytner and Andy Hunter report from the ground. 6pm Week eight clockwatch NFL The Minnesota Vikings, the last unbeaten team standing, put their 6-0 record on the line in Detroit where the Lions will need to be at their best to close the gap at the top of the NFC North. Elsewhere, the Bills welcome the Ravens to Buffalo and the Browns and Steelers meet in a game that will have a major impact on the race for the AFC North. Graham Searles will be padded up and across every play. 8pm Mexican Grand Prix Formula One Can Kimi Antonelli clinch the title in Mexico City? He needs only to finish in the top nine, something he has managed in 16 of the 18 races so far this season. Beau Dure has lap-by-lap coverage. Giles Richards reports from the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

headline: Jimmy Anderson reveals ‘sadness and shock’ at Lancashire exit
trail_text: Jimmy Anderson has revealed the shock he felt at his surprise Lancashire dismissal while he weighs up whether his future involves playing cricket or ‘something different’
body_text: Jimmy Anderson has revealed the “sadness and shock” he felt at his surprise Lancashire exit while he weighs up whether his future involves playing cricket or “something different”. Speaking for the first time since being told he will not have his county contract renewed, the England great told the BBC’s Tailenders podcast that the decision even made him question whether there is “something fundamentally wrong with me as a person”. The 44-year-old, his country’s leading Test wicket-taker, had played for Lancashire for 26 years since making his debut at the turn of the century and was let go despite taking 50 wickets, at an average of 17, while captaining the side amid their struggles in Division Two of the County Championship this year. “I went in for what I thought was a conversation about how the team moves forward,” Anderson said on the podcast. “It wasn’t a great year for the team. Being captain, I thought it was a chat about that. A couple of minutes in I realised it wasn’t a conversation. I was being told they thought the best way for the team to move forward was without me. I was quite shocked. It was quite brief.” England also chose to drop Anderson in similar circumstances in 2024 as they sought to build a fresh attack for the 2025-26 Ashes in Australia. “All of the way through the season myself and the head coach were like: ‘Is it something we are doing? Could we be doing more to help the team?’” Anderson added. “I finished the season thinking: ‘Was it something I did? Was I doing something wrong?’ – and then I get this news – now I am thinking that even more. I’m thinking: ‘This is happening again – is there something fundamentally wrong with me as a person?’ Your head just races. “I wanted to see my career out with Lancs. I don’t know if my career is done, we will have to wait and see, but it would be nice at some point if someone would let me retire.” The seamer, meanwhile,remains optimistic about a future within or outside the sport. He said: “I’m starting to get excited about the future, whether it’s something different or playing cricket again. It’s exciting. There are exciting challenges ahead. I have to attack it like that and not dwell too much on how or why it finished at Lancs. “ I am sad the way it ended with the club I supported as a kid but now I have thought about it I am quite excited for the future. I am always going to support Lancashire.”

headline: England rugby league reaches defining moment after men face early World Cup exit
trail_text: England’s Rugby League World Cup campaign is all but over despite victory over Papua New Guinea in their final group stage game
body_text: Game over. Two ultimately straightforward victories from three group games would ordinarily be enough to secure qualification in the Rugby League World Cup, but the format means that, barring a rugby league miracle from Tonga on Sunday, England are heading home early. That format – 10 teams in lopsided groups and England in a unique position of being effectively out after defeat on the opening weekend – has been a point of discussion since that defeat by the Tongans a fortnight ago. But at some stage, the attention has to turn internally and the tough, uncompromising questions have to be asked of English rugby league. Those questions can wait for another 48 hours after England defeated Papua New Guinea to ensure qualification for the semi-finals remains mathematically possible. But on a day when they had to not only win, but erode away a 68-point margin on Samoa before hoping they slipped up against Tonga later this weekend, the game is now almost up. A 22-point winning margin here was simply not enough. Tonga are capable of beating Samoa, without question. But given how their biggest-ever winning margin in that ferocious Pasifika rivalry is 32 points, it is safe to assume that head coach Brian McDermott and his side can start packing their suitcases now. England or Great Britain, for the first time in the history of the Rugby League World Cup, will not be in the last-four. It had all begun so brightly in Wollongong, though. For the opening 20 minutes England were sensational, opening up a 22-0 lead at a rate which suggested they could rack up the points they needed; with 67 enough to ensure a Tongan win of any kind on Sunday in Sydney would be enough to sneak through to the semi-finals. But England fell away from their gameplan in spectacular fashion. It would take them another 50 minutes to score a fifth try and by then Papua New Guinea had scored twice to take the points-difference permutations off the table. Late tries from Morgan Knowles and Mikey Lewis at least ensured it would be two wins from three, but England’s journey should end here. This should serve as a defining moment for English administrators who, for too long, have had their heads buried in the sand. Within the space of four hours in Wollongong, their men’s and women’s teams were effectively sent home on what should be looked back upon as a dark day for the game. An obsession with club rugby league, a congested domestic calendar which means England do not even have mid-season camps, let alone Test matches, and a decision to increase the overseas quota in Super League last year are all contributory factors to this mess. They have a monumental task ahead to reverse that decline; it should start with agreeing a partnership with the NRL to allow them to get a grip on the English game, but that would rely on those in charge agreeing to take a step back and letting the grown-ups of rugby league run things efficiently. McDermott wants to continue through to the next World Cup in 2030, and he should be given the chance – but he needs help from those above him. “It feels like we’ve lost the game,” he reflected post-match. “Something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through. If all we’d needed to do was win, we’d have handled it better … but it looks like we’re going out.” The required margin of victory looked entirely likely early on. Tries from Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Dom Young and Harry Smith all came from front-foot, attacking rugby that had the Kumuls scrambling. Leading 22-0 after the opening quarter, the points required felt within reach: but England spurned at least three more glorious chances as half-time approached. They drifted from the rugby which had served them so well early on, allowing Papua New Guinea a foothold. Dudley Dotoi and Gairo Voro’s tries within five minutes after the break suddenly then made it 24-12 and as England continued to labour with the ball, it was now suddenly about holding on to win, not winning big. Thankfully, they were at least able to do that. But when their fate is officially sealed on Sunday, the inquest should really begin into how English rugby league has found itself in the position among international rugby league’s new-age pecking order it is in. Talk about who should coach the team or who should play half-back are distractions. If those in charge do not wake up, England will continue to drift from the world’s elite. England women crash out to pile on misery England 6-24 Samoa Meanwhile, England’s women have failed to reach the final stages of a Rugby League World Cup for the first time, as the increasing gulf between the northern and southern hemispheres was once again exposed in a 6-24 defeat to Samoa which ends their tournament prematurely. Stuart Barrow’s side were in a winner-takes-all showdown in Wollongong against the Samoans, who were looking to reach the semi-finals of the World Cup for the first time. Their star-studded side, packed with NRLW talent, ultimately got the job done to inflict more misery on English rugby league and underline how they are being left behind on the international stage. England’s 78-0 defeat to Australia last week felt damaging enough, but failing to qualify from a group for the very first time is another damning indictment of where the English game now appears to sit in the pecking order. There will be a lengthy inquest back home for not just the men’s side, but the women’s too. Credit must go to Samoa too, though. Their rise in the international game has mirrored that of the men’s and while they too were beaten heavily by Australia in the opening weekend of the group stage, they are deservedly in the semi-finals for the very first time. They were much the stronger of the two sides in Wollongong and worthy winners. It did not take long for Samoa’s superiority to shine. The outstanding Freedom Crichton Ropati crossed twice in the right corner in the early exchanges, before the Parramatta Eels winger completed her hat-trick on the stroke of half-time. In contrast, England had showed little promise when they were in possession and looked comfortably second best. They had to score first after the break, but instead went further behind when Mercedez Taulelei-Siala crossed to make it 16-0, with only missed goal kicks from the Samoans keeping it somewhat respectable. Evie Cousins would take advantage of a marvellous Hollie-Mae Dodd break to get England on the board, but it was already looking like nothing more than consolation. That proved the case when Fanua Rimoni’s late try put the seal on a wonderful win for Samoa, and ensured England would be heading home early. The sobering reality for the women’s game in England is that there does not appear to be a quick fix to close the gap, however. The NRLW is making huge strides year on year, with players now fully professional and the talent pool growing at an exponential rate. There is progress in England, but much slower – with only a handful of competitive teams, and none yet professional. Barrow opted to take a young squad to Australia, with 11 of the group that travelled 23 or under. That is perhaps with the 2030 tournament in mind, but with the disparity in investment between the two hemispheres only widening in women’s rugby league, England will head home early knowing there is a difficult few years ahead: and the prospect of the gulf only getting wider.

headline: NCAA basketball 2026-27 predictions: from JuJu Watkins to Tyran Stokes, the names you’ll know by March
trail_text: Can Florida’s continuity trump the transfer portal? Will JuJu Watkins come back strong? And who will survive an expanded March Madness? Our writers weigh in
byline: Ella Brockway, Bryan Armen Graham, Stephanie Kaloi and Nicholas Levine
body_text: What are you most looking forward to, on or off the court? Lots of stuff. The return of JuJu Watkins at USC after her 19-month injury layoff, the debut of Tyran Stokes at Kansas, the potential turnaround of the Big East on the men’s side, and the stacked ACC on the women’s side. Ella Brockway JuJu Watkins’ return from injury, obviously, but also the question of whether college hoops can maintain any sense of continuity in the transfer portal era. Michigan won the men’s natty in April, then lost their coach to the NBA and watched much of their roster disintegrate. Florida, meanwhile, have managed to keep the majority of the core from their 2025 title team together. Which model wins out? Bryan Armen Graham Multiple things, but top of mind: Like many fans of women’s college basketball, I’m already excited by what JuJu Watkins has shown in the preseason. She’s been away from the court for a long time, and it will be thrilling to see the presumptive No 1 draft pick take over again. Stephanie Kaloi The new-look Pac-12 Conference. This nine-team league has only two schools that were previously in the Pac-12 and adds five schools from the Mountain West, plus powerhouse Gonzaga from the WCC and Texas State from the Sun Belt. An interesting mix of playing styles, from one of the nation’s best defenses in San Diego State to one of the most efficient offenses year in and year out in Gonzaga. Nicholas Levine The new 76-team format for men’s and women’s March Madness is … … not good nor necessary nor something that I think will affect most people’s consumption of March Madness. If the tournament is going to expand, I think we should full-send it and go to 128 with first-round games on campus. EB … a solution in search of a problem. When the deadline for most office pools is still Thursday at 12pm Eastern, the games on Tuesday and Wednesday have always felt like the tournament’s waiting room. Now we’re just making that waiting room bigger. BAG … potentially cool! I’m cautiously optimistic that this is more than just another money grab for the NCAA. Hopefully, it means more surprise wins from underdog programs that might not otherwise get a shot at the tournament. SK … fine. Like most people, I’m a “64 just feels so clean and right” guy. I like seeing more quality teams get a chance to compete, but expansion also hurts more of the lower-seeded automatic qualifiers, who now have to play in the First 12 on Tuesday and Wednesday. NL The surprise package of the season will be … The Miami men won 26 games last season but were knocked out in the second round of the tournament. With 6ft 9in forward Malik Reneau back for a fifth year, they’re a top-10 team and a Final Four contender. I’m also excited about Jasmine Bascoe, one of the best point guards in the country last season, running it back for year three with the Villanova women. EB The Michigan women have never reached a Final Four, but they return their top six scorers from an Elite Eight team. Olivia Olson, Syla Swords and Mila Holloway have grown up together and the Big Ten could be there for the taking with defending champions UCLA in a rebuild. BAG I think the Michigan women will make more noise than they have in recent years. They finished third in their conference last season, and beyond the usual suspects like South Carolina and UConn, the women’s game feels less predictable than it has in some time. SK The Arizona State men. Randy Bennett spent 25 seasons building Saint Mary’s into one of the country’s most consistent programs, winning 20-plus games 19 times and reaching 12 NCAA Tournaments. An early adopter of the ball-screen-heavy offense now commonplace across the sport, Bennett brings his tactical acumen and attention to detail to a Sun Devils roster loaded with size and skill. Look for ASU to shake up the Big 12. NL Which team in either preseason top 10 will struggle? In a world where 76 (seventy-six!) teams make the NCAA Tournament, all of these teams should be safe. For the sake of the exercise, I’ll pick the Tennessee men. Of the top teams in the SEC, they probably have the lowest possible floor. EB The Michigan men lost four starters, coach Dusty May to the NBA’s Mavericks and blue-chip recruit Brandon McCoy to a season-ending knee injury. Elliot Cadeau and Trey McKenney give them an elite backcourt, but expecting the Wolverines to remain among the top flight of contenders after so much upheaval feels optimistic. BAG The Notre Dame women are in an interesting position. Missing the tournament entirely feels like a stretch, but they’re relying on a lot of young talent this season. UCLA are also rebuilding after losing several seniors to graduation, though the defending champions have earned some breathing room as they put together their next contender. SK Texas Tech men. There is no one in the country more reliant on their fifth-year players remaining eligible than the Red Raiders. If they don’t go three-for-three in their eligibility lawsuits, they simply won’t have enough talent to earn a high seed in the NCAA Tournament. NL The men’s national player of the year will be … Jeremy Fears Jr, Michigan State. Last season’s national assists leader takes a step up – and maybe even takes the Spartans to their first Final Four since 2019. EB Thomas Haugh, Florida. The 6ft 9in forward could already be earning an NBA paycheck, but instead he’s back in Gainesville alongside Alex Condon and Rueben Chinyelu. His versatility and experience make him the centerpiece of a team with legitimate title ambitions. BAG Thomas Haugh, Florida. He’s a player I’m watching closely. Passing up strong NBA draft prospects to stick with the program is already a compelling storyline. SK David Mirković, Illinois. The 6ft 9in forward from Montenegro suffered a foot injury over the summer and has yet to be cleared to play. Once healthy, the skilled big man will be the best player on one of the best teams in the country. Coach Brad Underwood gives his players the freedom to play to their strengths, and Mirković should be highly productive on both ends of the court. NL The women’s national player of the year will be … JuJu Watkins, USC. The four-way race between Watkins, Sarah Strong, Hannah Hidalgo and Mikayla Blakes will be the highlight of the season. I’m picking JuJu. EB Sarah Strong, UConn. With Azzi Fudd having moved on to the WNBA, the reigning national player of the year becomes the undisputed centerpiece of Geno Auriemma’s offense. Strong’s cocktail of scoring, rebounding, passing and defensive instincts is almost unfair. Watkins will generate more headlines, but Strong could put together the more complete season. BAG JuJu Watkins, USC. Sarah Strong is a close second, and I think we’ll see these two battle it out all season. Vanderbilt’s Mikayla Blakes is another to keep an eye on. SK Juju Watkins, USC. Not only could the consensus 2024-25 All-American win national player of the year honors, but she could go down as one of the greatest college players of all time. If her supporting cast can take some of the offensive pressure off her, look for Watkins to lead the Trojans on a deep tournament run. NL The hottest NBA prospect is … Tyran Stokes, Kansas. The 6ft 7in freshman is the front-runner among the standout freshman prospects. On the older end, Motiejus Krivas could boost himself into the top-five pick conversation with another year at Arizona. EB Tyran Stokes, Kansas. He looks like he was designed in a lab for maximum appeal to professional scouts: explosive, versatile, capable of creating his own shot and jumping out of the gym. His jump shot and decision-making remain works in progress, but the physical tools appear to have no ceiling. BAG Everyone is very excited about Tyran Stokes at Kansas, so I’ll hop on the bandwagon. But he’s got a lot to learn in just a handful of months. Caleb Holt is another dynamic player who should cause a ruckus at Arizona this season. SK Tyran Stokes, Kansas. The best high school player in the country last season should follow in Darryn Peterson’s footsteps as a one-and-done Jayhawk. The 6ft 7in wing has an NBA-ready body and the athleticism to guard almost any position. Early signs suggest he can get into the paint and be productive once he’s there. If he continues to develop his perimeter game, he could be the first player taken in the 2027 NBA draft. NL The hottest WNBA prospect is … Watkins will go No 1 in 2027, but the No 2 pick should be Madison Booker of Texas. The pro scouts will be watching to see what jump her already well-rounded game can take. EB Hannah Hidalgo, Notre Dame. At 5ft 6in, she defies the prototype of a modern professional guard. But few players in the country can match her combination of scoring, defensive disruption and sheer competitive motor. The question is whether her diminutive frame limits her professional prospects. I’m betting her talent and tenacity win out. BAG I’m going to stick with JuJu Watkins, but Madison Booker cannot and should not be ignored. Ultimately, this may come down to what each team needs most. SK JuJu Watkins, USC. She appears to be a no-brainer as the best WNBA prospect. Not only does she have great size and athleticism, but she also checks the “smart, tough, skilled” boxes all coaches are looking for. NL One bold prediction The expanded tournament won’t generate much of a reaction. Expansion is the way of the future, from the World Cup to tennis majors to leagues themselves, because more teams means more games means more money. This year’s tournaments will probably feel bloated and include a few more lopsided results, but I suspect most fans will either begrudgingly enjoy an extra upset or two – or just skip the play-in round entirely and tune in starting Thursday. EB Rick Pitino takes St John’s to the Final Four. The Red Storm have won 61 games and two Big East tournament titles over the past two seasons, but haven’t advanced beyond the Sweet 16. With a formidable NIL war chest and a 74-year-old Hall of Fame coach who cannot go on forever, the urgency is palpable. This is the year Pitino delivers the program’s first Final Four appearance since 1985 – an outcome that suddenly feels natural with the Liberty and Knicks having primed the pump by ending decades-long droughts of their own in recent years. BAG After an OK first season and an absolutely brutal second under head coach Kim Caldwell, I think Tennessee’s women will surprise a lot of people. They’ve brought in a strong, enthusiastic group, and there’s something powerful about rebuilding a roster from scratch. Caldwell is such a unique force in college basketball. I think they’ll make a serious push come tournament time. SK The New Mexico men win the new-look Mountain West and make a tournament run. Eric Olen is in his second year in Albuquerque and has retained All-Mountain West first-teamer Jake Hall, the preseason conference player of the year, along with backcourt partner Uriah Tenette. The Lobos have also added a mix of European pros and transfers. The last time Olen had this much skill and positional size, he led UC San Diego to 31 wins and an NCAA tournament appearance. Grand Canyon will provide the stiffest competition in the conference, but look for Olen and the Lobos not only to secure the automatic bid but also to reach the Sweet 16. NL Men’s Final Four Arizona, Duke, Florida, Illinois. EB Arizona, Florida, Illinois, St John’s. BAG Duke, Florida, Michigan, UConn. SK Arizona, Illinois, Louisville, Michigan State. NL Men’s national champion Duke. I’ve spent too much of my life watching the Blue Devils (albeit from the other side of the Tobacco Road rivalry) to believe they’ll let a third straight NCAA Tournament heartbreak happen. They have a deep roster, but their biggest threats will be from Florida and Illinois, who also spent the offseason retaining and retooling. EB Florida. In a sport increasingly defined by roster turnover, Todd Golden has achieved something remarkable: keeping much of his 2025 championship core together. Haugh, Condon and Chinyelu give the Gators the kind of experienced, physically imposing frontcourt that grinds out wins in March. Duke may have more individual talent, but the Gators have something harder to manufacture: continuity. BAG UConn. That loss to the Wolverines was a tough pill to swallow, and I expect they’ll come back laser-focused on getting the biggest win of all this season. There’s plenty of motivation to go one better. SK Illinois. The Fighting Illini have experienced returners who are proven winners. With an international-heavy roster and great size and skill at every position, they’re a matchup nightmare for opponents. At one point last season, they had the highest offensive efficiency rating of the KenPom era. The health of David Mirković and Andrej Stojaković will be critical, but their combination of skill and winning experience gives them the edge over powers like Duke and Florida for me. NL Women’s Final Four Notre Dame, South Carolina, UConn, USC. EB Michigan, South Carolina, UConn, USC. BAG Michigan, South Carolina, UConn, USC. SK LSU, South Carolina, UConn, USC. NL Women’s national champion South Carolina were embarrassed in the national title game against UCLA last season. Dawn Staley and co will use that as fuel. The Gamecocks have a gauntlet of a schedule, but they also have valuable depth that will pay off in November and in March. EB South Carolina. Dawn Staley has enough frontcourt talent to field two formidable teams, with Joyce Edwards, Chloe Kitts and Ashlyn Watkins headlining an embarrassment of riches. Add Tessa Johnson’s experience and a promising collection of newcomers and the Gamecocks look built to withstand just about anything. Last April’s title-game humiliation against UCLA should provide all the motivation they need. BAG South Carolina, probably, and I’m making my peace with it, despite always enjoying the possibility of a surprise. Dawn Staley continues to build teams that are light years ahead of the rest. And after losing last season’s championship, I suppose the Gamecocks are underdogs in a way. Their talented freshmen should fit in nicely alongside the veterans. SK USC. I’m sticking with the JuJu theme and predicting she’ll lead the Trojans past their crosstown rivals UCLA. The generational star will most likely turn pro after this season, but not before cutting down the nets in Columbus. NL

headline: Chess: English prodigies have proud record of giantkilling across the generations
trail_text: From Jonathan Penrose to Bodhana Sivanandan, young English talents have specialised in defeating established stars
body_text: Nearly half a century ago, at Brighton 1977, the 10-time British champion, Jonathan Penrose, faced a 12-year-old boy, Nigel Short, in round three of the national title contest. Short already had a fast-growing reputation after defeating the legendary Viktor Korchnoi in a simultaneous display in London the previous year. David Bronstein, watching that game, compared the winner’s rook infiltration via the fifth rank after move 40 to José Capablanca’s strategy against Aron Nimzowitsch at New York 1927. Penrose disliked his position from the opening and offered an early draw, which Short declined, going on to score in 41 moves. The final stage illustrates the aphorism, attributed to Adolf Anderssen and Wilhelm Steinitz, that with a knight on the sixth rank, you can go to sleep and let the game win itself. More than a quarter of a century earlier, at Southsea 1950, Penrose had himself been the star of a game against a leading grandmaster when the then 16-year-old defeated the former world championship challenger Efim Bogolyubov in round three. It is an occasion I remember only too well, as I had drawn easily with the black pieces against Bogolyubov in round two and had been complimented for my play in Harry Golombek’s Times report, a feat which was instantly forgotten when Bogolyubov turned over his king. Giantkilling upsets continue. When England’s prodigy Bodhana Sivanandan defeated the grandmaster Ameet Ghasi at the 2026 British Championship, the game was awarded the best game prize for its strategic depth. Meanwhile, important English chess events lie ahead and Guardian readers have the opportunity to participate. The English Championships reach their final rounds this weekend, with the Olympiad grandmasters Michael Adams and Gawain Maroroa Jones fighting a flock of ambitious rivals. The pair met in round five and, in a display of mutual respect, swiftly hoovered the pieces off the board for a draw. After six rounds (of nine) the leaders were GM Jones and IM Jonah Willow on 5, with GM Adams, IM Marcus Harvey, GM Neil McDonald and GM Danny Gormally on 4.5. From 24 November to 6 December, the XTX Markets London Classic will be played at Hammersmith, with Sivanandan entered for the Fide Swiss, while the traditional Hastings congress celebrates its 100th edition, starting on 28 December. Hastings had its giantkilling moment in 1970, when the little-known student Martyn Corden shocked the former world champion Vasily Smyslov. This year Hastings has already announced the participation of three young 2500-rated grandmasters: Brewington Hardaway (2509) of the US, Nikoloz Petriashvili (2522) of Georgia, and Leonardo Costa (2555) of Germany. Meanwhile, England’s 12-year-old prodigy Supratit Banerjee is bidding for his first GM norm in Stockholm. The Sutton grammar schoolboy, who is already England’s second youngest IM, began well in a closed,tournament where three competitors are GMs and the other seven are all aspirants to the title. In the third round, he defeated Ireland’s Tarun Kanyamarala, but he later dropped back with successive defeats. 4048: 1…Rh1+! 2 Bxh1 Qh5 3 Kg2 Qh2+ 4 Kf3 Qxf2+ 5 Kxg4 Be6+ 6 Kh5 Qh2+ 7 Kg6 Qh6 mate.

headline: Beach volleyball in Morecambe Bay? An Olympics of the north sounds like a winner
trail_text: Our sport-loving PM is willing to risk a bitter north v south furore, all for the sake of table tennis in Teesside
body_text: As someone who barely understands their own finances, let alone the country’s, I will admit that budget day doesn’t always register with me. Perhaps if there were outre outfits or horse-drawn carriages involved, like there are at the state opening of parliament, I’d get into it, but the only accessory of note is a briefcase and it doesn’t even glow mysteriously when you open it. This week, however, the chancellor of the exchequer did manage to catch my attention. Somewhere amid the household energy payments and defence spending, he slipped in a cheeky £7m to assess a possible Olympic bid for the north of England. That’s only a preliminary step and a fraction of the cost of any actual bid – Tokyo and Paris spent more than £50m on theirs. Still, it’s enough to put thoughts in people’s heads of beach volleyball in Morecambe Bay or a British eight rowing to victory along the Tyne. The idea has gained traction since February, when a group of mayors from the northern cities first wrote to the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, asking her to bring the Olympics to their neighbourhood. Three months later, Nandy had thrown her support behind the proposal – “It’s time the Olympics came north” – and announced an initial assessment. The new funds will support a more comprehensive one, with a view to hosting in the 2040s. And it surely doesn’t hurt to have a recently installed, sport-loving prime minister, who was previously mayor of Greater Manchester. Andy Burnham is in the early, giving stages of his premiership and he can generate a lot of goodwill by spending a comparatively small sum exploring the option. The “detailed feasibility study” by UK Sport isn’t due until 2029, but you can still expect it to stoke a lot of excitement in the meantime. There has already been positive reaction to the news, not least from the former boxer Luke Campbell, the 2012 Olympic bantamweight champion who became Reform UK’s mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire last year. Campbell has been a vocal supporter of the plan; he has also been on the ropes recently, with police investigating allegations – which he denies – that he showed naked pictures of himself to a female member of staff. Still, he came out of his corner to praise the funding. “I’m proud to be working with other northern mayors and leaders to get this idea taken seriously,” said Campbell, calling it “a legacy worth aiming for”. London’s mayor, however, will be far less impressed. Sadiq Khan has been talking about bringing the Games back to the capital for the past five years. His office has been actively consulting the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and working up a plan to reuse 2012 venues to create “the greenest Games ever”. Khan has lobbied for it with Conservative and Labour governments. “The great thing to remember is the power of sport,” he said on the 10th anniversary of the London Games. “It’s above party politics, it’s above north versus south.” Unfortunately, it seems he may be wrong about that. Perhaps Khan needs to remember that North v South has been a fundamental part of England’s sporting landscape since the Victorians first codified its favourite physical pursuits. Some of the earliest fixtures in England were literally played between North and South, be they in football, cricket, water polo or draughts. Even rugby union had North v South games, before the establishing of two separate codes would create a geographical divide of its own. It’s one more aspect of the divide baked in to the country’s social history. And as John Healey’s £7m demonstrates, an Olympic bid is also, very much, politics. In this case, the politics of regional disparity – from the failure of levelling up to the devolution revolution, from No 10 North to Pride in Place. Whether the members of the IOC will vote for swimming in Sheffield, modern pentathlon in Manchester and table tennis in Teesside remains, for now, entirely moot. The government’s feasibility study answers the call of a more immediate voting base, who care as much about the promise of outside investment and regional infrastructure that an Olympics may provide as they do about the fortnight’s fiesta itself. And hey, how about that mythical high-speed rail line, while you’re at it? It should be said that there’s nothing wrong with ambition or even just testing the waters. If an Olympics bid did come off, it would be a more than fitting way to celebrate the north’s prodigious athletic legacy. And that’s something to which Burnham, an Everton season-ticket holder and former president of the Rugby Football League, has shown a longstanding commitment. Indeed, he has a literal track record: last month, he became the first serving prime minister to complete the Great North Run (in a very respectable sub-two-hour time). For now, however, the whole thing remains little more than a theoretical possibility and a politicians’ talking point. Perhaps we can find some other North v South contests to fixate on in the meantime. Unfortunately, the promised all-star footballing fixture at the Valley last year – with the North managed by Robbie Fowler and the South managed by Harry Redknapp – never materialised. But I see that England lacrosse has revived the fixture this year, after a hiatus of four decades. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

headline: Exeter’s Tom Hooper: ‘Sometimes you’ve just got to suck up a little bit of pain’
trail_text: The Chiefs’ latest Wallaby talks to Robert Kitson about dealing with English weather, the positive side of rehab and Australia’s World Cup chances
body_text: The list of Australian rugby players who have found a spiritual home in Exeter is a long and illustrious one. Dean Mumm, Dave Dennis, Nic White, Scott Sio, Greg Holmes, Julian Salvi, Ben White, Mitch Lees, Lachie Turner, Len Ikitau … almost without exception they have pitched up in the south-west of England and relished the experience. As Rob Baxter, Exeter’s director of rugby, drily observes: “They seem to like the pasties and the cider.” Perhaps the surfing opportunities and the area’s beguiling beaches have also played their part, although Baxter has his own subtly different theory: “Maybe Exeter and Devon is more like Australia than anywhere else in England. There’s plenty of open space and we tend to be a relatively old-school type of club. The Australian guys really seem to like that environment.” None more so, it seems, than Tom Hooper, the club’s current resident Wallaby who is hoping to upset England next Sunday. Hooper hails from cattle farming stock in rural New South Wales and while not a cider drinker – “I love Guinness” – the personable forward is a country boy to the tips of his beaten-up toes. “I was always going to be a meat eater, that’s for sure,” says the 25-year-old, reflecting on his sizeable childhood appetite growing up near Bathurst in New South Wales. “Getting tucked into the sausage sizzle with my little brother at our local rugby club was always a good way to get our fill.” Any misplaced worries before he arrived in Exeter a year ago have also long since vanished. “I’ll be honest, when I first came here I thought the international players were going to be wankers. But they weren’t at all … they were the loveliest, most humble guys. You feel so welcomed in this environment. And the other thing I’ll say is that the British weather’s not that bad. You can deal with it. It’s only one or two months of the year. I’ve only had one winter, though. I’ll see how this one goes.” It emerges, though, that Hooper is not quite as 100% “Strine” as he sounds. “My family heritage is actually Cornish. Way, way back before we get sent out on the boats.” He has certainly been enjoying the tors of Dartmoor and the coastal life so far. “I go freediving a little bit with a few of the boys.” Where exactly? “I can’t let you know my diving spot, mate. But there’s plenty of places; the whole coastline is absolutely beautiful.” So presumably he is living in an idyllic thatched cottage in the middle of nowhere? “Nah, I thought that’s where I was going to be but I’m right in the centre of town. I’ve got a landlord – I call him Grandad – who looks after me.” This most friendly of giants, however, is very much here for the rugby. Few top players worldwide have stacked up more games across both hemispheres in the past couple of years and the Chiefs could not wish for a more wholehearted recruit. Even a fractured shoulder blade against Ireland last July and multiple long-haul flights have failed to dilute his enthusiasm. “Spending a little bit of time in rehab was a blessing in disguise. It gave me a little bit of time off to strengthen the rig and get back into it over here. “A lot of people allude to how much rugby I play but if I look back to 12-year-old Tommy Hooper running around for Bathurst Bulldogs, he’d be pretty happy playing 30 games [a year] as a professional rugby player. Sometimes you just gotta suck up a little bit of pain and push through it.” Which is the sort of can-do attitude every coach respects. The 125kg, 6ft 6in Hooper has won 25 caps for the Wallabies and found it hard when they recently faced New Zealand without him: “It’s strange watching when I’m not injured. We had training at the same time as the game so I was trying not to see the score. Then I walked into Sandy Park, turned right into the brekky room and the score was on the telly. I think I let out a few profanities. The boys knew I wasn’t happy.” Hooper also misses Saturday’s game at home to Harlequins after he picked up a knock against Bristol last week. He remains adamant nevertheless that Australia, injuries permitting, can be a threat when they host next year’s Rugby World Cup. “Our squad on paper is looking really strong for that World Cup,” he says. “Then it’s just about having an individual onus on work rate and doing your job for the team. “I think the Wallaby back row, whether that’s the starters or the finishers, are bringing that in spades. And if we can get front-foot ball we’ve got some electric guys out wide. Get everyone on the field and firing and I think we’ll go a long way. It would be great to bring a buzz for the sport back into our nation.” Much the same, he agrees, could be said about England. He particularly rates Tom Curry – “The work he does off the ball is really underrated” – while his good friend Josh Kemeny at Northampton – “I hear a lot from him about how their team works” – has been educating him about Henry Pollock and others. “England are very similar to Australia in terms of the squad depth they possess. When everyone’s fit they can be one of the best teams in the world. So, yeah, it’s an exciting prospect to be facing them first off.” England, for their part, may yet bump into a second Hooper one day. His 22-year-old younger brother Lachie is highly rated – “He’s an absolute freak, he will be better than me” – and Tom says both aspire to be positive role models for country boys everywhere. “I loved my time growing up in the country … it teaches you a lot of good values. When I go back to Australia, it’s quite often the country kids who say ‘please’ and ‘thank you’. They’re often the ones I give my pair of boots to after the game.” And every time he lines up to sing Advance Australia Fair, he also feels a swelling sense of gratitude. “Rugby’s just been so intertwined in our life,” he says. “Mum and Dad met at a rugby field and Dad coached us all the way up through juniors. Then when we moved to Canberra they were on the road to watch us. I even met my partner on a rugby field … she was playing for the Brumbies’ women’s team at the time. “This sport has given me so much and I really want to give back, whether that’s to my team or future generations of country kids like me. I think I’ve got a duty to do that – and, hopefully, rugby’s got a bit more to give me.”

headline: Packers beat Panthers as Green Bay’s Christian Watson returns after mid-game hospital visit
trail_text: Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to beat the Carolina Panthers
body_text: Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to beat the Carolina Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night. Love went 30 of 41 for 288 yards with touchdown passes to Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Jacobs plus an interception. Although he rushed for only 39 yards on 21 carries against the NFL’s lowest-ranked run defense, Jacobs scored on a four-yard catch and one-yard run for the Packers (5-3). After trailing 27-10 in the third quarter, Carolina cut Green Bay’s lead to 27-19 on Bryce Young’s 26-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Coker on a fourth-and-three play with 5:37 remaining. Young’s ensuing two-point conversion pass was incomplete. The Panthers (3-4) got the ball back at their own 45 before losing the ball on downs at midfield with 2:41 remaining. Carolina got one last chance from their own 20 with 22 seconds and no timeouts remaining, but Dani Dennis-Sutton’s sack essentially ended any comeback hopes. Young went 23 of 31 for 209 yards with one touchdown and one interception. Carolina’s Chuba Hubbard had 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown and seven catches for 38 yards. Green Bay’s Christian Watson was involved in a remarkable sequence of events. He hurt his chest making a 53-yard catch in the second quarter. The Packers feared he may have sustained a serious injury, and he was taken to a local hospital. However, after being passed fit by doctors, he returned late in the third quarter, then caught a six-yard pass on the opening play of ‌the fourth. He finished as the game’s top receiver with 113 yards on eight receptions. “I never wanted to go [to hospital], I was hoping they’d let me off,” Watson said after the game. “They said there were a couple of signs that made them want to take me over there, so I was just praying it was good enough that I could come back out here. Luckily it was … I’m happy to be out here on a football field. There was no internal bleeding [nothing] that was raising suspicion. I cleared everything and I was able to get back out.” Watson said he had been able to follow the game while he was in hospital. “One of the doctors had his phone out, so I was watching the play-by-play,” he said. Carolina cornerback Will Lee hurt his hamstring while diving to make a tackle on the same play in which Watson was injured, and he was carted into the locker room. Carolina already have three other cornerbacks on injured reserve: Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), Mike Jackson (groin) and Jaycee Horn (quadriceps). Brewers get big welcome There was a warm welcome for another Wisconsin team on Thursday night. Several members of the Milwaukee Brewers, including team captain Christian Yelich and Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski, received a huge ovation as they arrived Lambeau Field one night after winning the first World Series title in franchise history. Brewers pitcher Brandon Woodruff held the Commissioner’s Trophy aloft as he emerged from the tunnel during a timeout before the second quarter. A few of the players attempted a Lambeau Leap into the crowd, with outfielder Sal Frelick having the most success. Those Brewers players later were shown on the video board cheering as they wore cheeseheads that included the message, “2026 WS Champions.”

headline: George Russell determined not to let disappointing F1 season define career
trail_text: George Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and still has plenty of time to win the world championship
body_text: George Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and believes he still has plenty of years left to come back and win the world championship. Russell has been outdriven by his 20-year-old Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli in a bruising season for the British driver. Antonelli is set to win the title and become F1’s youngest world champion at this weekend’s Mexican Grand Prix if he finishes in ninth place or above. He has taken nine wins thus far to Russell’s three, with the British driver struggling for consistency in adapting to the demands of the energy management required by the new cars which, alongside the tyres in use this year, does not suit the 28-year-old’s driving style. Russell has delivered some impeccable weekends, including commanding victories in Austria and Baku, but more often than not has been left baffled as to why he cannot make the car work to the same effect as Antonelli, a process which he conceded had been hard to deal with. “I’ve probably learned more about myself this year than I would have liked to, in all honesty,” he said at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. “You know, the highs and lows you go through in sport are immense and that’s because we all care so much for what we’re doing. “But I remind myself I’m 28 years old. I see Lewis [Hamilton] still competing extremely well at 41 and Fernando [Alonso] at 45. Lewis won the majority of his titles in his thirties and this year is absolutely not going to define my career as a whole.” Russell has suffered with no little bad luck this season but has offered praise to Antonelli, admitting the Italian has been the better driver and is thoroughly deserving of taking his first title in only his second season in F1. The British driver had opened the season strongly with a win at the Australian GP but was then battered as Antonelli took five wins in a row and the lead of the championship which he has not relinquished since. However, Russell maintained he would learn from the experience to return stronger in 2027. “It’s not going to break me. If anything, it’s going to make me stronger,” he said. “I’ve been pretty proud of my resilience and how I’ve sort of bounced back from very tough moments. “Through my lowest points of this season, I’ve generally bounced back really, really strong and then I had another bad race after the good one. So, maybe it’s something I need to analyse as well because I always perform best after my worst races. Maybe it’s just a coincidence, maybe there’s something in it. “I don’t think any athlete, no matter how great, has every single year of their career performing at their highest level. Unfortunately, this year for me has come at maybe the time when I needed it most. By no means the end of my journey, I have still got a good 12 to 15 years left in me.” Russell is in a tight battle for second place in the championship, just one point ahead of Hamilton and six in front of Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Antonelli did not take part in media duties on Thursday as the team said he was unwell with a “viral illness”. He was given leave by the FIA to not take part, as the team noted, as “a precaution to give him the chance to rest ahead of the weekend”. He is expected to be in the car for free practice on Friday.
