The Cadillac team also withdrew Valtteri Bottas from his media duties on Thursday in Mexico, noting that he was “unwell” and subsequently that “the team has taken the decision to allow him a day of rest, to support his recovery”.

headline: Dream serve up lunchtime rout of Valkyries to force historic WNBA finals Game 7
trail_text: Atlanta shook off two straight defeats with a commanding Game 6 win over Golden State to take the WNBA finals to a decider on Saturday
body_text: The Atlanta Dream had no intention of letting a matinee become their curtain call. Facing elimination at a lunchtime tipoff, the Dream overwhelmed the Golden State Valkyries 80-69 on Thursday afternoon to force a decisive seventh game in the WNBA finals, rediscovering their offensive touch just as their title hopes were threatening to slip away. Atlanta buried six three-pointers and shot 73.3% from the floor in a blistering opening quarter at State Farm Arena, built a lead that ballooned to 25 points before half-time and held on to send a series that had swung sharply towards Golden State back to San Francisco’s Chase Center for Saturday night’s winner-take-all finale. Both teams are seeking their first championship. Allisha Gray scored a team-high 23 points including five threes, Rhyne Howard added 21 while Angel Reese notched her fourth double-double of the series with 15 points and 14 rebounds to go with six assists. Gabby Williams finished with a game-high 26 points for the Valkyries after being held to four in the first half. Tiffany Hayes chipped in 15, but Golden State shot just 31.4% from the field and 25.9% from three-point range. Veronica Burton endured a particularly frigid afternoon, making just two of her 13 shots from the floor and missing all six three-point attempts. “It’s do or die. It’s win or go home,” Howard said. “I knew that coming in, we had to be aggressive from the jump, and that starts with me. You know, I have to be a good leader for this team. I have to set the tone early, and I feel like that’s what I did today.” The Dream had managed only 62 and 55 points in back-to-back defeats that erased their 2-1 series lead. On Thursday, they scored 32 in the first quarter alone, making 11 of their first 15 shots and moving the ball with a fluidity Golden State had largely disrupted over the previous two contests. Reese said a players-only meeting before a film session had helped restore Atlanta’s confidence, with Dream forward Naz Hillmon urging her teammates to remember who they were. “All of us have been superstars on a team at some point,” Reese said. “We needed the best out of every single person tonight.” It wasn’t quite a first-round knockout, but the Dream were never seriously threatened even when the Valkyries found their footing after the intermission. Golden State trimmed the deficit to 13 early in the fourth quarter, only for Gray hit a three-pointer followed by another from Reese to restore a 74-55 advantage with 5min 43sec remaining. The Valkyries made one final push, getting as close as 77-69 on Williams’s three-point play with 1min 15sec to go, which fouled out Howard. But Gray, compromised by an injury to her shooting hand for most of the postseason, answered with her fifth three-pointer off a Reese assist to remove all doubt with 56sec left. Golden State opted not to extend the contest by fouling in the closing seconds, leaving a final margin that barely hinted at the scale of the hosts’ dominance. “We needed the opportunity. That’s all we needed, and we maximized it today,” Reese said. “I’m just really proud of this group. The job is not done, and I’m looking forward to it. One more. Job’s not done.” The performance came amid the controversy surrounding a 12.30pm tipoff, a scheduling compromise that placed the biggest home game of Atlanta’s season in the middle of a work day. The Dream nevertheless announced a sellout crowd of 17,099. “I had no doubt that they would show up,” Howard said. “Everybody kept asking me about 12.30, 12.30. Now they can leave with a better taste in their mouths, go get the bottomless mimosas, you know, enjoy the rest of the day, ‘cause I know nobody’s going back to work.” For Golden State, the start was equivalent to 9.30am on their normal California clock, but their coach, Natalie Nakase, refused to blame the unusual start time. “No. That had nothing to do with it,” she said. “We played at one o’clock last week.” She added: “We knew they were going to play desperate. We knew they were going to play like their life depends on it. For us not to match that is disappointing and frustrating.” The WNBA adopted a best-of-seven finals last year, only for the series to end in a four-game sweep. This time, the extended format has delivered the ultimate decider. After six games have left nothing to separate the Dream and Valkyries, the first Game 7 in league history on Halloween night will settle everything. “Both teams want it, and so the mindset is a sense of urgency,” Burton said. “It is do or die, officially.”

headline: Australia gain edge in Test decider after late Bavuma blow hurts South Africa
trail_text: South Africa lead by 40 runs with six wickets remaining after Temba Bavuma was dismissed for 35 as they reached 140-4 on the third day of the Test decider
body_text: If Temba Bavuma was decisive for South Africa as he batted through day after day in Gqeberha, his fall in the shadow of stumps on the third day might prove as decisive at Cape Town. Bowled by a Nathan Lyon classic with eight balls to go, he saw his team reach stumps at 140 for 4, with a lead of just 40 to build on. Australia had started the day at 330 for 4, their lead exactly 100 by the time they were bowled out for 429. It was Josh Inglis and Alex Carey resuming a partnership at 145, calmly adding another 40 while sleepy South Africans gave up boundaries with misfields. A peaceable surface and a sunny morning had the Australian pair set to go large, especially with Kagiso Rabada not allowed to bowl for seven overs due to time spent off the field. Somehow, though, this series always has Simon Harmer in the thick of things, a grizzled competitor from the English county game making the most of his late-career Test renaissance. First he nearly pulled off another screamer at slip, one-handed and low to an edge from Carey in Rabada’s first over, pace on the ball ripping open the fielder’s middle finger. Then, after taping up the wound on his non-bowling hand, the off-spinner was asked to take the next over. The first ball saw Inglis crunch a reverse sweep for four to celebrate a century, but the sixth drew him into a defensive push to be caught behind for 102. Two overs later, Harmer had the left-handed Carey do the same to slip for 80. A less polite individual might have considered raising that bandaged finger to the opposition. It had been a mighty innings from Inglis, coming off injury, in the side for the first time in nearly a year. For the time being, at least, he is one of only six players in history with two centuries and no fifties, and two tons in a six-Test career indicates that he belongs in this side on a permanent basis. What configuration will permit that is a future headache for selectors. With Australia’s lead at 50 when Carey fell, much was in the balance. Twice the previous day, South Africa had been unable to turn a double strike into further wickets; here, they made it a triple as Pat Cummins was trapped lbw, a narrow umpire’s call on leg stump going Rabada’s way. It was a tough gig for Cooper Connolly at number seven, newly arrived both at the crease and more broadly in Test cricket. Matt Renshaw in Durban had joked about telling off Nathan Lyon for aggressive shots, but it’s hard to imagine a 23-year-old in his second Test assuming the seniority to marshal the tail. Yet to a point he did, batting up to lunch and beyond, collecting singles and twos, working towards doubling that lead. He was badged viciously by Marco Jansen, ducking into the short ball and half turning his head as it crashed into the front of his helmet, but continued to play bouncers with confidence, riding the next ball off his armpit and down past short leg. Mitchell Starc was caught behind driving Gerald Coetzee, Lyon edged Wiaan Mulder’s outswinger to Harmer, and when Connolly finally had a swing, he smacked one back to Jansen. His 29 won’t break any records, but he had overseen another 50 runs since losing Cummins. Early in South Africa’s reply, Aiden Markram cover-drove loosely at Starc, letting Head make up for the catch he dropped off the same combination in the first innings. David Bedingham made another poor choice to hook, caught at long leg. Marques Ackerman made his second half-century for the match with 62, again free-scoring with risky pulls through fine leg and slashes through the cordon, wiping off most of the deficit with Bavuma’s quiet support. But this has been a match for Starc interventions, and with the score on 95, venomous bounce from around the wicket, lefty to lefty, he smashed Ackerman in the grille so hard that it ricocheted to slip. Ackerman saw so little of the ball that he didn’t know he’d edged his pull shot on the way through, eventually challenging the umpire, but he had taken too long. Not happy at being told the clock had run out, that refusal saved his team a review. Late-day tension rose each over. In a fierce Cummins spell, Matthew Breetzke edged him just short of Renshaw at slip, while Bavuma gloved a nasty one over leg gully. Lyon was getting increasingly serious turn. And with the shadow of a silly mid-off stretched across the pitch, Lyon ripped one back a mile from outside off-stump as Bavuma missed his swing towards leg. In a big day for “effectively”, South Africa are effectively 40 for 4. They won in Gqeberha from there, but it’s a hard search in the clear blue skies of Cape Town to find lightning for a double strike.

headline: Duckett and Dawson steer England to victory over Sri Lanka in tri-series farewell
trail_text: Ben Duckett scored 167 and Liam Dawson took four wickets as England secured a consolation victory over Sri Lanka in the tri-series
body_text: Not this time. Sri Lanka threatened a repeat of Rawalpindi, and a target of 387 in Lahore was within reach. Pavan Rathnayake was the thorn again with another century but, unlike his captain Harry Brook’s last week, Ben Duckett’s epic was not in vain. The left-hander struck 167 before Liam Dawson took four wickets, setting up a consolation 55-run victory for England. Sri Lanka had already booked their place in Saturday’s tri-series final against Pakistan but looked ready to take this dead rubber, too. With 87 runs required from the last 10 overs, and Rathnayake’s low hands working their magic, the game looked theirs. But England’s attack kept calm and Dawson, back for his final over, nabbed Rathnayake for 118 as the last five wickets fell in a rush. The win rounded off a bizarre tour for England who lost two seemingly unloseable games. Here, they were grateful for their left-arm spinner’s steel in another run-fest. Four for 49 in a 700-plus game is a special return. “I wasn’t getting nervy,” said Brook. “We had a clear plan and a lot of clarity at the top of the mark with the bowlers. The lads have learned a hell of a lot from that game we played a couple of days ago. To finish the game off like we did there was an exceptional effort.” Duckett was the leading man in the first half. He struggled in the 430 game, way off his best with a scratchy 29 while everyone else teed off. Move forward a week and he has two more ODI tons, 105 in the low-scorer against Pakistan followed by a career-best. With Tom Banton punching his way to his fifth 50-plus score in six innings, the first-wicket stand was worth 163 from 25 overs. England now have a healthy problem: where does Jacob Bethell, back next month in Australia, fit into the picture? Banton taking the gloves could be an option if England want to keep this opening partnership intact, with Bethell going to the middle order. Banton will undoubtedly be peeved that he failed to turn three half-centuries in the series into at least one helmet-raising moment. He fell for 74 when his footwork went missing, dragging a Dasun Shanaka delivery on to the stumps. But Duckett, in love with Lahore, was on for the big one. He reached his third ODI hundred on this ground off 89 deliveries, and the southpaw swung freely from there, his next 50 taking only 29 balls. Middling his pull shots, Duckett eventually tired, though only after he had gone past his 165 against Australia at this venue last year. Brook promoted himself to No 3 as England pushed towards another gargantuan total, but an errant scoop limited him to 44. Will Jacks, Jordan Cox and Sam Curran kept England moving at pace but Brook’s dismissal still felt significant, the moment that eliminated the chance of another 400. Asitha Fernando, armed with his tailing yorker, helped limit the damage with figures of two for 63, but England still made their way to the highest-ever ODI total at the Gaddafi Stadium. Joe Root was not even required. Sri Lanka had no reason to be daunted, even with an early dismissal: Sonny Baker dropped Avishka Fernando at deep fine leg but went through Kamindu Mendis not long after. Kusal Mendis’s bat split in half early on when facing Gus Atkinson, but the replacement blade worked just fine. England looked short with the ball having left out Adil Rashid once again, and Henry Crocombe was barely called upon in his second ODI. At 177 for two off 26 overs, Sri Lanka were more than well-placed on a dewy pitch. Brook called for Root’s off-spin, a move that felt desperate but quickly worked. Kusal edged down the leg-side on 89, into the gloves of Cox, and Dawson had Shanaka leg-before three overs later after a successful review. Spin was tightening things from both ends, but Root’s third over was expensive as Janith Liyanage thumped over the on-side. Curran was handled comfortably, his moon ball punished, and Jacks was too short as Rathnayake made up for a patient start. Nonetheless, England rediscovered some composure as the game closed in. Baker had been expensive against Kusal but he prompted the removal of Liyanage on 27. Crocombe had bowled only two overs when Brook called him in for the 43rd, and Sahan Arachchige launched the newbie into the hands of the captain at long-on. Curran’s tricks began to work too, setting up the run-out of Dunith Wellalage, and Dawson returned for one final over, getting Rathnayake to lob an edge to short fine leg. Next up for England: Australia.

headline: Brewers manager Pat Murphy takes shot at ‘horseshit’ Yankees team after World Series win
trail_text: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy was captured taking a shot at a teh 2023 Yankees after he celebrated his team clinching the World Series
body_text: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy was captured taking a shot at a “horseshit Yankees team” after he celebrated his team clinching the World Series on Wednesday night. A video of Murphy talking to Jake Bauers emerged in which the manager tells the Brewers’ soon to be a free agent: “You’re going to be a rich fucker. Just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself? Just remember, say, ‘This is the way we used to do it.’” Bauers played for the Yankees in 2023 before he was traded to the Brewers. The Yankees finished fourth in the AL East in 2023, missing the playoffs for the first time since 2016. Bauers did little to help them, batting .202 with 12 home runs in 84 games that season. However, he has thrived at the Brewers: in the 2026 regular season he hit .266 with 26 home runs and an OPS of .874, all career bests. He was also named the National League Championship Series MVP as the Brewers swept the Los Angeles Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982. Murphy also had another excellent season and is favorite to be named the NL Manager of the Year for a third season in a row. Murphy is not the first person to joke about the Yankees in a World Series. When the Dodgers overwhelmed the Yankees in the 2024 edition, Los Angeles veteran Joe Kelly said New York were “sloppy” and “can’t make a play”, while his teammate Miguel Rojas called out their “lazy” defense. The Brewers did not limit their attention to the Yankees after their win. Pitcher Trevor Megill was asked if he had a message for his team’s fans after they clinched the World Series. “Have fun talking shit to Chicago next year,” Megill told MLB reporter Ben Verlander. “We have a ring.”

headline: The low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lie
trail_text: Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s owners, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction
body_text: For the entirety of the 2026 baseball season, the overlords of the game have stood on the single position that what has now happened could not happen, and the result was a year that has been treated like an appetizer for the main course of the offseason: the shutting down of the game until the players, after 40 years of resistance, finally agree to a salary cap. The insistence that the game had been predetermined undermined the Milwaukee Brewers, who spent 149 days this season atop the standings. Baseball dismissed Milwaukee’s 22-0 demolition of Seattle on 18 August, the 20-0 waxing of Cincinnati a month later, and the comprehensive dusting of their division – their fourth consecutive National League Central title and fifth in six years – by 14 games. Baseball’s owners, at their persuasive best, would have their paying customers believe that the Brewers’ franchise-record 103 regular-season wins also were an illusion, or worse, the dreaded outlier, even though Milwaukee have won 770 games since 2018, the fourth-most in all of baseball. Even when Milwaukee exhaled and made the Dodgers look old in a stirring four-game sweep, ESPN’s Jeff Passan reported the owners’ position remained unchanged. The Brewers to that point had not helped dispel the notion. They had sputtered badly in recent postseasons, giving life to the thought that maybe their summer wins really were empty. Only one thing could ever change that perception: winning in the playoffs. Surrounded by so many friends that a Wednesday evening at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg felt like a home game – the good folks of Milwaukee and points beyond will remember the date specifically as 28 October 2026 – the Brewers rejected the notion they could not win both because of the economic forces against them and the intangibles champions possess but seemed to go missing from their group when the clocks fall back. They did so by winning the World Series for the first time in their 58-year history, and doing so resoundingly, destroying the Tampa Bay Rays in five games. The final score was 4-1, ending a month that will be played and replayed in the minds and DVRs of Milwaukeeans. Few teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchs. Few teams so emphatically demanded so much of themselves. What had been accepted as fact has always been decidedly fiction – but fiction can live as truth until it is exposed, killed once and for all on the ballfield. No matter the argument to concede the season to the inevitability of money and not having it, the truth is the Brewers have been an elite team for the better part of the decade, and the signature joy of this World Series run has been the joyous, ruthless attention this team paid to the task of not merely believing they were championship level, but proving it, to every team that opposed them this season, but more thrillingly, to themselves. Nothing else mattered but emerging from this month as champions – not the payroll or the labor battles that will almost certainly shut the game down over the coming weeks and quite likely wipe out spring training and at least a portion of the 2027 season and the Brewers’ title defense, or the mystique and riches of the two-time defending champion Dodgers; not the twin histories of having never won the whole thing since that long-ago day near the end of spring training in 1970 when the Seattle Pilots’ equipment truck loaded in Tempe, Arizona, but the team didn’t know where home would be as a court order determined if the truck was headed back to Seattle or to a new home in Milwaukee, or the Dodgers’ long record of torturing Milwaukee baseball. That torture dated back to losses to Brooklyn in 1956, Los Angeles in 1959 before the Braves left town for Atlanta, and to the recent postseason defeats to the Dodgers in 2018, 2020 and 2025, when the Brewers began their second decade in the National League by being as good as the franchise had been since the big American League years of Yount and Cooper, Molitor and Fingers, only to suffer the familiar NL fate of being good, but not good enough to beat the Dodgers when it counted. The Brewers were nowhere men – only the World Series would heal the past wounds that have stayed with them, highlighted by last year’s humiliating four-game sweep in the NLCS by the Dodgers – and they played with a buoyant and calm desperation, a gorgeous certainty that could not last, but did. The Brewers won the requisite 11 games to claim the trophy and needed only 13 games to do it, but trailed in eight of them. Yet, as an example of their belief, none of their series this postseason was tied after two games. Both Brewers losses in these playoffs were by one run. When they faltered, they did not panic as desperate teams too close to the prize do; they got tougher. Jake Bauers’ soul-snatching at-bats against the Dodgers offered a sign, the youthful charges of Series MVP catcher William Contreras, Jackson Chourio, and the too-young-to-care stardom of Cooper Pratt was another, coming back from down 4-0 against the Dodgers and Rays was still another, and the two-out, eight-run fifth in Game 3 seemed to end the Series – except that it didn’t. Most impressively, responding to losing Game 4 three outs from the title in the bottom of the 12th not with the doubts that create suspense and pave the way to epic collapse, but by returning the next night unfazed and champagne-ready, demanding they be taken not as a cute story but a hard-edged team ready, at long last, for its close-up. Neither the doomsday rhetoric of an unnecessary work stoppage or the fearsome reputation of the former champions, nor the feisty underdog spirit of an admirable Tampa Bay could block the sunlight, too long in arriving, of this Brewers team. They played pure, determined baseball and responded to the insult – and it is an insult – that the decimal points on the balance sheet meant more than winning 103 games and 90-plus so many times before that, meant that once it was time to deal the cards they couldn’t win. The Brewers won 114 games in 2026, finished the regular season 15-3, and then went 11-2 in the playoffs for a grand total of 26-5 since 7 September. Baseball’s finances need addressing, but they don’t require shuttering the place. Even with the game the owners are playing in their quest to increase franchise values, their words speak an untruth – Brewers owner Mark Attanasio purchased the team from Bud Selig in 2005 for $223m and the team that supposedly cannot win (but did) has a valuation by Forbes at $1.9bn. The game that matters, however, is the one on the field, the one that belongs to the players, and this October, there was absolutely nobody better. Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He also writes on Substack

headline: Pasifika pride finds a home at Rugby League World Cup: ‘Passion brings us together’
trail_text: Supporters in western Sydney are adding colour and community to the tournament as their home nations compete on the global stage
body_text: At Harold Wood Uniting Church in Auburn, Viliame and Talita Latu are the centre of attention. The local Tongan congregation, which revitalised the 116-year-old church building in 1997, is celebrating the couple’s first Sunday church service as husband and wife. But the number of Tongan flags fluttering from cars outside show the pair aren’t the only thing on people’s minds this week. Tonga’s representative rugby league team, Mate Ma’a Tonga, handily beat Lebanon’s Cedars in front of more than 25,000 fans at Commbank Stadium in Parramatta the Friday before in the Rugby League World Cup. In a case of terrible timing, the match clashed with the couple’s wedding day. “The game was on my wedding night! Made it hard for me to watch it,” says Viliame, who goes by Laka. “In the video of our wedding reception, there are going to be so many people watching the game on their phones,” Talita adds. “There was someone on their iPad, too.” Despite the usual hand-wringing about blowout scorelines between wildly mismatched sides in the pool stage, this year’s World Cup has already produced enough unforgettable moments to lay claim to being the best ever. The tournament opener, where Australia pipped a ferocious New Zealand at the death 24-22, was a classic that sold out Allianz Stadium. A fast and courageous Fiji took the Kangaroos all the way, going down 36-22 in a result that flattered the defending champions. Tonga made history in their first Cup game, beating England for the first time. Even before the tournament kicked off, western Sydney had well and truly caught World Cup fever. Parramatta Road is a sea of Ford Raptors, delivery vans and garbage trucks bearing Tongan, Samoan, Fijian, Lebanese and New Zealand flags. Team jerseys and national colours are becoming part of the unofficial dress code at church services. Samoa and Penrith Panthers winger Brian To’o broke the internet the week the tournament began, ripping his shirt off and doing the splits onstage in front of thousands of Samoa supporters at a fan day in Mount Druitt. Demand for tickets has been so great it has caught organisers flat-footed. A plan to move Sunday’s Tonga-Samoa blockbuster from Commbank to Accor Stadium at Olympic Park, which the NRL believes would have brought in 60,000 fans, was only unsuccessful because it would have clashed with pre-booked concerts. Aisea Taufa, one of the congregation’s lay preachers, says plenty of congregants missed out. “We tried to book [tickets for the Samoa game], but we were too late. It sold out two weeks ago,” he says. Supporters who can’t get to games are flocking to off-field fan events instead. Rugby league legends of Lebanese heritage like Hazem El Masri, Tim Mannah and Josh Mansour led thousands of Cedars fans on a march through the Parramatta CBD before the Tonga game, complete with drums and a contingent of Tongan fans joining in the dabke. (“Pauline Hanson is in cardiac arrest [right now],” reads one of the top comments on the Cedars’ Instagram.) “When the fans marched to the stadium, they marched as a group. We didn’t let Lebanon march by themselves, we all went together,” Laka says. “That passion, it brings us together as a community.” While Lebanon are yet to post a win (though hopes are high ahead of their meeting France on Sunday), their fanbase has been one of the most passionate of the entire tournament. Speaking to Triple M after the Tonga game, lock forward Jalal Bazzaz explained why. “Our little nation, we’ve been through a lot,” Bazzaz said. “To get out there with the boys, the brotherhood, and give a little hope to our little nation, it means the world to us.” Tongan fans can take more bragging rights than most for this World Cup’s success. It was superstar North Queensland Cowboys forward Jason Taumalolo who breathed life back into international rugby league when he decided to represent Tonga rather than New Zealand at the 2017 tournament. While Taumalolo attracted plenty of criticism at the time, he and other Pasifika players who chose to represent their heritage rather than cashing paycheques from Australia or New Zealand kickstarted the Pacific-nation revolution that has made this year’s tournament so compelling. “[Taumalolo] did that to inspire the younger generations who are coming through now,” says Laka. “He showed that it’s not all about the money. It’s about representing your home country, the place where your family’s from.” Given Tonga and Samoa’s unbeaten runs, anticipation is at fever pitch ahead of their meeting on Sunday, with fans believing Australia’s decades-long dominance of the international game could be coming to an end. “Tonga can go all the way,” Laka says. “Our defence against England was so solid. With halves like Isaiya Katoa, we can go all the way.” “Here on Sunday, it’s gonna be red,” Taufa vows. “This week, we’re the Church of MMT.”

headline: England urged to hold nerve as Rugby League World Cup hopes hang by a thread
trail_text: Brian McDermott urged his side to keep their nerve as they attempt to secure what would be a remarkable qualification for the semi-finals
body_text: The England head coach, Brian McDermott, has urged his side to keep their nerve as they attempt to hold up their end of the bargain on Friday and secure what would be a remarkable qualification for the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup. Defeat by Tonga in their opening group game a fortnight ago appeared to all but consign England to an early exit, owing in no small part to a complex and shortened format, with the tournament reduced to 10 teams. However, the margin of their 82-0 win against France last Saturday means qualification is still possible, albeit unlikely. They need to defeat Papua New Guinea in Wollongong and hope Tonga beat Samoa on Sunday, with a 68-point swing required in points difference between England and the Samoans. That essentially means McDermott’s side will once again have to pile on the points against a capable Kumuls side who will pose a sterner challenge than the French. McDermott described the circumstances and permutations as “remarkable” this week, knowing his side must win big to stand a chance of avoiding becoming the first England side in history to fail to reach the semi-finals of the tournament. But he warned his players not to be distracted by the unique task at hand and the need to score points. “I don’t know how many coaches have been in this position before where they know they need to win by a big score,” he said. “It’s a difficult situation to negotiate because you don’t want to show any disrespect to the opposition. So to suggest we would want to score a lot of points, it sounds disrespectful. “There’s a discipline in that we don’t start looking for things or searching for things outside of how we want to play. And that was a really impressive trick against France because we knew we had points in us and they weren’t coming for that first 20 minutes. We can’t get to the points first, we’ve got to get through the physicality.” That patience will be key against a Papua New Guinea side who have a large contingent of England-based players. They were initially resolute against Samoa last week in Port Moresby, trailing 14-6 at half-time before imploding in the second half to lose 64-6. They, like England, need a huge victory to stand any chance of qualification. But the spotlight is undoubtedly on England, who start as heavy favourites. In the pursuit of points, McDermott’s one significant team change has the Hull KR hooker Jez Litten starting in place of the reigning Man of Steel, Wigan’s Brad O’Neill, who drops down to the bench. Litten has provided a spark in both games so far and his dynamic attacking play will be key again. “It’s more about the best fit for the gameplan,” McDermott said. “They all understand the concept of it being a squad effort. It’s not just a team effort. We’ve got a specific task against PNG and I think it’ll be a stiffer test than against France. And we find ourselves in a similar situation, because we don’t just need to beat them, we need to beat them convincingly.” McDermott’s expansive style which produced points aplenty last week will be key again, as will the performances of Mikey Lewis and the captain, George Williams. Lewis will start from the bench and look to stretch a tiring Kumuls side, while Williams has drawn praise from McDermott for his displays so far. Both possess the running threat that could unlock the requisite scoreline England need to at least ensure Sunday morning’s game between Tonga and Samoa has meaning. “George was the guy who broke the game open for us last week against France,” McDermott said. “We faced a really determined France in that first 20 and George was the guy who ran. “That’s why he’s in the team, he’s in the team because he’s the captain and because he’s a good player, but he’s also a runner. And he ran, and broke France’s defensive line down and opened it up for us a bit.” Meanwhile the permutations for England’s women, who kick off earlier on Friday morning, are more straightforward. Beat Samoa, they and will be in the semi-finals – but defeat means they are going home. England’s wheelchair side begin the defence of their World Cup title against Wales in the early hours of Friday, with Tom Coyd’s side heavy favourites to go all the way once again.

headline: Everybody hates Pat: is a cabal of college kids really trying to bring down ESPN’s star meathead?
trail_text: Pat McAfee’s reaction to a few mild jokes shows how the ubiquitous ESPN host he’s happy to whip up a crowd into a hostile frenzy but is terrified of any criticism
body_text: It was all shaping up to be a golden year for Pat McAfee. The man who landed a five-year, $85m deal in 2023 to take The Pat McAfee Show to ESPN had cemented himself as the star attraction of the sports broadcaster’s bold new era of stunts, stupidity and memebrain swill. His persistently honking presence on the set of ESPN’s College GameDay had helped push ratings to new heights. ESPN executives were so impressed with McAfee they were reportedly in negotiations to award him a new contract worth between $60m and $65m a year; one even went so far as to describe him as a “generational” media talent. Then, over the weekend, disaster struck. A handful of college kids attacked him online ahead of his appearance with College GameDay at the University of Utah. Well, “attacked” is maybe overstating things: they made a few mild jokes at his expense. But it was all too much for ESPN’s brightest blimp. Suddenly, McAfee’s world came crashing down. His initial reaction, to be fair, was mild: “The university’s Instagram account posted something talking a little trash about me last night, which I certainly love,” he said ahead of the Utes’ clash with the Houston Cougars last week. But by Monday the narrative had changed. On his eponymous show, McAfee said he had “never felt more uncomfortable” than he did on the Utah campus, alluding to the assassination of Charlie Kirk as a reason for his unease: “I thought to myself: Has anything really scary happened at, like, a college gathering in the state of Utah recently? Do you think we should be amplifying reasons for why people hate my guts as a university? I don’t know.” Well, Pat, neither do I. To read this comically melodramatic retelling of his time at Utah you might assume last week’s College GameDay was uncommonly vicious and antagonistic. Instead, it was the usual chop-up of hype, half-assed technical analysis and shouting, in which McAfee supplied his standard mix of meandering rants and basic crowd work and the gathered masses, in turn, responded with cheers and (good-natured) boos as expected. The video that McAfee implied had him fearing for his life, posted to the university’s Instagram and TikTok accounts, involved a handful of students poking very light fun at the ESPN host for ripping off his shirt on set (which he does often) and spouting “corny” lines in place of real analysis (ditto); one of McAfee’s would-be assassins even emphasized that “we love you bro” as he implored McAfee to “keep the shirt on”. The wokes and the leftists are always the most precious snowflakes on earth until some kid does a mild impersonation of Pat McAfee ripping his top open; when that happens it’s a federal emergency and the national guard needs to be called in to set things right. Any more of this mild banter from the brutes and ingrates of the American undergraduate population and McAfee will be calling his buddy Donald Trump to request Secret Service protection. Even more bizarre than McAfee’s amazingly thin-skinned overreaction to this absolute non-event is how seriously his claims of imminent danger to his life (stemming, once again, from a video in which a few students say they don’t want to see McAfee’s naked torso) have been taken by those around him. The school published a groveling apology for its actions and deleted the offending video from its social media channels, while ESPN issued a statement of support for McAfee and “the very real and valid concerns he has around safety and security”. During his ascent at ESPN, McAfee has perfected all the attributes of a WWE-style heel – the gift for offense, the shirtlessness, the penchant for writhing on the ground like an upturned beetle – with the exception of one: he absolutely cannot stand it when he’s the butt of the joke. The man is a machine at whipping a crowd into a hostile frenzy then runs in fright the moment the first boos hit his ears. McAfee is perhaps the leading light of the rightwing sports bros who’ve come to prominence in the age of Trump: these men love sports, love their country, love their president, and are unsure what to make of women. Trump himself made his debut appearance on The Pat McAfee Show late last year, and over this summer McAfee was on hand to lend some primetime meat to the inaugural Patriot Games, the president’s Hitlerian exercise in uplift for the white youth of America. It’s perhaps no surprise, then, that McAfee has absorbed completely the personality traits of the president: to the casual misogyny, the constant moaning about “woke”, the boorishness and the egomania can now be added McAfee’s Trumpian inability to take a joke or any kind of criticism, however mild or well-intentioned; in the deranged McAfee worldview it now seems even college kids, a big part of College GameDay’s own audience, are part of the shadowy network of villainy working to bring ESPN’s star beetroot down. Whether it’s punching across at critical media outlets or punching down at fans who don’t like the kind of shirt-ripping frattiness he’s introduced to College GameDay, McAfee never seems more engaged in his work than when snarling about the “rats”, “marks”, “losers” and “puppets” snapping at his feet. It cannot be emphasized too much how stupid and overblown this whole concocted controversy is. What is really going on here? Is this all reflective of a desire for attention on McAfee’s part, another demonstration of his continuous need to make everything – in sport, on TV, in culture at large – About Him? Or is ESPN so heavily degraded and virality-brained now, so in thrall to the Magaverse and its perverse understanding of the world, that the empty suits who run the place genuinely feel the operation will collapse without a happy McAfee – placated and kept safe from the everyday terrorists roving the college campuses of America – at its core? Perhaps it’s a bit of both. As Soft Pat’s star at ESPN has risen and he’s been handed more prestigious on-air assignments, the statements emanating from the C-suite hailing his “generational” and otherworldly talent have become more and more ludicrous; amid reports of his monster new contract, McAfee is now involved in Monday Night Football and there’s talk of potentially using his Super Bowl alt-cast for even higher honors on screen. “Pat can do whatever he wants,” ESPN executive vice-president Mike Foss recently mused, and there’s a real sense that the whole network is under the spell of McAfee’s bare breast, that – if only as a cultural project – the erstwhile “Worldwide Leader in Sports” now belongs to McAfee. The wholesale enrollment of a once-proud network into the cult of McAfee does not reflect the man’s talent: he’s good for ratings, sure, but any old rightwing purplehead could curl up into a topless ball, screeching, and do what he does. Instead, it’s a sign of the profound confusion that has gripped traditional media in the post-cordcutting era of vertical video and endless slop. Nothing else works, seems to be the thinking; maybe this idiot will. In another context, or another era, the TV triumph of the outcast, the oddball, the unlikely star might have heralded a deepening of the culture, a growing sophistication in our collective understanding of what it takes to be appealing as a popular media talent. But so much of what McAfee represents is the kind of meatheaded insensitivity that sports broadcasting – with its polish and professionalism – was historically designed to supersede, especially at a place like ESPN. Figures like McAfee drag us all back into the frathouse, the kegger, the swamp, and now they won’t even let us joke about it.

headline: The NFL has a host of Hall of Fame caliber receivers. But which one is the best?
trail_text: Quarterbacks in 2026 have a series of dazzling weapons at their disposal. We rank the best of the receivers in the NFL at the moment
body_text: NB: We have restricted the list below to players in their prime years, so excellent, older receivers such as Mike Evans and Davante Adams have been left out. 1) Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Seattle Seahawks The quality of receivers across the NFL at present is sky high. And Smith-Njigba is a cut above the rest. There are faster and more physical wideouts, but none have the precise, impossible to cover route running of JSN. Most receivers have a tell that hints at their next move. Not Smith-Njigba though: defensive backs have to guess and second guess his movements, which leads to consistent, easy separation and massive yardage totals. The 24-year-old’s talent is so great that he quickly ended DK Metcalf’s time in Seattle and took over the offense, leading them to the Super Bowl last season. Smith-Njigba is the key to Seattle’s offense, not Sam Darnold at quarterback. Any league average passer could be elevated to playoff success throwing to Smith-Njigba. After seven games this season he is closing in on 1,000 receiving yards. He almost broke 1,800 yards in 2025 but, at this pace, he could be the first NFL receiver to crack 2,000 yards in a season. 2) Puka Nacua, Los Angeles Rams Not a lot was thought of Nacua heading into the 2023 draft. He was seen as a decent option as a slot receiver or a gadget guy. NFL analyst Lance Zierlein’s assessment wasn’t exactly glowing: “Nacua is an athletic wideout lacking the twitch or speed to attack man coverage at a successful rate. However, the ball skills and competitive nature he brings to the field give him a fighting chance to make a roster.” Teams were put off by his lack of speed – his 40-yard dash was the 37th-best among wide receivers drafted in 2023 – and he fell to the Rams in the fifth round. But the NFL isn’t all about straight-line speed. He did well in the combine’s gauntlet drill – which involves running across the field while catching balls fired from either side – and Nacua reached the highest top speed of any receiver who did not miss a catch. What’s even more special is how quickly he adapted to the NFL. His first game: 10 receptions for 119 yards. Lucky start? Nope. Game two: 147 yards. He had an off day on his third outing with “only” 72 yards. Game four he roared back with 163 yards and a touchdown. The only knock on the 25-year-old is his availability – he has only played all 17 games once in his career – and he has been mired in off-field issues. But when he’s on the field he has been ultra consistent, and could go for 1,500 yards this year, despite missing a couple of games. 3) Ja’Marr Chase, Cincinnati Bengals The Bengals top receiver in yards this season is Tee Higgins by a wide margin, but Chase is still the leader – alongside Joe Burrow – of Cincinnati’s offense. That includes in the locker room too. On Sunday, Chase gave a stirring half-time speech after the Bengals went into the break 13-0 down. “I came in here screaming, saying, ‘Somebody’s got to make a play for us, somebody got to make a play,’” Chase said after the game. “And I told our offense we can’t look at our defense the whole time. We’ve got to step this shit up and make something work.” And they did. The Bengals scored five unanswered touchdowns to obliterate the Ravens for a vital victory in the ultra competitive AFC North. Chase’s elite speed, agility and phenomenal hands are a nightmare for defenders. He often starts seasons slowly, so expect great things to come from a player capable of unparalleled production. Chase’s has three career games of 200 or more receiving yards, the best in the NFL among active players. 4) Justin Jefferson, Minnesota Vikings The Vikings star is in a tricky spot. His talent is undeniable, as is his track record. At the start of the season his 8,480 yards receiving since 2020 were the most for any player in the first six years of their career. That total includes last year though, when Jefferson recorded his lowest total for receiving yards, touchdowns and first downs. Then again, he did have JJ McCarthy, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer throwing him the ball. And in another season in which Minnesota’s defense is doing the heavy lifting, Jefferson is still on good form despite an uninspiring cast of quarterbacks. He already has more touchdowns (3) than he did in the whole of last season, and there are signs that Kyler Murray could be able to give him the service he deserves. Against the Saints, Murray went all-in with a fastball to Jefferson in the back of the endzone amid blanket coverage. It all looked so simple as Jefferson popped and came down with the ball, while falling backwards, for the touchdown. Hopefully Murray can give Jefferson a few more moments like that as the 6-0 Vikings builds towards the playoffs. The best of the rest Zay Flowers, Amon-Ra St Brown, Chris Olave, CeeDee Lamb, Christian Watson, (honorary tight end inclusion) Trey McBride and Higgins all have a case here but Drake London gets the nod owing to untapped potential and immense physicality. He always appears to be open, thanks to a 6ft 4in frame, brilliant hands and great route running. He lacks speed but the 25-year-old is as close as it gets to a Mike Evans clone. He would be accruing similarly impressive stats if the Atlanta Falcons had more competent quarterback play. A rogues gallery of Desmond Ridder, Kirk Cousins, Marcus Mariota, Taylor Heinicke and Cooper Rush have stymied London’s numbers since he joined the NFL in 2022, but in 19 games with Michael Penix at quarterback he has 1,822 yards and 10 touchdowns. Penix is good but by no means great, and London still has much more to offer.

headline: ‘I’m no special guy. We can all do this’: Loek Hartog on rescuing Ollie Millroy from a burning car
trail_text: Last month in Shanghai, the Dutch driver saved Ollie Millroy’s life after a crash. The incident created a unique friendship and a shared determination to improve safety
body_text: Winter is coming and, at eight in the morning, Amsterdam is dark as Loek Hartog and I walk towards the park. The GT motor racing driver is only 24 but, after all he did last month, when he showed extraordinary courage in saving the life of his fellow racer Ollie Millroy, we talk easily about life and death. Hartog sips a takeaway coffee and, as we stroll, he asks if the world seems to be in a worse state than usual. Paris is burning, Kyiv is reeling, Vladimir Putin is being hailed as “a humanitarian” by Donald Trump’s envoy and the robots are coming for us. These are grim times, but I remind Hartog that he gave us hope as, after ripping off the doors of Millroy’s burning car as if he had stepped out of a superhero movie, his humanity was remarkably moving. Hartog dragged Millroy to safety before trying to comfort the 36-year-old Briton after an accident that left him with six broken ribs, a damaged lung, a splintered collarbone, a broken hand, a fractured C6 neck vertebrae and a stunned sense that he had almost died at the China GT. We sit near a small lake and Hartog explains he will soon fly to Shanghai again for the next round of racing in the GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup. This weekend he is back on the same track where he and Millroy shared something profound, and driving the same kind of car that almost killed his new friend. A low sun rises over Vondelpark, the birds are singing and cyclists whir past in an unbroken hum as the young Dutch driver resists being called heroic. “Maybe the biggest thing to process was that a lot of people actually had the balls to tell me: ‘Oh, I would have never done the same,’” he says. “That made me more emotional than the actual circumstances and this is why I’m sitting here. We need to do better as a society. We need to stand up for each other. You already touched on this, with what we see in the news. We’re all humans and we need each other. Why be against each other?” Has the accident changed Hartog? “Of course. I look at things with a completely different angle now. But it’s like an additional angle. It’s not that I’ve changed my character. I’m still the same guy with just one experience more.” He adds: “The biggest thing I’m conscious of now is not every time somebody calls this a heroic act, which is a very nice appraisal. It’s when people say: ‘I wouldn’t have acted the same.’ I’d love to trust people. I know you can’t expect these things but the world would be a better place if we can. I came away from it unscathed and, as humans, it’s not that hard. Really, I’m no special guy. We can all do this.” It’s worth recounting what “this” amounted to for Hartog. He was driving at “around 270km/h” down a straight when he saw fire engulf Millroy’s Ferrari after he had been hit by a car involved in a different collision. “I saw a lot of flames,” Hartog remembers. “I’m quite tall, 6ft 6in, but I think the flames were twice my height. So I knew there was a high chance of him not getting out himself. It was quite serious.” Did he feel afraid? “It’s kind of similar to stepping on a surfboard for the first time. You don’t know what you’re doing. It was more that kind of feeling – not really scared. For me there was no other scenario than I would get him out.” Hartog didn’t consider the danger that Millroy’s car might explode. “No, you don’t think of that. It was like the movies because it felt like slow motion. When I watched it back for the first time I was like: ‘That was it?’ It felt so much longer.” He tried to open the driver’s door before running round to the other side of the car. Hartog yanked the doors off but says, with a smile: “It looks a lot more spectacular [than it was].” When a marshal finally arrived, Hartog took the fire extinguisher from the man, who was not wearing flame-proof clothing. He doused the worst of the fire before, after two attempts, pulling Millroy out of the burning wreck. It took just over a minute and Hartog says: “Ollie was confused and not aware he was in a car in flames. It was like he was knocked out in a boxing match and not able to breathe. He kept repeating: ‘Where am I? What happened? I think I broke my back.’ The help was not the best because not many people were speaking English. So they kept moving him and I kept telling everyone [to stop]. That was maybe the worst thing for me because I felt the most helpless.” Hartog and Millroy sat near a barrier as they waited for the medics. “That’s where we became a bit more emotional because I was telling him: ‘You’re going to be OK. There’s help on the way.’ I was making eye contact, but he was in shock.” After Millroy was taken away, Hartog drove his car slowly back to the pits. “I was like: ‘I need to stop [racing].’ You think like that in those moments which is human and natural. But then you think of all that [racing] means to you. So [his doubts] very quickly turned into: ‘When can I go out back again?’ It’s like a drug, racing.” Hartog visited Millroy in hospital that night. “He was very drugged, but I showed him on my phone what happened and he kept saying: ‘Oh my God, nobody told me it was this bad. Oh my God, is that me?’ He realised it would have been very different if I wasn’t there.” It felt as if fate had intervened because, as Hartog says: “I was doing very bad in the race and, usually, I’m not running so far at the back. But that actually put me in the position to respond the way I did. So it’s such a strange turn of events that led to this. It’s unbelievable.” Before the race on 5 September he had “a very bad feeling. I reflected more on myself, like something would be wrong for me. In the end, it turned out differently.” Millroy has a wife, Fern, and three children. That night, everything they could have lost hit Hartog. “That was really emotional for me,” he says. “I couldn’t sleep because I was overloaded and then Wiep, my partner, sent me a picture of Fern, the kids and Ollie at Disneyland. She was like: ‘You did it for them.’ That really struck me.” The deep gratitude felt by Ollie and Fern meant they flew to Amsterdam to surprise him this month. “My birthday is 5 October,” Hartog says, “and I thought I was going for lunch with Wiep. She said: ‘Oh, we need to get a big frame for my masters’ degree before lunch.’ I was like: ‘Why can’t we get it after lunch?’ She was saying: ‘We need to get it now.’ I was like: ‘OK, OK.’ Then we walked into this restaurant [near the framers] and I asked for a table for two. We were taken to one where Ollie and Fern were sitting.” Hartog’s shock gave way to delight and then appreciation. “It was really special and they gave me a very special gift. They gave me a watch, because I gave them more time.” That simple gesture is laced with deeper resonance and Hartog asks if I would like to see it. He spreads the Rolex across his open hand, and we think how time would have stopped for the Millroy family had he not saved Ollie’s life. Did he and Millroy know each other before the accident? “No. We’d heard of each other but we’re from different generations. Ollie has been a benchmark and a competitor to some of my mentors.” Despite their difference in age, Hartog and Millroy are determined to work together. “Absolutely. That’s the most important thing – that something positive comes out of this. If the headline had been ‘British racing driver had a fatal accident’ rather than ‘was saved’, it would have been a completely bad story for our sport. We don’t want that to happen, ever.” It took 47 seconds for a marshal to appear and more than four minutes for medical assistance to arrive at the Shanghai track. We discuss the anger of Betty Chen, Millroy’s teammate at Ferrari, who wrote: “The measures taken by the organisers following today’s incident, particularly the lack of an immediate and adequate emergency response, are something we cannot accept. The safety of drivers and team members must always come before anything else. What happened today and the way the situation was handled is truly unacceptable.” Hartog understands Chen’s anger. “Absolutely. First of all, an incident like this should never happen. And, secondly, there should be no driver that needs to stop to help in a case like this.” He continues: “Lots of people told me the marshals are not allowed to cross the guardrails on their own, which makes total sense on paper. But once something like this happens in front of you, I cannot believe you’re telling people to go against their feeling. If your gut tells you to do something, it should be your cue to act. We should mandate rules that are more human.” There is something deeply human in Hartog as, walking back to his apartment, he talks about his hope that he and Millroy may race each other again next year. But we sense the difficulties Millroy faces when we have a WhatsApp video call with him. The injured racer talks openly about how he is struggling since he took himself off his strong painkillers. He compares it to the withdrawal symptoms a heroin addict might suffer, while the pain has become excruciating. We postpone our joint interview until the next morning. Hartog and I are convinced that Millroy won’t be well enough to talk and we agree to leave him in peace during his long and painful recovery. But 24 hours later Millroy messages me to say he is ready to chat on a Zoom call from Dubai. “I was hoping to be in better shape six weeks on, but I’m really struggling,” Millroy says. “I’m in a lot of pain. It’s really hard and I’m getting frustrated. The meds gave me a false sense of security because the team are testing at Sebring [in Florida] in four weeks and I’d thought I might be all right for that. But since I’ve come off the painkillers, I can’t even imagine getting anywhere near a racing car. I can’t even get in a road car at the moment, it’s that sore. I’ve got an appointment this afternoon to work out a plan but it’s made me realise I’m a lot further away than I thought.” Hartog leans towards his friend on screen and says: “It’s pretty insane what your body has been trying to heal the last six weeks.” Millroy nods. “I guess this is one thing I can’t rush, I can’t force, I can’t influence, other than doing what I’m doing, which is eating the right things and trying to rest. But I’m in so much pain I can’t even sleep. It’s just in my head that I want to move on. It’s in our nature, right? I guess it’s why we do what we do. We’re not the most patient. “It’s a really weird feeling because I’m also enjoying time at home with my wife and kids. So am I desperate to switch back to all the travel? I don’t think so. The bit I love about motorsport is driving a racing car and that’s not been impacted at all by what’s happened. I’m excited to get back behind the wheel and compete. But I don’t feel like my life’s been put on hold because I’m not at a circuit next weekend.” The two friends talk engagingly about the addiction of racing and it’s striking that Millroy’s son, Mylo, has already fallen for karting. “It was pretty crazy,” Millroy says. “We were still in hospital when he had his first race. My wife flew out a couple of hours after the accident. She was watching it live on TV at home [in Dubai] and got the first flight to China. She told the kids I had food poisoning and she needed to come to China to help me get home. But news of the accident spread around the school and, even though they’re just eight years old, kids were seeing it on YouTube and parents were talking about it. “On the Wednesday after the accident Mylo called us in tears because he’d seen it. He’d watched enough racing to know that that doesn’t happen very often. He said: ‘I want to be with you.’ We said: ‘The best thing you can do is have a great weekend and just enjoy everything on the track.’ And he did. Even at his age you can see the addiction and passion for racing.” Mylo finished third and was awarded the top novice prize at the UAE International. “He’s off to a great start,” his dad says. “But the most important thing is that he’s enjoying it.” Hartog had told me the previous day about his own start in motorsport that had been fuelled by his father’s love of GT racing. “The best thing is the time you get to spend with your parents or with your dad,” he says before talking directly to Millroy. “Ollie, you and Mylo will spend a lot of time together in the winter. That’s great.” The drivers are determined to bring about change in racing. “We want to try to save more lives by pushing for better safety,” Millroy says of their joint objective. “Safety has improved so much in the last few decades. But we’ve got to a stage everybody has sat back and said: ‘Motorsport can’t get any safer than it is now.’ But my accident proved it can, especially in some parts of the world. It’s been a wake-up call for a lot of organisers, a lot of circuits. We’d like to get the whole motorsport community together to make sure steps are taken to make the sport safer – because it’s very clear there are still areas in need of improvement.” This weekend Millroy will turn on his TV and watch Hartog race in Shanghai while remembering his traumatic accident. He says: “I’m not particularly angry about anything that happened. All the positivity since then massively overwhelms any anger.” He amuses us as he recalls the look on Hartog’s face when he and Fern were surprise guests at his birthday: “It was pure shock as he had absolutely no idea. It was brilliant.” I know how often Millroy has thanked Hartog but is there anything else he would like to say to the man who saved him? “Thank you again Loek and don’t change. I know you won’t. This is in your nature and you’re an inspiration to all of us in sport and life in general. Fern and I now think about life differently because you really put everything into perspective. So thank you for myself and also on behalf of so many millions of people that have seen this story. You’ve been really inspirational.” Hartog’s face fills the screen and he says: “Thank you, Ollie. I’m really looking forward to the friendship that comes out of this, talking about Mylo’s career and the fun stuff which keeps us busy every day. In the three times we’ve met each other in person it has been very special and always too short. I look forward to it being normal and to seeing Ollie being fully himself again and smiling a big and really complete smile. That would be special.”

headline: Milwaukee Brewers close out Tampa Bay Rays to end 57-year wait for first World Series title
trail_text: Milwaukee ended a wait of nearly six decades for their first World Series championship, beating Tampa Bay 4-1 to clinch the title in five games
body_text: The Milwaukee Brewers captured their first World Series crown on Wednesday night, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 to complete a four-games-to-one victory and end more than half a century of waiting for baseball’s biggest prize. Rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt drove in two runs and Jacob Misiorowski pitched five and two-thirds scoreless innings as Milwaukee put the finishing touches on a charmed season that began in spring training with championship ambitions and ended with a maiden title in the franchise’s 58th year. Trevor Megill was mobbed by his teammates on the mound after Richie Palacios grounded to second baseman Brice Turang, who threw to Jake Bauers for the final out before a sold-out crowd of 40,489 at Tampa Bay’s Tropicana Field. “It’s the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city’s waited a long, long time for this and we’re so happy to bring it home to them,” said Christian Yelich, the 2018 National League MVP and the Brewers’ longest-tenured position player. “Can’t wait to get back there and celebrate.” William Contreras was named Most Valuable Player of the series after batting .381/.435/.429 with four RBIs across the five games, including a run-scoring double in the clincher. The 28-year-old became the eighth catcher to win the award and the first since fellow Venezuelan Salvador Perez for the Kansas City Royals in 2015. Contreras also helped contain Tampa Bay’s vaunted running game, throwing out four would-be base stealers, including two in the opener, while using the automated ball-strike challenge system to overturn 10 of 13 calls behind the plate. The honor capped a year in which he won the World Baseball Classic with Venezuela. “I don’t want to offend any of the other catchers in the league,” Contreras said through a translator. “But sitting up here today, champion of the world, I feel like I’m the best catcher in the league.” The Brewers, who arrived in Milwaukee in 1970 after one season as the Seattle Pilots, had reached the World Series only once before, bowing to the St Louis Cardinals in seven games in 1982 as American League champions. They switched to the National League in 1998 as part of the realignment accompanying the arrival of the expansion Rays and Arizona Diamondbacks, ensuring an even number of teams in each league. But that narrow defeat had remained the nearest they had come until this year, when a team blending young talent with October experience finally went one step further. Milwaukee had been three outs from completing a sweep on Tuesday night in Game 4 before letting a 12th-inning lead slip away. Given another opportunity less than 24 hours later, the Brewers stacked a four-run advantage behind Misiorowski, the brilliant right-hander who scattered two hits and one walk while striking out two before departing with a calf cramp. Tampa Bay’s best early opportunity came in the fourth, when Liam Hicks was hit by a pitch and Chandler Simpson singled, with Sal Frelick’s fielding error leaving runners at second and third with two outs. Misiorowski induced a groundout from Ben Williamson, whose pinch-hit single had won Game 4, to leave both runners stranded. He then put down the Rays in order in the fifth. “I don’t even have words,” said Misiorowski, the overwhelming favorite to win the NL Cy Young award who broke the World Series velocity record with a 103.5mph fastball on the first pitch of Game 1 last Friday. “I know they’re going crazy in Milwaukee.” Asked about the Brewers’ fans, thousands of whom had transformed the drab domed stadium in downtown St Petersburg into a home away from home, he added: “They’ve been nothing but supportive this year and in years prior and it has been amazing.” Pratt, the 22-year-old who made his major-league debut in June and collected four hits in Tuesday’s defeat, again supplied an important part of Milwaukee’s offense. Turang doubled in the second inning and, after Frelick was hit by a pitch, scored on Pratt’s single to center. Pratt was caught trying to reach second, but the Brewers had the lead. “This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real,” said Pratt, whose seven RBIs matched the rookie World Series record set by the Gil McDougald with the 1951 New York Yankees. “This is surreal. It only took four months!” Tampa Bay starter Drew Rasmussen, pitching on three days’ rest, kept the deficit at one through four innings before manager Kevin Cash turned to his bullpen. Milwaukee immediately doubled their advantage. Pratt singled off Kevin Kelly, Garrett Mitchell followed with another single and David Hamilton’s ground-ball single to right brought Pratt home for a 2-0 lead. The Brewers widened the gap in the sixth. Yelich was hit by a Garrett Cleavinger pitch and scored on Contreras’s double to left. Turang singled, then swiped second after Tyler Wells entered. Following a Frelick strikeout, Pratt lifted a sacrifice fly into foul territory in right, scoring Contreras to make it 4-0. The Rays conjured one final threat in the ninth. Hicks doubled with one out and, after Jonny DeLuca struck out, Simpson lined an RBI double to right off Megill, cutting Milwaukee’s lead to 4-1 and bringing the potential tying run into the on-deck circle. But Megill stranded Simpson at second to bring down the curtain on Tampa Bay’s campaign. The championship capped a season in which Milwaukee posted a major league-best 103-59 record before winning the NL pennant for the first time with a sweep of the deep-pocketed Dodgers in the NLCS, joining the 1923 Yankees as the only teams to eliminate a postseason opponent the year after being swept by them. For Pat Murphy, it was the crowning achievement of his third season in charge the Brewers. The 67-year-old had already won consecutive NL manager of the year awards before helming Milwaukee to the promised land. “The years of getting eliminated or being beaten last year by the Dodgers, that was a blessing because we learned from it and we grew, and we came in with a different attitude,” Murphy said. “We came in with a spirit about us, and we weren’t going to be denied.” “We weren’t great at a lot of things, but we were relentless,” he added. The Brewers established total command of the matchup with three consecutive victories: a narrow win in the opener, a comeback from four runs down in Game 2 and a 10-1 rout in Game 3. Tuesday’s setback denied them the chance to become the first team since the 1976 Cincinnati Reds to sweep both the League Championship Series and World Series, but merely postponed the inevitable. Tampa Bay, who won an AL-best 98 games despite one of Major League Baseball’s smallest payrolls, were left with a third World Series defeat following losses in 2008 and 2020. “Tonight we ran into a team that had elite starting pitching, very good pitching, and then as elite of a bullpen as I’ve ever seen,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said. Milwaukee’s relievers finished the postseason with a 1.38 ERA, the fourth-lowest in history among teams with at least 40 relief innings. The Brewers’ triumph marked the city of Milwaukee’s first World Series championship since 1957, when Lew Burdette’s three complete-game victories powered the Braves past the favored Yankees in a seven-game white-knuckler, delivering the city’s first professional sports title. The Braves relocated to Atlanta nine years later. This year’s Fall Classic guaranteed a first-time champion for only the second time in 107 years and the first since the Philadelphia Phillies faced Kansas City in 1980. Milwaukee claimed that distinction, leaving the Rays, Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners as the four active major-league franchises still seeking their first title. Amid the celebrations, Yelich remembered the beloved Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker, who died last year aged 90. “He’s smiling, man. He’s smiling. I really wish he could have been here to see this,” he said. “This one’s still for Bob and this is still for you.”

headline: Canada women snap eight-game skid against USA to avenge Olympic hockey heartbreak
trail_text: Canada beat the US for the first time since 2025 as two newcomers scored in a 5-3 victory, eight months after their Olympic gold-medal heartbreak
body_text: Canada ended an eight-game losing streak against the United States with a 5-3 victory on Wednesday night in Windsor, Ontario, as newcomers Caitlin Kraemer and Rosalie Tremblay scored their first senior international goals in a rematch of February’s Olympic gold-medal game. The win marked Canada’s first victory over their archrivals since 2025 and came eight months after the Americans snatched Olympic gold in Milan, where captain Hilary Knight scored the equalizer with 2:04 remaining in regulation before Megan Keller struck in overtime to deny Canada a fifth Olympic title. Sarah Fillier scored the winner with 8:15 remaining in the third period after the Americans had erased a two-goal deficit at the WFCU Centre. Laura Stacey added an empty-net goal with six seconds left to seal the victory in the first of two exhibition games ahead of next month’s women’s world championship in Denmark. Daryl Watts opened the scoring on a first-period power play before Kraemer, 20, doubled the lead off a pass from Nicole Gosling. Knight pulled a goal back for the Americans at 5:37 of the second period, but Tremblay, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Wisconsin, restored Canada’s two-goal advantage just over four minutes later with a rebound goal. The Americans mounted their comeback in the third period, with Abbey Murphy cutting the deficit to 3-2 at 3:48 before Caroline Harvey tied the game at 7:53. Fillier put Canada back in front with a shot high past US goaltender Aerin Frankel, and Ann-Renée Desbiens made several late saves to preserve the lead. The Americans entered the two-game series with all 23 members of their Olympic gold-medal team among a 31-player training camp roster. The teams meet again on Friday in Plymouth, Michigan. The women’s world championship will take place in Herning and Esbjerg, Denmark, from 6 to 16 November.

headline: Chiefs sign Justin Tucker in wake of sexual misconduct allegations as Butker struggles
trail_text: The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad
body_text: The Kansas City Chiefs have signed the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad after Harrison Butker’s poor start to the season. Tucker was widely considered one of the best kickers in NFL history until the Ravens released him in May 2025. The Ravens said his departure was a “football decision” after a slump in form, but the move came months after he was accused of inappropriate sexual behavior by massage therapists. Tucker denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges but he served a 10-game NFL ban for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. More than a dozen massage therapists from spas and wellness centers in the Baltimore area accused Tucker of inappropriate sexual behavior. One therapist who spoke to the Baltimore Banner, which broke the story, described Tucker’s alleged behavior as “really degrading”. Another said: “I can’t watch sports anymore. I see his face everywhere.” The 37-year-old has not played in the NFL since he was released by Baltimore. During his time with the Ravens, he made seven Pro Bowls and won the Super Bowl in his rookie season. His final season in Baltimore, in which he made just 73.3% of his field goals, was statistically the worst of his career. Tucker’s career average for field goals is 89.1%. On Wednesday, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid said he was not worried about Tucker joining the team. “He’s done his suspension, took care of that business there,” Reid said in response to a question about what message the move sent to the team’s female fans. “I’ll leave it at that.” When asked about Tucker’s past, Reid said: “We try to do our homework the best way we possibly can and talk to a lot of people, make sure things are OK.” Butker, who has won three Super Bowls with the Chiefs, has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts this season. The 31-year-old Butker has also been involved in off-field controversy. During a commencement address at Benedictine College in 2024, he criticized Pride month, working women, Joe Biden’s leadership during the Covid-19 pandemic and abortion. “I think it is you, the women, who have had the most diabolic lies told to you,” Butker said during the speech. “Some of you may go on to lead successful careers in the world, but I would venture to guess that the majority of you are most excited about your marriage and the children you will bring into this world. I can tell you that my beautiful wife Isabelle would be the first to say her life truly started when she started living her vocation as a wife and as a mother.” Reid said Butker had not been “as consistent as he wants” this season. “We love Harrison,” Reid said. “He’s one of my favorite guys. Sometimes things don’t go quite the way you want them, and you work on that. He understands the business and how it works. He’s struggled a little bit. Butker will get most of the reps this week. We’ll just see where it goes. It’s fluid.”

headline: Ernie Johnson, beloved host of Inside the NBA, to step away from show at end of season
trail_text: Ernie Johnson, the widely loved host of Inside the NBA, has announced he will step away at the end of the current season after 37 years in the role
body_text: Ernie Johnson, the widely loved host of Inside the NBA, has announced he will step away at the end of the current season after 37 years in the role. Johnson made the announcement on social media on Wednesday. “This is by no means the end,” Johnson said. “It’s just a turning of the page, and I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with Inside the NBA. And lastly, I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support, and on this day, for your understanding.” The 70-year-old said he had undergone bypass surgery 14 months ago and wants to spend time with his wife and grandchildren. He has dealt with a series of health issues during his career. In 2003, he was diagnosed with non-Hodgkins lymphoma and he missed presenting duties during the 2018 MLB playoffs due to blood clots in his legs. Johnson joined Inside the NBA in 1990 and works alongside arguably the most popular panel of analysts in US sports: former NBA stars Kenny Smith, Charles Barkley and Shaquille O’Neal. Barkley has said he will retire from the show at the end of this season. During its run, Inside the NBA has won 19 Sports Emmys. In 2025 it moved from its longtime home on Turner networks to ABC and ESPN. “Ernie Johnson is one of sports media’s most respected and beloved figures,” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. “For more than three decades, he has been the heart of Inside the NBA, helping create one of the most iconic and entertaining studio shows in sports. We are grateful for Ernie’s extraordinary contributions and look forward to celebrating him throughout the season.”

headline: British racing chief warns budget tax hike may have ‘devastating’ impact on sport
trail_text: Horse racing’s ruling body will ‘urgently engage with the government’ after the duty on the profits from fixed-odds gaming machines was raised in the budget
body_text: Brant Dunshea, chief executive of the British Horseracing Authority, said on Wednesday that the sport’s ruling body will “urgently engage with the government to establish how we can work together to reduce the impact” after John Healey, in his first budget as chancellor, raised the duty on the profits from fixed-odds gaming machines in betting shops from 20% to 25%. The widely expected rise in machine games duty (MGD) was well below the doubling of the rate, from 20% to 40%, recommended this year by the Social Market Foundation thinktank, but Dunshea warned that the move could “still prove devastating for our sport” since it presented a “clear risk” that “hundreds, if not thousands” of betting shops nationwide faced closure as a result. There are about 5,500 betting shops in the UK and the average shop contributes approximately £25,000 to racing annually via the levy and rights payments for live coverage and data. “British racing derives nearly a third of its £350m annual income from betting via high street shops,” Dunshea said, “[and] is now set to potentially lose £57m a year, based on independent modelling that was shared with the Treasury before today’s budget. “While the MGD rate increase is not as severe as some called for, this change could still prove devastating for the future of our sport, impacting prize money, the viability of racecourses, thousands of jobs and vital horse welfare projects and research. “[Closures] will also significantly impact a large part of the sport’s fanbase for whom a visit to their local bookie is the primary way they engage with horse racing.” Gideon Salutin, co-author of the report by the Social Market Foundation (SMF) that called for a much bigger rise in MGD, said that while the organisation was “pleased” that MGD had been raised, “reflecting the higher harm associated with this form of gambling”, the rise was also “relatively limited”. The SMF, Salutin added, remained “sceptical that such a small rise will have a significant impact on industry behaviour”. The share price of several major high-street gambling businesses rose after the budget speech on Wednesday. Shares in Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, were up 8% shortly after Healey’s announcement while share in Evoke, which owns William Hill, rose by 3.5%.
