headline: Carey and Inglis counterpunch to put Australia on top in South Africa
trail_text: Keepers rebuild the innings to reach 330 for four at the close Green sparkles but Labuschagne duck is ominous
body_text: If Cape Town’s first day was a rollercoaster, the second was some more sedate form of transport, though it continued with ups and downs fitting its mountainous backdrop. Twice, South Africa produced double strikes to stall promising Australian positions; twice the Australians rebuilt. Finally, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey pushed Australia in front, 330 for four to South Africa’s all out 329, ready to surge on through day three with those six wickets left in hand. While Travis Head was there, Australia’s first session threatened to match South Africa’s the day before, when Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman had piled on 140 against a bewildered attack. Head threw his hands at width, mixing luck with skill for seven boundaries. His new foil Matthew Renshaw showed contrasting temperament for the opening role, leaving and defending the new ball with the clarity he had shown in the middle order in Durban, underlining why he was the original candidate to replace Jake Weatherald at the top before the selectors’ brief and ill-fated Nic Maddinson excursion. Head’s contribution of 41 out of 58 will continue debate about his batting position. It’s clear at a glance, given an opener’s average of 49 is titanic by modern standards, but the detail is stark: that average breaks down to 23 in the first innings of a match, 43 in the second, 71 in the third, and 60 in the fourth. Head smashes up teams later in games set up to suit his approach, but hasn’t batted time when doing so is essential in tricky early conditions. Having more of a shield up top, leaving Head to plunder in the middle, may still be the best use of a precious resource. There is also his current problem with chopping on to his stumps, today via an awkward cut against Simon Harmer’s off-spin. That makes eight times bowled in his last 15 dismissals, up from 20 out of 66 before that span. Harmer struck again in the same over, teasing Marnus Labuschagne into a catch at slip on what must be Labuschagne’s last chance at Test cricket before the opportunity comes to blood a replacement during the Australian summer. Labuschagne’s problem is not so much the duck, which can happen to anyone, but its tentative provenance: a player who has trained so hard to move dynamically against spin had both feet in cement, poking uselessly at a ball that would have carried on past the stumps. In theory, he has one more innings left to save himself, but that was the shot of a player who is in no state to use it. Cameron Green arrived for a rebuild, but South Africa were fuming after the third umpire denied a catch from Gerald Coetzee’s bowling. Harmer at second slip was convinced, and replays looked identical to precedents where a player with fingers flat on the ground gets the ball to bounce up into their palms. This time it wasn’t given. Australia added 85 before the stand ended, including an explosive over when Green hooked the returning Rabada’s bouncer barrage, with some risk, for a consecutive six, six, and four. Harmer also had Renshaw given not out to a gorgeous ball that drifted across the left-hander, spun back past the edge, and hit his back pad, but was umpire’s call for height. It was Marco Jansen who ended the frustration, needing third-umpire recourse to prove that extra bounce had nicked the top edge of Renshaw’s half-hearted uppercut, then in Jansen’s next over, Harmer at slip inked in the Green catch that had been whited out. Just before tea, Australia’s set pair had been removed for 74 and 65. Still trailing South Africa by 144, at 185 for four, more was needed. It came from Inglis and Carey, both wicketkeeper-batters, though Inglis adopted the traditional counterpunching style of their kind, while Carey tended more to defence between moments of creative scoring. Again a partnership grew with both contributors heading towards half-centuries. Harmer was milked, Rabada remained ineffective, and as Inglis opened out after passing 50, he hit a six off both, and consecutive fours cutting Coetzee. There were moments of peril mixed in, like Harmer spinning one back to Inglis that almost took off-stump, and a couple of top edges that landed safe, but Australia’s scoring kept the field spread, and unlike Mitchell Starc’s demolition derby with the new ball the previous evening, South Africa’s use of it just sped up the scoring. By stumps the stand was 145, with Carey 51 and Inglis 85, and after captain Pat Cummins was sufficiently unsure of his batting that he chose to bowl on day one, the new configuration had come good on day two. Next is whether day three sees Australia move into a decisive lead, or whether South Africa can rein them in.

headline: London Broncos to go without £1.3m RFL funding if they enter Super League next year
trail_text: London Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs that they must relinquish any rights to around £1.3m in central distribution funding if they are to enter the competition in 2027
body_text: London Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs that they must relinquish any rights to about £1.3m in central distribution funding if they are to enter the competition in 2027, with the Rugby Football League expected to ratify their elevation imminently. A partnership between Super League and Australia’s National Rugby League (NRL), which would mean the latter taking administrative control of the English game and injecting tens of millions of pounds of much-needed financial support, is now not expected to begin until 2028. Despite that, the expansion of Super League to 15 teams to include London has moved a step closer. Many of the existing top-flight clubs were aware the NRL would insist on London’s inclusion in Super League when a partnership eventually starts. It was initially suspected that would be in 2027, but the two competitions have failed to agree a deal in time, though the NRL will assist in ensuring four Super League games per week are shown on Dazn next year. That partnership not beginning until 2028 appeared to have consigned London to another season in the Championship, which they won at a canter this year. But Super League clubs informed the Broncos they would still be willing to include them on the proviso they came in with zero distribution. The other 14 clubs currently get around £1.3m in central funding. It is understood that London have now accepted those terms. They were only due to get around £140,000 in distribution had they remained in the Championship, such is the harsh financial reality of life outside Super League. But London were also fearful they would lose their best playing talent if they decided against agreeing to the stringent financial conditions. York and Toulouse joined Super League with half the central distribution of the other teams, around £650,000, this year when the competition expanded to 14 teams. It will now grow again with London set to be included as a 15th team – with Super League clubs now ultimately expected to vote on expansion shortly. Super League clubs cannot handpick new teams though, only decide on the size of the league. That decision will then go to the RFL, who will launch a process to decide the 15th team. The governing body would probably use the IMG gradings system which decides the makeup of Super League as a metric for London’s elevation. Broncos actually finished 16th in this year’s gradings but the team that finished 15th, Barrow, have already said they are not ready for Super League. Their facilities also do not meet minimum standards – meaning the RFL can approach London as next in the pecking order and invite them into Super League.

headline: David Boon on front foot as Cricket Australia hands new boss a sticky wicket
trail_text: Australia’s former No 3 faces one of his biggest tests as he takes the reins as CA interim chair with BBL privatisation only the first task of many
body_text: David Boon walked on to one of the stickier wickets in Australian sport on Wednesday, after Cricket Australia warned the national pastime faces years of financial losses and a period of “cost minimisation”. The outlook is grim, and that’s without a glance towards a cricketing world of emboldened match-fixers and upturned by Indian interests, facing an Australian summer that is no longer the country’s own. The moustached former Test No 3 batter was sent into the middle due to the ousting of Mike Baird, whose place as chair was pulled out from under him by New South Wales officials unhappy at the manner of his pursuit of BBL private investment. Millions may flow from sales of the Melbourne Renegades – for whom a buyer could be found before the end of the year – and other franchises. That would soften the bruising of the financial fall in the down phase of Australian cricket’s four-year, Ashes-to-Ashes cycle, courtesy of the international sports investment community. A comfortable bed of banknotes not unlike that kept by Scrooge McDuck, given the price touted for the Renegades alone would single-handedly turn around three years’ worth of CA deficits. With the “right protections, right safeguards, the right investment, the right opportunities”, as Baird espoused on Wednesday, young cricketers might even end up with something that benefits them more than MI Melbourne. Yet landing the not straightforward privatisation is only the first task of many for Boon in a delicate time for the sport. The Tasmanian – who has spent his post-playing career as a selector and ICC match referee – is formally taking on the role in an interim manner, though he has wide support to take the post on a permanent basis, working in concert with a board and chief executive Todd Greenberg. From his throne alternating between Hobart and Jolimont, Boon will oversee a cricketing fiefdom being dragged into the present day. Cricket Australia officials are desperate to muscle out the likes of the UAE and South Africa from the late-summer franchise cricket window to preserve its status – alongside the IPL and The Hundred – as one of the three major global men’s short-form competitions. So desperate, in fact, they are prepared to “march ahead” – as Baird said – with privatisation despite falling short of consensus with the states and, so far, the players. “We’ve got a strong belief that private investment, with appropriate safeguards, can keep the Big Bash as the dominant league, it can keep the January window the dominant window for Big Bash outside of the IPL, and we certainly think it connects us into global franchises,” Baird said. Opening Wednesday’s AGM with a short address, Boon wasted no time in declaring it was full steam ahead for privatisation, “a huge and important project”, despite the presence in the room of new board member Ed Cowan. The former Australian opener was elevated as the new board nomination from New South Wales and is a prominent critic of the BBL plans. Boon’s stance reflects that of Cricket Tasmania officials, who have sought interest from partners without the help of investment firms managing the Renegades process. Talks are under way with six parties interested in a slice of the Hurricanes, with investment set to be finalised within 12 months. The Renegades deal might even be locked in before one is reached with the players, a potential source of consternation for investors wanting buy-in from Australia’s top talent before they write a cheque. On negotiations with the Australian Cricketers Association, Greenberg sounded hopeful but admitted: “We’re a little way apart in that there’s a difference of opinion contractually about how the proceeds of the sale would operate.” Uncertainty also surrounds the future of the Australian men’s side. The contract of coach Andrew McDonald is due to expire at the end of next year’s ODI World Cup. “He’s held in incredibly high regard by the Cricket Australia board and by all of us. I think he’s done an outstanding job, and I think his results tell you that,” Greenberg said, before delivering a reality check. “But in saying that, there’s also an eye on what’s coming next, and there’s no doubt that there’ll be a transition of this team, and we want to make sure that we can have oversight of that so that we protect and thrive into the next phase, whoever that might be.” In reflecting on his time as chair, Baird volunteered the most pressing decisions that face Boon, and others within international cricket, including the “reinvigoration” of Test cricket, a downturn in TV rights values and corruption. The NRMA chief executive was close to Jay Shah, the well-connected former BCCI official now chair of the ICC. Although no longer in a formal role, Baird promised to ensure Boon was introduced to the people he needed to meet at the next ICC meeting in Bali next month, and in Chennai when the Renegades meet the Scorchers in December to open the BBL season. “In that period, I hope I’m able to connect Boonie – he’s someone that’s known and loved across the game, so I’m sure it’s not going to be hard for him to pick it up – but we can’t underestimate the time and effort that goes into that because it’s significant and it’s required for the game,” Baird said. “We need to be at the table shaping it, not watching it take place.”

headline: Dream say WNBA finals concerns went unheeded as teams prepare for 12.30pm Thursday start
trail_text: The Atlanta Dream say their concerns about finding a suitable home venue for the WNBA finals went unheeded as they prepare to play the Golden State Valkyries
body_text: The Atlanta Dream say their concerns about finding a suitable home venue for the WNBA finals went unheeded as they prepare to play the Golden State Valkyries in a crucial Game 6 on Thursday. The Dream’s normal home, Gateway Center Arena, has a capacity of about 3,500 people. To accommodate the increased interest in the team during the finals, the Dream have played their two home games so far at the Atlanta Hawks’ State Farm Arena, which can seat more than 17,000 fans. However, the Hawks play the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday night, meaning the Dream and Valkyries will play Game 6 at 12.30pm EDT on the same day. That means Valkyries fans in their home state of California will watch the game at 9.30am local time. Golden State lead the best-of-seven series 3-2. In an open letter to their fans on Tuesday, the Dream said they had raised concerns about a possible scheduling clash months ago, but the calls went unheeded. “This incredible run by our players has … made something else abundantly clear: the Atlanta Dream has earned the right to be taken seriously,” the Dream wrote in the letter. “Two months ago, when the WNBA finalized playoff dates and times, we raised concerns that the W Finals schedule conflicted with NBA games at State Farm Arena. As we moved through the playoffs, we reiterated those concerns. Our concerns did not receive the attention, nor the urgency that they deserved.” The letter did not elaborate on the exact concerns the team raised, or who they raised them with at the WNBA. According to ESPN, WNBA teams were told the dates for this season’s playoffs in December 2025. The WNBA, NBA, Dream, Golden State and the finals’ broadcasting partners had discussions over the weekend about the best solution to the venue problem. In Tuesday’s letter, the Dream said playing Game 6 during the afternoon was the best option available. “As much as we have great affection and nostalgia for Gateway Center Arena, we believed that our fans and the city wanted the opportunity to be a part of this historic series, and to see it played on a world-class stage,” the letter said. “That meant State Farm Arena.” The Valkyries’ Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton have urged fans to call in sick so they can see their team potentially clinch the title in only their second season in the WNBA. Meanwhile, the Dream’s Allisha Gray said her main focus was the game itself, not the start time. “It’s the finals,” Gray said. “We just got to do what we’ve got to do. We are locked in on winning Game 6 whether it’s 8am, 10pm, midnight. We got a championship to win.”

headline: Marco Jansen belongs to a great tradition but top all-rounders are hard to find
trail_text: The South African stands out, not just because of his height, but England and Australia now find themselves looking for an equivalent
body_text: If you were to bioengineer a cricketer in a laboratory, which attributes would you give them? You would make them tall, with long limbs and a whiplash action to extract steep bounce. Add speed, movement both ways and a left arm to offer a point of difference. With the bat, make sure they can whack sixes but also go down the gears when an innings starts to unravel. For an added trait, have them catch meteorites in the outfield and the cordon. You might end up with Marco Jansen. At the start of the third Test, the 6ft 8in South African had taken 99 Test wickets at 20.81. His 85 against Australia at Gqeberha in the second Test came after South Africa had slumped to 110 for six before his counterattack helped turn a precarious position into an innings victory. Jansen is still developing as a batter, but his 25.66 average before this current Test understates his potential. Jansen belongs to a great South African tradition. The country’s finest sides have often been built around players who can do more than one job. Mike Procter, Shaun Pollock, Lance Klusener and Jacques Kallis, who scored 13,289 Test runs and took 292 wickets, came to embody the quintessential South African cricketer. That heritage continues in Jansen and Wiaan Mulder, whose wobble-seam bowling comes with the capacity to make 367 not out. But what makes someone an all-rounder? A recent essay by the analyst Jarrod Kimber argues that “a true all-rounder is not just their numbers, it is the effect they have on the entire team”. The tidy statistical definition, in which a player’s batting average exceeds their bowling average, is inadequate. By that measure Joe Root and Don Bradman qualify. The more useful question is whether a player could be selected for either skill. That separates the all-rounder from the batter who sends down a few overs, or the bowler who can hang around at No 9. More than that, the best all-rounder lets a captain add a bowler without weakening the batting. A more emphatic measure is a player’s capacity to score a century and take a five-wicket haul in the same Test. It has happened only 41 times, by 29 players. Ian Botham did it five times, more than anyone else. He belonged to a golden quartet alongside Richard Hadlee, Imran Khan and Kapil Dev, who seemed like cheat codes in a sport without substitutes. England have never quite let go of that romance. Botham, Andrew Flintoff and Ben Stokes embody the free-spirited maverick who can arrive with a cigarette dangling from his mouth and the smell of beer on his lips, then produce a match-winning show. Does that help explain why Sam Curran can seem to receive less love? He is a useful left-arm bowler and inventive batter, but does not fit the same heroic silhouette. England’s idealised all-rounder can cast a long shadow over anyone who does not live up to those standards. Australia’s problem is stranger. They have produced fine all-rounders, but few who have matched the sustained excellence of Kallis or Garfield Sobers. Keith Miller made 2,958 Test runs at 36.97 and took 170 wickets at 22.97. Alan Davidson, a left-arm fast-medium bowler and accomplished lower-order batter, scored 1,328 runs and took 186 wickets at 20.53. In the first tied Test, against the West Indies in 1960, he became the first player to score over 100 runs and take 10 wickets in the same match. Since then, Australia have had useful options: Andrew Symonds, Shane Watson, Mitchell Marsh and now Cameron Green and Beau Webster. The issue is not an absence of all-rounders, but the rarity of one who sustains elite contributions in both disciplines. For a country that prizes natural athleticism and power, it is curious how rarely the complete package has clicked. Perhaps that is because outside Asia we still picture the all-rounder as a fast bowler who can bang it in or seam it off a length. Ravindra Jadeja and Shakib al-Hasan complicate that picture. Both are frontline spinners and serious batters, capable of reshaping a team’s balance. Are they given their due in the west, where a pitch that seams on day one is often treated more kindly than one that offers turn? They are recognised as all-timers, but the language of all-round greatness still favours the pace-bowling showman, which might explain why Moeen Ali felt undervalued for most of his England career. Wicketkeepers raise a related question. If a keeper bats in the top six, as Adam Gilchrist did on 23 occasions in 96 Tests, are they an all-rounder? They offer two skills, but keeping is a specialist discipline in its own right. Sometimes cricket’s labels are less tidy than its scorecards. Maybe the most charming all-rounders were the less imposing ones, like New Zealand’s Chris Harris, whose looping “dibbly-dobbly” deliveries and lower-order runs made him useful in a dozen small ways, or Sri Lanka’s parade of batters who could send down darted spin. Perhaps we love all-rounders because batting and bowling are each so difficult that doing both at an elite level feels like the truest measure of a cricketer. Faf du Plessis recently said he wished Jansen had been in his team when he was captain of South Africa: “He’s two players in one.” Dale Steyn called Jansen “currently the best cricketer in the world”. The laboratory may have produced a unicorn. Now Jansen has to show how many jobs one cricketer can do. This is an extract from the Guardian’s weekly cricket email, The Spin. To subscribe, just visit this page and follow the instructions.

headline: Jay-Z is the perfect Super Bowl shill for a league of billionaires
trail_text: The rapper lends the NFL a veneer of credibility but is unlikely to push back on the establishment figures who run the league
body_text: On Monday the NFL named Jay-Z as the headliner for this season’s Super Bowl half-time show. His company, Roc Nation, produces the show under a 2019 deal reportedly worth $5m a year, and the agreement was extended for another five years in 2024. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said his one request when the partnership began was that Jay-Z “take the stage himself one day“. Goodell’s wish makes total sense: Jay-Z is the perfect choice for the half-time show, and that’s not a compliment. The NFL wants a shill who can still pass for a rebel, and nobody in American music plays that part better than Jay-Z. Jay-Z’s origin story has become an American legend. Years before he sold records, Shawn Carter grew up in Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses and sold crack as a teenager. When labels passed on him, he hawked CDs from the trunk of his car on college campuses. Then he put out Reasonable Doubt in 1996 on his own label, Roc-A-Fella. “Nobody would sign me,” he said later. The money followed. In 2013, he performed Picasso Baby, a track about the paintings he wanted to own, for six hours straight at a Chelsea gallery, and Marina Abramović joined him. By the time of The Story of OJ in 2017, he was handing out financial advice. Forbes puts his fortune at about $2.8bn. He raps for the rich now, a Black oligarch who seems about as cut off from the rest of the country as the rest of the billionaire class. His bootstraps story mirrors the platitudes Americans have been told for decades – work hard and you’ll get what you deserve. On paper, he’s the perfect avatar for America’s polluted ideas of capitalism. But the country Jay-Z is rapping to is in terrible shape. How many of us can relate to his lyrics in 2026? Gas and grocery prices have rocketed. SNAP enrollment fell more than 13% in a year as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tightened the rules. Only 63% of adults say they could cover a surprise $400 expense. You can see why the NFL would use Jay-Z as someone who can give the appearance that the league, with its huge conservative fanbase, is actually progressive. He wore Colin Kaepernick’s jersey on Saturday Night Live in 2017 after the quarterback had sparked a protest movement against police brutality by kneeling for the national anthem. Jay-Z then dedicated The Story of OJ to Kaepernick onstage. A year later, on Apeshit, he bragged about turning down the Super Bowl and told the NFL it needed him more than he needed it. Things would soon change. In June 2019, Forbes named him hip-hop’s first billionaire. A few months later, Roc Nation signed its deal with the NFL. But at the news conference announcing his NFL partnership, Jay-Z no longer appeared as receptive to Kaepernick’s approach to protest. “We’ve moved past kneeling,” he said. That same year, Kaepernick settled his collusion grievance against the league after he said his protests had effectively ended his playing career. The 2019 deal also put Roc Nation to work on Inspire Change, the league’s social justice initiative. It’s safe to say that Kaepernick was unimpressed. “I just want you to know, one, you’re serving the culture up to a bunch of racists and, two, they don’t care about you,” Kaepernick later recalled saying to Jay-Z. “You’re the music guy to them. They quite literally need a Black face – and have said as much.” Seven years later, Jay-Z is still battling Kaepernick, the man who says he was blackballed by the NFL. This summer, Jay-Z linked up with Target, which had been boycotted by many Black customers after it rolled back its diversity and inclusion policies. Kaepernick, on the other hand, said he would not allow his memoir to be sold at any of the chain’s stores. At a concert in July, Jay-Z rapped that Kaepernick had allowed himself to be silenced by signing his grievance with the NFL (sources close to Kaepernick have denied this). “Buddy took a check, I ain’t even mad at him, but along with that check you have to sign a non-disparagement. I’m the one [the NFL] can’t control,” Jay-Z rapped to the crowd at Yankee Stadium. Maybe that’s true, but it doesn’t appear that Jay-Z is doing much to control – or change – the league either. In 2021, USA Today’s Mike Freeman wrote: “There isn’t a single, tangible thing you can point to that shows Jay-Z helping with the league’s social justice efforts.” That’s a little unfair; through Inspire Change the NFL has funnelled millions into charities across America. At the same time, the NFL is mostly run by the same old, rich conservatives it always has been. There is still no Black majority owner of a team, and Forbes now puts the combined value of the league’s 32 teams at more than $300bn. In 2025, Donald Trump, who once called NFL players who protested during the national anthem “sons of bitches”, became the first sitting president to attend a Super Bowl, and that same week the league pulled “End Racism” from the endzones in New Orleans. That slogan had been on NFL fields since 2020 as part of Inspire Change. Conservatives have noticed. A column published on Sport & State hailed Jay-Z as a “legend” and told readers there likely wouldn’t be any anti-ICE activists onstage at this season’s halftime show, adding that “after last year’s Bad Bunny debacle, Jay-Z offers a compromise.” That’s about right. Jay-Z won’t have anybody to push against at the Super Bowl. The NFL is Roc Nation’s client, and the team owners are its partners. As we saw with the Target debacle, whatever Jay-Z says up there, he’s unlikely to go against the people who pay him.

headline: Jimmy Anderson’s stubborn refusal to give up has fuelled his greatest achievements
trail_text: Lancashire have moved on without him, but the 44-year-old England stalwart wants to keep going as long as his body allows
body_text: Jimmy Anderson could teach Philip Marlowe a thing or two about The Long Goodbye. England’s leading wicket-taker in Tests is of that sporting breed who have no interest in bowing out at the top. Like Andy Murray before him, he has shown little enthusiasm to bow out at all, as long as his body allows him to keep doing the thing he loves: getting opposition batsmen out. It was little surprise, then, that when Lancashire announced this week they would not be renewing his contract after 25 years, there was no immediate retirement announcement. Instead there was an irked Instagram post, then silence, as the one-club man considered his options. One of those, apparently, was a T10 cricket tournament in Rome. And lo, it is now confirmed that Anderson will lead (and even “co-own”) the Napoli Knights for 12 days next month. It may not seem an obvious encore to an illustrious red-ball career, but neither was putting himself up for auction in the Indian Premier League at the age of 42, having played no short-format cricket in a decade. Anderson has always been more interested in playing the game than his own ego. Will Italy be the final act for this anti-diva? It seems unlikely: Anderson’s GOAT status has always encompassed that animal’s legendarily stubborn qualities, and his farewell tour now rivals Elton John’s. Remember the time he and Stuart Broad were dropped from the England squad to tour the West Indies, and everyone assumed both men’s careers were over? That was nearly five years ago. Broad’s retirement in 2023 only made Anderson more determined to continue; by the following March he had his 700th Test wicket. When England’s director of cricket, Rob Key, did call time on his international career that summer, Anderson immediately showed the Bazboys what they were missing, taking seven for 35 on his County Championship return against Nottinghamshire. Since then there have been two more summers with Lancashire, including 50 championship wickets at 17.68 this year, despite a recurring calf injury. Now that his county, like his country, wants to move on without him, no one will begrudge him a little of his trademark grumpiness. Anderson’s stubborn refusal to give up has, after all, fuelled his greatest achievements. With his significance to the game well established it’s easy to forget how much turmoil Anderson endured at the beginning of his career, a quarter of a century ago. His first county season put him under an immediate and intense spotlight. Having taken two wickets in two balls in his first game against Surrey, aged 19, he finished the season as Lancashire’s third-highest wicket-taker, just a handful behind his teenage hero Peter Martin. He was drafted into England’s one‑day international side that winter, before he even had a county cap. Selection for the national side with a wafer-thin CV was not as common as it has become under the current regime (Anderson’s England Academy roommate, Gordon Muchall, assumed it was a joke, and told him to stop packing his gear). And his inexperience was an issue. While his raw pace and prodigious swing could trouble the best – witness the way he out-yorked Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis in England’s 2003 World Cup match against Pakistan – he lacked the wisdom and discipline to marshal his skills. There were wild and expensive spells. In October 2003 his nascent career was English cricket’s hot topic. Sporting blond tips in his hair, he grabbed a five-fer on Test debut against Zimbabwe, before being taken to pieces by a South African top three of Graeme Smith, Herschelle Gibbs and Gary Kirsten. I was interviewing him for the launch issue of the Wisden Cricketer magazine: wanting to kick off with a bold statement, we put the 20‑year‑old on the cover (in a designer T-shirt, shock horror, rather than traditional whites). Tacitly, and in spite of his rocky start, we were anointing him the future of English cricket. New to the media carousel, it was natural for Anderson to be shy. But his signature style was already present. “Laconic”, “terse”, and “an exaggerated languor” were phrases I felt fit to include. Beneath the article we ran an analysis of his technique by Bob Cottam, England’s former bowling coach. “He needs to perfect an in-swinger with the new ball,” said Cottam, who nevertheless confirmed that “with experience, Jimmy can become a world-class bowler, the attributes are all there”. What strikes me just as much is how Anderson, even at that stage, recognised his greatest strength as “being able to come back stronger”. It was something he would have to draw on plenty in the years that followed as his form – and selection – remained inconsistent. There was an unsuccessful remodelling of his action and a stress fracture. It wasn’t until he paired with Broad to open the bowling on the 2007-08 New Zealand tour that his performances began to bear out that almost outrageous early promise. Between the 90s and the noughties England were on a desperate hunt for new heroes. Plenty of all-rounders suffered under the burden of that cursed appellation, “the new Botham”. Anderson’s rapid propulsion from Burnley CC to the World Cup stage was followed, predictably, by a backlash of scepticism. It didn’t just take determination to weather that: it took devotion. Anderson’s obsessive love of bowling saw him through. It’s also why he improved so much as he aged – always evolving, experimenting, developing a mastery of swing and seam bowling few could match. His early days at Lancashire may have impressed but no one could have predicted he would finish as one of the all-time England greats. The “future of English cricket” secured his legacy through a relentless dedication to his craft. It should be no wonder to anyone that he’d like to continue practising it.

headline: Cricket Australia takes $20m revenue hit from two-day Ashes Tests with more losses ahead
trail_text: Governing body reports $82m surplus for the 2025-26 season but projects two years of deficits with less interest in upcoming tours
body_text: The financial blow struck to Cricket Australia due to the pair of two-day Ashes Tests last summer amounted to $20m, hurting the sport’s bottom line as it prepares for multiple years of losses. The governing body reported a $82m surplus in 2025-26 supercharged by strong broadcast interest, ticket sales and commercial revenue associated with the men’s Ashes, the traditional peak in the four-year cycle adopted by Cricket Australia. More sobering is the outlook, however, with two years of deficits projected. The anticipated sale of parts of BBL franchises have not been factored in to those calculations. CA’s outgoing chair Mike Baird joked to his replacement, former Test batter David Boon, during Wednesday’s AGM that he needs to ensure future matches go the full five days. “We’ve had a record Ashes crowd at the MCG, 94,000, only going two days there,” Baird said. “Let’s mark it down that five-day Tests are a good thing, Boonie.” The revenue shortfall due to the abbreviated MCG match was initially estimated at $10m, but the total was even higher. The Perth fixture, which also did not reach day three, left an even deeper hole. Chief executive Todd Greenberg said the combined shortfall was worth “give or take $20m” and it was a “significant” blow, though the organisation still managed to meet its financial targets. “That’s a pretty solid outcome given the fact that we have two two-day Test matches, but we’ve over-achieved in some other areas like non-broadcast revenue, our sponsorship program outperformed, some of our other revenue lines outperformed, so we were able to make up the difference.” Annual revenue rose to a record high of $601m, an increase of almost $150m over the previous year, leaving the governing body with $87.5m in cash and investments after the peak of its financial cycle. Cricket Australia is warning of at least two years of financial losses, however, reflecting the lower level of interest in the tour by New Zealand this summer, and Pakistan and Sri Lanka the next, and one of its priorities in coming years will be “cost minimisation”. That partly explains the pursuit of private investment into BBL franchises, which is set to proceed initially with the Melbourne Renegades despite opposition from New South Wales officials and no deal secured yet with the player association. “We want to get to a position where we’re sustainable,” Baird said. “Part of the Big Bash work is, not only looking for the private investment, we also think that’s going to lead to increased capability and it’s going to help drive fan experience, and whole different ways it’s going to grow the Big Bash and the game. “That’s going to bring more revenues to it, but we’re also talking to states about kind of resetting the financial model if additional resources come in.”

headline: England’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blow
trail_text: Steve Borthwick has lost two key England squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg
body_text: England’s head coach, Steve Borthwick, said he will be monitoring this weekend’s domestic Prem games with some trepidation. Already he has lost at least two potentially key squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg, with doubts still hanging over his first-choice fly-half, Fin Smith, and fresh injury uncertainty emerging on virtually a daily basis. Pepper’s involvement always looked improbable from the moment he sustained a nasty-looking ankle injury against Gloucester last Friday. The young Bath flanker will be sidelined for several weeks, as will the Bristol centre Van Rensburg who has been advised to rest and recuperate after two heavy concussions within the past three months. Smith, meanwhile, is still being treated for the calf problem he sustained against Leicester last Saturday. Borthwick says it remains “unclear at this stage” whether the Northampton fly-half will be available to face Australia next week. Calf injuries and kicking are not a great combination and England also need their tactical hub to be at the heart of their preparations. Borthwick, accordingly, will effectively want to make a call by the end of this week although England are slightly helped by the fact the Wallaby fixture is on a Sunday rather than 24 hours earlier. “Typically I would name the team for a Sunday game around the Wednesday, so that would still be my aim,” said Borthwick. “But if Fin’s not available for selection we also have some quality fly-halves in George Ford and Marcus Smith.” The Bath hooker Kepu Tuipulotu has also limped away from training in Bagshot with a leg injury that will now be assessed, but there is more encouraging news regarding Seb Atkinson (knee) and Manny Feyi-Waboso (hamstring), both of whom should be available to play for Gloucester and Exeter respectively this weekend. Borthwick’s preference would probably be for both players to be tucked up on their sofas but under the terms of the joint agreement between the Rugby Football Union and the clubs, the latter can pick their international players once they are cleared by England’s medical staff. “If they’re fit then they’re available for selection,” said Borthwick. “That then comes down to the head coach or director of rugby of the club.” Either way it is a tense time for the national management who are having to do without their customary full extra week of training because of the need to shoehorn the new Nations Championship finals weekend into the calendar. Rugby players need to play rugby but, invariably, it comes with an element of risk attached. “Certainly there is a part of me watching these games and hoping the players get through the 80 minutes and are fit and available for next week,” said Borthwick. The stakes are further heightened by next year’s looming World Cup, with Borthwick having pointedly reminded his players that only nine Tests remain before England’s World Cup preparations enter their final stages. The primary message is that, for those intending to be on the plane to Australia, performing at the requisite level starts now. “This series of games this autumn is the last opportunity we have playing southern hemisphere opposition before we’re at that World Cup,” said Borthwick. “I’m looking forward to seeing players compete and perform against this calibre of opposition. You look at the power many of these southern hemisphere teams have. That’s a different challenge. When they come into camp again on Monday night, having recovered from their games, all that matters is performing the way we want to against Australia.” Borthwick also brushed aside suggestions of potential discord after the fractious East Midlands derby between Leicester and Northampton where several of his squad were at loggerheads. The RFU sought to try to dilute any notion of friction by issuing a photo of Ollie Chessum and Henry Pollock with their arms cheerfully around each other and Borthwick has not yet deemed it necessary to pull anyone aside. “I actually think it’s a real strength of the game to be able to compete like that in that kind of full-blooded encounter – and then they’re perfectly fine. It’s a strength of English rugby that the players have such pride in their clubs … in modern day sport I see that as a positive. But when you come in [here] it’s all about the England team.”

headline: Australia fight back in rollercoaster start to deciding Test against South Africa
trail_text: Decision to bowl first was almost disastrous but the hosts were dismissed for 329 after being 140-0 at lunch
body_text: For a time, it was heading up there with the worst. David Gower at Leeds in 1989, when Australia topped 600 and declared. Nasser Hussain in Brisbane, 2002, when Australia were 364 for two by the end of the day. Edgbaston 2005, where England lamped 407 from 80 overs. Those were the looming comparisons for captains deciding to bowl at the toss, after Pat Cummins did the same in the third Test at Cape Town, only for South Africa’s openers to smash 140 by lunch. Yet, by day’s end, Australia had taken 10 for a further 189, Mitchell Starc destroying the tail with four wickets in six balls, 329 all out constituting a serious Australian comeback. What a rollercoaster. The Australian setup has looked frazzled on this tour: confused player selections for the squad, then for the XIs, confused shot selection in the middle, players bouncing around the order with nightwatch duties and injury absences. Here they chose to leave out their best player from the second Test, Scott Boland, for Nathan Lyon, and were forced to leave out their best player of the last decade, Steve Smith, for Josh Inglis, as well as dropping Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster for Cameron Green and Cooper Connolly. The last time a touring Australian side made four non-disciplinary changes was in the West Indies in 1984. So it tracked that there was confusion in the decision by Cummins as well. He has been a bowl-first enthusiast relative to captaincy convention, this being the ninth time he has made that call in 25 opportunities, and perhaps was banking on there being more juice in the surface on the first morning than on the second afternoon. But with locals describing a Cape Town surface that is known to run easy, and on a morning of bright sunshine with plenty more predicted, surely the safest move was to try to build a score? That is what Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman did, Markram setting the tone with some early blows, then Ackerman following his lead until surpassing it. Starc and Josh Hazlewood bowled poorly, too short and too wide on too many occasions, and with no swing and no lateral movement from the pitch, Markram laid into front-foot drives, back-foot punches, and even a shockingly audacious smash from Hazlewood on the up. When Cummins came on to play enforcer, Markram pulled him for six. Lyon, the spinner, was bowling by the 12th over rather than waiting to influence day five. Before long, Ackerman took over. Happy to hook whenever the opportunity came, he cleared fine leg for six from Cummins and belted Lyon out of the arena over midwicket. When Starc returned for a later spell, Ackerman smashed 18 off one over, hitting four boundaries in a row. Australia were shambolic, Travis Head dropping one of the easiest catches of his life at cover, spliced to him by Markram from Starc, then Lyon letting a return catch go through in the first over after lunch. With the score on 158, South Africa were 13 short of the record opening stand against Australia for a team being sent in, and the tourists looked set for a dismal day. It was Lyon who found a way through. With Ackerman determined not to temper his approach on 95, he ran at Lyon only to be outfoxed, a wider and slower ball evading his bat to bring about his stumping. Markram also perished while forging on, pulling a Hazlewood ball that had bounced nowhere high enough out to long leg, the first of many false shorts to short balls that found the hands of a fielder. That opened the door for Lyon to bowl Temba Bavuma, past the defensive outside edge, and Connolly to get his first Test wicket by burrowing past Matthew Breetzke’s inside edge, lbw on review. David Bedingham had played beautifully, driving with precision, and finally reached 50 having been out for 46 and 49 earlier in the series. But he went no further, also caught at fine leg hooking, Hazlewood dancing over the boundary and back to complete it, followed by Wiaan Mulder top-edging a hook off Starc for nought. Wicketless for 158 had become 216 for six. So it was time for South Africa’s rollercoaster to climb up again. Marco Jansen, so often the Australians’ chief cause of frustration, took them on once more, flaying the ageing ball for another half-century after his match-turning 85 in the second Test. With Ryan Rickelton alongside him, they added 95 in good time. But the first over with the new ball brought about the rollercoaster’s death-drop finale. Now with cloud cover at the end of the day, the ball began to swing, and Starc went back to his roots. No wobble-seam, no bouncers, just left-arm, over the wicket, inswinging menace. Rickelton nailed on the back pad, fourth ball of the over, for 42. Jansen two balls later, trying to drive, curling back to kiss the outside of off-stump, bowled for 52. First ball of Starc’s next over, Gerald Coetzee was bowled off his pads, backing away from that inswing, and while Kagiso Rabada survived the hat-trick ball, he was smashed in line with leg-stump from the one that followed. South Africa had lost four wickets for two runs, Starc finished with six for 72 and a day of Test cricket containing almost everything one could ask for was called to a close. The jury might remain out overnight if asked to decide who should be happier. Look for a verdict later this week.

headline: England need to unearth World Cup core despite derby friction and injury chaos
trail_text: England’s Nations Championship games against Australia and Japan should be the end of experimentation for Steve Borthwick
body_text: Even on the most serene days no one would describe coaching England as a relaxing gig. With his side’s opening November Test looming on Sunday week, Steve Borthwick is already faced with assorted injury-related complications at precisely the moment he needs to start finding lasting answers to a range of fundamental selection questions. The untimely training field absence of Fin Smith, pencilled in to be England’s starting No 10, is a prime example. With the two leading midfield candidates to face Australia – Seb Atkinson and Bernhard Janse van Rensburg – also unable to train this week, Smith’s calf injury has materialised at the worst possible moment. Add the Bath flanker Guy Pepper, who limped off against Gloucester last Friday, and suddenly there is a hint of pre-Halloween gloom hanging over England’s preparations. There is also the bigger picture. At various times, Borthwick has been urged to base his selections around dominant club sides in Northampton, Bath and Saracens. How unfortunate, then, that all three went down in a sodden, windblown heap at the weekend. Nor does it help that the two most effervescent England‑qualified back-rowers this season, Jack and Tom Willis, ply their trade in France and are ineligible. On top of everything else, there is the small matter of Borthwick being required to manage the increasing number of squad members itching to punch Henry Pollock’s lights out. To say Ollie Chessum and the other Leicester players who squared up to the Saints back‑rower during the East Midlands derby on Saturday were unhappy with their England “buddy” would be putting it mildly. Competitive tension is an inevitable part of the game, but, from Borthwick’s perspective, a “them and us” split within the national squad would be ruinous. Because, in the end, there is only one overarching question that matters: how can England win the World Cup next year? The debate then becomes less about week-to-week contingencies and necessitates some longsighted vision. This next month is effectively Borthwick’s last chance to identify his preferred combinations before the World Cup and that opportunity absolutely cannot be wasted. Nor can England afford a repeat of the turmoil that compromised their plans before the last World Cup. In the semi-final against South Africa, there were a mere seven surviving starters – Freddie Steward, Jonny May, Manu Tuilagi, Owen Farrell, Jamie George, Maro Itoje and Tom Curry – and 10 of the matchday 23 from Eddie Jones’s last hurrah as head coach against the Boks less than a year earlier. Given the circumstances, England did well to scramble as far as they did. Compare that with England’s World Cup-winning squad in 2003 when only two players – Josh Lewsey and Trevor Woodman – were not involved in a thrilling victory against the Wallabies at Twickenham 11 months previously. While there was movement on the bench, where injuries played their part, 17 of Sir Clive Woodward’s 22-man squad from November 2002 featured at the World Cup. Hence why this autumn matters so much in terms of nailing down certain positions. There has been some judicious filleting with Theo Dan, Ben Spencer, Ollie Lawrence and Elliot Daly nowhere to be seen. Charlie Ewels, similarly, finds himself on the outer. Kepu Tuipulotu, Noah Caluori and Arthur Clark have earned the nod, with Cadan Murley and Ben Curry seeing off the respective challenges of the unlucky George Hendy and Fitz Harding. Tom Pearson, similarly, has profited from the injury to Chandler Cunningham‑South and Borthwick’s reluctance, for now, to summon Max Hicks, Courtney Lawes, Hoskins Sotutu, Ethan Roots or Jack Clement, among others. The Bracken brothers, Jack and Charlie, must be close too. At least there is an A international to encourage the aforementioned, but, equally, those not required in Bagshot this week now know something truly special is required. Borthwick has to settle, as a matter or urgency, on who should wear six, seven, eight, nine, 12 and 13 this time next year – not guys who might conceivably have the highest ceiling at some unspecified future date, but individuals capable of turbocharging an England side that, lest we forget, have lost five of their past seven Tests. With any luck, then, Borthwick is not just thinking about the Australia game in isolation, but the opening two weekends as a package. If all 36 players in training this week have some involvement against Australia and Japan it would also help to separate the wheat from the chaff: the management then can identify a 23-man squad to face New Zealand that, ideally, mirrors the one that will kick off the knockout stages of the World Cup less than 12 months from now. Admittedly, that strategy becomes harder if Smith, Atkinson, Janse Van Rensburg and Pepper are unavailable. On the other hand, Marcus Smith is back in form while Sale’s Joe Marchant, if required, has plenty of experience. Alternatively, Gloucester’s fleet-footed Will Joseph could just prove the answer to England’s endless midfield conundrum; a partnership with his clubmate Atkinson would certainly work in terms of cohesion, pace and balance. Anyone who has watched Northampton attack will also be eager to see the alert Archie McParland in an England No 9 shirt sooner rather than later. Then, suddenly, with Itoje, Chessum, George Martin and Alex Coles all scrapping for a start at lock and Pollock, Ben Earl, Tom Curry and Greg Fisilau vying for back-row prominence, England could be in clover. The time for experimentation, however, is almost over. This is an extract from our weekly rugby union email, the Breakdown. To subscribe just visit this page and follow the instructions.

headline: NFL today: How to watch Cowboys v Eagles, TV channels & live stream Monday 26 October
trail_text: How will Dallas and Philadelphia fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
body_text: There is “reeling”, and then there is whatever the Eagles are doing heading into Monday Night Football against the Cowboys. Philadelphia have lost four games in a row to fall within a whisker of last place in the NFC East. Jalen Hurts’s blood clots rapidly escalated and have probably knocked the franchise QB out for the season. Backup Tanner McKee has inherited a legitimate crisis. And it’s not as if all was hunky-dory before Hurts went out. The Eagles had already blown a 10-point fourth-quarter lead to the Rams and let the Jaguars come back on them in shocking fashion in London before the Hurts news. The Cowboys have their own enormous issues. Former Eagles assistant Christian Parker joined up as defensive coordinator, aiming to fix a bad unit, but the Cowboys are still struggling to keep teams from racking up big point and yardage totals. Facing the Cowboys defense has been a salve for struggling offenses, as when a Packers team who couldn’t convert a third down for their life suddenly converted nine of their first 10 against Big D last weekend. Despite these issues, both teams are within reach of the first-place Giants in the East. This is a critical game even though it is mainly compelling for the anxieties on both sides of the rivalry. Date: Monday 26 October 2026 Time: 8.15pm ET/5.15pm PT/12.15am GMT (Tuesday) Stadium: Lincoln Financial Field (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) How to watch United States: Watch on ESPN or ABC, or stream through Fubo or ESPN Unlimited. Fubo’s ABC availability depends on location. Canada: Stream on Fubo Sports Pro or DAZN. Fubo Sports Pro includes NFL Game Pass on DAZN. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN. What to watch for For Philly, McKee’s comfort level will be the most important thing. In his first 2026 outing, last week’s 25-14 loss to the Panthers, McKee threw 45 passes and prioritized getting the ball out quickly to leave less time for bad things to happen. McKee averaged 3.1 completed air yards per attempt, which ranks 40th in the NFL so far this season, according to Pro Football Reference. (The idea there: McKee did not successfully complete many passes more than a few yards beyond the line of scrimmage.) Most troublingly, the Eagles got just 2.9 yards after the catch per completion, a comically low rate that would have McKee last among regular starters. The Cowboys will be on high alert for blitzes from Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, who has surely observed Dak Prescott’s trouble against the blitz over his past two games. Fangio is one of the least-blitzy defensive coordinators in the league this season, but teams have drastically escalated their blitzing against Prescott, who has poor numbers against it (no touchdowns and a passer rating of 67 when blitzed in his last two games). Could it be that the much greener McKee is not the only QB to have an ugly time in this one?

headline: Bookies fear budget hit but gaming machine self-harm killed off the old-fashioned shops
trail_text: A wholesale plunder of local communities via casino-gaming took place and racing was content to sit on sidelines
body_text: Has it really been almost a year since racing’s last bout of Budget-related anxiety? Apparently so, because having successfully persuaded Rachel Reeves to exempt racing from a (modest) hike in betting duty in 2025, here we are again, nervously anticipating Wednesday’s budget amid warnings that John Healey could effectively sound the death-knell for high-street betting shops. Healey is widely expected to raise the rate of machine games duty (MGD) in the budget, a move which could, according to some predictions, lead to the closure of thousands of high-street shops with significant knock-on effects for racing’s income from off-course gambling. The prospect of a significant hike in MGD this week was initially floated by a report from the Social Market Foundation (SMF) thinktank in June. The report recommended doubling the duty rate on the profits from high-street gaming machines, from 20% to 40%, to reflect the significantly higher rates of harm associated with machine gaming compared to traditional betting on racing and sport. The gambling industry’s response was swift and indignant. Citing a report from the consultancy firm Regulus Partners, the industry warned that if Healey took the SMF’s advice, up to 4,000 of the UK’s 5,500 betting shops could be forced to close over the next three years. That, in turn, could cost the racing industry an estimated £92m in annual income – a third of its total from betting. The British Horseracing Authority also expressed its concern. “This would have devastating consequences for British racing,” Greg Swift, the BHA’s director of communications and corporate affairs, said in a statement this month, “hitting prize money, Levy funding and our ability to continue investing in our world-leading equine welfare and veterinary research projects.” Subsequent rumours ahead of Wednesday’s budget suggest that Healey is considering a less dramatic rise in MGD, from 20% to 25%. Yet even this, according to the gambling industry, could lead to hundreds of shop closures and tens of millions in lost revenue for racing. So, is the end really nigh for the high-street betting shop? Its demise has, after all, been forecast with some regularity over the last couple of decades since the advent of online gambling, and above all when the campaign to cut the maximum stake on the high-street fixed odds betting terminals (FOBTs), from £100 to £2, was at its height. Suggestions at the time that most or all of the UK’s shops would be shuttered within months if the cut were imposed proved to be a long way short of the mark. The current total of around 5,500 shops is well below the 9k around a decade ago, but that also reflects the fact that the gambling market as a whole, and among younger generations in particular, is increasingly moving online. At the same time, though, there can be little doubt, however, that racing remains painfully exposed to a major reduction in the number of shops. The sport’s income from the retail sector is tied to media rights contracts for live pictures and data agreed on a “per-shop” basis. The Regulus report suggests that racing receives around £27k in media rights and Levy payments from the average shop’s total annual revenue of £440k. If a sport that derives a significant chunk of its income via betting is caught up in the fallout from a tax rise on casino-gaming, however, there is an extent to which it can only have itself to blame. The BHA took offence when, shortly after being installed as prime minister, Andy Burnham lumped in betting shops alongside vape shops and adult gaming arcades as undesirable presences on the high street. But if an outlet cannot absorb a 5% rise in MGD, there is an argument that it is no longer a betting shop at all. It is a mini-casino, with betting on the side. At the turn of the century, a betting shop (or maybe two) was a familiar and largely accepted part of the high street landscape. But that consensus was swept away in the headlong rush to squeeze as many shops as possible into areas of high population density, in order to install the maximum number of four FOBTs in each one. It was the bookies themselves that killed off the old-fashioned betting shop, amid a cynical and deliberate orgy of corporate greed that sucked hundreds of millions of pounds from what were already the UK’s most deprived areas. They did not want or need five or six “betting” shops in a row, but they got them anyway. At one stage in the mid-2010s, there were 18 on the main high street in Hackney alone. It was a wholesale plunder of local communities via casino-gaming, and even as the campaign to restrict FOBT stakes gained irresistible momentum, racing was largely content to sit on the sidelines and keep counting the cash from its media rights deal. While Matt Hancock, the culture secretary in 2018, was consulting on whether to cut the maximum FOBT stake to £2, the BHA actively supported the gambling industry’s warnings of imminent disaster – including wholesale shop closures – if the cut was imposed. So while the rise of online gambling was always going to see a steady decline in the number of betting shops, it is thanks to the FOBTs that there will be very few in the general public to mourn their passing, if or when they close their doors. And racing, which did little or nothing to stand up for betting while the FOBT scandal unfolded, can have few genuine grounds for complaint if, after Wednesday’s budget, it continues to pay the price for its complicity.

headline: England fret over Fin Smith’s fitness for looming Australia match
trail_text: Steve Borthwick has been handed a dilemma at 10, with the Northampton fly-half unable to join the England training camp this week
body_text: England are fretting over the fitness of the fly-half Fin Smith in the lead-up to the Nations Championship home opener against Australia on 8 November. The Northampton player damaged a calf in the second half against Leicester on Saturday and will be unable to join the national squad who have a three-day training camp in Bagshot this week. Losing Smith so close to the Wallabies game would be a significant blow given the 24-year-old started at 10 in all three of England’s Tests in July and was instrumental in Saints’ domestic title triumph last season. England’s management say they remain hopeful he will be back in time to face Australia but, with limited preparation time available, there will inevitably be some disruption to Steve Borthwick’s plans. Borthwick has responded by calling up Gloucester’s Charlie Atkinson as cover, with Marcus Smith and George Ford the other specialist 10s in the squad. Since deposing Ford after England’s defeat against Ireland in the Six Nations, Fin Smith has staked a firm claim and is very much the man in possession of the 10 jersey. Marcus Smith’s last start at fly-half for England was against Ireland in Dublin in the opening round of the 2025 Six Nations. There will be an official update on Smith’s condition on Tuesday with injury doubts hanging over several other players. Bath’s Guy Pepper appeared to be in pain as he limped off against Gloucester on Friday, while Benhard Janse van Rensburg has not featured since suffering a heavy concussion in Bristol’s second Prem game of the season. The inside centre Seb Atkinson is also unable to train this week but has not ruled out playing for Gloucester at Northampton on Saturday. It leaves Borthwick and the squad’s other specialist centres – Henry Slade, Joe Marchant, Max Ojomoh and Fraser Dingwall – waiting to see what will unfold before the formal squad announcement next Monday. Marchant, for one, is delighted to be back in the frame for the first time since the 2023 World Cup. He then moved to Paris to play for Stade Français, having previously been told his England career was over, but is now back and eligible again after joining Sale Sharks. The 30-year-old Marchant, who married Alan Shearer’s daughter Hollie this year, said he would love to feature at the World Cup in Australia next year. “When I was a kid I wanted to play for England and that’s not changed,” he said.

headline: Doubles players sign open letter pleading with tennis chiefs to ‘protect’ format
trail_text: More than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board, imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms
body_text: More than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board and management imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms and “protect” the format in professional tennis. The subject of potential reforms to the ATP has been a significant issue since players were informed in a meeting during Wimbledon that the ATP was conducting a review of its doubles regulations and potential changes could see doubles draws being halved at the ATP events in 2028. Under these proposals, ATP Masters 1000 events would host only 16 doubles teams and the main draws at ATP 500 and 250 events would accommodate only eight teams. The proposals could also lead to the total prize money distributed to doubles players being halved from 20% to 10%, with the remaining money allocated towards singles players. The news provoked significant criticism from a large group of doubles players at Wimbledon, and they have spent subsequent months organising to resist the reforms. In addition to more than 150 active players, the letter has been signed by more than 20 national federations and legends of the sport. In the open letter, the players state: “The current plans would shift about $20m (£15m) in prize money from doubles to singles, while cutting a significant number of professional opportunities for doubles specialists. That shift would make it much harder for talented players to build and sustain a doubles career. A healthy professional sport cannot rely solely on a small group of top stars; it needs pathways for players to develop, compete and earn a living.” Sem Verbeek, the 2025 Wimbledon mixed doubles champion and one of the players spearheading the campaign, told the Guardian that the doubles players feel the ATP’s potential reforms threaten the future of doubles and that the ATP has not sought to collaborate with doubles players to shape the future of the discipline. “The A to B with these proposals is really threatening not only the history, but also the present and future of the whole discipline of professional men’s doubles,” he said. “The livelihoods of a lot of players are at stake here, and not only that, I think also the dreams of any young player that wants to pursue a doubles career are really in big jeopardy. “I think that one of the big reasons that we have so much support for this open letter is to really provide the ATP with a platform to get in touch with us and make this more of a collaboration rather than a one-sided review that they keep saying is ongoing. But any real data and real numbers and real requests that we have have not been answered so far. And I think that’s why a lot of active players are so frustrated with this because we have a lot of ideas.” The ATP management views doubles as an unsustainable loss leader, and it intends to redistribute some of the money currently reserved for doubles to singles players, an initiative doubles players believe pits singles and doubles players against each other despite the fact that they are all members of the same association. “The main message that we want to send is the ATP really has to balance short-term economic growth with the legacy that it has built,” Verbeek said. “We understand that the ATP and tennis as a whole is entertainment, is a business but you also have a responsibility to all of your fans worldwide to protect and grow the legacy of both disciplines of your sport. “It’s been clear so far I think for a lot of people, if you look at how inaccessible doubles is from a viewership standpoint, that the ATP has under-invested and under-marketed the discipline so far. So we really just want to invite the ATP to really meaningful collaborations and meaningful discussions on how we can grow this part of the sport without damaging the future of it and allowing people to have a celebratory career in doubles. And I think that’s part of the reason that so many legends have signed on. “For some reason the generation of decision makers that are in the ATP right now feel like a doubles career is not a real tennis career. And that to us is ludicrous. It should be celebrated. It’s a discipline that has provided a lot of history and should provide a lot of future and it shouldn’t be looked at as, let’s say, a failed singles career or something like that.” This month the ATP announced widespread reforms to the calendar, schedule and rule book. In a Q&A attributed to the ATP chief executive, Andrea Gaudenzi, on the ATP website, the men’s tennis governing body addressed its potential doubles reforms. “Doubles will continue to be a core part of the ATP Tour,” Gaudenzi wrote. “The review is focused on identifying a model that gives the discipline a sustainable long-term future, works effectively for tournaments and fans and supports the wider player pathway.”

headline: Liam Dawson reveals England are ‘gutted’ after latest ODI tri-series defeat
trail_text: Liam Dawson has revealed that the England cricket squad are ‘gutted’ after two agonising defeats have left their chances of making the ODI tri-series final hanging by a thread
body_text: Liam Dawson has revealed England’s disappointment after the two agonising defeats to Sri Lanka and Pakistan that have left making the ODI tri-series final in serious doubt. “That changing room is gutted, we’re desperate to win,” he said. To reach the final, England need Pakistan to beat Sri Lanka on Tuesday and then they have to thrash Gary Kirsten’s men on Thursday, but Dawson is optimistic the losses can help them in the World Cup in 12 months’ time in southern Africa. “If you look at the last two games, we’ve been in positions where we should have won, so that is a massive positive as a group,” he said. “To lose those two games from a position we’re in is frustrating because we should have won those games. “If, in a year’s time, we do get to those situations again and bank on our previous experiences then we’ll look back at this tri-series as a huge positive.” The 36-year-old said he is not drawing any conclusions from usurping Adil Rashid. For more than a decade, the leg-spinner has been the No 1 spinner for England in white-ball formats and he needs 26 more dismissals to become their all-time leading one-day wicket-taker. After missing September’s home series win over Sri Lanka because of an injury, Rashid has been overlooked for the defeats to Sri Lanka and Pakistan. The explanation given is Dawson’s skiddy slow left-armers are more suited to the conditions in Rawalpindi and Lahore, with Rashid expensive in his only tournament outing against Pakistan last week. In Rashid’s absence, Dawson has impressed, but a bowling unit light on experience has been exposed as England let seemingly surefire wins slip away. The former England captain Nasser Hussain told Sky Sports last week that Rashid’s recent performances had “dropped off”, although Dawson believes the double World Cup winner remains a stellar operator. “I don’t think I can be compared to Adil, he’s a phenomenal bowler,” he said. “You don’t play 165 ODIs and become a bad bowler. I don’t think you can compare us at all because we’re so different in our roles in the team. He’s a fantastic bowler, he’s been exceptional for England and I think he still will be.” Without an express paceman or mystery spinner, England let Pakistan off the hook from 154 for nine chasing 242 in Lahore on Sunday as Shadab Khan and the No 11, Haris Rauf, sealed an extraordinary win for the hosts. The pair’s 89-run stand set a record for the highest 10th-wicket partnership in a successful chase and came three days after England, despite Harry Brook smashing a double hundred, were unable to defend 429 against Sri Lanka After being a fringe England player for much of his career, Dawson has established himself as a mainstay in the T20 side under Brook and is more involved in the ODI setup. “Up until a year or so ago, I said to numerous people I didn’t think I’d play for England again,” he said. “I’ve really enjoyed the time I’ve had so far. You’re desperate to do well, but each time I get to play for England is a really special thing. I didn’t think it would happen at the age I got to so to play the amount I have in the last year and contribute has been really pleasing and hopefully that can continue.” Dawson retired from first-class cricket in May after 19 years with Hampshire and having played four Test matches, but he will not be reversing that decision even if approached by the new England Test head coach, Stephen Fleming. “Those days are gone,” he said.

headline: TNT Sports close to securing live UK rights for England white-ball cricket tour of Australia
trail_text: TNT Sports is close to securing live UK rights for England’s white-ball tour of Australia next month in a deal that could see one of the matches broadcast free-to-air
body_text: TNT Sports is close to securing live UK rights for England’s white-ball tour of Australia next month in a deal that could see one of the matches broadcast free-to-air on Channel 5. The Guardian has learned that Channel 5 is also in advanced talks with Cricket Australia over a highlights package for the eight-match tour, with the terrestrial broadcaster also in discussions over securing live rights for one of the five T20 internationals. Channel 5 has live rights for two home men’s and two women’s T20s each summer in a four-year deal that began this year, but has never broadcast an England match from overseas. While the finer details are still being discussed, the opening T20 of the five-match series in Melbourne on 21 November is the game of greatest interest to Channel 5, as the start time of 8.15am on a Saturday is likely to attract the biggest UK audience. If the deal is completed it would be the first time an England overseas game has been broadcast FTA since Channel 4 picked up the rights for a Test series in India in 2021 during the final Covid-19 lockdown. TNT Sports has broadcast England’s past three Ashes series in Australia so its decision to bid for a white-ball tour, that also attracted interest from Sky Sports and Dazn, comes as little surprise. Channel 5’s involvement is an intriguing development, however, which raises the prospect of more cooperation between the two over sports rights given that they are both owned by the US media giant Paramount Skydance. Channel 5 also picked up a highlights deal for the Commonwealth Games in the UK last summer with the event broadcast exclusively live on TNT Sports. Brendon McCullum’s white-ball squad fly to Australia at the start of next month following a brief return home after the conclusion of the one‑day international tri-series that is taking place in Pakistan, where England are struggling to reach the final after due to successive defeats to the hosts and Sri Lanka over the past seven days. After criticism of their preparation for last winter’s Ashes series the England and Wales Cricket Board has scheduled a 50-over warm-up game at the WACA on 7 November ahead of a three-match series that begins at the Perth Stadium on 13 November, with five T20s beginning the week later. The value of overseas cricket rights has fallen in recent years with the result that most of England’s winter tours have only been sold at the last minute. Sky Sports have bought the rights for England’s Test series in South Africa over Christmas, and are broadcasting the tri-series in Pakistan, but have moved away from signing long-term deals with overseas boards. TNT Sports declined to comment, but Cricket Australia is understood to be confident that the deal will be completed.

headline: Wolff hails Antonelli’s US Grand Prix demolition as the Italian’s ‘best race yet’
trail_text: The Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has paid tribute to his driver Kimi Antonelli and hailed his victory at the US Grand Prix as the Italian’s ‘best race yet’
body_text: The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has paid tribute to Kimi Antonelli, who all but closed out his first Formula One world championship with a victory at the US Grand Prix that Wolff described as the Italian’s best race. Wolff was at pains to point out the considerable efforts made by a number of other people in bringing the young Italian to the verge of a record-breaking title. After his victory at the Circuit of the Americas, Antonelli needs to finish ninth or better at the Mexican Grand Prix this weekend. He could even finish outside the points as long as neither his teammate, George Russell, nor Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, the other drivers in the running, win the race. If he seals the title in Mexico City he will become F1’s youngest world champion at 20 years old. Antonelli led from pole position on Sunday with a controlled, dominant run largely at the front of the field, for his ninth success of the season. “On Kimi’s side, the main headline is that [it is] for me the best race that he’s delivered,” Wolff said. “Getting off the start with the inferior tyre and then controlling it at all times. Exceptional. I think he’s outperformed the car.” When asked if it matched Antonelli’s superb drive from 19th to victory at the Italian Grand Prix in September, Wolff acknowledged it was special, but that Austin was up there with that drive. Antonelli concurred. “Monza was a super special one and one I will remember for ever,” he said. “But this one, probably in terms of execution, was better because the way we built the performance throughout the weekend was very good.” Wolff believed it was all the more impressive given how difficult Antonelli’s rookie season had been in 2025 when at times he struggled with the car and made mistakes that caused some to question whether Mercedes had been correct to promote him to the team so soon. Those are doubts he feels Antonelli has comprehensively silenced. “There are many people that said last year after nine races without points he shouldn’t be in a Mercedes,” Wolff said. “People in other teams that said he shouldn’t even be in Formula One. “All of that now is extremely satisfying to see what he’s able to deliver, how he’s working with the team, with Bono [race engineer, Peter Bonnington] and yielding the results. But it wasn’t an easy road. “It’s been 30 or more years that I’ve tried to understand racing drivers’ brains and I still don’t know what has happened over the winter. His ability to process and deliver something that’s outstanding, which we didn’t see coming.” Mercedes took on Antonelli as part of their driver development programme when he was 12 years old and have supported him through karting and in the feeder series to F1. Wolff was the driving force behind bringing Antonelli into the team to take Hamilton’s seat when the Briton left for Ferrari. Wolff was insistent he felt the youngster was ready to step up and he maintained that Antonelli’s success should not be viewed as having come from nowhere, but rather the product of many years and the input of many people. “I wasn’t the one responsible for it,” Wolff said. “It was teamwork.
