It was our junior team around [the Mercedes driver development adviser] Gwen [Lagrue] that discovered him when he was 11. “Credit to that group that have developed him over the many years. I read an interview [with the Ferrari vice-chair] Piero Ferrari last week where he said: ‘What a talent, he reminds me of Niki Lauda.’ And I’m thinking, people don’t get that this is the work of nine years. “The development of nine years, the hardship over nine years, the integration of the team, the working with the engineers, millions in the development of his career, of his ability, of his character together with his parents. It’s just not that it landed like this.”

headline: Creaking, smug … and a contender? Aaron Rodgers may yet get his Super Bowl farewell
trail_text: The 42-year-old remains a polarizing figure. But the Steelers have a formidable defense and a quarterback who has seen it all before
body_text: Aaron Rodgers is nowhere near this NFL season’s MVP conversation. At times in his second season with the Pittsburgh Steelers, the almost-43-year-old has shown glimpses of the player he was in his prime, slinging the ball with zest and precision, able to suss out any coverage. Other times he has looked like, well, a guy in his 40s playing a young man’s game. Rodgers looked more like prime Rodgers in the Steelers’ gritty 16-10 win over the New Orleans Saints in Paris. He wasn’t satisfied with his side of the ball, telling reporter Molly McGrath, “I don’t think we played very good on offense today.” But Rodgers did enough to secure the win, including a 51-yard strike to DK Metcalf in the second quarter. He later scrambled for a first down on third-and-six to secure the win. Sure, there were points left on the table – the Steelers had several stalled drives and scored only one touchdown in four red-zone trips – and 16 points against a two-win team isn’t impressive. But the Steelers left France with a win, a 5-2 record and a ton of upside. So here’s a crazy thought: could Rodgers win a Super Bowl in his final NFL season? But when you consider the parts around Rodgers, perhaps it’s not so crazy. As competent as Rodgers was against the Saints, the defense stole the show. It smothered Saints quarterback Tyler Shough, and shut down the Saints’ run game as Steelers linebacker Patrick Queen had predicted. This Steelers run defense is punishing and only improving. In Weeks 1 through 4, it allowed 4.5 yards per carry. Over the last three weeks, that has dropped to 2.8 yards per carry. All told, Pittsburgh’s defense has allowed just three touchdowns in the last 15 quarters. That is some 2025 Seahawks-level domination. Offensively, Rodgers is no worse than Sam Darnold was last year when the Seahawks won the Super Bowl. He’s thrown 13 touchdown passes and five interceptions for 1,699 yards through his first seven games – Darnold had 12 TDs, four picks and 1,754 yards over the same span in 2025. Saints linebacker Kaden Elliss likened Rodgers to a point guard, noting the advantage he has over other NFL quarterbacks. “Even though he’s up there in age, I think that’s an advantage to him, his mind,” Elliss said after Sunday’s game. “And I think he used that today.” Maybe Rodgers’s football IQ could catapult Pittsburgh to a deep playoff run in the AFC. Yes, there are the perennial Super Bowl contenders like Kansas City and Buffalo, but no AFC team this season is a winning machine like the Patriots in the Brady-Belichick era. And, after a ho-hum Super Bowl from a star power perspective, a Rodgers return to the big stage would set off fireworks. Of course, Rodgers comes with plenty of baggage due to his commitment to his “own research” during the pandemic, his ridiculous antipathy towards Anthony Fauci and his habit of calling out coaches and teammates. Recently, though, he appears to have realized keeping his opinions to himself is probably the best course of action. His worst take over the weekend was appearing to think Peaky Blinders was set in France rather than England. He’s not exactly likable, but considering what he’s said in the past, his recent behavior seems like progress. Not that he’s completely quiet. In Paris, when asked about the International Series, he let it be known that NFL owners had considered a 16-game schedule with two byes and an entire international week, where teams play all over the world. Instead, according to Rodgers, they opted for the 17-game schedule to rake in extra cash. Rodgers added that the league “may be a little tight on money”, a refreshing level of shade that will win him some fans. Realistically, Rodgers and the Steelers will need a good deal of luck to make it to the Super Bowl this year. But that’s the case for plenty of teams. A run to the title game would send Rodgers’s smugness off the charts, but you have to admit that his final game coming on Super Bowl Sunday would be interesting. MVP of the week Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. Down 13-0 at the half, the Bengals looked destined for an infuriating loss, an art they specialize in. They had mustered just 49 passing yards, and were struggling to sustain drives. Meanwhile, the supposedly retooled Bengals defense couldn’t get the Ravens off the field. At the half, Baltimore, led by a backup quarterback, had dominated the time of possession 22:20 to 7:40. Yet again, Cincinnati looked like a fringe playoff team not meeting their full potential. And after locking up star receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins for Joe Burrow in his prime, being a fringe playoff team isn’t acceptable. Chase’s half-time team talk seems to have worked. “I told our offense [that] we can’t look at our defense the whole time. We’ve got to step this shit up and make something work,” he said after the game. Burrow, who is chasing his first league MVP, duly played out of his mind. He was essentially perfect after the break, dicing up the Ravens secondary for four touchdowns on four drives with 243 yards and an 89% completion percentage. Burrow made it look effortless as he tends to do at his best. Stat of the week 64. How do the Tampa Bay Buccaneers win a game 43-13 when Baker Mayfield threw for only 64 passing yards? They faced a Carolina Panthers team who were a walking comedy of errors. Mayfield threw just 11 passes in his first game back from dislocating his thumb, and did connect with Tez Johnson for a score. The damage unsurprisingly came on the ground – Tampa rushed for 258 yards and three touchdowns, including two from Bucky Irving, who eclipsed 100 yards. The Bucs also strip-sacked Bryce Young and returned it for a touchdown. Imagine the score if Mayfield was slinging the rock. Video of the week Bo Nix came into Sunday’s game with just 37 rushing yards all season. So when the Broncos quarterback nearly doubled that total in one play – a 62-yard touchdown run that gave Denver a late second-quarter lead over Arizona – hell yeah, he was going to add a flourish. The spin move at the goalline might not have been necessary, but it must have been cathartic. Nix has been criticized for not providing an offensive spark, even though Denver entered the game at 4-2 after negotiating one of the league’s toughest schedules. But Nix looked far more comfortable – and at times electric – in Sunday’s 30-16 win. He finished with the one long rushing touchdown, and 222 passing yards. Elsewhere around the league -- The Chiefs were undefeated going into their game with the Super Bowl champion Seahawks but we knew Kansas City had flaws. Patrick Mahomes has been good rather than great, the receiving corps is ravaged, and their schedule was soft to start the season. On Sunday Night Football, they were overwhelmed by Seattle, whose defense became the first unit this season to make former Seahawk Kenneth Walker III look human. And Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba was terrifying once again, hauling in 150 receiving yards in his team’s 20-3 win. “One hell of a game from Sam Darnold,” Smith-Njigba said, slightly underplaying his own contribution. –- The Miami Dolphins are no longer winless after humiliating the New York Jets 28-25 at MetLife. Geno Smith was outplayed by Malik Willis, who played clean football and was able to scramble at will, especially in the first half. Jeff Hafley outcoached Aaron Glenn, not a hard feat. Given New York’s talent advantage, they have no business losing at home to a 0-5 team with severe salary cap issues. But when the Dolphins have the ball for the final nine minutes of the first half and Glenn enters the break with all three timeouts remaining, winning is difficult. The Jets’ star receiver, Garrett Wilson, has cut a frustrated figure recently and was targeted just three times Sunday. CBS cameras caught him yelling on the sidelines, although he later denied his anger was directed at his quarterback, Geno Smith. “We were collaborating,” Wilson said. “I don’t even think I was talking to Geno.” This fan on Reddit summed it up best. –- The Minnesota Vikings moved to 6-0 after an ugly 16-10 win over the Indianapolis Colts. This was not the game that will leave the rest of the NFL believing the Vikings are a juggernaut. Colts kicker Spencer Shrader missed two field goals, and Minnesota sealed the win after Daniel Jones delivered a ball right to safety Harrison Smith. But the Vikings are the only undefeated team left in the league, something few would have predicted at the start of the season. –- The Houston Texans fell to 2-5 after a 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants, who move to 4-2-1 and are very much in contention in a weak NFC East. It was a masterclass by the Giants’ offensive line and running backs against a Houston team who were favored by 10.5 points. Cam Skattebo tore through the Texans line with 17 carries, 124 yards and a touchdown, a week after being benched. In his first start for New York, JJ McCarthy was sensational. While he had no passing touchdowns, McCarthy (20-of-28, 252 yards and no turnovers) was comfortable in the pocket and able to anticipate coverage under pressure. One bright spot amid the disappointment for Houston: Tank Dell caught his first pass in 673 days. Dell suffered a torn ACL, MCL, LCL and a dislocated kneecap in late 2024, and his return is miraculous after a plethora of surgeries. –- The Atlanta Falcons handed the San Francisco 49ers their first loss of the season. The Falcons were opportunistic in the 29-20 win after a series of miscues by the 49ers. Brock Purdy threw two interceptions, including one on a pass he meant to be thrown away. The absence of the injured Mike Evans was felt keenly, and Christian McCaffrey missed a chunk of the game with a thigh injury, though he did return. Given the thin wide receiver corps in San Francisco, perhaps there’s an unhappy camper they can pursue.

headline: ‘We’re not doing great’: Gilgeous-Alexander in tears after Williams suffers gruesome leg injury
trail_text: Shai-Gilgeous Alexander scored 34 points and the Thunder stayed undefeated but they lost guard Jalen Williams to what appeared to be a serious leg injury
body_text: Shai-Gilgeous Alexander scored 34 points and the Oklahoma City Thunder stayed undefeated but they lost All-Star guard Jalen Williams to what appeared to be a serious leg injury during their 108-101 victory over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday night. Oklahoma City won their third straight game to start the season but lost three players to injury, including Williams, who went down hard on a drive to the basket with 1:14 left. The guard’s left leg gave way as he landed and his foot bent at an unnatural angle. The 25-year-old left the court on a stretcher with towels covering his injured leg. He covered his mouth with his hands when he looked down at the injury while Gilgeous-Alexander and players on both teams appeared to be in shock. “We’re not doing great,” Thunder coach Mark Daigneault said after the game. On Monday, it was confirmed that Williams suffered a fractured fibula and a dislocated left ankle. He is likely to miss the rest of the season. Gilgeous-Alexander was in tears as he spoke about Williams after the game. “I just feel bad for him,” Gilgeous-Alexander said. “It’s obviously going to be tough without a player like that. But he’s not gone for ever. He’ll be back better than ever, and we know it. We’ve just got to hold the fort down until he comes back.” Williams missed 49 games last season due to a variety of injuries but was a key part of the Thunder’s title campaign in 2025. Thunder guard Cason Wallace (left shoulder soreness) and forward Jaylin Williams (right wrist soreness) left the game in the first quarter and did not return.

headline: Kimi Antonelli looks forward to drivers’ title after victory in US Grand Prix
trail_text: The F1 champion-elect, now two points from his first championship, said: ‘Hopefully we can clinch it soon,’  but Max Verstappen was unhappy with his car
byline: Giles Richards at the Circuit of the Americas
body_text: Kimi Antonelli has acknowledged the Formula One world championship is within his grasp after the Italian took a dominant victory at the US Grand Prix which has put him just two points away from clinching his first title at the Mexican Grand Prix next weekend. Antonelli beat the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second place and the Red Bull of Max Verstappen into third. With his title rivals George Russell and Lewis Hamilton finishing eighth and fourth respectively, Antonelli will take the title if he finishes ninth or better in Mexico City. The 20-year-old, who stands to become Formula 1’s youngest champion, was jubilant as he crossed the line at the Circuit of the Americas. “Yeah! That’s how we do it,” he exclaimed to his engineer Peter Bonnington. “Another small step,” the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, told Antonelli over the radio after the victory. “Another small step.” With Mercedes having worked hard to iron out issues with their recent upgrades to the car, the victory was important to the team, who pulled off a coup in opting for a one-stop strategy which paid off handsomely for their world champion-elect driver. Antonelli paid tribute to his team. “We’re very close [to the title], hopefully we can clinch it soon,” he said. “It was a result we needed, to be fair, the whole team deserved it all this time – working to bring this new package and finally seeing the result is very pleasant. It was a perfect execution of strategy to call the one stop. Today was a great team effort.” This view was echoed by the Mercedes deputy team principal, Bradley Lord. “It felt like everyone was getting a bit excited but all Kimi could do today is go out and win,” he said. “Amazing job by everyone on the pit wall and the strategists back at base. What a drive, what a win.” However Verstappen, whose Red Bull team opted for a two-stop strategy, was far from enamoured with his afternoon and a car that was suffering from problems. “Yeah, that was terrible,” he said. “The pace, the wrong tyre, shit pit stop, shit engine braking. Nothing worked.”

headline: Kimi Antonelli storms to US F1 GP victory but is made to wait for title glory
trail_text: The 20-year-old championship leader won from Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen and should become F1’s youngest world champion next week in Mexico
byline: Giles Richards at the Circuit of the Americas
body_text: With a calm assurance that belies his tender years, Kimi Antonelli delivered another masterclass at the US Grand Prix, ensuring that while he could not quite seal the Formula One world championship in the Texas sunshine, it is a coronation that is surely only delayed for a week. The 20-year-old has made it almost a formality that he will seal the deal at the next round in Mexico. Antonelli’s dominant victory in Austin at the Circuit of the Americas, with a controlled and composed drive to beat the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second place and the Red Bull of Max Verstappen into third, was described by the Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff as “one small step” towards the title in what has been a season of giant leaps for the Italian. Those leaps were exemplified by Antonelli’s run in Austin where he did everything required of him, taking pole and converting it to a dominant race win, his ninth of the season. “The race of a champion who isn’t the champion yet,” was Wolff’s accurate assessment. However, while it was a perfect weekend for the Italian, it was not quite enough to claim the title in Texas. With his teammate George Russell finishing in eighth place and Lewis Hamilton in fourth for Ferrari, the fight remains alive but only just and Antonelli is now in position to finish the job next weekend in Mexico City. Antonelli leads Russell by 123 points and Hamilton by 124. With nine wins, the Italian cannot be caught on countback and needs to be only 100 ahead after the Mexican GP. Any finish in front of Russell and Hamilton, or ninth or better regardless of where his two rivals finish, will be enough for him to become the youngest driver to claim the sport’s crown and the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari in 1953. The joy when Antonelli climbed from the car was palpable as he allowed himself the chance to acknowledge the feeling that he really is now world champion-elect. It was not a thrilling victory in what was something of a stately affair, but again Antonelli had its measure and was all but untouchable in a race enlivened really only by a split strategy. The Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell opted for a one-stop strategy over the two-stop choice of Red Bull and Ferrari, and the former proved to be the right call. Antonelli led from the off and after putting in a long first stint while his rivals dashed in for new boots, he emerged able to regain the lead without having to stop again. The strategy split made the procession at least open to debate for the mid-period until it became clear that the one-stop option was the quicker. The late phase did see some feisty passing by Verstappen, who took advantage of his fresher rubber to hustle through the field, as in his wake did Leclerc, who was equally brave and ultimately took second place. Verstappen finished in third, although he was suffering with engine-braking problems. Hamilton, too, made a late pass to claim fourth , with Lando Norris in fifth for McLaren The race belonged to Antonelli, however. He did not put a foot wrong with a cool-headed display as he assuredly put one hand on the title. The Italian went into the weekend insisting he just wanted to have fun, to perform at his best and without letting the title play on his mind. He did so with no little success. The pole lap had been brilliant, his first since Belgium in July, and in the race he demonstrated the same imperious form as when at his very best this season and which has brought him to within touching distance of his record-breaking achievement. Just as his five-race run of victories at the start of the season had given him command of the title fight, he is closing it out with nerveless control. The pole, he admitted, had been something of a surprise given how strong Red Bull have been of late but the victory was an emphatic reminder that these are the performances Antonelli is always capable of delivering. Moreover, the result was welcomed with open arms at Mercedes. The minor wobble they experienced when their upgrades brought to Malaysia did not deliver as expected and left the team having to work at bringing the package up to speed, looks to be over. The upgrade is not where they want it to be, the car’s operating window is narrower, but they have a handle on it that the victory demonstrated even if, as Wolff noted, the car remains unsuited to Russell’s style. That is particularly true in comparison to Antonelli, in whose hands the Mercedes once more looked like it was on rails. He went into this race needing to win and he delivered, ensuring that the title race is all over bar the shouting.

headline: NFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Seahawks, TV channels & live stream Sunday 25 October
trail_text: How will the Kansas City and Seattle fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
body_text: Sunday Night Football this week is a blockbuster. The Chiefs take their undefeated record to Seattle, where the defending-champ Seahawks should have an early sense of urgency. Mike Macdonald’s team enter at 3-3, already a full three games (plus, for now, a tiebreaker) behind the gangbusters 49ers. To have any real shot at a home playoff game — a critical edge in last year’s Super Bowl run — the Seahawks need to get a win against a resurgent Chiefs squad who nothing like the husk they appeared to be down the stretch last season. In addition to a clash between two marquee franchises, the evening is a homecoming for one of the most important players of the young season: Kenneth Walker III. The Seahawks-turned-Chiefs running back has been key to KC’s offensive revitalization after signing as a free agent following his Super Bowl MVP nod with Seattle. The Chiefs were in the bottom half of the league in rushing yards per carry last year but this season hold a whopping lead over the second-place team, averaging 5.5 yards to the Bills’ 5.1. The 26-year-old Walker is having a career year and has worked his way from “good player” to “maybe the Offensive Player of the Year.” Date: Sunday 25 October 2026 Time: 8.20pm ET/5.20pm PT/12.20am GMT (Monday 26 October) Stadium: Lumen Field (Seattle, Washington) How to watch United States: Watch on NBC, or stream on Fubo. Canada: Stream on Fubo Sports Pro. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN. What to watch for The Seahawks need to get Sam Darnold on track. Sure, leading the club to a Super Bowl win has bought the veteran some goodwill, but Darnold has been bad enough that the Seahawks fan in your life has probably texted you at least once to call for the elevation of backup Drew Lock. Darnold, who was hurt earlier in the year, is throwing interceptions on a career-worst 4.7% of his throws. His passing success rate reached a career high 50% last year but has dipped to 40% in the early going here, one of the lowest marks he’s posted. Meanwhile, the Chiefs don’t have big problems right now, but they do have little ones that they should address in the near term. One of them is that Patrick Mahomes has had pedestrian numbers in three of the team’s five games, only really lighting it up in a Week 3 win over the dreadful Dolphins. This hasn’t been a big issue with Walker setting the world on fire, but as Mahomes gets deeper into the season and further from the ACL and LCL tears that ended his season last year, you’d hope to see some growth. The bad news here: Seattle is giving up 4.3 adjusted net yards per attempt, by far the best mark in football. One might expect that for the Chiefs to stay unbeaten, Walker will need to keep doing the heavy lifting.

headline: Joe Marchant recalled to England training squad for Nations Championship
trail_text: Joe Marchant has been recalled to England’s training squad for the Nations Championship next month as Steve Borthwick faces injury disruption to his midfield options
body_text: Sale’s Joe Marchant and Gloucester’s Will Joseph are two notable inclusions among Steve Borthwick’s 36-man England squad, announced on Sunday, for the conclusion of the Nations Championship in November, with both boosting the head coach’s midfield options. The 30-year-old centre Marchant last appeared for England at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, and spent two seasons at Stade Français in the Top 14, before returning to the Prem with Sale Sharks for this season. Will Joseph, the 24-year-old younger brother of the former England player Jonathan Joseph, has illuminated the table-topping Gloucester’s strong start to the domestic season. He was called up by Eddie Jones for the tour to Australia in 2022, making one brief appearance off the bench in a second-Test win against the Wallabies in Brisbane. Henry Slade, Max Ojomoh and Fraser Dingwall are Borthwick’s other centre options, with Benhard Janse van Rensburg of Bristol sidelined by a concussion sustained against Northampton this month. The Gloucester centre Seb Atkinson is among three players called up to continue their injury rehabilitation, along with Manny Feyi-Waboso of Exeter and Bath’s Guy Pepper. The scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet, who helped Leicester to defeat their local rivals Northampton at Welford Road on Saturday, is included along with the Saints pair of Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland. The 21-year old McParland is uncapped, while there is no place in the squad for Ben Spencer of Bath. Kepu Tuipulotu, the Bath hooker, is another uncapped 21-year-old called up by Borthwick. Fin Smith, Marcus Smith and George Ford are the specialist fly‑halves – while in the forwards the captain, Maro Itoje, having been rested in the summer, will return to the international stage. Alex Coles, Ollie Chessum, George Martin and Arthur Clark, another player flourishing at Gloucester, will be candidates to start with Itoje at lock. But there is no place for the 37-year-old lock Courtney Lawes, who like Marchant returned from a spell in France to sign for Sale. Tom Pearson (Northampton) and Ben Curry (Sale) return to a squad packed with back-row talent, and will compete for starting spots with Tom Curry, Ben Earl, Henry Pollock and Greg Fisilau. The prop Fin Baxter, who impressed for Harlequins in their victory against Saracens on Sunday, is back after almost a year sidelined with a foot injury. His clubmate Marcus Smith made a strong case to start in November by dismantling Saracens in Quins’ 33-15 win. Borthwick’s squad assembled on Sunday at Pennyhill Park for a three‑day training camp, with the players due to return to their clubs for the Prem’s fifth round next weekend. England begin their November programme against Australia at Twickenham on Sunday 8 November, before facing Japan on Saturday 14 November. A high-stakes encounter against the All Blacks follows on Saturday 21 November, with fixtures for the concluding Nations Championship weekend, on 27/28/29 November, to be confirmed.

headline: Marcus Smith produces timely reminder of his class as Harlequins sink Saracens
trail_text: Marcus Smith starred for Harlequins in their 33-15 derby victory against Saracens
byline: Luke McLaughlin at the Twickenham Stoop
body_text: Marcus Smith celebrated his 200th Harlequins match in magnificent style. Perhaps there is a danger, at times, of taking his immense talent for granted, but he was unstoppable here. A powerful visiting Saracens side barely got a look-in, with Smith reminding us all of his ability on the day Steve Borthwick named his England squad for a packed November. Smith’s sensational running, distribution and tactical kicking masterfully controlled Quins’ attack for a badly needed success. They were nought from three in the league and this was a vital result for reasons more important than Smith’s personal prestige. Defensive discipline and forward muscle was as significant as the customary soft hands and creative vision. It is only one victory but the storm clouds gathering around Jason Gilmore, the head coach – and the rest of the club’s hierarchy – have cleared to some extent. Gilmore paid tribute to Smith: “The work he puts in, the way he cares about the club, he’s only 27 and played 200 games for us. We’re so lucky to have him. He led us around the park and I’m really proud of Smithy.” Saracens – despite the presence of Maro Itoje, George Martin and Ben Earl – struggled to make an impact, hardly helped by their indiscipline; Earl and Fergus Burke were shown yellow cards before half-time. Brendan Venter’s rotation policy may begin to raise eyebrows: Noah Caluori, Owen Farrell and Charlie Bracken were doing shuttle runs 10 minutes before kick-off. There are not many clubs who would ignore players of that quality as a matter of course. “We have chopped and changed, so I understand why people are asking that,” Joe Shaw, the Saracens head coach, said of his side’s obvious lack of cohesion. “It’s not some random thing we’re trying to be quirky with. We believe there is merit in what we’re doing.” The Prem weekend had been characterised by stormy weather and old-fashioned wrestles at Welford Road and Ashton Gate, in conditions that did not favour free‑flowing rugby. A stiff breeze remained but the appearance of the sun played into Quins’ hands. Smith proved the point within three minutes, launching an attack down the left before capitalising on slick handling from George Furbank and Cadan Murley to sprint over. The crowd were on their feet. The tone was set. The prop Fin Baxter, returning from a 10-month injury layoff, soon demonstrated Quins are about more than silky skill, producing a muscular carry in the 22 before a delightful one‑handed offload for the openside Seb Driscoll, who smashed through the Sarries No 9, Tomos Williams, and over the line. The wing Rotimi Segun did get Saracens on the board with a fine twisting finish after the visitors worked through the phases into the Quins’ 22, with Martin, Rhys Carré and Theo Dan making inroads before Williams’s looping pass to the left. But Quins, as if to prove a point, soon went to the driving maul at the other end, culminating in a penalty try and Earl in the sin bin for collapsing it. Smith’s afternoon got better when Max Malins was sent cantering over the line on 26 minutes thanks to more sharp work by Segun. The England back, hungry to make a difference at both ends, chased a seemingly lost cause and batted the ball out of Malins’s hands. Saracens’ media strategy has been debated recently and a three-word message on social media last week – “Their cup final” – raised the pre-match temperature. Rather like Northampton’s Henry Pollock and his embarrassing involvement in a scuffle at Leicester on Saturday – that only served to motivate the opposition – it was a provocative move from Saracens that seemed to backfire. Before half-time, Burke was shown a yellow card for an upright tackle on Rodrigo Isgró before Murley pounced for Quins’ fourth: bonus point secured, 26-5 at half-time. Saracens had missed 22 tackles and conceded 10 penalties. On 55 minutes Quins twisted the knife. Williams flung a long pass out for Segun on the Saracens left where he knocked it on: Will Porter, the No 9, kicked ahead, collected and took advantage of some halfhearted defending to score Quins’ fifth and final try. It was a ragged effort from Sarries and will be a horrible one for their post-match analysis. Tottenham’s 2-0 win against Chelsea on Saturday – another significant London derby – was distinctly un‑Spursy. Here was a heartening, notably un‑Quinsy, victory for Smith, the player of the match, and his suddenly resurgent team. “He’s brilliant isn’t he?” Shaw said of Smith, adding the derby defeat left him with an “awful feeling”. “We planned for him not to be that brilliant. He can pick you off. It’s a disappointing day at the office.”

headline: England stunned after Shadab Khan’s miraculous century delivers one-wicket win for Pakistan
trail_text: Shadab Khan made an unbeaten 113 in a thrilling last-wicket stand with Haris Rauf as Pakistan, chasing 242, beat England in a thriller
body_text: Shadab Khan whipped the rug from under England’s boots with an eye-popping 113, a blitz of boundary peppering when hope was lost, the one-wicket win guaranteeing Pakistan a place in the tri-series final. England, for the second time in four days, watched a sure thing swirl down the drain. With Pakistan 154 for nine in their run chase, 88 away from victory, queues were beginning to build at the Gaddafi Stadium exits. But Shadab had other ideas, and with No 11 Haris Rauf providing adhesive company, went on the rampage. Balls disappeared over this boundary and that as England giggled nervously into their hands. The drama doubled when Shadab was given out lbw on 97, slamming his bat into the turf in frustration, hands shaken with England, before an inside edge was discovered on a what-the-heck review. From there 21 were needed, and 21 were hit, nail-nibbling minutes encompassing Rauf arguing a Sam Curran wide with Will Jacks having to be placated by Joe Root, a first hundred in any international cricket for Shadab, and Rauf driving Henry Crocombe for four to win the game by one wicket. Their partnership of 89 was the highest for the 10th wicket in any successful ODI chase. After the cut-throat chubbiness of Thursday’s 859-run glut, this was pared-down cricket. Pakistan, in West Indies World Series salmon pink for breast cancer, had looked in command at the halfway stage, after England left runs in the middle, all out with 20 balls to spare for just 241. But England’s bowlers kept their nerve and Pakistan’s batters faltered, until Shadab and Rauf’s last stand. Pakistan’s chase started under a purple Lahore night sky, with the ground filling up late. Like England earlier in the day, Pakistan had a tricky power play. A frustrated Fakhar Zaman flashed a drive straight into the giant paws of Jamie Overton at slip in the fifth over to give the immaculate Gus Atkinson his first wicket. The debutant Crocombe, all baggy shirt and rosy cheeks, coltish arms and legs working overtime, shared the new ball. He was on the money with his first over, and a more erratic nine-ball third finished with the wicket of Saim Ayub, who ladled the ball straight to Overton as Crocombe was mobbed. The crowd had one name on its lips and Babar Azam, at his home ground, made them sing with a pure off-drive matched by something equally majestic on the on-side. But just as the glory hit the veins, Atkinson whistled through the gate, firing the top of off, wagging his finger in celebration. Saad Baig picked up the pace with an otherworldly 32, until a bullet was collected by Jacks at backward point off Overton, who had pulled up in his delivery stride earlier in the over. From there, it was cat and mouse: could England frustrate Pakistan into giving wickets away? Yes they could, as Liam Dawson and Overton bowled on a button, and finally Hasan Nawaz yahooed Dawson into the stratosphere, Harry Brook waiting for his prize. Arafat Minhas lasted just three balls before directing Overton to Root, who had just been ushered to short fine leg by Brook. Salman Ali Agha had a meaty slog at Dawson, Razaullah, also on ODI debut, got a gorgeous ball from Jacks between bat and pad to leave Pakistan nine down. It looked like game over. Earlier, Ben Duckett’s fifth ODI century was the backbone of an England innings that sparked in places but was blotted by clusters of wickets. His second century at Lahore was dominated by sweeps of various hues, but after Pakistan won the toss and bowled, England’s first four wickets lined up like a pin number: 4, 5, 1, 6. Tom Banton clipped the superb Shaheen Shah Afridi’s fifth ball to cover to give him a 150th ODI wicket. Root had time, just, to dispatch Afridi to the boundary before leaning back and enveloping him to point. Brook, fresh from 202 against Sri Lanka, was undone coming back for a second, fractionally too slow for an inspired Razaullah pick up and throw. Then Jordan Cox tried to nuzzle Rauf to third man but was met by Babar diving to his right at slip. In Curran, Duckett at last found sticking power, and the pair added 93 until Shaheen brought himself back on and Curran took on his shorter ball. As the black kites circled above, England’s last five wickets added 96, Duckett celebrating his first hundred against Pakistan with a low-key kiss of the badge, but they looked underdone and so it proved. To reach the final, England need Pakistan to beat Sri Lanka on Tuesday before thrashing Sri Lanka on Thursday.

headline: The WNBA finals are a basketball wonderland – unless you’re part of the Maga machine
trail_text: The Dream and Valkyries are tied at 2-2 after four absorbing games. Many in America would rather we revisited the national anthem debate
byline: Andrew Lawrence at State Farm Arena
body_text: When Tyler Perry leading lady Crystal Renee took center stage at State Farm Arena to sing the national anthem before the Atlanta Dream’s WNBA finals clash with the Golden State Valkyries on Saturday afternoon, a smattering of photographers, game officials and event security took their familiar places around her as the capacity crowd stood for the flag. The teams, as is now customary, spent that time in their locker rooms. As soon as the lights went back up, the teams returned to the floor to resume their shootarounds. Anyone genuinely invested in the finals would have been unfazed by them briefly stepping away – if they remembered it at all after the Valkyries’ 67-62 win tied the series at two games apiece. But for many watching the game, basketball is beside the point. Seven years ago, Jay-Z declared that the culture had “moved past kneeling” and similar national anthem protests, seemingly sounding the death knell for an era of sports activism that had helped raise awareness of racial disparities as a broader social movement gathered force. The line cemented his partnership with the NFL as the league bowed to political pressure to crack down on anthem protests, with other major US sports eventually following the NFL’s lead. But rightwing media and politicians never got the memo. They’re still making sports a battleground for patriotism, with basketball as the war’s chief casualty. Credit OutKick, Fox’s renegade sports arm, for providing the spark that reignited the right’s outrage machine. They tipped off the WNBA finals by making a story out of Atlanta and Golden State leaving the court during the national anthem, then amplified the indignation aimed at LeBron James for appearing to practice his golf swing during the anthem at a Philadelphia 76ers game that same week. That was all the scene-setting Donald Trump needed. “You know the NFL did that for a while and they stopped because people stopped watching games. I think you should do the same thing with women’s basketball,” Trump said. In a Truth Social post, he called James a “disgrace” and demanded he “apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” Basketball has grown accustomed to this kind of punching down from the White House and the familiar cycle of provocation and outrage, especially when the administration’s poll numbers are dragging. James dismissed Trump’s diss as a sign of a “slow news day at the office” and the WNBA declined to engage, beyond noting that players haven’t been on court for the anthem for years now. Meanwhile, the Dream and Valkyries have been too preoccupied with winning their first championship to really enter the chat. “For me, it’s staying off social media. It’s just going inward with our teammates and staff,” said veteran Golden State center Kiah Stokes, who helped drive her team’s victory with her stout defense of Atlanta star Angel Reese. “Staying together. That’s been one of our keys all season.” But no matter how hard the WNBA resists the urge to clap back, no matter how valiantly it tries to keep the spotlight on basketball, there will always be someone on the right looking to steal it for their grievance grift. As OutKick and Trump reheated the stale anthem controversy, former NBA player turned Maga wannabe Enes Kanter Freedom was making a grand show of his latest appearance at a WNBA game, asking for special security arrangements so he could watch Game 3 of the finals from a courtside seat. The Dream offered to accommodate Kanter Freedom – who has disrupted WNBA games in the past – with a fully stocked suite, courtesy of the team and State Farm. But Kanter Freedom refused and beat a retreat with his camera crew. Jennifer Sey, the red-pilled former US gymnastics champion, has attended this year’s finals in her anti-trans athletic gear – and her efforts to incite a reaction from the W’s progressives went largely unnoticed, too. It is unfortunate that these finals have become a microcosm of the WNBA season, a tug-of-war between a basketball product that has never been better and a political class desperate to bend it to its own agenda. But the longer the right keeps up its fight, the more it gives its game away – exposing the hypocrisy beneath its moral posturing. We’ve seen how urgently conservative culture warriors believe women need protecting when the alleged assailant isn’t transgender. “Cornell’s a fine school,” Trump said in response to the university’s handling of a student’s gang-rape allegations. “I’m sure they’ll do what’s right.” We’ve seen how much this administration cares about its great American heroes as it sends them into an open-ended conflict, keeps sailors at sea for record stretches and downplays casualties, injuries and damage to US assets in the war with Iran – all while slashing veterans’ jobs across the federal government. We know why basketball makes such a ripe target for attacks from Maga’s crusaders of the American way: the game’s politics lean left, its players are well-traveled, culturally sensitive and have no qualms about dunking on trolls. And we know why the WNBA, in particular, gets under the right’s skin: it is so Black and queer, and its players have set the tone for political protest in American sports. The Dream, specifically, helped usher Raphael Warnock, the Atlanta pastor who delivers sermons from Martin Luther King Jr’s pulpit, into the US Senate. We see the play Kanter Freedom is trying to run by seeking out an altercation with a player in front of Atlanta’s largely African American crowd, and the statement Sey hopes to make by swanning around queer-friendly Ballhalla in her statementware. We see how closely these grifters actually follow women’s sports. That much was clear again in a recent episode of The Georgia Gang, Atlanta’s long-running political TV roundtable, when the talk turned to the home town team’s WNBA finals berth. “Go Sophie Cunningham, she my’s girl not Angel Reese,” said panelist Phil Kent, a conservative consultant – a contrarian move that also betrayed his refusal to appreciate the absorbing WNBA finals matchup we are being treated to: Maga It girl Cunningham and her Indiana Fever crashed out in the first round. When others at the roundtable praised Reese’s selection as defensive player of the year, Kent doubled down (“I question that”) – and the clip has since drawn a torrent of criticism. “These white men are so broken,” said one Twitter user. “It’s never been about basketball.” The Valkyries enter Game 5 with momentum on their side (“Block out the noise and understand the gameplan” was coach Natalie Nakase’s recipe for victory on Monday), but how the rest of the series unfolds is anyone’s guess. Will Stokes keep holding Reese in check? Will the Dream be forced back into their rinky-dink home arena for Game 6? Will the series go the distance and break more ratings records? The storylines are almost too juicy – and they’re the last thing anyone on the right will want to talk about.

headline: ‘If it was up to me it wouldn’t end like this’: Jimmy Anderson confirms Lancashire exit
trail_text: Jimmy Anderson has expressed regret at how his 25-year spell with Lancashire has come to an end after the club confirmed he will not be offered a new contract
body_text: Jimmy Anderson has confirmed he will leave Lancashire when his contract ends this year, after the county decided not to extend his deal for the 2027 season. The 44-year-old has not said whether he will retire or continue playing elsewhere. Anderson reflected on his Lancashire career on Instagram. “I’ve supported Lancashire since I was a kid, and so to get to play for them for 25 years was a dream come true,” he wrote. “I have always found it special walking out to play at Old Trafford and have some incredible memories of doing so, including the honour of being captain. “If it was up to me it wouldn’t have ended like this, but I wish the players and fans all the best for the future.” Anderson made his Lancashire debut in 2001. He took 443 first-class wickets for the county in 112 appearances, plus 83 List A wickets in 61 matches and 50 T20 wickets in 40 appearances. His 50 wickets in the 2026 Championship at an average of 17.68 earned him Lancashire’s Championship player of the year award. The county finished second-bottom in Division Two and exited both limited-overs competitions in the group stage. Paul Farbrace, Lancashire’s incoming director of cricket, said he had told Anderson the club would not extend his contract after a meeting with the chief executive, Richard Kenyon, on 19 October. Farbrace said the club wanted to rebuild its squad to secure promotion and then challenge in Division One over the next three to four years. “Lancashire Cricket can confirm that, following a remarkable 25-year association with the Red Rose, Sir James Anderson’s playing career with the club will come to an end at the conclusion of his current contract,” read a statement from the county. The former England captain Nasser Hussain said Anderson’s departure was “a hugely sad way” for the bowler to leave the club. “I’d say most counties in the country would take Anderson, even at the age of 44,” he wrote for Sky Sports. “I’d rather not focus in on how it ended, both for England and for Lancashire – I’d rather be thankful that we’ve had 26 years of Anderson giving it all for England and Lancashire.” Anderson’s Lancashire exit follows his retirement from international cricket in July 2024. Anderson’s 188th and final Test was against West Indies at Lord’s. He finished his Test career with 704 wickets, the most by any fast bowler.

headline: Australia survive almighty Fiji scare to stay unbeaten at Rugby League World Cup
trail_text: The Kangaroos eventually proved too good for Fiji but not before the hosts were given a run for their money in Brisbane
body_text: The naysayers have questioned this increasingly provincial sport and its sometimes laughable and often one-sided, so-called World Cup. But against the favourites and hosts Australia, the Fiji Bati showed – from the tears on the players cheeks during their anthem, their wondrous pre-match hymn, right through 80 minutes of fearless effort in attack and defence – why this tournament is worth persisting with. The inspiring Fijians appeared to have answers to every criticism, a response to every question, except three. The quality on the Australian bench, the class of James Tedesco and the finishing of triple try-scorer Tom Trbojevic finally took down the likeable underdogs, in front of a healthy Sunday night crowd in Brisbane and no doubt millions watching on prime time television. Fiji had taken the lead early in the second half when winger Semi Valemei – who also ended with a hat-trick – slid into the corner off a cut-out pass from impressive five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe. The Dolphins playmaker almost set up another score moments later to put his side two tries ahead with half an hour to play. As staggering as that might have been, it was no less than Fiji deserved. But that four pointer was disallowed due to obstruction, and from the ensuing set the Kangaroos got on a roll, and Sam Walker and Tedesco combined to put Trbojevic over in the corner to level the scores. Within minutes, Walker had knocked over a penalty goal to secure a lead they would not relinquish. Trbojevic picked up a Tedesco grubber minutes later, and the Kangaroos began to feel comfortable. The Manly player completed his hat-trick on the edge of a flowing move featuring Tedesco again, that put the result beyond doubt with 15 minutes to go. Though Trbojevic scored three tries, his right edge alongside Kotoni Staggs was rarely comfortable against the Fijians, and Donoghoe created another try down that side in the final 10 minutes. It proved only a consolation score for Fiji, but it will be food for thought for coach Kevin Walters ahead of the challenge looming at the end of the tournament. Tedesco was playing his first Test since 2023, and the Roosters’ Clive Churchill medallist was influential early. After three handling errors ruined a promising Fijian opening, the 33-year-old drew two tacklers and a short ball put Staggs over for the first try. The veteran had entered the tournament as a man reborn after two superb seasons were capped off by a premiership, making him the player many thought should be the Australian No 1. As Tedesco rested against New Zealand, however, Reece Walsh roared with a match-winning display, adding intrigue to an already difficult decision facing coach Walters later in the tournament. As the first half ticked on, the Bati reminded the 41,108 fans at Suncorp Stadium this was more than an Australian selection trial. Trbojevic made an error running out of his end, and Donoghoe took advantage of a miscount by the Australian defence with a cut-out pass that left Trbojevic clutching at air as Valemei crossed. A penalty and set restart left Fiji camped in the Australian 20-metre area, and another two sets left Australia reeling. The pressure was temporarily released when Waqa Blake ran around a teammate to give up an obstruction. But a Lindsay Smith ruck penalty gave Fiji another opportunity, and Brandon Wakeham grubbered through for Taane Milne to put the upstarts in the lead against the favourites. Suddenly, the tournament’s first upset was on the cards. Tom Dearden and Walker were named in the Australian halves, teammates in green. But they were also competing to partner Cam Munster at the pointy end of the tournament following the injury withdrawal of Mitch Moses. Neither were perfect in the first half, behind a pack being monstered by the Fijians. But they both helped wrestle the match back in control on the cusp of half-time. A terrific long kick from Dearden relieved pressure, and then Walker combined with Trbojevic and the elusive Tedesco to score a long-range try to put the hosts back in front. Walters had made a range of changes to spread the minutes throughout his squad, but the starting side – with Smith and Keaon Koloamatangi as middles – looked overpowered, made worse by a head injury to lock Cam Murray. But into the second half, Walters’ high-end rotations of Tino Fa’asuamaleaui and Pat Carrigan and the recovered Murray helped take control of the yardage battle. They might not have got the result, however, were it not for Tedesco, who finished with more than 150 run metres and three try assists. He was supported by his Roosters’ teammate Walker who looked increasingly comfortable on his debut. The Kangaroos wrap up the pool stage with a match against the Cook Islands in Townsville on Saturday. Their opponents in the semi-final will not be known until the final pool stage fixture, the much-anticipated clash between Tonga and Samoa in Parramatta next Sunday night. Fiji need to upset New Zealand on the Gold Coast on Saturday if they hope to sneak into the final four.

headline: Kimi Antonelli seizes F1 US GP pole and chance to seal first world title
trail_text: Kimi Antonelli claimed pole position for the US Grand Prix with a hugely impressive lap at the Circuit of the Americas as he closes in on a first world title
byline: Giles Richards at the Circuit of the Americas
body_text: Kimi Antonelli claimed pole position for the US Grand Prix with a hugely impressive lap for Mercedes at the Circuit of the Americas. In beating Red Bull’s Max Verstappen into second place, Antonelli did exactly what was required to give him the chance to close out his first world championship title this weekend. Isack Hadjar did well to secure third for Red Bull, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in fourth and fifth for Ferrari, and Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate George Russell in sixth. Antonelli’s first pole since the Belgian GP in July could not have been better timed as he attempts to take his first title. The Italian has a 102-point lead over Russell and needs to be 125 points in front after this race. To take the title he must win on Sunday and have Russell finish outside the top eight, with Hamilton outside the top four. The win certainly looks to be a strong prospect but he still needs his rivals to stumble on Sunday. He can only do his best and knows that even should the title not be secured here, on this form it will surely be done and dusted by the next round in Mexico. “We got pole, so we’ll try to win tomorrow,” Antonelli said. “Max has been very quick and did an incredible job in qualifying so it’s not going to be easy. Hopefully we’ll be leading into turn one and we’ll try to set the pace, even though it’s going to be very tight. Very happy with qualifying today, Q3 was very tough with the wind, gusty, unpredictable but happy to stick it on pole.” It is another striking achievement from the Italian, not least because the Mercedes upgrades applied in Malaysia have made the car more of a handful to drive. Indeed, Russell was a full four-tenths off his teammate, and it was a strong return to form for Antonelli as he looks to become the youngest F1 world champion at just 20 years old. He was flawless for the lap that proved unbeatable in the Texas sunshine but it was a performance by which Mercedes, too, will be buoyed given they were hoping to extract the maximum from their recent upgrades which had not delivered as expected on their opening salvos in Malaysia and Singapore. With the team having found a way to exploit them, Antonelli gave a reminder of just what a formidable opponent he is. His engineer, Pete Bonnington, admitted it was somewhat unexpected given both the team’s work on their upgrades and the form of the recently resurgent Red Bull, with Verstappen taking pole and the win at the last two rounds. A sentiment echoed by the beaming Antonelli. “It was unexpected, we felt it would be close but it was a good surprise,” he said. “I am happy because we have been working very hard on this package and since Singapore we have taken a big step further. The team have done a tremendous job and finally we are seeing the results.” For the first runs in Q3 in what had been a tightly contested session, with both Red Bull and Ferrari looking to be very much in the mix, it was Antonelli who set the pace. He put in a blistering lap with a time of 1minute 34.035seconds, almost two-tenths up on Verstappen, with the Italian hooking up what was one of his very best laps of the weekend. On the final runs Verstappen gave his all but could not improve and, although Antonelli too could not go quicker, he had done enough. His time was not bettered and a somewhat unexpected pole was secured with no little style. “Yes man, it’s good to be back,” he said. For Antonelli, in a season of milestones, including eight wins, his first pole in Austin is his seventh of the season and the first for Mercedes here since Valtteri Bottas last took the top spot in 2019, from which he went on to win – a feat Antonelli will hope to emulate. The Italian looked very much at his best and has given himself the chance to potentially finish the job. But as Verstappen observed, if not here on Sunday, then at the next round or the round after. The hard yards are over.

headline: Winds of change are coming for Australia as selection storm brews in South Africa
trail_text: Crushing defeat in second Test raises fresh questions about visitors’ fragile batting lineup before Cape Town decider
body_text: The old adage that it is harder to get out of the Australia cricket team than into it is about to be put to the test. The horror show against South Africa in the second Test that ended in defeat for Australia by an innings and 31 runs exposed familiar fractures in the lineup that have less than a week between matches to be repaired. The Australian selectors have shown in South Africa they are prepared to change a winning formula with the ball, while they have long been reluctant to cut ties with proven performers with the bat. But the first innings capitulation as Australia were all out for 99 in Gqeberha could force their hand to make a tough call or two – or perhaps more – as a selection storm brews before the series decider in Cape Town. Marnus Labuschagne remains a persistent problem though arguably not the most pressing concern with Australia forced to consider other selection dilemmas. Even with three scores in the 30s from four innings in this series against South Africa, Labuschagne’s numbers are damning. So was his decision to loft off-spinner Simon Harmer into a stiff breeze and toward the long on fence when time at the crease was Australia’s only hope of escaping St George’s Park with a series lead. The 32-year-old’s barren spell without a Test century has now extended well beyond three years and he has averaged 22.09 in 47 innings since last raising the bat against England at Old Trafford. He has not averaged more than 40 in a Test series since compiling 207 runs with three half-centuries on home turf against Pakistan in 2023-24. A Test average that sat above 61 in late 2022 has now dropped to 43.36. Labuschagne had been clinging on to his spot since long before he was left out of the side for three Tests against West Indies that followed the 2025 World Test Championship final. Even with the numbers stacked against him, Labuschagne could still be handed one more last chance with a vacancy widely expected to open at the top of the order to partner Travis Head. The most likely route to another Test lifeline could therefore be for Labuschagne to open the innings in Cape Town, just as he did in the WTC final defeat last year. Cameron Green and Josh Inglis are expected to be available for the third Test after recovering from injuries sustained during the one-day leg of the tour of South Africa. Green is nearing a return after suffering an abdominal strain in the third ODI and spent time batting in the nets as the second Test played out at St George’s Park. The 27-year-old once rivalled Labuschagne as the batter most under pressure, until he earned some credits with a defiant ton and a half-century from No 5 in the drawn series against Bangladesh. Head coach Andrew McDonald has said Green is unlikely to bowl in the Test series against South Africa but his batting alone should be enough to ensure selection, if fit, with Australia needing reinforcements to help fill the top six. Inglis, on the other hand, remains far from a walk-up starter. The keeper-batter has become a mainstay of Australia’s white ball sides but has been unable to make the most of his opportunities in the longest format since a century on debut against Sri Lanka. Cooper Connolly is also back in the frame though the spin-bowling all-rounder’s hopes of adding to his one Test could rest on whether selectors are prepared to back the versatile but underperforming Beau Webster as well as the conditions at Newlands. The three batters forming a queue just as Australia weigh up their options are all best suited to the middle order, just as gaps appear to be forming at the top. The selection gamble to recall Nic Maddinson after almost a decade in the Test wilderness and more than 18 months without first-class cricket, in part while recovering from testicular cancer, has shown few signs of paying off. The 34-year-old looked out of his depth as he returned with a 33-ball duck and even a quick-fire 48 in the second innings in Durban only left a glimmer of hope that better was to come. Kagiso Rabada has troubled more established batters than Maddinson but the manner in which he was dismissed by the South Africa quick for another duck and eight in Gqeberha is likely to bring an abrupt end to the left-handed batter’s shock selection. Shifting Matt Renshaw back to the top order and letting him settle in a position where he has been comfortable at domestic level could resolve the most glaring issue. It would also open up a spot for Green to return in the middle order while leaving the door ajar to perhaps call in Inglis or Connolly for the third Test against South Africa. Australia have not lost a bilateral Test series since early 2023. They have not been defeated by a side other than India since Pakistan claimed a 1-0 series victory in the wake of “sandpapergate” in the UAE in 2018. The natural flow state of the side under captain Pat Cummins has been to ride out the highs and the lows. But the long journey through the top end of Australia, a tour of South Africa and home series against New Zealand, then the renewal of the tensest of rivalries in India and England already looks like being blown off course. Winds of change are finally coming for the Australia Test team. And this time, even Cummins’ unwavering calm might not be enough to weather the storm.

headline: Leicester turn up the hostility as Steward caps old-time beating of Northampton
trail_text: Leicester scored four unanswered tries in the second half to overturn a 7-3 interval deficit and beat Northampton 28-7 in the Prem
byline: Michael Aylwin at Mattioli Woods Welford Road
body_text: We have seen this before. It is easy to forget, amid all the tries and sunshine, that rugby has a darker side too: a wet, windy, deafening ferocity that not even the most twinkle-toed can transcend. And they practically invented it here. This is not the first time Leicester have welcomed their beloved neighbours to the lair as champions and disabused them of any notions of grandeur. It took the Tigers 40 minutes to whip themselves into the necessary fervour, but when they did, all else followed: the rocking stadium at capacity, the win, the bonus point, the obliterated opposition. “The crowd was brilliant,” said Geoff Parling, Leicester’s head coach. “The crowd is outstanding. This stadium is iconic. It’s rustic, I know it is. I’ve said it before. It’s old. But I wouldn’t change it for the world.” It was not just the 40 minutes of directionless fumbling by the home team, but a mass fracas with a number of those visiting friends, which spilled into the stand, that sparked them into life, pretty much from the moment they re-emerged from the break. The second-half Tigers showed the first-half version how a lineout and drive is executed, when Jamie Blamire scored their first try within four minutes of the restart. That earned them a one-point lead and normal service was resumed. Half-time’s highlights analysis probably centred on that, well, we can’t really call them fights these days – this is the age of the camera, after all – but certainly pushing and shoving long after the referee had brought the first half to a close. There were Alex Coles and Freddie Steward at each other’s throats. On it went, up the steps of the Crumbie Stand, where Henry Pollock, obviously, seemed more interested in tying his shoelace than getting in for an orange. Ollie Chessum and Steward, his England teammates, did not find it funny, shoving him all the way to the changing room. “These games are going to be hostile,” said Phil Dowson, the Northampton coach. “In the current game, you can’t throw anything. It’s just push and shove and talk crap. That happens every derby. So I don’t think that had any impact. It’s not as if anyone got filled in. Well, you just can’t any more.” Such discord was in keeping with a first half in which neither side could quite find their feet on the slippery turf. Saints seemed more in tune with the kind of rugby that has prevailed before the rains came. Theirs was the only try of the first half, early on, when Finn Smith, with an advantage, chipped in behind, where Billy Searle spilled and James Pater gathered to score. Leicester could not make anything of a stream of penalties in the first half, sending four of them to the corner in the first quarter and spilling or, often, not even securing the subsequent possession. How that was going to change. Once Blamire’s try had restored order, the Tigers tore through the Saints at set piece and high ball. The champions deteriorated in the swirling rain. Cameron Henderson was next to rise to take a lineout, after a ferocious scrum had earned the penalty. Henderson then finished in the corner like a winger, sent away by Gabriel Hamer-Webb. That put Leicester six ahead and five minutes later they were more than a score clear, this time Finn Carnduff finishing after another attacking lineout. The bonus point came in the final 10 minutes after one of the more bizarre swings of fortune. Smith’s cross-kick had sent George Hendy away from his own 22, Adam Radwan’s slap-down earned him a yellow card. But way back earlier in the move Tom Lockett’s head had collided with Solomone Kata’s. It was another totally innocent accident, Kata not only changing direction, but rising sharply to clash with the covering Lockett. Even by rugby’s standards, the yellow card was absurd punishment. But it also meant Radwan’s was rescinded. On he came, off Lockett went, and over strolled Steward for the bonus point from the subsequent lineout. When it is not your day, it is not your day, Saints must have rued. But when it is your day, especially at this grand stadium in the wet and windy twilight, it really is.

headline: Northern Olympics campaign to get £7m in Healey’s budget
trail_text: Fund will support feasibility study for potential bid to host Games in 2040s, backed by northern mayors and top athletes
body_text: John Healey is to announce a £7m fund to examine a potential future bid to host the Olympics in northern England in his first budget as chancellor. The fund will be used to carry out a full feasibility study for a northern Games, which, if successful, would be held in the north of England in the 2040s. In May, before Andy Burnham entered No 10, the government commissioned an assessment by UK Sport which could inform a bid for the international sporting event in the 2040s. If the campaign were successful, it would be the first time the Olympic Games and Paralympics were hosted in Britain since London 2012. There was further momentum behind the idea in June when mayors from across the north of England met in Sheffield to discuss the possibility of a northern Olympic bid. More than 40 Olympians, Paralympians and elite athletes, including Laura Kenny, Jason Kenny, Sarah Storey, Beth Tweddle and Tom Pidcock, have signed a joint statement “to express our strong and united support” for the idea to hold a “box office Games” in the north of England. Announcing the fund, Burnham said an Olympics bid would “unlock opportunity across our towns and cities” and that “we can put on the greatest show on Earth”. He continued: “Few things bring a country together quite like the Olympics. I want people to feel that sense of excitement again, and to experience it in their own towns and communities, not just watch it on the telly. “The Games would unlock opportunity across our towns and cities for the whole country. From north to south, it would be something everyone could get behind and be proud of. “We know we can put on the greatest show on earth. Now we want to explore how we can do it again, with the whole country behind it.” The full feasibility study will look in greater detail at how the Games would work in practice, including types of venues and transport links needed and the prospects of developing a winning bid. It will also look into how much it could cost and examine the chances of a bid succeeding. The work will involve the government, UK Sport, the northern mayors and the British Olympic and Paralympic Associations, who would ultimately be responsible for a bid. Healey said: “The north hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable. “Britain’s experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I’m picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious Games. “It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost.” The British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport released a joint statement welcoming the news. “Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements,” they said. Sydney, Tokyo and London are among the mega-cities that have played host to the Olympics in recent years but Brisbane, Australia’s third-largest city, will be hosting the 2032 Games. The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has previously criticised plans to explore a bid to host the Olympics in northern England, saying that excluding London would be a “missed opportunity”.

headline: The World Series of the have-nots is here. But baseball’s money problem isn’t going away
trail_text: Baseball’s two best regular-season teams are also among its lowest spenders. But their unlikely World Series comes with a warning about the sport’s future
body_text: The best pitcher in baseball led the best team to victory over the second-best team? Weird. A World Series that makes the logical feel novel began on Friday as the Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 1. Of course the Brewers, with their MLB-topping 103 regular-season victories, should be facing the 98-win Rays on the grandest stage. But of course, since these are two of the smallest and lowest-budget franchises in the sport, they shouldn’t. That this best-of-seven title decider is at once a shocking cold shower and a comforting warm bath is largely explained by the absence of the two-time defending champions, the Los Angeles Dodgers, who were swept 4-0 by the Brewers in the National League Championship Series. That was a philosophical battle with a drop-mic ending: the revenge of the nerds. Analytics over affluence, a triumph for the teams who scrimp and strategize rather than simply lobbing money at the best free agents each offseason. The Dodgers have parlayed financial dominance into winning the National League West division in 13 of the past 14 years. At the start of this season there was every reason to expect they would win their third World Series in succession. But instead of spending this title fight lamenting the Dodgers’ dominance and fretting that money has made baseball dull and dynastic, we have the first match-up in 46 years – and second since 1920 – between two teams that have never won a World Series. A country where the world’s richest person has reportedly made political donations in excess of $442m in this election cycle is culturally conditioned to believe that wealth wins. Yet baseball is, after all, still a sport where the won-lost standings and the salary tracker are not fully interchangeable. Here are successful teams, boasting talents as luminous as Rays third baseman Junior Caminero and Brewers catcher William Contreras, with payrolls less than half the size of the most lavish spenders. Milwaukee’s annual outlay ($146m according to Spotrac) ranks 19th in the 30-team league with Tampa Bay ($96m) in 28th position. And the Rays reached this point by beating the Cleveland Guardians, who have MLB’s smallest payroll, in the American League Championship Series. Only the Dodgers, Brewers, Atlanta Braves and New York Yankees have more regular-season wins in the 2020s than the Rays, who are in their third World Series. Tampa Bay, founded as an expansion franchise in 1998, reached the final in 2008 (where they lost to the Philadelphia Phillies) and in the Covid-wracked 2020 season, losing to the Dodgers at the makeshift site of Globe Life Field in Texas. The Brewers’ only other World Series appearance was a loss to the St Louis Cardinals in 1982. Though there are suspicions that national television audiences will be meager for a series between small-market teams lacking superstars, the games in Milwaukee are some of the hottest tickets in World Series history. On one resale site the asking price for standing-room only tickets to Saturday’s Game 2 in Milwaukee was north of $3,000. The first clash held moderate value for the neutral spectator. It was a night with a fast start, a false finish and some messy, unmemorable baseball in the middle. Where ordinary pitchers throw fastballs, Jacob Misiorowski, MLB’s strikeout leader in the regular season, hurls fireballs. Pitching on 11 days’ rest, the 24-year-old started his night with the quickest pitch ever recorded in a World Series, a 103.5mph screamer to leadoff hitter Yandy Díaz. Misiorowski surrendered one run in five innings’ of work. “Not perfect, but good enough to get a win,” he said. Milwaukee led 3-1 after the seventh but Tampa Bay mounted a late rally, scoring a run in the ninth to induce a tense, if gauche, finish. The visitors loaded the bases but catcher Liam Hicks appeared to hit into a game-ending double play. The Brewers celebrated but the fireworks and high-fives were premature. The Rays challenged the decision, which was overturned on review. This confirmed that shortstop Cooper Pratt had taken his foot off second base too early as he threw to first, and also that Milwaukee fans can boo almost as loudly as they cheer. Still, there was more than enough air left in the lungs of the fans at American Family Field to reboot the celebrations after the teams returned to the field and closer Trevor Megill struck out outfielder Jonny DeLuca for the win, for real. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after. You know, you kind of have that emotional dump and then you have to get back on it.” Brewers slugger Christian Yelich told Fox Sports. It was perhaps early evidence that in a series that is likely to be decided by fine margins, Milwaukee’s formidable bullpen might ultimately make the difference. Pat Murphy, the Brewers manager and Bruce Springsteen superfan who was FaceTimed by The Boss in midweek, declared Contreras the “player of the game” after he drove in a run and threw out two attempted base-stealers, neutralizing a key strategy for Kevin Cash’s aggressive Rays. “Money isn’t everything” is a nice narrative as far as the action goes, but the peculiar genius of American sports is how they generally preserve parity and uncertainty on the field while embracing rapacious capitalism. Three years ago, the Brewers, who are owned by Mark Attansio, a Los Angeles-based investor who also controls Norwich City FC and has an estimated net worth of $2bn, managed to squeeze $500m out of lawmakers in taxpayer-funded upgrades for a 25-year-old ballpark that cost less than $400m to build in the first place. A high-stakes financial duel engulfing the entire league played out to gaggles of reporters before the game as two power-brokers dug in to entrenched positions near the first-base dug-out. Bruce Meyer, the interim head of the players’ union, called the owners’ proposal of a salary cap a “nuclear bomb” and - more reasonably - argued that the presence of two small-market clubs in this year’s World Series proves that competitive balance is possible without a cap. Meanwhile, MLB commissioner Rob Manfred broadened the context as he made the case for a limit: “It’s been 40 years since we’re here. Once every 40 years is not enough. It’s not that no small market can win, it’s just that it’s pretty rare.” Milwaukee has a retractable roof, and Tampa Bay an indoor dome, but storm clouds are gathering above all the same. The owners are virtually certain to lock out the players on 1 December in a row over money that will threaten the start of the 2027 season. So this is a sport freighted with growing anxiety about the future, even during its showpiece event. Perhaps this, as well as the novelty factor of the match-up, is amplifying the party atmosphere of the last spectacle before the stoppage.

headline: Rising US star Fred Richard wins first world gymnastics title as Skye Blakely adds two more medals
trail_text: Richard becomes the first American man to win a world floor title since 2003 as Blakely takes her medal haul to four in Rotterdam
body_text: American Frederick Richard won the floor exercise title at the world gymnastics championships in Rotterdam on Saturday, finishing ahead of Britain’s Jake Jarman and Israel’s Artem Dolgopyat. With US gymnastics great Simone Biles looking on as a spectator in the Netherlands, the 22-year-old Richard secured his first world title, edging out Jarman by just 0.033 points after scoring 14.633. Jarman, the defending world champion, was among a field that included the last two Olympic gold medallists. “I hope this is a lesson to everybody that you don’t have to wait to get the win to say you will be a champion,” Richard said afterward. “You don’t have to know when it’s going to happen or how it’s going to happen, but believing it every second of every day does pay off. I’m proof of that now.” Richard became the first American man to win a world title on floor exercise since Paul Hamm shared gold in 2003. He is also the first American man since Danell Leyva to win medals across team, all-around and individual apparatus events at the Olympics and world championships. Richard, who won bronze in the all-around event at the 2023 world championships in Antwerp, also helped the United States win team bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. Elsewhere on Saturday, Newly minted all-around champion Skye Blakely added to her medal haul in Rotterdam, earning bronze on vault and uneven bars during the event finals on Saturday. The 21-year-old from Dallas, who soared to gold in the all-around on Friday after recovering from injuries that wrecked her Olympic hopes in 2021 and again in 2024, hardly looked tired in what has quickly become the meet of her life. Blakely averaged a score of 14.166 on her pair of vaults to share the podium with gold medalist Rebeca Andrade of Brazil and American teammate Claire Pease. Andrade, the Olympic champion on vault and the Olympic silver medalist in the all-around in Paris behind Biles, edged Pease for gold. The 27-year-old Andrade, who is competing as an event specialist at the moment while eyeing a run at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, averaged 14.666, a bit ahead of Pease at 14.233. Kaylia Nemour of Algeria recovered from a misstep on vault in the all-around finals on Friday that cost her a medal to easily defend her gold on uneven bars. Nemour’s intricate and technically demanding routine – perhaps the hardest currently being done by any gymnast, male or female, on any event – earned her a 15.333, the highest score of the day. Helen Kervic of Germany captured the silver at 14.833, with Blakely in third at 14.600. Blakely, who joined Olympic champions Biles and Nastia Liukin as well as Rebecca Bross as the only American women to win at least four medals at a single worlds, will have a chance to add to her medal total on Sunday when she competes in the beam final.

headline: ‘Like a fairy tale’: USA’s Paula Moltzan becomes oldest first-time World Cup winner by 0.01sec
trail_text: The American skier produced a stunning second run to claim her maiden World Cup victory, edging Albania’s Lara Colturi by just one-hundredth of a second
body_text: American Paula Moltzan became the oldest woman to claim her first Alpine skiing World Cup victory on Saturday, pipping Albania’s Lara Colturi by just one-hundredth of a second in a thrilling season-opening giant slalom at Sölden, Austria. Moltzan, who was fifth after the opening run, produced a superb second descent to finish with a combined time of 2min 14.82sec, narrowly denying her Italian-born Albanian rival, who finished in 2min 14.83sec.
