Germany’s Emma Aicher completed the podium, 0.52sec behind the Minnesota native. “It feels like a fairy tale right now,” Moltzan said afterward. “Pretty unreal and I think it will take a minute to settle in.” The victory marked a long-sought breakthrough for Moltzan, who debuted on ski racing’s top flight in 2012 and was dropped from the US team a decade ago. The 32-year-old, who won an Olympic bronze in the team combined event at the Milano Cortina Games in February, had finished second or third in 10 previous World Cup races across 13 seasons without ever reaching the top step of the podium. Starting the second run in fifth place, the American clocked 1min 7.86sec in increasingly foggy conditions to move four spots up the standings and set a target that none of the remaining contenders could beat. “In the second run I knew I had to send it,” Moltzan said. “A lot of people tend to back off when it gets dark and, for me, I just want to push harder. It’s just an opportunity to be brave and take a chance.” She added: “You have to kind of fake it till you make it. And yeah, I guess I faked it well enough today.” The 19-year-old Colturi, who had been sixth after the opening run, came agonizingly close to denying Moltzan her moment, crossing 0.01sec behind the winning time to come up short by the slimmest of margins. Aicher also made a significant move, climbing from ninth after the first run to third, while Sweden’s Sara Hector slipped from second to fourth, 0.63sec off the pace. Moltzan’s American teammate Mikaela Shiffrin, seeking a record-extending 111th World Cup victory, had led after the opening run but struggled amid the deteriorating visibility, sliding wide on one turn, and fell to seventh overall, 0.83sec behind the winner. Shiffrin, who equalled the women’s record with her sixth overall World Cup title in March, has described the new campaign as an “exploration season” in which she plans to race less frequently in her signature slalom discipline to concentrate on giant slalom and super-G. The 31-year-old has not won a giant slalom race since December 2023, despite holding the women’s record with 22 career victories in the discipline. Saturday’s race also saw the return of Slovakia’s Petra Vlhová, the 2022 Olympic slalom champion and 2021 overall World Cup winner, who finished 23rd in her first appearance on the World Cup circuit since January 2024 following a 33-month injury layoff. Italy’s Federica Brignone, who won Olympic gold in giant slalom and super-G on home snow in February, was absent as she continues her recovery from surgery in August. For Moltzan, the result represented an immediate reward for a bold late-career equipment change. In May, she ended an 18-year association with French manufacturer Rossignol to join Van Deer–Red Bull Sports, becoming the first woman to race for the Austrian brand, which had previously supplied only male skiers. “I’ve been working a really long time for my first victory, but also, I never would have expected it would have happened first race on new material,” Moltzan said. “I guess it just proves that we’re doing something right.” The result also gave the United States two skiers inside the top seven, with AJ Hurt finishing 13th, Elisabeth Bocock 14th and Nina O’Brien tied for 16th. It also made Moltzan the first American woman other than Shiffrin to win a World Cup tech race since Lindsey Vonn claimed giant slalom gold in Åre, Sweden, in December 2015. Moltzan has also been making headlines away from the slopes. In an interview with the Athletic published on Friday, she discussed her campaign to expand fertility treatment coverage for US Olympic athletes, a cause she has promoted by racing with a floral uterus design on her helmet. The Minnesotan has argued that female athletes should not have to choose between pursuing their sporting ambitions and starting families, and is pushing for greater fertility benefits through the US Olympic and Paralympic Committee. For now, Moltzan has every reason to savor the biggest victory of her career, achieved on the Rettenbach glacier slope in the traditional opening race of the World Cup season. “I can’t imagine a better start,” she said. “I’m really, really, really excited and I can’t wait to see everybody who’s here cheering us on.”

headline: Australia crush England in women’s Rugby League World Cup statement win
trail_text: The Jillaroos defeated England 78-0 as the reigning champions ran in 15 tries in a one-sided Rugby League World Cup contest in Perth
body_text: The Jillaroos sent a reminder to English rugby league that it is losing touch with the best in the world with a 78-0 hammering in Perth. The 15-tries-to-none victory confirmed the gulf in athleticism and skill between the two hemispheres and reminded fans the rugby league universe now orbits the Pacific. The one-sided result showed last year’s 90-4 embarrassment in Las Vegas was no outlier and England’s women’s team must urgently refocus in time for next week’s showdown with Samoa if they are to reach the semi-finals. England had not beaten the Jillaroos in four previous meetings and they made it hard for themselves with a dismal opening five minutes. They were offside from the kick-off, putting them on the back foot immediately. The Australia full-back, Tamika Upton, slipped through the England line on her first carry. Seconds later, backrower Tiana Penitani-Gray – shifted into the starting lineup – drew two tacklers and passed to winger Jaime Chapman, who walked over. It got worse with England’s debutant half-back, Jenna Foubister, put the ensuing kick-off out on the full. Jillaroos’ five-eighth, Jocelyn Kelleher, who made her own bow for Australia last week, launched it on the last tackle with precision, arcing it over the England winger Anna Davies. Chapman read the trajectory and leapt into the sky, coming down with the ball over the line for a sparkling try. Chapman’s afternoon had started perfectly, but a knock-on handed England the ball inside 20m. Davies appeared to sneak around the Australia defence early in the set for a try, but the video referee spotted her knee sliding on to the sideline before the ball was grounded. It was as close as England would come and from there the match was played almost exclusively up the other end. Upton was having it all her own way. Another two linebreaks, including another on a kick return and she had accumulated more than 100 metres before the 20-minute mark. In one remarkable effort, Upton appeared to be held by the England full-back, Fran Goldthorp, but she shrugged her off and put Kelleher over for Australia’s third try. Julia Robinson, shifted into the centres from the wing, crossed for the fourth. Robinson was forced off when the shoulder of Shaylee Bent collected her in a tackle and she walked off clutching her arm. That injury – suspected to be a broken wrist – triggered another debut and on came the Roosters’ NRLW premiership winner Sariah Paki, a two-time Olympian in rugby sevens. The difference in strength and athleticism between the sides was stark and after Olivia Kernick almost barged over the ball went left to emphasise that skill also favoured the hosts. Half-back Tarryn Aiken engaged the line, freezing the cover defence with a straight decoy run from Paki, and Kelleher powered over the line. The contest was already over, but the Jillaroos captain, Isabelle Kelly, showed no mercy in crossing to make it 30. Winger Abbi Church, brought into the starting side, finished a flowing attack and it was 36-0, more points than minutes at half-time. Aiken, Kernick and replacement Quincy Dodd crossed early in the second half to post the half-century as the Jillaroos cut through the defence seemingly at will. With twice the possession, three times the run metres and 13 line breaks to none and still 20 minutes on the clock, this was a contest between colonial frenemies that was long over. Fortunately, the best team of the world were in the mood for entertaining. One chip and chase from Kelleher was regathered then handed off to Upton who put over Church. It was the best moment of the match and proof even a shellacking like this can draw a smile. Forward Makenzie Weale scored a try on debut after coming off the bench, sprinkling the stacked scoreboard with an ounce of storyline. Penitani-Gray, Kelly and Bent added late four pointers to bring the final score to 78-0, giving the England fans in Perth after their men had earlier defeated France 82-0. Australia play Wales next Sunday in Sydney, another almost automatic victory for the hosts. The going will get tougher in the semi-finals. A likely clash looms against Fiji, who pushed the Kiwi Ferns in the opening round and easily accounted for Papua New Guinea 40-4 in Port Moresby earlier on Saturday. England face a challenge in their third match against Samoa, who thrashed Wales 76-0 on Friday. After this defeat they will need a win on Friday to make their way into the semi-finals, where they will probably meet New Zealand. But given the Samoans held the Jillaroos to 40 points last week, the underwhelming England might want to have their bags packed.

headline: England crush France by 82 points to keep Rugby League World Cup hopes alive
trail_text: Herbie Farnworth and Dom Young grabbed hat-tricks as England’s men beat France 82-0 in Perth to maintain their slim hopes of earning a semi-final spot in the Rugby Leaguer World Cup
body_text: England will only really know next weekend whether this record-breaking result means anything, but when not only a win but a convincing one would keep their hopes of reaching the World Cup semi-finals alive, this was a case of job done for Brian McDermott and his side. With the shortened and controversial group stage format meaning just one defeat is near-ruinous, even the head coach broke ranks this week and admitted England’s chances of qualification are slim at best after the 30-12 loss to Tonga on the opening weekend. Samoa’s 64-6 win against Papua New Guinea earlier on Saturday meant the permutations became simple, but daunting. Samoa beat France 78-4 last week, giving them a +132 points differential; England now have a +64 points differential. Above all, England need a favour from Tonga against Samoa next Sunday. Should Samoa win, England are going home. But if Samoa slip up – entirely possible in a hotly contested game akin to State of Origin – then a second big England win could be enough. When kick-off arrived in Perth, England knew they had to overturn a 150-point swing on Samoa. To that end, eroding more than half that deficit in one match represented a positive outcome as McDermott’s pre-tournament promise of expansive rugby bore fruit. That said, it was not clear if England were mindful of the permutations during a tense opening quarter. At the midway point in the first half, the game was scoreless, with France doing a wonderful job of resisting England’s challenge, some frustrating attacking play. But Dom Young’s try 15 minutes from the break opened the floodgates. In 55 minutes England scored 14 tries, with a string of outstanding individual performances. Should England beat Papua New Guinea by a margin of 68 points in Wollongong on Friday, a Tonga victory would allow McDermott’s side to sneak through to the semi-finals. If the winning margin is smaller than 68, they would need Tonga to pick up the slack in their own winning margin. Unlikely? Perhaps. “What we’ve done today is enormous given the context,” McDermott said. “We knew we had to win big and we’ve done it without getting distracted.” France have conceded 160 points in two games, raising again questions about the strength of French rugby league. They did frustrate England early on, but once Young crossed, France could not halt the points. By half-time, England had 34, with another five tries. Three of them went to Herbie Farnworth, who underlined his status as the world’s best centre with a devastating display. George Williams and Matty Ashton were the other first-half try-scorers, but even with the game over as a contest England could not afford to let up. There were eight more tries after the break, with Young completing his hat-trick. The introduction of the Hull KR duo Jez Litten and Mikey Lewis was also key, with the pair exploiting an exhausted defensive line. Litten finished a fine break for his try before Lewis scored twice in six minutes. Victor Radley and Jack Welsby also crossed and at one stage in the final quarter, England were 76-0 ahead, with a real chance they could reach 100. Yet there was only the late try AJ Brimson’s display merited as England declared on 82. Time will tell whether that is enough, but on a day when the pressure was at its highest, England did what was required.

headline: The sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow?
trail_text: Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down
body_text: It has been 10 years since the Indianapolis Star published allegations of sexual abuse by Larry Nassar, the former team doctor for USA Gymnastics, setting off a chain of events that would lead to a reckoning for the sport. Hundreds of women came forward with their own allegations against Nassar, who also worked at Michigan State University, leading to his conviction and jailing. The exposure of his crimes sparked a wider investigation into how gymnastics had allowed predators to abuse young athletes around the world. While Nassar was the worst recorded case, it emerged many other countries had questions to answer about the failure to protect victims from not only sexual but physical and emotional abuse. But a decade later, on a large houseboat moored in Rotterdam three tram stops away from the Ahoy Arena, where the World Gymnastics Championships are taking place this week, survivors and advocates raised fears about the slow pace of change. The impact of the Nassar case was seismic, not least because of the decision of Judge Rosemarie Aquilina, on agreeing to Nassar’s plea deal, to allow his victims to have their say in her courtroom. People tuned into Aquilina’s courtroom from all over the world to watch as 169 people took to the stand across seven days, delivering blistering, emotionally charged and brave testimonies of Nassar’s abuse and the impact of that abuse. Aquilina sentenced him to up to 175 years in jail with other convictions, federal and state, making a total of 300 years to life. “I know, dealing with so many victims, that when they speak publicly you see them shed their pain and get taller. You see them have a relief, an automatic release,” says Aquilina, perched on a seat in the helm of the boat. “The most interesting thing was that at first I had a list of maybe a dozen names who wanted to speak, then it was 20, then it was 30, and then it got up to 80, 100, etc. “What happened was that one girl empowered the next, who empowered the next. It was the beginning of their healing because they felt finally heard and believed, in a safe space, and they got to tell him to his face, eyeball to eyeball: ‘You hurt me. I am not a number, I am a name, how dare you?’” “Nassar constantly wanted control. He wanted to continue to control me, to control the girls, and to say: ‘Look what I’ve done. I took the plea for you’. That was constant … Did he deserve my respect? No. Did he give me respect? No. Did he give any of the victims respect? No. He never owned it. That infuriated me. It should infuriate everyone.” Among the victims motivated to speak after hearing others’ statements was the Olympic gold medallist Aly Raisman, who was excoriating in blaming USA Gymnastics for enabling Nassar. She was joined by fellow gold medallist Jordyn Wieber, Olympic bronze medallist Jamie Dantzscher and former US national champion Mattie Larson. The mother of the athlete who first complained about Nassar, Maggie Nichols, read out a powerful statement on her behalf. Simone Biles, the most famous gymnast of her generation, revealed she was a victim on social media and later testified publicly in front of the US Senate Judiciary Committee. Two years after Nassar’s sentencing, a documentary film named after Nichols, called Athlete A, was released, shining a spotlight on the traditional coaching system of compliance, fear and silence and how it allowed Nassar to operate. The documentary opened the global floodgates. Kim Shore, who was a gymnast in Canada in the 1980s and “experienced all forms of abuse, but also all forms of joy”, was then on the board of directors of Gymnastics Canada, the national governing body, after stepping into governance when her own experiences and direct intervention had failed to prevent the cycle of mistreatment repeating with a family member. “I absolutely love the sport. I love how it feels in my body. I love so many aspects of it. And yet I spent most of my time surviving it,” she says. Shore, who is an independent safe sport advocate, says of the impact of the Nassar case: “I was floored, understanding: ‘OK, I wasn’t a bad kid, I wasn’t a bad gymnast, this is why I was treated that way, it’s endemic.’” Yet the reaction from the organisation was “absolutely lacking”, says Shore. “I remember I sat and watched those girls tell their story in the courtroom and I just bawled. I encouraged the board members that I was associated with to watch it as well.” She does not believe any of them did. Eloise Jotischky, 23, who in 2022 won the first civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuses she suffered in the sport, says the impact of the film was being able “to articulate what you’ve been through and find the terms to understand and talk about your experience”. “It’s very hard to explain it to people who are not within that culture, that sport,” she says. “The only way I can really describe it is that it’s sort of like a cult in a lot of ways. It’s a very closed system, you’re very isolated, in a lot of cases you’re pulled out of school, you’re removed from your friends, you’re travelling to competitions all the time and you’re deprived of a normal social life. I’d say it’s very similar to a coercively controlling relationship in a domestic setting, there’s a lot of parallels there, but you’re a child, so there’s the duty of care issue as well.” Jotischky stopped training at 14. “By the end, it wasn’t joyous. I think I hated it. You just blame yourself and you think that you’re the problem, until Athlete A comes out. That was about sexual abuse, but the underlying themes of Athlete A are about the physical and emotional abuse, the non-contact physical abuse, which made it get to that point. That’s what all resonated.” At the same time, the life of former British gymnast and athlete Claire Heafford was in transition. She was splitting from her husband, leaving her dream job and taking up wrestling. “Those major changes were partly taking place because I hadn’t yet realised I’d been so badly abused and that I had some psychiatric issues,” she says. “I got into professional wrestling when I saw it and felt very drawn to it. I didn’t really understand why, but it’s a performance art that is largely about the performance of masculinity and the violence is clear and obvious. I was really attracted to that being the inverse of my own experiences. I couldn’t understand that at the time. I was like: ‘I’ve gone mad, I’m 36, I’m learning to be a Mexican wrestler. I’m splitting up with my husband. What the fuck’s gone wrong in my life?’ “It was only when Athlete A came out that the penny dropped.” The documentary made Heafford want to act; she decided to set up Gymnasts for Change, an alliance to bring about safer sport. As the head of Gymnasts for Change International, she brought together the advocates and survivors in Rotterdam. “Athlete A was seismic. It came out just as Me Too had started,” she says. “On the one hand, Athlete A showed how awful the sexual abuse was and on the other it demonstrated to everybody in the world that gymnastics was a coercively controlling environment built on control and power. It showed that was just what the sport was, that everybody in it had experienced it and that they almost believed that it was necessary.” The Nassar case triggered a series of reports and new measures in the US including the FBI acknowledging its handling of the case was “inexcusable” and Congress establishing the US Center for SafeSport. That organisation has since faced heavy criticism. USAG went through four presidents in less than two years, said it would adopt 70 of the recommendations in an independent report into preventing sexual abuse and set up an Athlete Bill of Rights. USAG now says athlete safety has been its “top priority since establishing a new board of directors and leadership team in 2018-2019”. It emphasises that “a culture of safety is something that has to be worked on every day, at every level”, requiring all adult USAG members to be trained in safeguarding. Eight members of the board are former elite athletes and one seat is dedicated to that of a survivor. The case also inspired athletes around the world to speak up about their own experiences of abuse, including in Australia, Brazil and Britain. In Britain, an independent review led by Anne Whyte QC found that physical and emotional abuse were systemic, leading British Gymnastics to launch a 40-point plan aimed at changing the sport. That included a zero tolerance approach to abuse and a gymnast-coach led environment where “both feel empowered to create safe, positive and fair experiences at every level”. Such an environment is something Aimee Boorman, who is Simone Biles’ former coach, has spent her career advocating for. Boorman channelled her anger at her own experience of negative coaching as a child gymnast into her coaching philosophy. “I knew that I never wanted to make another child feel the way that I felt as a child. So, that was the basis of everything,” she says. “So many times I was told that I wouldn’t be successful because I was too nice. I was like: ‘Well, then I guess I’m not going to be successful by your metrics, your standard, your qualifier for success’. For me, success is having happy, healthy athletes who want to put their children in gymnastics because they have such a good experience. “Then, I went from being too nice to just being lucky that I had Simone, she’s successful and I’m successful because I was lucky that I had her. No, the reality is that Simone never would have gotten to where Simone is without the training she had from me and the other coaches that she had growing up. So, I’ve just had to hold on to my core beliefs.” Across Europe, too, gymnasts have spoken out to force change. Former Dutch gymnast Petra Witjes and Germany’s Adina Hausch document falling out of love with the sport because of their experiences. “At the elite club in the city I moved to it wasn’t fun anymore,” says Witjes, whose book, Silenced for Gold, is a memoir about the systemic abuses within sport and her battle to expose it. “My dad taught me to let my voice be heard but in the gym it was the opposite.” Witjes was terrified of speaking to her parents, she was taught not to trust them. “I didn’t feel safe at first, because my coach always said that parents don’t understand elite gymnastics,” she says. “They push your parents away from you. We were in total isolation.” Hausch says an injury that forced her from the sport was a relief. “I was on beam and I slipped with one leg and fell with the other on to the beam and then crashed down,” she says. “The leg was pushed sideways so much that it broke. From the age of 13 I don’t think there was a week without training through pain. When I left after the injury, the worst injury I’ve ever had, I was really happy that I didn’t have to go to the gym anymore.” In Rotterdam, survivors vary in age from their 50s to their teens; it is hard not to view the issues as systemic and global. And ongoing. Charlotte Jacobs, who is only 18, quit the sport after suffering emotional abuse when training in the UK. “It got to a point where I was like: ‘I can’t do it anymore’,” she says. “My experience was strange because it wasn’t physical, it wasn’t sexual, but it was emotional. You were ridiculed all the time, constantly. You weren’t allowed to cry, you weren’t allowed to talk, you weren’t allowed to sit down, if you were caught leaning on anything you’d have to run, you needed permission to go to the toilet, you needed permission to drink, and it’s that sort of really controlling, consistent and dismissive behaviour so that no one really felt safe that was prevalent.” Shore, who is a member of G4C Canada, argues that if a big list of cultural reforms comes from the top, that is then normalised within the national federations and then the clubs “all the way down to grassroots, then I think we would see faster reform and less resistance”. “The more I learn that the stories are consistent internationally the more it says something about the need for World Gymnastics to take a leadership role,” she says “The treatment across the world is pervasive and coaches are moving from space to space, country to country, more frequently now or they’re not even staying in this sport, they’re moving into other sports, especially if they’ve come into trouble.” World Gymnastics has moved to address the cross-border issue within the sport at least, publishing a new safeguarding policy last week which notes that the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, which it launched in 2019 and has handled nearly 500 reports, has the power to extend sanctions imposed by member federations providing they are compatible with the rules of the governing body and general principles of law. Among the efforts of World Gymnastics to address safeguarding concerns was the launch of the 10 Golden Rules of Gymnastics in 2021, the establishment of a safeguarding commission in 2022 and, this year, the launch of a safeguarding newsletter and the appointment of a full-time Safeguarding Manager. Shore believes the pace of governing bodies fully engaging with the change needed has been slow, however, “because to admit that there is harm going on in the sport puts organisations into a liability risk. Also, they have been able to deflect responsibility for so long. They don’t know how to solve it and they are getting pressure from all sides. By putting their head in the sand for literally 50 years we’ve now got to a crisis.” A statement from World Gymnastics said: “Creating a safe environment for current and future generations of gymnasts is a responsibility that World Gymnastics takes extremely seriously and shares with all stakeholders across the sport. The priority for World Gymnastics is not only to strengthen safeguarding rules and policies, but to ensure that they lead to meaningful changes in everyday practice.” Heafford alleges that British Gymnastics isn’t entering into meaningful engagement and collaboration with Gymnasts for Change and other survivors in the sport and says that she finds that “extremely frustrating”. She is also hugely critical of the processes gymnasts have to go through in raising a complaint against a coach or gym and what resolution looks like, saying: “In six years, we haven’t had one outcome that we can stand by and say that was a good outcome.” British Gymnastics, however, insists it has engaged with the organisation regularly which has “helped shape its approach”, including a meeting with G4CI and others in Rotterdam as well as introducting a new complaints and disciplinary process “to improve transparency and fairness” . Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, fears the situation could worsen. “Sport is getting younger. There’s a youth Olympics about to launch in Senegal. There’s going to be thousands of athletes, every one of them 18 or younger. They’re all children and they’re at a very elite level,” she says. “These children are being monetised and they are not protected because we know the systems are not in place to protect them.” Hausch wants to see “measurable boundaries, for example increasing the competition age to 18,” she says. “I would root for Germany not to join youth international competitions. Having a 13-year-old do youth European championships is the same as doing it as an adult, it’s the same amount of work you have to put in, the same amount of pressure, it’s not a softer version, it’s the full version, and it doesn’t make sense.” All agree there needs to be more done to help athletes advocate for themselves and others. Jacobs says: “There needs to be a sort of package of what to look out for. I think there needs to be more training for coaches in terms of mental wellbeing, disability, neurodiversity, all that, alongside what are and are not best practices. “We need more regulation,” she adds of the British landscape. “Look at the new guidance that’s come out about keeping children safe in education. That’s all been updated. Where’s the guidance for anything sports-wise, extracurriculars, whether it’s swimming, gymnastics, dancing, anything like that?” British Gymnastics says that it “recognises there is always more to do” but that prevention is “at the heart of our work. We have overhauled learning and development … and set clearer policies and guidance to drive meaningful change.” It says a coach developer network, regional teams and safeguarding and welfare officers in every club support communities. Jotischky, who is now studying law off the back of her experience, says there are changes needed there too. “The legislative gap that exists is astonishing. You have the 2015 Serious Crime Act section 76, which talks about coercive control, but it’s limited to domestic and familial relationships. Then you have the 2021 Domestic Abuse Act which lists personally connected individuals as only being family members. In a coach-to-athlete relationship where you spend 30 hours a week in the gym with your coach, and some gymnasts even go and live with their coach because they’ve formed such a close relationship, of course coercive control and emotional abuse can happen but it’s not recognised within the law. So, we have very little legislative ground to deal with the most serious cases in particular.” Listening to this group of women in Rotterdam, what becomes clearer is that while federations, to differing degrees, make changes in the name of athlete safety, survivors are still being failed. Meanwhile, these survivors and knowledgeable advocates remain isolated from the very structures that should be embracing them and channelling their knowledge and understanding of their experiences into the changes necessary to ensure the future health of the sport. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

headline: Daniel Stewart, former Port Adelaide AFL player, dies aged 37
trail_text: Key forward played 36 games and kicked 31 goals between 2010-2013 as the Power will wear black armbands at first home game of 2027 season
body_text: Former Port Adelaide player Daniel Stewart has died suddenly at the age of 37. The Power confirmed Stewart’s death on Saturday as the club said it was “deeply saddened” by the news that had come as a “shock”. Stewart played 36 AFL matches and kicked 31 goals for the Power between 2010 and 2013 after being selected with pick No 35 in the 2009 rookie draft. The 200cm key forward was recruited from North Adelaide in the Sanfl, after coming through the Eastern Ranges and Queensland club Labrador. Stewart was promoted to the Power’s senior list at the end of the 2009 season and the next year made his debut in round four against Geelong. He booted a career-high four goals, including two in the final term, to help the Power hold on for a tense victory against Richmond in the last round of 2010. “On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel’s family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh,” Port Adelaide chief executive, Matthew Richardson, said. “We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him. “Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton. “The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel’s passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him. We will honour Daniel by wearing black armbands in our first home game at Adelaide Oval in 2027.” Former Port Adelaide teammate and current AFL analyst Kane Cornes joined the messages of condolence sent to Stewart and his family. “A true tragedy. A brilliant and caring teammate who always had a smile on his face,” Cornes said in a post on X. “I loved watching him and his beautiful family from afar. He built a thriving business and shared a special friendship with Matty Thomas. Heart goes out to his family.” • This article was amended on 26 October 2026 to display a photo of Daniel Stewart. We regret that an earlier version mistakenly pictured another former Port Adelaide player.

headline: Red Roses suffer back-to-back defeats for first time in 10 years as Canada make statement
trail_text: Canada beat England 31-22 in WXV match in Ottawa for reigning women’s rugby world champions’ third loss in past 74 matches
body_text: History-makers, era-enders, giant-slayers. Breaking England’s unbeaten run was a statement for Canada last Friday but they backed it up in a 31-22 win to deal the Red Roses their first consecutive loss in a decade, sending a formidable message to the rest of world rugby. Some may view it as too early to call but Canada are serious contenders for the World Cup trophy in 2029, especially if they progress at the same rate that their performances have improved in just a year from that World Cup final loss to England in 2025. On a cold Ottawa night, Canada played with freedom and pace to down England once again. The captain, Sophie de Goede, laid bare why she is the reigning world player of the year with a hat-trick and some excellent defensive work, and Julie Omokhuale also stood out among a good team performance. England were looking for a response to that record-ending defeat but it never came. A strong and confident start ebbed into a scrappy and hesitant overall outing which they will want to put right for their final WXV Global Series match against the USA next Friday. But there were some positives for the visitors, namely Meg Jones. The captain, who turned 30 on Friday, was imperious in defence and Maddie Feaunati had another good game in the hour she was given. An Owellian atmosphere was created for those watching from home with the pitch having a grey tinge to it, a dystopian world isn’t usually compared to that of the vibrant and action-packed women’s rugby sphere but it may have felt like another world for England players losing back-to-back games. It was their third loss in 74 matches, so the panic won’t set in, but this result will unsettle the Red Roses. Jones said she told the team in the post-match huddle that they are “not broken, we just need to grow”. The captain added: “We’re a high-performing team in a high-performance situation. Our mindset is our biggest asset and it always will be. I genuinely believe we have the best players in the world and when we are firing we are genuinely unstoppable.” The Tests between these two this autumn have been ferocious and it was an utterly brutal start. A key part of Canada’s win last week was their defensive set and keeping England from scoring for a long time but that was a different story with Feaunati over in the seventh minute. Canada put England’s defence under its first proper stress test next and the white wall was impressive with a particular focus on double tackles, but it eventually buckled as Omokhuale dotted down. But the second Canadian try came all from England’s scrappy attack. A bouncing ball didn’t sit well for Zoe Harrison, who knocked on as a result and Gabrielle Senft pounced. De Goede tracked her run and was on her shoulder to receive the ball to finish it off with Canada’s secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, who announced new funding for Rugby Canada during the match, in the commentary box to celebrate the score and add: “I love it!” Several knock-ons and a try being held up stifled England from hitting back and so it was Canada who held a 12-7 lead at the break. The Red Roses’ need for points was made very clear when they opted to kick a penalty to start the second 40. England reverted to their deadly rolling maul from the 22 in an impressive score by Amy Cokayne. However, captain fantastic De Goede struck twice in quick succession for her hat-trick, with Savannah Bauder putting England out of sight despite a consolation score by Emma Sing. Head coach John Mitchell was critical post-match and said the referee Aurélie Groizeleau did not have a connection to the television match official. “I think the game potentially needs an improved standard with TMO, there was no TMO connection tonight,” he said. “We have got to improve that. These games are so meaningful and there are going to be situations where there are going to be major turning points and I think the girls deserve quality decision making.” Canada can ride the high of this victory into 2027 where their next games are slated to be in the Pacific Four tournament, while England have one more WXV match against the USA. The Americans are in form but they should heed a warning: this England team are not used to losing and they will be pursuing a big response.

headline: ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
trail_text: Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress
body_text: Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention. Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies. Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature. Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets. The UK is set to meet just three of the 23. After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade. During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss. Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement. “A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.” He also argued that the UN should host a single environmental Cop each year to tackle the climate, biodiversity, plastics and other issues in one go. “This just makes my blood boil, because while we fiddle, Rome burns,” he said. The negotiations in the Armenian capital have seen Argentina, Saudi Arabia and Russia water down language on environmental ambition in the final agreement, while wealthier governments were divided on who would contribute more financial resources. European nations would like to see additions to the list of donor states, as China and several of the Gulf states are still classified as developing countries in the UN process despite decades of rapid economic development. The final agreement in Yerevan left this issue open. Key decisions on a fund to mobilise resources from firms that make money from digital forms of biodiversity, such as pharmaceutical companies, were postponed to the next summit in Ecuador in two years’ time. It had been hoped that the fund would generate £1bn a year for nature conservation, with a significant share going to Indigenous communities, but it has so far raised just over $10,000. The calls for changes to the biodiversity Cop process echo an intervention by leading policy experts during climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024 who said the summit was “no longer fit for purpose” and needed to shift to focus on implementation. Ruth Davis, the UK’s nature envoy, said she recognised that the meetings could be “extremely frustratiing”, but a huge amount of implementation was happening around the world. “We’ve got to make the system actually deliver outcomes for people, otherwise they’ll lose confidence in it,” she said. “In the end, this is a process that is owned by governments who are parties to it. But I know we are going to find friends and allies in making the process work for the citizens of countries for whom this is really important, not least because they are the ones facing the impacts.” Efforts to reform the UN’s sprawling environmental agenda are already under way. Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, said that the current systems were driving change, but they were moving too slowly. “Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands. “Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that.”

headline: ‘This is a robust recipe’: the experimental farm bucking the decline in UK birds
trail_text: Allerton Project attracts abundant wildlife and its success can offers clues to reversing the sharp drop in populations
body_text: Farmer Alastair Leake is standing in a field of sprouting winter wheat, pointing at his experiment. One side was ploughed before planting, with green shoots breaking through neat rows of upturned soil. On the other, the crop was drilled directly into the earth, emerging through a messy carpet of “trash” – stems, stubble and crop residue from previous harvests. “When we’re watching to see where the birds are landing to feed, none of them are going on to the ploughed side,” says Leake, the director of the Allerton Project farm, standing on the trashy side. “They’re all coming and feeding down here. “That’s because that’s where the seeds, the earthworms and the insects are. On the ploughed side, they’re all buried.” It is experiments such as these that have enabled the Allerton Project to buck the decline in farm bird populations across the UK. Farm bird abundance at Allerton has risen 145% since 1992 when monitoring began, compared with a 23% decline nationally over the same period. “This is not some study that’s been done overnight,” Leake says. “We can be fairly confident that this is a robust recipe that we’ve got here.” The Allerton Project is a working farm and research centre on the Leicestershire-Rutland border, where farmers and scientists have spent more than three decades testing how farming can produce food while supporting wildlife. Frequently hosting farmers, policymakers and businesses, the 320-hectare “demonstration farm” uses a range of sustainable agriculture, habitat creation and landscape management methods to show how agriculture can be a part of environmental action. “I don’t want people to come here and say: ‘Oh, that’s a nice nature reserve they’ve got going there’,” Leake says of his guests. “I want them to go back on to their farms and say: ‘Do you know what, I can do that.’” Changes in farming practices across the UK have devastated farmland bird populations. An increase in pesticide use and a loss of suitable habitats have driven some species to extinction, according to the RSPB. But at Allerton, farm bird numbers are at their highest level since records began, with song thrush, blackbirds and linnets in particular on the rise. Leake points to a “bird table”, a channel of dedicated wildlife seed mix that splits the field. In these unkempt strips found all over the farm, kale, teasel, sorghum and millet are grown to supply seeds to birds through winter. “That is probably the most important thing we’ve done, [making] sure that there is food in the landscape for those birds to go and feed on,” he says. “If they manage to survive what we call the ‘hungry gap’, which is January, February, March, that means they’re ready to breed again.” Goldfinches love the teasel, he adds. Adjoining the bird table is the “beetle bank”, a strip of uncultivated land planted with long, tussock-forming perennial grasses. As the grass dies down year after year, it falls over and builds a thick, fibrous blanket of dead plant material, where beetles move to hibernate. “When it warms up in the spring, they go out into the crops and they eat the pests that attack the crops,” says Leake, adding that the beetles mean the crops do not need to be sprayed with pesticides. “But also they provide insect food for birds.” In a nearby field, Leake showcases an innovation found in gardens all over the country: bird feeders. “We fill the barrel up with wheat and the birds come and feed off it in the wintertime,” says Leake. “It’s just what people do in the gardens, feeding birds and things, but we’re doing it for farmland birds instead.” The less-discussed aspect of wild bird protection is predator control. Foxes and crows, for example, can prey on eggs and chicks, sometimes holding back the recovery of vulnerable ground-nesting birds. Killing predators can be contentious. Leake says Allerton’s approach is as humane as possible, targeting predators only during nesting season, the most vulnerable time for birds. “Our approach is a much more managed one,” he says. “So we are just reducing the pressure at the critical point.” He says these measures prove it is possible to reverse the decline in wild bird populations. “We have reached the highest number [of birds] against the backdrop of the national figure continuing to go down,” he says. “This is because we’re learning how to manage the whole estate better for nature as time moves on. We come up with new ideas, we put them in place, and that is bringing nature recovery. “There’s no reason why this couldn’t be done across the whole country. No reason at all, given the right incentives for people to do it.”

headline: Healey to veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills
trail_text: UK chancellor’s plans add to concerns government is moving away from pro-renewables agenda
body_text: John Healey has said he will veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government is moving away from the pro-renewables agenda. Announcing his plans, the chancellor said clean power is “how we break the grip of international gas prices on our bills”, but added the shift towards it “has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it”. New offshore wind projects lodging bids for subsidy contracts will only get signed off by ministers if they believe that all the power generated could be accommodated by Britain’s electricity grid without pushing up costs for consumers. Writing in the Times, he said: “There’s no sense building power that can’t connect and then paying to switch it off. We will take that approach into our next renewables auction, only buying projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security.” The move appears to be a further shift away from Labour’s target of having clean power by 2030, after Healey revealed more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget in the budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending. The cuts caused alarm among renewables experts, who warned they meant that Britain was unlikely to hit its targets on green heating, and were seen as a dismantling of former energy secretary Ed Miliband’s green agenda. There is concern in government that wasted wind charges could add to energy bills, with the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is funded through energy bills, being forced to pay wind turbines to switch off when there is not sufficient cabling capacity to transmit their power to consumers. A National Audit Office report in September warned that homes and businesses could be faced with a potential annual bill of £7.8bn by 2030 to deal with the issue. Healey appeared to preemptively address criticism of the plans. He said: “This is not a retreat from clean power. It is the credible route to it. Cheaper electricity will make it easier for businesses and households to electrify, strengthening our energy security and helping us decarbonise the wider economy.” He added that “without the renewable generation added in recent years”, this year’s gas price shock “would have hit families and firms even harder. “Those who want to rip up renewables would leave Britain more exposed to volatile markets and the dictators who exploit them.” One casualty of the cuts announced in the budget was a reduction in the amount of money available for the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions were being undermined. Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30. Some believe the cuts, much of which will pay for higher defence spending, are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. Allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever, pointing out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed. Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments. Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.

headline: Country diary: An impromptu birding trip with a total stranger – and it was magical
trail_text: Slimbridge, Gloucestershire: A chance meeting led me and my partner into an afternoon of discovery and generosity that is nothing like a certain YouTube documentary on birding
body_text: “What did you just see?” a bearded man asked, through the open window of his old Mini Cooper. “Just some crows in that tree.” “Slimbridge Wetland Centre is closed. I just missed it!” We too had been greeted at Slimbridge by a shut door at the visitor centre, dashing our hopes of some late-afternoon birdwatching. “I’m gonna find another way to the estuary. Want to hop in?” Before I had a chance to contemplate this stranger’s offer, my partner, Beth, had jumped into the back seat of the Mini, and we motored away into the unknown. We set off on foot down a promising track, following our new friend, Phil. With each step towards the shore he became more alive, extolling the weather, the ancient churches on the hills, and our fortuitous meeting. I’m not an expert birdwatcher, but Phil has a lifetime of honed skill – he cupped his ear to the curlew’s cry, pointed to long-tailed tits, shelducks, dunlins and a medley of geese. We learned that he’s a composer, and helps to run a museum in the mid-Wales town where my sister lives. As we approached the Severn seawall, roe deer with glowing antlers stared at us. I couldn’t help but think of Listers, a rip-roaring YouTube documentary about two young men who enter the cut-throat world of competitive birdwatching, spending a year chasing glory and rare birds across the US. They found that an ostensibly nature-based activity can become a Pokémon-style “Gotta catch ’em all” exercise, in which underhand strategy and toxic behaviour can be hard to avoid. Not so here, as we followed our excited leader’s stream of identifications and free-flowing observations. The moment we mounted the seawall, we saw a horizon ablaze with a sunburst of burnished copper. The mudflats were dotted with countless waders and gulls, and the Severn’s mighty tide was already starting to rush in. “See the marsh harrier? Incredible, incredible,” Phil murmured. We watched as the harrier glided over, sublime, sending ripples through the assembly. And there wasn’t a whiff of competition. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Twice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says report
trail_text: More than 100,000 species are traded globally, whether illegally smuggled, sold as ornaments or in fisheries, timber and fashion industries, study finds
body_text: The number of plant and animal species in use or sold in the wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought, researchers have discovered. A study, published in Science Advances, warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded, and that past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as the boom in the online exotic pet trade, where sellers offering to post spider eggs across the world or sneak reptiles on to planes are just a click away. “The dimensions of trade have changed. Without monitoring it in a representative way, we cannot manage it,” said Alice Hughes, a professor at the University of Melbourne and lead author of the study. “At the moment, we are completely underestimating what modern trade looks like – for the pet trade and for the ornamental trade, we are not capturing it. And it poses a major risk to species.” The study comes as the US-based nonprofit, the Center for Biological Diversity, filed a petition asking the US Fish and Wildlife Service to list the Javan slit-faced bat under the Endangered Species Act, warning that consumers are buying the bat for decor, placing it at risk of extinction. Taxidermy bats are sought after, particularly by US consumers, who are looking for gothic or spooky decorations for Halloween or Christmas gifts, the centre said. The wildlife trade study identified 107,356 species that are either in use or traded globally – far higher than a previous estimate of about 50,000, which was made by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES). The study draws on more comprehensive datasets, as well as newer research papers that have tracked species sold online for decoration. It shows flaws in our understanding of what species are at risk; for example, the number of butterfly species found to be traded is greater than the IPBES’ entire estimate for all traded terrestrial invertebrates. Molly Brown, programme officer for wildlife use and trade at the International Union for Conservation of Nature and a co-author of the paper, said the findings were a reality check. “The number of species that we are talking about is still an underestimate, and that’s really clear in the paper, because we cannot access and we do not have the type of monitoring data that we really need,” she said. Discussions about the wildlife trade often focus on criminal activities, such as illegal smuggling of ivory or pangolin scales. However, the wildlife trade encompasses sectors such as fisheries and the timber trade as well as fashion and the sale of species as ornaments. This includes activities that may be sustainable, as well as trade that is driving species to extinction. Even assessing the value of the legal trade compared with the illegal trade is challenging. The under-regulation of wildlife trade has created loopholes that allow species, including sought-after exotic pets, to be “laundered into legality”, researchers said. Four years ago, nearly 200 countries agreed to ensure that trade of wild species was “sustainable, safe and legal”, as part of a landmark set of targets aimed at ending the destruction of nature. Efforts to meet these targets are hampered by a lack of data about what is being sold and where it originated. The main data point for measuring progress on a globally agreed wildlife trade target refers only to fish stocks, which would account for at most 3% of all traded species, said Hughes. Experts say there needs to be more systematic data collection and sharing. Globally, fisheries are monitored by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, while the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites) monitors and regulates international trade in about 40,000 species to protect them from over exploitation. However, researchers said that this excludes large numbers of potentially vulnerable species, warning the Cites system is too slow moving to keep up with new trends in threats to wildlife. Most countries lack any systematic data outside Cites, the study says. “Sometimes, it is years before things get listed and that means that they can be virtually extinct in the wild by that point,” said Hughes. Species that are newly described are often rare and have a small range, meaning they are especially valuable to trade, and can be quickly wiped out. Chris Shepherd, a conservation advocate at the Centre for Biological Diversity, who was not involved in the study, added that he had observed the wildlife trade for decades and that new species were continually appearing. “The demand for wildlife, especially live wildlife traded for pets, is growing fast, as is the number of species involved,” he said. “This trade is pushing an ever-growing list of species towards extinction, and as such, putting in place mechanisms to better monitor this trade are essential.”

headline: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey
trail_text: Turkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expected
body_text: Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible. Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so. Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone. Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

headline: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets
trail_text: Ex-energy secretary Ed Miliband’s agenda appears undermined as money is diverted from renewables to defence
body_text: Britain is unlikely to hit its targets on green heating after the cuts announced by John Healey this week, experts have warned, as critics of Ed Miliband claim the former energy secretary’s green agenda is being dismantled. The chancellor unveiled more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget this week, much of which will pay for higher defence spending. One casualty of the cuts is the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined. Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda. Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that a Labour government will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.” Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments. Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps. Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30. The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned. “It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.” The cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband. Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system. One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.” Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean. “This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.” Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.” But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed. They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels. One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.” A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes. “We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”

headline: ‘You can see the water going down’: residents on edge as one of England’s worst-hit reservoirs dries up
trail_text: After UK’s hottest summer on record, Ardingly near Haywards Heath is just 19% full – and next-closest reservoir is unusable due to broken treatment works
body_text: “You can see the water level at Ardingly going down and down. I don’t remember ever seeing it this low,” says Caroline Allan, a lifetime resident of Haywards Heath, the nearest town to one of England’s most depleted reservoirs. The Ardingly reservoir, managed by South East Water and serving about 95,000 properties in and around Haywards Heath and Uckfield in Sussex, is currently 19% full. The day the Guardian visited, the weather was grey and rainy, incongruous with the muddy reservoir bed that should have been submerged under six metres of water. Earlier this month a severe drought was declared in parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex, with urgent measures being taken to secure public water supplies after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record. Severe drought is the highest level of drought and is declared when evidence shows drought is causing or will soon cause serious harm, and when emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services. “They will probably never lift the hosepipe ban and it just seems so unfair that they’re making the area more and more crowded but they’re not increasing the capacity to store water,” said Allan. There has been a steady stream of new housing developments around Haywards Heath, sparking local opposition, with concerns that a growing local population is putting pressure on already strained resources. Water demand is increasing as the population grows and new industrial demands from datacentres and energy infrastructure require more water. Plus, the water available to supply those needs is reducing as the climate crisis worsens, resulting in greater variability and unpredictability of rainfall and greater water demand during hotter, drier summers. There has also been a lack of investment over several decades in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs. Most of Europe has endured back-to-back climate crisis-driven heatwaves this summer. The extreme heat, coupled with little rainfall, means 82% of England and large parts of Wales are still in drought or severe drought. The Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year and yet supplies at several reservoirs are critically low. This includes Ardingly and Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers and is 14.5% full. It is estimated that 120% of average rainfall is needed between now and April for all areas to be considered out of drought. The government’s national drought group was told on Wednesday that despite the “weather whiplash” brought by Storm Austen and Boelo, the recent rain has not changed the drought outlook. Less than six miles away from Ardingly, Southern Water’s Weir Wood reservoir is 80% full because a water treatment works at the site has been out of action since 2018. “It’s crazy that they’ve got Weir Wood next door and they’re not using it. I think that’s madness,” Allan said. Graham Ward, who has lived in Haywards Heath for his whole life, also said it was “crazy” that there was a full neighbouring reservoir that cannot be used. During the drought in 2025, South East Water announced emergency plans to connect the Ardingly and Weir Wood reservoirs together by an overground pipeline. When the rain came and the drought conditions eased, these plans were shelved. Southern Water is now seeking to rebuild the treatment works at Weir Wood by 2030, and South East Water is conducting a feasibility study of a buried pipeline to connect the two reservoirs. But after government guidance to stockpile essential goods, water scarcity has become a pressing concern for local residents. “We’re really not that far away from Weir Wood, and we’ve got Ardingly with hardly any water in it and we’re told to buy water. It’s just crazy,” said Allan. Ward said he has already been storing water for some time in anticipation. “I am worried, but I also think there should be responsibility on the water companies to get the reservoirs working as they should be. The infrastructure is crumbling and it’s not fit for purpose any more; if we continually have hot summers, this is going to be a problem every year,” he said. Delphine Hazeldon, who has lived in Haywards Heath for more than 20 years, also said she has never seen the Ardingly reservoir so low. “Our relatives in Australia, they’re always asking for updates and they’re horrified. It is a definite worry, we’re approaching 80, but we think well, it’ll be our children and our children’s children facing the problem. The whole thing is a mess.” A spokesperson at Southern Water said: “Weir Wood reservoir is being rebuilt to ensure long-term water resilience for the North Sussex region, in the face of climate change and population growth. The existing treatment works date from the 1950s and reached the end of its operational life, with significant reliability and water-quality challenges. The site was therefore taken out of supply in 2018. “While a number of options were considered, a complete rebuild was identified as the best long-term solution to provide a reliable and resilient water supply for customers in the area. While we already supply water to South East Water through an existing interconnected network, Ardingly’s current situation would not be resolved if Weir Wood treatment works were operational.” Water minister, Emma Hardy, who chaired a national drought group meeting on Wednesday, said: “Despite the recent rain, the situation remains serious. As we move through autumn and winter, we now face the challenge of having drought and flood simultaneously as the rain struggles to be absorbed by the hardened ground. “Resilience to our changing climate is key and we need to be thinking about next year now. Water companies must continue to take every available measure to secure current supplies while also ensuring that we start the spring in the strongest possible position.” South East Water declined to comment.

headline: Biodiversity Cop17 seems to be stalling. Is it time to reform the process?
trail_text: In this week’s newsletter: There are too many meetings, and not enough decisions, say experts – and time is running out
body_text: When things are not going well at an environmental summit, organisers often tell delegates that the “world is watching” in an attempt to focus minds. But spend any time at biodiversity Cop17 in Armenia and it is clear that the world’s attention is elsewhere. The negotiating halls of Yerevan’s Meridian centre are subdued. Environment ministers have arrived from all corners of the world to plan their response to being so far behind the biodiversity targets they agreed four years ago. Right now, they appear on track to miss nearly all of them. They risk continuing the miserable record of never having met a biodiversity target they have set for themselves. More from Cop17, after this week’s most important reads. Essential reads The climate crisis will destroy our economies – we learned this 20 years ago. When will we act? Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn Angry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on Rosebank In focus I write this during a good week for the environment. Lula’s incredible comeback in the Brazilian presidential election will probably guarantee four more years of low deforestation rates in their part of the Amazon rainforest, one of the most alive places on our planet. Serbia’s new Student List government could tackle the country’s dreadful environmental record. But these hard-won achievements have little to do with the increasingly fractured multilateral process. In a side room on Wednesday, I sat down with Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, to discuss how the process could be reformed. The organisation is working with governments to streamline the sprawling set of agreements and bodies that make up the global environmental calendar, in an attempt to improve their impact. “The process is delivering but it’s going too slowly. This is what the secretary-general [António Guterres] said when he was here: ‘Thank you. Good. Do more, but faster, because we are not where we want to be’,” she said. Implementation has always been one of the most challenging parts of any Cop process. Painfully negotiated agreements lack ways to meaningfully highlight which countries are falling behind or punish bad behaviour. It will always be up to national governments to deliver on their promises. During the climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024, leading policy experts called for a radical overhaul to climate summits, describing the process as “no longer fit for purpose”. They said they needed to shift from a focus on negotiation to implementation, and argued that only the most environmentally ambitious countries should host, although some in the group later walked back on that statement. Even so, they are not alone in their calls for reform of the international patchwork of agreements and initiatives. “Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. It will be very interesting for members states to look at the issue. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands. Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that,” she said. By the end of Friday, governments are scheduled to sign off an action plan to get back on target with this decade’s biodiversity targets. Few in Yerevan are expecting major moves. But without change soon, calls to reform the Cop process will only grow louder. The health of the planet demands it. Read more: • Four years ago countries made a historic deal to save nature. Is it dead in the water? • World’s climate fight needs fundamental reform, UN expert says: ‘Some states are not acting in good faith’ • Cop summits ‘no longer fit for purpose’, say leading climate policy experts • To read the complete version of this newsletter – subscribe to receive Down to Earth in your inbox every Thursday.

headline: Greener front gardens could help combat air pollution and summer heat
trail_text: Scientists call for incentives to preserve vegetation as study highlights benefits of plentiful planting in London
body_text: Your front garden could be a first line of defence against air pollution, according to a year-long field study in two London neighbourhoods. The UK’s 26m gardens cover nearly 5% of the country’s land area, but they account for a much larger share in urban areas. In Greater London, domestic gardens cover 41% of the city, compared with 27% of Cardiff and 23% of Edinburgh. Previous studies have shown that, apart from providing direct access to green space, gardens have wider benefits for mental health, biodiversity and flood resilience. Research from the 1980s found that patients recovering from surgery who could see trees from their hospital windows recovered faster. In the first study of its kind, researchers measured air pollution in eight gardens alongside busy roads. One set of gardens was about 10 metres from North Circular Road in London; the other was about 15 metres from a busy road in the east of the city. The research found that gardens with hedges and plentiful vegetation had the lowest levels of particle pollution. The best-performing garden had up to 80% lower particle pollution than paved gardens. Gardens with lawns also had stable and consistently low levels of air pollution. Hedges, shrubs and trees can alter the flow of air pollution from nearby roads. Plants can filter the air by trapping particles on their leaves, while gaseous pollutants can be absorbed through pores in the leaves. While the gardens shielded homes from local air pollution, they offer less protection in spring, when air pollution from agriculture and farming could spread across wide areas. Paved gardens had the highest temperatures and highest levels of air pollution. In summer, temperatures could be up to 6C hotter than in gardens with abundant vegetation.
