Prof Prashant Kumar, of the University of Surrey, who coordinated the study, said: “The cooling effect is especially clear. Given the recent hot summers in the UK, keeping plants in front gardens could make a meaningful difference, particularly during hot nights. “Greener front gardens can deliver real benefits. A front-garden hedge can help improve local air quality near the home. If air pollution is reduced directly outside the home, it is reasonable to expect that less pollution may enter indoors.” Dr Karina Corada-Pérez, of the University of East London and first author of the study, said: “Our message is simple: keep gardens green wherever possible. The pressure to pave front gardens is very real. We recognise why many residents pave front gardens, including the need for low-maintenance spaces or off-street parking.” She said there was a clear opportunity to design front gardens that met practical household needs while retaining vegetation. “We need guidance and incentives that balance parking, accessibility and maintenance with the health, climate and environmental benefits of greener front gardens,” Corada-Pérez said.

headline: Country diary: The light and shade of autumn’s shortening days
trail_text: Loch Insh, Cairngorms: In my three decades in Scotland I’ve adjusted to the darkness of this time of year, and found glory in the quality of light
body_text: It is the one clear day in a fortnight of heavy cloud, wind and rain, so I am out by the loch, basking in the rays of light, breathing them in, hoarding for the weeks to come. This time of year makes them all the more precious. Here in the Highlands, once we are past the autumnal equinox, we can almost feel the Earth tipping away from the sun as the light grows shorter each day and the night steals back. It’s a turn that is especially obvious when the clocks change and our evenings are suddenly dark. As an Australian brought up in south Asia and raised on sunshine, when I first moved here I found this shift dismaying and I dreaded the months ahead. For a few years a light box sustained me through the depths of winter. But in my three decades in Scotland, I have acclimatised. I’ve found increasing reasons to glory in autumn, when the encroaching darkness is offset by a particular radiance in the light, especially at either end of the day, as the low sun cuts through cold air. It seems to gain greater clarity, drawing sharper lines around shadows and making every twig and rock stand out in high relief. And there’s intensity to its long-reaching rays, casting a glow on the fire palette of the berries and the changing leaves. When shafts of sun break through on otherwise slate-dark days, the trees seem lit from within, like the golden halo in an icon. Today, the first snows on the hills are brilliant white, echoed in the gliding swans on the loch. But even the darkness no longer feels such a threat. Its cloak falls gently now, each day giving more ground to the velvet night, studded by a silver brooch of moon. I feel myself tipping away from the sun myself to stare at thousands of stars, planets, meteors, comets and the soft glitter of the Milky Way. And I am drinking and breathing it in, hopeful for the winter to come. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order at guardianbookshop.com and get a 15% discount

headline: Wildlife Trusts hit £30m target to buy and rewild huge Northumberland estate
trail_text: About 25,000 members of public chip in £17m towards 3,800-hectare Rothbury estate, described as ‘once-in-a-generation opportunity’
byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
body_text: One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland. The Wildlife Trusts’ bid to buy the Rothbury estate, an area the size of Athens, had been championed by David Attenborough who on Friday thanked the public for their help. “The Wildlife Trusts called for your support and you answered in your thousands,” he said. “The opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality. This will be a place where nature, community, farming and heritage can combine to create something very special for generations to come.” The fundraising campaign was launched two years ago after the estate was put up for sale by the Duke of Northumberland’s youngest son, Max Percy. At more than 3,800 hectares (nearly 15 sq miles), the Rothbury estate is the largest piece of land in single ownership to have come up for sale in England for more than 30 years. Campaigners said buying it was “a once-in-a-generation opportunity”. Mike Pratt, the chief executive of Northumberland Wildlife Trust, said he felt “elated” at the success of the campaign and “humbled” by the public support. “We are absolutely elated, it has been a long haul and it hasn’t all been easy,” he said. “The other word is humbled. There was £17m from the public to make this happen and that is at the forefront of my mind – we’ve got to honour that support and make sure that people come here and really enjoy getting close to wildlife.” The estate is a thrilling, spirit-lifting mosaic of different habitats, including the looming Simonside hills, sweeping wild moorland, valley woodlands and farm fields. Pratt was talking to the Guardian at Lordenshaws, the site of an iron-age hill fort and one of the largest clusters of strange, ancient cup and ring marked rocks in England. He thinks people rallied to the campaign because it “represents hope … a positive view of what the future can be”. The trust has big plans and hopes that by making interventions, restoring and extending habitats, it can increase numbers of species which are already there, whether mountain bumblebees or red squirrels. “We should have water voles in this landscape,” said Pratt. “Maybe we can help bring them back. Pine martens are making their own way back, maybe we can encourage them. Hopefully we’ll see more curlew.” The eventual hope is that the Rothbury estate will be the “beating heart” of a 40-mile nature corridor from the coast at Druridge Bay to the Scottish-English border at the Kielderhead and Whitelee Moor national nature reserves. The trust also believes that more nature tourism will bring benefits to the town of Rothbury itself. Sophie Bulgin, the Rothbury project manager, said the enthusiasm of volunteers in the various projects that had been running had taken her aback. “It has overwhelmed me,” she said. “I didn’t imagine that much interest and enthusiasm. People are taking ownership.” One of the projects is eco-acoustic monitoring, with “people walking for miles across the estate in bracken as high as their shoulder” to install and retrieve monitors which record the sound of small mammals, bats or anything else that might be close by. In a fortnight, there will be earthworm counts which might reveal more about the health of the soil. As well as gifts from 25,000 members of the public, the National Lottery Heritage Fund gave a gamechanging £5m. Large donations also came from charitable foundations and philanthropists, and the government this week pledged £1.94m. Not everyone supported the campaign, however, with some farmers calling it a “folly”. Guy Renner-Thompson, a councillor and the chair of Northumberland Conservatives, this week questioned the government’s priorities after its decision to give money. “Farmers on the estate have already raised concerns about food production, changes to traditional land management and whether their businesses can remain profitable,” he said. “Those concerns deserve answers before ministers reach for the chequebook.” Pratt said the trust had been working closely with farmers. “We want to demonstrate that you can have lots of wildlife and still have a productive business model.”

headline: Feral deer will become Australia’s next feral pig problem without prompt action, report warns
trail_text: The invasive species has increased in spread and numbers and is costing farmers millions of dollars
body_text: An unpublished government report on feral deer shows Australia is failing in its efforts to stop the spread of what one advocate warns could become “Australia’s next feral pig”. The five years from 2020-2025 over which the national feral deer action plan was assessed covers a period in which the famously elusive species has increasingly encroached upon major cities, leading to more frequent encounters – including a memorable occasion in which two men in various degrees of undress were fined after becoming lost in the bush when they were spooked by deer while nude sunbathing. The report says deer, one of the country’s “most rapidly increasing invasive pests”, have both increased in numbers and spread in territory, costing more than $91m in production loss and management time every year. Deakin University’s Prof Euan Ritchie, president of the Australian Mammal Society, said he was “not at all” surprised by this year’s national vertebrate pest management report card. “This report shows that governments are failing miserably to invest enough to control deer populations and the severe impacts that they can have on agriculture, native wildlife and the environment, road safety and culturally significant sites,” Ritchie said. “This is what sustained failure to act sufficiently results in.” Six species of feral deer are established in Australia – chital, fallow, hog, red, rusa and sambar – with well-established populations across south-eastern Australia, where densities are highest. There are smaller, more localised populations in South and Western Australia and the Northern Territory. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The report card, produced by the National Vertebrate Pest Coordinators, shows every state and territory is failing or floundering in their efforts to control feral deer – with one notable exception. South Australia, which launched an ambitious statewide eradication plan in 2022, received a green in all four categories assessed under the traffic light system of marking. The report showed – with high confidence – that the state had decreased the abundance, distribution and environmental and agricultural impacts of deer. New South Wales and Tasmania were given reds in all four categories, while Queensland and the ACT both received three reds and a yellow. No jurisdiction but SA received a single green pass mark. Invasive Species Council advocacy manager Reece Pianta said the report confirmed what land managers had been seeing on the ground for some years. In May 2025, the council released footage and images that it said showed the Gold Coast “under feral deer siege”. Pianta said the report, leaked to his organisation, points to “a long-term systemic underfunding of deer control”. He said deer did not have the recognition of other more notorious invasives, but controlling them was every bit as necessary. “Deer are the next feral pig,” he said. “The difference with deer is that an intervention now could make a significant difference to the population numbers and contain, or even reverse, that spread.” While Pianta said deer “probably can’t be eradicated” from the entire continent, he said South Australia’s “A+” report score showed it was possible to do so in some states and territories, while others would require a long-term effort to contain the spread of deer and mitigate their impacts. Adelaide University Environment Institute director Prof Andrew Lowe said the report was a “good news story” for his state that rang true with what he was seeing on the ground. Lowe, who is also member of the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, which is involved in managing deer, said SA grappled with its “massive problem with deer” in earnest from 2022, after an agricultural impact estimate showed the $36m worth of damage done every year by deer there was set to increase to $241m by 2031. But although deer had “massively declined” in the few years since a $4m eradication program began, Lowe said deer were seeking refuge on the fringes of urban areas, where culling was more expensive. He said functional eradication of deer from SA would take about another $10m over 10 years. The cost of inaction, though, was of a different magnitude. “If we don’t do that, then the population will go up again and we’re going to be in the same situation,” Lowe said. “So $10m versus $240m – do the math.”

headline: Angry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on Rosebank
trail_text: Exclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decision
byline: Jessica Elgot, Kiran Stacey, Pippa Crerar and Fiona Harvey
body_text: Furious Labour MPs have been lobbying the prime minister and chancellor not to overrule the energy secretary should she decide to block the Rosebank oilfield. MPs say they are alarmed at the cabinet splits that have emerged over the issue after sources told the Guardian that Miatta Fahnbulleh was minded to refuse environmental permission for the field. Sources close to the chancellor, John Healey, have since made it clear he is in favour of the scheme, while some in government believe the prime minister, Andy Burnham, also wants it to go ahead. Backbenchers worried about the environmental impact of the project are now urging their whips and Downing Street not to allow other ministers to intervene in Fahnbulleh’s decision. Catherine Fookes, a Labour member of the energy select committee, said: “Approving Rosebank will blow a hole in our green credentials. A group of us is making it clear to leadership that this should be Miatta’s decision and I hope they listen. “Labour MPs are really, really concerned about it – it would go against the thrust of our manifesto.” Another MP said: “If Healey pushes through Rosebank, there will be blood. It’s economically shortsighted as well as politically explosive – they aren’t listening at all to the discomfort on the backbenches.” Another commented: “Lots of us have raised this. I think the position Miatta has been put in by these briefings is intolerable.” Concerns are understood to also have been raised with Healey directly in budget meetings with MPs. Fahnbulleh’s parliamentary aides have circulated a memo to MPs insisting she would have the final say on the proposals, after a number of MPs contacted them to raise concerns that she would be overruled. “No decision has been made on Rosebank,” the memo said. “The energy secretary will consider all relevant factors in a case before reaching a decision. “The energy secretary is the only decision maker and will consider all relevant factors as part of the quasi-judicial process. No other cabinet member or minister has any role in this decision and does not see the advice on it,” it added. Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil drilling, calling the Jackdaw gasfield, which the government approved last week, “a bridge to the future”. The prime minister insists the decision over Rosebank will be for Fahnbulleh alone to make. But he prompted speculation about his support for the project on Wednesday, when he told the Commons: “Use of our reserves can support and accelerate a clean energy future, and that was very much the logic behind the decision that the government announced on Jackdaw last week.” Many in government believe Fahnbulleh can approve the bigger Rosebank scheme without breaching the UK’s carbon commitments, in part because most of its oil would be exported. The Guardian also revealed on Tuesday that the Treasury had already factored in tax revenues from the scheme, which are expected to hit about £500m by the end of this parliament. Treasury officials said on Wednesday the money had been included in forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) since 2019, and that doing so would not prevent the energy secretary from blocking it. The OBR said in its budget forecast on Wednesday: “The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the North Sea Transition Authority’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries. “The forecast annual pace of decline [in oil and gas production] would be around 14% a year if there were no production from any new fields.” The memo from Fahnbulleh’s aides added that decisions to score Rosebank as part of the forecast would be a decision for the OBR. However, some Labour MPs believe the Treasury has been using aggressive tactics to strong-arm the energy department, with one describing the approach of No 11 as “macho bullshit”. Clive Lewis, another Labour MP, said: “You cannot claim global climate leadership while approving new oilfields simply because you’ve already pencilled in the tax receipts. Tax ‘receipts’, as I understand it, that will be the operator’s estimate and not actual Treasury revenue.” Analysis by Uplift, a campaign group, found that on the government’s and industry’s estimates, the tax take from Rosebank would probably be limited and could be outweighed by the tax breaks and incentives likely to be offered for the development and decommissioning of the fields. Areeba Hamid, a co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said: “Any tax revenues from this far-off field in a rapidly declining basin don’t just leave our public services at the hostage of future oil prices, they also leave taxpayers on the hook for the costs of decommissioning for decades to come. The truth is that approving new oil drilling in the North Sea will only add to the costs of climate impacts, costs not fully factored into forecasts such as those from the OBR. Any economist should be able to see that.” MPs said there would be a significant parliamentary rebellion on Rosebank, unlike Jackdaw, where they were prepared to accept the argument to allow gas to be extracted for domestic consumption. Fookes said: “The case was made for Jackdaw to some degree and we remained quite quiet over that. Rosebank, however, is a different issue.”

headline: Country diary: A new chapter for the farm – we’re going organic
trail_text: Tebay, Cumbria: Historically it’s been a tricky thing for hill farms to do, but we’ve always run ours on organic principles, and now we’re fully converting
body_text: From 1 November we have change happening on our farm. We have decided to become an organic farm and have started the two-year conversion process with the Soil Association. We’ve always run the farm on organic principles, but now, with our small shop selling our beef, lamb and pork, we’ve decided that we will convert, prioritising soil health and biodiversity without the use of chemicals. It has historically been tricky for hill farms to go organic because many are on commons with shared grazing and no physical boundaries between “hefts”, and with shared routes to and from the fell. Now the certifiers are keen to be flexible and adapt, so we have decided to give it a go. The process is funded by the government’s sustainable farming incentive scheme, which we were lucky to get into this year as so many farmers missed out. Practically it will mean more record-keeping, vet permission needed for dipping sheep and longer withdrawal periods on many medicines. When we plant trees, we will need to source organic trees, or ask for a derogation if they’re not available. It will be the culmination of the change in our farming system, from the conventional upland beef and sheep farm we bought in 2018, to a regenerative model where biodiversity is considered something we produce as a public good. It would also be very unusual here – the north-west has only 2.4% of the UK’s organic land. It’s a challenge, but it’s something we want to do as my son’s wife’s family farm has become organic and it has worked well for them. What we’re hoping to achieve for the farm is to increase biodiversity, produce quality breeding stock that can thrive outside all year without any additional inputs, produce food for local people to buy direct from the farm, and allow people to visit and understand the farmed landscape. It will be a talking point on future farm walks as well. Our latest batch of beef will be in the farm shop for Christmas. It won’t be certified organic this year, but in future years we hope it will. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order at guardianbookshop.com and get a 15% discount

headline: The Jackdaw gasfield, net zero and climate adaptation
trail_text: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which the prime minister said the government’s gasfield approval was part of its commitment to a greener future
body_text: Andy Burnham writes that his determination to tackle the climate crisis is “unwavering” and that the transition must not leave communities behind (We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan, 22 October). Whatever one thinks of Jackdaw, the test of that pledge is whether people are also protected from climate impacts that are already here. The research that you reported on last week attributed two-thirds of the heat deaths that it estimated – 4,354 of them in the UK – to climate change. The numbers from that study were not available when the health secretary took questions in the Commons last Tuesday, but the signs were – stretched ambulance services, cancelled operations and overheated wards. Heat was barely mentioned. The prime minister says that he will not be “so careless with people’s lives” as oil and gas workers face the transition. He is right, and the same care is owed to older people in care homes, pregnant women, patients on hospital wards and outdoor workers facing the next heatwave. So the government must commit to practical action before next summer. That means effective cooling and heatwave plans in hospitals, maternity units and care homes, stronger early warnings, welfare checks for isolated older people, and protections for workers in dangerous temperatures. The Climate Change Committee has shown that the investment needed is manageable and the cost of inaction far greater. Net zero and adaptation are not alternatives. Mr Burnham should say what he will deliver, and when. Emma Howard Boyd Chair, National Heat Risk Commission • The idea of using fossil fuels as a “bridge” to green energy has been touted by polluters and politicians since the 1980s. It’s mind-boggling that we’re still at this point. Energy security, national security and avoiding climate catastrophe all come with rapidly expanding green technologies such as heat pumps and renewables. The benefits there far outweigh those produced by gas drilling, and it’s these that should be Andy Burnham’s full focus when he talks of a green transition. After decades of delay, the world’s transition now needs to be fast. Thanks to the failure of the politicians who came before, we need heaps of gas to heat our homes this winter, but the idea of baking that in for more decades isn’t just stupid – to myself and my peers who look ahead with fear at an increasingly precarious future, this decision is an insult. Gwydion Elliott Sheffield • Andy Burnham – “not a climate guy”, according to one of his MPs – argues in his opinion article that an increase in CO2 emissions is required to bring down CO2 emissions. George Orwell would appreciate that. Douglas Currie Edinburgh • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Country diary: A vial of water from the rivers, becks and springs of Yorkshire – but not without permission
trail_text: Wharram and York, North Yorkshire: It’s the nervy few days before a ceremony that will honour our local waterways, and I have work to do
body_text: I visit the source of the tiny stream called the Gypsey Race now and then, drawn by the everyday miracle of its water welling to catch sunlight like a plaything and alchemise it into colours and sparks. Today, though, is different, because I’ve come to ask for something. Something like permission, or approval maybe. I’ve been helping to organise a gathering of river advocates to co-draft a regional charter of river rights – making explicit our responsibilities towards them. We will be holding a ceremony to blend waters from across Yorkshire to make ink in which the charter will be written. I want to collect water from the Gypsey, but I also want some of its potent reputation. Its course is regarded as auspicious thanks to an extraordinary concentration of nearby prehistoric barrows, cursuses and henges, not to mention England’s tallest standing stone. Local folklore insists that its capricious flow holds the power of prophecy. I address my request to two sentinel trees rooted in the water – sister salixes, willow and sallow – then begin to walk around the spring. I’ve barely gone 10 steps when the clouds part and the recently tilled soil at my feet starts glimmering. I look up and the field is alight with what must be hundreds of miles of spider silk. Is this the answer I was hoping for? Early on the day of the ceremony, I meet my collaborators and we decide to swim at the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss. On the slipway, a gleam of colour reveals itself to be small lost brooch with an enamelled kingfisher. Minutes later, as we’re towelling off, a young lad comes hurrying along the path with a net containing a monstrous green, gold and russet pike, magnificent and terrible, with a judging eye and, as Ted Hughes put it, “the grin it was born with”. I choose to read the cobwebs, the kingfisher token and the pike as positive omens, but I remain nervous about the ceremony. Will the pragmatic Yorkshire folk we’ve invited get it? I soon relax: the first offering is a vial the woman says contains not only local rivers, but water from sacred springs around the world. I think this might just work. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warn
trail_text: President has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather events
body_text: Sweeping cuts to the premier US climate agency under Donald Trump have severely hampered the country’s capacity to forecast, research and respond to extreme weather events, former government officials and scientists have warned, as the US faces a cascade of hazards fueled by a potentially historic El Niño this winter. From the start of his second term, the president has taken aim at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), slashing staff levels, canceling contracts and grants, and shutting down databases and research laboratories. The agency that has long been considered a global crown jewel in climate science and forecasting has lost roughly 20% of its staff since January 2025. The National Weather Service, which is housed within Noaa, has also taken a hit. Weather stations have had to delay data collection and cut operating hours, with hundreds of meteorological and other technical positions still vacant across its 122 forecast offices. The effects have already been felt at Noaa, where a chaotic and volatile environment has sent morale plummeting, increased burnout and hampered vital work. While capacity has quietly unravelled, a large-scale disaster will quickly expose the most dangerous gaps. “The system has not really been tested since all the cuts happened,” said Tom Di Liberto, a former Noaa climate scientist who now works as the media director of Climate Central. That test could soon be coming. This year’s super El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the ability to fuel extreme weather events around the world. It’s already climbing off the charts and is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter. Along with dangerous spikes in temperature, El Niño will supercharge storms in parts of the American west, raise sea levels in California by up to a foot, and set the stage for debris flows, landslides and flash floods. “Whether we as a country can handle the kind of coast-to-coast extremes that could potentially happen this winter is a big question,” Di Liberto said. Noaa plays a pivotal role in public safety and provides key insights and forecasts relied upon by a vast array of communities and industries, from weather shifts that could affect crop schedules, to emergency response preparations when hurricanes are brewing or fire conditions are aligning. The agency operates early warning systems for tsunamis, monitors seafood supply chains and provides ocean data needed for safe shipping and port operators. While the losses are expected to have a profound effect on the American public, they will be felt globally, too. Scientists and forecasters around the world depend on Noaa satellites, studies and intelligence, including data-sharing arrangements that track severe weather across Europe, coordination for disaster response in the Caribbean, and deforestation monitoring and the effects of the climate crisis in the Amazon rainforest. “I worry about loss of life and about our inability to be protected at a time when we need our government the most,” said Monica Medina, who served as the principal deputy administrator of Noaa during the Obama administration. The risks are but a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. “If this is a real test” of a hotter, more precarious future, she added, “we’re going to flunk”. Budget and research cuts Gaps in staffing, operations and engagement with the public are the top three concerns for Rick Spinrad, who spent three decades at the agency and served as Noaa administrator for the Biden administration. The agency was already shorthanded in those areas when Trump took office, according to Spinrad. But since January 2025, Noaa has lost more than 3,000 staffers, according to workforce data from the US office of personnel management that was last updated in August this year. It’s the biggest staffing drop in the last decade, and includes hundreds of people who lost their jobs during massive layoffs or who took incentives to retire or resign as the administration worked to systemically shrink the size of the federal government last year, along with those who left voluntarily. Some departments have been hit harder than others. The public affairs team that helps disseminate important information was roughly halved. Information technology management workers, who provide vital support for forecasting and data infrastructure among other things, were reduced by roughly 27%. The data showed a loss of more than 500 staffers across a range of science positions with only 46 new hires. There were also about 10% fewer meteorologists and meteorology technicians as the US went into autumn this year, even after the National Weather Service rushed to staff up in the aftermath of the Trump administration’s massive 2025 layoffs. The NWS analyzes and collects roughly 6.3bn observations each day. They release 1.5m forecasts and up to 50,000 warnings each year. Cracks have begun to show as the agency has tried to takes on its enormous and essential workload with fewer people. Staffers had to work double shifts to keep some forecasting offices open, the Washington Post reported last September. Staffers who spoke to the Post at the time described an agency pushed to its limits. Only 40 meteorologists were added to the ranks across Noaa between January and August this year, with hundreds of vacancies across the country still open as a tumultuous winter approaches. Overall, the agency was able to bring on just 525 new hires since January 2025, leaving a gaping 2,500-person deficit. Already, staffing limitations have shown up in delayed or limited weather balloon launches that left parts of the Great Plains unprepared for tornadoes and limited warnings to rural communities in Alaska, where more than 1,500 people were displaced by floods earlier this year. The NWS also failed to adequately provide multilingual weather alerts due to staffing and funding cuts, the government accountability office (GAO) found, leaving 26 million people in the US at higher risk. “There has been this hollowing out – there’s no time to do anything other than the very basics,” said Dr Anna Zivian, a climate researcher and policy expert. “I suspect we haven’t seen the worst outcomes from the loss of capacity yet. You can’t pick up that kind of slack.” Meanwhile, the Trump administration terminated dozens of grants representing a loss in more than $28m in funding for states, cities, non-profits and universities, according to calculations from Grant Witness, an organization that tracks science-related grant making by the federal government. Climate research has been the most affected, according to their analysis, which found that the number of grant awards in fiscal year 2026 was 37% lower than the 2021-2024 average. Despite these concerns, the administration has outlined more plans to slash budgets and research capacity. Trump has proposed cutting $1.6bn in Noaa funding – a 26% drop – for next year’s budget. While many of the cuts won’t make it through the budget process, they showcase how the president views the essential services the agency provides the American public and puts more pressure on the staff still working at Noaa. “People at Noaa are nervous,” Di Liberto said, adding that employees across the organization were afraid they would get in trouble if they said something that conflicted with the administration’s anti-climate narrative. “You want people doing their best work when we face these extremes,” he said. Denials of human-caused climate crisis coming from the top have only made their jobs harder, as scientists and forecasters work to put urgent information into context for the American public and others around the world. “It’s incredibly difficult,” Di Liberto said. “Imagine being told the number six doesn’t exist and then being asked to do math.” A missed learning opportunity An El Niño year can be high risk, but it’s also an incredible chance to learn and prepare, offering a glimpse of what the world might expect as temperatures rise. In that regard, experts worry a shrunken Noaa is missing a vital research opportunity. “This El Niño is so useful in a sense of getting an understanding about where we stand for dealing with extreme weather around the world,” Di Liberto said. “Unfortunately we’re going to learn a lot this winter about our ability to deal with multiple extremes happening at the same time.” He and other experts have also expressed concerns that not enough has been done to ready communities for the coming hazards or capture important data that will inform the future. “When it comes to preparing for El Niño events – or any weather extreme – the preparation happens during the off season,” he said. During the last strong El Niño a decade ago, the agency deployed planes, weather balloons, unmanned aircraft and a research ship to collect data. This year, only “a handful of unmanned watercraft” will be deployed into the Pacific, NPR reported in September. The Trump administration had also begun removing ocean monitoring systems that provide important data during El Niño, but restored them after widespread outcry from scientists, fishers and public officials. Roughly $6bn has been shaved off an investment secured for weather satellites that would have propelled major advancements in future weather predictions. The sharp reduction could create a gap in satellite coverage, according to an analysis from the government accountability office, severely disrupting data. Funding for a decade-long project to monitor the oceans using autonomous robotic devices called biogeochemical-argo floats – part of a global effort – will also expire at the end of October. A Noaa spokesperson responded that efforts to monitor and collect data this year have built on past efforts by using “new, cutting-edge technologies” that were previously unavailable. “NOAA has never been more equipped to study, prepare for and respond to an ENSO event [El Niño southern oscillation event],” a Noaa spokesperson said in an emailed statement that highlighted updated modeling tools and the use of uncrewed systems. “These advanced capabilities have allowed NOAA to streamline resources and study this year’s El Niño more effectively than ever before.” Spinrad and other experts agreed that new technologies had helped advance data collection and improve forecasting ability. “We are more capable than we have been in the past because of the developments in the technology, the satellites that we’re flying, the observing systems that we’ve put in place,” Spinrad said. “But everything that this administration is doing suggests that we cannot and will not sustain those capabilities. So the real question is – are we at a turning point now?” • This article was updated on 27 October 2026 to include a response from Noaa issued after publication and to add that an ocean monitoring program had been reinstated.

headline: Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders
trail_text: Emissions from exported oil would not count against carbon budget, insiders say – reasoning likely to draw dismay from climate campaigners
body_text: The giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead. The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval. Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one. A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction. On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth wrote to the prime minister urging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation. But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected. “The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.” Greg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong to approve the Jackdaw gasfield last week and would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions. But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.” Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time. A judge ruled in 2024 that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it. Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes. Fahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C. In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035. Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets. Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank. He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated in Scotland with the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield. Fahnbulleh told the Guardian last week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank. Her allies say she is leaning away from approving it because the climate damage it would create, while arguably not enough to violate legal limits, would not be overriden by the potential benefits, which those who support its approval argue includes tax take, jobs and investment. In recent days, however, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project. The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”

headline: Britain’s fridge disposal crisis and what to do about it
trail_text: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Sam Wollaston about Norfolk’s fridge mountain
body_text: Sam Wollaston (What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain, 21 October) highlights an urgent issue, but misses a key underlying driver: the reality of climate change and increasingly hot UK summers. Many standard UK fridge-freezers are only built to normal (N) ambient climate classes, rated to operate in temperatures up to +32C. During recent heatwaves, indoor temperatures in many homes regularly exceed this limit. Even subtropical (ST) rated units fail when ambient temperatures push past 38C. When ambient limits are exceeded, cooling systems fail, leading to compressor breakdown, spoiled food and premature appliance disposal. We need higher regulatory standards requiring manufacturers to produce more durable, resilient appliances rated for higher ambient temperature classes (such as Tropical T or SN-T). Until manufacturers are held to these standards, UK consumers will continue to be left with failing fridges and our landfill waste will keep growing. Alistair Beattie London • The problem of fridge disposal needs government action. A “polluter pays” levy should apply to all new fridges, and should go proportionally to local authorities responsible for waste management. They could use the levy to commission companies to recycle fridges in an environment-friendly way. Steve Rowell Solihull • There is a simple solution when fridges and freezers are being thrown away simply because the owner wanted an “upgrade”. Appliances in working order can be given away to others via apps such as Olio and Freecycle, or community Facebook pages or WhatsApp groups. This is how I disposed of all my functional white goods when my house was renovated. Jacky Rowland London • I have just had to buy a new fridge as I can’t find replacements for the door seals on the the old one. Fridges should be repairable. Now the old one, which still functions in a rattly sort of way, has to join the recycling queue simply because of a bit of perished rubber. Diana Dalasini Molesey, Surrey • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

headline: Slovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summer
trail_text: Extreme heat accelerated disappearance of Triglav glacier from mountain revered as a symbol of Slovenian identity
body_text: The final ice patch has vanished from Slovenia’s Triglav glacier, the latest Alpine casualty of Europe’s scorching summer. The once mighty ice mass lost 93% of its surface area between 1983 and 2003, shrinking to cover less than a hectare of overheated rock, but went on to surprise researchers who feared its imminent demise, clinging on to the mountain for two more decades. In the last five years, which includes Europe’s three hottest years on record, the remaining ice has melted to a handful of isolated pockets, with the final remnant of the main body measuring just a few metres by the end of summer. New photos of the mountainside – taken either side of snowfall this month – confirm that no ice remains. Matija Zorn, director of the Anton Melik Geographical Institute, said Mount Triglav “holds a central place in Slovenian national identity” and the demise of the glacier represents the loss of an important data source and indicator of climate change. “Every year I knew that the ice was going to be less and less,” he said. “But I was shocked every year [by] how much less ice was up there.” Fierce heatwaves made hotter by carbon pollution have ravaged the Alps and reduced big white glaciers to what scientists have called “moonlike” rock deserts. Last month, Swiss glaciologists found that nearly a fifth of the country’s ice had disappeared in the last five years, with a 5.5% drop in volume in 2026. In Slovenia, home to the south-eastern tip of the Alps, the Triglav glacier suffered most of its decline in the last century. Historical photographs and documents suggest the glacier covered about 40 hectares in the mid-1800s. By 1946, when scientists conducted the first formal measurements, its area had shrunk to just 14 hectares. Zorn, who first took measurements at the glacier in 2001, said the rate of change was surprising even in the decades in which the glacier defied expectations. The spot at which he had to put on crampons to prevent slipping jumped back year after year as the glacier receded. “The melting is incredible,” he said. “In 2022 … we took a core of ice out for some geochemical analysis and it was like 5 metres [deep]. The next year, I was standing on the same spot … not on ice, but on rock.” Triglav is Slovenia’s highest peak, a cultural touchpoint that every person in the country of skiers and climbers is expected to climb at least once. Although the glacier has vanished, scientists have found ice in the caves beneath Triglav as its retreat has exposed new shafts. A second glacier on the Skuta mountain has also shrunk and thinned, but the remaining patch of ice is better shaded than Triglav and is expected to hold out for a few more years. Western Europe suffered through its hottest summer on record this year, causing at least 50,000 estimated heat deaths and costly secondary effects that ranged from failed harvests to power plants being forced to shut down. Scientists are still assessing the damage done to ecosystems. Miha Pavšek, a glaciologist and mountain guide, said “nature is changing in front of our eyes” but people were not yet taking it seriously. “With the melting of the glacier, a part of me is also going away,” said Pavšek, who has a photograph of his parents there in 1957. “There are some things that humans thought were eternal. Glaciers are obviously not.” • This article was amended on 29 October 2026. In an earlier version, due to a misunderstanding, Matija Zorn was quoted as saying: “In 2002 … we took a core of ice out for some geochemical analysis...” This date has been changed to 2022.

headline: UK spending on ‘fairytale’ carbon capture tech is a national embarrassment, chancellor told
trail_text: Chris Packham says £24bn earmarked for projects with ‘ludicrously uncertain results’ should be redirected to help lower bills and cut emissions
body_text: Campaigners are calling on the chancellor to cut the government’s £24bn spending plans for “fairytale” carbon capture technologies in favour of funding green schemes that can reliably cut emissions and lower energy bills. The environmentalist Chris Packham is leading an 11th-hour appeal for the Treasury to use this week’s budget to scale back the government’s “exorbitantly expensive” support for carbon capture, which is now more than the planned spending for the US, the EU, Norway and Japan combined. He said it was a “national embarrassment” that the government had earmarked £24bn to support a series of carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects developed by big oil companies, including BP and the Norwegian state oil company Equinor, and urged ministers to “put things right”. “CCS is a tech fairytale,” the naturalist and broadcaster said. “It should be a national embarrassment that the UK is pumping more taxpayer money into it than any other country in the world. This budget is a chance to put things right.” The intervention comes as the government reportedly plans to reduce the grants available to households hoping to swap their gas boiler for an electric heat pump. This shift is considered crucial to cutting the carbon emitted when heating buildings, which makes up around a fifth of the UK’s total greenhouse gas emissions. Packham called on the government to safeguard funding promises “that empower households to lower bills” rather than “bankrolling exorbitantly expensive projects with ludicrously uncertain results”. The leaders of many economies have backed carbon capture technology designed to trap the emissions from fossil fuel infrastructure before they are released into the atmosphere. Proponents believe that piping carbon dioxide into underground storage could provide a permanent climate solution for industries that are unable to replace fossil fuels with cleaner alternatives. Although there are instances where the technology has worked successfully, many high-cost projects have struggled to progress and there are many examples where carbon savings have proved to be far less than expected. Green groups fear the technology has been promoted by fossil fuel companies to prolong the use of fossil fuels. Packham said a failure to rein in the planned CCS spending “would be yet another strong signal that this government is putting big oil above people and the planet”. Aled Dilwyn Fisher, a senior researcher at Oil Change International, said: “It’s worrying that spending on climate is being cut in favour of defence, but cutting support for proven climate solutions while continuing to bankroll unreliable carbon capture projects would add insult to injury. “This budget should be an opportunity to put public money where it can make a real difference to the climate and help cut people’s energy bills, rather than continuing to gamble billions on the fossil fuel industry’s latest expansion plan.” Work on the UK’s first CCS projects has begun at the East Coast Cluster near Teesside and Humberside, in north-east England, and at the HyNet Cluster near Merseyside and north Wales, in north-west England. The second phase of the government’s CCS support plan includes £200m to support the Acorn project in Aberdeenshire, alongside £80m from the Scottish government. Rosie Hampton, a campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said over the summer that the government’s climate response was being built on “fantasy plans about turning the North Sea into Europe’s carbon dumping ground” while politicians should be focused on “climate solutions that will improve people’s lives, such as warm homes, better public transport and decent green jobs”. Martin McCluskey, the parliamentary undersecretary at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, told an industry event this month that the government remained committed to carbon capture but fiscal pressures may require decisions on the pace of the industry’s development. The Carbon Capture and Storage Association (CCSA) said the UK’s first projects had already awarded more than £4bn in supply-chain contracts, which could support about 350 UK companies and 5,500 construction jobs. “Pulling back now would undermine investor confidence, risk leaving infrastructure underused and deepen industrial decline,” said Mark Sommerfeld, the CCSA’s UK director. “This budget must honour existing commitments, turning today’s progress into lasting growth, energy security and reindustrialisation,” he said. The government has been contacted for comment.

headline: ‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts
trail_text: Boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £9,000 for sustainable alternatives, expected to be slashed in budget
body_text: When Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical about whether the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said. “I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.” But despite a surge in interest in cheap and sustainable ways to warm homes, the government is understood to be slashing the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as it looks for ways to cut spending in Wednesday’s budget. Businesses that install the renewable systems are fearing the worst. “It’s going to damage us as a company,” said Tuck, the operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford. About 75% of his customers pay for their pump using the government subsidies. “It’s the foundation of the business. If that’s to go, it’s extremely damaging. “Of course, we will do what it takes to keep everybody’s jobs going and the business afloat. But it’s a tough one – I don’t know how we will do that.” The boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) was introduced in 2022 to help people decarbonise their homes and businesses. It provides upfront grants worth up to £9,000 to help property owners replace fossil fuel and direct electric heating systems with low-carbon alternatives such as heat pumps and biomass boilers. Heat in buildings is responsible for approximately nearly a fifth of the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions, the latest government data shows. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has described the 2020s as a “critical decade for decarbonising heat”, but now appears to be putting the cost of decarbonising on to the consumer. The UK lags far behind other European countries with heat pump installation; Norway, the global leader, has 632 in every 1,000 households, while the UK has a paltry 19. Jim Lacey, who has been installing renewables with his business JLN Plumbing & Heating for 20 years, said: “No one’s going to save the planet if it really hits their pocket.” “We can go in [to homes] now and go: ‘It’s a few hundred pound more than having a normal boiler, but you save so much on your energy usage.’ That whole argument’s gone.” Adam Killa, the founder of Ask Renewables in Burscough, Lancashire, saw what happens when subsidies are removed after the 2022 closure of the Renewable Heat Incentive, a scheme that paid households for generating clean heat. “As soon as that stopped, we went from doing six, seven, eight [installs] a week down to zero. The customers say: ‘Well, I know they’re good, but 15 grand – I can buy a new boiler for three grand. What’s the point?’ While the government continues its drive to increase numbers of young people earning while learning, heat pump installers say cuts to the subsidy will put their apprentices – and the future of the industry – are at risk. “Unless we start bringing the young generation through, we’re going to have a huge lack of installers, repair engineers, and more importantly, heat pumps as well,” said Tuck. A nascent industry, installers fear manufacturers will go under too. According to the Heat Pump Association, about a third of heat pumps sold in the UK in 2024 were produced domestically. “This isn’t just down to us fitting the heat pumps, it’s the people delivering them, it’s the people manufacturing them, it’s all the associated trades that go with it that make the little bits, the little bobs, everything,” said Lacey. “There’s so many knock-on effects” James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the green thinktank Verdant, said removing money from green jobs and manufacturing would damage Andy Burnham’s mission to effectively reindustrialise Britain. “It’s at a point where his blank spot on climate is working hard against other things he wants to do,” he said. Lacey said that, while he had not thought the grant would last for ever, he had expected business and consumers to be weaned off gradually as the technology became more widespread and production costs fell. “But to suddenly axe some off the BUS grant or get rid of it completely is just catastrophic for all the work that we’ve put in so far,” he said. A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on budget speculation. “We remain committed to bringing down bills for families now, while investing in the clean, homegrown energy and warmer homes that will protect households from volatile fossil fuel prices for good.” • This article was amended on 28 October 2026. An earlier version said the UK had 3.5 heat pumps for every 1,000 households; this should have said 19 heat pumps. The figure of 3.5 refers to the number of heat pump sales for every 1,000 households in 2024.

headline: I struggled to come to terms with my mum’s death. Then I swam in the sea and suddenly felt connected to her
trail_text: My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away
body_text: It was early morning in late September, off the coast of Kaş in Turkey. Watching the slightly choppy sea from a boat, the last thing I felt like doing was embarking on another 5km (3-mile) swim. Mind fog had sapped my energy, and my mood was decidedly Eeyore-like. But as I pulled on my cap and flippers, adjusted my goggles and took the plunge, something shifted. Head in the water, the knotted feeling in my throat began to loosen. Breathing came properly. There was respite. My swimming is far from sophisticated – my strokes are messy and I am mostly kicking from the knees. Still, I manage to move forward, albeit slowly, hugging the coastline of Turkey’s Lycian Way, turning a corner and entering an area of calm. The water is blue-green. Fish glide purposefully beneath, and I’m uplifted when I see a turtle navigating around a rock on the seabed. I came to Turkey with SwimTrek, a Brighton-based company offering guided open-water swim tours. The plan is to complete 25km over five days. On the one hand, it is a holiday; but for me, the combination of swimming and the sea has become something more than that. It began in Croatia in June 2024, eight months after my mother died unexpectedly, when a friend persuaded me to sign up to swim 3km a day for a week. I had been feeling lost as I tried to come to terms with my mum not being here any more, and generally anxious, made worse by sleepless nights. Even on calm days, at times it felt difficult to breathe, the tightness in the throat unrelenting. The only thing that seemed to help was swimming, especially with the focus on the Croatia challenge. My preparation was mostly in the pool, pretty much all of it breaststroke. I had a rude awakening on the first day of the trip when I tried to swim either breast or backstroke – the latter steering me wildly off course. On day two I was kitted out with flippers and one of the SwimTrek guides taught me the basic front crawl technique. From that point, my confidence in the sea grew. The sensation of being immersed in the open water is difficult to describe, but it brings me instant relief. I feel weightless yet anchored by the buoyancy. The rhythmic movement while watching the sea life helps to clear my mind of clutter. This is a far cry from my early experience of swimming. Growing up in the south London town of Croydon, the closest I got to the water was a municipal pool. I was taken there by my mum. I would bob around in the freezing water of the children’s pool while she would swim laps in the adult one. Going swimming in those days – the 1980s – was synonymous with verrucas and posters featuring cartoon images warning against “bombing” and “heavy petting”. The latter made me and other children giggle although none of us really knew what it meant. The changing rooms were grim and you would travel home with wet hair, laden down by a damp towel and stink of chlorine for days. The highlight was a post-pool Curly Wurly from the snack machine. On a hot summer’s day, my mum would take us on the train to Brighton. I would go reluctantly, more enthused by amusement arcades than the sea. But I was lucky. There were glimmers of the sea winning me over. With an Italian father, every two years we would go on holiday to Italy, travelling by train from the UK to see relatives in Turin and then along the Mediterranean coast to see those in Sicily, where my dad was born. When we were at the beach, my mum would swim up and down, seemingly for hours. I would look out for her now and then from the shore. It is only now, since I have started swimming myself, that I wonder what those swims meant to her. My mum lived with depression and anxiety, and I believe the sea might have given her the same kind of respite it has given me. I don’t know because we never spoke about it. The only time we really talked about her swimming was when she called needing help to buy a cap, which had to be of a particular variety, or goggles, online. My mum, who was 73 when she died, did other things to keep active, too – going to the gym every morning, at least until Covid, and she loved playing tennis and walking. After years of talking about it, my parents moved to Bexhill-on-Sea in East Sussex a few years before she died. So now, whenever I return to the UK from Italy, Bexhill is where I go. I appreciate the UK coastline much more and find that walking by the sea when there, or even just listening to it for a few minutes, helps to centre me. Now and then, I brave a cold-water dip. But it is the swim tours that have become a powerful source of all-round wellbeing, helped also by a welcoming swimming community and new friendships made. A year after Croatia, I did a 4km-a-day trip in Greece, where I celebrated my 50th birthday. I managed to complete the Turkey one, too, feeling a huge sense of achievement and absolutely no shame about being the slowest in the group. I’m already planning next year’s swim. And even though I’m sad that I can’t tell my mum about it, the sea makes me feel connected to her.

headline: Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners
trail_text: Letter to PM argues series of wrong choices on North Sea oil, Heathrow, EVs and heat pumps will scupper net zero plans
body_text: Andy Burnham will “sleepwalk” into climate disaster if he fails to get a grip on a series of important policies whose combined impact could scupper plans to reach net zero, campaigners have said. Big decisions on North Sea drilling, the expansion of Heathrow airport, electric vehicles (EVs) and grants for heat pumps are awaiting decisions from ministers. But they should be considered in the context of their cumulative impacts rather than be taken separately by different government departments, according to Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth (FoE) in a letter to the prime minister. Taken together, the emissions resulting from approving drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, expanding Heathrow airport, watering down the UK’s EV targets and cutting heat pump grants would be 402m tonnes of CO2 over the next 25 years, the letter says. The emissions would be greater than those of 106 coal plants running for a year, more than enough to prevent the UK meeting its carbon budgets and net zero. Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace, said: “The Burnham government is facing a series of big decisions over the next few months that could define its legacy on climate. This administration seems to get the urgency of cutting the emissions causing deadly heatwaves and droughts, but there’s a real risk they could still sleepwalk into reversing the strong progress the UK has made so far.” Last week, the government gave the go-ahead to drill the Jackdaw gasfield, despite warnings that it would create only 27 new jobs, fail to cut the cost of living, and add little to UK tax revenues. Now, the North Sea fossil fuel industry is pressing for a green light to the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, which would produce higher emissions. Car manufacturers have lobbied hard for the government to water down its mandate to ensure all new car and van sales are electric by 2035, by allowing as many as half of sales to be petrol or diesel in 2030, which would mean falling far short of the current target of 80% electric by then. Given the long life of vehicles, this could produce future emissions equal to about 60% of the emissions from Rosebank, according to analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank. Airlines are also pressing for an expansion of Heathrow, which the chancellor, John Healey, strongly favours in the belief that it could increase economic growth. Campaigners challenge this analysis, arguing the UK is already embarking on airport expansion at Gatwick. In his budget on Wednesday, Healey is also likely to cut the boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants to households installing heat pumps in place of gas boilers, despite the savings on gas use that it represents and the slow speed of the transition to electric heating so far. Parr said: “Decisions about Rosebank, Heathrow expansion, electric vehicle targets or heat pump funding should not be rushed through or made in isolation – ministers need to be far-sighted and keep track of their cumulative impact on our climate. The carbon bill may take a while to turn up, but there’s hell to pay when it does.” If Burnham were to reject these high-carbon plans, the UK could build a cleaner, more equal and more prosperous society, added Imogen Dow, climate lead at FoE. Renewable energy could bring down bills, particularly amid soaring oil and gas prices, and the net zero economy has grown faster than the rest of the economy, according to the CBI. Dow said: “Delivering on our climate goals is not solely a win for the planet – it will also strengthen the economy, lower household bills, improve public health and protect the places we call home. “At a time when powerful vested interests are pushing the world towards climate catastrophe, it’s more important than ever that governments like the UK stand strong.” A government spokesperson said: “Reindustrialisation will never mean reneging on our climate obligations and net zero. Over the past two years, clean power has secured £110bn in announced investment and supported thousands of jobs through our record renewable energy auctions.”

headline: Country diary: Our tiny island is awash with waxcaps
trail_text: Calf of Man, Isle of Man: Such is the wealth of Manx fungi, a map is being built to plot it all. We took a special trip as part of that project
body_text: The bird observatory on the Calf of Man was sulking under a low cloud base as we stepped ashore at South Harbour. The dank mist was perfect for our surprise visit to the island, as it was not for the birds we had come across, but fungi – in particular, waxcaps. My wife, Liz, and I had taken the chance to accompany Nev Kilkenny, a visiting mycologist, who would help identify and study some autumn mushrooms and toadstools – and contribute to a map that is being assembled of Manx fungi. Autumn gales make visits to the Calf (off the south-west corner of the Isle of Man) difficult to plan, but Nev’s visit coincided with a calm spell, and so an impromptu expedition was arranged. A whole kingdom of life was literally at our feet. We weaved back and forth across the fields muttering words like parrot, spangle, golden, garlic and goblet, all wonderful names of waxcaps previously found on the island. The fields were tightly cropped by sheep and rabbits, the soil bare in places – ideal conditions for unusual species. Indeed, it was at a burrow entrance that we found a date waxcap, one of Britain’s rarest fungi. The waxcaps kept coming: we found butterscotch, snowy and glutinous varieties, and over our two-day survey we identified 18 – doubling the Calf’s known waxcap species. The study of Manx fungi has had a resurgence recently. The island has four sites that qualify for the top European status (compared with just one in the whole of the Netherlands), and many areas are expected to become sites of special scientific interest for their fungi alone. Doing their bit, the Isle of Man Fungus Group, under the tutorship of Nev and Liz, has identified more than 400 species including blushing waxcap and mealy waxcap, both on the global red list for species at risk of extinction. All of which makes the map of Manx fungi – to be used at government level for conservation purposes – all the more important. Every fungal foray is a vital piece of the jigsaw. With our Calf visit done, we look forward to our next one, at the Creggans, a nature reserve set up to protect fungi. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Super-rich get ‘double dividend’ from causes and costs of climate crisis, report finds
trail_text: Oxfam says investing by rich in disaster recovery widens inequality and gives incentive to delay climate action
body_text: The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic consequences, according to a study by Oxfam. The global equality organisation has found that the richest 0.1% of the world’s population are heavily invested in disaster preparedness, recovery and reconstruction – a market that is projected to grow from $70bn to $92bn a year by 2029. This gives the planet’s wealthiest and most powerful people a “double dividend” from the climate crisis and, more alarmingly, an incentive to delay or disrupt action to solve the problem, the NGO says. It also worsens global inequality as those least responsible for global heating end up having to pay those most responsible in terms of higher food prices, repairing homes damaged by extreme weather or relocating to other areas. Jean McLean, Oxfam’s chief influencing officer, accused billionaires of turning chaos into profit. “The super-rich benefit at both ends of the crisis: first, through continued investment in polluting industries, and second, through investment in the booming ‘adaptation economy’ – recovery and rebuilding services are sold back to a warming world,” she said. “The populations who contributed least to the climate crisis are absorbing its worst consequences, while those who caused it are best equipped to protect themselves.” The richest 0.1% on the planet, a group of 8 million people, are responsible for more carbon emissions than the poorest 3.5 billion combined, the report says. As a result, this group have reportedly contributed by 125 times more than the average person to extreme heat events. This is partly due to lifestyles. The world’s private jets, for example, release more CO2 in two seconds than most of the world’s people emit in an entire year. But the biggest impact of this group comes from their investments. Oxfam’s new destroy and rebuild index identifies 217 corporations that either fuel climate breakdown or do business in adapting to it through provision of cooling devices, flood barriers, firefighting equipment, transportation, food, insurance and loans. Last year, these companies made an average of US$1.8bn and paid out $1bn in dividends to shareholders. Six major asset managing firms, which advise wealthy investors, are on this list in their own right and are heavily invested in other members. Two of the biggest, BlackRock and Vanguard, have shares in 92% of the companies in the index, worth a total of more than $1tn, Oxfam says. Similarly, it notes that crises – caused by extreme weather or war – have tended to boost the profits of major food trading companies that are dominated by billionaires, whose wealth has increased by $120bn since 2020. When drought, floods or storms hit crops, any subsequent increase in food prices tends to disproportionately benefit big corporations and their investors at the cost of small producers and regular consumers, Oxfam says. The group cites the case of a 231% surge in cocoa prices after extreme weather in west Africa in 2024, when it says local farmers saw none of the gains. Such inequality has consequences. The annual emissions for the richest 1% will cause 1.9m excess deaths due to heat, Oxfam says, based on estimated impacts on human health, agricultural productivity and sea level rise. More than three-quarters of those deaths will occur in low- and middle-income countries, which are far less responsible for the crisis because they produce only 8% of emissions. Wealthy nations and wealthy individuals are somewhat insulated – at least for now – from the climate crisis because they are more likely to be able to afford higher food prices, robust houses, emergency evacuation, private healthcare and personal security. This makes them less likely to use their considerable lobbying power to support climate action, and may even encourage them to slow or block emissions cuts that could affect their personal wealth, Oxfam says. Instead, some use disasters to push privatisation agendas or encourage poor nations to take out loans. Alex Maitland, one of the lead authors, said the very richest people were not just passive beneficiaries of the climate crisis. “This is deliberate,” he said. “When you take into account their political influence, this is pretty damning evidence that they’re able to orchestrate that is happening.” Oxfam is demanding higher taxes on the rich, private jets, oil and gas companies and polluting companies. The group calls on the UK government to improve international climate financing commitments based on grants rather than loans, and to end profiteering from climate disasters. Nafkote Dabi, the climate change policy lead at Oxfam International, said: “What’s complex about talking about climate change is everyone likes to think it’s a shared problem, but it’s not. Addressing the climate crisis is really easy. Control the richest, curb their power, curb their emissions, and also tax their wealth.”

headline: UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’
trail_text: V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand
body_text: Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers. Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand. If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand. The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteries can do the same job. Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need to pay renewable generators to switch off. However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years. Carmakers could earn a “credit” for selling cars installed with V2G technology, also known as bidirectional charging, according to plans detailed in a government consultation that closed on Friday. That credit would allow the carmakers to sell another petrol car without facing the risk of fines if they miss the ZEV targets. The government is preparing to cut electric vehicle sales targets under the ZEV mandate. Environmental groups are braced for changes that could mean an additional 147m tonnes of carbon emitted into the atmosphere by 2050. Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, a thinktank tracking the transition to electric cars, said: “Vehicle to grid is exciting technology that could help balance the grid and cut bills, but carmakers should only be rewarded if it’s actually used, not just for fitting it. “Under these proposals, one or even two extra credits worth around £4,000 each would hand manufacturers thousands per car for kit that costs a few hundred pounds, even though few drivers own the expensive charger needed to use it. Ministers should make sure the people who benefit from V2G are drivers and billpayers, not carmakers’ shareholders.” Some people already sell their electricity back to the grid through companies such as Octopus Energy in the UK, Renault in France, and BMW in Germany. Octopus Energy has claimed that drivers could save £620 a year with the service. Vicky Edmonds, the chief executive of the Electric Vehicle Association England, which represents drivers, said: “We have millions of EV drivers in the UK, but only a fraction are using vehicle to grid or storage technologies.
