These technologies have enormous potential but consumers are still getting to grips with more immediate questions around the cost of their car, the cost of charging, and whether an EV meets their day to day needs. “It is far too early to be giving manufacturers a credit that effectively allows them to sell fewer EVs, for a technology that has not even been tried and tested, at scale, by drivers in the real world.” Once the technology takes off, electricity supplied by V2G cars could add up to the equivalent of a power station by 2030, able to provide 1.2 gigawatts of power on demand, according to the National Energy System Operator, which balances Great Britain’s grid. That could grow to as much as 41 GW by 2050, Neso forecasts, enough to meet more than a quarter of peak energy demand.

headline: Typhoon Champi declared strongest storm of year so far
trail_text: One dead and 527 injured as winds of up to 185mph hit Taiwan and southern Japan, while Greece issues flood alerts
byline: Megan Davies and James Parrish for MetDesk
body_text: Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan. So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday. For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas. The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible. A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Cyclone Arnab is expected to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast by Wednesday. The India meteorological department has alerts in place for extreme heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong surface winds across the eastern side of the country. Models are forecasting gusts of up to 85mph, and six-hourly rainfall totals of up to 100mm, as the storm makes landfall, currently expected on Wednesday. From then, the system is set to drift to the north before gradually dying out over north-east India at the end of the week.

headline: Country diary: Jackdaws carve up the sky as dusk descends on the moors
trail_text: Eldwick Crag, West Yorkshire: In the low light and the high wind, these corvids are preparing to roost for the night. And they seem to be enjoying themselves
body_text: Jackdaws like blustery weather the same way dolphins love choppy seas. There are faster flyers and more graceful flyers, but I can’t think of a bird that just enjoys flying as much as a jackdaw does. They bob and bank and yaw and wheel. And right now it’s roosting time in the copse above the quarry. A jackdaw roost – or rather the prelude to the roost, the bedtime gathering, the swirl of small, clacking crows above and about the trees, like particles about to be drawn into a plughole – isn’t a murmuration. It’s neither as spectacular nor as enigmatic as the twilight displays of starlings; it’s a flock, plain and simple (plain as the jackdaw’s call of its own name, “jack”). But like everything jackdaws do, it’s full of bustling, garrulous life. Behind the jackdaws, the evening sky is a deep, soft pink. We’ve left behind the belted galloway cows and calves browsing watchfully on the upward meadow slopes, and now, as we pick our way north, we throw tall shadows sidelong across the bracken. Ahead of us, on the moor, the faded heather is copper-coloured in the late sun. Linnets come zipping overhead, high on the wind. A red grouse does its noisy gottle-of-geer act (we’re on the south brink of a sprawling grouse estate here). My son picks out three small honey waxcap toadstools in the grass, like nuggets of unpolished gold – no, we can’t eat them (“reputed to be edible but of poor quality”, I read later). And then, further along, I have to steer him and his sister a little way wide of the path, as the long body of a dead hare is stretched out on the peat, partly plucked, the eye sockets empty. Jackdaws and their crow kin aren’t always playful. On the way home, with the day almost all gone, a white ghost of the dusk, a barn owl, comes shearing through the twilight ahead of us, following a purposeful line of pursuit into the undergrowth on the flank of the hill. A different kind of bird flight: all business. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Cabinet split emerges over controversial Rosebank oilfield decision
trail_text: Chancellor is in favour of North Sea project, but energy secretary has said she is leaning towards rejecting it
body_text: A cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, with the chancellor, John Healey, in favour of the controversial North Sea project. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is ultimately in charge of the decision, and the Guardian reported last week that she was leaning towards rejecting it after granting permission for the smaller Jackdaw gasfield. It is understood, however, that Healey backs approving the licence, which is on hold over concerns about the project’s environmental impact. The chancellor hinted at his support last week when he told ITV he expected oil and gas revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, suggesting he was anticipating income from Rosebank. The prime minister would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision. No 10 declined to comment on Sunday after the Mail on Sunday reported that Andy Burnham and Healey had agreed to try to push the project through, saying it was a matter for the energy secretary. Fahnbulleh is responsible, but the views of Burnham and Healey will hold weight in the choice over whether or not to go ahead. She told the Guardian the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it. “One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.” If the Rosebank field is rejected, it would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. A final decision is expected before the end of the year. Labour MPs said on Wednesday that there would be a big pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessary part of the transition to net zero. MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent. Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet made her decision. Rosebank would produce emissions about seven times greater than Jackdaw, and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe it would do less for UK energy security, given that most of the oil would be exported. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We do not comment on speculation. The North Sea remains a vital national asset, and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come – alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis. “Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process.” Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through an energy wealth fund. She said last week that the fund would be given £2bn in the budget. “When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes. She could not, however, say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the fund, or how much that may generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

headline: Neville Fay obituary
trail_text: Other lives: Founder of Tree Aid and champion of ancient trees and healthy soils
body_text: My friend Neville Fay, who has died aged 78, set up the reforestation charity Tree Aid in 1987 and then went on to reshape understanding of ancient trees and the soil. During the Dutch elm disease epidemic in the 1970s, Neville bought an old Transit van and chainsaw, felled dead trees and sold firewood door to door. This eventually evolved into Treework Services, expanding into milling timber, tree surgery, landscaping, hardwood flooring and kitchen manufacturing; by 1982 it had become a co-operative of more than 30 people. The images of famine in Ethiopia that prompted Live Aid in 1985 proved a turning point. Believing emergency food aid could never be a credible long-term response, Neville gathered friends at his local pub in the Somerset village of Chew Stoke, founded the charity Tree Aid in 1986 and started fundraising. Rather than using money raised to develop new projects in Africa, funds were directed to existing community-led initiatives in the semi-arid Sahel region, south of the Sahara, helping to accelerate ecosystem restoration. With the charity successfully running, in 1992 Neville stepped away from the organisation, with Tree Aid continuing to thrive. To date it has planted almost 50m trees across Africa. Neville was born in Durban, South Africa, to Jewish parents – Dolly (nee Goodman), a school teacher, and Raymond Fay, a dentist – whose own parents had fled persecution in eastern Europe. Opposed to apartheid, in 1956 they left South Africa for Liverpool. Neville attended Merchant Taylors’ school in Crosby and the Jewish youth club at Harold House, where he discovered the communal ethos that would anchor his politics. Dropping out of Aberdeen University to form a local tenants’ union and summer camp for disadvantaged children, he later finished his sociology degree having embraced communal living. In 1975, Neville and his wife, Kate – whom he had met at Aberdeen and married in 1970 – moved to Bristol with their two children and ran a halfway house for ex-offenders. The following year, with a group of friends, they squatted in an abandoned rectory in Chew Stoke, forming the Lodge Co-operative Housing Association in the building, which has continued to provide affordable homes for many families, and disabled and elderly people. The couple went on to have two more children once settled at the rectory, and Neville remained living there with Kate until the end of his life. Treework Services had, meanwhile, evolved into an arboricultural consultancy, Treework Environmental Practice, run by Neville’s elder son, Luke, with his daughter Rachael also at the company. Studying ancient woodlands in the UK and Europe, Neville published widely, developed the Veteran Tree Survey for English Nature and co-authored Veteran Trees: A Guide to Risk and Responsibility (2000), Tree Surveys: A Guide to Good Practice (2005) and Trees - A Lifespan Approach (2016). He was pivotal to the Ancient Tree Forum and the establishment and achievements of the National Tree Safety Group, and his “innovations in arboriculture” seminars popularised the principles of conservation arboriculture. In 2009 he received the Arboricultural Association’s award for services to arboriculture. With his daughter Ellen he founded the Sustainable Soils Alliance in 2017. A fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, the Linnean Society and the Royal Society of Arts, Neville also cared devotedly for Kate through many years of illness and never formally retired. He is survived by Kate, their children, Luke, Ellen, Gabriel and Rachael, and six grandchildren.

headline: Koalas are cute, furry, iconic – and dying of chlamydia. But how well does the approved vaccine work?
trail_text: Queensland researchers say a published study contains ‘silly mistake’ that over-inflates vaccine’s efficacy but the regulator is standing by decision to approve it
body_text: At wildlife hospitals across eastern Australia, many koalas brought in have distinctive brown patches on their bottoms – a sign of urinary incontinence and a painful inflamed bladder. Others have red, weeping eyes, pointing to a bacterial disease that can cause blindness in the endangered marsupials. Chlamydia infection, also known as chlamydiosis, is the most significant disease affecting the animals. The culprit is most commonly the bacterium Chlamydia pecorum, which is spread via mating or close contact. “Relatively inevitably, infected females will become infertile, and quite rapidly,” says Mark Krockenberger, a professor of veterinary pathology at the University of Sydney. Dr Freya Russell, a postdoctoral research fellow at the Queensland University of Technology (QUT), add: “In the animals that are heavily diseased with chlamydia, they can also be quite emaciated too … more boney rather than the robust kind of koala we’re used to seeing.” Infection rates vary geographically but in some koala populations the prevalence of chlamydia is as high as two in three. Populations in northern regions tend to be worse affected than those in the southern states. Researchers have struggled for years to devise a solution to bring koala chlamydia rates down. Two separate chlamydia vaccines have been in development in Queensland for more than a decade. One was approved by the veterinary medicines regulator last year but questions have been raised about its efficacy. What will it take to save the iconic animal from one of its key existential threats? The problem with antibiotics Since 2022, koalas in Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory have been listed as endangered by the Australian government. Chlamydia is only one of a handful of threats facing the emblematic species, along with land clearing, habitat fragmentation, vehicle strikes and other disease such as koala retrovirus, which causes an Aids-like illness. In humans, chlamydia infections – caused by Chlamydia trachomatis – are easily treatable, usually requiring a single dose of antibiotics. In koalas, antibiotic treatment is less straightforward – and often less successful. “We can kill the chlamydia … but the problem is that in the process, you can easily kill the koala as well,” Krockenberger says. The animals are highly dependent on gut microbes to digest toxic eucalypt leaves. Antibiotics – which kill bacteria – result in a “shift in the abundance of good microbes that help the koalas digest eucalypt”, says Dr Lyndal Hulse, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Queensland. “When you get that shift in those microbes … that’s when the koalas get into trouble – they have weight loss, they have diarrhoea, and the worst-case scenario is that they go on to dysbiosis [a microbial imbalance] which can prove to be sometimes fatal.” On top of that, some chlamydia strains have developed antibiotic resistance. “There are very few effective vaccines against chlamydia,” Krockenberger says. None exists to treat the infection in humans. “There’s one in sheep that has variable efficacy, and that’s about it.” Russell is part of a team at QUT developing a two-dose vaccine that contains proteins found on the outer membrane of chlamydia bacteria. In trials, they have vaccinated more than 500 koalas in the Currumbin region of the Gold Coast, with promising results, such as a reduction in chlamydia-related admissions to the local wildlife hospital. But the researchers have not yet conducted placebo-controlled studies, which are the gold standard for determining how effectively a new vaccine or drug works. “When we first started doing trials … the population was rapidly declining,” Russell says. “Our team decided it wasn’t really ethical to be doing placebo controls in this heavily diseased population” – as it amounted to withholding treatment they believed to be effective from sick animals. Given the difficulties of catching wild koalas to deliver a booster shot 30 days after an initial jab, the researchers have developed an implant that they insert at the time of first vaccination, which degrades over a few weeks to deliver the second dose. “It’s completely biodegradable and non-toxic,” Russell says. “We’ve found in a captive study at Currumbin that it had the same efficacy when compared to the two-shot vaccine in stimulating antibody responses.” The delayed-release implant vaccine is now being trialled in wild koalas, and has not yet been approved by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA). ‘Silly’ data error A second protein-based vaccine, available as a single-dose, has been developed by University of the Sunshine Coast (UniSC) researchers and was approved by the APVMA in September 2025. Prof Keith Chappell, a molecular virologist at the University of Queensland, a third Queensland institution, has since questioned the efficacy of the vaccine. Last month he took issue with a 2024 paper the researchers published in npj Vaccines, which had found that the vaccine significantly lowered disease incidence and resulted in a 64% reduction in chlamydia deaths over a 10-year period. In a pre-print – which is yet to be peer-reviewed – Chappell and colleague Dr Michaela Blyton said they had identified an error in data analysis “which resulted in survival from birth to time of vaccination incorrectly being attributed to vaccination”. After correcting for the error, they wrote, “there was no significant difference in the survival or disease rate between vaccinated and unvaccinated koalas”. They argued that the vaccine’s use by veterinarians “should not be recommended”, advocating for “the continued development and testing of an improved vaccine formulation”. Speaking with the Guardian, Chappell described the data error as a “silly mistake”. Commenting on the approval of the vaccine by the APVMA, Chappell said: “The regulatory system has failed … There should be an independent review of science to make sure that it’s done according to best practice.” “I’ve had … setbacks as well,” says Chappell, who was a co-developer of the molecular clamp Covid vaccine, which stalled when trials returned false positive HIV results. “It made me realise the importance of high quality, transparent research.” In a statement, an APVMA spokesperson said it “does not accept that issuing the permit represents a regulatory failure”. “The permitted claim – that the vaccine ‘may aid in the reduction of clinical signs of the disease’ – is qualified and limited and does not mean the vaccination prevents chlamydial disease or mortality in koalas,” it said. “Any concerns must be assessed against the permitted claim and the complete body of relevant evidence, not solely against interpretations of a single publication. The APVMA will assess credible new scientific information relevant to the permit and determine whether regulatory action is warranted.” In a statement, a UniSC spokesperson said: “We welcome scientific scrutiny of our work, and disagreement between researchers is not unusual in any active area of science. “What is being debated here is one aspect of a much larger research program. It does not invalidate more than a decade of peer-reviewed science or the substantial evidence supporting the continued development of a vaccine to help protect koalas from one of their most significant disease threats.” The UniSC vaccine was also studied last year in a randomised controlled trial. That study, which involved Sydney researchers, followed for 12 months three populations of wild koalas in NSW, which were either vaccinated or given a placebo treatment. The inclusion of a control group was so researchers could be “100% sure that whatever you’re looking at is not just by chance”, says Dr Valentina Mella, a senior lecturer in animal behaviour and conservation at the University of Sydney, and a collaborator on the project. The study found that vaccination did stimulate an immune response in the koalas, but “did not translate to any effect on chlamydiosis”. “The immune system was doing something, but that response was actually not enough to do anything useful to stop the disease,” Mella says. It was a disappointing result: “We wanted a very strong effect of the vaccine and we didn’t get it.” The study concluded it was “possible that vaccination has a more modest effect and could benefit koala populations with a lower disease prevalence or be useful in conjunction with additional management strategies”. Prof Peter Timms, a microbiologist at UniSC who has led the vaccine’s development, says: “We’ve published 29 papers in the whole vaccine story and they’ve all been reviewed scientifically by experts. We publish everything with the attitude that we’re there to share it, and do it openly and transparently.” “We’re very confident that what we’ve got is a strong health benefit, but it can keep being improved,” he adds. “It’s a journey, right? There’ll be ups and downs.”

headline: Policy U-turn could stall Britain’s take-up of electric vehicles
trail_text: The 2030 target for 80% of new cars to have zero emissions could be cut to as low as half
body_text: Electric cars make people happy. More than nine in 10 EV drivers – 94% in a recent poll – are saving money, and a similar number would stick with electric for their next purchase, and recommend them to family and friends. Sales are soaring: more than half of the new cars sold in the UK last month were electric, if hybrids are taken into account, and about 28% of new car sales overall were electric only. This is hardly surprising, given that soaring petrol and diesel costs have pushed up the price of a full tank to about £120. EV drivers are paying about 2.4p a mile. Why then is the government considering a major U-turn on electric vehicle policy that, if followed through, could stall the take-up of EVs, help to close off a route to lower living costs, and dent the UK’s ability to meet its carbon targets? Andy Burnham, the prime minister, wrote in the Guardian this week that he would push ahead with the target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Despite the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield this week, sources in government also hinted to the Guardian that another large project, the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, was less likely to be greenlighted. However, analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank, seen by the Guardian, shows that the looming decision on the future of electric vehicles could also have a major impact on net zero and carbon budgets, though it has received far less attention. Under the zero emissions vehicle mandate, all new cars and vans sold from 2035 must be fully electric, with interim targets for 80% of new cars and 70% of new vans to be ZEVs by 2030. The end goal of 2035 is likely to remain, but under a consultation that ended on Friday, the 2030 targets could be weakened to 70% or even as low as 50% of new cars. Taken with previous watering down of the policy to allow more sales of hybrid cars – which use both electric and combustion engines – that change would lead to emissions greater than burning all the gas in the Jackdaw field, according to the ECIU. If the mandate were cut more drastically to require only 50% of sales to be EVs by 2030, this could mean an additional 147 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, which would equate to about 58% of the likely emissions from burning the oil produced by the Rosebank field. Jess Ralston, an analyst at the ECIU, said weakening the target would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China as increasing numbers of people opt for EVs. It would also not benefit the public because EVs can be £1,750 a year cheaper to run, and potentially more with oil prices rising. “With climate concern high among the public after extreme heat and persisting drought, and public support for net zero up above two-thirds, a decision to U-turn could look very odd,” Ralston said. “Ministers have talked about getting families off the fossil fuel rollercoaster – this would be the opposite, locking in higher driving costs, more air pollution and higher carbon emissions.” Burnham faces a further complication: in 2024, the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, and now wants to limit public subsidies to vehicles made in Europe, under pressure from European carmakers. If Burnham wants closer integration with the EU, and more favourable trade terms, he may be forced to slap matching tariffs on Chinese imports to the UK. This would raise the cost of EVs in the UK and cut off one route to lower living costs. If fully implemented as originally planned, the ZEV mandate could be the largest single carbon-saving measure the government has yet proposed, according to previous research. But after intensive lobbying from carmakers for a weakening, Labour MPs are deeply divided. Car manufacturers in the UK have been slow to retool their plants to EVs, and some have pursued hybrid vehicles instead. Many analysts consider hybrids, which combine a polluting petrol engine and a smaller battery, a technological dead end. By contrast, China has rapidly ramped up its EV manufacturing, and now dominates the global market, producing about three-quarters of all EVs. Sales of EVs have soared, now making up about a quarter of all new car sales around the world. Some Labour MPs in constituencies with car plants side with the manufacturers, while others argue that with petrol prices soaring and unlikely to abate, EVs are a way to lower the cost of living and get Britain off the fossil fuel hook. Chris Hinchliff, Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, told the Guardian: “Weakening the EV target would be another nail in the coffin of a livable future.” Barry Gardiner, Labour MP for Brent West and former environment minister, said a U-turn would hurt forward-looking companies and favour laggards. “Watering down the mandate means that good companies, who moved straight away to comply, feel they have been unfairly burdened with additional costs while their lazy competitors have sneaked an advantage,” he said. “Government flip-flops are a huge problem for business. State the regulation clearly and then stick to it. Business will then adapt and do what it does best because it knows it has a level playing field.” A government spokesperson said: “We are reviewing the ZEV mandate to ensure it continues to support British industry and investment, and no decisions have been taken. Crucially, the end goal has not changed – we will phase out all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and be fully zero emission by 2035, and remain committed to our legally binding net zero targets.” Consumer research shows the 2 million people currently driving EVs in the UK tend to like them: polling by the Electric Vehicle Association found 94% of EV drivers reported they were saving money compared with petrol or diesel cars. A similar number would stay electric for their next car, and recommend an EV to friends or family.

headline: The Australian reports ‘widespread errors’ in BoM temperature data. Where is the evidence for those big claims?
trail_text: An ‘audit’ of the Bureau of Meteorology main dataset for measuring climate change claims it contains ‘widespread errors’. It doesn’t stack up
body_text: Australia’s climate has warmed by more than 1.5C since 1910, according to the Bureau of Meteorology’s main long-term temperature data. If you were so motivated, you might think if you could discredit this data, then you would undermine the whole climate change story and even – perhaps – the rationale for cutting Australia’s greenhouse gas emissions. Over the past week, The Australian newspaper has launched a major reporting campaign based on a “forensic audit” that attempts to discredit the data, claiming it has found “widespread errors” that raise “questions about the integrity of records used for climate analysis”. These are big claims indeed, that would require remarkable evidence. Former prime minister and climate science denier Tony Abbott called for an independent review, while News24 (formerly Sky News Australia) and 2GB also promoted the story, which sent climate science denial blogs into a flutter. On Thursday night, the bureau released a statement saying the claims were based on “several misunderstandings” and accusations of human intervention in the data were “false and unsubstantiated.” The bureau’s temperature records have been a constant target for climate science sceptics for more than 15 years. So what is going on? First, a primer. When it comes to temperature records, the bureau makes the raw temperature data from its weather stations available to the public. But the bureau’s main temperature dataset for measuring climate change – known as ACORN-SAT (Australian Climate Observations Reference Network – Surface Air Temperature) takes observations from 112 weather stations and performs a quality control process to remove the effects of local changes (like a station moving) that could artificially alter the readings. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter There are of course multiple other datasets that show Australia’s climate, just like the rest of the planet, has warmed and how this heating presents a troubling laundry list of risks that leave almost no aspect of life in the country untouched. The Australian’s reporting – that includes at least eight pieces of coverage from stories, follow-ups and cartoons to editorials – centres on an “audit” of the raw data, which it said was carried out by a retired scientist and a former computer engineer. There are too many claims to list here, but they range from accusations that sequences were detected showing “obvious patterns of human intervention” to missing or duplicated data. How was this audit done? The audit report does not outline its methodology, saying only it had used statistical software and computer coding. This lack of a methodology might cause some to pause, but not The Australian. The most striking example from the report, wrote The Australian’s environment editor, Graham Lloyd, came from the minimum temperature readings for August 1907 for Sydney’s Observatory Hill that were found to have been duplicated in the record for August 1867. This deserves an explanation from the bureau. But it is also true that data before 1910 is not used in ACORN-SAT and so, in the context of what the bureau’s data says about Australia’s changing climate, it is irrelevant. A bureau spokesperson said it had examined the claims made in the report and less than 200 observations from the 7m in ACORN-SAT data had been affected by duplication. The spokesperson said 10 months of observations had shown duplicate data for minimum temperatures at Observatory Hill, but only three of those months were after 1910. A fourth month of duplicate temperatures had been identified at Charleville in Queensland. They are all from handwritten records of pre-1946 data that have been manually digitised. The “resultant impact on Australia’s long-term temperature record is so small as to be statistically irrelevant,” the bureau said. No further duplicate months had been found in the entire network of weather station readings. But how could these duplications have happened? A spokesperson said a “working hypothesis” was that the errors likely occurred in the 1950s or 1960s. “This is when the original handwritten records (field books) were transferred to a punch card system,” they said. “It is plausible that the manual handling introduced the duplication. Discussions with former bureau employees indicate the digitisation in question occurred prior to the 1980s.” Data failure? What about the claimed “patterns of human intervention” in temperature data? Another claim of the audit was that a run of 17 consecutive days of 31C maximum temperatures at Palmerville on Queensland’s Cape York in 2004 was evidence of “data failure”. “The probability of this occurring naturally is effectively zero”, the audit report claimed, and “less likely than winning the lottery every week for a year.” The bureau rejected this and said the audit had appeared not to have taken into account how some historical raw observations were recorded to the nearest degree, as was the case with the Palmerville site at the time. “In combination with lower temperature variability in the tropics, this makes repeated patterns in the raw data more likely.” ‘Secret climate business’ In one follow-up piece, David Evans, a climate sceptic, made the odd declaration that “secret climate business” at the bureau had to end and repeated it in an editorial he wrote for the newspaper. I say odd, because the so-called audit could not have been done had all the data not already been made public. The ACORN-SAT has already been the subject of two independent reviews and the methods it uses have been published in peer reviewed journals. The recent audit report had two authors. Lloyd described one, Tom Berger, as an investigator and “former computer engineer and specialist in data-based deception analysis”. According to Berger’s own website, he has also been a corporate entertainer for more than 30 years and had “mesmerized corporate audiences worldwide” blending “mind-bending entertainment with neuroscience-backed insights – revealing thoughts, predicting actions, and cracking the code of persuasion”. A second author, Geoff Sherrington, was described only as a “retired scientist”. Sherrington described himself as a retired geochemist at a mining company when he signed a declaration in 2022 rejecting the role CO2 plays in the climate. ‘Red meat to its audience’ Lloyd wrote that the audit report had been sent to the bureau “on behalf of Mr Berger” by the independent Tasmanian MP Andrew Wilkie, who received a letter back from the bureau explaining its investigations, and saying accusations of fraudulent or deliberate data manipulation had “no basis in fact”. Wilkie told Temperature Check he wasn’t asked by The Australian to comment and “felt uncomfortable” the article might have been interpreted as him having doubts about the bureau’s integrity or its climate data. “I found The Australian’s coverage of the matter to be quite feverish, and red meat to its audience, which flooded one article with about 1,000 comments,” he said. He had “no reason to reconsider my trust in the bureau,” he said. Attacks on the bureau’s temperature records have been orchestrated by climate science deniers for more than 15 years. Previous episodes have been described by scientists as “harassment”. One former bureau boss described the source of previous attacks as a “fever swamp” of climate science denial that had wasted scientists’ time. On each occasion, The Australian newspaper, rather than the scientific literature, was the journal of choice for sceptics to make claims of a conspiracy within the bureau. In the meantime, the climate isn’t paying attention. Guardian Australia approached The Australian for comment. Graham Readfearn is Guardian Australia’s environment and climate correspondent

headline: ‘False autumn’: stressed trees drop leaves early after scorching English summer
trail_text: Season will be less vibrant with trees such as birches, which usually offer a striking burst of yellow leaves, already bare
body_text: Among a canvas of copper, red and purple autumn leaves on display at Wisley garden in Surrey, south-east England, one tree stands conspicuously naked. “The birch has lost all its leaves,” says Guy Barter, the chief horticulturist at the Royal Horticultural Society. “That’s the effect of drought, so it’ll have no autumn colour this year.” Where a burst of sunny yellow foliage would normally brighten the display, the birch can offer only its ivory-white bark. After the hottest summer on record, the tree has dropped its canopy early, stressed from months of high temperatures and choosing to not lose any more water through its leaves. This is also known as a “false autumn”, where the stress of extreme summer conditions prompts trees and plants to behave as if the season has changed. The birch illustrates how extreme weather driven by the climate crisis is reshaping the flow of the UK’s seasons. Thousands of plant varieties at Wisley are still displaying vibrant hues, but the drought-sensitive, yellow-leafed trees such as birches, beeches and sycamores had shed their foliage by mid-October. Normally, autumn’s effect on trees is triggered by shortening daylight, dropping night-time temperatures and adequate ground moisture brought on by rain. But severe summer heat and drought has disrupted this usual cycle by forcing stressed trees into early defoliation and premature colouring, resulting in a display that kicked in earlier than expected. The majority of England and Wales remains in drought, and six areas of England were declared in severe drought this month with river and reservoir levels running low. Unlike deep-rooted species such as oaks, trees with shallow root systems are unable to tap into deeper groundwater, making them vulnerable to leaf drop when surface soil dries out during a drought. “Birch, beech and sycamore have been among the trees worst affected,” says Barter. “It’s at least as colourful as it is most years, but some of the trees are not giving their best, so it’s not the perfect autumn colour.” The RHS expects an earlier autumn colour peak in drought-hit areas, with intense but potentially fleeting displays. Reds, ambers and purples could stand out as some trees normally prized for yellow foliage lose their leaves. Tim Upson, the director of gardens and horticulture at the RHS, says the colour peak historically comes toward the end of October, but this year’s drought has brought some trees into colour earlier. “Quite often now it’s going into November when you get that crescendo,” he says. “So for me, this is quite unusual.” As Storm Austen blows in, the Met Office has warned of strong winds that could damage buildings and bring down trees. Experts warned in September that high winds brought by El Niño could decimate already drought-weakened trees. Although shallow-rooted and yellow-leaved trees are struggling, other species remain vibrant, including the biggest liquidambar tree in the UK with its flutter of pink, red and purple leaves. Barter says gardeners here are likely to plant fewer birches and more “trees of the future” such as liquidambar going forward. “There are different scenarios under climate change,” he says. “The generally accepted one is that we’ll have milder, wetter winters, but we’ll still have the occasional really cold one. So it’s no good planting tender trees, because when we have a really cold winter, they’ll succumb. “We’re looking for trees that are completely hardy in cold winters and have also got deep, wide-ranging roots that can tolerate hot, dry summers.” He lists Lebanon cedars and swamp cypresses as trees that Wisley will plant more of to adapt to changing conditions. Upson says adaptation is nothing new at Wisley; it was happening when he started working in horticulture 40 years ago. “There are some wonderful Californian oaks and Mediterranean oaks which we planted as an experiment 30 years ago, and they’re thriving now.” Familiar species will still have a place as temperatures change, he says, but beech and birch could become less spotted, surviving better in sheltered or damper locations. “I think what will happen is that we won’t necessarily lose plants, but they will either become shorter-lived or they won’t grow in the most exposed and stressful situations,” he says. “It’s going to be very much a changing landscape.”

headline: ‘You need persistence’: the Norfolk couple who took on environmental regulators three times – and won
trail_text: Tim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk Broads
body_text: Polluters and regulators who fail to stop pollution must quake in their boots when they receive a letter from the lawyers for Tim and Geli Harris. The couple, who farm 460 acres in the Norfolk Broads, have now scored a hat-trick of landmark legal victories to save an internationally important wetland after they won again in the high court this month. Lady Justice Lieven found that Natural England failed in its statutory duty to protect Catfield Fen from pollution after nitrates and phosphates washed from arable fields into one of the finest examples of calcareous fen in western Europe, home to 2,500 species including rarities such as the fen orchid, crested buckler fern, breeding bittern and swallowtail butterflies. In a scathing assessment of Natural England’s inaction since the Harrises first reported the pollution to it in 2021, the judge said the cause of the pollution was “the most basic level of common sense” and required action by the government’s conservation watchdog. The Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money taking action to hold to account government agencies for failing to protect the fen, which is part of a special area of conservation (SAC), an internationally important wetland protected by law. The marshes lie within the Broads national park. “This is bigger than a little ditch in Norfolk,” says Tim. He fears that “regulatory inertia” is preventing pollution from being halted on waterways across the country. “Inertia is prevalent throughout all the regulatory bodies. It’s a landmark judgment because it says they can’t just do nothing.” The couple are big fans of Dirty Business, the recent Channel 4 dramatisation of a maths professor and a retired detective’s battle against sewage pollution, the water companies and the Environment Agency. “It’s just like that film when you go to a meeting,” Tim says. “The language is from [George Orwell’s] 1984. What we call the light side doesn’t have the money. The dark side does. That’s where the money is. Of course it is.” “They are slippery snakes,” Geli adds. Tim held senior roles in the shipping industry, collecting “the wages of sin”, before turning to environmental campaigning in retirement. “She’s the greenie,” he says of Geli, who grew up near the forests around Heidelberg, Germany, and has always loved the natural world. They bought their farm, which came with a large chunk of Catfield Fen, in 1994, wanting to live closer to nature. They turned their arable fields into pasture to prevent soils and pollution from washing into the fen, and continue to tend English white park cattle, sheep and rare-breed Eriskay ponies. “It is beautiful,” Geli says of the fen, which requires a careful rotational cut to preserve its rare plants, invertebrates and birdlife. “It’s a little bit of wildness. It’s mysterious. There are places here where we’ve never been – they are pure nature.” Tim says: “It’s taken 1,000 years to create this and people could destroy it very quickly.” Geli adds: “If you water your plants with the wrong water, they die quite quickly.” The Harrises take conservation advice from the experts at Natural England. “We get on well with Natural England, apart from suing them,” Tim says. “They all came to tea and we talked about everything but the thing [the legal case]. It was a very British occasion. They have some very good people. The trouble is too many no longer have fire in their bellies. They are apparatchiks. We respect them but we wish they had more ‘go’.” Natural England said it accepted the court’s verdict that it had not done enough to protect Catfield Fen but it would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. In 2016, the couple won a public inquiry that demonstrated that too much groundwater was being taken from the valley by water companies and local farmers, causing Catfield Fen to dry out. They won a second battle in 2022, forcing the Environment Agency to limit the abstraction of water close to other nature-rich sites on the Norfolk Broads. Their principles have cost them local friendships. They say National Farmers’ Union reps rejected their application for membership of the local branch, saying half their members would resign, with farmers upset at restrictions on their abstraction of water to boost lucrative crops such as potatoes. “We’re farmers, we’re not anti-farmer,” Tim says. Since their 2022 legal victory, the Harrises have noticed an improvement in the water levels and biodiversity of Catfield Fen’s dykes. Geli says: “We are a Noah’s ark until things get better and nature can spread outwards from here again.” The fen and its wildlife may be in a better condition under their stewardship, but they are not confident that nature is winning. “The evidence this summer was that the insect numbers are going south, according to the experts who survey here,” Tim says. “We are not complacent; we are very worried.” The judge is to make further rulings on what Natural England must do to stop the pollution of Catfield Fen. For the Harrises, the answer is simple: arable farmers must be paid to put in buffer strips of grassland between their ploughed fields and the ditches leading to the Broads to reduce the nitrate-filled soils washing from arable fields into the fen. More widely, Tim argues that regulatory bodies must simply put their resources into monitoring and compliance. He fears most breaches of environmental rules go unnoticed because of a lack of both. The Harrises say they do not want to spend their time campaigning. “I don’t want any of this, believe me,” Tim says, gesturing at the box files that take up two walls of shelving. “I’m 79. I want to read books.” He believes the Broads Authority, the government agency responsible for the national park, should be leading the fight against pollution. Nevertheless, they are considering another legal challenge to stop the Broads from being polluted. Their stewardship of Catfield Fen will continue after they go. Their daughter will take on the farm, and she is a lawyer by training. So is their granddaughter. “The agencies are not getting rid of the Harrises when we die,” Tim laughs. Do they hope their example can inspire others to believe they can act to protect nature and clean water? “You need enormous persistence,” Tim says. “You need passion,” Geli adds. “Evil can happen when people do nothing.”

headline: Counting crows (and cockatoos, and kookaburras): BirdLife Australia’s Aussie bird count takes flight for 2026
trail_text: With more than 3.7 million birds counted already, the annual bird survey is on track to beat last year’s record by the time it closes on Sunday 25 October
body_text: Maths class looked more like owl-gebra for students at Cedars Christian College in Wollongong this week. With BirdLife Australia’s Aussie bird count under way, teacher Karen Jooste has blended birdwatching into the curriculum for her year 2s, using the count to learn about data collection, along with avian-themed narrative writing and lessons on biodiversity and conservation. It helps that there’s a tree-lined creek running through the school grounds, a gathering place for all manner of birds. There’s a resident family of tawny frogmouths with two fluffy chicks; nesting magpies and magpie larks; wood ducks; pacific black ducks; king parrots and rainbow lorikeets. There’s even a local bowerbird that has been known to build an astonishing bright blue bower in spring. And, if her students catch the mournful cry of yellow-tailed black cockatoos in the distance, Jooste has been known to take the whole class outside to look for them. “There’s never any shortage of birds,” she says. Jooste has a whole week of bird-based activities centred around the count. She’s made up her own tally sheet with pictures to help with identification, and even had some students doing counts during their lunch break. “Today in our free reading time we all grabbed a bird book, we all grabbed a cushion and we went and sat under the trees and read with the birds around us. I try to make the most of it, and they actually love it,” she says. “We really do have a very unique school environment, with the trees and the creek, so I want to make the most of it.” With more than 3.7 million birds counted already and tens of thousands of Australians participating in the wholesome and unadulterated joy of counting birds, this year is already on track to beat 2025, according to BirdLife Australia’s Sean Dooley. The annual snapshot runs until midnight Sunday. “We usually have a big flurry of people doing surveys over the weekend – it’s the six o’clock swill version of birding,” Dooley says. Anyone who is outside for 20 minutes – whether waiting for a train, watching children’s sport, or on their lunch break – can wing it. The app makes it easy to record the data, with a built-in bird finder showing 30 of the most commonly recorded birds within 10km. If you spy one that’s not on the list, the app lets you search by characteristics like size, shape and colour, he says. Dooley loves seeing people join in from cities, remote communities, outback properties and offshore islands. “The thing we want people to discover is that you don’t need to be in a remote national park to see birds,” he says. Much like Jooste’s class, primary and even preschool children tend to get a kick out of it, he says. “It’s great because they have to look up and look out and connect with something in the real world.” “The advantage of doing it on the app is it’s still got that gamification aspect, they still get to enter something on a screen, and there is that competitive element; which bird species will you see the most of? Or, can we beat last year … can we beat Tuesday’s total?” Speaking of competitiveness, Dooley hopes to top last year, when 64,000 Australians counted more than 5 million birds. The Australian magpie, rainbow lorikeet and noisy miner were among the most commonly spotted species. He encourages everyone to “keep counting right up to the end”. “We just want to spread the love. Know that you’re not the only birder in the village.” Birdlife Australia’s Aussie bird count ends at midnight, Sunday 25 October

headline: At Cop17, the pressure is on to rescue a deal that could end the destruction of nature
trail_text: ​As world leaders struggle to meet deadlines to halt nature loss set four years ago, a rare leopard in host country Armenia offers a symbol of what is at stake
body_text: The Armenian capital Yerevan is chock-a-block right now with officials, scientists and environmentalists from all over the world gathering for Cop17. Everyone is here to try to rescue a historic deal to end the destruction of nature. The pressure is on. Targets set for 2030 are woefully off track, and the nearly 200 countries present need to agree on a plan to speed things up. All this is happening at a time when national budgets are tight and leaders are distracted by conflict, protests and the global energy crisis. But first, this week’s most important reads. Essential reads This Norwegian village is one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. How can its people save it? What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? US extreme weather survivors are a growing group – now they want to be a political force In focus There have been snippets of positive news. Just a week before the conference began, a Persian leopard, one of Armenia’s rarest and most endangered animals, was spotted in the southern-central region of the country. “It was late, we came home and then one of my caretakers [rangers] called me and said, ‘I have amazing news,’” Syuzi Karapetyan, a teacher who also leads the Gndasar Social-Environmental NGO, explained when I visited her village on Saturday. She had goosebumps when she heard the news, she said. Persian leopards, also known as Caucasian leopards, were once widespread across western and central Asia, but their range has shrunk dramatically. There are thought to be no more than 10 leopards in Armenia, as poaching and habitat destruction have devastated its population. The discovery of a new individual, never spotted before in the country, has delighted Karapetyan and local people, who in partnership with WWF have rebuilt the population of bezoar goats, one of the leopard’s key prey species, and found ways to protect its habitats. The question of how to save our most endangered species is a critical issue being discussed at Cop17. Scientists have warned of the rapid annihilation of wildlife, far above natural background levels, with some saying we are in the midst of a mass extinction event, driven by human overpopulation and overconsumption. A commitment to protect endangered species was one of 23 targets that governments set four years ago, and which they are not on track to meet. Lots of governments still haven’t mobilised resources, partly because they don’t know where to focus, says Dr Kira Mileham, who co-chairs the Reverse the Red Action Partnership, which supports governments to tackle species loss. There might be hundreds of species at risk within a country’s borders; which should they prioritise? This week, Armenia and Colombia announced an initiative, the Coalition of Action to Recover Endangered Species (Cares), a government coalition that aims to help countries assess where to focus their efforts. Some species might not need much dedicated action, as long as parallel efforts – for example to protect their habitat – are under way. Others might need more focused, species-specific interventions such as protection from disease or, if their numbers are very low, help to enable them to breed. The Cares alliance will help governments to assess which of the species in need of specific support are already receiving attention from NGOs or research institutions, and which are falling through the cracks, and connect them with experts, says Mileham. Reverse the Red will serve as the secretariat of Cares. It’s then up to governments to develop a plan, and find resources to support it. So far, 17 countries, including the UK, have joined the Cares alliance to share best practice. Separately, nine private funders and organisations, including Leonardo DiCaprio’s Re:wild, have said they will commit more than $500m over the next five years to recover the world’s most threatened species. The money has been welcomed, but it also matters how it is spent. There is still a huge bias in how conservation funding is allocated, with larger, charismatic animals such as leopards, tigers and elephants sweeping up the majority of resources. “Decisions need to be taken based on the scientific information that is available, and not just because some are cute, which unfortunately is what happens,” says Benoit Guénard, associate professor at the University of Hong Kong, who has researched the distribution of conservation funds. Many conservationists hope money will be better targeted, with resources spread more evenly – and that fungi, algae and amphibians might see some of the success enjoyed by the Persian leopard. Read more: • ‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline • World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says • As a former minister who once climbed a tree to save it, I know there is passion to protect nature. We just have to show it | Steven Guilbeault • To read the complete version of this newsletter – subscribe to receive Down to Earth in your inbox every Thursday.

headline: Country diary: Slugs? Dull? This one is pure showbiz
trail_text: Falmouth, Cornwall: The rainbow sea slug is a bizarre and breathtaking animal, and with warming seas it’s gaining a toehold in the south-west
body_text: I have never seen a species quite so flamboyant in appearance. A couple of centimetres in length, it was curled beneath the submerged rock like a piece of gaudy costume jewellery. When the cry went up that one had been found, I had to prevent myself from breaking into a run as I navigated the slippery seaweed-covered boulders to catch my first glimpse of this rarity. A sea slug. And yet a species that does everything possible to dispel any idea that slugs are drab and dull. The extravagant rainbow sea slug comes with a “ta-da!”. Typically found along the coasts of Spain and Portugal, this multicoloured member of the Aeolid nudibranchs family has spread north with warming seas, and was first recorded in the UK off the Isles of Scilly in 2022. It has since secured a toehold in southern bays of Cornwall and Devon. I had joined a “bioblitz”, run by the Rock Pool Project, on a low spring tide in Falmouth. The community organisation’s monthly challenge engages members of the public in a citizen-science survey of seashore life. The rainbow sea slug was a star find, drawing an admiring huddle of enthusiastic rockpoolers. Breathtaking and bizarre, its outlandish confectionary of candy colours looks almost artificial. The vivid pink body is decorated with a mane of blue finger-like projections known as cerata, which are topped with yellow and orange. A pop-art palette of colours designed to warn predators that it is unpalatable. This one was found on the underside of a rock beside white circles of recently laid eggs – the next generation of these sensational little sea creatures. The project volunteer and marine biologist Ellie Maynard told me that she encountered her first rainbow sea slug last Christmas. “Since then I have seen upwards of 20 here,” she said. “It has been really rapid how they have grown in number.” It was far from the morning’s only rarity. Others included the wonderfully named hair curler slug, which first reached the UK last September and has wavy brown cerata that give it a permed appearance. The rainbow sea slug we were watching eventually trundled off, like an overdressed performer late for a carnival. Show time was over. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order at guardianbookshop.com and get a 15% discount

headline: Decomposing whale near Sydney’s Coogee beach should be towed out to sea, Indigenous rangers say
trail_text: The juvenile humpback carcass is wedged between rocks and attracting sharks, but is too decayed to be moved for burial
body_text: A First Nations ranger group says a whale carcass that closed two of Sydney’s most popular beaches after washing up this week should be towed out to allow it to decompose in the ocean. Coogee beach reopened on Friday after closing on Thursday, when a whale carcass, believed to be a juvenile humpback, was found washed up in Lurline Bay, between Coogee and Maroubra beaches. Randwick city council confirmed the reopening on Friday but said Maroubra beach remained closed due to “dangerous surf conditions”. But the council said the carcass remained wedged among rocks after high tide had failed to move it out to sea as hoped. “People should avoid Lurline Bay and not swim or enter the water in the immediate area. The area remains barricaded off,” the council said. They said a drone flyover on Thursday evening had not spotted any shark activity, so lifeguards decided Coogee was safe to reopen. Swimmers were urged to swim between the flags. But they added that high tide on Friday evening could move the carcass closer to the water’s edge one again, potentially attracting sharks. The whale is an important totem animal to the local Bidjigal people. Robert Cooley, a senior ranger at the Gamay Rangers, who have been working with the council on a culturally respectful way to deal with the remains, said the tide had pushed the carcass higher up towards a coastal walkway, requiring an intervention. “The preferred option now is to tow it back out to sea.” he told Guardian Australia ahead of an afternoon briefing with the council. “Now that it’s up there and decaying and several vertebrate and other bits of bone are showing, people have a habit of taking collections home, which is quite distressing to us.” The Gamay Rangers undertake natural and cultural resource management activities like protection work, conservation, and threatened species management in the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council area. Cooley said that because the whale was in an advanced stage of decay, it was too challenging to lay it to rest on conservation land owned by the land council, as a young humpback that washed up on Cronulla beach earlier this year had been. “It’s just a big pile of blubber now, but the priority is to let nature take its course [out at sea]. The second priority would be lay it to rest on our conservation land.” He said the Gamay Rangers did not support taking the whale to landfill. “It’s really distressing to know that a significant ancestor of ours is taken to landfill with the rest of the city’s rubbish.” Concerns were raised earlier this year about the towing of a sperm whale carcass along a 20km stretch of coast south of Sydney to Wollongong before being taking it to landfill, resulting in increased shark activity and catching swimmers off guard. Olaf Meynecke, manager of the whales and climate research program at Griffith University, has been involved two successful whale tows this year in New South Wales and one in Queensland. He said taking whale carcasses to landfill was “unethical, and … not very environmentally friendly”, towing them far out to sea, typically to the start of the continental shelf – up to 50km offshore – allowed them to decompose naturally and support the marine environment, including sharks. “We actually do want the sharks to bite into these carcasses because it helps to decompose it quickly,” he said. “It’s actually a pretty good thing because then you get rid of the sharks from the nearshore areas where people are bathing.” He said while explosives had been used in the past to break up whale carcasses onshore, now they were typically only used while towing to “open up one side of the whale so that the decomposition will happen a lot faster”. “The only thing that keeps the whale buoyant is is the intestines and the methane that’s being created through gut bacteria. “Once that compartment is opened and the guts release all the methane, the whale will start sinking.” In Western Australia this week, the popular Cottesloe beach was closed amid fears of shark activity due to a three-metre decomposed partial whale carcass. The Cottesloe mayor, Melissa Hawkins, told the ABC the council had organised a bulldozer to take the remains to landfill. With whale migration season in full swing, the ABC reported that watchers in Jervis Bay off the NSW south coast were greeted by the a rare sighting of an orca pod, believed to be hunting a humpback.

headline: Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn
trail_text: People succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating toll
body_text: Heat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, new research suggests, with scientists blaming climate breakdown for two in every three of the deaths. Morgues and funeral homes filled with bodies from June to August as the heat added by planet-baking pollution cut short an extra 32,000 lives in urban areas, the researchers found. Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering. The “staggering” death toll, modelled using historical relationships between heat and health in 854 cities, was the worst on record, the study found. Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years. “In some sense, the absolute numbers of the heat-related deaths estimated across the 854 urban areas are indeed staggering,” said Malcolm Mistry, a climate and health scientist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who co-authored the study. “But perhaps what is even more alarming is the proportion of these deaths that we attribute to anthropogenic climate change.” The share of deaths due to climate breakdown has risen from about 40% at the start of the century to 65% this summer, the study found. People succumbed to heat at the highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, while absolute death tolls were greatest in Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Because death certificates rarely record contributing factors – such as dangerous temperatures that push a stroke victim or lung cancer patient past their limits – families rarely know that heat and human activity hastened their relatives’ death. “These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost a loved one this summer due to the climate crisis,” said Katie White, the climate transition minister for the UK, where scientists estimated 4,354 heat deaths this summer.” In Naples, the hardest-hit city on the continent, 815 people per million died from the heat, according to the study’s age-standardised estimates. Mario Guarino, an emergency doctor at Ospedale CTO in the north of the city, said he witnessed a 15% increase in emergency room visits during the hottest weeks. The “defining characteristic” of the period was the complexity of health problems exacerbated by heat, he added, with loneliness and poverty worsening the situation further. “We took in a terminal cancer patient who lived in a hot attic simply because his family couldn’t find a company to install air conditioning during the summer,” said Guarino. “An elderly man with dementia was abruptly abandoned by his Ukrainian caregiver who returned home to say goodbye to her son, who had been called to war. Emergency services found [the man] lying on the floor one night with a fractured pelvis, desperately trying to call the tenant next door.” The study found people over the age of 85 made up almost half of the death toll, though younger people were not immune, with 833 people between the age of 20 and 44 also thought to have died due to the heat. The scientists said the death toll from the cities studied, which account for about 40% of the European population, could not be easily extrapolated to estimate the full death toll including those in towns and villages. The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, the EU’s climate monitoring service announced this month, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Slightly less punishing temperatures in eastern Europe brought the continental average to its third-hottest level on record. Greenhouse gases have warmed Europe about twice as fast as the global average, exposing more people to intolerably hot summers and fewer people to dangerously cold winters. While cold is a bigger killer than heat, scientists expect rising temperatures to claim more lives than they save, as heat deaths are projected to rise faster than cold deaths fall. The study combined established relationships between heat and mortality with temperature data for 2026 to rapidly estimate the fallout from this summer’s heat. The death tolls for individual countries differ from what national public health agencies have calculated using their own methods. David García-García, a researcher at the mortality monitoring system at the Carlos III health institute in Madrid, who was not involved in the study, said it was a “valuable contribution” that allowed for comparisons across the continent. “However, it is important to bear in mind that these are estimates based on observed temperatures and epidemiological models, which do not incorporate actual data on deaths occurring in the summer of 2026,” he said. Doctors have urged governments to burn fewer fossil fuels – the core driver of rising temperatures – while bolstering health systems, greening cities, rolling out air conditioning and encouraging people to drink water and seek shade. They have also stressed the benefits of people checking in on vulnerable neighbours and family members so they can get help before tragedy strikes. “The real epidemic these days is loneliness,” said Guarino. “Many elderly people are left alone during the summer, abandoned by their families, and due to their low income, they can’t afford air conditioning or, if they do have it, avoid turning it on because of the cost of electricity.”

headline: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval
trail_text: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
body_text: Andy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050. The comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block. Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets. “There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,” the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian. He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity. Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis. “Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote. “More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.” Meanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury. The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments. Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.” Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action. “It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.” The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.” Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas. “At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.” He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.” Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.” Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”. It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts. The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain. “Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.

headline: Unsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leak
trail_text: People near south Wales river were told to keep windows and doors shut after thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site got into the water
body_text: Oily slicks of kerosene still appeared to be leaking into the River Taff this week, several days after a breach of thousands of litres was spotted by members of the public. The breach into the Welsh river was identified last Friday, after people reported strong chemical odours emanating from it. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) officers arrived on site soon afterwards to identify the source of the pollution and were assisted by the south Wales fire and rescue service, which placed absorbent mats and booms to contain as much kerosene as possible. Residents along the Taff were advised to keep windows and doors closed last week, after it emerged that thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cynon Taf had entered the river. Four kilometres (2.5 miles) of waterway were affected, according to NRW. GE Aerospace is a US multinational company that designs and builds military and commercial aircraft systems and engines. Its site in south Wales is among the world’s largest maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities for commercial aircraft engines, employing more than 1,350 people. In 2017 GE Aerospace was the recipient of £5m in funding from the Welsh government, intended to support innovation and sustainability in the aerospace sector. Despite early estimates of a volume of about 25,000 litres of kerosene spilled, NRW was unable to confirm what quantity entered the river, and could not comment on possible enforcement action while its investigation was under way and it gathered information. Public Health Wales advised that the community should avoid all contact with contaminated areas along the busy stretch of river, which runs parallel to many popular trails on both banks, including the Taff trail. People near the river had been complaining of sinus problems and headaches. “Kerosene vapours may be mildly irritating to the respiratory system. Our current assessment is that people who can smell kerosene may experience temporary irritation, particularly if they are exposed for prolonged periods,” said the health body. Sarah Llywelyn, who lives in a riverside home in Glan Y Llyn downstream from the GE Aerospace facility, was among those who reported the leak to NRW. “The smell was absolutely unbelievable. My eyes burned as soon as I opened our door into the garden. I knew it must have been huge because of the smell, and it’s a fast-flowing river – it was essentially unsafe from the point of contamination to Cardiff Bay. We moved here because of the river. What I want more than anything is for lessons to be learned. This should never happen again.” A visit by the Guardian to the site found oily slicks still leaking into the Taff five days after the incident began. NRW believes that the pollution has now been stopped from entering the river. An NRW spokesperson said: “Fuel that entered the drainage system before the leak was stopped by the operator could remain within parts of that network and whilst containment measures help reduce and capture pollution, they are not always able to separate all fuel from flowing water. Our work to investigate this incident and assess environmental impacts is ongoing.” Prof Steve Ormerod, from Cardiff University’s Water Research Institute, confirmed that the photos of the leaks appeared to show the kerosene still entering the waterway through the bunding (a secondary storage system, usually to catch overflows). “The Taff has been recovering from its grossly polluted past,” he said. “So this incident is a potential setback to clean water species such as salmon, dippers and kingfishers that have been recolonising the river. “Kerosene is a mixture of paraffins, naphthenes and benzene-like chemicals that risk direct toxicity to aquatic organisms, reductions in oxygen transfer across the water surface, and suffocation through impaired gill function in fishes or insects. Effects on feather waterproofing are also likely in the birds that have no choice but to enter the water to feed.
