Overnight rain was insufficient to raise river levels and flush the Taff, so kerosene will still be lurking in backwaters and eddies along the river.” Gerwyn and Jordan Lewis from Ynysgau farm, directly opposite the site of the main spill into the river, said they were advised by NRW that the river was unsafe for animals to drink from due to kerosene pollution, meaning that areas of the farm with access to the river could not be safely grazed. “We simply cannot take the chance of our animals becoming seriously ill or dying. Our winter feed stocks could now be depleted at an alarming rate, leaving us facing the possibility of having to purchase substantial additional feed at considerable expense. “We also operate a tourism business comprising campsite pitches and glamping accommodation, a sauna and cold plunge facilities, all beside the affected river.” A GE Aerospace spokesperson said: “The safety of our employees, neighbours and environment remains our top priority. We are continuing to work closely with Natural Resources Wales to address a fuel spill that occurred during repair work at our site on Friday 16 October. The source was identified and isolated on Friday, and containment and clean up are ongoing, with specialist teams working both on and off site.”

headline: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say
trail_text: Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’
byline: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent
body_text: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers. About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%. Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism. Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said. But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter “The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at Cordio (Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment. “We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.” The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations. The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution. Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating, one assessment finds. The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed. The critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075. The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals. The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record, the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed. That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching event on record for reefs in Western Australia where a heatwave killed corals across 1,500lm (930 miles). Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease. Gudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”. He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.” Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming. “We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.” Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable. But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for. Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”. “Reefs are like Picasso paintings under water,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives. “To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.” This story was amended on 23 October 2026. An earlier version misstated Mishal Gudka’s organisation name.

headline: Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill
trail_text: New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after Deepwater Horizon disaster
body_text: Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and has still not fully recovered, according to a new study. The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published on Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade. Conducted using acoustic sonar, multi-depth trawling nets and genetic studies, the study revealed dramatic population drops across the gulf between 2011 and 2015: fish declined by 63.5%, macrocrustaceans including shrimp and krill fell by 62% – severely affecting a primary food source for whales – and cephalopods such as squid and octopus dropped by 59.7%. Researchers found that the post-spill population crash outpaced any decline recorded in similar waters over the past 60 years. They also noted that natural factors like temperature, oxygen and food availability did not vary with the decline, confirming the spill as the primary cause. The marine species most severely affected were also among the most vital to open-ocean ecosystems and global food webs. Krill, a primary food source for deep-sea fish and shrimp, plunged by 72.8%. Bristlemouths – probably the most abundant backboned animals on Earth – fell by 69%. Meanwhile, lanternfishes, which sustain seabirds, dolphins, sharks and commercial fisheries, dropped by 62.9%. A 2023 survey of the area found that many of these populations have not recovered sustainably. Because large amounts of marine species were instantly killed or affected due to chemicals stored in their eggs, this led to sharp reductions in population sizes, in turn leading to reduced genetic variations, the study found. Scientists examined genetic diversity in three lanternfish species that suffered severe population crashes, which subsequently led to inbreeding among the survivors. “The rate of genomic diversity decline is remarkable given the short temporal scale,” the study noted. The study also examined chemical dispersants applied during the oil spill cleanup. While these agents break oil into smaller droplets, they also spread polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) – among crude oil’s most toxic components – deep into the water column, increasing toxicity exposure for mid-water and deep-sea marine life. Six years after the spill, researchers found elevated levels of PAHs in deep-sea fish eggs and cephalopod tissues, which severely impaired reproduction. The study further highlighted that residual oil – even at sublethal concentrations – may have hindered the ability of certain species, including damselfish and stingrays, to locate mates through olfactory cues. “If you keep the oil from coming to the surface, then it won’t be affecting as many shallow water [animals] or humans that were there to work on the spill,” the study’s lead researcher, Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Florida’s Nova Southeastern University, said. “That was the idea [of the dispersants]. What that tends to do is break up the oil into smaller droplets, which allowed it to stay deep in the water column. So that probably was not a good thing for these deep pelagic things that we work on, because now you’ve got this kind of minefield of small oil-laden particles floating around and staying at depth instead of coming to the surface,” he added. “We need to consider the deep ocean to be a very fragile system, not this thing that is so large we can’t disturb it. We need … to be as absolutely careful as can possibly be,” Sutton continued. Similarly, Pedro A Peres, one of the study’s co-authors and a researcher at Florida International University’s Institute of Environment, said: “Our findings are particularly concerning because these are species that are abundant, widespread and historically might not have been considered vulnerable. What we are seeing suggests that even species that appear abundant can experience substantial changes that may go unnoticed without monitoring.” Meanwhile, a BP spokesperson, Paul Takahashi, in a statement said: “We will never forget the 11 people who lost their lives. Sixteen years later, we remain keenly aware that we must always put safety first … We have worked hard to build a safer and stronger BP. We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again.” He added that the company had spent more than $69bn for the Gulf region’s recovery. In 2015, BP agreed to pay a record $18.7bn in penalties and damages after the US justice department and four states sued the company over the spill. The disaster also affected coastal communities in Mexico, which, as of 2020, had yet to receive any compensation. BP has denied that the oil from the spill reached Mexican waters. Since the spill, thousands of people have also filed lawsuits over long-term health problems they attribute to their involvement in cleanup efforts. Research conducted after the disaster has linked exposure to the spill with a range of health issues including increased cancer risks, higher rates of chronic respiratory conditions, heart disease, headaches, memory loss and blurred vision.

headline: Big pharma accused of ‘free-riding on nature’ as global fund attracts just $7,000
trail_text: The Cali Fund, set up to raise $1bn a year for biodiversity from drug companies, remains near empty
body_text: Big pharmaceutical companies have been accused of “free-riding on nature”, after a landmark biodiversity fund that invites businesses to put some of their profits back into conservation was left virtually empty. The Cali Fund set out to raise $1bn (£750m) annually, by asking companies that profit from nature’s genetics to contribute towards conservation in low-income countries. But more than 18 months after the fund was launched, it remains far below this target. As of Monday, at the start of the Cop17 biodiversity summit in Armenia, the fund had received just $10,656 in commitments, of which $7,085 had been deposited. No money has so far been given by major pharmaceutical companies, despite the industry’s reliance on genetic information from organisms around the globe for the development of lucrative new medicines. The industry’s participation could prove pivotal to the fund’s success. A study by Zero Carbon Analytics (ZCA) found the top 15 pharmaceutical companies could have contributed $756m based on their performance last year, if they had followed guidelines set out by the fund, which suggests companies make a voluntary contribution of 1% of their profits or 0.1% of revenue. In 2025, the top 15 pharmaceutical companies generated about $161bn in profits, according to ZCA’s research. “Look at how much profit these pharmaceutical companies are getting – and we’re only asking for a tiny percentage,” said June Rubis of Macquarie University, who is an Indigenous peoples and local communities representative from Asia and sits on the Cali Fund’s steering committee. “Definitely, they’re free-riding” on nature, said Rubis, who added that businesses did not appear to recognise the importance of protecting nature or of supporting “communities who have been in the frontlines of defending biodiversity conservation and therefore their future profits”. The Cali Fund is a key issue to be discussed at the UN biodiversity conference – Cop17 – in Yerevan, this week, and is part of wider efforts to plug a $700bn gap in funding for nature conservation. At least half of the money from the Cali Fund will be directed towards areas identified as priorities by Indigenous peoples and local communities. “The future of health is written in nature’s DNA,” said Victoria Kalyvas, who authored the Zero Carbon Analytics analysis. “The pharmaceutical industry stands to lose a great deal from its destruction, as do patients.” According to Zero Carbon Analytics, the total sum given to shareholders by the top 15 companies in 2025 was 175 times more than the suggested contribution to the Cali Fund. Ensuring that companies pay for their use of nature has become increasingly complex, due to advances in biotechnology that mean large volumes of genetic information, known as digital sequence information (DSI), can now be stored in public databases. The Cali Fund was designed to plug loopholes that have emerged as research has shifted from a reliance on physical samples to use of DSI. However, pharmaceutical companies have criticised the fund, saying the blanket amount they are asked to contribute is not appropriate, arguing that not all medicines are built using DSI, and that the fund overlaps with existing laws. Since its official launch in February 2025, the fund has received just three contributions by small private-sector companies: $5,000 from the UK-based biotech firm Prozomix; $1,000 from TierraViva AI, also based in Britain; and $1,085 from the Belgian firm E-Biom. “More money has been spent on meetings talking about the Cali Fund than there is in the Cali Fund’s coffers,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature, who said it was too optimistic to expect companies to contribute voluntarily and that they should be compelled to do so. Guilherme Cintra, director of innovation policy at the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations, said the industry was committed to biodiversity but had “ongoing questions about the design and implementation of the mechanism”. “The current mechanism overlaps with existing law, relies on inaccurate assumptions about how data is used in the discovery of medicines, and asks companies to hand over a share of their total revenue, whether DSI was used to develop a medicine or not,” Cintra said. A spokesperson for the Cali Fund said the amount raised so far was “disappointing but not entirely surprising”, adding that “comparable financial instruments have generally taken two to three years before contributions began to scale [up]”. The spokesperson said: “Contributions will likely remain modest while the operational infrastructure is being completed and until the Cali Fund becomes better known.” They added that discussions at Cop17 would give greater information to companies, enabling them to come forward with commitments. A spokesperson for the French pharmaceutical multinational Sanofi said the company recognised “the critical importance of biodiversity and healthy ecosystems to human health and the long-term resilience of healthcare systems” and that protecting nature was a core component of its environmental sustainability strategy. A spokesperson for the British biopharmaceutical company GSK said open access to DSI was “critical to enable continued medical innovation and rapid response to public health emergencies, including pandemics”. They added: “We support the intent behind the Cali Fund and will make a decision regarding voluntary contributions when there is more information about how the Cali Fund will work alongside other national and multilateral access and benefit-sharing mechanisms.” Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features

headline: ‘This isn’t greenwashing’: thousands of butterflies surprise experts on restored West Sussex farmland
trail_text: Rare small blues and dingy skippers among species found on former wheatfields two years after start of transformation under commercial nature project
body_text: An “amazing” abundance of 5,290 butterflies, including rare small blues and dingy skippers, has appeared on land that was barren wheatfields just two years ago. The speed with which nature has bounced back at Halnaker Hill farm in West Sussex has surprised experts after 133 hectares (330 acres) of intensively farmed land were turned into a commercial nature restoration project. The farm’s relatively unproductive soils on the South Downs were cropped for wheat for 40 years, but after a final harvest in 2024 the arable land was sown with a special wildflower mix. Seven kilometres of hedgerows have been planted, seven hectares (17 acres) of new woodland created, three ponds dug and 54 hectares (133 acres) of herbal leys seeded, with carefully controlled mob-grazing on existing chalk grassland to improve its wildlife and biodiversity. Halnaker Hill Natural Capital is a commercial nature restoration project that derives its income from selling biodiversity net gain (BNG) credits, which enable houses to be built in the wider region. Under BNG rules, developers are legally obliged to deliver an increase in nature on new housing estates or by buying credits for nature restoration elsewhere. The independent ecologist Neil Hulme, who has advised Halnaker Hill on nature restoration and surveyed for butterflies, said he found “clouds of butterflies” on the former wheatfields last summer. “The speed has amazed me, from a sterile landscape to one brimming with butterflies,” he said. “Despite being tiny, the small blue is very good at sniffing out its foodplant, kidney vetch. I knew it would come, but what I didn’t expect was it to come so soon and multiply so soon. “Some people are a little bit unsure about BNG and the idea of monetising nature, but projects like this are showing so clearly how BNG can deliver nature by the bucketload. This isn’t greenwashing; this is the real deal.” As well as seeing a profusion of skylarks, corn buntings, hobbies and dragonflies on the site, Hulme recorded 85 small blue butterflies and seven dingy skippers, which have never previously been recorded on the fields. Surveys also found 547 small heath butterflies, and scores of common blues and green hairstreaks, alongside eight sulphur pearl moths, a highly localised species restricted to coastal areas of southern Britain and usually observed in ones and twos. Halnaker Hill farm, which is delivering more than 850 units of BNG, forms part of the South Downs national park authority’s “ReNature” programme, which is tackling biodiversity loss and adaptation to global heating in the region. More than 7,700 hectares (19,027 acres) of land is being transformed into natural havens. Nick Heasman, the head of natural capital for the South Downs national park, said: “It’s been wonderful to work with the team at Halnaker Hill to bring about real, positive change, demonstrating that BNG can make a big difference for nature, and this survey proves that. Just two years ago this was largely an arable landscape – showing how quickly nature can bounce back, given space, time and love.” According to Hulme, it is relatively simple for any land manager to boost nature on chalk, simply by scraping off nutrient-rich top-soil and sowing specialist chalk grassland wildflower mixes if the site is not near any existing chalk grassland. Next year he is planning to reintroduce the rare Duke of Burgundy butterfly to the site, with wild pansies also being sown to attract the Queen of Spain fritillary, a once-rare migrant that is increasingly common visitor to southern Britain. “Projects like this fill me with optimism,” said Hulme. “If we can achieve this in just two years, the sky is the limit.”

headline: Country diary: From Mexico’s Day of the Dead to a Shropshire allotment
trail_text: The Marches, Shropshire: Symbolically a flower of the ancestor-honouring Mexican festival, the dahlia appeals to the British gardener’s appetite for the spectacular
body_text: Gardeners are a deviant lot. Despite our passion for wildlife gardening and the drive to be sustained by, and share, our own fruit and veg, our appetite for novelty, aberrancy and even the spectacularly monstrous is insatiable. Take a look at this. The flower is the size of a plate and the brightest orange, like Mark Rothko’s painting No. 210/No. 211 (Orange), with a kind of vibrating stillness, maybe the colour of a sugar maple in autumn sunlight. The ray florets are a mass of long, pointed, half‑curled petals, wildly dancing, writhing away from the central boss of golden disc florets. This exotic vision is a dahlia. We bought a bag of dahlia tubers from the supermarket and planted them in the allotment back in May. We lost the label and, anyway, they grew into three different varieties together, so we’d be none the wiser. One was a small white-tinged pink pompom that flowered in the heatwave, another was a larger white-orange-yellow ball and now this, a semi-cactus in audacious orange. These flower shapes are part of a dahlia culture that has flourished since their introduction from Mexico in the 18th century. The semi-cactus type originated from a single tuber of Dahlia juarezii sent to Holland in 1872. Since then, hybridisation from all forms of dahlia seeds has resulted in 50,000 varieties. Although the dahlia’s position in gardening fashions waxes and wanes, dahlias are respectable again, but they have long been an allotment favourite as a cut-flower crop or grown competitively for shows. Our allotment neighbour has rows of gorgeous blooms and immaculate veg in the vernacular tradition. The stories dahlias have travelled with add to their exoticism. Their symbolic role as the flower of Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) has made them the national flower of Mexico, and the festival’s link to Halloween is a potent folklore connection. Even so, the marigold is more historically correct as the primary flower of los Muertos. Much of what we read about dahlia history from the Aztec and Inca periods is myth, curated by European imperialists. Nevertheless, just like tomatoes, also from Mexico, funky and transgressive dahlias now have a special place in the traditions of British allotments and in our deviant little hearts. Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
trail_text: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners
byline: Kiran Stacey, Jessica Elgot and Fiona Harvey
body_text: Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea. But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year. In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it. “One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.” In contrast, Healey told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision. Labour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero. MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent. Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.” On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments. “As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.” She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.” The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said. But they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.” Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies. The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”. Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.” Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households. While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences. The Greens said on Wednesday they intended to fight seats directly on the issue of Jackdaw and Rosebank. The Green MP Carla Denyer said: “We have identified dozens of seats where we are Labour’s main challenger and the climate is one of the top issues and voters have been mobilised by the heatwave and wildfires. “Our strong advice to Labour MPs is to stand up to Andy Burnham and his act of climate violence, both to save your seats and, far more importantly, to protect the planet for future generations.” Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. She said the fund would be given £2bn in the budget. “When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes. However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

headline: More than 1 million mice used in Australian research annually, ‘overdue’ study finds
trail_text: Advocates say having national data about numbers of rats and mice used in research can help boost public trust in science
body_text: More than 1 million mice and nearly 47,000 rats are used in scientific research in Australia annually, according to the first ever nationwide count. Dr Malcolm France, a veterinarian who compiled the data, described the count, released today, as “an overdue first step” towards publishing national statistics for all animals used in research, including fish, rabbits, birds and monkeys. National statistics on the use of animals in research are important for establishing public trust and informing policy, he said, but unlike comparable countries Australia has historically lacked overall data. “Publishing national statistics has long been the norm in the United States, Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom and New Zealand, where year-on-year comparisons help inform animal welfare priorities and resource allocation and also contribute to greater transparency, which is important for public trust in science,” he said. The research, undertaken for the Australian and New Zealand Council for the Care of Animals in Research and Teaching, found 1,193,619 mice and 46,961 rats were used in scientific research, teaching and testing in 2024 (the most recent comparable year), although the total did not include animals that were bred for research purposes but not used. The pilot study focused on mice and rats in the first instance as they are widely used laboratory animals with clearly defined roles in biomedical research. Establishing a national figure required a range of approaches, including in one case a freedom of information request, France said. Only three states – New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania – consistently publish their animal use data, while other jurisdictions collect statistics without sharing them and some did neither. “What the whole process has shown is that there is a pathway to get national statistics,” he said. Bella Lear, the chief executive of Understanding Animal Research Oceania, said nationwide data is “absolutely vital” for Australia to be able to demonstrate the scope and capability of its research, alongside its animal welfare practices. “It’s very hard to show that you are a great place to do research, and that your research is very welfare-focused and top of the line, if nobody can say for sure how much research takes place or how many animals are used,” she said. Lear said mice are commonly used, particularly in biomedicine, because the mouse genome was one of the first to be sequenced. The animals also breed quickly, enabling scientists to study subsequent generations. Rats are also routinely studied, in part because they were easy to train and keep. Dr Suzie Fowler, the chief science officer at RSPCA Australia, said transparency and accountability were critical for establishing trust and understanding with the public and that included public reporting on animal use and welfare outcomes. Mice and rats are social and intelligent animals, she said, and enjoy a variety and activities such as exploring and building nests. While some behavioural preferences could be provided for in a research environment – such as nesting material for mice, or more social interaction for rats – some practices and procedures could significantly affect their ability to have a good life and could negatively impact their welfare, she said. Paula Wallace, director of the Liberty Foundation – which earlier this year opened Australia’s first adoption centre specialising in small research animals – said statistics would assist organisations like hers in identifying how many animals might be suitable for rehoming. “Animals used in research are no different from the dogs and cats and rabbits we call pets,” she said, adding that the animals deserved the chance to find loving homes and experience a different kind of life beyond facilities.

headline: Giant tunnel proposed to tackle Windermere sewage discharges
trail_text: United Utilities, Environment Agency and local campaigners say 12-mile tunnel could take sewage away from England’s largest lake
body_text: Plans are under way for a new giant tunnel to transport sewage away from Windermere, England’s largest lake. Windermere, in the Lake District, has suffered from widespread raw sewage and bacterial pollution driven by discharges from United Utilities. Campaigners say this pollution has caused more frequent toxic blue-green algal blooms, with the public advised to avoid swimming in the lake. Modelling indicates the climate crisis will exacerbate these challenges, with the catchment expected to experience more intense rainfall over the coming years, placing further pressure on the wastewater infrastructure. A new project, backed by United Utilities, the Environment Agency and local campaigners, has set out a vision to end sewage discharges into the lake by building an 12-mile (19km) tunnel to transport sewage away from the lake. The water company said the use of tunnelling techniques would minimise the disruption to local communities. Windermere is at the heart of the Lake District Unesco world heritage site and has been the inspiration for poets, storytellers and lyricists for generations, with an estimated 17.7 million people visiting every year. The treated effluent would then be discharged into either the River Leven or the Irish Sea at Ulverston. It is estimated the project will cost £3.6bn, with United Utilities to seek permission from the government to raise customer bills to pay for it. It said the programme could add up to £3.17 a month to water bills in 2035. The project will now enter the detailed design phase during which specialised engineers will work out the technicalities of the build, which is expected to take two years. If granted permission to raise bills to pay for the project, United Utilities said the project could be complete within seven years and would provide a “one and done” solution with an immediate impact. Matt Staniek, a campaigner at Save Windermere, which is a partner on the project, said creating the feasibility report had involved weekly meetings over 15 months. Staniek, who has been calling for the end of sewage discharges into the lake for more than five years, said he was concerned at first about partnering with the company causing the pollution, but said they were the only people who could actually fix it. “This has demonstrated that it is possible not to dump sewage in Lake Windermere,” he said. In planning for the project, the team considered the transformation of Lake Annecy in France, which is widely recognised as one of the cleanest lakes in Europe. In the 1950s, Annecy faced similar pollution problems, but the authorities invested in long-term infrastructural improvements to eliminate the sewage discharges. “This is up to the government now. The plan is there, it’s in place, we’re not going to stop until Andy Burnham is on the shores of Lake Windermere with a spade announcing that the construction has begun on this project,” Staniek said.

headline: What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain
trail_text: This summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sight
body_text: Not much is happening in the tiny Norfolk hamlet of Little Hautbois on the day I visit. The pub, once popular with airmen from RAF Coltishall, stopped being a pub a long time ago, even before RAF Coltishall stopped being RAF Coltishall. It’s not Saturday, so there are no weddings at Hautbois Hall. Nor is it 19 May, so the restless, headless ghost of Thomas Boleyn isn’t driving his carriage across the bridge over the River Bure, as he is said to do on the anniversary of the execution of his daughter, Anne. Today, a lovely autumn one, all is as it should be. But half a mile down a narrow country lane is an incongruous and baffling sight: a strip of gentle hillside made up of large white rectangular blocks, piled up and sparkling in the sunshine. A glacier, you might think, if you were in Norway rather than Norfolk. (And ice is involved, as it happens.) As you get nearer, the picture becomes clearer; the blocks have coils on one face, doors and handles on the opposite one, plus the manufacturers’ names. It’s a glacier of fridges, more than 3,000 of them. Kate Murrell, the assistant director of waste management at Norfolk county council, is here to let me in. The fridges are surrounded by a security fence with CCTV cameras. “It’s not what we want to see here, or what the local residents want to see either,” says Murrell. The nearest local resident, Stuart Brown, tells me over his garden fence that it is “a bit of an eyesore”. These eyesores are not particular to Norfolk. All around the UK, old fridges are piling up, including in Nottinghamshire, Durham, Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire and Newport, the last of which found itself with a mountain of 80,000 appliances over the summer. So what is behind it? In part, it is because fridges and freezers are difficult to dispose of. David Santillo, a senior scientist with Greenpeace Research Laboratories, based at the University of Exeter, explains that they contain gases and materials that are harmful to the environment if the appliances are not dismantled correctly. Thus, by law, fridges have to be dismantled at specialist processing plants. The problem is that the number of these plants is shrinking rapidly in the UK. In Norfolk, a fire at an electrical waste and treatment facility in Thetford in April meant there was nowhere to recycle fridges and freezers for two or three months, which caused a pile-up. “If you got a new fridge and took the old one to the tip, they turned you away,” says Murrell. Then came this summer’s record-breaking temperatures, which caused more fridges and freezers to break down – and some processing plants to shut temporarily. As Murrell says: “During Covid, people upped their refrigeration capacity at home,” so there are even more appliances to deal with. After the Thetford fire, Norfolk council ran out of treatment facilities to which it could send fridges. Thetford was one of just eight full-scale processing plants for fridges in the UK; another major plant in south Wales shut down when the recycling company Unimetals filed for liquidation and a plant in the West Midlands closed in February due to a fire. This summer alone, 26 local authorities had to stop accepting fridges and freezers. Compared with Newport’s 80,000 fridge mountain, this Norfolk site maybe doesn’t look so terrible, though the stark contrast with its bucolic surroundings certainly adds to the shock value. “It’s nationwide,” says Jon Hubbard, the chair of the Local Government Association’s neighbourhoods committee. “I’m hearing more and more reports of councils struggling. In my own local authority in Wiltshire, I see large quantities of fridges and freezers piling up. It’s certainly not getting any better.” Santillo says the main danger with these appliances is the refrigerants. “Lots of different chemicals are used as refrigerants. Very old fridges could contain CFCs, which are ozone-depleting substances. There are almost certainly going to be HFCs, which are potent greenhouse gases. Others will contain propane and isobutane. Commercial fridges can contain ammonia.” Once removed and isolated, he says: “The refrigerants can be recycled and reused or, in the case of some of the old ones, they would need to be incinerated. Then you have the foams used for insulation, which can contain hazardous substances such as fluorinated compounds that also have to be recycled or incinerated.” While some of the fridges at Little Hautbois are clearly quite old, others look pretty recent – in working order even. Murrell says they probably are. Often the fridges are disposed of because the owner wants an “upgrade, or it’s a new kitchen and they want one that fits in with this, not that”. Some just aren’t built to last or are impossible to repair. Santillo says manufacturers could do a lot more to stop fridges and freezers needing to be disposed of. “They could find ways of making them last longer. They’re a significant investment and some of them aren’t very robust.” It doesn’t help that we no longer get things fixed. “The weakest link is always the compressor; once that goes, it becomes so expensive to fix that people tend to just get a new fridge.” Hubbard points a finger in another direction – at the producer compliance schemes that coordinate the collection, recycling and disposal of fridges and freezers in the UK. The idea is that the polluter pays, but because treatment capacity has been hit so hard, producers haven’t been able to keep up, so councils are having to handle and fund the collection, storage and treatment of these goods. “We’re picking up the phone, and they’re not answering,” says Hubbard of the schemes. “They need to come up with a proper business plan to get back up to full-scale recycling again. In the short term, they need to come up with a solution to storage.” At the moment, this is also falling to local authorities. “It’s costing money that should be spent on libraries, sports centres, fixing potholes, delivering health and social care,” he says. Murrell says more help needs to come from central government: “What the country needs is a more resilient infrastructure to deal with fridges and freezers at the end of their lives.” The other worry, says Hubbard, is the risk of fly-tipping when council disposal services are forced to halt. “Council-tax payers are being scammed by people who claim to be legitimate waste disposal organisations, collect your fridge and then dump it where they shouldn’t. And if that fridge can be tracked back to a resident, it’s the resident who gets prosecuted.” He advises people to take photographs of any disposal company’s licence. And the piles of fridges building up? “Recycling fridges should be about containment,” says Santillo. “You have to take the refrigerant out, contain it, then that goes on for further treatment. That’s clearly broken down and they’re just being dumped. They certainly shouldn’t be left to fall apart and fragment in the environment.” He has an additional concern. “If you have piles of fridges and freezers, they’re going to become home to wildlife; they’re great places to attract animals that like to live in small spaces.” Murrell says that here in Norfolk, pest control come in regularly and haven’t discovered any new residents, gnawing away at fluorinated insulation. But looking up at the kestrel hovering overhead, I wonder. I don’t think it’s after putrefied turkey twizzlers. Norfolk is now accepting fridges, but only at seven of its 19 recycling sites, which is all that can be managed. “That’s a way of reducing the volumes we get in,” says Murrell. “Customers might have to travel a bit further and so think twice about disposal at the moment.” A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs says these delays are “frustrating” and that the minister responsible for waste crime has written to producer compliance schemes asking them “to take all reasonable steps to fix this fast, as this cannot go on any longer”. The spokesperson added: “We appreciate the challenges facing local authorities, and are working closely with them, the Environment Agency and industry to manage the impact of capacity shortages, including allowing temporary storage sites and looking at long-term solutions to ensure this does not happen again.” In the meantime, the site here outside Little Hautbois is full, with no room for any more fridges. Nor are the ones already piled up here going anywhere at the moment, and Murrell is not hopeful that this will change any time soon. “Until we see national capacity really increase, councils like us are going to see disruption to the services. I think this one’s stuck for quite a while.” Chances are then that next 19 May, when Thomas Boleyn comes riding through with his phantom horses and carriage, he’ll look to the side of the road and think: “What an eyesore!” • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
