headline: UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
trail_text: Decision was widely expected after lobbying by Shell but will dismay environmental campaigners
byline: Peter Walker, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu
body_text: The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely expected move that will nonetheless dismay environmental campaigners and a number of Labour MPs. While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project, which is being decided on separately, have sought environmental approval for existing licences. The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. The decision on Jackdaw had been expected last month but was delayed, seemingly to take it beyond the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October, where Labour was defending a seat against a Green challenge and ultimately won. The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said after approving the scheme. Andy Burnham has said drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter”. “At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” the prime minister said. “We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” Announcing the decision, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “Following careful consideration of all relevant factors, I have agreed that the regulator can grant consent for gas to be produced at Jackdaw, which will begin to supply the UK with gas from this winter thanks to the highly skilled and vital North Sea workers. When asked to clarify how many jobs the gasfield would create, Fahnbulleh said: “It will create 27 jobs. It will secure 273 jobs. But, look, that was not the primary consideration. “This decision will support the country’s energy security with homegrown gas this winter and help minimise the UK’s use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear. “The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050.” Fahnbulleh also said the government would launch a new energy wealth fund with a £2bn downpayment to reinvest oil and gas revenues into the climate transition. It hopes this fund will demonstrate that approving new gasfields is not at odds with Britain’s climate commitments. Environmental campaigners have called for Jackdaw and Rosebank to be abandoned, while Donald Trump has urged Burnham to open them. Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.” She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.” The oil and gas industry says the fields will provide 10% of the UK’s output at their peak. But campaigners say they will cause so much environmental damage as to obliterate any economic benefit. The UN’s Environment Programme has said global carbon emission targets need to be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, an independent joint venture half owned by Equinor and half by Shell. Both have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled that the companies needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce. The companies have been lobbying hard for the green light. Adura commissioned a report this week that said rejecting the two projects would cost the UK economy nearly £10.8bn over the next decade. The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling. That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and about half of 18- to 24-year-olds. Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer. If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.” The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, called the decision “climate vandalism”. He said: “Today’s decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change. “The energy secretary has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills, the health secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS and the industry’s own assessment is that will create only 27 jobs. This is a victory for Shell over the people.” Ami McCarthy, the head of politics for Greenpeace UK, said: “Approving Jackdaw shows the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy. Andy Burnham promised pragmatism, but there is nothing pragmatic about rubber-stamping a project that won’t lower energy bills, won’t boost energy security and will create just 27 full-time jobs. “What Jackdaw is guaranteed to do is generate record profits for Shell and Equinor while supercharging the climate chaos hitting families here and abroad. Going on to approve Rosebank would detonate an even bigger carbon bomb, releasing as much carbon as 56 coal plants operating for a year. “True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates.”

headline: Climate campaigners condemn ‘maddening’ decision to approve Jackdaw gasfield
trail_text: Critics say move will jeopardise climate targets, fail to cut cost of living and distract from need to decarbonise energy
body_text: Climate campaigners and green experts have condemned the government’s decision to allow the drilling of the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. They said approval for the site would jeopardise the UK’s climate targets, fail to reduce the cost of living, and distract from the need to decarbonise the UK’s energy sector. Many drew parallels with the record-breaking heatwave and drought, fuelled by global heating, that the UK experienced this summer. “Is the prime minister living in a parallel universe? One where we haven’t just endured our hottest summer on record, with droughts, wildfires and, in all likelihood, the most heat-related deaths on record?” said Danny Gross, climate campaigner for Friends of the Earth. “And where the UN hasn’t warned that we’re on the brink of breaching the all-important 1.5C warming limit?” As the gas from Jackdaw will be sold on international markets, Gross said it would not bolster the UK’s energy security, but would add to global greenhouse gas emissions. “The disconnect [between the government’s green ambitions and its actions] is maddening,” he said. “This benefits oil giants and their shareholders and doesn’t make life more affordable as Burnham promised,” said Tessa Khan, the executive director of the campaigning organisation Uplift. “Clean energy is how we lower bills, reindustrialise regions and increase public control – not by caving to an oil industry making obscene profits while pushing up bills, laying off workers and driving the heatwaves we saw this summer.” As the North Sea is a rapidly declining basin, any rise in jobs is likely to be small and short-lived, analysis suggests. Kyle Lischak, the head of UK at the legal pressure group ClientEarth, said: “The companies drilling our oil and gasfield will soon leave the empty oilfields with record profits, whilst we pay the price of extreme weather for decades to come.” Ami McCarthy, the head of politics for Greenpeace UK, said: “Approving Jackdaw shows the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy. Andy Burnham promised pragmatism, but there is nothing pragmatic about rubber-stamping a project that won’t lower energy bills, won’t boost energy security and will create just 27 full-time jobs.” The Conservatives, Reform and some trade union leaders, including Sharon Graham’s Unite, cheered the government’s decision but 10 unions, representing firefighters, healthcare workers, teachers and others, signed a statement last week opposing development of the Rosebank oilfield. Many Labour MPs have been sorely disappointed by the government’s green light, but some are seeking a compromise by which in return for staying quiet over the Jackdaw decision – and potentially over the Rosebank oilfield, a decision on which is still in the offing – they want to stave off any watering down of the mandate on electric vehicles, which is also under consideration. “The EV mandate is a bigger issue, in terms of emissions in the long term,” one Labour MP told the Guardian. But the Green party sees a potential electoral advantage in Labour’s divisions over the North Sea. There are now scores of seats in which the Greens could be the main opposition to Labour at the next election, and where concern over the climate is a key priority. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said of the Jackdaw decision: “This is climate vandalism. Today’s decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change. “The energy secretary [Miatta Fahnbulleh] has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills; the health secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS, and the industry’s own assessment is that it will create only 27 jobs. This is a victory for Shell over the people.” Burnham and Fahnbulleh are expected to attend the next UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey next month, where governments will be asked to show they are living up to their climate commitments. Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, warned that the UK’s power to persuade was damaged by further fossil fuel exploitation, which would encourage other countries to ignore climate science and pursue markets for their own reserves. “Approving Jackdaw is a serious blow to Britain’s international climate credibility,” he told the Guardian. “The UK cannot expect developing countries to move away from fossil fuels while giving the green light to new drilling in its own back yard. That double standard will not go unnoticed by countries already suffering the consequences of climate change.” He added: “Britain has spent years presenting itself as a climate leader, but leadership is about what you do, not what you say. At a time when the world urgently needs to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels, approving new gas developments sends completely the wrong message.”

headline: This Norwegian village is one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. How can its people save it?
trail_text: As glaciers melt and permafrost thaws, Longyearbyen, on the remote Arctic islands of Svalbard, faces climate-induced problems from tap water to housebuilding to landslides
body_text: On a rugged mountain plateau of snow-dusted rocks, in the remote archipelago of Svalbard, a glaciologist, Andy Hodson, points out the “ears” of ice, white against the rock, that gave Foxfonna glacier its name, after the arctic fox. The small glacier, on a mountain 8 miles (15km) outside the Norwegian village of Longyearbyen, is a popular summer hike for tourists who come here seeking the Arctic experience. But in Svalbard, where glaciers cover 57% of the land and temperatures are rising up to seven times faster than the global average, making it one of the fastest-warming places on Earth, Foxfonna is changing rapidly. “It is slowly dying,” says Hodson, a professor at the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS). The telltale signs include a concave profile: Foxfonna is no longer accumulating snow. Precipitation here is increasingly falling as rain. Its thinning rate is between 1 and 4 metres a year, making it unrecognisable from when Hodson was last here a few years ago. Out in the fjords, on the other side of the coastal village, the large glacial fronts extending into the sea that are characteristic of the islands are melting at an even faster rate: over the past two years, 10 have retreated entirely on to land. In 2024, “things went crazy”, Hodson says, after record-high summer temperatures led to a big ice loss, of 1%, across the archipelago. It is affected by Arctic amplification – a feedback loop in which sea-ice retreat and atmospheric warming make each other worse. “Pretty much the whole island is losing ice now,” says Hodson. Longyearbyen, a scatter of brightly coloured houses, research institutes and tourist hotels at the bottom of a steep valley, lies at a latitude of 78 degrees north, the last stop in the high Arctic before the north pole. An important outpost of Arctic science, it attracts explorers, adventurers and nature lovers. The village’s 2,600 inhabitants are used to extremes: winter temperatures can drop as low as -20C (-4F) and, from late October to early March, the sun does not rise, plunging the valley into more than 100 days of darkness. But they are now facing new and unsettling challenges – things that many point out should serve as a warning for other Arctic regions. Not only is snow melting faster but now the permafrost – ground that once remained frozen all year – is thawing. This is having unexpected but significant consequences. People have recently been warned not to drink from their taps due to heavy metals contained in the bedrock leaching into the village’s water supply. Instead, they now have to fill up containers from a central tank of filtered water in the village’s supermarket, while the municipality investigates and works out what to do in the long term. The thaw has also caused landslides, damaged foundations and cracked walls, rendering some homes uninhabitable and threatening the long-term stability of other buildings. As a consequence, there are no longer enough homes for the number of people who need them. The authorities in Longyearbyen have been forced to learn lessons, acclimatise and try to adapt to the changing conditions. On the rooftop of the Svalbard Science Centre, which featured in the opening scenes of Vigil, the recent BBC thriller set in Svalbard, Gunhild B Sætren points out the scene of the most devastating avalanche in the archipelago’s history. The avalanche, in December 2015, buried nine people, killing one man and an infant in their homes in the shadow of Mount Sukkertoppen. “It was terrible,” says Sætren, a professor of safety psychology, who manages the Unis Arctic Safety Centre (ASC), established after the tragedy to focus on hazard management and climate adaptation. “Climate change is impacting us in very many ways. The greatest risk is avalanches. The area used to be an Arctic desert, but now there is more rain.” The tragedy, which was followed by another, non-fatal avalanche that damaged two houses in 2017, happened as the result of warming strong easterly winds and drifting snow. At the time, the avalanche danger from Sukkertoppen was known about, but no avalanche warning system was in place. Since then, snow fences to reduce drift and a wall of avalanche traps have been installed on the mountain and some houses pulled down, including Sætren’s own. The centre now provides weekly snow observations for the municipality’s avalanche warning system. Sætren also works on a programme with other high Arctic remote settlements in Iceland and Greenland, to look at common problems, such as evacuation procedures for avalanches. A new tour guide approval system, introduced by the governor of Svalbard to better assess climate and other risks, is expected to be in force by 2027. Arctic geology is complex and changing fast, with tour operators saying the changes are curtailing certain activities. At the Husky cafe, Matilda Weihs, 30, a guide for Svalbard Wildlife Expeditions who was trained by the ASC, says that this year they had to move the snowmobiles seven miles out of the village to find enough snow cover for tours. “We are losing snow earlier and the melt is starting earlier,” says Weihs. “There are big changes in the fjords. You need to stay away from glacier fronts due to the danger of glaciers calving into the sea.” *** The loss of drinking water has been a huge shock to people, says Terje Aunevik, mayor of Longyearbyen and a former husky musher. “In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it’s challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water. People get angry, wondering ‘why don’t we have control over it?’” It has forced a rethink about how to tackle the problem longer term, says Aunevik. “Now we are using a lot of resources to clean our tap water, when we use maybe 1-2% of that for drinking. That’s crazy energy use. We could have two different water-supply systems into our households, one for drinking and one for grey water.” Aunevik says the challenges of thawing permafrost are also forcing a rethink of the way the village is built. The construction of new homes to tackle the housing crisis was held up while the village grappled with a transition to a new energy system (a former mining camp, it previously used waste hot water from the mines for heating). And then, in 2025, scientists discovered the heavy metals were contaminating the water supply. “I sometimes say that we are in the beginning of building a completely new town,” Aunevik says. “We need to change everything. “There is a saying that wood does not rot in the Arctic, but now it does. It challenges how we construct our buildings.” Ingvild Sæbu Vatn, a partner at the Longyearbyen architecture firm LPO Arkitekter, says one solution to the problem of melting permafrost affecting wooden foundations has been to drill into the bedrock. Another settlement in Svalbard, Ny-Ålesund, tried this, but Sæbu Vatn says some buildings began to be pushed up by the movement in the ground. “They thought, ‘we’ll put the foundations in the bedrock and then we’ll be fine’ but they were wrong,” says Sæbu Vatn, who adds that this needs to be done with care. “If you put foundations in bedrock but you don’t do it properly, the buildings will still jack up. We need to look again at how we are building foundations.” Those working on solutions have also not ruled out the extraordinary. “One solution being explored [to stabilise building foundations] is to freeze the ground by blowing cold air under the buildings in winter,” says Sæbu Vatn. She says that while Longyearbyen is undoubtedly struggling, her hope is that in finding a way to survive they can offer hope to other Arctic regions, such as those with Inuit populations in Greenland and Canada. “The big resource that Longyearbyen has is its population,” she says. “People are adventurous and resourceful, and a lot of companies are very innovative. Maybe we can build knowledge from this strange little place that is rapidly warming. That would be a nice goal.”

headline: World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says
trail_text: Action needed to avoid disastrous overshoot of climate targets, according to organisation’s environment body
body_text: The world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. Although the “window has closed” on holding temperature rises to 1.5C, in line with scientific advice, limiting the “overshoot” of that target is still possible, according to the UN Environment Programme (Unep). But countries are failing to translate their long-term targets on reducing emissions into short-term actions, a report on the “emissions gap” between climate goals and policies has found. Global carbon output appears to have stalled: the emission levels in 2025 were broadly similar to those of the previous year. But Unep analysts were wary of calling it a peak or plateau, given the vast uncertainties of geopolitics and an increased reliance on fossil fuels, despite strong growth in renewable energy. Cutting greenhouse gases by 18% by 2030, and by 45% by 2035, would yield a good chance of limiting temperature rises to 1.7C above preindustrial levels. This would still allow events such as the record heatwaves of the last few months to become frequent and common, but could help prevent them from getting drastically worse. Governments were warned for years that time was running out, said Inger Andersen, the executive director of Unep. “[We used to say] there’s still an opportunity if we make this herculean effort [to stay within the 1.5C limit],” she said. “It’s now clear the herculean effort was not made. We procrastinated, and now we are saying this window has closed.” Nevertheless, she urged countries to keep the 1.5C goal – the centrepiece of the Paris climate agreement. “We can make the overshoot as brief and as short as possible. It’s not time to throw in the towel and give up. This is about how to find our way back, as shortly and quickly as possible.” Under Donald Trump, the US – the world’s second biggest emitter, after China – has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement and is threatening to reverse its longstanding trend of falling greenhouse gas emissions. Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, said: “All governments have a job to do, but in particular it is time for major fossil fuel producers such as the US and Saudi Arabia, which produce 20-25% of fossil fuels globally, to stop playing politics and face the scientific reality. Right now they are looking at the fire, denying it exists and pouring more petrol on it, while their own citizens increasingly face searing heat, wildfires and other impacts.” Other countries appear to have been affected by US intransigence – pledges made last year on greenhouse gases were noticeably weak, according to UNEP analysis. At the Cop30 climate summit in Brazil last November, governments were supposed to make fresh commitments under the Paris agreement to cut emissions. But the commitments made were nowhere near strong enough. Even if all of those updated pledges were fulfilled, temperatures would still rise to 2.6C above preindustrial levels, according to Unep’s projections, endangering life across swathes of the globe. Policy has also not kept up with pledges: on current policies around the world, temperatures would rise to 2.8C. Every five years of greenhouse gas emissions at current levels pushes up forecasts of global heating by 0.1C. Scientists also fear that the greater the margin by which we exceed 1.5C, the greater the likelihood of triggering tipping points in the climate system. Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, said: “The tragedy is that we have the solutions within our grasp. Solar and wind power are growing far faster than anyone expected, yet governments are still failing to move away from fossil fuels quickly enough. The technology is racing ahead while political leadership is dragging its feet.” The shortfall in countries’ commitments is supposed to be corrected under a Paris agreement mechanism called the “global stocktake”, an assessment of emissions targets next scheduled for 2028. But that has also been thrown into doubt: this week, the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change failed to set a timetable to publish its latest report before the global stocktake, which would prevent governments from assessing their progress against the latest science. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and one of the world’s leading climate scientists, said rows over the timing of IPCC reports must not be allowed to stall government action. “If all current national commitments are implemented, global emissions are projected to reach approximately 50 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually by 2035, when they should be below 35 gigatonnes. The science is already clear. Closing that gap is a question of political action, not a lack of scientific evidence,” he said. One way identified by Unep to limit warming quickly would be to cut methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide. • This article was amended on 21 October 2026. The UN Environment Programme targets a cut in global carbon emissions of 45% by 2035, not by 2045 as an earlier version said.

headline: Country diary: What a privilege it is to witness bird migration on such a scale
trail_text: Poole, Dorset: At this time of year, migrants are constantly on the move here, whether leaving, arriving or just stopping to refuel
body_text: With the sadness of our summer migrants departing the UK for another year comes the joy of our wintering birds returning. Working in conservation at Poole harbour, I’m out most days, connected to the ebb and flow of this change. As it is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and located on the East Atlantic Flyway, birds are constantly on the move here, whether leaving, arriving or stopping to refuel. To name just a few, in recent weeks we’ve seen the departure of swallows for southern Africa, and meadow pipits for Europe and north Africa; teals and avocets have arrived in large numbers; and we’ve had sightings of passing curlew sandpipers – scarce here. Today is a sunny, abnormally mild October afternoon on the Wareham channel, and the tide is very low, exposing broad expanses of mudflats bordered by heather, gorse and reedbeds on the shore. The mudflats teem with aquatic insects, crustaceans and worms – a vast buffet for waders. As we cruise near the shallows, taking care to remain in the deeper channels, I get a better view of the birds that have stopped to feed – curlews, oystercatchers, black-headed gulls, Icelandic black-tailed godwits. A bird that always catches my eye is the dunlin. They often congregate in huge flocks, and in the bright sunshine, I can just about make out their short, downcurved bills, brownish-grey upperparts and plain white underparts. They move erratically and constantly probe the mud. Every so often, they are spooked by something and lift into the air, their white undersides catching the sunlight. This group of dunlin may have travelled thousands of miles to reach the harbour. Despite weighing only around 50g, these little waders could have bred as far away as eastern Europe or Russia. They breed in the UK too, mainly on grasslands and moorlands in northern England and Scotland, moving south to spend the winter in continental Europe and north Africa. Here in Poole harbour, their numbers can exceed 2,000 by January. Bird migration is such an incredible spectacle; I feel privileged to see it happening on such a scale. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Jackdaw North Sea gasfield to get go-ahead in blow to climate campaigners
trail_text: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials
body_text: The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs. Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments. The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it. It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis. Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.” She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.” When fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production. Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status has become symbolic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated. The field was approved by the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting to have to make a decision on Jackdaw or Rosebank. However both fields were cast into doubt last year by a landmark ruling that said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted. A judge ruled that when deciding whether the two fields would violate the UK’s climate commitments, regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas they would produce. Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it. Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”. Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the US president’s arguments earlier this summer, promising to take a “pragmatic approach” to the decision. “There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.” He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.” Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns. Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence. Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later this year. The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling. That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds. Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer. “If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.” Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it will produce around seven times the CO2 emissions of Jackdaw and partly because most of the oil produced there will be exported. Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”

headline: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
trail_text: Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices
body_text: A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study. The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems. A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished. Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning. They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%. Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest. Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.” There is increasing recognition of the importance of Indigenous stewardship of the Amazon and other biomes that sequester carbon, shelter biodiversity and provide vital ecological services to the planet. But this role is increasingly difficult as Indigenous lands are threatened by miners, loggers, farmers and land grabbers, and as many of the young people of these often economically poor communities are exposed to the internet or lured away to wealthier cities. How to sustain, encourage and reward Indigenous stewardship is a hot debate in the international aid and environmental community. Many previous payment schemes came with strings attached, such as the Brazilian government’s bolsa família, which has child education obligations, or bolsa verde, which has conservation activity requirements. The authors of the new study say the project – which was drawn up with local women’s groups – is the first to offer an unconditional basic income to an Indigenous community in the Amazon. The lead author, Dr Neil Howard, said: “All of this helps ethical conservation. The incentive to exploit or abandon land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.” To boost the impact, the project delivered a voluntary “cash plus” complementary programme of community-led education on finance, conservation and climate change. Other academics are more cautious about the environmental impacts of cash transfers, pointing out that similar studies elsewhere have found they can lead to an increase in deforestation as people use the extra cash to expand agriculture. In some parts of the Amazon, cash payments are used to buy motorbikes and cars, which increases demand for more roads. There are also reports of Indigenous communities becoming more exposed to drugs when they visit cities to collect transfers. The authors of the new report acknowledge that wider research is needed on the ecological impacts of unconditional basic income. Their two-year study was small, covering little over 500 hectares (1,235 acres) of forest. They did not measure changes in vegetation or soil quality, nor account for the influence of any separate projects that might have been affecting community behaviour. Despite these limitations, they say the early results have excited the cash-for-conservation network of civil society organisations. “Yes, this is an experimental pilot and and we could do with something much larger,” Howard said. “But this is very pioneering. My hope is that the trade-off between scale and innovation tips in this direction.”

headline: Why have countries been pushing for a vital global climate report to be delayed?
trail_text: Saudi Arabia, Russia and China among those claiming developed countries have skewed findings of IPCC review
body_text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change suspended an important meeting on Friday in Addis Ababa without setting out a firm timetable for its next report. The world’s governments are due to meet in less than a month for the Cop31 climate summit, and this leaves the future of scientific advice to governments on the climate in doubt. What has happened? The IPCC – the UN-convened body of the world’s leading climate scientists – met for a week but, despite progress in many areas, was unable to come to agreement on the substantive issue of setting a launch date for its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of climate science. The seventh assessment report, known as AR7, was expected to be published in 2028, seven years after the last report in 2021. But some want this timetable to be delayed to 2029, or later. Who wants a delay and why? A loose group of governments led by Saudi Arabia, Russia and India, and also including China and Kenya, have raised objections to publishing the report in 2028, arguing that climate science is dominated by developed countries, which they say has skewed its findings. But many scientists, and experts, worry that a delay would prevent AR7 being used to inform the next round of pledges of emissions cuts, due to be discussed by governments at the Cop33 climate summit in late 2028. Under the timetable set out by the 2015 Paris agreement, 2028 is a crucial year as it will be the second “global stocktake”, by which governments’ pledges on emissions are scrutinised to ensure they are in line with the goal of holding temperature rises to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Saudi Arabia has a long history of obstructing climate action, including seeking to water down previous IPCC reports, and has employees of its oil company and scientists with oil links on the IPCC committees. Would a delay enable more science from developing countries? Most of the science that will be in AR7 has already been published and is now under review. IPCC reports take years to compile, combing nearly every possible source of data, and that is done at an early point in its reporting cycle. Establishing new sources at this late point is more difficult. The IPCC argues that it already takes pains to include scientists from around the world and keeps a critical eye on equity to ensure against developed country bias. Much of the basic science it relies on is based on the global workings of the climate system, and understanding the underlying physics and chemistry, which do not differ from developed to developing countries. Critics also point out that Saudi Arabia, Russia, China and India are all powerful economies with well-established scientific institutions and research bases – if they wanted to produce scientific models themselves, they could have done so by now, or could have provided financial assistance to other developing countries to do so. One possible compromise is for the IPCC to start working now on new ways to bring in more science from the developing world, and undertake a critique of its processes to that end, while keeping to the 2028 timetable for the first part of its four-part report, which deals with the underlying physical science, and allowing the other parts – which cover the impacts of climate breakdown around the world, and solutions to it – to be delayed. What do civil society activists think? They are divided. Some are against a delay and view it as a danger to progress on cutting emissions. Some leading figures support it, arguing that whose research informs the science, and whether scientists from developing countries can participate meaningfully, is as important as speed. Others have issued statements deploring the row while carefully not taking sides. Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, said: “It is deeply frustrating that governments have failed to agree a way forward. Developing countries must have a meaningful voice in shaping that science, and wealthy nations must provide the funding needed to make that possible. But legitimate concerns about fairness cannot become an excuse for endless delays.” Oscar Soria, director at the Common Initiative group, said: “The failure to agree the timeline is not a procedural detail, it has real consequences.. The answer is not to choose between urgency and equity, but to provide the resources and support needed to achieve both.” What happens now? A group of 117 scientists, many of them from developing countries, including several from China and one from India, have written an open letter vowing to push ahead with their work. “Our message to governments and to the world is simple: we will keep working,” they wrote. “Equity is built into how our assessment is being drafted. Author teams are working from a far wider evidence base than in AR6. It includes literature from the global south, non-English sources, grey literature and Indigenous knowledge and local knowledge.” The IPCC’s chair, Jim Skea, has also pledged to reconvene as soon as possible. The issue is certain to come up at the Cop31 talks in Turkey next month, where governments will be asked what they are doing to show a sense of urgency in tackling the climate crisis, in the face of what is likely to be the strongest El Niño in decades, supercharged by global heating, and likely to cause huge amounts of damage – in developed and developing countries.

headline: The pest I’ll never forget: the maggots that rained down like hail
trail_text: The record-breaking heat in London, in summer 2022, resulted in an appalling problem in my neighbourhood – which one man took on, armed only with a jet wash
body_text: It was that terrifying summer in 2022 when London reached 40C. I was staying in a friend’s flat while she was away for a year, a former housing association property where the living room ceiling permanently had a hole in it. Each day, the air felt thicker and the leaves looked more limp. Dust clung to every surface. With no wind, the stench of the bins lingered. I’d nicknamed the guy next door “Techno Guy” because his life’s great pleasure appeared to be sitting in the driver’s seat of a parked red convertible, stereo on full volume, revving the engine but going nowhere. Maybe it was to preserve his car battery, maybe it was to get away from his wife. His music genre of choice, Shazam told me, was Romanian techno (though he was also fond of the Cher megamix). He smoked constantly, each drag like a first breath. The sound of him hawking up phlegm in the morning became a kind of alarm clock. One Sunday, I was working from home and the smell of the barbecue had been going since breakfast – long rows of sausages, chicken, chops. I popped on my noise-cancelling headphones, thinking the couple next door were settling in for a big party, but later in the afternoon I realised it was just the two of them, having a magnificent feast. “Good on them,” I thought. A few days later, the heat became unbearable – then record-breaking. I wasn’t alone in taking an umbrella with me if I left the house. It was pressing and cloying. The bins, meanwhile, had reached a crisis state – the smell from next door’s in particular was so heinous I’d learned to hold my breath when I left the front door until I’d cleared them. The day it happened was alarmingly quiet. No techno, no Cher, not a single rev of the engine. I looked out the window and saw Techno Guy, his torso hidden, elbows-deep in his wheelie bin, groaning like an animal in pain. There was a small but growing pile of bags next to him – all torn and mangled, a brownish sludge seeping out of them – the remnants of the barbecue. At first I thought the sacks were moving, before realising it was a swarm of bluebottles creating a halo. My neighbour disappeared briefly, and returned carrying a jet washer. There was splat, a yell and a blossom of what looked like rice grains were blasted into the air. With steady horror, I realised what had been breeding in the depths of my neighbour’s bin, and what had compelled him to empty it and – for some incomprehensible reason – attack it with pressurised water. Maggots. Hundreds – maybe even thousands – of maggots, propelled into flight and falling on windows, walls, cars, gardens, hedges, pavements and bins all around. I thanked the universe I’d kept my window closed, as they landed on the windowsill, still wriggling their last wriggle. Some neighbours obviously thought that rain had finally come in the form of hail. They opened their doors to see. And then they too were hit by the unfolding horror. I’m sure someone yelled, but we were all in a sort of stasis. There stood the neighbour, stray maggots in his hair and on his face, before he went inside to fetch the dustpan and brush.

headline: Country diary: A species brought to the edge of extinction, recovering in the fens
trail_text: Ouse Fen, Cambridgeshire: The great egret’s story is remarkable, as is the conversion of this low-grade agricultural land into one of the richest wetlands in Britain
body_text: In keeping with this region’s summer of torrid heat and drought, the field by the path was an expanse of burnt, dead thistles. What was totally unexpected were the 13 great egrets among it. Ironically, the birds may well be here as a consequence of the climate crisis, but their appearance in a parched brown expanse felt strange. First, they are creatures of freshwater marsh and routinely hunt fish. Second, great egrets are the size of grey herons, but pure white, aside from lemon eyes and dagger-like beaks of pale autumnal orange. What was weirdest of all was the gestalt whole; the way they threaded through that horizon of brown, long necks extending and retracting like winding snakes, and all this gleaming intensity focused on catching voles. Then a bird would fly, the white rope of its neck rising, followed by a ragged cloak of wings, turning eventually to the stolid beat of heavy flight. What is perhaps strangest of all – although birdwatchers have long since normalised those developments – is that here’s a species that was brought to the edge of extinction by the Victorian trade in feathers for haute couture. The species slowly recovered and expanded massively in Europe until it colonised our shores at the beginning of the century. It started to breed in 2010, and by 2019 there were 24 nesting pairs. But the winter total may reach four figures. Great egrets hunting in a Cambridgeshire field of dead vegetation might be a good news story. Yet the wider tale of Ouse Fen is astonishing. In an innovative partnership between a gravel-extraction business and the RSPB, the whole floodplain has been gradually converted from low-quality agricultural land into one of the richest, most dynamic wetlands in Britain, whose total area will be 3,000 hectares (7,410 acres). It is already hoaching with wetland wildlife such as water voles and bitterns, spined loaches and marsh harriers. Extensive archaeological work on the other parts of the site has revealed that its most abundant bone material from the Neolithic is remains of beavers and dalmatian pelicans. Given this evidence of its past, who would dare predict what its future might be? • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order at guardianbookshop.com and get a 15% discount • The Nature of Seeing by Mark Cocker is published by Vintage at £20. headline: ‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline
trail_text: As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps
body_text: Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, a study has found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia. Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive. The data, which covers 88% of bee and hover fly species across the continent, suggests pollinator communities have been reshaped by the “gradual loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few”, according to the scientists. They warned of “deeper functional disruptions” if existing trends were not addressed. Nearly 90% of wild flowering plants, as well as more than three-quarters of major food crop types, depend in part on animal pollination. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization has warned the decline of pollinators sets off a chain reaction that threatens wildlife and weakens the ability of ecosystems to withstand climate change and environmental stress. Carlos Martínez-Núñez, an ecologist at the Spanish National Research Council and lead author of the study, said the findings showed that biodiversity loss could remain hidden behind apparently stable species numbers, “giving us a crucial opportunity to act before further declines occur”. “The fact that some species are increasing today does not mean they will remain winners as climate change and habitat loss intensify,” he added. The findings come as diplomats gather in Yerevan for the 17th UN conference on biodiversity. The summit, known as Cop17, will focus on the conservation and sustainable use of the natural world, and the shared benefits of its genetic resources. The study found 91% of the species logged over the last century had also been recorded at least once in the modern period, between 2001 and 2020. Although this suggests as many as 9% of species could have been wiped out in Europe, many of the species not spotted recently occur only rarely in the historical record, and the researchers said they “do not expect widespread extinctions to have occurred yet”. However, the species’ occupancy – the probability of being found at a given site – had mostly fallen. Ainhoa Magrach, an environmental researcher at the Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3), who was not involved in the study, said it “confirms what has long been suspected: many pollinator species are losing populations, and the decline is not affecting all of them equally”. “Until now, most of the evidence came from a few north-western European countries, such as the UK, Belgium and the Netherlands,” she said. “This work shows that the pattern extends across the continent, although some regional differences exist.” Wildlife is dying out at an unprecedented rate as humans destroy habitats, spray pesticides, and warp the weather with planet-heating pollution. Despite far-reaching consequences for humanity, including threats to food systems and further breakdown of the climate, governments have not met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created in Rio in 1992. The Cop17 summit is expected to focus on assessing progress toward this decade’s targets, which include protecting 30% of land and sea, reforming $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies and restoring 30% of the planet’s degraded ecosystems.

headline: Stop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MP
trail_text: Exclusive: Chris Hinchliff urges environment watchdog to block rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in one of UK’s most protected areas
body_text: The environment watchdog is being urged to intervene in “cash to trash” planning rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in the Norfolk Broads despite the damage to one of the UK’s most environmentally protected areas. Labour’s flagship planning reforms allow damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked if developers pay into a central nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date. These environmental delivery plans (EDPs) have been called “cash to trash” by critics, who say they roll back decades of environmental law and are a “licence to kill nature”. The Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected biodiversity hotspot that is home to more than a quarter of the UK’s rarest plants and animals, is the guinea pig for the first EDP. Developers will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – and in return get permission to build 15,780 new homes in the Broads. The government’s nature adviser, Natural England, which created the plan, states the development will cause environmental harm in the form of physical, chemical, hydrological and biological damage to the habitats and rare species from increased nitrogen and phosphorus pollution. The Broads are already in ecological decline and require cuts of 91-97% in nutrient pollution to recover. Chris Hinchliff, the Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, is calling on the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP) to intervene and stop the approval of the plan. He said the first EDP – which will be used as a blueprint for others – is in breach of the requirements of the government’s Planning and Infrastructure Act, is not based on the best available science and does not address pollution. In a letter to Natalie Prosser, the chief executive of the OEP, he said: “Unless the OEP acts now, those failures will be locked into the first plan of its kind and repeated in every future EDP that follows. “On Natural England’s own figures, the conservation measures it funds would leave about 83% of the extra nitrogen and up to 61% of the extra phosphorus going into the water, every year and permanently. These are protected sites that the plan itself says need pollution inputs cut by up to 97% to recover,” he said. Hinchliff said measures that would have reduced nutrient pollution from the new homes, such as upgrading septic tanks, using small-scale underground treatment plants for homes not connected to the mains sewers and planting riverside buffer strips, were not included in Natural England’s EDP. “In their place, the plan relies on indirect measures: fen cutting, deer control, catch-dyke works, removing one weir and restoring one kilometre of river,” he said. “A plan that leaves most of the pollution unaddressed, that ‘locks in’ ecological degraded status, does not ‘address’ the harm in any ordinary sense of the word,” he added. Ministers say the EDPs are needed to unblock growth as they pursue a target to build 1.5m new homes by the end of this parliament and are a “win-win” for nature and economic growth. The nature restoration fund, they say, will deliver coordinated, larger-scale conservation measures rather than piecemeal offsets. Broadcaster Chris Packham, who is supporting the campaign against the Norfolk EDP by the charity WildFish, said environmental laws fought for over decades would be cancelled at the stroke of a pen. “The Norfolk Broads are among Europe’s most precious wetlands: swallowtails and fen orchids, bitterns booming in the reeds and lamprey and bullhead in the gravels of the Wensum, one of England’s finest chalk rivers,” said Packham. “But … they are drowning in pollution and the government has devised a cunning scheme to pour in a whole lot more.” The push for growth comes as the UK is in a nature crisis: wild bird populations have fallen to their lowest level since records began, with nearly half of species in decline, hedgehog numbers have plummeted by 66% and sewage, agricultural runoff and chemicals have left rivers suffering with a toxic cocktail of pollution. The Norfolk Broads EDP is out to consultation, which ends on 27 October. The Wildlife Trusts said the EDP would allow phosphorus from new homes to increase existing pollution levels on the rivers Yare, Bure and Wensum – a delicate chalk stream – without sufficient action from developers to mitigate for the impact. “Even minor increases could be enough to tip the health of these rivers over the edge, with calamitous consequences for the Norfolk Broads,” said Matthew Browne, the head of public affairs at the Wildlife Trusts. Bradley Tooze, the nature restoration fund director at Natural England, said: “The environment delivery plan aims to deliver better outcomes to protect the precious habitats of the Norfolk Broads while enabling sustainable development, including through river restoration measures and wetland habitat creation. “We welcome all views on our proposals and encourage stakeholders to share their expertise to help shape this new approach to nature restoration.” A government spokesperson said: “The aim of this environmental delivery plan is to protect and boost the natural environment. It’s based on the latest evidence and has been scrutinised by a scientific panel including independent experts. We welcome contributions to the ongoing consultation where people or organisations have views about how best to secure the aims we all share – protecting and restoring nature at a scale the status quo isn’t delivering.”

headline: Four years ago countries made a historic deal to save nature. Is it dead in the water?
trail_text: So far not a single target of the plan has been met. As negotiators convene for Cop17, the pressure is on to find a way to honour the commitments made at previous summits
body_text: Passersby could smell the dead fish before they saw them. In August, more than 3,000 pike, roach, carp and rudd were found lifeless along the River Wensum in Norwich. Some gasped for air in their final moments, desperate for the oxygen that heatwave conditions had depleted in the water. Investigators believe that the die-off was triggered by heavy rainfall that flushed through high concentrations of pollution at a time when wildlife were already struggling. The 45-mile (70km) chalk river is one of about 250 in the country. They are a geological accident almost unique to Britain – and one of Earth’s rarest habitats. They emerge from chalk aquifers and are home to species such as freshwater shrimp, otters and stoneflies, also providing drinking water for millions of people. But just 11 have formal protection, with many ravaged by sewage pollution and overextraction. The Norfolk river is one of the few that does have legal protection, but it is in poor ecological health. “We are a world away from the crystal clear, free flowing and mineral-rich waters they could, and should be,” says Eliot Lyne, head of the Norfolk Wildlife Trust. This decade was meant to signal a change in humanity’s relationship with the natural world. At the end of 2022, nearly every government on Earth committed to an ambitious deal to better protect the world’s rapidly disappearing biodiversity at a summit in Montreal, Canada. Negotiators shook hands on targets that included protecting 30% of the planet for nature, restoring nearly a third of the planet’s most degraded ecosystems, and reforming at least $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally harmful subsidies. Some scientists say that we are living through the largest loss of life since the time of the dinosaurs, putting a million species at risk of extinction. This time, humanity is the meteor. The Montreal agreement was the response. But four years later, governments look almost certain to miss nearly all of the deal’s targets – potentially continuing the record of never having met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. The UK, one of the loudest voices demanding ambition in Montreal, is on track to meet just three of the 23 targets by the end of the decade. This week, countries gather at Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, to decide what to do next. On the eve of the summit, at the launch of a report showing just how far off track the world is on meeting those commitments, António Guterres, secretary general of the UN, warned that lack of progress means “the war on nature has not ended” and that “nature will not survive on good intentions”. Following this, in an address to leaders at an event in Armenia, Guterres once again emphasised the importance of action on subsidies in particular. “Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said. “They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.” “There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, former UK government minister when the deal was reached. “That’s where we are today.” British conservationists point to a growing gap between government rhetoric and action. “The UK is back on the international stage on nature,” then environment secretary Steve Reed declared while standing under the skeleton of a blue whale at the Natural History Museum in the first few months of the Starmer government. Since then, the government has weakened rules on biodiversity net gain in England, slashed tens of millions of pounds of funding for rainforest protection schemes as part of aid cuts, and rejected an outright ban on bottom trawling in marine protected areas. No new sites of special scientific interest have been designated by Natural England to protect rare wildlife and habitats since 2023. “For us to go around the world telling other countries that they must achieve these targets without us having a plan how to deliver them at home is a form of neocolonialism,” says Craig Bennett, head of The Wildlife Trusts. “We’ve got to pull our socks up and get serious about delivery at home. We are the nation of Sir David Attenborough. We are animal and nature lovers.” A UK government spokesperson said it has backed a nature recovery and climate resilience with £7bn of funding, and implemented new powers to tackle water pollution, fund species recovery and support international conservation work. The UK has also reinstated its climate aid commitments, apparently abandoned earlier this year, pledging around £6bn of international climate finance from the aid budget over the next three financial years, with around a quarter expected to be spent on nature. Jonathan Hall, managing director of Conservation International UK, told the Guardian: “Re-instating the ditched goal for international nature funding as part of UK climate aid is smart politics, given UK public support, and a smart investment in our global security and resilience in the face of ecosystem collapse. This very welcome re-commitment now needs to be accompanied with increased transparency so we can ensure this approximately £1.5bn is disbursed as impactfully as possible.” But the urgency of the warnings has not changed. Earlier this year, a report by intelligence chiefs warned that ecological collapse is a national security risk, threatening the country with food shortages, economic strife and global disorder. But nature has been unable to escape the swirling global current of populist culture wars. In the Netherlands, efforts by the EU, in 2019, to crack down on nitrogen pollution to protect vulnerable ecosystems sparked nationwide farmer protests. While the discontent predates this decade’s biodiversity targets, the nature restoration law, the EU’s flagship package of laws resulting from the deal, also became embroiled in a bitter disagreement with the rightwing bloc in the European parliament, who tried to block the regulations due to the impact on agriculture. It was eventually passed, but only after it was substantially watered down. “In the Netherlands, they tried really hard and you saw this huge backlash. It’s an extremely sensitive issue politically,” says Steven Guilbeault, Canada’s former environment minister, who helped guide the 2022 negotiations alongside China’s environment minister, Huang Runqiu. “Governments are not always the best at communicating these complex policy pieces. It is easy for a critic to come up with a totally meaningless slogan that gets picked up on social media,” he says. The second presidency of Donald Trump has also been catastrophic for the conservation sector. Hundreds of projects had previously received support from Washington DC – from stopping illegal fishing in the Galápagos islands to backing the restoration of Gorongosa national park in Mozambique after the civil war – but Trump’s brutal cuts to USAID and other government agencies have meant funding evaporated overnight for many schemes. Many European nations have followed suit – despite signing up to a target to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade. The UK has cut back funding for the Darwin Initiative, removing eligibility for at least 89 countries earlier this year. Efforts to get the private sector to help have struggled; a new fund to get companies that use digital forms of biodiversity for commercial discoveries, which proponents had hoped would raise hundreds of millions each year, has so far raised just $6,000. It is not a universally gloomy picture. A majority of countries have responded to significant parts of the agreement. One estimate shows that countries could come close to meeting the land portion of the 30x30 target, and the deal has seen the formalisation of more Indigenous territories in many countries. Even bigger protected areas could come: places such as French Polynesia have established huge new marine parks. Countries such as Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort, bringing back the Caspian tiger. But the gap between what the science demands to avert ecological crisis and the current pace of change remains huge – and an urgent task for negotiators in Armenia. “Protection targets are falling short, promised national plans have yet to materialise, and committed finance is not reaching where it is needed. This is increasingly a shared dynamic across environmental processes: making commitments is the easy part; delivering on them is much harder,” said Li Shuo, director of China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “Sustainable change will only happen when countries internalise the urgency to act and translate commitments into domestic action. More than halfway through this decade, most countries are still moving far too slowly.” • Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features. • The Guardian’s climate forum 2026 On Tuesday, October 20, join Zoe Williams, and our panel of experts—including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.
