headline: Seabird numbers bounce back in Solent region after 2022 avian flu wipeout
trail_text: Conservation work by RSPB has led to recovery of terns, gulls, plovers and oystercatchers on English south coast
body_text: The colony of sandwich terns nesting at Pagham harbour, West Sussex, was completely wiped out by bird flu in 2022. But numbers have bounced back from zero to 756 breeding pairs in just three years after conservation work in the Solent region. Populations of breeding little terns, ringed plovers, oystercatchers and black-headed gulls have also increased along the same coastline. The turnaround comes thanks to work by RSPB staff and volunteers at the Pagham harbour nature reserve and similar efforts across 52,000 hectares (128,000 acres) of coastline and estuary between the south coast and the Isle of Wight. The sandwich terns produced 570 fledglings at Pagham harbour this summer, one of the largest colonies ever recorded in the Solent region. Numbers of black-headed gulls increased 10-fold from 51 fledglings in 2025 to 504 in 2026, while little terns were up from 21 last year to 34. Avocets also prospered, with 18 pairs nesting on newly created islands within a saline lagoon at Ferry Pool, which provided safer nesting areas for shoreline birds. Other conservation work included special fencing to exclude mammalian predators of ground-nesting birds such as foxes, monitoring for the presence of rats, in-person patrols to reduce predation and the selective removal of vegetation to make space for shorebirds to nest. Wez Smith, senior project manager for the RSPB, said: “In 2022, sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and Mediterranean gulls were hit severely by HPAI/bird flu, leading to the abandonment of their breeding colony at Pagham harbour. It’s taken several years of dedicated conservation action, but the situation began to ‘tern’ around last year, and the site is now thriving with record breaking populations using it.” Volunteers and rangers have also carried out patrols to raise awareness among visitors and local people of the vulnerability of ground-nesting birds to disturbance, with dog-friendly exercise areas provided away from the nesting birds. At nearby RSPB Medmerry, floating rafts for nesting birds have provided predator-free spaces for common terns and black-headed gulls to nest without being disturbed by dogs or boats, while rafts have also boosted common tern breeding numbers at West Hayling, another RSPB coastal reserve in Hampshire. The efforts are part of the Solent Seascape project, a long-term partnership of charities and institutions led by Blue Marine Foundation to restore coastal nesting sites, seagrass beds, oyster reefs and saltmarsh along the coast.

headline: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian village as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
trail_text: Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the world’s fastest-warming places
body_text: Residents of a remote village in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost. Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond. Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade. Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining settlement. “The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard. When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.” The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”. Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants. Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched. Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulphate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place. Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous”, government guidelines had to be followed. The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise”, he admitted, with some residents angry at the inconvenience. The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” may be needed. Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around. Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said. “In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources.” Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities. “These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the Arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.

headline: Burnham urged to launch inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
trail_text: Letter from 150 scientists, MPs and activists calls for action to protect lower-income and minority-ethnic communities
body_text: The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air pollution, 150 scientists, MPs and activists have urged. Research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that across England, lower-income areas have persistently higher levels of air pollution than wealthier areas. The same research found that minority-ethnic populations were exposed to air pollution levels that were about 6% higher than those experienced by white populations. In a letter coordinated by the charity Enact Equality and signed by 150 scientists, MPs and activists, including the climate activist Greta Thunberg, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been urged to hold a national inquiry into the impacts of air pollution on these groups. Exposure to air pollution is linked to heart disease, strokes, cancer, asthma and effects on lung development in children. Despite this, the letter says, the UK does not have a dedicated mechanism to address the health inequalities. Air pollution can come from a wide range of sources, from wood-burning stoves to industrial fossil fuel burning. But the leading threat to clean air is posed by traffic emissions, with petrol and diesel vehicles emitting a variety of toxic pollutants. Measures such as London’s ultra-low emission zone have had a significant impact on improving air quality, with children’s lungs found to have grown bigger and stronger as a result of the policy. While there has been marked progress in reducing air pollution in cities like London, new government data shows that in 2025, parts of London, Glasgow and Bristol still had illegal levels of air pollution. Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, the mother of a nine-year-old girl who became the first person in the UK to have air pollution cited on their death certificate, said a “failure of inaction by all the main political parties over so many years, has meant the UK population is exposed to illegal levels of emissions”. This warning comes as new data, obtained through freedom of information requests by the campaign group Mums for Lungs, shows that in 11 English cities and areas, including London, Greater Manchester and Birmingham, more than 200,000 children were taken to hospital with breathing difficulties in 2025. The research found that younger children were the most affected, with more than 120,000 babies and toddlers admitted to A&E or hospital. Children are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs are still developing and they breathe more air relative to their body size than adults. In the city of Manchester, there has been a stark increase in admissions of babies and toddlers, rising from 653 in 2023 to 1,072 in 2025. Mums for Lungs said the decision in 2023 by Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, to scrap plans for a clean air zone raised important questions about whether sufficient action was being taken to drive down pollution levels. Jemima Hartshorn, the campaign group’s founder, declared the situation an “air pollution emergency”. “Behind every number is a child who is struggling to breathe and a family looking for help. We cannot keep treating dirty air as inevitable or acceptable,” she said. A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “Air quality continues to improve over the longer term and while most air quality standards are being met, more action is needed to protect communities. “Our ambitious new targets will cut harmful particle exposure by nearly a third by 2030. Working together with local authorities will keep driving progress through clean air plans and robust monitoring.”

headline: Country diary: At this time of year, an ancient urge to forage kicks in
trail_text: Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: Rosehips, sweet chestnuts, sloes – there’s an order and a rhythm to their gathering, tied to the season and folklore
body_text: The government suggests stockpiling, and while tins and candles might prove useful, a more ancient urge kicks in for me at this time of year. Walking the hedgerows, the colours of jewels entice me, and my pockets fill with rosehips or glossy conkers. It’s ingrained. For a vast stretch of human history, we survived by foraging for food and medicine, even after agriculture became widespread. My blackberries are stashed in the freezer. Folklore advises picking them before Michaelmas on 29 September – or 10 October in old folklore, when the devil spits on them. It’s reasonable, thus avoiding mouldy or frosted fruit. There is an order and a rhythm. Next, rosehips. I plan to make syrup, rich in vitamin C, but it’s a faff. Instead, they end up dried in the oven, making healthy treats for the Connemara pony. Elderberries, tiny dark pearls that must be cooked before eating, are added to crumbles and apple pies. Sweet chestnuts are roasted on the wood burner. My favourite is the sloe gin ritual. Unlike blackberries, sloes are best picked after the first frost. In recent years, that’s not been until well into December, so I pick now and cheat the process by freezing them for 24 hours before adding them to gin and sugar. By Christmas, the syrupy liqueur will be ruby red. Ribena for grownups. Last year was a mast year of widespread bounty. You’d expect this autumn’s yield to be much lower, but it’s not. The hedgerows are once again heaving. Maybe it is a reaction to a summer of drought, a panic effort in case the main plant does not survive. I’m always mindful of taking what is not mine, but this year, more than usual. The land I have walked for my lifetime is for sale. As tenants, we’ve always had the same family of excellent landlords. Our position is secure – the tenancy is fixed for three generations, and the current landlords assure us the farm will only be sold to someone with a respect for conservation and the communities that love it. The air is cooler today, with the promise of much-needed rain. My stockpiling complete, I’m ready to face winter and all that it may bring. Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

headline: Cop17 at a glance: everything you need to know about the UN’s nature summit
trail_text: This month’s biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, aims to push governments to meet the 23 targets agreed at Cop15 in 2022
body_text: This month, nearly every country on Earth will return to the question of how to stem the rapid destruction of the natural world. Humans are driving it, but so far we have not found a way to stop it. In late 2022, governments reached an ambitious once-in-a-decade deal to better protect nature amid scientific warnings that the planet is going through the largest loss of life since the extinction of the dinosaurs. Now, they are assessing their progress on the targets for the first time. What is Cop17? Every two years, signatories to the UN convention on biological diversity (CBD) hold a summit. The convention is one of three created at the Earth Summit in Rio in 1992 alongside climate change and desertification (the latter’s Cop17 having been held in Mongolia in August). The diversity Cop covers three main areas: conservation of the natural world, its sustainable use, and how to share the benefits of its genetic resources. This year will be the 17th time that signatories have formally met, where the main focus is assessing progress on this decade’s targets such as protecting 30% of land and sea for nature, reforming $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies, and restoring 30% of the planet’s degraded ecosystems. Governments have never met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created in Rio in 1992, and there has been a big push to make sure that the next years until the 2030 deadline are different. When and where is it? Who is in charge? Armenia is the host for Cop17, which will take place in the capital, Yerevan, between 19 and 30 October. They are tasked with corralling governments to take action on their weak progress towards the targets. Ahead of the summit, countries met in Nairobi to discuss their priorities for the summit, concluding that they are off track on every single one of the 23 targets they agreed in Montreal in 2022. In Armenia, environment ministers must decide what they are going to do about it. But it will be a challenge: the last biodiversity summit, Cop16 in Cali, Colombia, ended in disarray with no clear agreement on key topics after negotiations ran out of time. Another round of talks were needed in Rome to finish the meeting. Are the 2030 biodiversity targets out of reach? Not quite. It may seem like history is repeating itself, but there are signs of progress on some targets. The aim of protecting 30% of Earth for nature is the headline target this decade, inspired by the Harvard biologist EO Wilson’s vision of protecting half of the planet for the long-term survival of humanity. According to one estimate, governments are close to reaching this number for land, so far agreeing to place 27.5% of terrestrial areas under protection as nature reserves, national parks and other areas. But the target is not about simply creating new protected areas on paper: it emphasises effective conservation management of areas that are particularly crucial for the healthy functioning of ecosystems, such as wetlands, rainforests, grasslands and coral reefs. Other targets have seen almost no progress. An aim to reform and repurpose $500bn of environmentally damaging subsidies has received almost no action from governments. From tax benefits given to fossil fuel companies to state support for destroying rainforests in order to expand agricultural frontiers, governments remain a major driver of biodiversity loss. What might an ambitious deal at Cop17 look like – and what might prevent it? In terms of the latter, in a word: money. Governments need to do more – and fast – if they want to meet some of this decade’s targets. “This is a really important opportunity for parties to do a serious course correction,” said Guido Broekhoven, head of multilateral policy at the World Wide Fund for Nature, adding that countries need to commit to concrete actions to get the world back on track. But the world has changed a lot since the deal was reached in 2022, when there was enthusiastic support for action to better protect nature after the Covid-19 pandemic. While the US is not a signatory to the UN convention on biological diversity, it was a major funder of conservation through USAID, which has been dramatically cut by the Trump administration. Britain and other European countries have also curtailed their funding for conservation around the world. Developing countries have long been clear that there cannot be more ambition on conservation without extra resources. Without funding – not just agreed, but delivered – it is unlikely there will be more progress on achieving this decade’s targets. Some countries – such as Norway and Sweden – have paid up, but others are slower to do so, research has shown. “Japan stands out as a very large economy that is not putting much in terms of international nature finance forward,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of the Campaign for Nature. Private finance for biodiversity has also been falling since 2022. In 2025, the Cali Fund was launched to encourage private companies that benefit from nature’s genetic resources to contribute to conservation. It remains virtually empty. As on Monday, at the start of Cop17, it has received just $10,656 in commitments, of which $7,085 has been deposited – far short of a target to raise $1bn annually. Another challenge is the sheer volume of issues negotiators will need to thrash out. “It’s a very busy agenda,” said Catherine Weller, Fauna & Flora’s director for global policy. “There’s a genuine risk that they might not get through it all.” Additional reporting by Rebecca Ratcliffe

headline: EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds
trail_text: Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriers
body_text: The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerous Pfas compounds – Pfoa and Pfos. The EPA has found that virtually no level of exposure to either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies Pfoa as “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoa has been found to leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m barriers annually for plastic containers used across the US economy. The containers present an “ongoing serious and ongoing threat to public health,” said Kyla Bennett, a former EPA scientist who is now science policy director with the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (Peer) non-profit. Inhance has denied that the chemical leaches out in measurable levels, and told the Guardian in a statement that any Pfoa from its products are an “impurity”. The EPA has written that the company is “manufacturing” Pfas. The “phase-out” was put in place after documents made public during landmark early 2000s litigation on DuPont’s Pfas pollution in West Virginia laid bare the ubiquitous chemicals’ dangers and serious health risks. In 2015, facing intense pressure to act, the EPA reached an agreement with eight Pfas producers to “phase out” production of Pfoa and Pfos, a similar chemical produced by 3M. Though the agency stopped short of a ban, the “phase out” was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution. Officials often repeated the claim that the chemicals had been phased out, giving the impression that they were no longer produced or used in the US. Last month, the EPA quietly changed wording on its website that claimed Pfoa and Pfos had been phased out. In fact, both have been produced in the US this whole time, and at levels that independent science suggest are quite high. The EPA site previously stated: “The manufacture and import of Pfoa has also been phased out in the United States.” It now reads: “Quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported, and used by companies …” The change was made in response to a complaint filed by Peer, which pointed out that the EPA was allowing Pfoa to be produced in the US. Under the Information Quality Act, data and information made public by federal agencies must be complete and accurate. “They were giving the false impression and saying, ‘Nothing to see here because Pfoa is not being produced in the US,’” Bennett told the Guardian. “But that was demonstrably false, and now they have admitted it.” An epidemiological panel convened during the West Virginia DuPont case found Pfoa and Pfos probably causes cancer, heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease. The panel’s findings were the scientific basis for the phase-out. The EPA did not immediately provide a comment to the Guardian. Inhance in its statement to the Guardian stressed that there was never a ban in place and it was not one of the eight companies that agreed to stop producing Pfoa. The reversal underscores why phase-outs are inadequate, and the EPA needs to put in place bans, Bennett said. “If you have a chemical and there’s no safe level of it, then why on earth would you allow it to be manufactured?” she said. “This all makes perfect sense if you understand the reality that the EPA is an arm of industry, especially under the Trump administration.” The EPA’s reversal marks the latest twist in a six-year legal battle over Inhance’s Pfoa-infused containers. The EPA seemed unaware that Pfas were being “manufactured” during plastic container barrier production until late 2020 testing by Peer found high levels of Pfas in pesticides stored in Inhance bins. The subsequent EPA investigation unearthed wide-scale contamination of plastic containers, prompting the agency to subpoena Inhance for information. It publicly reminded the plastics industry that companies must submit for a safety review if they manufacture Pfoa. Inhance dismissed the agency’s evidence and claimed its containers did not leech Pfoa, but the EPA disagreed, again ordering Inhance in March 2022 to “immediately cease” production. Two weeks later, Inhance put out a press release stating that its products did not “impart” Pfoa, and it did not cease production. Subsequent EPA testing found the containers still contained Pfoa. Facing legal pressure from Peer, the EPA by December 2023 again ordered Inhance to stop making the containers. That ban was overturned by a federal appeals court. Peer later sued, but the case was dismissed because a federal judge ruled that the group lacked standing. In its statement, Inhance said that it made adjustments to reduce by 90% the level of Pfoa “impurities”. “Published peer-reviewed third-party risk assessments conclude that estimated exposure does not present an unreasonable risk to human health or the environment,” Inhance’s chief commercial officer, Patricia van Ee, wrote. “We have shared our process data with EPA throughout its review.” The EPA appears to have given up on enforcing the phase-out and legally pressuring Inhance. Still, the EPA maintained on its website that Pfoa had been phased out of production, drawing the formal complaint from Peer. In a response dated 18 September, EPA assistant administrator for chemical safety and pollution prevention, Douglas Troutman, wrote: “In response to Peer’s request, the EPA is updating its websites.” The update also notes that Pfos is in US production in some “limited, ongoing uses”. “This rare touch of candor by EPA is welcome, but it does not address the free flow of toxic Pfas saturating our food, water and soil,” Bennett said. “Now that EPA has admitted that these two legacy Pfas are still manufactured in the US, it is past time to take effective enforcement action.” This article was amended on 18 October 2026 to correct Patricia van Ee’s title, and the story previously stated that Inhance manufactures plastic containers. They make the containers’ barriers.

headline: The next ayahuasca? Gabon fights to protect sacred plant from US drug companies
trail_text: Iboga root, central to several Gabonese ritual traditions, is believed to have huge potential for use in treating addiction and some mental illnesses
body_text: The temple is dark, its sandy floor edged with candles. People sit shoulder to shoulder beneath palm fronds hung from the rafters. Through the night, they swallow what they have come here for: a bitter root bark called iboga. Tabernanthe iboga is a slow-growing central African rainforest shrub, the root bark of which has long been used in several Gabonese ritual traditions. In Gabon’s villages and forests, iboga is cultivated and sometimes gathered from wild populations, often collected under ritual conditions. But nothing in its cultural usage, at sites such as this temple on the outskirts of Libreville, is comparable to the potential wave of demand fast approaching from abroad. A US executive order has turned a spotlight on ibogaine, a drug made from the plant, which pharmaceutical companies believe has huge potential for use in addiction treatment. In the Bwiti (also known as Bwété) spiritual tradition, iboga is used in many different ways. Apollon Obolo, a practitioner of Misoko Bwiti, a branch concerned with healing and divination, describes the ceremony taking place that night, called Mubindu, as a way of lifting the burden carried by relatives and friends after a death. But, he stresses, iboga is only one part of the practice. “In Gabon, we don’t talk about iboga. We talk about Bwiti. Iboga is just an element,” he says. “For me, Misoko is like a microscope to see clearly about details in the life of someone.” Obolo believes it can “restructure” a person and resolve what ordinary medicine cannot. In Misoko, Obolo says, knowledge of iboga is received “from generation to generation”, and accumulated “time after time”. A 2012 report by Yann Guignon, an intercultural and sustainable development consultant and president of the NGO Blessings of the Forest, records practitioners describing wild iboga as something that must be considered in relation to the whole forest, including by following animals that eat the fruit. This stands in contrast to the interest now being taken by pharmaceutical companies. Ibogaine has a fast-developing reputation in addiction treatment, with early observational studies reporting sharp reductions in opioid withdrawal and craving after a single treatment. In a study published in 2024, 30 male US special operations veterans, most of whom were diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury, received ibogaine combined with magnesium. A month later, average PTSD, depression and anxiety scores had fallen by at least 81%, while disability scores moved from mild-to-moderate impairment into the “no disability” range. The study was small, uncontrolled and included complementary therapies, meaning it could not establish eﬃcacy. Its authors have called for further controlled trials. The former Texas governor Rick Perry has become one of ibogaine’s most visible political champions. Texas has granted $50m (£38m) for a multicentre trial, and on 18 April, the US president, Donald Trump, signed an executive order specifically naming “ibogaine compounds” and directing federal agencies to create a treatment pathway for eligible patients. A therapeutic economy already exists elsewhere: Beond, a clinic in Cancún, lists programmes costing from $13,500 to $19,500. *** Beyond the last paved streets in Libreville, Gabon’s capital, up a rutted hill and behind a concrete compound, stands the temple of Madame Djédjé Stéphanie Djoungounda, known as Maman Djédjé. The temple’s entrance is guarded by a painted mermaid. Djédjé specialises in Mbomba Ossoundo, a branch of the Mbomayano, which she describes as concerned with rebirth and restoration. It involves a plant she calls ikasô alongside small amounts of iboga administered during vigils. “We don’t heal only with ibogaine,” she says, standing among the iboga plants growing at her temple. “We heal with the whole iboga: the flower, the leaf, the bark, the trunk, the roots.” Not every dose of ibogaine abroad comes from Gabonese iboga. The molecule can be made semi-synthetically from voacangine, found in the related African tree Voacanga africana. But the iboga root bark is particularly in demand for ceremonial use, and for the manufacture of extracts containing several of its alkaloids. Even before the US announced its interest, demand had already begun to pose an ecological problem. Small amounts of root bark can be removed without uprooting the shrub, according to Guignon’s report. But commercial extraction can incentivise something faster: taking the entire root system, which yields more bark at once but kills the shrub. The report documents collectors doing exactly that – without replanting. Recognising the danger, Guignon’s organisation has worked with communities on iboga cultivation and conservation since 2015. For a species now discussed as pharmaceutical feedstock, the ecological ledger on iboga is startlingly thin. Lee White, who led Gabon’s national parks agency before serving as environment minister, calls wild iboga “rare and poorly studied”. His parks law-enforcement teams found evidence of severe local over-harvesting between Libreville and Cocobeach, as well as recurring problems around Mayumba and Lambaréné. White says he tried to initiate a study of iboga’s distribution and genetic variation, but was unable to secure financial backing for it. When asked why medicinal plant research in central Africa draws so little funding, Djédjé answers bluntly. “There isn’t any,” she says, suggesting that finance flows to higher-profile areas such as the Amazon. What did arrive, she says, were students sent from institutions to extract her remedies and “take the money themselves”. Eventually, she says, she stopped sharing with researchers. To Master Mulema, an initiator and scholar in the traditions of the Fang people, the plant’s vulnerability is clear. “Iboga can disappear,” he says. If it is to help humanity, “it must be surrounded by regulation”. From a Gabonese perspective, the story of iboga is potentially a familiar and depressing one: export the raw material and watch the high-value part of the supply chain form elsewhere, while the plant itself is pushed to the brink. In May this year, a government decree attempted to challenge that sense of fait accompli, recognising traditional knowledge associated with iboga as national heritage and requiring benefit-sharing in return for commercial use. Patent applications tied to iboga now must disclose the origin of the product concerned, and the decree also creates an iboga sovereign fund, financed in part by royalties and benefit-sharing agreements. On 18 September, Gabon’s council of ministers went even further, adopting a draft decree prohibiting the export of iboga and every derivative, in any form. The government says the measure is intended to protect the plant and the cultural knowledge attached to it. An export ban does not answer the question of who has the right to decide what happens next. There is no central Bwiti church to ask for official sanction. Tah Mombo, a Bwété Dissumba practitioner involved in efforts to marshall viewpoints from the many different traditions, explains the importance of Indigenous voices in the debate around the plant’s future: “We speak about our things, from our home, for us and by us.” Iboga is not the first plant medicine to become a global industry. Ayahuasca moved from Amazonian traditions into a worldwide retreat economy, followed by disputes over Indigenous authority, commercialisation and who should benefit. Gabon is hoping to avoid this by setting terms while the international ibogaine market is still being built. Ultimately, Obolo’s insistence that Bwiti, not iboga, is the key issue is a refocusing of the usual debate around natural resources. Ibogaine can be isolated and measured in milligrams, but the harder thing to protect is the culture that made the plant meaningful before anyone wanted the molecule. As world leaders prepare to travel to Armenia for Cop17, where the debate over biodiversity funding and benefit sharing will be central to negotiations, other countries with bioresources both known and as-yet-undiscovered will be watching with interest. Reporting for this article was supported by the Pulitzer Centre.

headline: US workers facing deadly heat embrace tactic that targets major brands’ reputations
trail_text: Program founded by tomato pickers has some of the strongest US worker protections – and its approach is being emulated by other groups
body_text: “It’s the kind of heat that makes you feel like you’re being dehydrated, like your skin is drying out,” said Lucas Benitez, after harvesting watermelons with his sons and wife this summer. “The heat that we had 30 years ago is not nearly the heat that we have today.” This summer was the hottest on record in the US, and most workers in fields, greenhouses and unconditioned indoor facilities still do not have heat protections on the job, putting their health at risk as the climate crisis is expected to make extreme heat more frequent and intense. Benitez began working in tomato fields in Immokalee, Florida, when he was just 16, and in the early 1990s went on to help found the Coalition of Immokalee Workers (CIW), named after the major tomato growing region in south-west Florida. Today, CIW’s Fair Food Program has some of the strongest heat protections for workers in the country, and its approach is being emulated by other groups – in the US and beyond – as federal, state and local efforts to protect people from extreme heat stall. The program’s protections were hard won after years of boycotts, hunger strikes and protests against food corporations, and now protect farm workers in dozens of crop types. The model, described as “market-based enforcement” by academics, works by targeting the reputation of the known brand-name of a company – say a fast-food retailer – to improve conditions rather than smaller entities in the supply chain. Retailers agree to pay a small premium to buy from farms that comply with a worker-protection code of conduct. Farms that violate the code can lose their preferred status, giving workers a powerful way to enforce protections without relying on government regulators. Miami-based WeCount is among the labor groups that are now adopting the Fair Food Program model for other hot, low-wage jobs. Worker organizations in dairy production in Vermont, construction in Minnesota, sugarcane production in India, and banana production in Ecuador have created similar human rights initiatives. Florida produces about 70% of all indoor plants sold in the US. The workers who grow these plants were exposed to temperatures over 100F (37.8C) this summer and reported heat-related symptoms and dehydration, said Oscar Londoño, the co-executive director of WeCount, a human rights organization led by immigrant workers and families in south Florida. “Workers feel like they’re on the verge of fainting,” Londoño said. “We have, unfortunately, far too many stories of heatstroke.” Extreme heat put other workers in danger this summer too. In September, 24-year-old Obed Azahel Hernandez Perez died from extreme heat exposure while harvesting sweet potatoes in Chickasaw county, Mississippi. And, last year, 47-year-old Marco Antonio Hernandez Guevera died after collapsing from the heat on his first day in the field at a tomato farm in Immokalee. In Texas, hospitals are seeing an increasing number of cases of kidney disease among outdoor workers, which research suggests could be linked to prolonged exposure to extreme heat. The state-level protection route For years, WeCount advocated for heat protections for workers at the state level. Despite largely being symbolic (it did not include enforcement or penalty measures), the legislation died in committee every year, Londoño said. In 2021, the organization, along with labor partners across the state, launched the “qué calor” campaign, meaning “how hot”, with the goal of securing heat protections for workers. Two years later, WeCount set its sights on passing a local ordinance. Unlike the drafted state legislation, the county bill had strong enforcement in the form of monetary penalties to make sure there was industry-wide compliance, Londoño said. The 19-page local ordinance included provisions when the heat index hit 90F (32.2C) for paid rest breaks, access to clean drinking water, and first aid procedures. In 2023, a five-member committee of Miami-Dade county commissioners voted 4-1 in favor of the ordinance and the full county commission passed the bill unanimously through first reading. But before the county commission’s final vote on the bill, the Florida state legislature blocked the local worker heat protection ordinance with a pre-emptive law banning local efforts to require heat protections for outdoor workers throughout the state. “It was devastating to see the legislature pre-empt commonsense protections,” Londoño said. “We believe every worker deserves these protections.” WeCount has also advocated for federal heat protections for workers through proposed Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) standards written under the Biden administration. “Unfortunately, it looks like that heat standard is stalled. Workers can’t depend on that,” Londoño said. Proposed legislation introduced last November by the Indiana representative Mark Messmer would block Osha from implementing the heat protections. Without federal heat standards, many people remain unprotected, said Roy McAllister, director of occupational safety and health at the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union (UFCW), which represents 1.2 million workers. Few slaughterhouses at meatpacking and poultry plants are air-conditioned, and workers are exposed to heat from lack of ventilation, hot steam, meat carcasses, salt tanks, steriliser tanks and ovens, he said. In warehouses and in grocery store receiving areas, some people work their shifts in areas that are hot, stuffy and lack adequate air circulation. “As we just saw, this is the hottest summer on record that we’ve ever had.” McAllister said. “It continues to get hotter every year. We’re starting to see more and more people exposed to high temperatures and there’s no federal protective measures to keep employers accountable.” A long fight for better conditions With today’s extreme heat, the Coalition of Immokalee Workers and growers within their Fair Food Program decided it was necessary for the tens of thousands of people in their program to have access to electrolytes on participating farms year-round. This summer, the CIW’s Fair Food Program added the new requirement to its heat protection standards in a matter of weeks, which already required participating growers to provide shade, cool drinking water, paid rest breaks, heat illness training for workers and supervisors, and the ability for workers to seek medical attention without fear of retaliation. But to get to this point – with 14 major participating food retailers, including Walmart, McDonald’s, Whole Foods and Trader Joe’s – workers in the Fair Food Program put pressure on retailers through protests and hunger strikes around the country. Benitez was among a group of Coalition of Immokalee Workers who held a hunger strike outside Taco Bell’s headquarters in Irvine, California, in 2003 in an effort to get the chain to agree to only buy tomatoes from farms that pay their pickers a living wage. “Taco Bell has a policy that it will not buy food from contractors that mistreat animals,” Benitez told the Guardian during his hunger strike in 2003. “All we are asking is that they have the same policy for humans.” At the same time, student-led organizations boycotted Taco Bell over the working conditions of tomato pickers, getting some of their universities to cut ties with the franchise. After three years of boycotts, Taco Bell agreed to the coalition’s demands in 2005. Later, the coalition took on McDonald’s, which agreed to pay more for tomatoes to increase the wages of pickers in 2007. WeCount is now in this phase of the strategy with its planting justice program and has set its sights on Costa Farms, one of the world’s largest indoor plant growers. The day after Labor Day, WeCount coordinated actions at Costa locations in Florida, South Carolina and Virginia. Costa Farms told the Guardian that the company has received requests to join WeCount’s planting justice program. “We take the underlying issues seriously, but the WeCount program’s core workplace protections are already part of Costa Farms’ existing systems and practices, including paid heat-prevention training, a comprehensive heat illness prevention plan, audited payroll and employee-controlled timekeeping systems, complaint-resolution processes and onsite medical support,” the company said in a written statement. “For more than six decades, Costa Farms has invested in the safety, training and development of our team members, and that commitment continues to shape how we care for and support our workforce today.” “We believe if Costa Farms becomes part of a new gold standard, it will set a precedent for others to do the same while signaling to the major retailers that growers are ready to adopt this program,” Londoño said. “If we can transform Florida, we can transform the entire industry.”

headline: The problem with telling people the world is ending
trail_text: In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?
body_text: These days, it’s easy to succumb to hopelessness. Whether you’re thinking about the climate crisis, the prospect of AI apocalypse, war or political turmoil, the list of challenges facing humanity can seem insurmountable. It certainly feels unprecedented, and much of it may be. The sense of impending doom, on the other hand, is nothing new. And what we have learned from the past is that doomerism can lead to paralysis. If everyone freezes, then nothing changes – but if we want to have a chance of mitigating some of the threats I’ve mentioned then action is what’s required. In 1947, The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists created an infamous magazine cover with a “Doomsday Clock”. The hands move closer to midnight whenever events push humanity a little closer to catastrophe. They move back when we make the world a little safer. The original setting was seven minutes to midnight, and the hands are now a mere 85 seconds away. The Doomsday Clock was a particularly memorable form of crisis communication. The idea was to wake people from their day-to-day routines and help them realise the grave risks facing us. As such, it stands in a long tradition of debate about how to inform, warn and inspire members of the public to take action. On one end of the spectrum are the doomers. These are often activists and whistleblowers who feel a genuine sense of dread about imminent disaster, and want to inspire the same alarm in others. Recently, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon made headlines by arguing that frontier AI models pose an existential risk to humanity. At the other end are critics who tend to dismiss these calls as either overblown or self-serving. These folks argue that hyperbolic claims either lead to needless panic or distract from more important issues. I find myself in a third camp of people who harbour sincere concerns about the problems facing humanity, but worry that feelings of dread will immobilise people. Inaction is a sensible response if you are led to believe that we are past the point of no return, or that the scope of the problem is so immense that anything you do won’t make a difference. The problem with doomerism isn’t necessarily that the risks are exaggerated, but that it may create a self-fulfilling prophecy – by engendering helplessness, rather than galvanising people. This aspect of human psychology has been well known for many years by experts on persuasion. When people hear messages designed to appeal to our fears, they can be moved to take action. But this only tends to work as a one-off, and only then when the messages convey a sense of efficacy – a belief that it’s still possible to make a difference. By contrast, if people are inundated with scary and overwhelming stories about the climate or AI, they tune out. Like the boy who cried wolf, those bearing these messages can quickly find themselves ignored. A big problem for us now, then, is that the modern information ecosystem tends to reinforce negativity. For decades, a core principle in the news business has been “if it bleeds, it leads”. This came from an understanding among journalists that humans are drawn to bad news. This principle now dominates what you see online. My colleagues and I looked at traffic to news stories on Upworthy.com. This was a website that became famous for conducting A/B tests of headlines to see which one drove clicks, and then using the most popular headline. We analysed 22,743 of these mini-experiments and found that each additional negative word in a headline increased clicks by 2.3%. Psychologists call this the negativity bias: bad is more attention-grabbing than good. So how does consuming these stories affect our behaviour? We tested the impact of negative messaging around climate in a massive study with 59,440 participants in 63 countries. We had climate experts create 11 different messages to determine exactly which of them changed beliefs and mobilised people to take real action. The messages included emphasising scientific consensus (for example, noting that “99% of expert climate scientists” agree on the facts), social norms (stating that a majority of people in each nation was concerned), consequences for one’s region (emphasising the increased frequency and severity of wildfires and floods) or the effects of climate change on future generations (asking participants to imagine writing a letter about their actions regarding the climate crisis that would be read by people decades from now). We also included a text loaded with doom and gloom that told participants: “If your anxiety about climate change is dominated by fears of starving polar bears, glaciers melting and sea levels rising, you are barely scratching the surface of what terrors are possible, even within the lifetime of a young adult today. And yet the swelling seas – and the cities they will drown – have so dominated the picture of climate change/global warming that they have blinded us to other threats, many much closer at hand and much more catastrophic …” This terrifying passage was the one that proved most effective at getting people to spread it on the internet or social media. But like other fear appeals, it failed in inspiring real action: it was the single worst message for getting people to make the time and effort to mitigate climate effects – by planting trees, for example. It also failed to increase belief in the climate emergency or support for climate policies. This absolutely doesn’t mean we should avoid sharing the facts about the climate crisis. The message that emphasised the overwhelming scientific consensus noted that the “Earth is warming and climate change is happening” due to human activity. It was more effective than negativity on every outcome we measured, except for sharing on the internet. It conveyed the facts in a sober manner, with the backing of 99% of climate scientists. What this shows is that, instead of making people feel inept and miserable, we need to take the exact opposite approach. Scientific consensus isn’t the only powerfully motivating message. My PhD student Danielle Goldwert has found that telling people about the potential emotional benefits of climate action – such as increased hope and connection – makes them significantly more likely to take action, be it political participation, advocacy, donating money to climate causes or changing their lifestyle. If we want to motivate people in the face of dire threats, we must give them a reason to hope. Without that, we are destined to doomscroll while the world burns. • Jay Van Bavel is a professor of psychology and neural science at New York University. Further reading Not the End of the World by Hannah Ritchie (Vintage, £18.99 Hope in the Dark by Rebecca Solnit (Canongate, £10.99) The Future We Choose by Christiana Figueres and Tom Rivett-Carnac (Vintage, £12.99)

headline: Heat pumps and insulation would cut UK living costs more than new oilfields, study suggests
trail_text: Warm homes plan would create 50,000 jobs, compared with about 1,100 for Rosebank oilfield, thinktank finds
body_text: Insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to cut the cost of living, create jobs and boost the UK’s economy than drilling for new oil, research suggests. The government’s £15bn warm homes plan, currently under threat of cuts as ministers seek budget savings, would slash £1bn a year from household energy bills across the UK, concentrated on those on low incomes, according to research by the thinktank E3G. It would also provide a £1.6bn yearly boost to the economy, and about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses. The Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, the analysis found. The jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of them – Equinor – an overseas investor. A decision on whether to give the green light to the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea was “imminent”, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said on Wednesday. A decision on Rosebank would take a little longer, she said. Labour promised in its 2024 election manifesto to halt new licensing for oil and gas, but Jackdaw and Rosebank could be exceptions because they were already in the licensing system. Equinor previously estimated 3,500 jobs would be created at peak for Jackdaw and Rosebank combined. Experts have repeatedly pointed out that new North Sea oil and gas would not bring down fuel prices or ease any supply constraints on the UK arising from the Iran war, because oil and gas are sold on international markets. Some proponents of drilling argue that the economic boost to the UK and tax revenues for the government are reasons to grant licences. But related research by WWF and the campaigning group Uplift shows that tax revenues are likely to be limited, given the concessions that drillers can expect. While the total profits from Rosebank for its backers, Equinor, Shell and Ithaca Energy, could be £1.5bn over its 25-year lifespan, the UK government faces a potential loss of £258m through tax breaks and incentives. Tax revenues from the North Sea were about £4bn in 2025-26, but upstream tax relief and support measures amounted to an estimated £3.26bn. As the North Sea is a basin in steep decline, tax revenues from drilling are projected to fall to about £100m by 2030. Decommissioning costs for drilling platforms are also a major factor: taxpayers are likely to be asked for £12bn as the North Sea’s infrastructure is dismantled. The warm homes plan, under which up to 5m homes would be insulated, would draw in a further £15bn in private investment, according to E3G, which would be spread across the country rather than concentrated in one area, in line with Andy Burnham’s pledge for economic growth “in every postcode”. E3G also estimates that delivering the warm homes plan in full would boost GDP by 0.08%, while AI modelling suggests Rosebank would add about 0.025% on average through its lifetime, assuming the average oil price returning to $70 a barrel from recent highs. If the UK taxpayer paid for decommissioning, this would outweigh any positive impact. James Huw Dyson, a senior researcher at E3G, said: “When the first cold snap rolls in, the public aren’t going to thank the government for cutting home insulation while giving big oil tax breaks to drill for polluting energy that keeps our bills high. If the government is serious about tackling the cost of living, and investing across the country, it should focus its attention on insulating homes and rolling out clean energy, which will cut bills and create good jobs across Britain at the same time.” Ten major unions wrote to the government on Thursday to oppose granting a licence to the Rosebank oilfield. Scores of Labour MPs also oppose the move, and 600 scientists wrote to ministers over the summer urging a rethink. Dhara Vyas, the chief executive of Energy UK, which represents the energy industry, said: “We need government to stick to its ambitions on electrification. Watering down the warm homes plan or making further changes to the zero emissions vehicle mandate sends mixed signals to a market that has been in a state of flux for far too long – these businesses cannot easily ramp up production again, and sadly for too many have already had to close.” The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero declined to comment on E3G’s findings or the future of the warm homes plan. A spokesperson for Adura, the joint venture between Equinor and Shell that owns Jackdaw and Rosebank, said: “Analysis has shown that approving Rosebank and other planned North Sea oil developments would support £35.3bn in UK economic value between 2026 and 2035. Rosebank alone represents private sector investment of £8.7bn, three quarters of which will be spent in the UK, and together with Jackdaw will contribute £4.1bn in additional tax revenue over the next decade.” These figures take in the company’s wider operations beyond Rosebank and Jackdaw, and also make assumptions about the wider supply chain and the spending of employees as economic benefits, which are uncertain. On the tax take, they do not take account of the large tax reliefs available, estimated at more than £2.4bn. Contrary to standard HM Treasury practice, Adura’s estimates do not appear to factor in a discount rate for future income.

headline: From little acorns … to his 1,000th article for the Guardian country diary
trail_text: As Mark Cocker approaches a landmark for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, he is still inspired by powerful encounters with nature
body_text: In the autumn of 1987, Mark Cocker sat in a field near Norwich and watched a jay burying acorns for the long winter ahead. He described the scene in his first country diary for the Guardian. Thirty-nine years on, some of those jay-planted acorns will be mature oaks now, and Cocker is completing his 1,000th diary for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper. In his next diary, he will reflect on the changing birdlife around Flint Clough, in the Peak District, where he first marvelled at rare birds aged 12 after devouring bird books in his bedroom. As a boy, he would find cuckoo, golden plover, ring ouzel and twite, a once-common bird which is now virtually extinct in England. On his latest visit a few weeks ago, he saw raptors he would have only dreamed of as a boy, “a whole slew of buzzards, two peregrines, two marsh harriers – the first I’ve ever seen in Derbyshire – and several red kites”. The Guardian country diary began in 1904 with the nature-loving dispatches of Thomas Coward, a retired textile bleacher from Cheshire. Today there is a diverse roster of about 30 diarists spread from Cornwall to the Cairngorms who include farmers, scientists, conservationists, a vicar, a thatcher and a forager, as well as writer-naturalists such as Cocker, who pens a fortnightly dispatch, usually from his local patch in Derbyshire. Despite honing his skills by working as a warden at Holkham national nature reserve in north Norfolk, while also becoming the first member of his family to attend university, where he studied English, Cocker says it took him 10 years to master the deceptively difficult craft of the diary – a compelling story about rural life in just 360 words. “You need quite a long apprenticeship to get it right because it’s so short,” he said. “It’s like a haiku. You’ve got to awaken the subject from its dormancy and get straight into the theme. And then the best diaries link it to something else. “You have a single shaft of light and, if you can, you excavate its relationship to the other parts. You have to often imply or adumbrate rather than specify. And it’s that connection between the part and the whole, the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.” For Cocker, who earlier this month published The Nature of Seeing, a collection of recent diaries alongside new essays exploring how we might experience nature more fully, the close observation required for appreciating nature is a discipline that benefits all writing. He points to the surprising number of literary greats who have also kindled a passion for wildlife, from Margaret Atwood to Vladimir Nabokov. Before he began writing, Cocker worked as a refuse collector, a road sweeper, a potato picker and, as a penniless student, posed nude for the local art college. His big break came after a conservationist friend wrote to the Guardian to complain about the surfeit of inconsequential diaries about cricket matches. “She said: ‘The Guardian needs to get its boots and hat and coat on, and get out into the wild,’” remembered Cocker. Cocker did that, writing early columns on chiffchaffs, silver-studded blue butterflies and sparrowhawks, before becoming a regular when the legendary Lakeland diarist Enid Wilson fell ill. Between them, Wilson and Cocker have covered a span of 76 years. Cocker shrugs off his own skills as a naturalist, which he says would be completely normal in another culture or era. In The Nature of Seeing, he writes about Inuit fishers who navigated home through the fog by recognising the subtly different patterns of snow bunting songs which corresponded to particular sections of the (invisible) coastline. “That is the level of attention to the living world which we’ve lost and need to recapture,” he said. He never steps outside with a preordained list of subjects to write about but seeks powerful encounters. “I have to feel the article viscerally. I have to feel that it moved me. That’s really where the experience begins and ends. If it doesn’t engage you personally, if you aren’t affected by it, the diary is a cheat.” After Phil Gates retired recently following nearly 40 years on the diary, Cocker is now the longest-serving diarist. The country diary editor, Paul Fleckney, said: “Mark is a gift to the diary. What you get from him is hyper-detailed knowledge with one eye on the bigger picture, and all written with such persuasion. Beneath it is a deep, deep love for the natural world, but also a rare kind of indefatigability. It’s as if all he wants to do is open people’s eyes and ears to the wonders around us, and it is infectious.” In a time of climate and biodiversity crises, as overconsumption imperils humanity, Cocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come. “Meaning has been poured on to the diary because it is a repository now for a sense of the impending crisis which assails all life,” he said. “We’re now recognising that the intensifying nature of capitalism, the rise of the right, migration, climate change, drought, starvation, overpopulation – everything is to do with one meta-story, and that is our relationship with the rest of life. The diary’s become a valuable philosophical place for big ideas to be shared.” The Nature of Seeing by Mark Cocker (Vintage Publishing, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

headline: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
trail_text: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation
body_text: US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth. Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found. US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation. The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States. In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December. Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States. It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026. The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill. Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondelēz eight meetings. Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House. Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR. The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”. Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance. “Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.” Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.” US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR. The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.” The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said. The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European Union Deforestation Regulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.” Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.

headline: How the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hope
trail_text: In an extract from his new book, the nature historian explains how technology could help the seabird survive
body_text: For centuries human beings have exploited puffins, harvesting them by the thousand on their breeding grounds for their food and feathers. Over time, though, this relationship has changed, so that today we have come to love them, celebrating their quirky character and comical appearance and giving them a central place in our affections – a journey described by the environmental historian Dr Rob Lambert as the shift “from use to delight”. How ironic, then, that just as we have come to truly appreciate them, our own existence now threatens theirs. The climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds, whose life cycle is so intimately connected to the timing and abundance of their food supplies. Warming oceans result in fish such as sand eels shifting their range into cooler waters, and thus either declining or disappearing from the seas around seabird breeding colonies. If puffins need to travel further to their feeding areas, or take longer to find and catch food once they get there, then their chicks have a lower chance of fledging. Even if they do, they are less likely to survive the following winter. Our changing climate has already led to an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as autumn and winter storms, which leads to a higher mortality of birds outside the breeding season. It is often forgotten that the climate crisis is not the only negative factor affecting these birds’ lives. As we have seen, increased marine pollution, especially from oil and plastic, along with less severe yet still serious issues such as disturbance and predation, are already reducing the puffin’s breeding success at many once-thriving colonies. The dire prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring. In early 2026, BBC News reported that following that winter’s severe storms hundreds of dead and dying puffins, guillemots and razorbills had been washed up on beaches in Cornwall, Scotland and north-east England. Conservation organisations have also reported more than 20,000 stranded birds, mostly puffins, along the Atlantic coasts of France, Spain and Portugal. Samuel Wrobel, the RSPB’s senior marine officer, noted that this was the worst wreck for over a decade, since the catastrophic events of winter 2013-14, and warned that “after the impact of avian flu this is the last thing our seabirds need”. Moreover, as most birds are likely to have died at sea, so will never be found, the true death toll is likely to be much higher. Peter Harrison has spent his life watching, painting and studying seabirds, and has a special affection for the puffin. I asked him what he thought about the species’ future, and he began by confirming the many threats the birds face, including a reduction in their prey due to the climate crisis, threats to nest sites and the resulting lower breeding success. Rather to my surprise, however, Harrison feels some optimism for the puffin’s future, pointing to that famous legal victory that stopped industrial sand eel fishing in the waters around England and Scotland. He is also enthusiastic about the use of technology to track the movements and survival of all seabirds, including the puffin, since this began in the 1980s. “Prior to that time, there was a huge void in our knowledge of what puffins and other seabirds did in their non-breeding period,” he says. “They simply went to sea, only to reappear again in their breeding areas the following season. Rapid technological advances over the last four decades have greatly increased our understanding of their movements, revealing details of seabird distribution and behaviour at sea, including important foraging areas.” And as he points out, this knowledge does not just benefit the puffin. “Auks – including puffins – fulfil a role as important canaries in the cage, indicators of global health and sustainability. If auks are doing well, the oceans will be doing well,” Harrison says. The one thing we have on our side, Harrison believes, is that, unlike landbirds which often only live for a few years, even small seabirds can live for several decades. As he notes, although they might have gone through bad times, seabirds have in the past shown that they can make a rapid comeback, especially if we are able to rid their breeding islands of invasive predators. Scientists have a crucial role to play, too. In 2004 BirdLife International developed the BirdLife Seabird Tracking Database (STDB) to collate tracking data using a range of different, and rapidly improving, technologies that can track the presence and movements of seabirds when they are away from their breeding colonies, as they are for most of their lives. The records enabled them to identify six previously unrecognised oceanic routes used by the birds on their journeys: the Atlantic Ocean, North Indian Ocean, East Ocean, West Pacific Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and the Southern Ocean Flyways. The data obtained is also used for seabird research and conservation by BirdLife scientists and their collaborators throughout the world. As Dr Stephen Kress, the scientist who has devoted his life to successfully bringing back puffins to the US, points out: “Seabirds were once abundant along the coastlines of North America and throughout the world, but the declines we’re seeing in their populations are directly related to things humans are doing – they would be fine if we weren’t tampering with their world and messing things up. “And so I feel that we have an ethical responsibility as stewards of the Earth to do something where we can. That’s why we’ve developed these restoration techniques. If we hadn’t done that, we wouldn’t be documenting puffin recovery, we’d be documenting extinction.” Yet perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds. They may be outside our day-to-day experience for much of our – and their – lives, yet the huge affection for the puffin, held by millions of people around the world, must surely count for something. This is an edited extract from The Puffin by Stephen Moss published by Vintage at £14.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

headline: Honeybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study finds
trail_text: As a surge in beekeepers has led to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers
body_text: Honeybees are outcompeting wild pollinators for resources by aggressively bumping into them and chasing them away from flowers, research has shown. The study, by researchers from Anglia Ruskin University, found that areas where there were higher concentrations of honeybees had fewer wild pollinators, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies. Honeybees were also most likely to instigate, and win, competitive interactions, pushing out rivals to collect more pollen and nectar. The number of managed bees has risen in the UK, as campaigns to “save the bees” resonate with the public, leading to a boom in hobbyists setting up beehives. The number of registered beekeepers has more than doubled, from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 in 2025, according to the National Bee Unit. However, there are growing concerns that this growth in managed honeybees is harming other, wild, pollinators including bumblebees, by increasing competition for food and passing on diseases, especially in areas where there are fewer flowers or an especially high density of hives. To better understand the nature of this competition, the study in Cambridgeshire observed pollinators over a two-year period as they foraged on bramble and ivy in areas close to honeybee colonies. The study documented the outcomes of 300 interactions between flower visitors from five groups: honeybees, bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies and “other”, which included types of flower-visiting and pollinating flies, butterflies, beetles and wasps. In each interaction, the study noted where an individual “won”, by gaining access to a resource, “lost”, or if a resource was shared. Honeybees won in most of the encounters across both plant species. Past research has suggested that honeybees outcompete other pollinators indirectly, by taking up resources. However, the Cambridgeshire study provides evidence that they are posing a more direct form of competition, known as “interference competition”, where a species might attack or chase others away. “That’s important because, of course, it means that the wild pollinators are facing a challenge from both those types of competition from honeybees,” said Victoria Buckle, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Anglia Ruskin University. Honeybees were actively avoided by other flower visitors in 28.4% of interactions on bramble and 35.6% on ivy. In competitive interactions won by a honeybee, the honeybee either displaced other flower visitors – for example, by landing on them or pushing them off flowers – or chased them away, in about 20% of cases. Bumblebees were also observed displacing other pollinators, though Buckle believes this was probably not intentional, and was instead a reflection of their less coordinated movements as they fly through confined spaces. “They bumble along the patch and then they’ll mistakenly bump into another pollinator and it just falls off a flower,” Buckle said. “With the honeybees, the aggression was more overt. You could tell that they’re specifically trying to move the other one off the flower.” The reasons for honeybees’ aggressive behaviour is likely to relate to the way in which they organise their social groups, said Buckle, adding: “Some castes of bees can be guard bees, so they have that capacity within them to show threat and aggression, to guard their hives and to look after the brood.” The only pollinator able to hold its own against honeybees was the ivy bee, which was first recorded in the UK in 2001 and feeds mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers. It was seen displacing and chasing honeybees. The study also found that higher temperatures led to an increased number of competitive interactions, probably because nectar was drying up and plants were going into heat stress. Given that mean summer temperatures are predicted to rise by up to 4C in the UK by 2080, such competition is likely to become more frequent, said Buckle. More research is needed to examine how wild pollinators can be better protected, she added. “A lot of beekeepers are environmentally minded and they want to make sure that they’re not impinging or having an impact on other pollinators,” Buckle said. “This research is important because it helps guide our planning and best practices for conservation.”
